en: *Fahua Zhizhang Shu*, Fascicle One, Part One.
Composed by the later student of the Xianzong lineage, Tongli;
proofread by his dharma-heir disciple, Mingyuan.

△ 9. General Explanation of the Title (The name reveals the reality; the title indicates the central tenet. Therefore, before explaining the sutra, this is explained in general. This means that the meaning of the entire sutra is explained within its title.

Furthermore, "name" refers to the name of the translator, and "title" refers to the title of the translated sutra. Both are now explained together; hence, it is called a "general explanation. Two parts: 1. The title of the sutra; 2. The translator.
First, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

the first two characters directly reveal the meaning of the Dharma. "Exquisite" (*miao*) is a name derived from its own essential nature; it does not mean "exquisite" in contrast to what is coarse. If...
If "sublime" were contrasted with "coarse," then the sublime would have limits; it would not be the perfect sublime. Furthermore, that which is sublime is sublime from the very beginning;

it is not something that was coarse first and becomes sublime later. If it were coarse first and sublime later, then the sublime would have a beginning and an end, and thus would not be eternally sublime.
To explain its meaning: it is called "sublime" because it is profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter. Moreover, it is only between Buddha and Buddha...

It is because it can be brought to ultimate completion that it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Furthermore, it is called "wondrous" because it is that which cannot be known by *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.
As the Sūtra says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is wondrous and difficult to conceive. Therefore, the title places the character "wondrous" before "Dharma.

This "Dharma" refers to the present sūtra, which takes the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence and taking the function of guiding and sustaining (*avasthāpana*) as its utility. Regarding its essence being the true aspect: because...
The seven axioms and the sublime texts were all expounded by the Tathāgata from within the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);
not a single word or phrase fails to reveal this true reality of the One Vehicle, and thus they constitute its essence (*tattva*). Regarding "guidance and maintenance" as its function:

"guidance" (*niyama*) means that it guides sentient beings toward understanding; "maintenance" (*dhāraṇa*) means that it maintains its own nature. As for "guiding sentient beings toward understanding," it refers to all sentient beings...

Sentient beings inherently possess the essence of the true aspect (*dharmatā*). However, because they are obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*) and closed off to the provisional teachings (*upāya*), resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) does not arise;

how then could they enter into realization? The Buddha, through this Dharma, opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true aspect, enabling sentient beings to borrow the teachings to contemplate their own minds—using the finger to see the moon.
This constitutes the function of generating understanding in accordance with living beings. It is as it is said: "Relying..."
Regarding "upholding the self-nature": this refers to the fact that the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is the One Vehicle Buddha-nature.
However, because their faculties vary in sharpness or dullness and their afflictions vary in thickness or thinness, the vehicle is split into three and the nature flows into five.

Through this sutra, the Buddha reveals and unifies them, causing those of the three vehicles to return together to the One Vehicle and those of the five natures to revert to the single nature. This is what is meant by "reposing."

This refers to the function of maintaining its own nature (*svabhāva*). However, although the preceding explanation of the meaning follows the root sūtra, the term "Dharma" (*dharma*) still risks being conflated with other assemblies.
Therefore, it is distinguished by prefixing it with the word "Sublime" (*miao*), thereby indicating that the other assemblies cannot be called "Sublime.

If one were to discuss this Dharma in its entirety, it would universally encompass all assemblies and could not be so distinguished. Thus, as stated previously, it is not that the sublime is spoken in contrast to the coarse; now, furthermore—

Regarding the term "selection" (*jiǎn*): it is precisely because [this teaching] universally encompasses all assemblies, whereas those other assemblies cannot universally encompass [it], that one is compelled to select this one.
Yet, even so, it does not contradict the principle of non-selection. Furthermore, as for why this Dharma is called "wondrous," I shall briefly indicate four meanings based on the scriptural text.
First, because the provisional and the real are mutually identical. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas..."
"By means of immeasurable powers of skillful means, I preach for the sake of sentient beings. Furthermore, it says: "I establish these skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
The first three phrases represent the real within the provisional, while the latter two phrases represent the real within the provisional.
This is because, in most assemblies, the various aspects cannot be mutually identified, whereas here the two—origin and trace—interpenetrate one another. As the Sūtra says: "I dwell eternally..."
This is because, through the power of various supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), I cause sentient beings who are subject to delusion not to see me, even though I am near them. Furthermore, it says:
"At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain. I then said to the sentient beings: 'I am always here and do not pass away.'"
The first four lines fundamentally apply to the provisional (traces), while the latter four lines extend from the provisional to the fundamental.

This is because, across most assemblies [of the sutras], these two levels cannot be mutually integrated; yet, here, principle and phenomena are unimpeded. As the Sūtra says: "This Dharma abides in its own dharma-position;

the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. (In this passage, "this Dharma" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle—principle. "Dharma-position" refers to the self-abiding state of all phenomena—phenomena. "Characteristics of the world" refers to conditioned phenomena—phenomena. "Eternally constant" refers to the unconditioned.)

(Dharma; Principle). The first phrase indicates that principle does not obstruct phenomena; the second phrase indicates that phenomena do not obstruct principle. This is because many assemblies are often unable to achieve non-obstruction.

Fourth, because cause and effect interpenetrate. As the Sūtra says: "The World-Honored One, throughout the long night, has constantly taken pity on us, seen us, and taught us, causing us to plant the unsurpassed vow.
It further says: "I now have no more doubt; I dwell securely in the Buddha."
The Way. Expedient means serve as the attendant. The first three phrases show the cause penetrating to the fruit; the latter three phrases show the fruit penetrating to the cause.

This is because, in most assemblies, these elements cannot interpenetrate one another. Nevertheless, these four meanings collectively belong to the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai fajie*).

As for the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious omens, the emergence of stupas and the transformation of the earth, and the appearance of spiritual beings from within the ground, and so forth— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end.*
This belongs to the realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratibandha*), an inconceivable state. Even "wondrous" (*miao*) cannot adequately describe it;

it is only out of necessity that we forcibly name it "wondrous. [Question: The sages of the Confucian tradition taught people solely through the Way of the Mean (*zhongyong*), yet they still remarked, "The people have rarely been able to abide in it for long. Why is it that the title of this present scripture begins by speaking of "wondrous"?

"Does this not cause people to be startled and alarmed, and hinder their spiritual progress? Answer: "The single character 'Miao' (Wondrous) is precisely intended to arouse people's admiration and stimulate them to advance in their practice. If one can truly accept it directly and suddenly turn back toward the source, then the Wondrous Dharma is not far away;
it has always been present within the activities of daily life. Regarding the two characters "Lian Hua" (Lotus), they are used as a metaphor for illumination.

Among the ancient masters, some interpreted them by taking the blue lotus, some by taking the white lotus, and others by taking the *Ruixiangdeng* (Flower-Fragrance Banner) from the Sea of Fragrant Water.
Now, based on the textual meaning of this very sūtra, it should be explained by means of the udumbara flower, for this flower corresponds precisely to the meaning of the text.
As the sūtra says: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only from time to time."
These two phrases correspond to the two characters "wondrous Dharma" (miao-fa). Next, it says: "It is like the udumbara flower, appearing only once in a great while.
These two phrases correspond to the two characters "lotus flower" (lian-hua).
Furthermore, this scriptural passage consists of the Tathāgata’s introductory words following Śāriputra’s three requests; thus, we know that such a "wondrous Dharma" refers to this single sutra.
The entire body [of the sūtra] is like the *udumbara* flower; taking this general metaphor from a single scripture to explain the title—what room is there for dispute?
If one explains the meaning, there are two aspects: first, it is translated as "Numinous Omen" (*ling-shui*).
This is because this flower either does not bloom at all, or if it blooms, a Buddha appears in the world, serving as a numinous omen of the Sage. The *Parnirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In Jambudvīpa..."
The Honored King of Trees is named Udumbara; it bears fruit but has no flowers. If it should have flowers, they must be golden in color, and only then does a Buddha appear in the world.
For this reason, it is called the "Auspicious Omen Flower" (*ṛddhipuṣpa*). It is also called the "Responsive Auspiciousness.
Since this flower may not appear at all, but when it does appear, a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) emerges in the world, it serves as a portent of a Sage-King. Thus, it is established [as such].
The Treatise says: Throughout Jambudvīpa, there is a royal road for the wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin), one yojana in width.
When there is no wheel-turning monarch, it is submerged by the waters of the ocean; when a wheel-turning monarch appears, the ocean recedes by one yojana, and this road becomes manifest everywhere.
The *udumbara* flower blooms only once in a great while; for this reason, it is called the "Auspicious Response Flower" (*ruìyìng huā*).
Both of these names are translations based on meaning. If translated according to its color and type, one should call it the "Golden Lotus Flower.

Since the color gold has already been seen in the term *nirvāṇa*, if you wish to know what constitutes a lotus flower, according to various sutras there are four kinds of lotuses. The first is called...
The *utpala* (blue), secondly the *kumuda* (yellow), thirdly the *padma* (red), and fourthly the *puṇḍarīka* (white).
Now, the *udumbara* is phonetically similar to the *utpala* in its Sanskrit pronunciation;

where they are not entirely identical, it may be due to a distinction between golden and blue colors. To take this as a metaphor is, according to the original sūtra, to refer to this [the *udumbara*].

The flower does not appear out of season; it appears only when the time has arrived. This serves as a metaphor for this Dharma, which is not taught out of season, but is taught only when the time has arrived.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this may be briefly categorized into three points:

First, this flower is named "King of Honored Trees" (*Kusumitarāja*), serving as a metaphor for this Dharma being the king among all sūtras. Second, this flower has fruit but no blossoms; its flowers are invariably golden in color.
This metaphor illustrates that this Dharma exclusively discusses the essence of the fruit, while occasionally mentioning causal practices; for such practices must necessarily accord with the Truth.

Third, this flower either does not bloom at all, or if it blooms, a Buddha will certainly appear; this metaphor illustrates that this Dharma either is not taught at all, or if it is taught, one is granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
According to the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, there are also three meanings: first, this flower appears on the road of a Wheel-Turning King.
1. This flower exists only on the Buddha-vehicle; this serves as a general metaphor for the entire sutra, as it is through the *Saddharma* (the Sublime Dharma) that [this vehicle] exists.

2. This flower appears together with the road; this serves as a metaphor for those who hear this Dharma, as they immediately reach the stage of Buddhahood. 3. This flower is offered solely for the enjoyment of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) during his excursions;

this serves as a metaphor for how this Dharma is provided solely for the enjoyment of the Dharma-King. These seven points above are all general metaphors for the whole sutra by means of the *Saddharma*.
The term "original" (*yuan*) belongs to the name of the entire scripture; "lotus flower" (*lianhua*) is likewise merely a metaphor for the entire scripture.

As for specific meanings within the text, there are naturally distinct metaphors provided in the relevant passages, which need not be discussed here in advance. (Question: If the *udumbara* is indeed a lotus flower, why was the Sanskrit term not retained in the title?

Why was "flower" not changed to "lotus" in the main text? Why did Master Kumārajīva not translate it as "auspicious omen"? Why did the ancient masters not translate it as "lotus flower"? Furthermore, in the preface to the commentary, which explains the scripture, why is it annotated as "a square flower that is simultaneously fruit"? (Answer: The reason the Sanskrit term is not retained in the title is to indicate the seed.

Because they belong to the same category. As for the fact that the Sūtra does not translate "flower" as "lotus," it is to demonstrate respect. As for Master Kumārajīva’s not translating "spiritual omen" (ling-shui), it is because the term "spiritual omen" does not exist in this land; he feared that if it were placed in the title, people would not recognize it as a metaphor.

As for the reason ancient worthies did not translate "lotus flower" (lian-hua), it is because although it is indeed a lotus, it is not like those found in common parlance; they translated it according to its meaning, wishing for people to know its extraordinary excellence. The preface of the *Śāstra* explains the Sūtra, while the commentary takes "square flower" (*fang-hua*) to mean "fruit";

this is because that [commentary] merely provides a brief outline of the meaning and lacks the leisure for detailed analysis, thus provisionally following conventional explanations without wishing to entirely discard the intent of the ancient commentaries. However, when it comes to a title that pertains to an entire scripture, how can it not be analyzed? How can it not be analyzed?
The word "sūtra" (經) serves as a summary to define its essential nature. In the Sanskrit language it is called *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Kie-ching" (契經).
"Kie" (契) means that it accords with the principle of all Buddhas above and accords with the capacities of sentient beings below. "Ching" (經) has many meanings, which may be condensed into four.

First is "pervasion" (guàn): it means to penetrate and comprehend all meanings that ought to be known. Second is "gathering" (shè): it means to sustain and guide all sentient beings who are to be saved.
Third is "constancy" (cháng): it means remaining unchanging throughout the three periods of time. Fourth is "Dharma" (fǎ): it means that the ten realms follow the same track.

The term "accordance" (qì) is not used here because, in this region, the sacred teachings are simply called "sūtras" (jīng); thus, to conform to local usage, the character "accordance" (qì) is omitted. Furthermore, as for the character "accordance" (qì)—
This refers to its function. The characters of the scripture constitute its essence (*tī*), for the essence encompasses all functions.

Furthermore, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* belongs to that which is explained (*vācya*), it inherently possesses the function of harmonious correspondence (*kaihe*) without depending on words. Setting aside such discourse, this title was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth;

it takes both dharma and metaphor as its name, unifying the capacity and the object, encompassing both essence and function, including both the general and the particular, and penetrating both the empty and the real. Therefore, it is so named.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The title of the scripture is concluded (with an appended explanation of the volume sequence). Volume One (*Jǐuàn dìyī*). [“Volume” (*juàn*) is spoken in contrast to “unfolding” (*shū*).

It means that it is unfolded for ease of recitation and retention, and rolled up for ease of veneration and offering. In ancient times, scriptures were mostly made into scrolls (*zhóu*) as volumes; today, although the format has changed, the name has not been altered. “First” (*dìyī*) refers to the sequential order. This scripture consists of seven volumes in total;
according to the sequence, this volume stands at the beginning, hence it is called the first. Subsequent volumes may be understood by analogy]. △ Second, the Translator.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Yao Qin period is indicated; for further notes, see the preface. "Tripiṭaka Master" signifies one who manifests virtue. "Tripiṭaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

The term "Piṭaka" (Basket) has two meanings: first, the sense of containing or storing. This means that the Sūtras expound the training in concentration (*samādhi*), while the Vinaya expounds the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*).

The *Śikṣā* (Training) treatises elucidate the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). This is because each is capable of containing and preserving the meaning of its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). Second is the sense of "giving birth":
that is, the Sūtras accord with the single mind, the Vinaya governs the three types of action (*tri-karma*), and the Śāstras distinguish between the false and the correct;

each is capable of giving birth to the functional utility of their respective outflows. There are likewise two aspects of the Dharma Master: first, self-benefit, which means being extensively versed in the noble Dharma of the Tripiṭaka and receiving it as one's own spiritual lineage.
Therefore, there are two ways of benefiting others: namely, by propagating the noble Dharma of the Tripitaka and serving as a model for humans and devas.

The emergence of Kumārajīva’s name is recorded in the *Huàfàn shílù* (Record of Chinese and Indian Names), both of which can be seen in the prefaces. The single character "yì" (translate) records this event; "yì" refers to translation.

Examining the *Zhōu lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), it states that the languages of the four quarters were each managed by their own officials: those from the north were called *yì*, and those from the south were called...

The elephant [is divided into] the "Eastern" (Dong) called *ji* and the "Western" (Xi) called *di*. Although the present sutra came from the West, it is called a "translation" (*yi*) because during the Han dynasty, the Northern Office was proficient in Western languages;
thus, when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, it was termed a "translation," and this convention has been maintained ever since.
Nevertheless, the master translator, having received vows and entrustments, forgot his own body for the sake of the Dharma. From the third year of Hongshi, he entered Chang'an and resided at Xisha...
Yao Yuan translated various sutras and śāstras totaling more than three hundred and ninety fascicles; this sutra is included among them.

When he reached the end of his life in the fifteenth year [of the Kaiyuan era], he made a vow, saying: "If the various sutras I have translated are indeed not in error with the Buddha’s intent, then after my body is cremated, my tongue shall not decay.
Later, it was exactly as he had said. Thus we know that the Master’s tongue was like those of all Buddhas in its capacity for extensive [teaching].
The Long Tongue [Bodhisattva] praised this sutra without exception. Furthermore, this is a translation based on the meaning that profoundly accords with the needs of the time and circumstances.
May the circulation of this sutra never cease, and may the grace of the translator be inexhaustible. Therefore, these words are inscribed at the beginning of the sutra to be shown to future students.
The general explanation of the title is concluded. △ Ten: The detailed interpretation of the textual meaning has three parts: first, the introductory section; second, the main body of the teaching;

third, the dissemination section. (Regarding these three sections: they originated with Dao’an and were validated by Bandhuprabha. This is because whether a sutra is extensive or concise, it invariably possesses these three. By classifying the sutra according to these divisions, it is like the head, torso, and feet of a body, each having its own distinct boundaries without confusion. Therefore, he was called "Mitiān" [the Sky-Covering Sage].)

The high-level structural analysis (*kōhan*). This has been universally followed throughout both ancient and modern times, and it marks the beginning of the practice of categorizing and analyzing the various sutras. First, the "Preface" (*jo*) describes the origins of a given sutra and clarifies the causes and conditions for its teaching. Within this section, there are chapter titles and the main textual body;
regarding the chapter titles: [text follows].
The Introduction, Chapter One, of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

First, the title of the sūtra is presented; next, the titles of the chapters are given. This is because, although the chapters are distinct, they are grouped by category and collectively subsumed under the sūtra.
Furthermore, the chapters are established based on the sūtra so that practitioners may know to which [section] they belong. "Introduction" (*nidāna*) is synonymous with "narrative" (*kathana*).
There are three meanings: first, enumeration, because it lists the sequence of guest and host, and basis and manifestation;

second, narration, because it recounts the origins and causes for the flourishing of transformation and the arising of the teachings; third, citation, because it quotes the wondrous meanings that should be expounded in the main body of the text.
As for "categories" (*pinlei*), this refers to groups of texts that follow a similar pattern, which are set apart as a single collection for the sake of easy retention and recitation.
According to the titles of various sūtras, they are either proclaimed by the Tathāgata himself, established by the compilers, or added by translators.
Regarding the two chapters of this present sūtra, "Bhaiṣajyarāja" and "Devadatta," these were proclaimed by the Tathāgata himself (as there are explicit words to that effect in the text).
As for the remainder, none can be definitively determined. As for the present chapter, it appears to have been added by the translator, for the compilers merely...

In recounting these events, it was not necessarily the case that their names were immediately assigned. "First" (*di*) refers to the sequence of sections; "one" (*yi*) is the beginning of a numerical series.
This scripture consists of twenty-eight chapters in total. According to the sequential order of the sections, this chapter is the commencement;
therefore, it is designated as the "First. (The scriptural text is divided into two parts: 1. The Prologue of Testimony through the Six Conditions. 2. The Illumination that Initiates [the Teaching].

Preface. First, regarding the six conditions (the six *pratyayas*): they are faith, the teaching, the time, the master, the place, and the assembly. If even one of these is lacking, the Great Teaching will not flourish; therefore, the ancient masters determined them to be the "sixfold accomplishment.

It is called the "Testimony of Faith" because the distinction between guest and host, and between the dependent and the primary, as well as the subjective and the objective, is clearly established, thereby testifying that this is the Buddha’s word and causing people to give rise to faith. It is also called the "General Preface," because these sixfold accomplishments are common to all sutras. It is also called the "Postscript," because it was established by the compilers after the sutra had been preached.

Regarding this establishment through compilation, there is both an intention and a cause. As for the cause of its establishment, according to the treatise of Nāgārjuna: when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was overcome with grief, and Aniruddha said to him, "You are the one who upholds the Buddha..."

The corporate body (saṃgha) should consult regarding future matters. A difficult question was raised: "What are these future matters? Puṇṇa replied: "You ask about what shall be done after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: whom shall we take as our teacher? Upon what shall we rely for our dwelling?

How shall we discipline monks of evil character? How shall the Dharma-piṭaka be compiled? And what words should be placed at the beginning of the sūtras? Ānanda received these instructions and inquired about each point one by one. The Buddha answered according to their questions: "After my parinirvāṇa, you shall take the precepts as your teacher;

you shall dwell relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni). Monks of evil character shall be expelled in silence. At the beginning of all sūtras, the words 'Thus have I heard' (evam mayā śrutam) and so forth should be placed. Consequently, all works belonging to the Buddhist scriptures include these words; those that lack them are entirely of spurious origin. This is the intent behind establishing [this convention]. There is [a further reason].

Third: [The purpose of] eliminating doubt, settling disputes, and distinguishing from heterodoxy. First, eliminating doubt: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the assembly requested Ānanda to ascend the seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka. He was moved by a spiritual power such that his physical marks and signs became identical to those of the Buddha. The assembly then gave rise to three doubts: first, they doubted that the World-Honored One had returned;

second, they doubted that a Buddha from another realm had come; and third, they doubted that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood. Upon the utterance of these words [by Ānanda], it was known that he was compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, and the three doubts were instantly severed. Second, settling disputes: Because Ānanda’s virtue and accomplishments were nearly equal to those of the assembly, if he had not been accorded the honor of following the Buddha, it was feared that contentious debate would arise.

By the utterance of these words, it was made manifest that there was a source for this transmission of the teachings, and the various disputes naturally subsided. Third, distinguishing from heterodoxy: This is because at the beginning of the sūtras of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) in the Western Regions, the two characters "A-yu" are placed. "A" is translated as "non-existent" (wu), and "yu" [is translated as] "sorrow" (you).

This is translated as "existence. The intention is that although phenomena are manifold, they do not transcend existence and non-existence, or the views of annihilationism and eternalism; such is generally the case. Now, setting aside these [worldly] terms, this reveals the supramundane True Dharma, distinguishing it from heterodox scriptures. This section is divided into two parts.
First, a general explanation of the five conditions; second, a specific listing of the audience. Regarding the first:
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Thus it is. Faith is accomplished; in accordance with this intent, one employs words of faith and compliance.
For if one has faith, one says, "This matter is thus"; if one lacks faith, one says, "It is not thus. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; it nurtures all wholesome dharmas. Hence, it is set forth at the beginning. Furthermore, "thus" (*evam*) signifies assent.
This is a term of assent. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: At the time of the council, all the bodhisattvas together requested, saying, "As you have heard it, so should you speak.
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma then granted permission, saying, "So shall I speak; as I have heard it... (and so forth).
Furthermore, the word "thus" (*evam*) is a term that points toward a phenomenon; it possesses the capacity to indicate both the indicator and the indicated.
They are distinct. That which can indicate refers to the person who compiled [the teachings], while that which is indicated refers to the Dharma that was compiled.
There are two types of persons who compiled them; as the *Zuǎnlíng jì* states: "The Mahāyāna Piṭaka was compiled by Mañjuśrī and Ānanda-sāgara between the Iron Ring Mountains.
As for the Dharma that is indicated, there is both the phenomenal (factual) and the principial (doctrinal). Regarding the phenomenal...
Explaining the empty text: from this point onward, until the moment he paid his respects and departed, all matters were of this nature.
As for the principle, it is the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that is explained. The Sūtra says: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are quiescent. It further says:
"This dharma abides in the station of dharmas; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," and so forth—these are all principles of this kind.
Whether as phenomena (*dharma*) or as principles (*naya*), they all belong to this dharma; therefore, they are not specified individually, but are simply stated as "thus" (*evam*).
If one connects this with what follows, it is the statement of the compiler addressing the assembly: "Such a dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha."

...is also [the case]. "I hear" refers to the accomplishment of hearing. This means that although one may possess faith and compliance, at the critical moment, one truly relies upon auditory perception.
Without auditory perception, how could the essence of the teaching be established? Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The true essence of the teaching in this land / Is pure in auditory perception.
To explain the meaning: "I" distinguishes the host from the guest; "hearing" refers to the sound arriving and reaching the ear. These two combined—[form the basis of the teaching].
The Treatise states: These [teachings] were compiled by those who claimed to have received them directly from the Buddha’s own lips and face-to-face;

they are not like those who privately study or read ancient texts. Furthermore, from the ordinary person to the Sage, it is taught that there are four kinds of "self": first, the pervasive conceptualization of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-parikalpita*).

There are four types of "self": first, the self-conceptualizations of non-Buddhist schools; second, the provisional self of the various sages; third, the true self of the *dharmakāya*; and fourth, [the self as it appears in] this text.

Therefore, there are three meanings for the name "Bhikṣu": First, the exaltation of the two virtues. This refers to having attained one's own benefit and achieving mastery over the mind. Second, the weight of reputation.

This means that precepts prevent physical misconduct, meditative concentration removes mental distraction, and wisdom realizes the emptiness of conceptualization; thus, one is able to destroy both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*). Fourth, the terrifying of Māras. This means that once...

As for why he is called a "Gentleman" (*śi*) after begging: it is because, having accomplished the work of the Path, he is worthy of receiving this food. He is also called a "Remover of Famine" (*kṣud-vinodana*), meaning:
Sentient beings have meager merit and constantly suffer from famine. Because a *bhikṣu* begging for alms can generate the power of merit, there are two kinds of *bhikṣus*:

These are the śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, they cause all to hear. This is merely a case where the name is the same but the reality is different.
"Assembly" (zhòng) is a term for harmony. In Sanskrit it is *saṃgha*, which here is translated as "harmonious assembly. There are two kinds of harmony:

This is because one realizes the unconditioned dharma of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). According to the present sutra, it is logically appropriate that the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is equal;

It is not explicitly stated because it can be understood through implication. The subsequent phrase indicates the number: "twelve thousand people. This refers to the assembly present at the gathering who received their predictions (vyākaraṇa).

Master Kumārajīva, however, based on the ultimate discourse at the conclusion [of the sutra], maintains that regardless of whether they were part of the general assembly or his constant followers, all were equally granted predictions, and thus all should be considered in detail.

It is the mind, because it is based solely upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons that the foundations of defilement and purity are established.

Such great Arhats, well-known to all, and so forth.

It is so. This refers to the aforementioned twenty-one individuals. Furthermore, although these twenty-one individuals belong to the rank of Arhat, they have all turned from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle;

"Śāriputra. Those listed above are the great arhats known to all. The term "and others" (等) refers to their companions;

when leaders and followers are combined, they together complete the number of twelve thousand. [Question: According to the prophecies, both Ānanda and Rāhula were still in the stage of training (śaikṣa).

Now, being listed among the assembly of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), does this not contradict what follows? Answer: There are three reasons for this. First, because he abandoned the provisional to follow the real. According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Ānanda said to Kāśyapa: "I possess the power; I could have attained the Way long ago."

Because he served the Buddha, Ānanda intentionally retained his residual fetters (*anuśaya*). The original sūtra also states: "Using skillful means, he acts as an attendant to protect and uphold all the Buddha-dharma. Based on this, Ānanda’s actual virtue had already realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); however, for the sake of serving the Buddha, he temporarily remained at the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*).

Now, relinquishing the provisional to follow the real, he is listed here. Rāhula may be understood by analogy. Second, it is to refute the attachment to the provisional: although the prophecies for Ānanda and Rāhula indicate they were still in the stage of learning, these were merely expedients to lead those of true practice and to manifest provisional rituals.

Those who cling to the provisional take these as signs of true practice; thus, to refute such attachment to the provisional, they are listed here. Although the first two characters [of the text] are restricted to this specific section, their meaning extends to the subsequent sections.

All [of them] turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma through the eloquence of unimpeded joy in preaching, up to the stage of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Dharma-body extends vertically through the three periods of time and pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions, for among all phenomena there is nothing superior to it.

This is the virtue of *prajñā*, for through *prajñā* one can awaken to and comprehend the true and false, the real and unreal natures and characteristics of all phenomena.

Mind. Because the desire to speak is manifested through the mouth, there is the *pratibhāna* (eloquence) of the desire to speak, which is one of the four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). As for the four types of analytical knowledge:

first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), because one is able to expound upon all phenomena; second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), because one is able to analyze all meanings;
third, the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because one can communicate through the words and expressions of various regions and different species.

Therefore, there is the fourth, the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Because one speaks joyfully and without weariness, in accordance with others' dispositions and desires, these four types of eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) are such that each subsequent one can encompass the preceding ones, while the preceding ones do not encompass the subsequent ones.

Now, by citing the latter as encompassing the former, it is simply called the "eloquence of joyful speech. *Vartana* (turning) refers to oral transmission; that is, to transmit to others what one has personally attained.
Therefore, whatever is taught by those of non-retrogressive nature is entirely for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle. The wheel has two meanings:

Furthermore, the former clarifies self-benefit, which is described as "non-retrogression from Bodhi. The latter clarifies benefiting others, which is described as "turning the non-retrogressive wheel.

it is distinguished from those who seek to quickly escape the triple world for their own sake and pursue personal nirvana. Observing the meaning through this classification:
When this was done, eighty thousand bodhisattvas all personally realized non-retrogression and entered the rank of Dharma Kings.
This concludes the clarification of the ranks. II. Praising their Virtues.
"Making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" (up to) "being able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
The first five phrases praise his virtues in terms of self-benefit. Regarding "making offerings": externally he practices the four types of requisites, and internally he attains single-mindedness.
Not realizing that the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty in essence is called material offering; realizing their emptiness in essence is called offering through principle.
This present case is an offering through principle. The phrase "immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" most clearly demonstrates the great number of Buddhas to whom the offering is made.
This refers to not having planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas. "To plant" carries the meaning of cultivating.
"Multitude of virtues" refers to the myriad virtues of the fruit of Buddhahood. "Root" is synonymous with "foundation.

This means that since a Bodhisattva has made offerings to many Buddhas, they must have cultivated the myriad practices; although they have not yet realized the myriad virtues themselves, they have already cultivated them.
This is the very root [of all things]. That which the Buddhas praise may be done so by extolling the profundity of its cause, or by extolling the proximity of its fruit;
examples include the present sutra’s revelation of the fundamental [nature] and the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).

Those who cultivate themselves through compassion borrow the practice of benefiting others to perfect their own virtues, as seen in this sutra where, following the bestowal of predictions, one continues to practice the causes for further eons.

This is of that sort. Regarding "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom": since it was stated above that one acts "with compassion," it must mean not abandoning the afflictions of the mundane world (*saṃsāra*).
Since it was stated that one "cultivates the body," it must mean being able to accomplish the Buddha’s wisdom.

It is precisely because one accomplishes the Buddha’s wisdom while not abandoning the mundane world that this is an "entering without entering"; therefore, it is called "skillful entry. This is unlike the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which sink into emptiness.
They incline toward quiescence; even if they should attain some slight realization, both fall into partiality and deficiency. Although they have entered [the path], it cannot be called "good.

Now, this section explains the meaning of non-retrogression from Bodhi. It is precisely because of their great offerings to the Buddhas and their manifold planting of roots of virtue that they are praised by all the Buddhas;
furthermore, they cultivate themselves with compassion regarding the wisdom of the Buddhas.

Having already been described as "skillfully entering," one is then able to practice and realize spontaneously until reaching the stage of non-retrogression. The phrase "thoroughly penetrating" and below praises his virtues in terms of benefiting others;
"great wisdom" distinguishes him from those of provisional or limited capacity, referring specifically to what is called "the knowledge of all modes."
"Reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*) refers to the completion of all matters. It does not imply grasping at the "this shore" of birth and death or the "other shore" of *nirvāṇa*.
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says: "The Great Perfection of Wisdom.

This means that because a bodhisattva has already attained mastery over great wisdom, that wisdom may be described as ultimately perfected; therefore, it is called "reaching the other shore. This is its renown.
"Universally heard" means that great wisdom fills the interior while fame resounds without; "immeasurable worlds" is said to describe the extreme distance to which it is heard.
"Able to deliver sentient beings" means that great wisdom is fully sufficient and its responsive manifestations are vast.
His fame and reputation spread far and wide because those who received his transformation were numerous—“countless hundreds of thousands” being used to express the vastness of those he delivered.
However, this section explains the meaning of the aforementioned "turning the wheel of non-retrogression.
It is precisely because one has attained great wisdom, whose renown is universally heard, and is already capable of delivering all sentient beings, that one may turn the wheel of non-retrogression.

And thus he enters the rank of the Dharma King. This concludes the section on praising his virtues by clarifying his position. △ Third, the summary by naming him, which has two parts: first, the specific enumeration of his names;

this is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*). The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Clearly seeing the Buddha-nature, just like Mañjuśrī," etc. It is also translated as "Wondrous Auspiciousness."

As for Xiang (Auspiciousness): because at the time of his initial birth there was an omen of auspicious light filling the chamber, this Bodhisattva traverses the three periods of time and transforms all realms as numerous as motes of dust.

Having realized the Way in a prior kalpa, he was titled *Nāga-gotra-rāja* (Dragon-lineage Honored King). Presently manifesting in the northern direction, he is called *Maṇiratna-akṣaya* (Jewel-Treasury Accumulation).
In the future, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name *Samantadarśin* (Universally Manifest). While in the causal stage, he served as the teacher to the eight kings. In... [text continues]
The fruit [of this practice] is the Seven Buddhas and the Patriarchs, who manifest their great transformation like shadows and echoes, appearing in the form of Bodhisattvas.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), whereas the present sūtra serves as its catalyst. Since the perfectly consummate and wondrous principle cannot be understood without wisdom, it is therefore set forth at the beginning.

Regarding Avalokiteśvara, there are two meanings: first, in terms of awakening through wisdom; second, in terms of transformation through compassion. As for awakening through wisdom, "Avalokita" (contemplation) refers to...
The "ability to hear" refers to the faculty of the sense organ (*indriya*). "World-Sound" (*loka-svara*) refers to the auditory object (*viṣaya*) that is observed;

for by means of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of sound as a "returning hearing," one attains entry into perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). Regarding the perspective of compassionate transformation: "contemplation" refers to the compassionate mind responding to and meeting [sentient beings]; "World-Sound" refers to the stimulus of those who invoke the name.
For the Bodhisattva responds to such stimuli with a compassionate mind, seeking out sounds to rescue them from suffering. This is eternally abiding in the Universal Gate (*samanta-mukha*).
Obscured [by ignorance], he manifested sovereign supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in their full perfection and had already attained perfect enlightenment.

In the past, he was titled Buddha *Saddharmaprabhāsa* (Light of the True Dharma), manifesting as one dwelling in the stage of causes. In the present, he serves as an attendant to Amitābha and shall succeed him upon the Buddha’s seat.

In the future, he will be named *Samantaprabhā-guṇa* (Universal Radiance of Virtue), thereby representing the gate of compassion and circulating his profound transformation. For these reasons, he is designated next [in the sequence]. Mahāsthāmaprāpta is, that is to say, Great...
He is Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Suyāmasūtra* states: "Wherever I set my foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra tremble;
therefore, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Furthermore, in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"Because you vowed to take hold of the trichiliocosm, I shall now name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Moreover, this Bodhisattva, by means of...

The Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection gathers those who practice the recollection of the Buddha and leads them back to the Pure Land; because he brings about transformation without exertion, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Only one endowed with great power can advance toward the goal of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna); therefore, his name is specifically listed.
Regarding "the ever-diligent," the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "This Bodhisattva, for the sake of a single sentient being, passes through immeasurable..."
For kalpas he has followed [the Buddha] without abandoning him; yet, even though [the Buddha] has not yet converted him, he has never for a single thought-moment harbored a mind of abandonment.
Because he exerts himself with body and mind, he is named "Ever-Exerting" (Sadāprarudita). The reason his name is listed here is, in essence, to attract and guide those of the Two Vehicles.
One generates the mind to deliver sentient beings and establishes the practice of diligent effort. Regarding "without rest," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Cintāviśeṣa-sūtra*) states:
suppose one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas constitute a single day and night; thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year.

If, after the passage of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one encounters a single Buddha, and one continues to encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the *Gaṅgā*, practicing all forms of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and cultivation...
Having cultivated meritorious virtues, they subsequently receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Because their minds never cease, they are named "Unceasing" (Avaivartika).

Now, in listing their names, it is intended to spur those who are weary on to progress, to bring their great aspirations to fulfillment, and to cause them to look with humility upon their former mentalities.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* asks: "For what reason is he named 'Jewel-Hand' (Ratnapāṇi)? It is because that Bodhisattva..."
When transforming sentient beings throughout all Buddha-lands, should he wish to touch all Buddha-worlds with his right hand, it is accomplished exactly as he desires.
From his hand issue the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, up to the sounds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the hands of the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the seven treasures emerge to provide for [beings]."
He bestows [gifts] upon all sentient beings and causes them to rejoice, enabling them to attain nirvana;
therefore, he is named Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Palmed). Furthermore, this sutra is profoundly deep and immeasurable; one who does not possess the jewel-hand of wisdom cannot fathom its limits.
Thus, I shall list their names to represent it. Regarding the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states that his former name was Jyotīrasa. From...

Having heard the discourse on the Buddha’s wisdom from the Venerable Sūryagarbha, he offered medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing that in the future he might heal the dual ailments of body and mind for all sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced and called him Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King).
In the past, he was the body named *Priyadarśana*; in the future, he shall be titled the Buddha *Ruci*.
In the present, he serves as the primary interlocutor (*pratimukha*) within the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" to symbolize universal salvation; therefore, his name is listed here.

As for the Bodhisattva *Vīradatta*, desiring to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, he practiced giving with diligence and a heart free from stinginess, even extending to his head, eyes, marrow, brain, and the flesh of his own body.
He gave his hands and feet to beggars without any sense of cowardice or weakness. To list their names here is because giving is the foremost of the ten thousand practices;
for one who wishes to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, this alone is essential. As for the Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, he is named by way of metaphor: the moon takes the *maṇi* jewel as its essence;
it is beautiful in the midst of the sky, yet its reflection appears in a thousand rivers. This serves as a metaphor for Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as his body; he illuminates the celestial nature so that the myriad forms manifest their shapes.

The reason for listing their names here is that this sutra fully reveals both essence and function; it is not like those [other teachings] which are insufficient for those engaged in conditioned activity.
As for the Bodhisattva Candraprabha: "Moon" symbolizes tranquility (*samatha*), and "Light" manifests wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, he is fully endowed with both tranquility and wisdom.
Only then does one accord with the Buddha-vehicle; therefore, their names are listed as a model for those who aspire to the Buddhist path.
As for the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, his noble wisdom of self-awakening is complete, like the moon on a full night.
However, this sutra can only be fully exhausted by Buddhas and Buddhas; it cannot be clearly understood by anyone whose noble wisdom is not yet perfected. Therefore, their names are listed.
Furthermore, as for the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he takes the salvation of sentient beings as his personal responsibility and regards the attainment of the ultimate fruit as his deadline.

Bearing such a heavy burden upon a long and distant path, he neither retreats nor yields. A person such as this is capable of continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom and transmitting the Buddha’s voice and teachings;
therefore, his name is specifically listed here. As for the one of "Immeasurable Power," he employs it throughout the three periods of time, and his transformation fills the ten directions.
The boundaries of the Dharma reach across all limits while its measure remains inexhaustible; the transformative functions interlace one another while its spiritual power is boundless.
That this sutra flows and circulates without end relies entirely upon such individuals; therefore, their names are recorded as a model for those who propagate the sutra.
Those who transcend the three realms dwell amidst the mundane without being defiled, and abide within existence without being fettered; they are fundamentally established for the sake of fulfillment.
Regarding sentient beings who are adrift and lodging within the three realms, he provisionally performs the Buddha-work of empty flowers;
yet in reality, he desires to purify the Buddha-lands without departing from the One True Reality, universally manifesting his playful supernatural powers.

Such a person is capable of serving as a bridge and raft for the Dharma in the age of the final law and circulating the sacred scriptures; therefore, their names are listed here as a standard for the four reliances. Bhadrapāla.
This is called "Well-Protected" (*Sugupta*). It means he is well able to protect sentient beings, causing them not to regress from the bodhicitta.
As the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states: "If sentient beings hear his name, they will ultimately attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

He is also called "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*), for his merit surpasses the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and his virtue exceeds the three levels of worthies (*tri-piṭaka-ārya*); thus, he is the foremost among all worthy ones. Now, he is listed [here].
As for his name, it signifies that this sutra must be transmitted only by one who is close to the ultimate. Maitreya is fully called Maitreyī, and is also called Maitriya;
this translates as "Kindness-Born" (*Maitreya*), which is his clan name. The *Siddhārthamati Sūtra* states:
"If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the samādhi of a compassionate mind. Therefore, he is called Kindness-Born. His personal name is Ajita.

"Many. This is translated as "Invincible" (Anabhibhūta), meaning that having ascended to the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Final Birth, there is no one capable of surpassing him, with the single exception of the Buddha.
Formerly he was known as *Qiuming* (Seeker of Fame); now he resides in Tuṣita Heaven and shall act as the host at the Dragon Flower Assembly.

These two chapters, the former and the latter, both serve as the introductory prologue (*nidāna*). It is intended that by means of this wondrous Dharma, the conditions for delivering sentient beings through three assemblies shall be brought to fruition.
Therefore, I have listed their names so that those who aspire to the Dragon Flower Assembly (Lónghuá) may apply themselves with all their heart to this sutra.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, Master Kumārajīva’s commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra states: "Because he accumulates the jewels of wisdom, he is named Ratnakūṭa."

The verse following the Parable of the Burning House states: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom; therefore, their names are listed here to encourage those who receive the Way.
As for the Guide Bodhisattva, he enters the marketplace to extend his helping hand, establishing a grand model throughout the three realms and leading the masses of the ignorant and deluded;
thus, he serves as the teacher of devas and humans. Accordingly, the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* says: "Regarding sentient beings on the paths of error..."
He gives rise to the mind of great compassion and leads others into the Right Path; therefore, he is called the "Guide" (*śāstṛ*).

Now, this sutra is precious in its propagation, and propagation necessarily relies upon virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). For this reason, the title of "Guide" is placed at the end of the assembly of all the sages.
The explanations of the names of these various sages provided above are derived either from their causal practices (*hetu-caryā*), or from their resultant virtues (*phala-guṇa*), or in relation to...

This is the realization through wisdom. Alternatively, regarding the transformation through compassion, I have likewise merely followed the precedent of the ancient masters by recording one or two examples.

One must understand that even an Arhat of the stage of no-more-learning cannot be confined to a single virtue; how much less so for a Bodhisattva who dwells near the ultimate—how could their manifold merits ever be exhausted?
This concludes the detailed enumeration of names. II. Concluding the Summary and Revealing the Extensive.
There were eighty thousand such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together.
The two characters "such as" (rúshì) refer to the various holy ones whose names were listed above; "equal" (děng) signifies their collective leadership. Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
This refers to the multitude under his command, numbering eighty thousand, which establishes the count of the principal figure and his retinue.
It is said that these eighteen assemblies, including the bodhisattvas who are their equals, are all *mahāsattvas*. When the principal and the retinue are combined, they total eighty thousand people.
Furthermore, the concluding phrase here differs slightly from the previous section on those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); previously, the word "equal" (*sama*) was placed [at the end].
Under the title of "Virtue" (德), it is known that the subject of equality is superior while the object of equality is inferior.

Now, because the character for "equality" (等) is placed above the title of "Virtue," we know that between the subject and object of equality, there is in reality no distinction of superiority or inferiority. Nevertheless, in the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
Is it that there are no new insights or those of shallow station? It is simply that they are difficult to enumerate one by one. The section on the intermingling of the Three Vehicles concludes. II.

The Inclusion of the Eight Classes [of Gods] (Although there are internal correspondences, external protection must necessarily be sought; therefore, following the Three Vehicles, the eight classes are listed).
This is divided into six parts: 1. The Heavenly Kings and their retinues; 2. The Dragon Kings and their retinues; 3. The Kiṃnaras; 4. The Gandharvas; 5. [The remainder].
The assembly of asuras; the six assemblies of garuḍas. First:
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra was together with his retinue—namely, twelve thousand devaputras—as well as his entire host.
"At that time," and so forth. The assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and Śakra Devendra—here translated as "The Able Lord"—is the sovereign of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
According to the *Sammitīya-nikāya-śāstra*, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha’s teachings, she was a woman who resolved to build a Buddhist stūpa;
thirty-two people assisted her in its completion. Consequently, the woman became the Lord of Devas, while the thirty-two people [became his retinue].
They serve as rulers for the various realms; these are what are known as the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
Together with their retinues, they represent the categories of beings under their jurisdiction. Since the Lord of Devas has assembled, his kinsmen and ministers all follow him;

thus, the "twenty thousand sons of devas" indicates the number of his retinue. Because they are the children of the Lord of Devas, they are all referred to as "sons of devas. Furthermore, there are those below...
Regarding the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings, ancient masters have said: the Moon King (Candraprabha) is the Moon Palace Deva;
the Universal Fragrance King (Samantagandha) is the Constellation Deva; and the Great Emperor Ziwei (Dhruva) is the Sun Palace Deva.

Of these three sons of heaven, only the Star宿 (Nakṣatra) Son of Heaven sits upright in the center of the heavens, presiding over and governing the celestial phenomena throughout the stars, distributing his office to illuminate them.
The other two sons of heaven dwell within the belly of Mount Sumeru and circulate around the four continents;
these are what are known as the "three lights that illuminate the world. As for the four Great Heavenly Kings: the first is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which in this language means...
Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holding the Nation) resides on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru, dwelling upon a terrace of gold; he governs the two classes of gandharvas and piśācas.
The second is named Virūḍhaka, which means "Increase"; he resides on the southern side of Mount Sumeru, dwelling upon a terrace of lapis lazuli;
he governs the two classes of kumbhāṇḍas and pūtanas. The third is named Virūpākṣa, which means "Broad."
Virūpākṣa resides on the western side of Mount Sumeru, dwelling upon a terrace of white silver and presiding over the two classes of the Viśvāsa and Vāsuki nāgas.

His fourth name is Vaiśravaṇa, which translates as "Much-Hearing. He resides on the northern side of Mount Sumeru, dwelling upon a terrace of crystal and presiding over the two classes of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Their respective abodes are situated at the waist of Mount Sumeru, level with the palaces of the sun and moon; each governs [their respective realms].
There are two classes of spirits who protect and shield the world, preventing them from harassing human beings; these are the so-called Four World-Protecting Kings (*Lokapāla*).
Together with their retinues, they generally refer to the three luminous *devaputras* and the four Great Heavenly Kings, along with the number of subordinate classes under their command.

Below [the Heaven of] Mastery (*Īśvara*) are the two heavens at the summit of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*): the Heaven of Mastery (*Īśvaradevaputra*) and the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*).
He is the Lord. When this deity desires the objects of the five senses, he manifests them with sovereign ease;
therefore, he is named Īśvara (The Sovereign). Mahā-Īśvara (The Great Sovereign) is the lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

When this deity desires the objects of the five senses, other deities manifest them for him, and his sovereignty surpasses that of the former; therefore, he is named Mahā-Īśvara. His retinue consists of three [thousand].

The "Ten Thousand" refers to the superior abodes (*abhibhvāyatana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as their retinues are also numerous. (According to the desire realm, above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and below the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, there are further two heavens:

Yāma and Tuṣita; they are not mentioned here because by citing the upper and lower limits, the middle is included. All those from this point upward collectively belong to the heavens of the desire realm.

Below the Sahā world are the celestial hosts of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). "Sahā" is translated here as "Endurance"; it is so called because [the beings there] are capable of enduring the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the eight sufferings (*aṣṭau duḥkhāni*).

"Receiving" means that there is no intention to seek escape. "Lord" carries the sense of taking [the realm] as a covering and protection above. According to the teachings, within a single set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), the first dhyāna covers above; thus, the first dhyāna is the lord of the four continents. Within a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), the second dhyāna covers above; thus, the second dhyāna is the lord of the small thousand-world system. Within a medium thousand-world system (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*), the third dhyāna covers above; thus, the third dhyāna is the lord of the medium thousand-world system. Within a great thousand-world system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*), the fourth dhyāna covers above; thus, the fourth dhyāna is the lord of the great thousand-world system. Furthermore, regarding the Brahma-heavens, the Great Brahmā is the lord of one set of four continents; the Ministers of Brahmā (*brahmapurohita*) are the lords of a small thousand-world system; the Great Ministers of Brahmā (*mahābrahmapurohita*) are the lords of a medium thousand-world system; and the Great Brahmās of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are the lords of a great thousand-world system. This is because they possess the power to govern and protect these respective realms.
