When the third dhyāna covers [the world], then the third dhyāna is the lord of a medium chiliocosm.
When the fourth dhyāna covers the great trichiliocosm, then the fourth dhyāna is the lord of the great trichiliocosm.

According to this, all four dhyānas of the form realm are called "lords of realms," though the extent of what they govern differs—just as there are lords of a household, lords of a district, lords of a nation, and lords of the world.

Regarding the category of "Lord" (*Brahmā*): the single word *brahmā* still belongs to the Western [Sanskrit] language; it is translated here as "Free from Desire," because by eliminating the afflictions of the lower realms, one ascends to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for "King" (*rāja*), he governs and oversees the Brahma hosts, attaining sovereignty within his own celestial realm.
However, since he is called both "Lord of the Realm" (*dhātupati*) and "Brahmā King," it is to manifest the realm he protects as well as to clarify the station in which he dwells.
Śikhin Mahābrahmā is the heavenly king of the First Dhyāna; he is called "Crest" (*śikhin*) because there is a spiral crest upon his head.
Prabhāsa Mahābrahmā is the heavenly king of the Second Dhyāna; his physical and environmental radiance is superior to that of the first.
Because they are meditative, the third and fourth [dhyānas] are equally included; this is merely a skillful turn of phrase in the translation.

There are twelve thousand followers, which is the number of the Brahmakāyika assembly under his governance. Above this, there is further the single realm of the Formless (ārūpyadhātu), where assemblies would likewise exist;
however, because form cannot be seen there, it is not listed. This is based on the words of celebration and dedication following Śāriputra’s reception of the prediction.
Thus, the various devas herein are all noble sages who have temporarily assumed their stations to manifest as reflections of the Great Transformation;
how could they be mentioned in the same breath as those ordinary worldly devas? △ Second, the dragon kings and their retinues.
There were the eight dragon kings, from Nanda Dragon King (down to [Upananda]), each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The first phrase provides the general heading; "Nanda" and those following provide the specific enumeration. Nanda means "Joy"; Upananda means "Excellent Joy.
These two brothers, the dragons, constantly protect the kingdom of Magadha; their winds do not rustle the branches, and their rains...
It does not break into clods; the five grains flourish in abundance, and it responds well to the hearts of men.
King Bimbisāra established a great assembly annually to compete [in its cultivation]. When the common people heard of this, they joyfully flocked there;
hence its name. Sāgara means "Salt Sea" (Salty Ocean); it is so called because it dwells beyond the Fragrant Water Sea. Vāsuki means "Jewel Renown" (Precious Fame).
Because his fame is honored and respected, he is also called "Many-Headed" (*Bahumukha*), as his form manifests with many heads. *Takṣaka* means "Manifesting Poison" (*Dhūmra-viṣa*);
because he poisons people by exhaling his breath, he is also called "Many-Tongued" (*Bahujihva*), as his form manifests with many tongues.
*Anavatapta* is also called *Anodadha*; this translates as "Without Heat-Affliction. It is the name of a lake. The *Āgama* states that it is located in the Snow Mountains.
Atop the mountain peak is Lake Anavatapta. Within the lake is a hall supported by five pillars, where a nāga resides;

this is none other than the present Nāgarāja. Maṇasvin—here translated as "Great Body" or also as "Great Power"—when the asuras fought with Śakra, they pushed back the ocean waters to submerge the city of Sudarśana. This nāga coiled his body to block the seawater. Because of this...
It is so named. *Utpala* means "blue lotus" in this [language]; it is the name of a pond. Because the nāgas dwell in dependence upon this pond, the word "etc.
(*ādi*) encompasses an exhaustive number. According to the *Vṛṣṭisamaya-sūtra*, there are eighty-four billion nayutas of nāga kings;
as for those now gathered in this high assembly, how could they be limited to only eight? Therefore, the word "etc. is used to include them all.

The final sentence provides a summary. According to the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there was a dragon girl named Prabhāvatī who, together with twenty thousand sea deities, received a prophecy from the Buddha that she would be born in the buddha-field of Aśoka.
The Sāgara Dragon King also received a prediction that he would become the Buddha Vimalaviśuddha.
In this very sutra, there is also the case of the eight-year-old dragon girl who suddenly realized the Way in the South;
how, then, can the profound roots of these multitudes be measured? △ Third, the assembly of kinnaras.
There were four Kinnara kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The first phrase provides a general heading. *Kinnara* refers to the gods of the Dharma-music of Śakra; they are also called *Cintāra*, which is translated here as "Doubtful Deities.
They have human bodies with a single horn; being like humans yet not humans, those who see them give rise to doubt. Thus [it is said of] the Buddha.

Regarding the passage, "When the Dharma is being preached, the various devas sing with lutes and chant the dharma-gates," this refers to these very spirits. In the subsequent line, they are listed individually:
the *dharma-kinnaras* who perform the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, because the Four Noble Truths possess the sense of providing a guiding principle (*dhāraṇa*).
The *Kinnara* of the Sublime Dharma performs the music of the twelve links of dependent origination, for the Dharma of dependent origination is considered more perfect than the Four Noble Truths.
The *Kinnara* of the Great Dharma performs the music of the six perfections, for by means of the Dharma of the six perfections...
This is to distinguish them from the Hīnayāna. As for the *Dharmadhara* Kinnaras, who collectively perform the three aforementioned dharmas:

they universally chant the truths, conditions, and the six perfections with a single voice; because this possesses the meaning of *dhāraṇī*, the concluding phrase summarizes the whole, as can be understood.
△ Fourth, the Gandharva assembly.
There are four gandharva kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The first phrase provides a general heading. Gandharva refers to the worldly music deities of Śakra. They are also called gandhara;
this is translated as "smelling fragrance" or "fragrance-aggregate," because these beings take fragrance as their food and sustain their aggregates with fragrance.
The following lines list them separately: "Music of the gandharvas" refers to those who perform dances with shields and feathers, such as the eight rows of dancers arrayed in the courtyard.
"Melodies of the gandharvas" refers to those who sing in accordance with the pitch-pipes, such as voices harmonizing with the five notes.
"Beauty of the gandharvas" compares favorably with the preceding "music of the gandharvas," for it represents the most refined and exquisite aspect of dance.
The Gandharva Beautiful Sound surpasses the preceding musical tones; his singing is truly harmonious and elegant. This concludes the final verse.

However, regarding these two preceding sections, it remains uncertain whether they represent inner secret virtues manifested through external provisional forms, or whether they involve those with karmic affinities from many lifetimes who were permitted to attend this sublime assembly. △ Five: Asuras.
The assembly of *asuras*.
There are four *asura* kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The opening phrase provides a general heading. *Asura*, also called *asura-loka*, is translated here as "the unattractive," for this reason...
There are females of this class who are handsome, but because there are no males of this class who are handsome, they are also called "non-devas" (asura).
Because their karmic rewards resemble those of devas, yet their status and virtue are not those of devas, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are four types. First, the egg-born:

within the realm of hungry ghosts, by the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon supernormal powers to enter the void and are born from eggs; they are categorized as belonging to the destiny of hungry ghosts. Second...
First, those born from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*). Among the various devas, they descend due to the diminution of their merit; their dwelling places are adjacent to the sun and moon.

Emerging from the womb, they are categorized within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*). Second, those born by transformation (*upapāduka*). They sustain the world-systems, their power penetrates all things without fear, and they are able to contend for authority with Brahmā and Śakra.
Because they exist through transformation, they are categorized within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*). Third, those born from moisture (*saṃsveda-ja*). They are born...
The Great Ocean Mind. [They] dwell in the openings of the aloeswood caves; they roam through the void at dawn and return to their watery abodes at dusk.
They exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryag-yoni*). In this sutra, they are referred to as *asuras*. Alternatively, all four [realms] may be present.

If one were to list their names, they appear to belong primarily to the realm of gods (*deva-yoni*), while also including humans and ghosts. In the subsequent line, they are listed individually: *Bali*, which here means "the bound. Together with...
Because he was once bound during a battle with the Lord of Devas, Khara-karṇa—translated here as "Broad Shoulders"—is so named because his two shoulders are wide and expansive;
he is the one who pushed back the ocean waters to submerge the city of Sudarśana.

Vemacitra—translated here as "Various Doubts"—is so named because his mind harbors many forms of doubt regarding his celestial status; he is also called "Pure Mind," for he returned to the Buddha and received transformation through his teachings.
Because his mind was thus pure, he is the father of Śacī, the consort of the Lord of Devas.
Rāhu—this means "obscuring the sun"—so called because when he fought with the Lord of Devas, he was able to obstruct the sun with his hand. The final phrase provides a summary.
△ Sixth, the assembly of Garuḍas.
There are four Garuḍa kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The opening phrase provides a general heading. Garuḍa is also called Kāruṇa; this is translated as "Golden-Winged Bird" because its wings are golden in color.
It is popularly known as the "Great Peng. The distance between its two wings is three million six hundred thousand li. It tears open the ocean...
It is this very creature that feeds upon dragons with water. When Zhuangzi says, "Its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky," he was likely referring to this.
Following the second phrase, it is listed separately: "Of great majesty" (*mahā-tejas*) means its majesty strikes terror into all dragons, while its virtue conforms to the Buddha’s transformation.
"Of great body" (*mahākāya*) means its body surpasses all its kind; it is what Zhuangzi called the Great Peng (*páng*), whose size one cannot know how many [leagues].
"Thousand Li" refers to this. "Greatly Puffed Up" means being self-important and conceited, looking down upon the multitude; thus it is named after the *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
If one has this jewel on the neck, one is named after it. The final phrase provides a summary. Thus far, these two sections [have been explained].
In the opening of the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," they are also recorded at length;
this must mean that throughout many lifetimes they shared a karmic affinity, were gathered into the True Dharma, and attained entry into the sublime assembly.

According to the subsequent text, prior to the Tathāgata’s emission of light and following Śāriputra’s reception of his prediction, there are further two groups—the yakṣas and the mahoragas—recorded at length alongside the Dharma Master.
These should also be present here; it is likely that the translator omitted them. As for the statement that there are "eight classes," this is established according to their specific meanings.
Once the eight classes have been fully encompassed: △ Third, the assembly of donors arrives together.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Vaidehī was the wife of King Bimbisāra and the mother of King Ajātaśatru; her name means "Contemplation.
Because King Ajātaśatru had murdered his father, she became weary of the Sahā world and relied upon the sixteen contemplations taught by the Buddha.
Sūtra: Because one maintains the visualization of the Western Quarter and contemplates rebirth there. Ajātaśatru—this is translated as "One Whose Enmity Was Not Yet Born.

Before he was born, a physiognomist predicted: "If this child is born, he will surely harm his father. Thus, he was named [Ajātaśatru] to record this. After he was born, his father ordered him to be thrown from a tower;
however, he did not die, though he lost a finger. For this reason, he was also called "The Fingerless One" (Anamika). He grew up to be faithful and harmonious.

Devadatta’s plot imprisoned his father within the palace; he took control from the royal residence himself. His mother, moved by virtuous words, was awakened to the truth and was just opening the gate to invite her husband when she found that her father had already died.
King Ajātaśatru, realizing for himself the gravity of his crime of parricide, returned to the Buddha to seek repentance.
Now, wishing to borrow the mother’s goodness to conceal the son’s evil, he is called "the son of Vaidehī. In reality, the mother has not yet arrived;
it is only the son who has come, and thus he is called King Ajātaśatru. The causes and conditions for his crime of parricide are detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

This is not urgent for the present purpose, so it is not recorded. Regarding the final phrase, it clarifies the multitude under his command: once the King of Men has emerged, the people fill the roads;
moreover, including the palace retinue and ministers, their number is unknown. Thus, it says "several" (*jiǎnrúan*) and so forth.

As for the classification as "the assembly of donors" (*tánzhòng*), although there is a distinction between the king’s kin and others, once they have reached the ground of the Buddha, they are all designated as "givers."

[The Master says: "Question: The Buddha preaches the Dharma among humans; why is the assembly so small? Answer: The text is abbreviated and does not record it, but in reality the people are not few. According to the *Anantārthartha-sūtra*, four wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) are listed, along with their kings, ministers, citizens, men, and women.

Furthermore, the later part of the present sutra also states: 'And all the minor kings, wheel-turning holy kings,' etc.; its full extent may be known from these sources. [End of] the detailed classification and listing.
△ Second, the conclusion by describing the ritual protocol.
Each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

The first phrase describes the ritual for requesting the Dharma; since the assemblies of the Three Vehicles and the eight classes of beings were not gathered together but were distinct, it says "each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The second phrase describes the manner of listening to the Dharma; having already prostrated at his feet, they divided into groups and took their seats, hence it says "withdrew."

"Sitting to one side" does not mean that the great assembly is all sitting together on one side. Furthermore, "each bowing at the Buddha’s feet" symbolizes the principle of using skillful means to conform to the ultimate reality and the convergence of the three vehicles into one.
"Retreating to sit to one side" symbolizes the meaning of equally receiving the prediction of enlightenment while attaining realization in different realms.
The six conditions for the sequence of testimony and faith are concluded. II. The Sequence of the Emission of One Ray of Light.

(1. A Single Ray of Light. This refers to the ray of light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows. Since the Great Teaching of the Lotus Sūtra arose from this, it is called the "Introductory Chapter on the Arising [of the Teaching]. Furthermore, this introduction is also termed the "Specific Introduction" (*pṛthag-nidāna*), because it pertains specifically to the present sūtra—just as the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* is initiated by the transformation of the World-Honored One’s physical appearance, and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* is initiated by Ānanda falling into lust;

thus, each sūtra has its own distinct beginning. It is also called the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra," because prior to the preaching of the sūtra, these questions and answers serve as a prologue that initiates the opening of the teaching.
This is divided into four parts: 1. Manifesting the Appearance to Accord with the Capacities of Beings; 2. Emitting Light to Shine Eastward; 3. The Assembly Raising Doubts; 4. The Question.

Answer: Regarding the "Initiation" (the first section, which clarifies the preliminary signs). Before the light was emitted, four signs were first manifested: first, the preaching of the sutra; second, entering meditative concentration; third, the raining of flowers; and fourth, the shaking of the earth. This was because the time for the assembly had arrived and their conditions were ripe;

as their great capacity was about to be awakened, these signs were displayed to engage them. Thus, the members of the assembly were filled with joy, joined their palms, and gazed upon the Buddha with single-mindedness, manifesting an air of eager anticipation and profound inquiry.

This section is divided into three parts: first, the preaching of the sutra and entering concentration; second, the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth; and third, the joyful observation by the great assembly. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly (up to) entering the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings, his body and mind unmoving.
Regarding "at that time": it refers to the moment when the great assembly of the Dharma-congregation had each paid their respects and withdrawn to their seats.

Regarding "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavat*): it is one of the ten titles; he is the teacher of the three realms and the father of the four modes of birth, revered by both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Out of respect [for this classification], the "fourfold assembly" consists of the two groups of the ordained and the two groups of the laity.

Although, when analyzed in detail through the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings, there are various distinctions, in general terms they do not exceed the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople.
Furthermore, the ancient masters further divided those within a single assembly into four types:

first, those with strategic wisdom and discernment who know the proper time and occasion, acting as initiators for the assembly, such as Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and others; second, those for whom conditions have converged and the time has ripened.
Those who attain the Way upon hearing [the teaching] are the "audience according to their capacity," such as Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and others.

Third, those who carry the fruit while practicing the cause to assist and support the transformation of the Dharma are the "shadow-and-echo audience," such as Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and others.

Fourth, those whose faculties were shallow in the past and do not understand in the present are the "audience for establishing karmic conditions," such as those who form causes through sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). Based on this, then...
By merely designating the fourfold assembly, all assemblies are thereby encompassed.
"Surrounding" means to cluster around the Dharma King from the front, back, left, and right, like ten thousand streams flowing toward the capital or the multitude of stars bowing to the North Star.

Furthermore, whereas it was previously stated that they "sat back," here it says they "surround" because this signifies the act of readjusting their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) as they are about to perform an offering. Regarding "offering": [it is] borrowed...

Sincerity toward external objects encompasses all three types of action (*trikarma*). "Reverence" (*gaurava*) involves manifesting ritual decorum to transmit the mind; it specifically belongs to the action of body (*kāyakarman*).

"Veneration" (*satkāra*) involves focused application of thought and mindfulness; it specifically belongs to the action of mind (*manaskarman*). "Praise" (*praśamsā*) involves verses extolling virtuous deeds;

it specifically belongs to the action of speech (*vākkarman*). According to the *Anantārthaviniścaya-sūtra*, offerings include such items as celestial incense and celestial robes; reverence includes...
The rituals such as joining the palms and crossing the hands; the words expressing reverence such as gazing with single-minded devotion;
and the verses of praise such as "How great! O Great Awakening!"—all these none fail to manifest the utmost sincerity for the Dharma. This is for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

The capacity of those to be transformed is distinguished as not being that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The Dharma taught—the Mahāyāna sūtras—is distinguished as not being the path of the Lesser Vehicle.

Furthermore, although the three vehicles assemble together, the fact that the Great [Vehicle] is taught specifically for Bodhisattvas is precisely to cause the three vehicles to feel shame for their smallness and to aspire to the Great.
This is what is meant by the saying: "The turtledove cries upon the tree, but its intent lies within the hemp field. This is called the "Immeasurable" [Dharmakāya].
Regarding the meaning: that sutra explains it through the Buddha himself, saying, "The infinite meanings are but a single dharma.

As for this single dharma, it is what is called "signlessness" (animitta). (This clarifies that the infinite is one, for even that one cannot be apprehended. "Signless and yet not signless" (this explains the meaning of signlessness;

it is because both signs and non-signs are absent that there is true signlessness. It is named "the true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa). (This sentence establishes the essence; precisely because it is truly signless, nothing can destroy it—this is the principle of the true mark.)

From a single reality-mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), immeasurable dharmas arise—namely, the two truths, the three vehicles, and the four fruits of sainthood (this clarifies that the one gives rise to the immeasurable;
whether it be the provisional and real teachings, the principles of the three vehicles, or the stages of the four noble fruits, all arise from this).
Based on this, the *Aparimitārtha-sūtra* likewise takes the reality-mark as its essence. Because this essence can encompass and give rise to all dharmas, it is called "immeasurable."

Regarding the meaning: "The Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas" is not expounded unless there is a suitable recipient; "that which is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" is not spoken unless the time is right.

This is because he feared that if it were bestowed upon or received by the wrong person, it would give rise to slander and incur transgressions; or if displayed at an improper time, it would conversely result in the loss of benefit.

What is meant in this sutra by "long remaining silent regarding this essential point and not striving to speak it quickly" is precisely this intention. [The section] beginning with "The Buddha spoke... [is as follows].

Having finished speaking, he entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The term "already" (*yi*) is used in reference to the capacity of the audience; for while the sutra itself has no beginning or end, it is "already" complete in its accomplishment of benefit.
"Knotting" (*jie*) refers to the mutual interlocking [of the legs]. "Half-seated" is called *jia* (cross-legged); *jia* means to add. This means first placing the left foot upon the right knee.
"Full-seated" is called *fu* (full-lotus); *fu* means to return. This means next placing the right foot back upon the left.
The knees. This is the procedure for entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Furthermore, there are briefly eight benefits to sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*):

first, it counteracts restlessness (*auddhatya*); second, it counteracts lethargy (*styāna*); third, it counteracts distraction (*vikṣepa*); fourth, it destroys the armies of Māra; fifth, it generates respect in others;
sixth, it brings delight to devas and humans; seventh, it is not a practice shared with worldly enjoyments; and eighth, it is uncommon to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
All Buddhas of the past practiced this dharma, and the present Buddha does likewise; therefore, it is called "sitting in the full lotus posture at the place of immeasurable meaning.
As for the term "immeasurable meaning," since the meanings are immeasurable, there is no fixed location, nor is there any coming or going.
Now, when wisdom merges with principle, all dharmas and meanings manifest before one; thus, "meaning" refers to the "place."

And it enters the ear. "Samādhi" is translated here as "Right Concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*); it is not shared with non-Buddhists, for they do not possess such wrong concentration. It is also called "Right Reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*);
it is not shared with ordinary worldlings, for they do not experience such worldly reception. Regarding "body and mind unmoving": externally, one maintains a solemn physical demeanor;
internally, one withdraws the spirit and mind. This refers to what is called: "The body, along with the hands and feet, remains still, peaceful, and unmoving. Its...

His mind was constantly serene and tranquil; it had never been distracted. Having finished preaching the sutra and entering meditative concentration, △ Second, the rain of flowers and the shaking of the earth:
At that time, the heavens rained *māndārava* flowers (extending to) the entire Buddha-world shaking in six ways.
At first, the devas offered worship because they had already received the benefit of the teaching upon hearing the Buddha preach the sutra;

now, seeing the Buddha enter meditative absorption, they wished to hear further instruction and thus rained down flowers as an offering to express their gratitude for what they had previously heard and their request for what was yet to come. At that time:

This refers to the time when the sutra was preached and [the Buddha] entered meditative concentration. Regarding the *mandārava* flowers and so forth: in older translations they were rendered as "small white" and "great white" because their color was white;
in newer translations they are rendered as "small pleasing" and "great pleasing," meaning that their fragrance and color are complete and thus perfectly accord with human preference.

Regarding the *mañjūṣaka* flowers and so forth: in older translations they were rendered as "small red" and "great red" because their color was red; in newer translations they are rendered as... [text ends].
"Small softness" and "great softness" refer to being radiant, light, and graceful; they are called "soft" because they are lovely.

"Scattering [flowers] upon the Buddha and the assembly" refers to the patron of the offering and their companions. If one provides an interpretation based on symbolic dharma (*dharma-pratibimba*), the flowers symbolize knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

The four [offerings] symbolize the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*), as well as opening, showing, awakening, and entering. This expresses that the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is inherently complete, just like the flowers.
The fundamental nature is originally perfected; however, because it has long been obscured by emotional consciousness (*kleśa-vijñāna*), it is like color and fragrance that do not manifest.
Now, in order to reveal, cause awakening to, and lead others into this reality, the falling of the four flowers from the heavens is used as a symbol.

Their scattering upon the Buddha and the assembly symbolizes the meaning of the thorough penetration of cause and effect through the stages of revealing, instructing, awakening, and entering. From "Throughout the Buddhas" [downward], the earth deities manifest their forms, stating that the aforementioned discourse on the sutra and entry into meditative concentration have concluded.
The original purpose was to incite the Great Mind (mahācitta). However, as for those of the Two Vehicles, they ultimately remained as if neither seeing nor hearing it;
therefore, the earth shook and its appearance transformed to demonstrate the intent of causing them to be startled and moved upon contact with their own eyes.
Regarding "the entire Buddha-world," according to the subsequent verse by Maitreya, this world refers to the sphere of transformation of a single Buddha. The six kinds of earthquakes...
Regarding "movement" (*dong*): An ancient master explained that a low, rumbling sound is called "thundering" (*zhen*); a crashing, resonant sound is called "roaring" (*hou*);
and that which causes beings to be startled is called "striking" (*ji*). These three are all sounds, collectively termed "thundering. That which sways and is unsettled is called "movement" (*dong*).
Rising from below and ascending upward is called *udaya* (rising). The undulating of mounds and depressions is called *utsada* (surging).
These three are all forms of physical movement; collectively, they are termed the "sixfold earthquake. Furthermore, within these six types, each is further divided into three:

for example, movement in one direction is called *cala* (shaking), shaking throughout the four continents is called *pracala* (shaking everywhere), and shaking throughout the great trichiliocosm is called *saṃpracala* (shaking universally). The same applies to the remaining five types.

Taken together, these are called the eighteen modes of shaking. Regarding the fact that the worlds of all Buddhas are now said to shake in six ways, this expresses the principle of using the general to encompass the particular.
If one explains this as a symbolic representation of the Dharma: the earth represents ignorance (*avidyā*);

the six movements represent the breaking and severing of the six stages—namely, the stages of abiding, practice, and heading toward the various grounds and the wondrous [Buddha-ground]. It is said that the ignorance of sentient beings is vast and pervasive, like the solid and firm nature of the earth.

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time are difficult to shake. Now, as they are about to hear this Dharma and completely destroy the ignorance of the six stages (*ṣaḍbhūmi-avidyā*), the earth shakes in six ways to symbolize this.
After the rain of flowers and the shaking of the earth, △ Third: The Great Assembly’s Joyful Contemplation.
At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly (up to) rejoiced, joined their palms, and with single-minded devotion gazed upon the Buddha.
First, the members of the assembly are generally designated: "bhikṣus" refers to Kauṇḍinya and others; "bhikṣuṇīs" refers to Mahāprajāpatī and others;
"upāsakas and upāsikās"—translated as "male and female lay followers"—refers to those who have long or recently served and made offerings to the Triple Gem.
Regarding those such as the men and women of this region who observe the fasts and uphold the precepts:
they are not recorded in the general narrative because the translator omitted them, and because they are subsumed within the category of the *dāna-pati* (almsgivers).

Furthermore, these four assemblies (*catur-parṣad*) also include bodhisattvas, since bodhisattvas consist of both householders and renunciants, each being subsumed according to their respective class. Thus, the four assemblies herein are identical to those in the general introduction.
These are the assemblies of the Three Vehicles. "Devas" refers to the celestial kings and their retinues. "Nāgas" refers to the dragon kings and their retinues.

*Yakṣa* translates as "fierce and evil," "valiant and strong," or "swift and agile"; this is because their nature is fierce and evil, their power is valiant and strong, and their movement is swift and agile.
*Gandharva* refers to the assembly of deities of worldly music. *Asura* refers to the non-... [text truncated]
The *devas* (gods); the *garuḍas*, which are the hosts of golden-winged birds; the *kiṃnaras*, which are the hosts of gods of dharma-music;
and the *mahoragas*, here translated as "great serpent deities. Kumārajīva said: "These are terrestrial dragons that travel on their bellies.
This is why, although the general introduction lacks the two classes of *yakṣas* and *mahoragas*, they are nonetheless categorized as the eight divisions. As for humans—
He encompasses the four classes of commoners, grasping the infinite capacities of the fourfold assembly;
he encompasses non-humans, grasping the infinite capacities of the remaining realms, as well as various minor kings—such as King Ajātaśatru and the King of Śaśibiṣa of the sixteen great kingdoms.

Regarding the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings (*cakravartin*), according to the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra* (A-pi-tan), there are four types: first, the Golden-Wheel King, [who appears when] human life expectancy is eighty...

When the human lifespan is ten thousand years, a Golden-Wheel King appears in the world. Riding upon the precious golden wheel, he rules over the four quarters of the earth, exercising sovereign authority over the four continents.

When the human lifespan is sixty thousand years, a Silver-Wheel King appears in the world. Riding upon the precious silver wheel, he rules over three quarters of the earth, but does not include the northern continent.
When the human lifespan is forty thousand years, a Copper-Wheel King appears in the world, riding upon the precious copper wheel.

The Wheel-Turning Kings of Iron rule over two continents; they do not include the two continents of the northwest. These four Wheel-Turning Kings of Iron appear in the world when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years.
Riding upon the precious wheel of iron, they rule over one continent, governing only Jambudvīpa. These are the four types of Wheel-Turning Kings.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, which extended upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

This was precisely the moment when the great assembly gazed with joy. As for the Buddha’s emission of light, it was because there were those present who possessed the capacity to be awakened and inspired;
thus, he first bestowed a teaching beyond words to initiate the occasion for their inquiry and request. "Between the eyebrows" refers to the space between the two...
Between the eyebrows, it is neither biased nor leaning, representing the subtle principle of the Middle Way, the virtue of the Dharma-body, and the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
As for the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) mark, it is one of the thirty-two marks. According to the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, when the Buddha was first born, its length extended five feet;
by the time he attained enlightenment, its length had extended to one zhang and five chi. It is like a tube of lapis lazuli, within which...
The outer brilliance represents the principle of true emptiness and purity, the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*), and the characteristic of the real mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

Since the light issues from this mark, it is called the "light of the white tuft mark" (*ūrṇā-kośa-lakṣaṇa-raśmi*). It represents the principle of wondrous existence and perfection, the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*), and the function of the real mark.
As for its illuminating the eastern direction: since the east is the head of all movement, it signifies that this sutra is the foremost among all sutras.

For this reason, furthermore, the East flows downward, serving as the ultimate convergence for all streams; this symbolizes that the present sutra is pure and perfect, acting as the central hub of all teachings.
One world-realm constitutes the transformative sphere of a single Buddha; eighteen thousand realms are mentioned to express the extreme vastness of its scope.

"Mí" (靡) means "none"; it signifies that there is nothing not universally pervaded, representing the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle which encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because there is no interval [between suffering], it is called *Avīci*. This is translated as "Without Interval," also as "Without Obstruction," and also as "Without Rescue.

This means that the experience of suffering is uninterrupted, being without obstruction or rescue. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Five hundred *yojana*s beneath Jambudvīpa is where this hell first begins;
therefore, it is called a 'hell' (*naraka*). *Akaniṣṭha* is translated as "Obstructive Matter" (*sapratigha*).
"Ultimate" (Kongjù) refers to the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha). This is because "form" (rūpa) denotes that which possesses material obstruction.

Now, this heaven is at the very summit of the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu), while the Avīci Hell is at the very bottom of the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu). From the highest above to the lowest below, the intermediate realms encompass humans, asuras, ghosts, and animals.

This manifests the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for it pervades the six realms of existence without exception. This concludes the section on the scope illuminated by the single ray of light.

because beings go from those states to these, and die to go to those, they are called "destinies" (*gati*). As for "sentient beings" (*sattva*), they are so called because they receive birth through the conjunction of manifold conditions.

The first two phrases concern the extinction and *parinirvāṇa* of the various Buddhas; this is translated as "perfect stillness" (*yuánjì*). It signifies that the manifestation of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has reached its fulfillment.

Because one withdraws the body and enters quiescence, it is also called "extinction" (nirodha). This refers to the temporary cessation of the activities that sustain birth. Alternatively, it is called "perfect quiescence" (yuanji):

because there is no reality that is not perfect and no delusion that is not quiescent. It is called "extinction" (miadu) because one extinguishes the flow of afflictions and crosses the sea of birth and death;
this is spoken in terms of realization through the severance [of defilements], rather than as a mere matter of physical events. Now, [to speak] by way of events...

Commentary: One should not adopt the conventional interpretation [of this passage]. This is identical in meaning to the present Buddha’s preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, his subsequent turning toward the twin śāla trees to preach the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and his entry into parinirvāṇa.

As for the latter four lines concerning the construction of stūpas after his passing, "after parinirvāṇa" refers to the time when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished, the smoke has vanished, and the ashes have flown away.
Regarding the construction of stūpas with relics (*śarīra*), there are two meanings. The first is as follows:
First, it is because one honors the Buddha’s śarīra as one would honor the Buddha’s sacred countenance out of gratitude for his benevolence and virtue.
Second, it is because it manifests the Buddha’s remaining influence, serving as a causal basis for merit for humans and devas. Śarīra is fully termed *śarīraka*, and is also called *śiloka*.
This is translated as "sacred bone" (*linggu*). As for why the bones are designated as "sacred," it is because they are perfumed by the Tathāgata’s precepts and meditative concentration;
they manifest light and signs, and will certainly respond to sincere petitions. "To erect" (*qi*) means "to construct. Regarding the requirement that a stūpa be constructed with the seven treasures:

although this serves to manifest reverence, it also symbolizes the true permanence of the *dharmakāya* and the meaning of being adorned with the seven riches. "Stūpa" is an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; its full form is... [end of fragment]

It is called a *stūpa*. This translates as "a high and prominent place. That the location must be high and prominent signifies that the Buddha’s virtues are towering and majestic, representing the meaning of being gazed upon by humans and devas.

This is identical in meaning to the practice of distributing the *śarīra* relics and erecting *stūpas* for worship after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (the events following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa are detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
