The Doubts of Maitreya, Part Two. First, the doubt of Maitreya; second, the doubt of the great assembly. Regarding the first:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought... [up to] "...this rare sign; I shall now question him."
First, he investigated the causes and conditions. As for "forming this thought," it refers to reflecting within one's mind without speaking aloud regarding the matter at hand;
thus, it says, "now. As for "manifesting the signs of spiritual transformations," a single ray of light shone toward the east, its divine efficacy unfathomable.
It is divine. The transformative manifestations of the Buddhas are inconceivable in their changing forms; they are transformations. Such divine transformations—how could they appear for no reason?
Upon repeated investigation and scrutiny, there must be causes and conditions. Therefore it is asked: "By what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen arise?"
This "omen" refers specifically to the radiance. It is called an omen because it is rarely seen in the course of a lifetime.
Now, as the Buddha descends [from his seat], he contemplates and intends to ask about the causes and conditions of this radiance; only the Buddha can know them.

Maitreya wishes to question the Buddha, but seeing that the Buddha has entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he does not know when he will emerge. Therefore, it is said: "Now the World-Honored One has entered into *samādhi*. Indeed.
Seeing that there was no one to resolve his doubts, he intended to seek resolution for himself. Then, another light shone from the east, transcending all words and thought.
As the transformative manifestations of the Buddhas were not of the ordinary kind, it was said that this was "inconceivable.
A rare event having been manifested, Maitreya reflected upon it repeatedly; he would surely come to master the facts and clarify the principles, for his causal roots were deep and his wisdom supreme.
Only one who possesses sufficient virtue to command the respect of others can clarify this matter and dissolve the multitude of doubts;
therefore, it is said, "One should ask whom? Who is able to answer? Furthermore, the subsequent passage points to a specific person to resolve these doubts.

When Maitreya was in right contemplation, he beheld Mañjuśrī; by shifting his thoughts, he found the one capable of resolving his doubts. Therefore, it is said, "He again formed this thought," which refers to this very person.
The designated term: Mañjuśrī is the one specifically pointed out as the resolver of doubts.

As for the "Dharma Prince," he does not take up the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because Mañjuśrī acts as a shadow-like manifestation to assist in transformation, being entrusted with the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He is named a Dharma Prince. Those who draw near him find that his shadow and echo never depart; those who make offerings cultivate both principle and phenomena together.
All of this is due to Mañjuśrī’s profound causes cultivated over many kalpas; thus it says, "In the past, for immeasurable [kalpas]," etc.

This speaks to the vastness of his close service. One must necessarily encounter these [conditions], for since the encounters with Buddhas have been so numerous, one's own realization and insight must naturally be manifold.
Furthermore, the text of Mañjuśrī’s response states: "In the past, I have witnessed such auspicious signs before the Buddhas.
Thus, Mañjuśrī’s profound inner treasury has now been thoroughly scrutinized by Maitreya. As for my current inquiry, the intent of the question is already resolved;
for Maitreya deeply understands Mañjuśrī and is able to resolve the doubts within his very root-mind. (Question: Regarding the passage praising his virtues, it says: "He made offerings...")

He has served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, yet he has never once singled out Mañjuśrī. For what reason did Maitreya not know of the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs, while instead deferring to Mañjuśrī for his great service to the Buddhas? Answer: That Maitreya did not know can be briefly explained through two meanings: first, from the perspective of ultimate practice (*satyācaryā*);

second, from the perspective of provisional manifestation (*upāya-pradarśana*). Regarding ultimate practice: one who is on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) does not know the second stage; one at the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi*) does not know the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The present emission of light and manifestation of signs is the realm personally realized by the Tathāgata;

it is not within the scope of Maitreya’s wisdom as a candidate for Buddhahood (*kṣetrajña*). Regarding provisional manifestation: Maitreya’s skillful means and discerning wisdom know the proper time and the capacity of beings. Desiring to establish the ritual of "tongue-tapping" (the formal protocol), he manifested the appearance of ignorance. His deferral to Mañjuśrī also has two aspects: first, from the perspective of symbolic representation (*saṃketika*).

Regarding the Dharma: secondly, concerning the representation through shadow and echo, and the representation of the manifest teaching. Mañjuśrī represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); by borrowing him to initiate [the discourse], it is shown that this sutra cannot be understood without wisdom. Regarding the representation through shadow and echo:

although Mañjuśrī has long since attained Buddhahood and Maitreya is compared as the one who succeeds him, even though Maitreya has made many offerings to Buddhas, he is nonetheless slightly inferior [to Mañjuśrī]. Thus ends Maitreya’s doubt. II. The Doubts of the Great Assembly.
"At that time, [who] shall now be questioned regarding the marks of supernatural powers (ṛddhi-lakṣaṇa) of the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas...?
"At that time" means simultaneously with Maitreya’s doubt; it does not refer to a different time. The fourfold assembly (catasraḥ parṣadaḥ) includes the bodhisattvas by implication.
The devas, nāgas, and yakṣas include the eight classes of beings (aṣṭau gaṇāḥ) by implication. "Etc. includes humans and non-humans, as well as minor kings and universal monarchs (cakravartin).
In this context, the assembly that harbors doubts is none other than the assembly previously described as "joyfully observing. The term *xian* (咸) means "all.
Since the matter was not ordinary and the entire assembly was universally in doubt, it is said that "they all formed this thought. This refers to the phrase concerning the Buddha’s radiance.

This precisely refers to the matters being contemplated. Regarding the characteristics of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): a single ray of light shines to the east, its breadth and narrowness being unimpeded;
a single transformation is manifested instantaneously, with extension and contraction occurring simultaneously—all of which are the inconceivable supernormal powers of the Tathāgata.
The assembly suspected that he was Maitreya himself, yet they had no means to identify him. Therefore, it is simply said: "Now, whom shall we ask? As an ancient worthy said:
"A great doubt leads to a great awakening; a small doubt leads to a small awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening.

Although the preceding events included the preaching of the sutra, entering meditative absorption, the raining of flowers, and the shaking of the earth, the great assembly at the Dharma-gathering merely knew to rejoice, join their palms, and focus their minds with single-minded devotion.

To contemplate the Buddha is to be free from doubt. Now, by moving through the marks of light and demonstrating that which transcends words, he causes the mind to be distressed and deliberation to be weighed;
thus, the response of the "beak and the egg" may be hoped for. The assembly’s rising doubts were finally resolved.
△ Fourth, the initiation through question and answer has two parts: first, Maitreya’s inquiry; second, Mañjuśrī’s response. The first of these has two sub-sections; the first is brief.
Question. Second, the detailed inquiry. First, the two parts: 1. The prose section; 2. The verse section. First [the prose]:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts... (up to) ...he saw all the adornments of those Buddha-lands.
At first, as he was about to question [Mañjuśrī], Maitreya was filled with anxiety and unease; his gaze was fixed upon Mañjuśrī.

Although the words had not yet left his mouth, his intention was already clearly manifest. Thus it is said, "I wish to resolve my own doubts"—this is the language used by the sūtra compiler to describe the scene.
Furthermore, observing the fourfold assembly and so forth reflects Maitreya’s intention to extend his own concerns to others; that is to say, "By means of me..."
Even those at the stage of the "Successor to the Position" (Kṣetrajñāna-bhāga) cannot know [this], let alone the rest of the assembly; therefore, he uses his eyes to survey them one by one.
This is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). As for the various devas, nāgas, and so forth, this refers to the meaning of using the eyes to proceed from near to far.

The intention is that even the fourfold assembly, whether they have been with the World-Honored One for a long time or recently, cannot know [this], much less the other members of the assembly who have only just entered this sublime gathering.
To survey them one by one in their entirety is what is meant by "reaching" (ji). Suspicion resides within, while its form manifests without;
by observing the exterior, one knows the interior. Therefore, it is said that "the minds of the assembly" refers to the aforementioned observation of the doubting minds of the assembled multitude.
The following inquiry constitutes the actual words of the question. As for why he necessarily asks Mañjuśrī: [it is because...]

Because he wished to provide support for great wisdom in order to resolve the doubts within the minds of those with dull faculties, this auspicious sign specifically refers to the manifestation of light.
Such signs are never bestowed in vain; therefore, he asks by what causes and conditions they exist. A single ray of light shines toward the east, its divine transformation unfathomable.

Throughout the course of his teaching during one lifetime, his adaptive manifestations are infinite; thus, it is called the "sign of supernatural power" (*abhijñā*). He emits a great radiance, raising up that which is capable of illuminating.
"Light" illuminates two phrases, citing the objects illuminated; it does not specify "reaching upward" or "reaching downward" because the inquiry is abbreviated.

"All are seen" cites the manifestations appearing within those objects. The adornment of the realms encompasses the beginning and end of a single cycle of transformation (*ekāvatāra*), for the realms are adorned by the presence of Buddhas preaching the Dharma and assemblies practicing the path. Part Two.

Regarding the verse sections (gāthā), according to various sūtras, there are two types: first, *geya* (translated as "repeated verse"), which refers to verses that repeat the prose (*prose-gāthā*); second, *gāthā* (translated as "isolated verse"), which refers to verses that arise independently. An example of *geya* is the repeated verse at the end of the preceding section;

an example of *gāthā* is the verse praise by the Dragon Girl. Furthermore, Tiantai further divides *geya* into two categories: first, "anticipatory verse" (*chao-song*), where the prose follows and the verse precedes it, because the verse anticipates and transcends the subsequent text;

second, "retrospective verse" (*zhui-song*), where the prose precedes and the verse follows it, because the verse follows up on what has already been stated. Now, beyond these anticipatory and retrospective verses, they are further divided into four types. First, "extensive verse" (*guang-song*), which refers to the prose...

1. *Liaoyi* (Abridged in the prose): This refers to cases where the meaning is concise in the prose (*changxing*) but expanded in the verse (*jiesong*). 2. *Guangyi* (Expanded in the verse): This refers to cases where the meaning is detailed in the prose but abridged in the verse. 3. *Bushi* (Supplementary verse): This refers to instances where the meaning follows the prose, yet the prose lacks the specific textual phrasing;

it should be understood as a verse added to supplement the prose where it was incomplete. This excludes those verses that are *gāthā*. 4. *Yiyi* (Meaning-based verse): This refers to cases where the meanings of the expanded and abridged versions are so intermingled as to be difficult to distinguish, or where the meaning resembles the prose while the wording is slightly dissimilar.

When a lecturer encounters such "transcendent verses" (*chaosong*) or "retrospective verses" (*zhuisong*), they must provide cross-referential instructions. Regarding places where the verse is expanded or abridged compared to the prose, one need not strictly follow the prose divisions; whether opening a single section into many or combining many into one, either is acceptable according to the convenience of the text. Up to this point...

Regarding the *padasaṃgīti* (verse summaries) and *arthasaṃgīti* (meaning summaries), it is not necessary for each one to correspond precisely to the prose (*gadya*). It is sufficient to analyze the meaning based on the text. What follows below is a re-verse of the prose, and as such, the phrasing is somewhat abbreviated; this is categorized as an *uddānasaṃgīti* (summary verse). (The summary verse states:)
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse.
"Thereupon" (*atha*) refers to that time. "This meaning" still points to the prose section. There are four reasons why he wished to restate it:
first, according to the local custom; for after the scattering of loose flowers in India, they generally use strung flowers, as is the case here.

First, following the sequence [of the text], he composed an inscription after the preface. Second, according to inclinations: since human sentiments include those that delight in scattered flowers and those that delight in strung garlands—just as in this land people delight in prose and poetry.
Third, according to the arising of understanding: since the nature of wisdom involves both the dispersal and the integration of flowers.
There is the interpretation of "stringing together flowers," which is like interpreting prose or poetry in this land. Fourth, there is the accordance with the capacities [of the audience].
Since capacities may be sharp or dull—the sharp understand upon hearing once, while the dull only comprehend after it has been explained twice—this present verse further possesses two meanings:
first, the earnestness of the request; second, the lack of weariness in teaching the assembly. Because it possesses all these meanings, one desires [to explain it].

To restate this: if one were to speak of "repeated verses" (geya) for the sake of future Buddhas, there are two further meanings. First, it expresses the earnestness and sincerity of compassionate instruction;
second, it serves to distinguish between the preceding and succeeding assemblies, as it does not pertain to the meaning of the present verses.

"Gāthā" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; its full form is *gāthā*, which is itself a corruption. The correct term is *ātodya-dvīpa* (or *āryā-gāthā*), which translates here as "laudatory verse. This applies regardless of whether the verse consists of four-character lines or otherwise.
From as few as seven syllables per line, through four lines or even more lines, all such compositions may be termed *gāthā*.

That it is now called a "verse inquiry" (*gāthā-praśna*) is because Maitreya has interwoven the meaning of the prose (*gadya*) to form a string of flowers with which to inquire. (This is the introductory verse; what follows is the main body of the verses.)

As for the phrase "Why does the Guide Mañjuśrī emit a great light from the white tuft between his brows that shines everywhere," the initial mention of his name indicates that the question has a specific referent. "Guide" (Nāyaka) is an epithet of the Buddha;

because he can expound the Dharma to lead the multitude and manifest signs to draw in the deluded, he serves as a teacher who guides them. "Why" (*kasmāt*) is an interrogative particle used to pose a question.
These words praise the meaning of "by what causes and conditions," etc. The two lines concerning the brow-protuberance refer to the light that previously illuminated and the objects illuminated;
they praise the meaning of "emitting great light to illuminate the eastern direction," etc.
The reason it does not mention the manifested forms is that the verse is abbreviated. The brief inquiry concludes. △ Second, the detailed inquiry (the previous section was urgent).

Because he sought a definitive resolution, there is a brief inquiry. Fearing that his presentation of the meaning might not be exhaustive, he asks again in detail. However, although this section of detailed questioning follows the sequence of the prose, the prose itself lacks the explicit textual markers; it is likely that Maitreya, relying on what he had previously observed, has provided these details in full as a supplement to the verses (belonging to the category of supplementary stanzas).

This is divided into four parts: 1) A combined presentation of the manifest signs; 2) The formal presentation of the emission of light; 3) The conclusion of the vision and the request for resolution; 4) Anticipating objections and formulating the questions. Regarding the first:

although the initial doubt was primarily concerning the emission of light, the falling of flowers and the shaking of the earth are also preliminary signs preceding the emission of light; therefore, they are presented together.
He recounted this (to show that his narration has its source).
It rained *māndārava* and *mañjūṣaka* flowers (until) his body and mind were refreshed, attaining what he had never experienced before.
First, it describes how devas and humans presented offerings. Regarding the "four flowers" and the mention of "two": this is because they do not distinguish between large and small varieties.
*Candana* is translated as "medicine," for it is the name of a fragrant substance; this is because this incense can eliminate illness. Now, the wind passes over these flowers.
Its fragrance is like this. Thus it is said that "sandalwood-scented winds come gusting forth one after another; their pure essence is pleasing to people.
This expresses the meaning of the universal dissemination of the flavor of the Dharma through the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
Flowers rain down and cover the ground, so that dust, soil, and pebbles are not seen. Fragrant winds strike the nose, so that no foul odors are perceived. Therefore it is said:
For these reasons, the ground is everywhere adorned and purified, signifying the meaning of the purity of the "mind-ground" following the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
Below this, the transformation of the terrestrial deities (kṣetrapāla) is described, as can be understood. The final four lines describe the joyful observation of the great assembly.
This refers to the various categories. There are four such categories: the two groups of those who have left the household life and the two groups of those who remain at home.

Thus, when it says "other groups" are not mentioned, it is because the close is cited to include the distant. "All were filled with joy" means they rejoiced that there was a cause for the rain of flowers.

The earth quaking with joy is a manifestation of the extraordinary sincerity within being expressed outwardly; hence it is said that "body and mind are filled with gladness. Regarding the phrase "never before seen or heard":

because one has now obtained what was previously unseen and unheard, it is said "one attains what has never been attained before" (*atulya-pūrva-labdha*). [Question: Before the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth, there were two further signs—the preaching of the sutra and the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Why are these not presented together? [Answer: The *Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* is intended specifically for the Bodhisattvas, and Maitreya has no doubts regarding it. Since he has no doubts concerning the sutra, he naturally understands the state of concentration clearly; therefore, these two are not presented together. △ Second, the main body.
II. Chen Fangguang’s Two Points: 1. The realms illuminated by each individual ray of light; 2. The manifestations appearing within those various realms. First:
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminates the eastern direction (extending) from the Avīci Hell upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The "phrase between the eyebrows" refers to the aforementioned light capable of illuminating. "Illuminating [the worlds]" refers to the aforementioned objects illuminated.
The "eighteen thousand lands" are discussed in terms of a single ray of light shining horizontally. That they are "all like golden color" is due to being reflected by the Buddha’s light.
This represents the entire Dharma-realm, for all are identical to the Buddha-realm. From the character "A" downwards, this is discussed in terms of a single ray of light shining vertically.
"Bottom" refers to that which possesses material obstruction; "summit" refers to the ultimate. These are spoken briefly according to their meaning for the sake of the verse’s convenience.

This concludes the section on the realms illuminated by a single ray of light. II. The Manifestations Appearing in All Realms (three parts): 1. The Responsive Resonance of Sentient Beings' Capacities.
Second, the transformation-response of all Buddhas; third, the cessation of transformation when the capacities [of beings] are exhausted. Regarding the first:
within all worlds, the sentient beings of the six realms—down to their receiving of retributions, whether auspicious or inauspicious—are all seen here.
The first phrase reiterates the aforementioned realm. "Dao" (道) means a path. There are three good and three evil [paths] through which beings travel back and forth;
since there are six such paths, they are called "sentient beings of the six realms. "Qu" (趣) means to head toward. One heads toward this [realm] when born and toward that [realm] when dying;
thus, they are said to be "those toward whom birth and death tend. Good and evil karma each consist of many varieties, which, when categorized, are merely...

Tenth: these refer to the three actions of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind. To uphold them is good; to transgress them is evil. Each is capable of binding one to the cycle of birth and death;

therefore, they are called "karmic conditions" (*karmapratyaya*). "Condition" (*pratyaya*) here carries the sense of "binding. There are many varieties of retribution for both good and evil deeds, yet when condensed, there are only six types.
For instance, as for a superior grade of wholesome cause, the retribution is rebirth in the heavens; for a middling grade of wholesome [cause], [the retribution is...]
Causes [lead to] retributions in the human realm; inferior-grade wholesome causes lead to retributions among the asuras—both are termed "favorable retributions.

Superior-grade unwholesome causes lead to retributions in hell; middle-grade unwholesome causes lead to retributions among the hungry ghosts; inferior-grade unwholesome causes lead to retributions among the animals—all are termed "ugly retributions.
If one were to divide these into subtle categories, the interplay of cause and effect is truly vast, as detailed in a single chapter.

Within the causal stage, these are further divided into three; thus, both good and evil each have nine grades. This results in the superiority and inferiority among devas, and the nobility and lowliness among humans.
Within a single path, the categories are not uniform—what is called the inconceivable realm of sentient beings and the inconceivable retribution of karma.
Now, the fruit is experienced in accordance with its cause, just as a shadow follows a form.

Therefore, it is said that according to the karmic conditions of good and evil deeds, one receives retributions that are either auspicious or inauspicious, as described above, without a single detail being omitted;
hence it is said, "one sees all of this. As previously stated: "In this world, one sees exhaustively all the sentient beings of the six realms in those lands."

This is merely a slightly more detailed elaboration than what preceded it. The section on the sentient beings' capacity for resonance and response concludes. △ Second, the various Buddhas’ transformative responses, which has two parts:
1. Manifesting the provisional from the real; 2. Returning the provisional to the real. The first [of these two] has two sub-sections: 1. From the real; 2. Manifesting the provisional.
First: Furthermore, he beheld the Buddha, the Holy Lord, the Lion (up to) teaching countless billions of bodhisattvas.
"Beheld" means seen. In eighteen thousand lands, there were World-Honored Ones who had attained the Way; therefore, they are called "all Buddhas. Since—
Having attained enlightenment, he transcended all sages and stood alone as the Honored One; thus he is called the "Holy Lord" (*ārya-nātha*).
His majestic radiance blazed forth, startling the Māras and heretics so that they hid their tracks; thus he is called the "Lion.

When he expounded the sūtras—referring here to his initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*—the Bodhisattvas who had accumulated merit were like fish with gills swollen at the Dragon Gate, while the Śrāvakas of superior virtue closed their eyes and ears to the sublime assembly.
Therefore, it is called "subtle and wondrous. It is like Mount Sumeru surpassing the heights of all other peaks, or like the bright sun eclipsing the radiance of all other lights;
therefore, it is called "foremost. This sound is the sound of preaching the Dharma. As for "pure," it means it is neither turbid nor mixed.
Peaceful and resonant; this is even the mark of the holy merit of the Sage. "Emerges" (chu) means "revolves" (zhuan).

Because sound, in its state of being a mere undifferentiated mass, cannot fully express the Dharma, it revolves into articulated and modulated tones. "Supple" (ruǎnrěn) is one of the eight qualities of voice;
it means neither urgent nor violent, but harmonious, gentle, and soft. This results from having cultivated gentleness and compliance during the causal stage. Seven.
He dwells in nine assemblies and reaches infinite capacities; thus it is said that he teaches "countless billions of bodhisattvas.
These are all those of the perfect and sudden great faculty, who, upon first seeing the Buddha’s body, immediately enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
What was stated previously—namely, "furthermore, seeing the present Buddhas of those lands and hearing the sutras and teachings spoken by those Buddhas"—refers merely to the speaker and the spoken.
This refers to the long exposition of the four lines on the purity of the voice, which encompasses both the capacity to bestow [the teaching] and that which is bestowed.
△ Second, the application of provisional means has two parts: first, a general presentation; second, a detailed presentation. First:
"The Brahma-voice is profound and subtle, causing all to delight in hearing it" (up to) "illuminating the Buddha-dharma and awakening sentient beings.
The first two phrases carry forward from what precedes and initiate what follows. "Brahma-voice" is one of the thirty-two marks [of a Buddha];

it combines the two meanings of purity and softness mentioned previously, as he constantly spoke gentle words during his causal practice, thereby eliciting this mark as a result. This refers exclusively to the Perfect and Sudden Great Teaching.

Because it is covered by the great capacity for the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], it is called "profound and subtle. This follows the preceding text’s discussion of the ultimate discourse according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which does not accommodate the various capacities of all beings.
To cause people to delight in hearing it, [the Buddha] restrains his original intention and speaks according to the inclinations of others.

This gives rise to the subsequent section on teaching the Dharma as appropriate, which skillfully accommodates the various capacities of all beings. That this must follow the preceding to give rise to the subsequent is because...

This reveals that the Buddhas employ skillful means; it is not that they have nothing further to attain. "Each in their own" below serves as a general statement. "Each in their own" distinguishes this from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) realm.
"World" distinguishes this from the *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment) realm. This is because the *dharmatā* lands and *kṣetras* are interpenetrating and fused, such that no boundaries can be fixed.

The *saṃbhoga* realm is where sages and worthies dwell for themselves and does not pertain to the field of transformation. Now, by concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior, each is established according to its own station.
It is a transformed land; therefore, it is said that [the teachings] are each [delivered] within their respective worlds. "Expounding" (*jiang*) and "explaining" (*yan*) differ:

"explaining" refers to direct pointing to the meaning, while "expounding" refers to analytical exposition. This represents the process of arising from the fundamental to the derivative, analyzing the one into three;

hence, it is called "expounding. "True Dharma" (*saddharma*) distinguishes this from what is partial or deviant. Because the Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* is difficult for the various capacities of beings to receive, it flows toward those at the level of ordinary people.
Externally, we now speak of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna) as an antidote to the biased attachments of ordinary beings and the false views of non-Buddhists;

therefore, they are designated by the name of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). The teachings of the Three Vehicles all take dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as their fundamental principle, though they differ in their degrees of depth.

There are distinctions between that which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), that which is provisional (*upāya*), and that which is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); hence, it is said to be "various. Regarding the use of "immeasurable analogies," there is a single cause...
There is one historical precedent that serves as an analogy. This was established for those who could not understand through direct discourse.

Regarding the illumination of the Buddha-dharma, when discussed according to the teachings, it is because those of small capacity do not harmonize with the Great Teaching that the Buddha-dharma fails to prevail;
this is what is meant by "lack of clarity. Now, using the torch of causes and conditions and the lamp of parables, one illuminates and realizes the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the Dharma: because it causes [the truth] to become manifest, it awakens sentient beings. This is discussed in terms of their capacities;
for if the Great Teaching were not adapted to the capacities of lesser ones, it would be of no benefit to sentient beings, and thus they would not attain awakening.

Now, by means of the method of causes and conditions and the expedient of parables, it is revealed and shown to sentient beings so that they may attain entry into awakening. Based on this, there are two aspects: illumination and awakening.
This sentence reveals the purport of the ultimate reality (*tattva*) and has already disclosed its general outline.

That even Maitreya still pushed back, claiming he did not know, is what is meant by "possessing the eye of the discernment of dharmas" (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*); it means he truly did not know. This section was not present in the preceding text;
it was likely left out here as an alternative presentation by the translator to avoid redundancy. The general exposition is concluded. △ Second, the specific exposition.
If there are those who encounter suffering and grow weary of old age, illness, and death—up to those who seek unsurpassed wisdom—for them he preaches the Path of Purity.
First, he preaches the Śrāvaka-yāna. Regarding "those who encounter suffering": because the faculties of śrāvakas are dull, they take the Truth of Suffering as their primary gateway;
thus, those of the śrāvaka disposition frequently encounter hardship and distress, for they first realize suffering and only thereafter sever the origin [of suffering]. All...

Among the various forms of suffering, old age, sickness, and death are the most severe; therefore, one feels a singular revulsion toward them. It is not that one does not feel revulsion for the others, but they are matters of secondary urgency.
This single word "revulsion" (厭) is precisely where the Śrāvaka gains strength. This is because those who encounter suffering are many, while those who feel revulsion toward suffering are few.

Once one knows to be weary of suffering, one will not end one's life in suffering. Furthermore, the single character "weary" (*yàn*) is also a point of narrowness and inferiority for the Two Vehicles;
it means that because they are weary of suffering, they quickly exit the Triple Realm, fail to resolve upon the Great Mind, and thus do not attain Buddhahood.
The teaching of *nirvāṇa* is intended to cause them to aspire toward cessation; *nirvāṇa* is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This...

It is translated as "extinction and crossing over" (*nirvāṇa*). It is called "extinction" because it extinguishes the afflictions of views and thoughts; it is called "crossing over" because it crosses over the death of the limited segments of existence. "Limit" (*anta*) refers to the ultimate boundary.

It is the limit of all suffering, the point where [existence] is reduced to ashes and utterly extinguished. If suffering were exhausted while the body and wisdom still remained, that would still be a boundary and not yet the final consummation.
Now, relying on the *Hīnayāna* nirvāṇa, one takes the fruit of the extinction of the ashes [of the aggregates]; hence it is said, "exhausting the limit of all suffering.

As for the omission of the two truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*), this is because the fruit is cited to encompass its causes. The subsequent four lines explain the *Pratyekabuddhayāna*.

If a person possesses merit, their faculties as a *pratyekabuddha* are sharp; thus, they take the truth of origin as the initial gateway. Therefore, those of the *pratyekabuddha* disposition are numerous.

It brings forth merit and happiness. This is because when one indulges in merit, it is easy for delusion to arise. Those who have previously made offerings to the Buddha possess the causes for having merit.
The "sublime Dharma" refers to the Dharma of causes and conditions, as it is superior to the aforementioned Four Noble Truths.

The two characters "aspiring and seeking" are precisely where the power of awakening resides. This is because those who possess merit are many, while those who seek the Dharma are few. Since this is known...
One who aspires [to this] will not be deluded by worldly merit. Regarding the explanation for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle:

the character "condition" (*yuan*) follows the teaching, which refers to the twelve links of dependent origination; the character "awakening" (*jue*) follows the capacity, which refers to the seventy-seven insights.

This means that the Buddha taught the twelve links of dependent origination so that [practitioners] might rely on the seventy-seven insights to awaken to the principle of ultimate truth. The final four lines explain the Bodhisattva vehicle.

The Bodhisattva possesses the Buddha-lineage and is destined to succeed to the rank of Buddhahood; therefore, they are called "Sons of the Buddha. To personally practice and realize [the teachings] is termed "cultivation" (xiū);
to establish the cause based upon the fruit is termed "conduct" (xíng). Herein, the six perfections (pāramitās) are briefly explained, though in detail there are many approaches;
thus, they are described by means of various categories. "Unsurpassed wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the Buddha. Because the Buddha’s wisdom is most supreme, it is called "unsurpassed."
The single word "seeking" (*qiu*) is precisely where the Bodhisattva gains mastery. This is because while those who practice cultivation are many, those who seek wisdom are few.
Once one knows how to seek wisdom, one will naturally not be obstructed by the causes of outflows (*āsrava*).

For those to whom the Path of Purity is taught, it is shown that the fruit of Buddhahood is the Path of Purity, so as to enable them to accomplish the cause of non-outflow (*anāsrava*). One does not cultivate various [practices] with a defiled mind through conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because of their practice. Previously it was said: "And he saw those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all those who had practiced and attained the Way.
Now, both the capacity [of the disciples] and the teaching are presented together; the three vehicles are each described separately.
Thus, one further knows that this concerns the turning of the light upon the three assemblies. This concludes the section on "Applying Expedients Based on Reality. II. Turning the Expedients.
Returning to the reality [of the preceding], there are two parts: first, concluding the previous section and initiating the subsequent one;
second, formally presenting the appropriate capacity [of the audience]. Regarding the first: "Mañjuśrī, I dwell here... (up to) "...these many [teachings] shall now be briefly explained."
"First, I summarize what was previously seen and heard: 'I dwell here' means not departing from Vulture Peak;
'what has been seen and heard is such as this' refers to that which was seen and heard above, meaning that by relying on the Buddha’s radiance, one does not depart from Vulture Peak."
What has been seen and heard is already as numerous as this. The final three phrases initiate a subsequent brief summary.
It states that what has been seen and heard is not only as numerous as described above, but there is even more that has not yet been set forth; therefore, it says "and ten billion matters."
"Affairs" refers to the practices of the six perfections and so forth that follow below. "Counted by thousands and tens of millions" is said to express the extreme abundance of these affairs.

"In this way" generally points to both those characteristics already presented and those yet to be presented. As for the characteristics already presented, they have already been described as numerous;
how much more so when it comes to those yet to be presented? Therefore, it is said they are "many and manifold. Even if one were to speak of them all, one could not exhaust them. There are...

Doubts linger in the mind; they cannot be resolved unless they are addressed. Therefore, it is said: "Now I shall briefly explain. Furthermore, there are two senses to this "brief": first, it refers to the brief teaching alone.

Whereas previously, when the provisional was established based on the real, both the capacity [of the audience] and the teaching were presented together, here, as the provisional is subsumed back into the real, the capacity remains while the teaching is abbreviated.
Second, it includes the abbreviation of the capacity itself. This is because the final, ultimate discourse encompasses a vast range of capacities.

How much more so for the eighteen thousand lands—how could they possibly be described in words?
