"I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.

This opening phrase reiterates the previously mentioned realm. "Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers to the disciples present at the great assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) is also called the *Kīṅ-ga* River; this is translated as "Heavenly Hall Coming. This river originates from the Snowy Mountains.
"Summit. It flows from Lake Anavatapta; its source is the highest point of all. Within the river, golden sand flows intermingled with the water, as fine as flour.
The present mention of this sand in contrast to the Bodhisattva is intended to express the extreme abundance of its quantity.
Various causes and conditions are as previously stated. The reason for not mentioning the characteristics of faith and understanding is that their meaning is set forth elsewhere.

Therefore, the final sentence concludes the core tenet. It states that although the causal conditions one upholds are manifold, when their original intent is traced back, it lies solely in the fruit of Buddhahood.
Just as a thousand paths and nine thoroughfares all converge at the royal city, it says: "and seeks the Buddha-way.
△ Second, the specific presentation of the characteristics of faith and understanding has two parts: first, a gradual and orderly exposition; second, a non-sequential exposition.
Speak briefly. First, the six [perfections]: first, giving; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, meditative concentration;
sixth, wisdom. Of these, the first three are: first, external giving; second, internal-external giving; third, internal giving. First [external giving].
There are those who practice giving gold, silver, and coral—[extending] up to that which is foremost in the three realms and praised by all Buddhas.
The word "or" (或) is an indefinite term, indicating that the eighteen thousand lands have manifold appearances and are seen as if in a state of visionary clarity.

Therefore it is said that there are those who practice giving gold, silver, and landed estates from the mines; these become increasingly refined through smelting and are universally esteemed as treasures throughout the world.
Coral is a treasure among stones, arriving from the kingdoms of Persia and Siṃhala;
its shape resembles deer antlers, and its color is red and lustrous. Because this land highly values the color red, it is prized by the world. This is true.

*Maṇi*. It is also called "pearl. Some originate from oysters and clams, while others come from snake-gems (*nāga-maṇi*). Because their types vary in quality—superior or inferior—their value is not uniform.
*Maṇi* is the name for a jewel; it is translated here as "Stainless" (*vimala*), because its substance is pure.

It is also called "Wish-Fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*), because if one desires whatever is needed, by burning incense and offering prayers, it can rain down [whatever is required] according to one's will. Entering through the Good Friend...

The sea is precisely where these are sought. Both *caichu* (musāragalva) and *mamanuo* (musāragalva) originate from stone; therefore, the four characters [of their names] are derived from the radical for "stone.
*Caichu* is the most pristine white among them, while *mamanuo* possesses various colors that are not uniform; it resembles jade but is not jade, yet both are treasures of the world.
The Vajra is the most firm and the sharpest; it can destroy all things, yet nothing can destroy it. As the ancient masters said:
"In the Sanskrit language it is called *vajra*, which here is translated as 'Vajra. It is the jewel possessed by Śakra and the mallet wielded by the Māṇibhadra spirits.
Beings of meager merit cannot even see it with their eyes. Based on this, one knows that it does not belong to this world.

The two characters "you zhen" (various treasures) encompass all rare and marvelous things; it means there is no jewel that he does not give away. "Nubi" (male and female slaves) is a general term for servants and attendants.
"Checheng" (vehicles) is a collective name for wheels and hubs. One who uses these as gifts provides them so that [the recipient] may fully utilize them for travel and transport.
As for "bejeweled palanquins and carriages," they are adorned with precious gems and are drawn by human porters; therefore, they are called *nian* (palanquins).

The character [for "chariot"] is composed of "husband" (夫) and "chariot" (車); it resembles the vehicle of a king, yet it is not for ordinary use. One who gives with joy forms the thought of benefiting others;
this is distinguished from giving out of compulsion or necessity, such as the cutting of one's own flesh. Such a person dedicates the merit toward the Buddha-way.
Dedicating these merits toward the Buddha-way means not seeking the rewards of fortune as a human or deva, nor the provisional vehicles of minor fruits.

This vehicle refers specifically to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). "Wishing to attain it" means relying upon it to resolve the mind for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) with the firm determination that it must be attained;
this is what is meant by "relying solely on the Supreme Vehicle to give rise to bodhicitta. This vehicle is indeed the most supreme.
The One Vehicle (Ekayāna). To attain it is to transcend the world and become a Buddha; thus it is called the foremost within the three realms.
This vehicle is the essential core of all Buddhas; to attain it is for one’s life-vein to be in communion with theirs, and for this reason it is praised by all Buddhas.

Although it may appear here to consist solely of the gift of material wealth, in reality its meaning encompasses the three types of giving (*dāna*). For example, through joyful giving, the seeker has no cause for fear.

This encompasses the giving of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). To vow to attain the Buddha-way and personally initiate the practice of transforming others encompasses the giving of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
When combined with the aforementioned material giving (*āmiṣa-dāna*), the three types of *dāna* are complete. Hereafter, follow this pattern. The section on external giving is concluded.
△ Second, internal and external giving (vehicles, horses, wives, and children belong to external wealth; body, flesh, hands, and feet belong to internal wealth).
There are some bodhisattvas who, seeking the unsurpassed path, give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, as well as their wives and children.

First, regarding the gift of the chariot and horses: "four horses" (*sima*) refers to a team of four steeds; "precious chariot" (*baiche*) refers to a noble carriage, one constructed from rare jewels.

It is drawn by four horses; thus it is called a "precious carriage of four horses. The *lánshǔn* (railing) refers to the front and rear balustrades. The *huágài* (canopy) is the covering over the top of the carriage.
The *xuān* (awning) refers to the side compartments on the left and right. Because they are adorned with various colors, it is called "adorned awnings.

As for "bestowing" (*bōshī*), it means to distribute everywhere, giving according to the requests of those who beg. By taking this as a cause and practicing it, one brings about the fruition of meritorious virtue. Furthermore...
[The text] proceeds to discuss giving the body and one's kin. "Body" refers to the entire person; flesh, hands, and feet—these three—are all subsumed under the category of the body.
A wife and husband are to each other as exterior and interior; a son and father are to each other as the author and the successor; these are all subsumed under the category of kin.

The single character "giving" (śī) comprehensively encompasses both the body and one's kin. Now, among all things that people value most highly, none surpasses body and life; [it is] what they love most.
There is nothing that surpasses wife and children. Now, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of the Way, forgets his own body; he regards his physical form as shackles and fetters.
Seeking the truth and loathing the false, he views his wife and concubines as painted vases; therefore, he gives them all away together. The final phrase summarizes the purpose of these actions.
Regarding the reason why a bodhisattva relinquishes both internal and external things: it is entirely for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path.
According to the later *Devadatta-parivarta*, the Buddha himself recounted: "Throughout many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, aspiring to seek unexcelled bodhi.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, I diligently practiced giving with a heart free from stinginess—elephants, horses," and so forth.
The seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and even one’s own flesh, hands, feet, and so forth—these are of this same category.
△ Third, internal giving:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas joyfully bestowing their heads, eyes, bodies, and limbs to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
To remove one's eyes or injure one's body merely destroys their form; such giving is relatively easy. To sever one's head or kill oneself involves the total extinction of one's life;
such giving is extremely difficult. That you now give with joy and delight to those who beg is precisely because that which is gained is weighty, while that which is lost is light.
According to the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), King Mahāprabha summoned a beggar for his head.

The Brahmin said, "You have come from afar to beg for my head. Out of a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for you, I shall not oppose your wish, so that in future lives I may obtain a head of wisdom to bestow upon you all.

Your current request for the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely that intention. [Question: "The physical body bequeathed by one's parents must not be mutilated; this is why Zengzi made a vow not to remove his own shroud. If [the text] states that both head and eyes..."

[The questioner asks: "If one gives away even their own body, will they not fall into the sin of filial impiety? [The answer: "Circumstances vary from the ordinary, and duties differ in weight. Have you not heard how one sacrifices their life to fulfill righteousness (*ren*), such as the case of Bi Gan who had his belly cut open?

To this day, no one can argue that such acts were wrong. How much more so when seeking the Great Way that transcends the world, which cannot be compared to worldly loyalty and filial piety; for by doing so, one brings infinite benefit to the parents of many lifetimes and inspires inexhaustible joy in the sages and worthies of the ten directions."
Furthermore, who can say that he was unable to preserve his life, and thus hold him guilty of the sin of filial impiety? The section on giving is concluded. △ Second, the observance of precepts.
Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings (up to) shaving their hair and beards and donning the dharma robes.
Since my exposition has been extensive, I fear you may have overlooked it; therefore, I repeat his name to inform you.

In the eighteen thousand lands, there are many princes who practice the Way; thus, when it says "I see various kings going to the place where the Buddha is," this indicates that those who go are none other than these, for they come with sincere intent to have an audience.
When it says "asking about the Unsurpassed Way," it means they themselves contemplate wholesome dharmas and teach them to the people.

It provides no salvation for the world; therefore, one seeks separately the path that transcends the world to universally deliver those whose minds are deluded—this is precisely the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha-śīla*).
To "abandon" means to cast it off with utter indifference. The entire realm of the land is what the King finds joy in, and is thus called a "land of bliss" (*sukhāvatī*).
The residence of the Emperor is called a "palace" (*gong*); it follows the regulations of vermilion pillars and carved rafters. The Ruler governs...
The palace is called the Hall; it bears the names of the *zhique* and the phoenix. The attendants are called ministers; they hold the offices of the "hundred officials.
The consorts and ladies are called concubines; they possess the beauty of three thousand women with powdered brows and dark mascara. All of these are the most difficult things to relinquish.
As for the statement that he "immediately abandoned [the world]," it was because he went to the Buddha to inquire about the Way and realized for himself that worldly pleasures are not true.
Therefore, he departed with a carefree air, never looking back. This was not because he held the Way lightly or esteemed glory; rather, he regarded the entire world as a pair of worn-out sandals.
It cannot be otherwise. This is precisely the precept of collecting wholesome dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). To shave off hair and beard signifies the deportment of transcending the mundane world;
to don the dharma robes signifies severing the formal appearances of worldly convention. This is precisely the precept of collecting ethical discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*).
Having completed the discussion on upholding the precepts. △ Third, patience (*kṣānti*).
Alternatively, one may see a bodhisattva acting as a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.

As for acting as a bhikṣu: having abandoned the secular world to pursue the Way, he shaves his hair and dons dyed robes; externally, he cuts off the five desires, and internally, he purifies the five categories of offenses.
This explains patience in terms of upholding the precepts. To not engage in worldly affairs is called "dwelling alone," which means remaining far removed from clamor and distraction.

It is said: "Seclusion and tranquility. Furthermore, one who dwells alone is so because they have severed all opposition; "seclusion and tranquility" refers to entering deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This explains patience (*kṣānti*) in terms of meditative absorption. To do so morning and evening is called "delighting in recitation. The established teachings of the sages and saints are called "scriptures" (*sūtra*).
It is because one wishes to borrow those established dharmas to support the arising of right wisdom; therefore, one recites them joyfully morning and night.

This explains patience (*kṣānti*) by way of wisdom (*prajñā*). As for explaining patience specifically by way of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), it carries the meaning of seeking to cut off the current by striving to sever its source.
This is because those who lack patience mostly give rise to it due to the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*), as in that [previous] case.
This appearance of greed leads to the arrival of mutual insults; this mutual anger leads to the point where one forgets both oneself and one's kin;
this deluded ignorance leads to the formation of grudges and harboring of resentment. Now, as the Bodhisattva’s three trainings are complete, the three poisons naturally subside.
Not only can he endure the insults of others, but there are also no insults to be endured. This is the patience of non-patience.
This is true patience. The section on patience concludes. △ Fourth, diligence:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, with courageous and vigorous diligence, enter deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
"Valiant" (*vīra*) means being fierce and tireless yet not cowardly, and bearing suffering without complaint.

"Diligent" (*vīrya*) means that various conditions do not cause distraction, but one moves straight forward with a single thought. "Deep mountains" refers to remote gorges and secluded valleys where human habitation is utterly absent;
dwelling there, one lives among trees and stones, and traveling, one roams with deer and wild boars. Eating parched grain and eating herbs, such solitude is difficult to endure.
What is now called "entering" must mean that one has forgotten worldly affairs and the mind has died within the streams and mountains. This is what is meant by:
"Carrying the knotted staff across the shoulder, one does not look back at others; straightway one enters among a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks.

It is also like being forced by the world to know one's whereabouts, or moving one's thatched hut into the deep mountains—such are the deeds of one who contemplates the Buddha-way. Thus, one binds together all that they have done.
As for why Bodhisattvas enter deep mountains, it is because the Way of the Buddha is profound and subtle, and cannot be ascended by those who are superficial or flighty.
They rely on precipices and sheer cliffs to enter right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) for the purpose of reflection.

This is precisely the meaning behind the ancients who, after attaining enlightenment within the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*), dwelt in the mountains for twenty or thirty years to nurture the "sacred embryo" (*ārya-garbha*). △
The five dhyānas.
Furthermore, he is seen to be free from desire and constantly dwelling in seclusion (up to) praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million gāthās.
Initially, one enters the dhyānas from the shallow to the deep. "Desire" refers to the five desires, namely: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. One must certainly leave them behind.
This is because [distraction] acts as an obstacle to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). A secluded place is a ground free from desire;
one must dwell there constantly so that, by temporarily departing from the realm of desire, one may achieve the unity of movement and stillness, using that environment to fortify the mind.
This refers to the shallow practice of beginners. For those who practice deeply, there is a gradual process of cultivation;

that is, by gradually penetrating deeper, one reaches the ultimate limit. "Zen" (禪) is a partial transliteration of a Sanskrit term; its full form is *dhyāna*. This translates as "meditative concentration" (*靜慮*, *jinglü*).
"Contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to subtle observation; it is distinguished from spontaneous conceptualization, and is therefore described as "calm.

"Concentration" (*samādhi*) is the antidote to distraction, and thus also carries the meaning of "calm contemplation. The two terms are spoken together here as a combined rendering of the Chinese and Sanskrit, so that the meaning may be easily understood.

There are six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the divine eye; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, recollection of past lives; fifth, the power of spiritual transformations;

and sixth, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Here, only five supernormal powers are mentioned because, within the Mahāyāna teachings, only the Buddha is permitted to possess the exhaustion of outflows, while for others it is not so permitted.
Nevertheless, although these five supernormal powers arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not constitute the ultimate stillness where the emotions are forgotten.
Those [of the previous stages] were also unable to attain it; that it is now said to be attained is the verification of having cultivated it deeply. As for the latter four phrases:

"entering deeply into wondrous dhyāna" and "abiding in dhyāna" distinguish this from the aforementioned seeking of dhyāna by departing from desire; it refers to attaining without thinking and hitting the mark without striving—this is what is called "deep dhyāna.
"Joining the palms" and so forth distinguish this from the aforementioned seeking of stillness in secluded places; it refers to...
Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, he manifests all modes of dignified conduct; this is what is meant by "wondrous dhyāna.

As for the "ten million verses," some praise the fruit by citing the cause, while others extol merit and discuss virtue; as their metaphors and allegories differ, their poetic compositions vary accordingly.
The Great Sūtra states: "When praising the Buddha’s marks and signs, one should wish that all sentient beings achieve the Buddha-body and realize the markless Dharma.

The present statement, "praising the Kings of All Dharmas," likewise intends to dedicate the merit toward the benefit of all sentient beings. Furthermore, "peaceful meditation" (an-zen) pertains to meditative concentration (samādhi).
Verses of praise belong to wisdom (*prajñā*). Since one is able to rest in dhyāna while composing verses of praise, it must be that concentration and wisdom are perfectly integrated (*samprayukta*).
Thus, one is not only unbound by deluded concentration, but also not misled by frantic wisdom. Dhyāna concludes.
△ Sixth: Wisdom.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm (extending to) rescuing those in the hells from suffering and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
This first clarifies the wisdom of great joy (*mahāmuditā*). "Profound wisdom" means that their natural endowment is sharp and acute; they do not abide in superficial understanding.

"Firm resolve" means that they joyfully and diligently seek, never retreating from their original aspiration. Because their wisdom is profound, they are thus able to question the Buddhas of antiquity.
What the Venerable Master called "knocking at the gate and striking the joints" refers precisely to skillfully inquiring into the essential points of the mind.

Because his resolve was firm, he heard everything and received it all for retention; this is what the ancient masters meant by "upholding both text and meaning," like pouring from one vessel into another without omission.

The next eight lines clarify great compassionate wisdom: externally ceasing all conditions and internally giving rise to right contemplation, which is why it is said that "concentration and wisdom are complete."
This is sufficient. It refers to that which is called "vivid alertness does not obstruct profound stillness; profound stillness does not obstruct vivid alertness.
This is because there is no duality between the two phrases. The meaning of applying expedient means according to the capacity of the recipient is established through their functional application.

As for the "immeasurable metaphors," they may clarify the obscure by means of the manifest, or illustrate the profound by citing the shallow; since the capacities of sentient beings are immeasurable, the skillful and expedient parables are likewise immeasurable.

"To act for the sake of the multitude" means to serve as an occasion for those listeners—beings among gods and humans—to hear the Dharma. "To expound the Dharma" means to analyze and explain dharmas such as the precepts, goodness, the truths, and conditions.
By employing the power of skillful means through such words and phrases, one causes all to rejoice; this is what is meant.

The two phrases regarding "rejoicing" carry the sense of praising principle and manifesting reality. To speak directly in accordance with principle, one’s original intent is finally fulfilled; hence it is said:
He delights in preaching the Dharma. When the conditions converge and the time ripens, those who hear him immediately attain the Way;

thus it is said that he transforms all bodhisattvas. "To destroy" (*po*) carries the meaning of crushing and annihilating. "Māra" is a term from the *bāṇa* language; its full form is *māra*. This is translated as "seizer of life.

Because it injures the *dharmakāya* and seizes the life-force of wisdom, according to the analogy of the crest-jewel, there are the *skandha-māra*, the *kleśa-māra*, the *mṛtyu-māra*, and so forth; therefore, [it is so called].
The "army" refers to the host of demons. The "drum" is the command that urges the army forward;
because its function is analogous to the Dharma’s ability to exhort practitioners, it is used as a metaphor. The word "yet" (猶) serves to connect the preceding with what follows.

It states that the reason Bodhisattvas expound the provisional and preach the ultimate is precisely to destroy the demonic hosts; therefore, they beat the drum of the provisional and ultimate Dharma to urge them on.
One merely battles with the army of the noble ones (ārya). Furthermore, looking downward clarifies the wisdom of great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).

"Tranquil" (*jiran*) means immovability; it refers to turning back to observe and illuminating within. "Serene silence" (*yanmo*) means peaceful stillness; it refers to the correspondence with contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Because of this correspondence with contemplative wisdom, one inspires the veneration of devas and nāgas, such as when Śūnyatāprasava sat in serene meditation and Śakra scattered flowers over him.
Regarding "not taking this as joy": when one is in accord with the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), both mind and objects are forgotten;

the forgetting of the mind is itself forgotten, and even the forgetting of that forgetting is forgotten. One does not yet know there is any dharma to be grasped, let alone non-dharmas such as reverence—how could they possibly move the mind?
This is what is meant by the saying: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas. These are the final four lines.

This clarifies the wisdom of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-prajñā*). "Dwelling in the forest" means that externally one is severed from the burdens of sensory objects; it refers to dwelling peacefully in the wilderness.

"Radiating light" means that the defilements of the mind have been washed away and the light of wisdom has manifested—this is what is meant by "the ultimate purity through the penetration of light. Furthermore, regarding "dwelling in the forest and radiating light":
by means of my own stillness, I contrast it with the suffering of the hells, thereby stirring great compassion and radiating light of the same essence (*sabhāva*).
It is light. The suffering of hell is fundamentally empty; yet because sentient beings lack the means to save themselves, they proceed from ultimate non-existence to ultimate existence.
Now, having received the salvation of the compassionate light, it is like snow doused by hot water or darkness dispelled by a torch; thus it is said that the suffering of hell is rescued.
The Buddha-way is fundamentally perfect; yet because sentient beings lack the means to sustain themselves, they proceed from ultimate existence to...
Ultimately, there was nothing [to attain]. Now, having been touched by the illumination of wisdom, it is like a seed meeting with moisture, or like wood encountering spring;

therefore, it is said that they are "caused to enter the Buddha-way. This is analogous to the passage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* where those in hell, upon receiving the light, suddenly transcend the stages of the ten bhūmis;

this is precisely of that category. The gradual exposition has now concluded. II. The Non-sequential and Urgent Exposition (The preceding section presented the initial inquiry and prepared the ground with meticulous detail; therefore...)

The six perfections are each presented in their proper sequence and explained with gradual detail. Now, because the phenomena of the eighteen thousand lands are manifold, we see here [the practice of] giving and there [the practice of] precept-keeping; here the cultivation of wisdom and there the practice of seated meditation, and so forth.

Since every eye beholds Bodhisattvas practicing the Way, there is no leisure for sequential order; thus, it is expounded with urgency, divided into six parts: first, diligence; second, ethical discipline; third, patience;
fourth, meditative concentration; fifth, generosity; sixth, wisdom. First [Diligence]:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, but practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) in the groves, diligently seeking the path of the Buddha.

"Never" (*cháng*, meaning "formerly" or "at any time") refers to the state of being awake. Sleep is one of the four indeterminate mental states; its essential nature is dullness and brevity (*mèilü*). [The term] "dull" (*mèi*) serves to distinguish it from states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[Briefly selecting the state of waking: Its function is to obstruct contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The *Śāriputra-dharmanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Do not, on account of sleep, allow this one life to pass in vain.
Now, the Bodhisattva fears that this life might be spent in vain; therefore, he never sleeps.

This is what the ancient masters meant by "three periods of the day and three periods of the night," resolving his will without wavering. Regarding the practitioner: although active defilements (*vṛtti*) have been suppressed, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)...
It still burns fiercely; one must again apply circular methods to dispel it, as is the case with the Pratyutpanna Samādhi today.
As for the requirement to stay in the forest, it is because there one is far removed from dust and severed from entanglements, making it easy to advance on the Path.
Such diligent effort has no other purpose than the sole aspiration to attain Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that one "diligently seeks the Buddha-way. 2. Observing the Precepts.
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts and whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is without defect, pure as a precious jewel, as they seek the path of the Buddha.

Regarding "possessing the precepts" (*śīlavat*), there are two meanings: first, the meaning of receiving and upholding; this refers to the three masters and seven witnesses receiving and upholding the dharma of the precepts.
Second, the meaning of being complete; this refers to the fulfillment of the prohibitive precepts, such that no section or category (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is deficient. Majestic deportment...
As for "ceremony" (*yi*): the Vinaya clarifies three thousand [rules]. By relying upon them, one possesses a majestic presence that inspires awe and a dignified deportment worthy of reverence.
As for "being without deficiency": one maintains rigorous and careful protection so that not even a flying insect is harmed, such as the case of the grass-tethered goose or the pearl.
A precious gem is transparent and clear both inside and out, pure and free from blemish; the purity of the Bodhisattva precepts is like this. An ancient master said: "The profound..."
A mountain stream is insufficient to match its clarity; flying snow cannot compare with its whiteness. Thus it is said to be "pure as a precious jewel.
The final phrase concludes the intent of upholding the precepts, which is evident. △ Third, patience.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha dwelling in the power of patience (up to) being able to endure all things in order to seek the path of the Buddha.
"Dwelling" means abiding securely; it refers to remaining amidst insults as if they did not exist, because the inner mind is able to remain at peace.
Regarding "power," according to the *Āgamas*, there are six kinds: namely, the crying of a child is its power; the anger of a woman is her power; and the arrogance of a king is his power.
Power. For Arhats, progress is power; for Buddhas, compassion is power; for Bhikṣus, patience is power. To explain the meaning: that which grows and excels others is called power.
Now, the Bodhisattva abides in the Samādhi of Flexibility and Compliance, taming and subduing sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce.
There is no one so stubborn they are not tamed, and no one so fierce they are not subdued; therefore, it is called power. [This counters] overweening pride.
These people belong to the class of those who have not attained what they claim to have attained, and have not realized what they claim to have realized.
Because their minds are permeated by such overweening pride (*abhimāna*), when they see someone superior to themselves, they harbor hatred and jealousy; thus, they revile and beat them.

That one is able to endure all of this is because the Bodhisattva has deeply realized the equality of true reality (*dharmatā*), wherein enemies and kin are treated as one, rather than through forced suppression.

"Na" means "to compare. Regarding those who seek the Buddha-way, this refers to cases such as Maitreya (Not-Light), who was universally prophesied despite enduring slander, until he finally perfected his practice and attained Buddhahood.
△ Fourth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, for billions of years, remain free from all frivolous laughter and merriment in their quest for the Buddha-way.

These first four lines concern the practice of the initial resolve. As for "all frivolous laughter," this refers not only to speaking of what is unwholesome with the mouth, but also to manifesting licentious gestures with the body and indulging unrestrained emotions with the mind;
all such things can obstruct and disturb one's primary spiritual task. Therefore, one must remain detached from them.
As for their "foolish retinue," these are disciples who do not recognize cause and effect and do not believe in sin or merit.
Not only do they obstruct and disrupt one's primary practice, but they also serve as a source of frivolous laughter; therefore, one should distance oneself from them altogether.

The wise person is broadly proficient in both phenomena and principle, possesses a transcendent perspective, and is endowed with the discerning eye that distinguishes between dragons and snakes, wielding the power to mold and refine the sages.

The hands of the wise; therefore, one must draw near to them, for they can serve as the provisions for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The latter four lines concern the methods for profound cultivation.
"Single-mindedly removing distraction" means that although one has abandoned frivolous laughter and the like, there may still be subtle, discursive thoughts;
thus, one must concentrate the mind and eliminate them. "Gathering mindfulness in mountain forests" means that although one has abandoned...

Belonging to the realm of delusion, one still possesses residual worldly thoughts; therefore, it is necessary to restrain and sustain the mind among mountains and beneath forests for billions of millions of years.
This means that although one may associate with the wise, the Buddha-way values self-acceptance;

thus, one must seek it with sincerity for billions of millions of years. [Question: "In human life within this world, a lifespan rarely exceeds a hundred years; such instances are seldom seen. Now you speak of seeking the Buddha for billions of millions of years."

Question: Is this perhaps an impossible occurrence, appearing falsely within the light? Or is it a reality that I have simply not yet reached? Answer: There are two meanings to this. First, through the sustaining power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), many eons may pass as if they were a single moment;

this is as described in the later passage regarding the fifty minor eons being like half a day. This is what the ancient masters meant when they said, "A single thought-moment contains ten thousand years," and "Ten thousand years are but a single thought-moment. Second, the lifespan of beings in other realms is not necessarily fixed at one hundred years.

In this manner, the lifespan of humans in Uttarakuru to the north is one thousand years; how much more so for the eighteen thousand lands—how could it be restricted to a mere hundred years? It is true that you have not yet reached those realms. If you claim that these are but false appearances within the light, [you are mistaken].

If that were so, the eighteen thousand lands and the transformative manifestations of all Buddhas would all become false and illusory; how then could they serve as the introduction to this present sutra? The section on meditative concentration concludes. △ Five: Generosity.
Or they see Bodhisattvas [offering] delicacies and food (up to) with joy and without weariness, seeking the Unsurpassed Way.

First, the various offerings of the assembly are listed individually: "delicacies" (*yáo*) refers to superior items; "dishes" (*shàn*) refers to exquisite meals; "drinks" (*yǐn*) refers to tea and juices; "food" (*shí*) refers to daily sustenance;

"broths" (*tāng*) refers exclusively to decoctions; and "medicines" (*yào*) includes both pills and powders. These are bestowed according to the specific ailment, hence there are as many as a hundred varieties. [They] bestow these upon the Buddha.

Regarding "and to the Saṃgha": this is for the purpose of sustaining the physical body and healing the sick frame. Most precious garments are called *ming* (named), while the robes of supreme honor are called *shang* (superior).
These include such items as the necklaces of Akṣayamati. Thus it is said that their value is worth ten million, or that they are "priceless garments.

These should belong to the celestial robes (*devavastra*), which are so called because they do not exist in the human world and are therefore beyond price. [These are] to be given to the Buddha and...
"Monks" refers to those adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, as they act in accordance with the proper seasons. "Of thousands of millions of kinds" indicates that the number is not small.
"Sandalwood jewel-houses" distinguishes them from ordinary materials, such as the Jetavana Monastery built by Anāthapiṇḍada.
"Requisites for lying and sitting" refers to bedding and seating; according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, when making new bedding, one should use two parts of pure black wool. Three...
The four types of white [robes] and the four parts were established by the Dragon King; the present term "various wonders" (*zhòngmiào*) seems not to be restricted to these alone.

This likely refers to silk, cotton, carpets, mattresses, and various jeweled couches and beds, which are bestowed upon the Buddha and the Sangha to fully provide for the summer retreat and to supply for sitting and reclining.
As for "pure groves and gardens," these are places where the dust of the mundane world does not reach, such as the Jeta Grove and others.
Regarding "the profusion of flowers and fruit": there is the excellence of rows of trees and jeweled nets. Regarding "flowing springs and bathing pools":

there is the seclusion of the seven treasures and the eight virtues. As for "bestowing upon the Buddha and the Saṃgha," it is because they provide the necessities for recreation and travel, as well as for washing and cleansing.
Thus, the final four lines summarize the intent of the giving. "Giving such things as these" refers collectively to the four matters mentioned above: the gardens and groves. *Pāṇ*... [text ends].
It is exceptionally refined and marvelous; hence it is said, "of various subtle and wondrous kinds. It is entirely without stinginess; hence it is said, "with joy and without weariness.
It seeks no other fruit; hence it is said, "seeking the unsurpassed path. The section on giving is concluded. △ Sixth, Wisdom.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescent extinction (yìmiè fǎ), [extending] up to seeking the unsurpassed path by means of this wondrous wisdom.

First is the *prajñā* of letters (*wénzì bānruò*). "Preacher" refers to one who expounds the meaning according to the capacities of beings. "Quiescent extinction" is the principle of ultimate truth (*zhēndì lǐ*).
Ultimate truth is without marks; therefore, it is designated by the name "quiescent extinction. As for why "principle" (*lǐ*) is not used but rather "Dharma" (*fǎ*), since—

To fall into verbal designations belongs to the realm of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics). "Instruction" (*jiao zhao*) refers to training and admonition. Because it accords with the various differences of capacities, it is called "various.
"Sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*) refers to those who are transformed; because they receive transformation according to the teaching, they are called "innumerable.

This Bodhisattva, by means of the *prajñā* of words and letters, initiates practices for the benefit of others and expounds the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). In the passage beginning with "Or he sees," he observes.

"Shining Prajñā. "Contemplation" (guan) refers to the meaning of silent realization beyond words. "All phenomena" (zhufa) refers to the characteristics of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Because conventional truth involves differentiation, they are designated by the term "all phenomena.
As for why "nature" (xing) is used instead of "characteristics" (xiang): once one has entered the realm of contemplation, it belongs to the category of the essential nature (svabhāva-bhāga).
Since it belongs to the category of the essential nature, there is only the single true substance; therefore, it is said that there are no two.
If even the two marks do not exist, how could all phenomena possibly exist? This is the true essence, quiescent and immovable, formless and markless, boundless and unmanifest;

therefore it is said to be "like empty space. By means of the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), this Bodhisattva initiates practices for his own benefit and harmonizes with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The final four lines refer to the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā-prajñā*), wherein the mind has no attachments.

This means that both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously dispensed with; this is the meaning of the "twofold forgetting" through contemplation. "Sublime wisdom" (*prajñā*) is none other than the Great Wisdom of Equality.

The "Unsurpassed Way" is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle. To speak of the two aforementioned [realms] as having words or having contemplation is entirely contrary to the Great Wisdom of Equality;

such views belong to the coarse and superficial and cannot be called subtle and wondrous. To maintain a distinction between the real and the conventional ultimately deviates from the true mark of the One Vehicle.

All things exist as pairs of opposites; how could they be called "unsurpassed"? Now, since it is said that both [subject and object] are forgotten upon contemplation, and both the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously discarded, it is stated:

"By means of this wondrous wisdom, one seeks the unsurpassed path. This bodhisattva, through the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), initiates a practice free from opposition to shatter all attachments.
Up to this point, two sets of six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) have been presented; this is because...
Maitreya expands upon the preceding text regarding the meaning of various types of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) and various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

[Question: Now, the three cycles of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) in this sutra do not yet clearly manifest the capacity for the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). On what basis, then, can one judge that this belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? [Answer: There are two bases upon which this may be judged. First, following the Parable of the Burning House, the Buddha entrusts the matter to Śāriputra, briefly clarifying ten types of capacities; these do not go beyond the six perfections.

Therefore, within the section concerning the appropriate capacities to be reached by the teaching, he specifically singles out [the six perfections] so that it may be known that bodhisattvas of the six perfections are precisely the capacities intended by this sutra. Second, it is based on the assembly that received the predictions during the three cycles, such as Śāriputra.

The wisdom of Śāriputra, the diligence of Mahākāśyapa, the undisturbed mind of Revata, and the lack of contention with others by Subhūti—all these were the inner, secret virtues of bodhisattvas, secretly practicing the conduct of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).

How much more so, then, in the case of Miaoyan’s renunciation, which was exactly like various kings visiting the Buddha, or the propagation of the sutras by Wubing, which truly accorded with the bhikṣu’s abiding in patience? By drawing such analogies, they serve as clear evidence. How can it be said that they did not manifest the capacity for the six perfections?

The transformation and response of the Buddhas are complete. △ Third, the cessation of transformation when the capacity of sentient beings is exhausted (according to the preceding text, there should be two meanings:

first, the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas; second, the erection of stupas after their passing. Here, the first meaning is missing, yet the latter meaning can be expanded). This is divided into two parts: first, making offerings to the śarīra; second, erecting stupas to adorn the land. First:
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics.

These bodhisattvas are those among the assembly who were transformed by him during his lifetime; after his passing, once the cremation has been completed, they enshrine the remains in precious vases and adorn them with incense, flowers, and the like—all of which are termed "offerings. Out of gratitude for having been transformed, they contemplate the Sage.
This is indeed how it ought to be. △ Second, the erection of stupas to adorn the land:
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha constructing various stupas and temples (up to) like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.

First, a brief clarification: In the past, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, having received the final charge of the Buddha Vimalaprabhāsa, collected his relics and fashioned eighty-four thousand precious vases, upon which he erected eighty-four thousand precious stupas.

According to this account, those who construct various pagodas and temples not only express gratitude, but also receive the Buddha’s radiance; even when measured by the sands of the Ganges, they remain beyond reckoning.
Regarding the term "numerous": this is said because the stupas are so many that they are as densely arrayed as stars in the sky. The śarīras shine like the moon and glow like lamps;
those who gaze upon them feel reverence, and those who see them experience joy. Thus, they serve to adorn the realm. Beneath these jeweled stupas...

This is explained in detail. The stupa is composed of jewels and is not made of ordinary materials. It is described as "lofty and wondrous" because the higher one looks up, the more lofty it appears, such that it cannot be reached;
it extends twenty thousand *li* from top to bottom, hence it is said to be five thousand *yojanas*. From north to south is called its length.

The east-west measurement is called "width. Being identical in all four directions is called "perfect symmetry. Its diameter is calculated at eighty thousand *li*, hence it is said to be two thousand *yojana*.

Regarding each stupa and temple having one thousand banners and streamers: this refers to the one thousand banners and streamers suspended from the flagstaffs (*khaṭvāṅga*) in the four directions, as described in the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter concerning the adornment of the spire, where various banners and canopies hang down.
It is so. "Exposed canopies" (*lù màn*) refer to multi-tiered rain-stopping parasols. As for "interlaced with pearls," it is because they are formed by the interweaving of pearl nets.
At the corners of these exposed canopies, bells made of precious jewels are hung; when stirred by a gentle breeze, their sounds harmonize with one another.
Therefore, it is said that the jeweled bells chime harmoniously. The Buddha leaves behind his *śarīra* (relics) to perform the work of a Buddha;
devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and others rely upon these *śarīra* to cultivate fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Thus, they offer worship with incense, flowers, music, and the like.
That such offerings are described as "constant" reveals the extraordinary excellence of the Buddha’s virtues: even after his parinirvāṇa, they continue to inspire offerings that never cease.
[This is] so. Below the section on Mañjuśrī, fearing that [the audience] might doubt the intention behind adorning the land, he again mentions the name to inform them:

"The sons of the Buddha erecting stupas is fundamentally not for the purpose of adorning the realm; therefore it is said they do so 'to make offerings to the śarīra and to adorn the stūpas and temples.
Once the stūpas and temples are completed, the territory consequently gives rise to radiance; therefore it is said the realm becomes naturally extraordinary, wondrous, and beautiful."
The final two lines serve as a metaphor to clarify the meaning of "wondrously excellent. Regarding the "King of Celestial Trees," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is a tree named Pārijāta. Its roots extend fifty yojanas deep, its trunk rises fifty yojanas high, its branches spread fifty yojanas wide, and its fragrance extends fifty yojanas. Because Śakra holds it in special affection, it is called the "King."
As for those flowers that have blossomed, they are endowed with both color and fragrance, admired by both devas and humans. This is a metaphor for when a stūpa is erected within a realm:
the field of merit is preeminent, benefiting both the hidden and the manifest. What is meant by "adorned" and "exquisite" refers precisely to this.
Having finished describing the emission of light, [the text proceeds to] three: the conclusion of the vision and the request for resolution.
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light; I and the assembly... [up to] the Buddha’s son Mañjuśrī, pray resolve the doubts of the multitude.

First, the phrase "initially bound" expresses the marvel of what was seen. "The Buddha emits" introduces the sentence. "Able to illuminate" refers to the light. "I and [the others]" refers to the objects illuminated.

The various phrases manifest the characteristics of the provisional; this is the vision of the provisional. To proceed from the Real to establish the Provisional, thereby rescuing sentient beings from the burning house—this is the rare and marvelous power of the Buddhas.
To bring the Provisional back to the Real, subsuming the three vehicles into the Buddha-wisdom—this is the rare and marvelous wisdom of the Buddhas.
Thus, Maitreya, by virtue of seeing the provisional and real aspects of the Buddhas, attained [this realization].

"It is fitting," he said, and marveled at it. This was his marveling. The subsequent six lines repeat the doubt to seek its resolution. "Let go" (fang) is one line, repeating the light that is the object of doubt.
"Illuminating" (zhao) is one line, repeating the realm that is the object of doubt. "We" and the following two lines repeat the characteristics that are the objects of doubt.
This restates the doubt. The final two phrases seek a definitive resolution; their meaning is clear. This concludes the section on "Seeking a Resolution Regarding Views. △ Four:

Anticipating Objections and Presenting Questions (The Ancient Masters established four layers of latent objections here, which Tiantai adopted and utilized. Although the present [text] follows that interpretation in brief, it does not entirely agree with it; therefore, this is categorized under "Anticipating Objections and Presenting Questions"). Divided into four parts: 1. Anticipating the first objection and presenting the first question. 2.

Anticipating the second objection and presenting the second question. 3. [Anticipating the third objection and presenting the third question. 4. [Anticipating the fourth objection and presenting the fourth question.]

He raises three defenses and poses three questions; he raises four defenses and poses four questions. Regarding the first [defense]: fearing that Mañjuśrī might take up the preceding objection and say, "You claim you wish to resolve the doubts of the assembly.
If the assembly had doubts, they would surely ask; since the assembly does not ask, they have no doubts. Since they have no doubts, what is there for me to resolve? he therefore offers this defense.
The fourfold assembly looked up with joyful reverence toward the Benevolent One and me, the World-Honored One, wondering: "For what reason has this radiance been emitted?
Maitreya thought to himself: "If the Benevolent One thinks that because the assembly does not ask, they have no doubts, he is mistaken."

Why is this? I observe that the fourfold assembly looks up to you with longing and gazes upon both you and me. Those who rejoice do so because I have asked the question; those who look up do so because you will provide the answer.
Those who gaze upon you do so because they see that you have not yet answered; those who look toward me do so because they are eager for me to ask further.
This is the appearance of being troubled by doubt and unease—a sign that anticipates an objection. The final two lines state the inquiry itself, as it arises from a lack of understanding.

He preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, [the interlocutor] asks why he emitted this light. Later it says: "I saw that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara’s original light was an auspicious omen such as this;
by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is the direct answer to this question. II.

Anticipating the next objection and presenting the subsequent question (fearing that one might further object: "The World-Honored One's emission of light is the domain of a Buddha; it is appropriate for us to ask the Buddha about it. Since the Buddha himself has seen and answered it, we should do the same"—therefore, he anticipates this and says):
The Son of the Buddha replied at the appropriate time, resolving doubts and bringing joy; what benefit was there in expounding this radiance?
Maitreya’s intention was this: "If you, O Virtuous One, consider this to be the domain of the Buddha, it would indeed be right to inquire of the Buddha together.
However, the assembly currently harbors doubts within their hearts, and they are anxious and uneasy. We await the Buddha’s emergence from meditative absorption, yet we do not know [how to proceed]."
"When? We pray that the Son of the Buddha will answer in due time, swiftly resolving the doubts of the assembly and causing them all joy.
This is a defense against potential objections. The final two lines present the inquiry; for while Maitreya already knew that there would be abundant benefit, he did not know exactly how it would be.
Thus he asked, "What benefit does this radiance provide? Later it says, "The appearance now is as follows..."
This auspicious omen is the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits light to assist in the elucidation of the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This correctly answers the aforementioned question. △ Third, preventing three difficulties and clarifying three questions: (Fearing that one might further object: "If you wish to resolve the doubts of the assembly, it is appropriate to deliberate together.
It is unreasonable for you alone to require me to provide the answer. Therefore, he provides this defense:)
The sublime Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment—does he intend to preach this now, or will he bestow a prophecy?
Maitreya thought to himself: "If you, O Benevolent One, believe that the doubts of the assembly should be resolved, and that we ought to deliberate together upon it, I know this to be so.

Yet, as for my own limited vision in gazing at the Buddha’s celestial realm, and my shallow measurement of the ocean of wisdom with a conch-shell, the merit of his transformative teachings has already been fully revealed."

The expedient means for perfecting [the teaching] have already been fully exhausted. There remains only the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment, which he has never disclosed for forty years; this is to prevent difficulties. The final two lines pose a question:

Maitreya already understands that the provisional returns to the ultimate and that he himself will receive the prediction of Buddhahood, yet he does not know that these matters constitute a single, unified principle; therefore, he says:
It is for the purpose of explaining this and bestowing a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that it is later said:

"All you people, know now! With palms joined and single-minded, wait; the Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way. This is the direct answer to the question. 4. Guarding against four difficulties and presenting four questions:

(Fearing that others might again object, saying: "If it is as you have explained, this already resolves the doubts and is sufficient to gladden the assembly; why trouble yourself to provide an answer? Therefore, he guards against this by saying:)
"Manifesting all Buddha-lands as adorned and purified by various jewels" (up to) "observing what the Honorable One is teaching.
Regarding the adornment of the Buddha-land with jewels: wherever light shines, it transforms defilement into purity; thus, the meaning omitted previously is presented here.
Furthermore, "beholding the Buddhas" encompasses the sense of preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; by mentioning the person, one includes the Dharma. By mentioning...

"Because the Lord acts as the leader who gathers his companions, this is no small matter," he said, meaning that he dared not decide it on his own authority out of respect for the gravity of the affair.
Maitreya’s intention was: "If you, O worthy one, think that what I have spoken constitutes the resolution of this doubt, you are mistaken. Why is this?
Although I have exerted my mind in deep reflection to fathom the interval between the teaching of the Dharma and the bestowal of the prophecy, yet..."
This is to manifest the characteristics of the primary and secondary [recompenses] and so forth; this is no small matter. How could it be resolved by the inferential knowledge of one such as I?
This is a defense against objections. The final four lines present a question. This is because the great assembly at the Dharma-gathering...
There was a state of urgent distress born of weary hearts and troubled deliberations, yet Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva appeared as if neither seeing nor hearing;
therefore, he spoke on behalf of the assembly to convey their sentiments, saying: "Mañjuśrī, you should understand that the fourfold assembly and the nāgas and devas present here..."
Each of you should look upon this worthy one with respect; do not be overly humble and thereby fail to meet the expectations of the assembly.

Now I ask the worthy one: what is it that you ultimately intend to teach? Later he says: "For those seeking the three vehicles who may have doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them, so that they are exhausted without remainder.
This is the direct answer to the question. Above, four questions were successively posed in succession. Layer upon layer...
Next, it proceeds in orderly fashion. It seems both empty and substantial, such that its measure cannot be determined. At first, it asks, "For what reason, World-Honored One, do you emit this light?
appearing entirely as if unaware. Next, it asks, "What benefit does the emission of this light bring? slightly revealing its edge. Then it says, "Is it to preach the wondrous Dharma?
Or is it to bestow a prediction of enlightenment? clearly setting it forth as plainly as placing a dish upon a tray. Finally, it says:
He observed the Benevolent One and asked, "What are you teaching? Yet, this again brought trouble upon Mañjuśrī.

*Kalpa* is translated here as "time-period. Since it is called "innumerable," it is already understood to be long; yet, that it is further described as "inconceivable" and so forth serves to manifest this Dharma to its utmost extent.
Its name is designated as being beyond *kalpas*, and its essence dwells prior to all phenomena—what is meant by "there being a thing before heaven and earth.
"Sun, Moon, and Lamp-Light" is an epithet of the Buddha. An ancient master said: "The sun [shines] with light..."
The sun illuminates by day; the moon illuminates by night with its cool radiance; and the lamp continues the light where the sun and moon do not reach.
The Tathāgata’s threefold wisdom is perfectly luminous, dispelling the darkness of worldly ignorance just as these do. Therefore, this serves as his title. "Tathāgata," "Arhat," and so forth...

These are the general titles of a Buddha. As for "Tathāgata" (Thus Come One): the Way of each Buddha is the same; when a later Buddha appears in the world, he is like a former Buddha returning, and his name is modeled after the title of previous virtuous ones.
As for "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings): because he is fully endowed with wisdom and the severance of defilements, he is worthy of receiving offerings;

this is the title meaning he is fit to be a field of merit. As for "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Complete Knower): he has forever departed from the false knowledge of non-Buddhists and the limited knowledge of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles.

The name [Buddha] distinguishes him from the heterodox and the partial; it is a title that excludes others. "One endowed with knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): "knowledge-endowed" means the perfection of wisdom; "conduct-endowed" means the fulfillment of merit.

This is the title signifying the simultaneous exaltation of both merit and wisdom. "Well-gone" (*sugata*): "gone" (*gata*) means to have departed. He has departed from birth and death without being separated from them; he has gone to nirvāṇa without having traveled there.
This is the title signifying the wondrous departure to enlightenment (*bodhi*). "Knower of the world" (*lokavid*): he understands the nature of the world.

He distinguishes between the true and the false; his name signifies penetration of falsehood and mastery of truth. He is called the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara) because he has realized the unsurpassed path and transcends the world.
He is called the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi) because he possesses the strength of a great man and tames all classes of beings.

These names combined constitute the ultimate title for one perfected in compassion and wisdom. He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām), preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

He is the "Good Guide for Gods and Humans," the title meaning he serves as a model for the three realms. He is called "Buddha" (the Awakened One), which signifies that he has awakened himself, awakened others, and perfected his practice of awakening;

this is the title meaning the three types of awakening are fully complete. He is called "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), signifying that he possesses the nine aforementioned virtues and is thus honored by all within the mundane and supramundane worlds;
this is the title meaning he is equally revered by the nine realms. These ten titles are possessed in common by all Buddhas from time immemorial.
