Being free from the five desires and, furthermore, being in accord with the Dharma of nature while also being free from craving, it is therefore called "Brahmacarya" (the Holy Life); this is because "Brahma" is translated as "free from desire.

From the phrase "for the sake of seeking" onwards, the text specifically clarifies the goodness of the middle [vehicle]. Because the faculties of the Śrāvakas are dull, they are incapable of receiving the Great Dharma;
therefore, he responds to them by teaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the Truth of Suffering. To cross over... [and so forth].

The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): because one must sever origination in order to transcend suffering. "To transcend" (*du*) means to be liberated from it. Nirvana is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The meaning of "ultimate" (*jìngjiù*) also encompasses the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), because one must cultivate the path in order to realize cessation. "Ultimate" here refers to realization and entry [into that state].
*Pratyeka* is fully called *pratyekabuddha*; this is translated as "Solitary Realizer" (*yuánjué*). Solitary Realizers possess sharp faculties and are able to know all phenomena.
Because of these causes and conditions, he responds by teaching through the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

The twelve links of dependent origination are as follows: ignorance conditions volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*); these two links belong to the past cause. Volitional formations condition consciousness (*saṃskāra-pratyayaṃ vijñānam*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*vijñāna-pratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*);

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*nāmarūpa-pratyayāṇi ṣaḍāyatanāni*); the six sense bases condition contact (*ṣaḍāyatana-pratyayaḥ sparśaḥ*); contact conditions feeling (*sparśa-pratyayā vedanā*); these five links belong to the present fruit. Feeling conditions craving (*vedanā-pratyayā tṛṣṇā*).
Craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming—these belong to the three factors of the present cause. Becoming conditions birth;
birth conditions old age, death, and so forth—these belong to the two factors of the future result. This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Phantom City.

The Bodhisattva possesses the great root of virtue, endowed with the aspiration to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below. Desiring to reach the other shore, he responds to this through the teaching of the six *pāramitās*.
Pāramitā. This is translated as "reaching the other shore. It means that by practicing according to these six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), one is able to reach the other shore of Nirvāṇa.

To explain the excellence of the conclusion separately: because it brings the three vehicles back to the One Vehicle and universally records that all shall attain Buddhahood, it says "enabling them to attain Anuttara...
[and so forth]. It enables one to know the path and Dharma of all Buddhas, and to know all sentient beings...
The causal seeds of birth are called "all-seed wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*). The former phrase causes one to attain the fruit; this phrase causes one to perfect wisdom.
Having completed the detailed citation of the first Buddha, [the text] proceeds to: △ Second, a brief citation of the succession of twenty thousand [Buddhas].
Next, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp), [up to] the Dharma he taught, which was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
First, the names are listed in sequence; furthermore, as below, his clan name is also given: Phalguna, which means "sharp faculties."
It is also called "Swift" (*Kṣipra*). Because his six sense faculties are keen and sharp, he takes "Swift in Perceiving Objects" as his clan name.
When Maitreya descends, he concludes by declaring their identity: that twenty thousand Buddhas share the same name and the same clan name is an event so rare that it is difficult to believe.
Therefore, one calls out the name and concludes the address. "Names" and "titles" are both designations.

When the general and specific names and titles are identical, it is because their actual virtues are the same, and thus their designations are likewise the same. That which can be expounded as the Dharma is precisely the True Dharma (Saddharma).

If one were to involve even a slight degree of deviation or falsehood, it would not be something that could be spoken by a Buddha; therefore, the excellence of the beginning, middle, and end is identical across all modes of transformation.
Based on this, the twenty thousand Lamp-Light Buddhas and the eighteen thousand Buddhas within the light performed their teachings during the three periods in exactly the same manner.
How could it be that for the present Buddha alone it is otherwise? Thus, Mañjuśrī cites this as an analogy, wishing to...
Maitreya contemplated this deeply and attained realization of it himself. This concludes the general citation of the *Dīpaṃkara* [Sūtra]. II. Specifically Clarifying Past Events.

(The past events witnessed are entirely contained within this section; therefore, they are clarified separately. Divided into five parts: 1. The time when the capacity of the disciples matured; 2. Manifesting signs to accommodate the capacities of the disciples;

3. Emitting light that shines to the east; 4. The assembly of the congregation giving rise to doubts; 5. Preaching the Dharma and bestowing predictions. Of the first two [parts], the first is a brief enumeration.

Regarding the "timely opportunity": two meanings reveal its full maturity. First, it refers to the opportune moment at that time; it is not only the prince who is meant, but the prince is cited as an example, which is why it is said to be "abbreviated."
Regarding the passage from "The last of those Buddhas, before he had left the household life" to "the seventh was named Hsiang-i (Intent on Renown) and the eighth was named Fa-i (Dharma-intent)":

the "last of those Buddhas" refers to Mañjuśrī himself pointing to his own original teacher. "Before he had left the household life" means when he was still a layman serving as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
As for the "eight princes," they must have long attained realization over many kalpas; they manifested birth into a Buddha-family [to serve as his sons].
Now, those such as the Buddha and Pulu-yun possess both the definitive and the expedient; they are able to remain constant and yet undergo transformation—this is called "Intentional Mind.

They govern the world with wholesome Dharma and instruct the people with virtuous administration—this is called "Wholesome Intentional Mind. Their strategic planning and schemes are difficult to fathom—this is called "Immeasurable Intentional Mind.
They treat the good as supreme treasure, ensuring it is never lost—this is called "Treasure Intentional Mind. As for evil intention...

Daily diminishing [of faults], with wholesome intentions increasing daily, is called "Increasing Intention" (*vardhamānāśaya*). Thoroughly mastering both phenomena and principles, being able to eliminate all doubts, is called "Eliminating Doubt Intention" (*vicikitsāpahārin-āśaya*).
Skillfully responding to the sentiments of beings, like an echo responding to a sound, is called "Echo-like Intention" (*pratiśrutkāśaya*). The regulations and governing principles of the Dharma...

All are clearly and fully prepared; this is called "Dharmamati" (Intention of Dharma). Since these eight sons all became wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), I shall briefly explain them by correlating their names with their respective positions.
If they are treated as symbols of the Dharma: the Buddha symbolizes True Suchness (*tathatā*). Before his renunciation...
"Manifesting True Suchness within the bonds of existence" refers to the eight princes, which symbolize the transformation of the eight consciousnesses.

"Having the mind" (yì) symbolizes the *ālaya-vijñāna*, because it receives perfuming, maintains seeds, and contains all phenomena. "Departing later and arriving first" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"Having good intention" (shànyì) symbolizes the *manas* (the seventh consciousness), for it successfully accomplishes the six transformations and serves as the basis for both defilement and purity. "Immeasurable intention" (wúliàngyì) symbolizes the six consciousnesses, which arise moment by moment.

“Extinction” (*nirodha*) signifies the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), because its measure is severed. “Precious Intention” (*ratnamati*) signifies the body-consciousness, because all sentient beings together cherish it as a treasure.

“Increasing Intention” (*vṛddhamati*) signifies the tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*), because attachment to flavors increases evil, while preaching the Dharma increases goodness. “Doubt-Dispelling Intention” (*vicikitsā-prahāṇamati*) signifies the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna*).
One knows this immediately within the synthesis; thus there is no doubt. "Sound-intention" (*śabda-manas*) represents the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), for it is able to hear sounds.

"Dharma-intention" (*dharma-manas*) represents the eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), for it observes the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Based on this, Master Prabhāsa (Wondrous Light) is the original mind of Master Dīpaṃkara (Lamp-Light).
Dīpaṃkara transmits to Prabhāsa, which is the transmission of the fundamental wisdom. The eight sons follow Master Prabhāsa, relying upon the original [mind].

Wisdom is that which accords with the fundamental mind. The wondrous light transforming the eight sons is the transformation of the fundamental consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) in accordance with the fundamental mind.
By extending this analogy, one sees that the entire pedagogical system of the Lamp-Light Buddha throughout his lifetime does not transcend my own single mind.
If one realizes one’s own mind, then the purport of the present Buddha’s radiant auspicious signs can be clearly perceived. This concludes the brief exposition on the timing and circumstances. △

The two meanings clarify the arrival at maturity (that is, the time has arrived and the faculties are matured; although the text does not explicitly state "maturity," it simply mentions "leaving the household life," "arousing the aspiration," "practicing the holy life," and "becoming a Dharma teacher," which are stated as such based on their underlying meaning).
These eight princes possessed majestic virtue and sovereign power; (up to: they had already planted various roots of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas.

First, to clarify their status while still in the secular world: "majestic virtue" means that their rank governed the four continents; they possessed awe-inspiring majesty as they taught and bestowed the ten wholesome actions, and they possessed admirable virtue worthy of emulation.
"Sovereign power" means that they balanced leniency and severity, and their authority did not rest with others. Regarding what they [governed]:

This means that rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments all proceed from the Son of Heaven. Those who each govern four continents are Gold-Wheel Kings; this distinguishes them from those with other wheels.
The following sections clarify the causes and effects of leaving the household life. Hearing that his father left the household life, he realized that royal status is of no benefit;
hearing that his father attained the Way, he realized that leaving the household life is efficacious. Thus, he realized that royal status is of no benefit.

Therefore, he renounced them all. Having verified that there is merit in leaving the household life, he likewise followed that path. What the ancients called "the father and the son" is seen here in its entirety.
One who gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind conceives the aspiration to seek the supreme above and transform those below, establishing the practice of benefiting both self and others;
such are the three minds and four vows, which constitute the Mahāyāna mind.
Because there is never any regression, it is called "constant cultivation. Because the practice that enters into principle is pure and stainless, it is termed "Brahmacarya" (the holy life).
This refers to wearing the iron wheel without retreating, remaining eternally as such through the profusion of activity. As for the Dharma Master:

To take up the propagation of the Dharma as one’s own responsibility and to serve as a teacher for devas and humans—how could anyone reach such a state unless their capacity had ripened at the opportune moment?

That the *Kōki* (Commentary) states, "The meaning is clearly revealed," is indeed for this reason. Below, it clarifies the profound foundation of the past, stating that the rank of a Dharma Master is not easily attained;
yet a Prince [of the Buddha] reaches it in a single lifetime. What is the cause of this? It is entirely due to oneself.
Having planted various roots of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas—what is called "deep roots and flourishing branches"—is indeed possessed by those who have faith.

(Question: According to the teachings, Wheel-Turning Kings appear during the *utkalpa* (increasing eon), while Buddhas appear during the *apakalpa* (decreasing eon). For what reason, then, were all eight sons Wheel-Turning Kings at the time when Dīpaṃkara attained Buddhahood? (Answer: The Dharma has both provisional and ultimate aspects, and phenomena have both variable and constant natures. If one discusses this in terms of variability and constancy:

perhaps Dīpaṃkara’s vow was made during an *utkalpa*, or perhaps the capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings in an *utkalpa* had matured; thus, his appearance in the world was a manifestation of change, not a constant rule. If one discusses this in terms of the provisional and the ultimate: Buddhas appear during the *apakalpa*, or perhaps it belongs to the provisional school.

These are words of dogmatic adherence; they are not the true discourse of the Mahāyāna, which does not restrict itself to such [limitations]. It is as when the Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara) preached the sutra for sixty minor kalpas, yet the great assembly perceived it as lasting no longer than the time it takes to eat a meal.

How could one raise difficult questions based on the increase or decrease of kalpas? If one understands this principle of the provisional and the real, and the transformation of the permanent, then the ancient masters’ difficulties regarding the "eight sons" and the "one son," as well as the attachments to Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, can all be resolved simultaneously.

When the time arrives and the faculties have matured—Part Two: Manifesting the Signs to Accommodate the Faculties, divided into three sections: 1. Preaching the Sutra and Entering Samādhi; 2. Rain of Flowers and Earthquake.
I. The Great Assembly’s Joyful Contemplation. First:
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [entered] the Samādhi of the Abode of Meaning; his body and mind were unmoving. △ II.
The Rain of Flowers and the Trembling of the Earth.
At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers (until: the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways).
△ Third, the Great Assembly’s Joyful Contemplation.
At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs within the assembly (until: with joy, they joined their palms and contemplated the Buddha with a single mind).

The three preceding sections are identical in both text and meaning to the present manifestation of the Buddha’s physical form; there is no need for further prolix commentary. The section on manifesting the form to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings is concluded.
△ Third, the emission of light illuminating the East.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows... (omitting the passage from "down to" as it appears now) "...these various Buddha-lands.
Within the realm illuminated by the light, the text regarding the upper and lower limits is omitted.

As for the final two phrases concerning the manifested signs—"the text says 'as seen now'—Mañjuśrī did not wish to describe them in tedious detail, intending instead that one should understand the past by analogy with the present. These..."
"Buddha-field" refers to the manifestations appearing within that Buddha-field. After the light was emitted and illuminated the east, △ Fourth, the assembly raised their doubts:
"Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly... [up to] ...if you wish to know the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested."
Regarding the instruction "you should know": this is intended to make you realize that the present and the past are identical, so that you do not harbor self-reproach for your lack of understanding.

The twenty billion bodhisattvas were precisely those in the assembly at that time who had raised their doubts. The reason the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings are not mentioned is that if even the bodhisattvas harbored such doubts, it can be inferred that the others did as well.
Thus, in the current passage where the Buddha addresses the raising of doubts, there are no longer many bodhisattvas mentioned. The four... [text ends]
This refers to the collective gathering. Those who desire to hear the Dharma, based on their previous state of joy and palms joined, single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha;
they immediately become thirsty for the teaching and stand waiting expectantly, manifesting the aspect of wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.

"Obtaining what has never been obtained before" means that although their original intention was simply to hear the Dharma, they unexpectedly encountered the Buddha’s light shining everywhere, as if they had seen an object never seen before—feeling both joy and...
Doubt arises; there is that which cannot be resolved within the mind. If one wishes to understand the causal conditions, one must likewise repeatedly investigate and examine their meaning.
Viewed from this perspective, the present and the past are identical; it is only by maintaining an open and empty mind that one may await [the truth].

(Following the raising of these doubts by the assembly, there is another section of questions and answers that has not been recorded here; this omission is intended to leave Maitreya in suspense, much like what the Zen school calls "letting the doubt remain. The assembly had finished raising their doubts.
△ Section Five: Preaching the Dharma and Bestowing Prophecies (2 parts). First, preaching the Dharma after emerging from samādhi; second, bestowing prophecies at the time of entering parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the first: At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light... [up to] ...neither in body nor mind did he give rise to weariness or fatigue.

First, the capacity of the recipient is clarified. Da Cheng says: "The Sage has no name; it is because of their virtue that they are made manifest. Their spiritual powers are unfathomable, thus they are called 'Mysterious' (miao);
they brightly illuminate the masses of darkness, thus they are called 'Radiant' (guang). I, Yong, say: "Mystery" represents the essence of wisdom, while "radiance" represents the function of wisdom.
The essence transcends thought and deliberation, while the function penetrates both the provisional and the real; therefore, he is titled "Mysterious Radiance. Learning follows after the teacher.
It is said: "The younger brothers are called *di*; those who receive wisdom from a teacher are called *zi*. The specific designation of "eight hundred disciples" serves two purposes:

first, to manifest that Miaoguang’s wisdom was profound and that those who followed him were numerous; second, to manifest that this sublime assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* possessed listeners of great capacity—what is meant by the phrase "the resonance of spiritual potential fills the space before one.
Da Cheng says: "In the past, the Buddha’s eight sons took Miaoguang as their teacher. When the Buddha emerged from meditative concentration..."
When Wondrous Light (*Prabhāpāla*) preached the sutra, the present Buddha’s disciple, Rāhula, was a teacher to Śāriputra;

that he emerged from meditative concentration to preach the sutra for Śāriputra is because their roles as teachers were identical. Some may ask: "Wondrous Light was a bodhisattva, whereas Śāriputra was a śrāvaka;
how can they be the same? The *Dacheng* commentary explains: "By the time his true identity was revealed, Śāriputra was also a bodhisattva. Wondrous Light... [bestowed]... upon him.
As for the "trace" (迹): it is not necessarily that he is not a śrāvaka; Mañjuśrī’s skillful exposition merely conceals or reveals [his status] through expedient means.

From the phrase "at this time" onwards, it clarifies the teaching capable of reaching [beings]. "Arising" is spoken in contrast to "cessation"; when one enters [the state], it is called cessation, because all conditions are extinguished.
Emerging from [samādhi] is called "arising," because one brings forth words and images. Now, wishing to preach the Lotus Sūtra, he therefore arises from samādhi.

As for the term "on account of" (hetu), it indicates that this is not done alone; rather, it serves merely as a means to open the beginning of the teaching. That he must rely upon Wonderful Light (Prabhāketu) is as follows:

This reveals that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* cannot be understood without wisdom; it is the same now with Śāriputra. According to what preceded, [the Buddha] stated his intention to preach the Great Dharma and further described it as a "dharma difficult to believe.
Yet, he had not yet explicitly revealed the title of this sūtra, likely out of concern that it would be difficult for others to accept in faith.
Now, by means of the deeds of Dīpaṃkara, he has spontaneously proclaimed it without deliberate intent; though he does not wish for people to believe it, it manifests of its own accord.
If one lacks faith, then Mañjuśrī may be said to be skilled in eloquent discourse. Those of shallow understanding, upon hearing this, become confused and fail to comprehend it;
therefore, it is called "the Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas. Having long remained silent regarding this essential point, he does not strive to speak of it hastily;

hence it is called "that which is protected and remembered by the Buddha. The phrase "sixty [years] below" clarifies the timing of the encounter. According to the teachings, this refers to the time when the human lifespan is ten years.
The son’s age doubles that of the father, increasing until it reaches eighty-four thousand years; thereafter, it decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years.
One such period of increase and decrease constitutes a *kṣudrakalpa* (small kalpa). Now, when it is said that sixty small kalpas have passed, that duration may indeed be called long.
Yet, although such a vast amount of time has elapsed, it is taught that there was no change of seat; therefore, it is said [that he remains].
He rose from his seat. Those in the assembly heard it as if they were not on different seats; thus it is said, "also seated in one place.

Form and the Way merge, and wisdom and principle are darkly unified; thus it is said, "body and mind unmoving. Length and brevity are simultaneous, and thought-moments and kalpas are without obstruction;
thus it is said, "as if for the duration of a meal. Da Cheng says: "In this sutra, fifty small kalpas are said to be as if..."
For half a day, they were all equal in this regard; not a single person felt weary or indolent.
This reveals that each was possessed of pure sincerity, such that there was not even a trace of weariness in either body or mind, manifesting sincerity both inwardly and outwardly.

Yet, this too was brought about by profound causes and superior conditions—the result of the teaching reaching those whose faculties had matured. Having finished preaching the Dharma after emerging from samādhi. △ Second, the Proclamation.
II. The Two Aspects of the Prediction of Parinirvāṇa: 1. Proclaiming Parinirvāṇa before the Assembly; 2. Bestowing the Prediction of the Concealment of Radiance.
Regarding the first: The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [prophesied] that after sixty intermediate kalpas (until) he would enter nirvana without remainder.

The first phrase, "at that very moment," serves as the introduction; it refers to the actual events—the preaching of the Dharma and the proclamation of his passing—which belong to a single assembly, hence the expression "at that very moment.

The proclamation of his passing at the end of the "Bao Ta Pin" (The Jeweled Stupa Chapter) in the present sutra is identical to this. *Brahmā* refers to the Brahma Heaven, the lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

*Māra* refers to the Māra Heaven, the lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). *Śramaṇa* is translated as "diligent and tranquil"; it encompasses the community of those who have left the household life.

"Brahman" (婆羅門) is translated as "Pure Conduct" (淨行). It encompasses the assembly of householders, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and the eight classes of beings—three of which are explicitly named, while the remainder are subsumed by the word "assembly" (眾).
These words are the utterance for entering parinirvāṇa. There are two reasons why this must be proclaimed within the assembly:
first, to generate goodness; second, to extinguish evil. Regarding the generation of goodness: because the Buddha remains for a long time, those of meager virtue [will not...]

They plant roots of goodness. Because they have planted roots of goodness by feeling longing, yearning, and veneration upon hearing the proclamation of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, their evil is extinguished.

As for those who would otherwise become indolent because the Buddha does not pass away, upon hearing the proclamation of his passing, they conceive the thought that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter.
Because pride and weariness naturally cease, the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is as explained in the preceding text. There are two types of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*:

first, the permanent cessation of the *paricchinna-vedanīya-kāya* (the body subject to分段 [segmental rebirth]) through the severing of the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-āvaraṇa*), which is called the *anupadhiśeṣa* of the Hīnayāna;

second, the ultimate exhaustion of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) and the eternal disappearance of the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*), which is called the *anupadhiśeṇa* of the Mahāyāna. That which the Buddha enters now is the Great, not the Small. Thus it is said: "He shall enter."
This means that his worldly tasks were completed and his work of transformation was already finished; even had he remained in the world, it would have been of no further benefit.

"Necessarily at midnight" signifies that his body returns to the Middle Way, expressing the meaning of his nature entering eternal quiescence. [Question: Now, in the text concerning the Buddha’s proclamation of extinction, it says, "The Tathāgata will not long remain;

he shall enter nirvana. Yet he still awaits another time. Now, however, you say "today at midnight. Is the distance between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* not too short? Could it be that the Buddha had not yet preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when he attained parinirvāṇa? [Answer: There is a reason for this.

There are two meanings. First, regarding the breadth or brevity of the Dharma, which is not fixed; second, regarding the duration of time, which is not fixed. As for the breadth or brevity of the Dharma being not fixed: although it is the same single Dharma, it may be explained exhaustively and endlessly, or it may be fully encompassed by a single word.

As for the duration of time being not fixed: although it occurs within the same period, it may be extended over many kalpas, or it may be condensed into a single thought-moment. This is entirely due to the Buddha’s sovereign power and inconceivable spiritual efficacy, manifesting according to the differences in capacities and in accordance with the measure of the mind.

How could this be questioned with ordinary sentiments? Having finished proclaiming his entry into extinction before the assembly: △ Second, the bestowal of the prediction concerning the concealment of his radiance.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa (Virtue-Treasury) who, at midnight, entered parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Regarding the first prediction for a bodhisattva in the position of the successor, the name Guṇakośa, according to the *Mahāsiddhi*, has two meanings:
first, the sense of "containing" (kośa), meaning that he is fully endowed with all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; second, the sense of "producing," meaning that by this...

Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*): it is because [the merit] is bestowed universally upon all sentient beings. First, this refers to personal realization; second, it refers to speech for the sake of transforming others.

To speak with holy words is called "bestowing" (*śāsana*); to recall and take up the realization is called "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*). At that time, there was Guṇagañja, to whom the prediction was bestowed.

There are three reasons for this: first, because the time for his parinirvāṇa was near; second, because the affairs of the lineage of the Way were urgent; third, because [other] persons were unsuitable.
Because [the previous teaching] was lost, he addressed the bhikṣus with two purposes: first, to have them serve as witnesses; second, to let them know their point of reliance.
Regarding the phrase "shall next become a Buddha," this is not a distant prediction like that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

rather, it is a prediction that he shall succeed the Buddha in the immediate future, similar to the prediction given to Maitreya by the present Buddha. One must understand that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is not without distant predictions; however—
Mañjuśrī did not wish to exhaust his words, fearing they might become a mere path of intellectual understanding and thus obstruct the gateway to future awakening.

Because he was endowed with all virtues, he was ultimately moved by the fruit of these causes to manifest marks of physical excellence; hence his specific title, "Pure Body" (Śuddhakāya). *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus Come One";
*Arhat* as "Worthy of Offerings"; and *Samyaksaṃbuddha* as "Perfectly All-Knowing. These ten [titles] are common to all [Buddhas].
[This is] the title. By citing what precedes, that which follows is subsumed. Regarding "The Buddha bestows [the prediction]" below: he bestows the prediction and then withdraws his radiance.

As for why he enters extinction after having bestowed the prediction, *Dacheng* states: "Because this Way has its reliance; because his original intention has been fully expressed; and because the conditions for his transformation are complete.
From this point upward, according to the major sections, there are five segments, which constitute the entirety of the Dīpaṃkara’s pedagogical methods throughout his lifetime.

Now, for forty years prior to this, the Buddha employed manifold methods to refine and purify [the assembly]. That the time has arrived and their capacities have matured is a past event, identical to that of the Lamp-Lighter (Dīpaṃkara).

At the beginning of the sutra, the manifestation of signs to suit the capacities of the assembly and the emission of light shining toward the east, causing the gathered multitude to give rise to doubt, are present events, identical to those of the Lamp-Lighter.
As for the preaching of the Dharma and the bestowing of prophecies, these still belong to subsequent matters; although...
Their commonality has not yet been seen, yet it can be known in advance. What was previously stated regarding the desire to preach the Great Dharma and so forth is fundamentally based on this.

One should regard the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa as a cause for sorrow, but one should not fear being without a refuge. This is the "Virtue of Being Inferior. Regarding the "Virtue of the Treasury of Prophecy" (the verse on its meaning):
the untainted true reality (*dharmatā*) is spoken of in terms of what all Buddhas have realized. It is said that although sentient beings possess this true reality, [they do not realize it].

Due to defilement by afflictions, one is like a broken or leaking vessel that can no longer be used; only when the Buddha has exhausted all delusions and perfected the principle is he called "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
Now, although the Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has not yet attained Buddhahood, regarding the reality-mark of being without outflows...

Having already been able to realize this through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is called "thorough penetration" (*prativedha*). The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the passage "The Buddha hereafter," it records that he has withdrawn his radiance (*antardhāna*).
Sentient beings' capacities are like firewood; the Tathāgata’s teaching is like fire. When their capacities are exhausted, the teaching ceases, just as fire is extinguished when the wood is spent.
As for the distribution of the *śarīra* and the erection of immeasurable stupas, these symbolize the equality of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).

Regarding the intent of the universal spread of transformative influence: "The bhikṣus below" refers to the assembly at that time who turned their minds [to the Great Vehicle] (the supplementary verse).

Those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were those who, upon seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, gave rise to a heart of longing and reverence—the assembly that had turned from the Small Vehicle toward the Great.

Although this assembly had previously been diligent, they could not yet avoid relying on the Tathāgata, occasionally giving rise to arrogance or weariness; now, seeing the Buddha’s extinction and being without reliance, [they are transformed].
Therefore, one should seek with redoubled diligence, desiring to create the conditions for attaining liberation in the future. As it says later:
"After the extinction of the Buddhas, if there are people with gentle and supple hearts—such sentient beings as these have all already attained the Buddha-way.

This refers precisely to this category. The verse explaining past events is concluded. △ Third, the verse concluding by correlating the ancient and the present, divided into two parts. First, the verse on the Teacher:

The causes of the younger brother [Mañjuśrī] are presented first. The two verses that follow synthesize and resolve doubts. Of these, the first verse concerns the original cause of Mañjuśrī, and the second verse concerns the original cause of Maitreya. First:
This Dharma Master Wondrous Light upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma (up to) the deliverance of immeasurable multitudes.
Regarding the fact that while Wondrous Light propagated the sutras, the *Dharmaguptaka* [Vinaya] says "upheld" (*fengchi*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says "widely proclaimed" (*guangxuan*):
although he propagated all the sutras, it was the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that he held most dear. From "These various... onwards, the eight sons received his transformation; thus, Wondrous Light...

The Way was attained through the Lamp of Wisdom and transmitted to his eight sons. As the father initiated it and the sons continued it, Miaoguang (妙光) has long served this sutra by carrying forward the past and opening up the future.
Regarding "making offerings" (*pūjā*) below: this most clearly demonstrates the profundity of the cause. Having made offerings to the Buddha, one’s merit (*puṇya*) is fulfilled.
Practicing the Way in accordance [with the teachings], one’s wisdom (*prajñā*) is fulfilled. Because both merit and wisdom are fulfilled, one attains the [Buddha-]marks.

He succeeded in attaining Buddhahood. His eight sons then transmitted and recounted [the teachings] to one another in succession, passing them down in turn; hence it is called "successive transmission and prediction" (*anupūrvika-vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "God among Gods" (*devātideva*), a general discussion of "gods" (*deva*) identifies four types: first, worldly gods (*laukika-deva*), such as secular kings; second, gods by birth (*upapatti-deva*), such as the various deities of the three realms;
third, pure gods (*viśuddha-deva*), namely those who have attained the four fruits of the path and the *pratyekabuddhas*; and fourth, gods of ultimate meaning (*artha-deva*), which refers to...
Because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive that all phenomena are empty in meaning, and because the Buddha transcends the four heavens, he is called the God among Gods (*devātideva*).
Regarding the "Teacher of the Sages" (*ṛṣi-guru*): there are also four types of sages. The first is the Earth Sage (*bhūmi-ṛṣi*), who migrates to dwell in mountain forests.
Those who are aged yet do not die: (1) the two classes of celestial immortals; (2) the various devas of the three realms who possess the power of flight and transformation; (3) the noble rishis;

(4) the pratyekabuddhas who have attained the fruits of realization and mastery over supernatural powers; (5) the four true rishis; (6) the three types of worthies and ten stages of sages who have partially realized the True Principle;
and (7) the four rishis transformed by the Buddha. For these reasons, he is called the Teacher of All Rishis. II. Verse on Maitreya’s Original State.
[Extensive Verse]. At that time, the Dharma Master Wondrous Light had a disciple (up to) whose number was immeasurable.

Initially, he suppressed his pursuit of fame and profit, for those who allow their minds to be enslaved by such things and become indolent are thieves that obstruct the right path; thus, he constantly kept this in mind.
One's daily cultivation and progress will slacken. Fame and profit are the bait that hooks the mind; if one becomes greedy for and attached to them, one's pursuit of them will deepen day by day.
As this pursuit deepens, it leads inevitably to insatiable greed and seeking, causing one to frequent the homes of the noble and wealthy more often.
As one's daily cultivation slackens, one will inevitably abandon recitation and study; through neglect and forgetfulness, one will become unable to master the teachings.

Judging by this, such a person merely covets empty fame and does not apply themselves to true practice. Therefore it is said: "For these reasons, they are called 'those who seek fame. Furthermore, regarding those who practice the lower [vehicle]:

their planting of roots of goodness and their meeting with a Buddha, as well as the fame and profit they seek, all serve to support the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Therefore it is said: "They practice..."

Regarding "the multitude of wholesome karmas": seeing the Buddha and making offerings again causes one to accumulate merit through merit; following and practicing the Way causes one to cultivate wisdom through wisdom.

When wisdom is profound, *prajñā* (wisdom) is easily fulfilled; when merit is substantial, the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*) can be accomplished. Therefore, it is said that he is "endowed with the six *pāramitās*.
Because the Buddha appeared among the Śākya clan, and because ninety-six types of practitioners roll back their tongues, he is called the Śākya Teacher (*Śāstṛ*).

My son, because you have made offerings [to me] throughout many kalpas, you are able to see me now. Since you currently serve as the one who succeeds me, it is said that you shall become a Buddha hereafter.
The reason both cause and effect are designated by the name Maitreya is to repay your past vows.

According to the *Sūtra on the Descent into the Tuṣita Heaven*, "All those who, during the final dharma-age of Śākyamuni, diligently cultivate merit—whether by sweeping stupas, smearing the ground with plaster, or even merely reciting my name..."
As for those who pay homage, at the end of their lives they shall all be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven; in the future, they will descend to earth together with Maitreya.

The present statement that they "extensively deliver sentient beings" and so forth refers precisely to this. Furthermore, because they followed the Buddha in practicing the Way during the causal stage, their karmic connections have become profound;
therefore, in the resultant stage, they preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in immeasurable numbers—namely, those who are ready to be matured, they mature.
"Deliverance means to be delivered. As the verse on Maitreya’s responsive manifestations says: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; his manifested bodies number in the billions.
From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet the people of this age do not recognize him themselves. This may serve as a commentary for this passage.
The verses on the original causes of the master and disciple are concluded. △ Second, the verses on the summary and the resolution of doubts:
"After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you who were indolent are now I myself, the Dharma Master Wonderful Light."
Regarding the phrase "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa," this indicates that the traces of indolence are most manifest after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
it does not mean that such persons exist only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, the specific reference to the period after the Buddha’s passing is intended to address a potential doubt:
namely, that even during the time of the Buddha, there were those who were characterized by indolence, as was the case with Dīpaṃkara.
His deeds prior to this life should naturally have been forgotten. As for what occurred today, do not be surprised that he asks questions out of ignorance.
This concludes the verses synthesizing the ancient and the present. 4. Verses on Responding to Questions and Concluding the Answers (The prose section provides a general answer briefly;

here, the response is given specifically and extensively, thus belonging to the "Extensive Verses. Furthermore, former masters established four latent doubts at this point to explain the Name, Essence, Substance, and Function. Since these verses consist of four sections, they correspond precisely to the four preceding questions of Maitreya; therefore, this section is titled "Responding to Questions and Concluding the Answers.")
This is divided into four sections: first, the answer to the first question; second, the answer to the second question; third, the answer to the third question;

and fourth, the answer to the fourth question. Regarding the first [section]: as previously stated, Maitreya asked, "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, gazing upon both you and me. For what reason, World-Honored One, do you emit this radiance? Therefore, having posed the question, the response concludes as follows:
"I have seen that when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara manifested such a portentous sign of light, I knew then that the Buddha was about to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
Mañjuśrī’s intention was this: 'Why does the World-Honored One emit this radiance?

If it is as I have witnessed in the past—that such a portentous sign of light from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was followed by the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra—then I know that the present Buddha likewise intends to preach it."

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is beyond doubt. △ Second, answering the second question (following Maitreya’s previous inquiry: “O Son of the Buddha, you have answered at the proper time; having resolved their doubts and brought them joy, what benefit has been bestowed?”).
He manifests this radiance; therefore, one should inquire and provide the following summary answer:

"The present signs are like the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits this radiance to assist in the revelation of the meaning of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)."

Mañjuśrī’s intention was this: "As for what benefit you ask regarding the manifestation of this radiance—if one observes the signs of this day, they are no different from the original auspicious light. It is sufficient to know that this light is identical among all Buddhas.
These Buddhas, wishing to reveal the true nature (*dharmatā*), first employ skillful means (*upāya*), borrowing the transformative manifestations of the Buddhas across eighteen thousand lands."
It serves to assist and stimulate its manifestation. Thus, the present radiance emitted by the Buddha likewise assists in manifesting the meaning of the true nature (dharmatā).

△ Third, the answer to the third question (as Maitreya previously asked: "Regarding the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment—is he intending to preach this, or is he intending to bestow a prediction [of Buddhahood]?"—therefore, one should ask, and the response concludes as follows):
"O people, you should now know: join your palms with a single mind and wait; the Buddha shall surely rain down the rain of Dharma to satisfy those who seek the Way.
Mañjuśrī’s intention was this: "Is your question intended for an exposition of the sublime Dharma, or is it for the sake of a prophecy? You should judge this by means of inference."
"You all, now join your palms with single-mindedness and wait with open hearts. Why is this?

The Buddha shall rain down the great Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way, so that even those whose sprouts have withered and whose seeds are ruined may each receive a prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
What is called 'bestowing predictions through preaching the Dharma' is entirely contained herein. △ Fourth, answering the fourth question.

Question: (As previously stated in Maitreya’s inquiry: "To show the various Buddha-lands adorned with all manner of jewels and purity, and to cause one to see the various Buddhas—this is no small cause. To what end, then, was this taught? Therefore, one should ask and provide the concluding answer:)
"Should there be those seeking the three vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them so that none remain.
Mañjuśrī’s intention was this: 'Since you previously stated that this is no small matter, you must surely ask what it is that is being taught.
I imagine that those seeking the three vehicles may not necessarily believe what I say; if they still have doubts and do not yet believe," or...

Regarding those who have faith yet subsequently regret it: [Mañjuśrī] shall wait for the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption and will cause them to sever [their regret], purifying it completely until nothing remains.
This was Mañjuśrī’s urgent intervention in the maritime matter;

he entirely shifted the responsibility for this affair onto the Buddha, thereby compelling the Tathāgata to speak once he had emerged from concentration. Thus, it serves as the introductory prologue. The Introduction is concluded.
