△ Second, the Section on the Correct Teaching (explaining the correct principles of the provisional and the real, and the fundamental and the manifested; demonstrating the central tenet of opening up and returning to the ultimate. From the "Expedient Means" to the "Supernatural Powers," there are twenty chapters, all of which constitute the text of the correct teaching). This is divided into two parts:
First, regarding the gateway of the present time, to manifest the Buddha’s original intention for appearing in the world (At this gateway of the present time, not a single dharma is lacking;

thus, there are distinctions in the establishment of teachings across three periods and the application of five doctrines to various capacities. However, if one traces back the Buddha’s original intention for appearing in the world, it is nothing other than opening up the provisional to reveal the real, and unifying the three vehicles into the One. From this point onward, up to the "Peaceful Practices" chapter).

This is fully manifested therein). Second, regarding the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), this reveals the wondrous function of response and transformation: "In the ground of ultimate reality, not a single dharma is established. Because not a single dharma is established, it is able to universally manifest all dharmas.

Therefore, though there is no birth, it manifests birth; though there is no cessation, it manifests cessation. It benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, with transformations following one another without end. From the section on the Ground of Self-Abiding up to the Chapter on Divine Power, this is fully revealed.

The first three [sections]: First, a brief clarification of the provisional and the real, so as to move one’s attachments and give rise to doubt; second, an extensive clarification of the provisional and the real, so as to sever doubt and engender faith;

third, a thorough manifestation of the merit of the sūtra, so as to entrust others with the propagation of the Dharma. Regarding the first [of these], there is a general title for the entire fascicle which should be explained first.
The title of the chapter is as follows:

In the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Expedient Means," although the meaning is contained within this section, I shall now explain "expedient means" (*upāya*) by integrating the preceding and following passages. "Expedient" (*fang*) refers to the essence that is fixed and unchanging;
"means" (*bian*) refers to the function that responds to things and follows conditions. When discussed individually, "expedient" is the reality itself.
It is indeed *upāya* (expedient means). From beginning to end, this chapter does nothing but elucidate the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūta-artha*);

therefore, it is titled "Expedient Means. To synthesize the discussion: "expedient" (*upāya*) refers to that which arises from the direction [of truth] as an expedient; it is designated solely by its aspect as an expedient.
This is precisely the meaning of "skillful means" (upāya-kauśalya) as commonly explained. Generally speaking, this chapter contains five levels of skillful means.
The first is that once Mañjuśrī and Maitreya have finished their dialogue and the assembly has no one left to ask questions, [the Buddha] speaks of his own accord through skillful means.
The second means that while provisional grasping remains unmoved, no doubt regarding the ultimate arises; thus, through skillful means, one praises, extols, and inspires others.

The third means that although the Dharma cannot be pointed out and the characteristics of words and phrases are quiescent, one provides analytical explanations through skillful means in response to requests.

The fourth refers to the principle of the provisional and the real, which is not easily elucidated; it is so called because it provides skillful, expedient instruction by describing both oneself and others.

The fifth refers to the first cycle of the Dharma teaching, wherein Śāriputra received his prediction; it is so called because the real was intended for those of middle and lower capacities through the application of skillful, expedient methods.

General Discussion: Every word and every phrase of this sutra flows forth from the heart of great compassion; they universally serve to gather in and deliver sentient beings, and none are not skillful means (*upāya*).
Therefore, it is titled "Expedient Means" at the outset to let [the reader] know that from beginning to end, everything belongs to expedient means.
I hope you will not regard them as mere literal characters. [This is the general title for the entire volume. The main text of this chapter is divided into two parts: First, the brief [explanation].
Clarifying the provisional and the real. Second, the movement of attachments giving rise to doubt. This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
The former has two parts: first, praising by way of the Buddha’s wisdom; second, manifesting by way of all phenomena. The former has two parts: first, praising the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Second, the praise of the wisdom of self-realization, which consists of two parts: first, the initial section; second, the sequential explanation and establishment. Regarding the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, emerging from samādhi with composure... [up to] ...that which even pratyekabuddhas cannot know.
First, the sūtra author describes the ritual setting. "At that time" refers to the moment when Maitreya and Mañjuśrī had finished their dialogue.
Since the profound mechanism [of the Dharma] had been revealed, it was no longer appropriate for them to remain silent; therefore, he rose from samādhi.

As for the term "serene and composed," it means adjusting his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) and gathering his *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), appearing with a dignified and relaxed air, neither hurried nor constrained.

"Addressing Śāriputra" serves as the heading for the praise that follows. "Addressing" (gào) means to speak to someone by way of a formal summons; it carries the sense of a spontaneous discourse delivered without being asked.
The reason he addresses Śāriputra alone is that Śāriputra had long desired to study the bodhisattva path and was no longer content with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

It can be seen from such remarks as, "I shall henceforth not participate in these matters," which express profound personal sorrow. Furthermore, the term *śrāvaka* (voice-hearer) symbolizes provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Since the present [teaching] seeks to bring the provisional back to the ultimate (*pratyakṣa*), he addresses them alone.

The phrase "all Buddhas" collectively refers to those of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as cited in the "Chapter on Preaching According to the Dharma. Wisdom here refers to the Great Equalizing Wisdom (*samatā-mahājñāna*); sentient beings are deluded regarding it.
The Buddhas have realized this; therefore, it is called "the wisdom of the Buddhas. "Profound" means that it reaches the bottom of the abyss of all wisdom, for no other wisdom can fathom its depths.
"Immeasurable" means that it exhausts the full extent of all wisdom, for no other wisdom can measure its limit.
This is the praise of the actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), spoken in terms of self-awakening (*sva-bodha*). Section on the Gate.
This refers to expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), which is able to lead to ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*); therefore, it is called "the gate of his wisdom. Regarding "difficult to understand":

expedient means do not remain as expedient means forever; if one clings to expedient means, it is because one has not yet understood the meaning of expedient means. Regarding "difficult to enter": expedient means are able to lead to the ultimate.

If one is deluded regarding the ultimate reality, it is because they have not yet entered the pinnacle of the provisional [teachings]. This is a praise of the wisdom of the provisional, spoken in terms of awakening others.
That which is unknown to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is illustrated by such examples as those in the *Avataṃsaka* who faint and fall to the ground;
those in the *Āgama* for whom the daily wage is sufficient; those in the *Vaipulya* who constantly remove filth; and those in the *Prajñāpāramitā* who have no hope for even a single meal. This...

This is a combined praise of the provisional and the real, spoken in reference to the fulfillment of awakening (*bodhi*). While discussing the fulfillment of awakening, one would still distinguish it from that of the bodhisattvas;

however, here we distinguish it specifically from those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. This is because this sutra aims to shatter attachment to the provisional, and since the attachments of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are particularly heavy, they must be addressed as a matter of urgent priority.
The praise of the two wisdoms is thus concluded. II. Explanation in Sequential Order.

Why is this so? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon [the Buddhas]... [up to] ...the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) of what he has taught according to circumstances is difficult to understand.
The opening phrase takes up the preceding section to raise a question: "Regarding the wisdom and the gates mentioned above, why is it that those who hear and rely upon them do not know [them]?

From the words "The Buddha has personally... onwards, the text provides the formal explanation. "Having personally attended upon the Buddhas" refers to those such as Maitreya (Aśvaghosa’s *Maitreya-sūtra* mentions the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, here likely referring to the practitioner of the *Adhimukta-asaṃkoca-sūtra*, i.e., the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging).

Regarding the period of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, when Prabhāketu was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara: because the cultivation [of roots] had come from afar, all who practiced the path of the Dharma were universally recorded with a single voice;

because the accumulation [of merit] had come from a great depth—such as increasing one's lifespan, preaching the sūtras, upholding the treasury of the Dharma, and widely proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the courageous, though encountering many Buddhas in close proximity, do not excuse themselves on the grounds of the length of time, but instead apply themselves with diligence.

Although he practices many dharmas, he does not become complacent because his practice is complete; this is what is meant by "wasting no weariness even as one traverses kalpas like a stone pillar," and "not retreating even while bearing the iron wheel.
As for the phrase "his fame is heard everywhere," it refers to the profundity of his established resolve and the sense of his renown overflowing.
Yet, once his renown has overflowed, his internal realization and true virtue must naturally be exceedingly profound.
It has not yet been [attained]. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] has "accomplished" it. This explains the profound and immeasurable meaning of the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Regarding "that which is taught according to what is appropriate": because the true wisdom is profound and immeasurable, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he expounds it in accordance with their individual capacities;
this is what is meant by "establishing provisional means based upon the ultimate reality. However, although the Dharma thus taught belongs to...

It is taught according to what is appropriate, yet its underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) lies in the ultimate reality; this is the secret intention (*sandhyābhāṣa*) of all Buddhas, and is therefore said to be difficult to understand.

This explains the meaning of the "gate of wisdom" being difficult to comprehend and difficult to enter. If the two types of wisdom are such as this, how could they be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas?
This concludes the praise of the Buddhas' wisdom. II. Praise of the Wisdom of Self-Realization (in two parts). 1. [The first part...]
This passage generally reveals their complete endowment. The text is divided into two parts for specific praise. First:
"Śāriputra, from the time I attained Buddhahood until now... [I have] seen that all perfections (pāramitās) are already fully endowed."
The initial reference to "the Dharma not being exhaustive" points to the period after the *Avataṃsaka* and since his attainment of Buddhahood.

Between the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were various teachings given according to the capacities of beings; because the causes and conditions for entering the Path differed, it is said that they were taught through "various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there were those whose faculties were dull or inferior who remained unable to understand even amidst these various causes and conditions. Moreover—
Furthermore, they are illustrated by what is easy to understand and compared by means of what is easy to see; thus it is said, "through various parables, he extensively expounds the verbal teachings.
Regarding "innumerable skillful means": the One Vehicle is opened up into the Three Vehicles according to the differences in individual capacities, as the skillful means vary accordingly.
"Guiding sentient beings to cause them to leave behind all attachments" means that, for example, when ordinary people are attached to existence, the Buddha teaches emptiness.
He guides them by means of this. The followers of the Two Vehicles are attached to emptiness; the Buddha speaks of existence to lead them away from it.
Based on this, what was previously stated—that he merely leads sentient beings out of their attachments wherever they may be—is not sufficient to exhaust the full extent of the Buddha’s wisdom.
What follows below serves to reveal that his wisdom is complete. First, as for the inquiry that arises: it refers to what was previously stated, which seems to...
The Buddha’s wisdom is already exhausted [in its perfection]. Why, then, does he speak only of leading the multitude away from attachment?

From the passage "The Tathāgata" below, two types of wisdom are raised together to explain this. Expedient means (*upāya*) is provisional wisdom; knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) is ultimate wisdom.
Since both have reached their consummation, they are collectively designated by the term *pāramitā*. That "all are already complete" refers precisely to this.
This does not exhaust what has been explained previously. △ Second, the text is divided to praise [the Buddha] individually:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision... his speech is gentle and pleasing to the hearts of all."
First, there is the praise for the perfection of true wisdom. Regarding "the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision": this refers to the true wisdom realized by himself. Regarding "vast":
this is discussed in terms of the horizontal, because it is fully endowed with all merits. Regarding "profound and far-reaching":

this is discussed in terms of the vertical, because it exhausts the depths of the ocean of all virtues. Regarding "immeasurable and unimpeded," and so forth: these further explain the words of praise.
The Immeasurables refer to the four immeasurable minds: first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; and fourth, equanimity.
The Unimpeded [Faculties] refer to the four unimpeded analytical knowledges: first, of phenomena; second, of meaning; third, of language; and fourth, of eloquence.

The Powers refer to the ten powers, beginning with the knowledge of what is possible and impossible and ending with the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. Because they cannot be surpassed and cannot be destroyed, they are called "powers. The Fearlessnesses.
There are four: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;

and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering. They are collectively termed "fearlessnesses" because, when speaking extensively of one's own and others' knowledge and abandonment within the great assembly, there is no apprehension.
As for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is as described in the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, and so forth, up to the sublime *śamatha*.
He [penetrates] the samādhis, dhyānas, liberations, such as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, up to the inconceivable realm of liberation;
the samādhis, such as the twenty-five kings, up to the Śūraṅgama King.
Because he has thoroughly exhausted the source of these various merits, it is said that he "enters deeply into the boundless. As for "the boundless," since he has already—
Reaching the ultimate source, there is no further limit; this is what is meant by "profound and far-reaching knowledge and vision.
"All" refers back to what has been explained above: from all-knowledge up to Buddha-wisdom, all are termed the "noble wisdom of self-awakening";
from all dharmas up to the Buddha-dharmas, all are termed the "ultimate fruit-dharmas. Therefore, they are all said to have never existed [prior to realization], yet each is perfectly complete.
Because it is fully possessed, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). "Accomplishment" carries the meaning of being perfectly complete and endowed with all qualities;

this refers to what is known as the vastness of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). [Question: Since you have explained that true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) should belong to the ultimate realization of self-awakening (*pratyātma-adhigama*), the names "immeasurable," "unobstructed," and "fearless" seem to imply the awakening of others (*parānugraha*).

Furthermore, the meanings of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*), and the three gateways to liberation (*vimokṣa-mukha*) appear not to be the ultimate realization. Is it not problematic to use these to explain true wisdom? [Answer: Only when the nature-endowed virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all fully possessed can one call it true wisdom. If these were not inherently present within true wisdom itself, [it could not be so named].

[Question: From where, then, does the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*) arise? [Answer: Śāriputra, below, praises the perfection of skillful wisdom. "Various distinctions" refers to temporarily suppressing one's original intention and speaking in accordance with the inclinations of others.
"Skillfully expounding all dharmas" refers to the provisional establishment of the Three Vehicles to skillfully adapt to the various capacities of sentient beings.
Without skillful wisdom, how could this be possible? Now, when the Tathāgata calls himself a "capable one," it is precisely because he perceives this.

The meaning of being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is explained by the final two lines, which further interpret the words of praise. "Having supple speech" means being well-attuned to the sentiments of beings;
because of this, one is able to perform various forms of discernment. "Delighting the hearts of the multitude" means observing their capacities and providing instruction accordingly;
because of this, one is able to skillfully expound all dharmas. This, in essence, is the very function of being fully endowed with skillful means and wisdom.

The praise by way of the Buddha’s wisdom is concluded. △ Second, the manifestation by way of all phenomena. (Previously, fearing that [the audience] might stubbornly cling to what they had previously heard, he praised by way of the Buddha’s wisdom to let them know that whether provisional or real, neither is ultimate, and one must still seek upward.

This was because he feared they would loftily defer to the sacred realm and limit themselves by drawing lines on the ground. Therefore, he now manifests by way of all phenomena to let them know that every dharma and every instance is nothing other than the provisional and the real;

one simply needs to realize it right before one's eyes. Thus, it is known that everything before and after is medicine; if it fits the ailment, it may be taken and ingested. I hope you will not remain silent at the gate of medicine, waiting for your own death. This is divided into three parts.
First, a summary that cuts off further words; second, raising a question to provide an explanation and establish the point; third, a further explanation of the terms. Regarding the first:
Śāriputra summarizes the essential points (up to) "The Buddha has fully accomplished [them]; stop, Śāriputra, there is no need to speak further."

First, to take up the essentials and reveal the realization: the provisional and the ultimate teachings are present in every single instance. Were one to attempt to express them all in words, speech would be unable to exhaust them;
therefore, it is said, "taking up the essentials to speak. "Immeasurable" means there is no limit vertically; "boundless" means there is no edge horizontally.
Such unprecedented dharmas as these, the Tathāgata has perfected each and every one; hence it is said, "the Buddha knows them all."
This is the accomplishment. This is stated by taking only the most essential points. "Ceasing and abandoning" (zhìshě) below means to cut off speech and not speak;

"cease" (zhǐ) is synonymous with "to desist. It means wishing to desist and not speaking. Because the Buddha saw that those of the Two Vehicles and others only know how to produce understanding according to the literal words, yet do not understand the manifest principle beyond the words, he used expressions such as "immeasurable and boundless" to awaken them.
Seeing them like birds waiting for food or the thirsty longing for water, he then hurriedly stopped them.
This was also in accordance with what Zhongni (Confucius) meant by "I wish to remain without speaking," as there was no further need for explanation because speaking would have been of no benefit.
△ Second, the inquiry and the explanation for its fulfillment.
Why is this so? Because the Buddha has accomplished [all things] (up to) being able to exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The first phrase poses the inquiry. Since it is said that the Buddha has fully accomplished these "unprecedented dharmas" (*adbhuta-dharma*), he should also briefly demonstrate them.

Regarding the meaning of these characteristics: why is it that they are set aside and not explained? It is because that which the Buddha has taught establishes that there are no worldly phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma;
only the Buddha realizes and knows this, and thus it is said to be "accomplished by the Buddha. Furthermore, there are no Buddha-dharmas that are not worldly phenomena.
Sentient beings are deluded and obscured; therefore, it is said that this is "the foremost rarity. All who see forms or hear sounds miss the mark at every turn;

therefore, it is called "the dharma difficult to understand. To realize that the emerald bamboo and yellow flowers are *prajñā* and *tathatā*, it is said that "only the Buddha has fully exhausted [this truth].

Thus, to exhaustively penetrate all dharmas is the ultimate realization of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and to exhaustively penetrate the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) is the ultimate realization of ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*).
Thus, true wisdom is perfected. Aside from Buddha after Buddha, who could possibly equal this? This is precisely why [the teaching] ceases and is not further expounded.
△ Third: Explaining the Etymology through a Reversal.
Regarding the passage "All dharmas have such characteristics, such nature" (extending to) "such beginning, end, and ultimate equality":
the two characters "so-called" (suǒwèi) are terms used to introduce what follows as an explanation of what precedes.

That is, they summon the meanings of "such" and so forth below to explain the preceding statement that "only a Buddha can fully investigate [them]. "Such" (rúshì) is a term that points to dharmas. Characteristics, nature, power, and essence, etc., are precisely...

The dharmas referred to—whether sentient or insentient—all possess them. Therefore, speaking in terms of all dharmas, the explanation of their meaning relies on the name "nature" (xing) for that which sustains characteristics (xiang).

For example, regarding the physical bodies of sentient beings and the fundamental substance of insentient things: because they are sustained by nature, the sustaining characteristic is called "nature.
For example, regarding the primordial luminosity of sentient beings and the primordial vital energy of insentient things: [the sustained characteristic is called] "characteristic" (xiang)...

Based on their dependence, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essence (*svabhāva*); for example, the hands and feet of sentient beings, or the roots and stems of insentient things, because they are what the characteristic belongs to.

"Power" (*bala*) refers to functional capacity; for example, the grasping and moving of sentient beings, or the lifting, supporting, and sustaining of insentient things, because they are what the essence possesses.
"Activity" (*karma*) refers to functional operation; for example, the virtuous or wicked, good or evil, of sentient beings. [The same applies to] insentient things...

The truth or falsity of sentient beings' domestic and wild [states] is established by power; thus, that which gives birth is called the cause (*hetu*), like the seeds that are the causes of sentient beings' good and evil.

Because they are accumulated through action, that which assists and triggers is the condition (*pratyaya*), like the father’s semen and the mother’s blood for sentient beings, or the rich soil and moist rain for non-sentient things. Because it is that upon which the seed relies, it constitutes the basis.

These are termed "fruits. For instance, the perfection of the material bodies of sentient beings and the completeness of the internal and external aspects of insentient things are called "retribution" because they are produced by conditions.

Furthermore, the fortune or misfortune, the adversity or success of sentient beings, as well as the lightness or heaviness and the nobility or baseness of insentient things, are called "fruits" because they are what is experienced as a result.
The initial characteristic is the root, and the subsequent retribution is the branch; ultimately, they are non-dual.
Because they share the same true reality as their essential substance, it is said that they are "equal. Altogether there are ten instances of the phrase "thus" (*tathatā*).
If one thoroughly understands each of the first nine, this is the exhaustive investigation of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

If one definitively realizes and witnesses the final one, this is the exhaustive investigation of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is precisely what was meant above when it was said: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively investigate [them]."
However, these three preceding sections, while manifesting the ultimate nature of the Buddha’s wisdom, actually clarify that worldly phenomena are none other than the Buddha-dharma.
Since worldly phenomena are none other than the Buddha-dharma, then all dharmas are nothing but expedient means (*upāya*), and there are no dharmas that do not reveal the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
This is the Tathāgata’s extraordinary skillful means, which, by uplifting and sustaining beings toward the higher state, spreads the teachings of the voice throughout the world.
At the gateway of the six sense organs, one clarifies the provisional and the real within the realm of myriad transformations.

One who understands this need not wait for words to grasp the intent of the teachings spoken according to circumstances—the profound meaning that is difficult to comprehend. [Question: Among the "Ten Suchnesses," the meaning of *xing* (nature) seems to refer to the true essence (*zhentti*). Why, then, is the meaning of *deng* (equality) designated as the *shixiang* (true aspect)? [Answer:

*Xing* refers to the individual nature possessed by each phenomenon, whereas *deng* points to the essence to which all phenomena collectively return. Although the four great rivers are all called "water," they cannot be called the "ocean" [until they reach it]. It is only when all waters converge that it is the ocean. Thus, while *xing* pertains to the distinct characteristics of individual dharmas, *deng* indicates the universal reality to which they all ultimately belong.
It is therefore called an ocean. Thus, the meaning of equality constitutes the true mark (*dharmatā*). The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

△ (The Main Verses are divided into three parts: 1. The main verses corresponding to the prose; 2. An extreme manifestation of what is difficult to know; 3. A brief exposition for the purpose of refutation.

The first two [parts] consist of: 1. One verse praising the Buddha’s wisdom; 2. Two verses manifesting through all phenomena. The first of these two consists of: 1. One verse praising the wisdom of all Buddhas; 2.
One verse praising the wisdom of self-realization. The first of these two consists of: 1. One verse indicating and praising the two [aspects].
Regarding "Wisdom," the two verses explain it in successive order. First:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; neither the various devas nor the people of the world (up to) are able to fathom him."
The Buddhas have reached the ultimate consummation of the two wisdoms and transcend both the mundane and supramundane realms; therefore, they are called "World-Heroes" (*lokanātha*).
"Hero" (*nātha*) here implies one who is preeminent. Regarding their being "immeasurable," this is also spoken of in terms of the ultimate nature of what has been realized:
since the wisdom realized is already consummate, how could the person who realizes it possibly be limited? As for the various devas and the people of the world...

Devas and humans dwell within the nine realms; therefore, they alone are singled out here. Beyond these, there are three types of sages above and four types of ordinary beings below, which together encompass all sentient beings.
As an ancient master said: "Those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment do not know the Sublime Enlightenment."
How much more so for other assemblies? Therefore, it is said in general that "no one is able to know. This is a verse that transcends [ordinary] meaning;

it is a passage stating that what the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know—such as the Buddha’s powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)—all belong to the sphere of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
These are distinct merits used here to praise the phrases regarding the wisdom of all Buddhas. As for the other various dharmas of the Buddha...
The preceding verse describes the gateway of his wisdom. Because within this wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*) there are also immeasurable differentiated dharmas, no one is able to fathom it.
This combines with the verse’s meaning that it is profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter. [Question:

The prose commentary merely states that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know [it], whereas the present verse says that among all classes of beings, including devas and humans, none are able to know it. Why is there such a difference in breadth and brevity between the prose and the verse? [Answer: [This is because] from the time the six classes of ordinary beings first plant the seeds [of enlightenment], until the Bodhisattvas are about to be liberated, they hear [the Dharma]....

The conditions are now fully matured; since the former [task] was the primary duty and required urgency, only "hearing the conditions" (*śruta-pratyaya*) was specifically mentioned. However, as this [present task] is the Buddha’s compassion, it ought to be universal; therefore, it also includes the rest of the assembly. This is done collectively to stimulate their aspirations and resolve, to give rise to the superior mind, and thereby enable them to enter the realm of true knowledge.
The verse concludes the praise of the two types of wisdom. II. The Verse Explanation in Sequential Order (Abridged Verse).
"From the beginning, following countless Buddhas, he has fulfilled the practices of all paths (up to attaining the fruit at the site of enlightenment).

This refers to the phrase "from the beginning. The verse above [describes] "approaching the various Buddhas"; this "fulfillment" verse praises the aforementioned "exhaustive practice of the Dharma," which is profound and subtle.
It points to the aforementioned "true wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*). The initial attainment of correspondence is called "vision" (*darśana*); having already achieved great penetration.
It is said: "To understand. Although many Buddhas have appeared over long or short periods of time, they all practiced the Way and the Dharma;

yet regarding this profound and subtle Dharma, they ultimately did not attain correspondence with it, nor did they achieve great penetration. Therefore, it is said that it is difficult to see and difficult to understand.

The two lines beginning with "Practicing the Way for billions of kalpas" praise the aforementioned courageous and diligent effort; one who lacks such courageous and diligent effort cannot endure [this practice].
Because he practiced the Way throughout kalpas, the fame of one who has established profound resolve and firm conduct naturally overflows; therefore, it is omitted here.

Regarding the attainment of fruition at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the verse praises the aforementioned accomplishment of the most profound and unprecedented Dharma, rather than the various teachings spoken according to the needs of beings, whose underlying intentions are difficult to understand. This is because true reality must necessarily be endowed with skillful means (*upāya*).
Because it can be known through words. This concludes the verse praising the wisdom of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the verse praising the wisdom of self-realization (a single line of verse that subsumes the entire prose section; this is a concise summary).
"I have fully known and seen.
The Tathāgata himself says this because, just as those Buddhas have realized it, I too have fully known and fully seen it;

this is intended to manifest his own realization by means of others, so that they may know through analogy. The verse concludes the praise based on the Buddha’s wisdom. △ Second, the verse based on [the Buddha’s power].
The Verses on the Manifestation of the Meaning of All Dharmas:
"Such is the meaning of the various natures and characteristics of the great fruit of retribution... [down to] ...the cessation of the characteristics of speech.
These verses consist of six lines, read as pairs of couplets. They correspond in reverse order to the three categories of the prose commentary; their meaning is extremely clear. First:
These two lines provide an extended explanation of the meaning within the etymological analysis (*nirukti*).

While the prose section follows the sequence of their arising and thus places "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*) first, here, following the thematic convenience of the preceding text, "fruition" (*vipāka*) is placed at the beginning.

This is because the two wisdoms constitute the fruition, and the attainment of this enjoyment constitutes the retribution. Furthermore, regarding the ninefold distinctions of the *tathatā* (suchness) in both sentient beings and Buddhas...
The same applies to both. The first phrase cites the "end" with respect to the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*), hence it says "great fruit and great retribution.

The second phrase cites the "root" with respect to the sentient-being realm (*sattvadhātu*), hence it says "various natures and characteristics. In reality, both the root and the end encompass the entirety of the sentient-being realm and the Buddha-realm.
However, the Buddha-realm is described as "great" while the sentient-being realm is termed "various," because the Buddha-realm is preeminent, whereas the [sentient-being realm]...

Because of the distinction between realms (*dhātu*), the meaning points to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since the nine types of beings and Buddhas alike return to the same source, they are mentioned later.
This is what the long prose passage refers to when it says, "The beginning and the end are ultimately equal.

The following two lines—namely, "Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter"—do not merely indicate their differences; rather, they serve as the inquiry that introduces and explains the meaning within the preceding section.
Furthermore, it is known that these [teachings] converge upon the same goal. As the prose section states: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The final two lines refer to the meaning within the prose section regarding "taking the essentials and transcending words. This Dharma refers to the Dharma of the "Ten Suchnesses" (*daśa-tathatā*).
Although only a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it, it is nonetheless something known only by oneself, like the sensation of warmth or cold; truly, it cannot be expressed in words.
This is why it is said that it cannot be shown. Since it cannot be shown, one’s desire to speak is lost; hence it is said that "words and phrases are quiescent.
An ancient worthy said: "The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly abundant; it is simply that the tongue is too short."
This is precisely that meaning. The formal verse (gāthā) corresponding to the long prose (vṛtti) is now concluded. △ Second, the extreme difficulty of knowing [this], in three parts:
1. Granting that it can be believed and understood; 2. Distinguishing that it is beyond the reach of discursive thought; 3. Clarifying that it is known only through realization. First:
Among all other classes of sentient beings, none are able to resolve the firmness of the bodhisattvas' power of faith, with the single exception of the Buddha alone.
Since this encompasses all nine realms, it is said that "all other classes of beings" are included. The six ordinary realms are entirely deluded, while the three noble ones possess partial awakening;
therefore, it is said that "none are able to resolve" it. The bodhisattvas' power of faith is so firm that in the future it cannot be [overturned].
Because it is limited, it alone is excluded; for there is ultimately a time when one can understand it. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit;
it nurtures all wholesome dharmas. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma..."
Faith is that which enables entry. The latter part of the original sutra also states: "Śāriputra, even you have gained entry into this sutra through faith.
How great, indeed, is the power of faith! Thus, it is placed at the head of the five powers (*pañcabala*).

That it is uniquely excluded here [from the four foundations of mindfulness] should be understood and heeded by those who aspire to the wisdom of the Buddha. 2. Distinguishing from Reflection (*vitarka*)

It does not reach three [levels]. First, it distinguishes [them from] the Śrāvakas; second, it distinguishes [them from] the Pratyekabuddhas; third, it distinguishes [them from] the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the first:
"The assembly of disciples of all Buddhas who have made offerings to all Buddhas... yet they too cannot know."

First, he distinguishes the disciples of the Buddhas by collectively referring to all *śrāvakas* throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; thus, they are called "disciples of the Buddhas.
That they offer to the Buddhas necessarily implies they have heard the Dharma, thereby manifesting the profundity of their wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*).

That their outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) signifies that their afflictions have ceased, thereby manifesting the perfection of their abandonment-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Those who dwell in their final bodies possess only the remaining fetters of fruition, thereby manifesting that they are persons beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

There are three meanings for those whose strength is insufficient: first, delighting in the small; second, fearing the great; and third, the application of the mind. Delighting in the small means being content with what one has attained.
Fearing the great means being timid and apprehensive, thus not seeking it. The application of the mind refers to the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
None of these are sufficient to exhaust the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, they are inadequate. "Hypothetically" (*jia-shi*)—this distinguishes the disciples of Śākyamuni.
"Hypothetically" (*jia-shi*) means "supposing that. Śāriputra’s wisdom was said to be foremost; even if people like him filled the world, their wisdom could be called vast.
"Exhaustively" (*jin*)—in the rising tone—means "exhausting one's thought," which refers to allowing one's reflections to proceed. "Measuring" (*du-liang*) refers to conjecture and estimation.
Regarding "comparing": it is said that the Buddha’s wisdom has non-discrimination as its essence, whereas the minds of those of the Two Vehicles are characterized by discrimination.
Since the mind and its objects are mutually contradictory, even if one were to exhaustively employ thought and deliberation to compare and measure them, they remain unfathomable.

As for "even if," this means that even if there were as many Śāris as there are in the ten directions—excluding only a single world-system—to compare with the aforementioned [Buddha's wisdom], [it would still be incomparable].

Those who fill the world are most numerous. As for the other disciples—such as Maudgalyāyana in supernatural powers, Pūrṇa in preaching the Dharma, and others like Śāriputra in wisdom—they are each as numerous as Śāriputra himself.
Therefore, it is said that they "also fill the lands of the ten directions. In sum, because their application of mind is erroneous, the more they seek, the further they stray.
It is like a person who urgently wishes to travel east but walks facing west; thus it is said: "exhausting one's thoughts."
Even when measuring together, they likewise cannot know it. △ Second, distinguishing the Pratyekabuddhas:
The Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom, free from outflows, in their final body—[up to] none can know even a small portion of it.
The Pratyekabuddhas have eliminated the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and rank above the Śrāvakas; thus they are called those of "sharp wisdom.

Since their conditions for rebirth within the three realms are exhausted, and only their physical bodies and gnosis remain before being extinguished, they are called "those with no-outflows in their final body" (*anāsrava-paścima-deha*).

As for the phrase "also filling the ten directions," their spatial extent is equal to that of the Śrāvakas. As for the phrase "their number is like a grove of bamboo," their quantity is even greater than that of the Śrāvakas. These...
As for the mind, it exerts effort equal to that of the śrāvakas; as for the immeasurable billions of kalpas, the duration of time is even longer than that of the śrāvakas.
Those who wish to contemplate true wisdom should apply their minds equally to that of the śrāvakas, yet they will not know even a small fraction of it.

It is not known that this is even more extreme than [the ignorance of] the śrāvakas. That is to say, it is precisely because their discrimination is subtle that their awakening and illumination are consequently delayed.
△ Third, distinguishing the bodhisattvas:
"A bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment... (up to) ...is likewise unable to know."

First, to distinguish those of the initial resolve: this includes those who have newly awakened the aspiration, such as ordinary worldlings at the very beginning of their practice, or those of the two vehicles of indeterminate lineage who have turned away from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle—all of these are included.
Making offerings to the Buddha manifests the purity and thickness of their merit; understanding the definitive meaning manifests the depth and breadth of their wisdom;
and preaching the Dharma manifests the simultaneous operation of compassion and wisdom. That the initial resolve can already manifest in such ways is significant.
This should not be compared to the provisional, gradual, or initial mind. As for "rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds," it is not merely comparable to a grove of bamboo;
"full" refers to being filled to the utmost. As for "wisdom" being called "sublime," this wisdom is no small matter.

As for "kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," these cannot be compared to even hundreds of millions of immeasurable kalpas; though all together should deliberate upon them, they cannot be known.

This is because that which belongs to deliberation is, by its very nature, conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); since it deviates from the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*), how could it possibly know? This is what is meant by the saying:

"As soon as one gives rise to a deliberative thought, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles. Regarding "not regressing" (*avaivartika*): this distinguishes the profound stages from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) upward.
In the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), one flows spontaneously into the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). All such states are termed "non-regression."

Their number is like the sands of the Ganges. Moreover, they cannot be compared merely to rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds; even if one were to contemplate them with a single mind, one would still not know them.
This is because as the assembly grows larger, the mind becomes more subtle, and as the mind becomes more subtle, wisdom reaches further.
Regarding these three preceding sections, from the Śrāvaka stage up to the stage of non-retrogression:
if one discusses the realization of the fruit, each preceding stage does not equal each succeeding one; yet if one discusses wisdom, each succeeding stage excels each preceding one.

As their number increases, the duration of time becomes longer, the application of the mind becomes more intense, and the depth of their ignorance becomes even greater. In sum, the Buddha’s wisdom transcends all thought.
The true mark is markless; it cannot be sought with a mind of conceptualization, but can only be attained through a mind of non-attainment.
