there is but one path. This concludes the brief analysis. II. Detailed Analysis (in three parts): 1. Detailed explanation of the provisional and real aspects of all Buddhas; 2.
Detailed explanation of the provisional and real aspects of self-realization; 3. Summary to demonstrate the identity of the Way. The first [section] has three parts, following the same pattern:
First, a general summary; second, a detailed enumeration of the text in two parts; third, a concluding summary of the original intent. Regarding the first:
"Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is likewise thus."
"All" encompasses all three periods of time. It is said that each of the three periods has its own ten directions, and within each of those ten directions there are various Buddhas;
therefore, it is called "all the Buddhas of the ten directions. "Dharma" refers to the provisional and ultimate teachings.

Although the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Buddhas have been briefly explained above, their specific distinctions have not yet been clearly manifested. Now, the three [aspects] of the ten directions are clarified...
The Buddhas of the world are no different from those mentioned above regarding the provisional and the real for oneself and others; therefore, it says, "the Dharma is also thus.
This example serves to indicate their commonality with what precedes. △ Second, the separate listing of the divisions of the text has three parts:
first, the commonality of past Buddhas; second, the commonality of future Buddhas; third, the commonality of present Buddhas. First:
Śāriputra, all past Buddhas, up to the ultimate end, have all attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
According to the original sūtra, these past Buddhas were Candrasūryapradīpa, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, and so forth.
“Cloud Sovereign” (Yún Zìzài) and others may also refer to the thousand Buddhas of the Auspicious Eon (Zhāngyán Jié).
“From the ultimate [truth], he establishes the provisional” refers to the Dharma-phrase; “bringing the provisional back to the ultimate” is a statement concerning the teaching (*jiào*).

“These various [beings]” and the two subsequent phrases—transforming the one into three—is the phrase of the ultimate; “bringing the three back to the one” is a statement concerning the capacity of the audience (*jī*). △ Second, the future.
The Buddhas are the same.
Śāriputra, all future Buddhas, up to the ultimate end, shall all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding these future Buddhas, according to the original sūtra, they are named Padmaprabha, Lakṣaṇa, Jambunadaprabhāsa, and Candanagandha.
"Sānhaì (Ocean-Mountain Wisdom)" and so forth may also refer to the teaching of the thousand Buddhas of the Constellation Kalpa (*Nakṣatra-kalpa*).

The rest is as above. [Question: Since the Buddha has not yet arrived, how can the provisional and ultimate aspects of his capacity and teaching be known in advance? [Answer: The principles of former sages and later sages are one and the same. For example, regarding the succession of a hundred generations after the Zhou dynasty, even Confucius said it could be known. How much more so for the Tathāgata, whose three types of penetration (*trividha-pratisaṃvid*) illuminate all and whose five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) are perfectly clear;
even until the very end of the future limit, he does not need to count on his fingers to discern them. △ Third, the present Buddhas are the same.
"Śāriputra, [from] the present [Buddhas] of the ten directions [up to] the ultimate, all have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

This first section provides a general clarification regarding the Buddhas of the present. According to the root sūtra, they are manifested by a single ray of light and assembled through the three transformations.

The "Pure Flower King of Past Constellations" (Śubhavyūha-rāja) of the "Exquisite Sound" chapter and the "King of Supreme Majesty" (Vimalacandraprabha-rāja) of the "Universal Worthy" chapter may also be understood as referring to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Regarding "benefiting and bringing peace and happiness": first, one benefits them through provisional teachings, causing them to attain the peace and happiness of the Three Vehicles;
subsequently, one benefits them through the ultimate teaching, causing them to attain the peace and happiness of the One Vehicle. It is thus.
"Benefiting and bringing peace and happiness. To explain in detail, there are multiple layers of distinctions; hence it is said, "in many ways. From "These various...
onwards, each is explained individually, as above. This concludes the separate listing of the sections. △ Third, the summary of the original intention.
"Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas... so that they may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The phrase "only teaching and transforming bodhisattvas" concludes [the section] by way of the capacities of the audience (*yōki*). From the words "desiring to" (*yoku i*) below, it explains by way of the teachings (*yōkyō*).

The two characters "showing" (*shi*) and "awakening" (*go*) differ from those above. "Showing" means pointing out that which is inherently possessed, causing [beings] to believe that they are no different from the Buddha. "Awakening" means...
It awakens the ignorant and enables them to understand that they are no different from the Buddha.

Once they have attained this understanding, one further desires to lead them to cultivate based on their inherent nature, gradually deepening their practice until they become identical to the Buddha; therefore, it is called "entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision."
The detailed explanation of the provisional and the ultimate of all Buddhas is concluded. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the provisional and the ultimate of self-realization:
"Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus... (up to) because they have attained the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes."

The first part provides a general explanation by way of illustration. "Knowing all [the various desires]" and below provide a detailed explanation through specific analysis. Regarding "various desires":

these may be the desire to seek the state of a śrāvaka, the desire to seek the state of a pratyekabuddha, or the desire to seek the state of a bodhisattva; they differ according to their distinctions.
Since each has its own particular desire, one will inevitably become intensely fond of it and refuse to let go; therefore, it is said that they are "attachments of the profound mind. Accordingly...
"Below" refers to the manifestation of provisional means (*upāya*). As it is said: "For those seeking to be *śrāvakas*, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths;

for those seeking to be *pratyekabuddhas*, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to Dependent Origination; for those seeking to be *bodhisattvas*, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Six Perfections.
"Śāriputra, below" refers to the convergence of the provisional back into the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*). As it is said: "Causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."

This is the realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). This concludes the detailed explanation of the provisional and the ultimate as realized within oneself.
△ Third, the summary to demonstrate the identity of the Way.
Śāriputra, even in the worlds of the ten directions there are no two vehicles, let alone three.
"The worlds of the ten directions" refers to this world and other regions taken together; it is thus a summary that encompasses both self and others.
There is only the One Vehicle (ekayāna), and even a bodhisattva cannot be found therein; therefore, it is said that "even two vehicles do not exist. Bodhi...
Since even a "being" (sattva) cannot be apprehended, it is not said that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can be known; hence it is asked, "How much less could there be three?
Based on this, one further confirms that for both oneself and others, there is no path other than the single way of transcending the world. This detailed analysis is now complete.

△ Third, raising the objection regarding turbidity to prevent difficulties (fearing that, based on the preceding difficulty, one might say: "If there are neither two nor three vehicles, why do the Buddhas appearing in the world not directly teach the One Vehicle, but must first teach the Three Vehicles?")

Is this, then, a teaching intentionally devised as a compromise? Therefore, the *Fangdeng* [Sutra] states: "The Buddhas appear in the five turbidities and evil worlds," and so forth. This is likely said twice or thrice; it is simply that the Buddhas have no choice but to act thus.
Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities (yugaṃśas). [From "until" ... they distinguish and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (ekabuddhayāna).
When the first Buddha appears in such a turbid world, the world was originally pure and peaceful; however, due to the afflictions of the kalpa, sentient beings accumulate and cause turmoil.
It is like throwing sand and soil into clear water: the natures of both vanish, and their appearance becomes turbid; this is called "muddiness.
In this age, many people are corrupt and evil, and for this reason it is termed an "evil world" (*kaliyuga*). Out of compassion for them, the Buddhas [appear].

He manifests his body through responsive transformation; therefore, it is said that he "emerges from this world. This is the general heading. The phrase "so-called" is a term used to point to what follows as an explanation of what precedes it.
The turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) has no separate essence; its essence consists precisely of the following four [turbidities]. They accumulate and converge together.

The characteristic of *tīvraruci* (intense burning) is uninterrupted continuity. The essence of *kliṣṭa* (affliction/turbidity) consists of the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*); its intrinsic nature is agitation, and its characteristic is the oppression of body and mind.

The essence of *saṃkleśa* (multitude of turbidities) consists of the conjunction of the three conditions; its characteristic is the continuous succession of rebirths within the six realms of existence.
The essence of *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (turbidity of views) consists of the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*); its characteristic is false cognition that clings to nihilism or eternalism.

To erroneously interpret this as being the characteristic marks is the defilement of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). It takes consciousness, warmth, and breath as its substance, and its characteristic mark is to maintain the continuity of matter and mind while hastening the decline of years and shortening the lifespan;

this is the specific explanation. The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) is a term for summarization, meaning that the substance and characteristics of the five defilements (*pañcakaṣāya*) are merely as described above.

From the words "Śāriputra," the text proceeds to explain three [defilements] according to their sequence; by citing the defilement of the eon (*kalpakaṣāya*), it is understood that the other four defilements are already included therein.

Because the four [defilements] constitute the substance of a kalpa, according to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years and decreases down to thirty thousand years, it is not yet called a "corrupt" age (*kaṣāya*).

When it reaches twenty thousand years, it is then designated as a corrupt age. Although it is called a corrupt age, compared to the time of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, it is still considered an era of relative peace and clarity.
According to the present appearance of a Buddha, it corresponds to the time when the human lifespan is...

A hundred years ago, compared to the time when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the ways of the world could not avoid becoming turbid and degenerate; the hearts of men were no longer as they were of old.
Things have become increasingly downward-trending and ever more deeply corrupted. Thus it is said that this is an age of turbulence during the *kalpa*-impurity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

This refers to the most chaotic period within the *kalpa*-impurity when the Buddhas appear in the world. "Sentient beings with heavy defilements" means those who give rise to delusions and commit [transgressions].

Karma. That which obstructs right knowledge is called *mala* (defilement). Being rigid, violent, and difficult to tame or subdue is called *guru* (heaviness). This is the correct explanation of the meanings of *mala* and *guru*.

*Mātsarya* (stinginess) refers to being parsimonious with oneself regarding others; *lobha* (greed) refers to taking what belongs to others for one's own benefit—both are defilements of greed (*lobha-mala*).
*Īrṣyā* (envy) refers to hating the virtuous and resenting the capable; *asūyā* (jealousy) refers to disliking talent and being wary of merit—both are... [defilements of envy].
The stain of hatred is also the stain of delusion. Once these three stains have arisen, all unwholesome dharmas are produced from them; therefore, they are called "roots.
Once the roots are established, they inevitably become difficult to regulate and difficult to subdue; thus, as stains, are they not exceedingly grave?
Because skillful means possess the power to uproot them, they are called "powers. Regarding the teaching of three within one:

Because defilements heavily obstruct wisdom, one desires to gradually eliminate them so that it may be gradually revealed. Based on this, how could the Buddhas' employment of expedient means (*upāya*) be anything other than unavoidable?
This concludes the section on the analysis and explanation. △ Fourth, the refutation of errors and the exhortation to practice, which has three parts:

first, a gentle refutation through indirect speech; second, a direct refutation face-to-face; third, the exhortation to believe and accept. Regarding the first: [The Tathāgata, though clearly aware of their faults, does not immediately point them out, but rather...]
He employs provisional speech and uses indirect expressions so that those who hear them may awaken on their own; this is the great sage’s virtue of warmth, gentleness, and harmony.
Śāriputra, if my disciples... [up to] ...are neither arhats nor pratyekabuddhas.

The initial statement was phrased with subtle intent: "If there be among my disciples such a person"—meaning, if among my disciples there is one who considers themselves an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha, that is, one of those content with a mere trifle—having become satisfied with a mere trifle, they pay no heed to the Buddha’s teaching on the Bodhisattva path, nor do they take it to heart; therefore, it is said: "No."
To hear and not understand—this is something the Tathāgata clearly knows regarding such a person. He uses indirect phrasing to point it out;

this is not a disparagement, but rather a rebuke intended to bring about awakening. He says that since one is a son of the Buddha, one ought to fully understand the Buddha’s work; yet now, you do not know it.

These are those who rely on the teachings of begging for alms; therefore, it is said they are not disciples of the Buddha. Having already realized the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, they ought to advance to hear the Great Dharma;
yet since they do not hear it now, they belong to the class of those who have not realized [the truth] but claim to have realized it. Thus, it is said they are not Arhats and not Pratyekabuddhas.
The three instances of the word "not" (*fei*) here carry a sense of profound censure and utter condemnation; other cases may be understood by analogy with this.

One must be profoundly awakened to this. △ Second, a direct rebuke face-to-face (The previous section used compliant and conciliatory words; because [the listener] was pleased but did not reflect upon them, this section uses words of the Dharma to rebuke him directly face-to-face.
This is the public impartiality of the Great Sage in loving the good and hating evil). Divided into three parts: 1. Directly rebuking his fault; 2.
Raising questions and providing an explanation; 3. Turning to further reveal his fault. First:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus (up to the point where it says) "you should know that all such as these are people of overweening pride.
At the outset, he points directly at them: "These bhikṣus," etc. He points specifically to individuals within the community of renunciants.
Those who say "I have already attained" and so forth are those who take provisional means to be the ultimate reality. Since they take provisional means to be the ultimate reality, regarding—
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they not only do not seek it, but furthermore lack the aspiration for it; thus it is said, "they no longer aspire to or seek it.

This indicates that the Tathāgata thoroughly understands their minds and points this out to them face-to-face. The phrase "one should know" and what follows below serves to censure their error so that they may understand:

since they have already reached the provisional fruit, they ought to seek the realization of the ultimate truth. Now, because they no longer aspire to or seek it, this is merely the provisional fruit.
It is not necessarily ultimate. Therefore it is said: "One should know that such people are those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Alas!
Those who were originally not overweeningly proud, yet sit with the name of "overweening pride" and no longer advance in their seeking—regarding this, one ought to feel deep pain.
II. Raising the Question and Providing the Explanation.
Why is this so? If there were a bhikṣu—or anyone else—who did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible.
The first phrase poses the question; "If there were... and so forth, provides the explanation. One who has truly attained arhatship would certainly never lack faith in this Dharma;
by this we know that one who no longer aspires [to further goals] is definitely not a true arhat. This is why it is said:
Such a person is one of overweening pride. △ Third, turning [the discourse] to reveal their faults:
"Except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before them... they will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma."
First, he accepts the previous exemption. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be times when the Buddha is not present;

it is possible that some arhats might not have faith in this Dharma, and for this reason, an exemption is granted. The following section raises a question to provide an explanation and establish the point:

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, regarding these sutras, one may seek to receive and uphold them even if they contradict the original [teachings], or read and recite them in comparison with the original, or understand them [through study].
As for their meaning, not even one or two in a hundred possess it; thus it is said that such persons are difficult to find.
Because such persons are difficult to find and lack a lineage of teachers, even if they are truly arhats, one cannot guarantee that there will be no stream of those who do not believe them.
This is the reason for excluding them. If, however, one encounters an inferior person who speaks with increasing clarity, claiming to be a truly realized arhat—
Although they may temporarily lack faith, it would be better for them not to encounter other Buddhas at all.

Should they, however, travel afar by means of supernatural powers or be reborn through the ripening of conditions and happen to meet another Buddha, they will immediately be able to resolve their provisional doubts and thoroughly comprehend the ultimate meaning.
Viewed from this perspective, those who persist in not seeking [the truth] further clearly manifest overweening pride; there is no doubt about it. Thus, he directly rebukes them face-to-face.

End. △ Third, the exhortation to believe and accept (Two rounds of rebukes have been issued; even a stubborn stone would nod its head. Therefore, this section concludes with an exhortation to believe and accept, bringing the meaning to its end).
"Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe and understand (up to: that there is no other vehicle, but only the single Buddha-vehicle.
The phrase "you all" specifically refers to a class such as Śāriputra who are faultless;
it certainly need not concern those among the assembly previously rebuked. Since you are not like them, you should therefore with one mind believe and understand.
Uphold the words of the Buddha. Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak without falsehood.
Since their speech is without falsehood, they would never, even twice or thrice, deceive sentient beings; therefore it is said that there is no other vehicle, but only the One Buddha Vehicle.
Since there is nothing else and only this one, do not be satisfied with what you have already attained; rather, you should...
This shall serve as the standard until [the goal] is realized. The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the introductory note to the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

△ (The main verses are divided into four parts: 1. One verse granting permission to speak and requesting attentive listening; 2. Two verses providing the formal analysis; 3. Three verses praising the Dharma and exhorting faith; 4.
Four verses censuring faults and concluding with an exhortation. First (a brief verse summarizing the meaning):
"Among the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, there were those who harbored overweening pride... (until) Śāriputra, listen well.

At the beginning, five thousand people withdrew from their seats (this introductory narrative is provided by the author of the prose; the following verses are spoken by the Tathāgata himself and do not belong to the category of *geya* [repeated verse], therefore I have directly annotated the essential points without labeling them as "verses.

Subsequent sections follow this pattern). Among the monastic community, many falsely manifested dignified deportment and feigned the appearance of meditative concentration; thus, they were particularly prone to harboring overweening pride.
Among the upāsakas, many harbor wealth and rely on their influence, clinging to appearances and seeking fame; thus they are specifically termed "those with pride" (māna).
Among the upāsikās, many place great weight on the sentiments of children and wives while regarding sin and merit lightly; thus they are specifically named "those without faith" (aśraddha).

According to the prose commentary (*gadya*), all four assemblies are termed "those with overweening pride" (abhimāna); here, however, each is described according to the predominant characteristic. As for overweening pride, it is focused primarily on external things.
Adorned [with external trappings], they do not know to reflect within. Arrogant, they only know how to pride themselves upon others; they fail to understand self-cultivation.
Lacking faith, they are ignorant of sin and merit, and deluded regarding virtue and fault; thus, they do not perceive their own transgressions.

Because they do not perceive them, these faults accumulate day by day and month by month, leading to deficiencies and omissions in the precepts. As for these deficiencies: the precepts are like a city wall and moat; once breached, they become...
[Text missing. Precepts are like an air-bladder; if they are damaged, they become leaky. "Guarding" refers to shielding [the precepts] out of fear that one's own shortcomings will be exposed.
"Cherishing" refers to fearing the difficulty of reforming them. A flaw within jade is called a *xia*; a flaw on its exterior is called a *ci*.

When precepts have deficiencies or leaks, it is just like this. Since the precepts already possess such flaws and leaks, as jade has its *xia* and *ci*, it is only right that one should confess and reveal them.
Reformation. Aiming for the perfection of the whole person, one should instead excel in protection;

to do otherwise, out of a singular fear of loss and cherishing [only oneself], is to be content with the lowly stream and unwilling to strive for higher advancement. Therefore, such a person is termed one of "small wisdom.

Because of this, they cannot bear to hear the Great [Dharma]. Thus, when the imperial decree was about to descend, it had already been issued beforehand. Among the multitude, the World-Honored One did not restrain them. (Long Chapter)

The author of the sutra records that he did not restrain him; the verses praising the Tathāgata clarify that he did not restrain him (the meaning of these two parts mutually illuminates one another). Those with overweening pride merely crave empty fame and do not apply themselves to genuine cultivation or actual realization.
They are like the dregs removed from wine or the husks removed from rice; therefore, they are called "dregs and chaff among the assembly.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror is impartial; he perceives their innermost hearts clearly. Although they wish to conceal their faults, there is [no way to do so].
He was unable [to do so]. Therefore it is said that he departed because of his majestic power (*vibhūti*).

Since he departed because of his majestic power, why did the Tathāgata not restrain him and cause him to become the one with the story of the tied jewel? It is entirely because this person’s precepts were deficient and his wisdom was narrow.

Those with meager merit and virtue are incapable of receiving this Great Dharma; it is just as a stagnant stream does not flow into a broken earthenware jar, and blessings do not descend upon the licentious.

Therefore, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not forbid them. This section [of the text] below, "This assembly... and so forth, serves to suppress the unworthy, exalt the worthy, and provide encouragement—this may be understood.
According to the prose commentary (*dīrghapada*), there is first the request for permission to speak, followed by the aspiration of those suited to the teaching to hear it.

Both [sections] are abbreviated. The verse concludes the instruction on "permission to speak" and "admonition to listen. △ Second, the verse for the formal analysis of the divisions (omitting the introductory verse), which has three parts:

first, one verse briefly analyzing the divisions; second, two verses citing turbidity to prevent difficulties; third, three verses providing a detailed analysis of the divisions. The first [part] has three [sub-sections].
First, a combined verse on the provisional [teachings] of self and others; second, a combined verse on the ultimate reality of self and others;

third, a verse of meaning that concludes by revealing the identity of the path. Regarding the first two: one verse concerns the provisional [teachings] of all Buddhas, and one verse concerns the provisional [teachings] of self-realization. First:
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through the power of immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*).

What the Buddhas have attained is true wisdom (*jñāna*); the immeasurable skillful means is provisional wisdom (*prajñā*). Because provisional wisdom adapts to the capacities of beings, it is said that they "teach for the sake of sentient beings.
This refers to what is described in the prose as "preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate. △ Second, the verse on self- [attainment].
The provisional [teachings] are twofold: first, those for the general capacity of all sentient beings; second, those specifically for the two vehicles. Regarding the first:
from "the various paths practiced according to the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings" up to the *Upadeśa Sūtra*.

First, regarding the capacity and nature of sentient beings: the single character "mindfulness" (*nian*) encompasses both the subject and the object. The mind of the sentient being is the subject that practices mindfulness;
the path they cultivate is the object of mindfulness. To explain its meaning: "mindfulness" refers to earnestly holding [the teaching] to one's heart, never forgetting it morning or night.

"The Path" refers to the primary and auxiliary methods of the Dharma cultivated by those of the Three Vehicles. As for these primary and auxiliary methods of the Dharma, their categories are manifold...
First: therefore it is said "various. This refers to the capacities and natures (*gotra*) of those of the three vehicles.
"Desire" (*chanda*) means the constant inclination of the mind, uninterrupted from moment to moment. Through this uninterrupted practice, one cultivates the capacity and nature of humans and devas;

hence it is called "desirous nature. Since these desirous natures are not uniform, they are called "numerous. Not only are the desirous natures numerous, but even the deeds performed in previous lives—

Karma also differs according to being wholesome or unwholesome; this is spoken of in terms of the spiritual capacities of humans and devas. "The Buddha fully [knows]" and below refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching and benefit.
"Having fully known this" means that he observes the capacities of beings with a standard. Through various conditions, parables, and so forth, he imparts the teachings without error.
Because he imparts the teachings without error, benefits are produced according to each individual's capacity, thereby causing all to rejoice. This is as described in the subsequent text.

This means that because their wishes are fulfilled, their minds each become courageous and sharp. Alternatively, it is said that this explains the distinctions within the Dharma-division (*dharmakāya*), the names and meanings of which are seen in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

2. Specifically for the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). (Although the Buddha’s compassion is universal, his intention to specifically address the Two Vehicles is great. This is because they were his former associates;

furthermore, having previously regressed from the Great Vehicle, compared to Bodhisattvas, their circumstances are pitiable, and compared to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are logically fit to be received.)
"Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are attached to birth and death—for them he preaches nirvana.

Within this, there are two types of dispositions among those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). If they originally came from within the Two Vehicles, they are of dull faculties and delight in inferior teachings.

If they originally came from among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are attached to birth and death. Regarding "those who delight in inferior teachings": [this refers to those whose capacities were previously developed through the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.]

Although one may encounter immeasurable Buddhas, if one does not practice the profound and wondrous path of a bodhisattva, that path is called "profound and wondrous" because it is the cause of non-abiding and is beyond the reach of the two vehicles.

Those who greedily cling to birth and death are entangled within the three realms and are constantly afflicted and disturbed by manifold sufferings; these sufferings are called "affliction and disturbance" because they oppress and torment the body.
Because their minds are agitated and distracted, for this reason I speak of *nirvāṇa*. This is because they do not practice the profound and subtle Path;

it is merely a temporary means to rescue those within the fortress of transformation. Because they are tormented and disturbed by manifold sufferings, I provide an urgent remedy like one whose eyebrows are on fire.

Such is not the original intent of transcending the world. The verse summarizing the provisional [teachings] regarding self and others is complete. △ Second, the verse summarizing the reality regarding self and others, in two parts.

The first verse concerns the reality of self-realization; the second verse concerns the reality of all Buddhas. Regarding the first two [verses], the first brings provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality, and the second shows how the three types of faculties obtain benefit. First:
"I have established these skillful means to enable [beings] to enter the Buddha-wisdom" (up to "for this reason I preach this sutra").

The initial separate assembly for the followers of the Two Vehicles, which establishes these skillful means to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom, clarifies the original intent behind the bestowal of provisional teachings (*upāya*).
"I have never said that you shall attain Buddhahood" clarifies that the provisional conceals the real, which is why it was not spoken of.

"The time for speaking has not yet arrived" clarifies the reason for concealing the real. "Now is precisely the time; I shall definitively proclaim the Great [Vehicle]" clarifies that the time has arrived and the teaching is revealed.
This means that the faculties and capacities of the audience are now matured; the opportunity must not be lost. Therefore, it is said: "Precisely."
At that time, [the teaching] reveals and clarifies the ultimate convergence; it teaches only bodhisattvas, and therefore it is said that "it definitively expounds the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, right and wrong arise in competition, and anger and affliction are produced. The production of affliction is precisely the delusion of anger.
Taking these three delusions as the root, the one hundred and eight afflictions arise from them; is this not the turbidity of afflictions? The passage beginning with "By means of all...
praises the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). With the aforementioned various desires as causes and conditions, greed, anger, and ignorance arise. The ground...
The retributions of hell, ghosts, and animals arrive before one has even turned a heel; hence it is said that one "falls into the three evil paths.

"Extremely received": does this not refer to the turbidity of sentient beings? Regarding "receiving the womb" below, the verse refers to the turbidity of lifespan.

This is because its substance is precisely the eight consciousnesses; entering the womb and receiving a life-span depend entirely upon them. As the *Jiugui* says:
"Going last and coming first, acting as the lord" refers to this. That it constantly increases from lifetime to lifetime is due to this cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*).

The union of heat and breath constitutes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). From lifetime to lifetime, it causes the physical body (*rūpakāya*) to grow; is this not the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*)?

Regarding those of meager virtue below, the verse refers to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*). Since the physical body has already grown, it is difficult to avoid discrepancies among the various classes of beings.
Among them, those of meager virtue and little merit lack the qualities for transcending the world and possess scant worldly fortune; therefore, they become...

Because these wrong views are numerous, they are called a "dense forest. Phrases such as "existence" or "non-existence" clearly illustrate the meaning of the multiplicity of wrong views.
"Existence" refers to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), while "non-existence" refers to the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); these two together constitute [the dense forest].
The extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), etc., include the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Taking these various views as their foundation, they are successively and falsely conceptualized, resulting in sixty-two types. For example: (1) reckoning that form itself is the self; (2) reckoning that the self is apart from form.
The form-aggregate is great and the self is small; the self is within the form-aggregate (3). The self is great and the form-aggregate is small; the form-aggregate is within the self (4).
As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with the other four aggregates. Together these constitute twenty views. When combined with the three time periods, they become sixty.

Adding the fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two views—this is what is called the "dense forest. Those who are deeply attached to these false dharmas [are trapped therein].

To regard what is not a fruit as a fruit results in no actual realization; this subsumes the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). this subsumes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). As for self-conceit (*atimāna*), it is to regard what is not a cause as a cause and to take pride in wrong precepts; this also subsumes [false views].
Regarding "precepts and views": the preceding text uses the term "etcetera" (ādi) ambiguously; this passage restates the characteristics of the four types of views. As for "flattery and crookedness":

[This is] the state of affairs. I know that when non-Buddhists hear this, their hearts and gallbladders will surely shatter together.
The *Zhao Yao Ji* says: "Those who adhere to false views have all their mental faculties deluded; they live as if in a drunken dream and die drowning in the cycle of rebirth.

"Encountering the Buddha in this world" means hearing the Dharma and practicing giving and so forth, which refers to cultivating practice according to the teachings. If one discusses the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), they constitute one of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Fundamentally, they are not distinct from external skillful means; however, because the capacity of the practitioners lies within the realms of devas and humans, their conduct pertains to phenomenal forms (*lakṣaṇa*), and thus what is cultivated is...
Their merit and wisdom were entirely of the outflowing (sāsrava) nature; thus, they differed from external expedients. By taking these as conditions, they assisted in manifesting the True Cause.
Although at that time they belonged to the outflowing realm, they gradually entered the outflow-free (anāsrava). Up to the present, they have all attained the fruits of the Way. Therefore it is said:
"All such persons as these have already attained the Buddha-way. △ Second, the assembly relying on the teaching after the Buddha’s extinction, in four parts. First:

1. The assembly that turns their hearts through longing for the Buddha; 2. The assembly that erects stupas and builds shrines; 3. The assembly that constructs physical forms and painted images; 4. The assembly that makes offerings to images while reciting the names [of the Buddhas]. Regarding the first:
after the parinirvāṇa of the various Buddhas, if there are people with gentle and supple minds, all such sentient beings have already attained the path of Buddhahood.

The Dharma-body is true and eternal; it is fundamentally indestructible. Because sentient beings saw that the Buddha remained for a long time, they became arrogant, self-indulgent, weary, and indolent, and thus [the Buddha] used skillful means to transcend the world. Therefore, it is said, "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Due to the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, having nothing left to rely upon, they finally realized the need to abandon evil and cultivate goodness, transforming their rigidity into flexibility; hence, it is called "a mind of goodness and gentleness. Nevertheless, although this assembly...

Even those who encounter a Buddha and fail to awaken may still turn their hearts toward enlightenment after his passing. One must know that a single thought of goodness serves as the foundation for Bodhi;
a single moment of softness is sufficient to open the gate to the myriad practices. Therefore it is said: "Such sentient beings have all already attained the Way.
This refers to those who, like a lamp whose light has been extinguished, redouble their diligence in seeking the Unsurpassed Way. △
Second, regarding the multitude who erect stupas and build temples:
those who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, made offerings to their *śarīra* relics (up to the point where it says) "have all already attained the Buddha-way.
Making offerings to *śarīra* relics should pertain to the capacities of humans and devas. According to the present account, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa said:
The relics of the Tathāgata are not our concern; there are kings, ministers, elders, householders, and others who delight in the field of merit—this statement can serve as proof.
Regarding the "ten thousand billion kinds of stupas," human capacities are not uniform, and thus there are many varieties of stupas, ranging from gold and silver to agate (*musāragalva*).
[Note: see the preceding text regarding *meigui*, which refers to *sphaṭika* (crystal) or *musāragalva* (lapis lazuli/agate). Xu...

The Master said: "Fire-crystal (huoqí) resembles pearls and is red in color; its layers arise with each stratum distinct from the others. One description says it is like mica opening in successive layers.
Although lapis lazuli (liúlí) and the aforementioned crystal (bōlí) are both found in this region, they differ from those of the Western Regions.
Those [Western varieties] are of natural substance, whereas these are produced through smelting and refining. 'Pearl' refers to the true [pearl]."
As for the "beads" (*maṇi*): if they are not lapis lazuli, they are indeed beads. As with the various jewels mentioned above, their substance is pure and their types are manifold;
they may adorn the exterior or embellish the interior. Thus it is said: "Pure, vast, and magnificently adorned.

In arranging and calibrating these [descriptions], one must ensure that the literary style and the underlying substance are in harmony. When the *stūpa* soars into the clouds, its stars-like patterns are seen spread out like a chessboard. Therefore...
Regarding the adornment of various stupas: as for stone temples, they are constructed of stone; those made of sandalwood and below are constructed of wood and other materials.
Sandalwood and agallochum are the most solid in substance and can be used for beams and rafters.

There is a type of wood called *shuǎn* (juniper) that can be carved and engraved to serve as decorative brackets and crossbeams. Other timbers of varying qualities are used for pillars and rafters, each according to its suitability.
And so they employ them: using bricks for the walls, tiles to cover the roof, mud to bind the structure together, and earth to accumulate as a supporting mound.
This is because they were unable to erect a stūpa, yet erected a shrine; unable to use precious materials, they used wood, earth, tiles, and stones.
As for the "vast wilderness," it is a place devoid of human presence; and within this place devoid of human presence, [the shrine] was established.
There are two meanings to a Buddhist temple: first, to provide a place for the construction of the Dharma; second, to enable those on the path of suffering to know where to return.
There are likewise two meanings to constructing it by piling up earth: first, because building materials are difficult to procure; second, because one desires to honor simplicity over ornamentation.

One whose emotional springs have not yet opened and whose innate purity has not yet been lost is called a "child" (*tóng*). One who is unburdened by worldly desires and enters into the realm of spontaneity is called "playful" (*xì*).
There are two meanings to the act of piling sand to form a stupa: first, the planting of seeds; second, the resonance with the environment. Regarding the planting of seeds:

through past reverence for the Buddha, seeds were deposited within the field of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṣetra*); at this present time, when one is unburdened by worldly desires, these manifest as a current realization.
Because it is through practice. Regarding "the object evoking [a response]": one builds a stupa because of having seen [the Buddha]. The object meets with the mind;

at the moment of entering this state of self-attainment, it is evoked by the sincerity of one's intent. However, while building stupas and constructing temples fundamentally belongs to the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), piling up earth or gathering sand remains merely incidental.
One must know that the cause of a single basketful of earth can achieve the momentum of a layered cliff; this is the first step.
It serves as a condition for reaching a journey of a thousand *li*. Therefore it is said: "All such persons have already attained the Way.
△ Third, the assembly of those who construct physical forms and painted images.
If a person, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images—[extending] to the point of liberating immeasurable multitudes—they establish these images as an offering to the Buddha.
Whether they manifest as compassion or majesty, concentration or wisdom, they accord with the mind of the creator;
thus, it is said "various. With the *dāna-pāramitā* and the other perfections as the substance, they are carved and sculpted into patterns, [displaying] the thirty-two marks, mark by mark.
Because they are complete, they are called a "multitude. However, the Dharma-body is without form; thus, one borrows form to manifest the Truth.

Since one has faith in the Truth and fashioned these images, the cause is spontaneously established, leading to the attainment of the fruit; hence it is said that "all have already attained the Way. As for those made of the seven treasures:
gold and silver belong to the category of casting and smelting, while the remaining treasures also involve carving and engraving. Brass and yellow copper resemble gold, as does bronze.

Regarding the category of gold: thus, the character for "copper" (tóng) is composed of the radical for "metal" (jīn) and the character for "same" (tóng). As for "color," two types are mentioned; hence it is called "red and white copper.
White tin, lead, and pewter belong to the category of "blue metal" (qīngjīn); the most refined among them is called white tin, while that produced in Shu is called lead.
Regarding the term *guǐyángshēng* (桂楊生), it refers to tin (*xī*). Although most circulating editions use the character "wax" (*là*), this is an error; it is now correctly rendered as "tin" (*lì*).
This is why the colloquial usage combines "tin" and "lì" as a single term. There are two types of iron: first, that which is cast by melting, and second, that which is forged by smelting.
Since the present work involves making images, it must belong to the category of casting. As for wood and clay: wood serves as the structural core, while clay...

[Some] take [the image] to be made of flesh; this increases the sense of its being an embryo. Others consist of three materials—glue, lacquer, and cloth—which are blended together to form a substance.

These are then adorned and refined, with patterns created through painting and the application of gauze. These various forms also arise from the differing capacities of human effort, such that the physical representations each differ.

Nevertheless, when one investigates the heart of reverence for the Buddha, they all originate from a single source. There is none that does not take the seed as its cause; therefore, it is said that "all..."
He has already attained the Way. As for those who create images of the Buddha through painting—whether on paper, silk, cloth, or fine fabric—they apply five colors to depict his form.
These "marks" refer to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). By citing the causes, one reveals the fruit; thus it is said they are "adorned with a hundred blessings.
This is because each and every mark is the result of being moved by the cultivation of a hundred blessings. One may do this oneself or have others do so.
As for those who have already attained the Way, though there may be distinctions of kinship—close or distant—in their causal stage, there is no difference in their resultant state.

The character is often written as "bi" (茟), but Master Padmasambhava said this is an error. "Bi" (筆) is derived from the "bamboo" radical and is pronounced *bi*; "bi" (茟) is derived from the "grass" radical and is pronounced *wei*.

"Bi" (茟) refers to the initial budding of flowers on grasses or trees. Regarding the children's game, it originally belongs to the realm of the mindless; whether it involves grass or wood, it pertains to both grasses and trees.
It arises at the very beginning; as soon as it is brought forth, it is put to use. Thus it is said: "Whether it be grass, wood, or a brush—even a fingernail may suffice.

Whether one paints an image of the Buddha on a wall or pierces it into the earth, regardless of whether it resembles [the Buddha] or not, if one's fundamental mind regards it as the Buddha, it is then called an image of the Buddha.
By this, the seed of Buddhahood is impressed upon the *ālayavijñāna*, and when it encounters conditions...
It gradually increases; through long accumulation, it becomes virtue. Therefore, it is said that one "gradually accumulates merit. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Vows," states:
"Because of sentient beings, great compassion arises; because of great compassion, the bodhicitta is produced; because of the bodhicitta..."
Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, he is said to be "endowed with great compassion. All have achieved the Buddha-way;
whatever they do is always for a single purpose, hence it is said that "he transforms only bodhisattvas. Guiding them step by step with skillful inducement, his teaching does not skip over stages;
thus he is able to deliver and liberate immeasurable beings. Viewed from this perspective, even childhood play—which originally belongs to the realm of the mindless—still gradually accumulates merit.

Virtue. Possessing a heart of compassion, they proceed until they attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings, being no different from the Buddhas themselves. How much more so for those of the Three Vehicles!
If they can abandon the provisional to follow the real, gradually accumulating merit without dwelling [on it], how could they be inferior to children’s play?
Those who lack self-confidence merely delude themselves and abandon themselves. △ Fourth, the assembly of those who offer to images and recite the name.
"If a person [makes offerings] at a stūpa or temple, to a precious image or a painted image... (down to) all have already attained the Buddha-way.

Regarding "if a person [makes offerings] at a stūpa or temple," this means that as for the location, it refers to both stūpas and temples; as for the images, it refers to both precious and painted ones;
and as for the objects, it refers to both incense, flowers, banners, and canopies. Provided one gives rise to a heart of reverence and makes an offering, one shall [attain the Way].

It constitutes a supreme cause. Music consists of five notes and twelve scales, with voices alternating in song and harmony to serve as the rhythmic measure for song, dance, and the eight musical instruments;
therefore, it causes people to produce them. The *jiao* is a large conch shell. The drum is the sovereign of all sounds.
The conch shell (*śaṅkha*) leads all clamorous sounds; therefore, it is explained first. The *xiāo* was created by Yù Shùn.
It is made by binding small bamboo tubes together, which are arranged unevenly to resemble the wings of a phoenix. The large version consists of twenty-three tubes and is one chi four cun long;
the small version consists of sixteen tubes and is one chi two cun long. There is also a bottomless variety called the *dòng*.
The Xiao (Percussion Flute). Explanation of its meaning: "Xiao" signifies solemnity (*su*). This refers to its sound being solemn and clear. The Di (Transverse Flute):
Emperor Huangdi commissioned Linglun to cut bamboo from Kunxi to craft it. It generally has seven holes, though there are also varieties with three holes.
It is called the *qiāngdí* (Qiang flute). It was made by Qiu Zhong during the time of Emperor Wu. It is one chi and four cun long. Regarding its etymology: "dí" means "to cleanse.
It signifies cleansing away depravity and impurity, and receiving [the mind] into that which is elegant and correct. The *qín* (zither) was made by Shennong; some say it was made by Fuxi.
It is three chi, six cun, and six fen long, corresponding to the number of days in a year. Its width is six cun.

The six sides represent the Six Directions; the five strings represent the Five Elements. The waist is four inches wide, representing the Four Seasons. It is broad in front and narrow behind, representing the distinction between the noble and the humble.
It is circular above and square below, representing Heaven and Earth. The thirteen rays represent the twelve months together with the intercalary month.
Later, King Wen added two strings, the minor *gong* and the minor *shang*. Some say that King Wen and King Wu each added one string.

Furthermore, Cai Yong of the Later Han dynasty added two more strings, bringing the total to nine to symbolize the nine stars. Regarding the etymological interpretation: the *qin* (zither) is "prohibition" (*jin*);
it means to prohibit and restrain depravity and lust in order to rectify the human heart. As for the *konghou*, it was created by the master Yan at the command of Zhou.
It was created as a music of seductive charm. It was likely preserved by lords from empty states; thus, it is named after the "empty" *hóu* (pipe) and its bamboo construction.
As for the *pípá*, the originator of its design is unknown. It measures three feet five inches in length, symbolizing the Three Powers (*sān-cái*) and the Five Elements (*wǔ-xíng*).
Its four strings symbolize the Four Seasons. When the hand pushes forward, it is called *pí*; when the hand draws back, it is called *pá*. It is played in accordance with the drumbeats.
Regarding the names: the *nāgaṇṭhā* and *tāla* can be understood accordingly. In summary, these nine types [of musical instruments] have rhythms that are perfectly suited;

thus it is called "such wondrous sounds. He commands those who hold them to chant praises to the Triple Gem; thus it is said, "offering all with devotion. To express one's inner feelings through the modulation of tones is called *gīta* (song);
to chant with pure and resonant *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice) is called *bhāṣya* (chanting). This is truly because the Buddha’s virtues are so preeminent that all who behold him rejoice. Desiring—
I rely on these verses to express my sentiments; thus, I entrust them to this pure and resonant *brahman*-sound to be chanted as a hymn. Even with only two lines, there is a profound implication:
if even a single sound, though small, has already attained Buddhahood, how much more so for those who offer various musical instruments and those who sing long songs and vast hymns!
The phrase "with a distracted mind" distinguishes this from an attitude of reverence. As for "a single flower":

"Selecting against many objects" means that regarding painted images, one selects against those made of precious materials; by taking these as the conditions, one gradually accomplishes superior causes, and thus is able to see countless Buddhas.
Since one can see countless Buddhas, the causes are perfected and the fruits are fulfilled;
it is clear that such a person has already attained Buddhahood. Regarding "prostration," there is no material object to offer, but one pays respect with the body. Regarding "joining the palms":

One does not have the leisure to perform a full prostration; rather, one raises the hands and focuses the mind. As for "one hand," this means holding the right and embracing the left; the half-palm signifies sincerity.
As for "lowering the head," this refers to those who drive carriages or ride horses, where nodding the head serves as a substitute for bowing.

Thus, although these forms of etiquette may be complete or deficient, and the palms may be joined as a pair or singly, they all originate from the sincerity of a single mind. And since the Buddha accepts only that sincere heart, therefore—
It says, "By means of this, one makes offerings to the image. The two phrases beginning with "Gradually seeing" clarify that through long accumulation, causes are formed;

this is the principle of attaining the fruit by means of the cause. The passage beginning with "Extensively saving those below" clarifies that after the fruit is attained, one manifests transformation; this is the principle of withdrawing one's brilliance once transformation is complete.

The reason these terms—both manifesting transformation and withdrawing brilliance—are used together is to provide an admonition for those of the Two Vehicles. The intention is that they [the Two Vehicles] are... [incomplete source].
Because of minor good deeds, and by virtue of not dwelling in self-conceit, you have gradually come to behold the various Buddhas and accomplished supreme causes.
Thus, you have now attained Buddhahood and completed the work of delivering sentient beings. Yet you, O Śrāvakas, still linger in the "City of Transformation"—how truly lamentable!
Those who enter stupas and temples with distracted minds do so because of incidental circumstances; it is not out of sincere devotion. To recite "Namo" even once—

Regarding "there being no Buddha": this refers to generating the mind of enlightenment upon seeing a physical sign; it is not the result of constant mindfulness. The *Sammitīyanikāya-śāstra* (Zhengliang lun) quotes:
"In the past, there was a woodcutter who was pursued by a tiger. As he climbed a tree, fearing he would not reach safety, he called out the name of the Compassionate One, 'Buddha,' once."
Taking the planting of seeds as the cause, one now plants [the roots of merit] for the World-Honored One’s attainment of enlightenment.

Based on this, the statement that even recollecting the Buddha with a distracted mind has already resulted in the attainment of enlightenment is not false. (Question: In this context, the invocation of the name with a distracted mind, as well as the previous instances of drawing images with grass and fingernails or piling sand to form stupas, are merely occasional moments of thought.)

In children’s play there is no conscious intent; how could they know that there is a teaching upon which to rely? When the Buddha has passed away, by what means can the assembly that relies on the teaching gather such [virtue]? Answer: Building stupas, painting images, recollecting the Buddha, and chanting his name—these are the clear instructions found within the Tathāgata’s teachings.

Although those acts may have been performed as a mere fleeting thought during children’s play without conscious intent, they nonetheless spread outward through the successive influence of the Tathāgata’s bequeathed teachings. If these matters had never before been seen or heard of, why would one heap sand to make a stupa? Why would one use grass and fingernails to paint an image? Why would one chant the name with a distracted mind?

Therefore, even though it was children’s play without intent and a fleeting thought, and they were unaware that there was a teaching upon which to rely, they nevertheless relied upon it spontaneously. This is brought about by the inconceivable power of the Buddhist teaching.
The section on the assembly that relies on the teaching after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa concludes. △ Third, the detailed record of the prophesied assembly:
"In all past buddhas, whether during their lifetimes or after their parinirvāṇa, those who have heard this Dharma have all already attained the path of the Buddha."
"When the various Buddhas are in the world, those who hear this Dharma refer to the assembly for whom the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* made its broad predictions.

After the various Buddhas have passed into extinction, those who hear this Dharma refer to the assembly for whom the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* made its remote predictions. This refers to the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) of the original sutra.

The *Guangji* (Extensive Commentary) states regarding the present: "As for those of such categories who, before the Buddha, hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoice with even a single thought of sympathetic joy—I shall bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, the text concerning the future prophecy states: "After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa..."

If there is anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment, I likewise grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The statement here that "they have all already attained the Way" is due to the power of the broad predictions and far-reaching prophecies of all Buddhas, as well as the force of their sustaining grace. (Question: This differs from the provisional and the real; why do you alone perceive this error?)

[The section on] "The Buddhas of the Past. Do the Buddhas of the present and future not also possess this? Answer: Because the past is easier to believe, it is mentioned alone. One must know that the Way of every Buddha is the same; by citing one corner, the other three can be inferred.

[The verse] praising the identity of the Buddhas of the past is concluded. △ Second, the verse praising the identity of the Buddhas of the future has two parts: first, the direct verse corresponding to the prose; second, the supplementary verse for preventing objections. First:
The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number (until there is not one who does not become a Buddha).

Initially, they employ provisional means based on the ultimate reality; eventually, all [beings] below [the highest level] will return from the provisional to the real. This differs slightly from the prose section.

The meaning is in fact entirely the same. △ Second, the supplementary verses to prevent objections, which have four parts: first, preventing the objection as to how it could be that "one" is not established;
second, preventing the objection that it is inconsistent to explain all dharmas extensively; third, preventing the objection as to why it must be solely for the sake of the One Vehicle.

The fourth defense is that there is only one principle which ought to be explained swiftly as a rebuttal. First, the objection states: "Although the Dharma originates from a single source, the capacities of sentient beings differ in a thousand ways.

It may be granted that if one hears [the teaching], various interpretations arise, some succeeding and others failing. How can you claim that merely hearing the Dharma ensures there is no one who does not attain Buddhahood? Therefore, this defense is stated."
"The fundamental vows of all Buddhas are: 'The Buddha-way that I have practiced, I desire that all sentient beings may likewise attain.

These are called the fundamental vows of all Buddhas; by means of the various practices they themselves have cultivated, they dedicate them to sentient beings so that all may universally attain this Way.
Therefore, anyone who merely hears the Dharma enters together upon the raft of the Tathāgata’s great vow, whether far or near."
They will all, without exception, attain Buddhahood. This is just as when many people—whether rich or noble, poor or lowly—board a single boat together;
by the power of that vessel, there are none who do not reach the other shore. 2. Preventing the objection that it is improper to explain the various dharmas extensively (*Nan-yun*:

"Since you vow that they shall all equally attain this Way, it is improper to explain the various dharmas extensively. If you must preach countless dharma-gates, for what purpose is this? Therefore, the following defense is given").
Although the Buddhas of future ages shall preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality they constitute but a single vehicle.
Regarding the Buddhas of the future, although they preach countless Dharma-gates, when one examines their original intent, it is solely for the sake of the One Vehicle.
This still does not contradict the original vow. △ Third, preventing the objection that why must it be exclusively for the One Vehicle (the objection states:

"At the gateway of manifested transformation, there is no lack of even a single dharma; since the extensive teaching has already been established as a provisional benefit, why must it be exclusively for the One Vehicle? Therefore, this defense is stated)."

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature; the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions, and for this reason they teach the One Vehicle.

To say "the Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings" means they have thoroughly realized that all phenomena are fundamentally without self-nature; this is what is called the "lineage of the Buddhas."
They also arise from conditions, yet that which arises from conditions is not real; it likewise lacks the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since all things are devoid of intrinsic nature, this single matter alone is real. For this reason, only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is taught, precisely because it is the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);

not a single dharma is established there, for apart from this, there is nothing else to be said. However, the commentaries of the ancient masters on this single verse are mostly profound and abstruse, causing students...
This is difficult to comprehend; I shall now explain it once more. "Knowledge" (jñāna) means thorough understanding. "Dharmas" encompass both the sentient and the insentient.

Both the sentient and the insentient arise from True Suchness (tathatā) following defiled conditions; they fundamentally belong to the false manifestations of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), and are therefore said to be "without intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva).
"Buddha-seeds" refers to the lineage (gotra) of all Buddhas. Although the Buddha-lineage follows True Suchness in its aspect of purity...
It arises through conditions and likewise belongs to the false manifestation of the dependent nature; therefore, it is said to "proceed from conditions.
All sentient beings do not understand this meaning and falsely claim that the Buddha and all phenomena exist as substantial realities.

This is to further give rise to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra*). Only the Buddhas are free from both pervasive conceptualization and the dependent nature; therefore, they are said to "know. Since—
Having understood this, one realizes that only the perfected state (*pariniṣpanna*) remains as the true substance of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Therefore, only the One Vehicle is taught. This is further evidenced by the statement in the preceding text: "This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true.

△ Fourth, preventing the objection that since it is solely for the sake of the One Vehicle, it ought to have been taught sooner (The objection states: "Since it is solely for the sake of the One Vehicle, it should have been taught immediately. Yet all Buddhas have long remained silent regarding this essential point. Furthermore...")
Why is this? Therefore, it is said: "This Dharma abides in its place;
the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Teacher speaks through skillful means.

To speak of this as the Dharma of the One Vehicle is to abide within the station of all dharmas. Since one abides within the station of all dharmas, then the characteristics of the world are none other than reality;

therefore, it is called "eternally abiding. If even the characteristics of the world are themselves eternally abiding, how much more so that which the Tathāgata has taught according to what is appropriate—how could that not be reality? Thus we know that the Buddhas are not unreal.

I have long remained silent regarding this essential point. This was because the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) already knew me; acting as a guide for sentient beings, I have merely taught the One Vehicle through skillful means.
If there is still anything unclear, let me attempt to explain it further: this Dharma is the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of the One Vehicle. "Abiding" means remaining.
The "dharma-position" (dharmasthiti) refers to the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all dharmas. The intrinsic nature of all dharmas is both [this and that].

Because they do not reach one another, they are called "positions" (*sthāna*). The "characteristics of the world" (*loka-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, as it is the characteristic by which the world is established;
therefore, it is "eternally abiding. The "eternal abiding" refers to the true reality (*tathatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);

because this true reality of the One Vehicle cannot be found when sought within the coming and going of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is eternal. Here, the first phrase clarifies that the ultimate dharma is present right here.

All phenomena (*dharmas*): in principle, they are events; in events, they are principle. The second phrase means that all phenomena, in their very substance, are the true dharma; in events, they are principle.

One who realizes this will not find it difficult to understand why [the Buddha] has long remained silent regarding this essential point. Regarding the section "In the Way" and below, the meaning is easy to clarify.
The verses on the commonality of future Buddhas are concluded. △ Third, the verses on the commonality of present Buddhas, in two parts: first, the direct verses on the Long [Discourse].
[The] Practice. Second, the supplementary verse preventing questions. First:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions currently present, who are honored by devas and humans" (up to) "in reality, they are for the Buddha-vehicle.

The first verse provides a general indication: because the Tathāgatas are fully endowed with wisdom and the abandonment [of defilements], they are worthy of being fields of merit for humans and devas; therefore, they are called "devas."
People make offerings [to him]. Initially, he teaches the Three Vehicles to cause them to rest at the illusory city; later, he teaches the One Vehicle to cause them to enter the place of jewels.
