"Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I observe [the world]... and give rise to great compassion.

This first clarifies the Buddha who has attained realization; wishing to detail the causes and conditions for his appearance in the world, he again addresses Śāriputra, instructing him that he "should know.
When I distinguish this from other Buddhas, it is likewise established in accordance with worldly convention and is not a grasping at substantial existence. As for "observing with the Buddha-eye":
Dacheng says: "To distinguish the capacities of sentient beings, one employs the Dharma-eye; yet, because the Buddha-eye is perfectly pervasive, it subsumes the inferior by citing the superior.
Furthermore, since the four eyes enter into the Buddha, they are all termed the 'Buddha-eye. Regarding the phrase 'seeing the six [realms]' below:

this clarifies the assembly of those who can be influenced—the sentient beings of the six paths. Having failed to cultivate superior causes, they lack the adornment of merit and virtue; thus, they are poor and destitute."

Furthermore, they lack the support of the Buddha-dharma; thus, being destitute, they possess no wisdom. Lacking both merit and wisdom, they cannot escape saṃsāra, and so they enter into the cycle of birth and death.
Regarding why birth and death are called a "perilous path," the *Sammitīya-śāstra* states:

"In terms of fame and status, one may serve in the imperial court in the morning and be banished to the coastal frontiers by evening. In terms of body and life, one may dwell in a magnificent hall yesterday."
Now, returning to the yellow earth, if we observe this process of rising and sinking, one is born as a human or a celestial being only to fall again into the evil realms;
is this not perilous? As for "continuity," once one has entered the cycle of birth and death, the wheel turns without ceasing. This is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* means when it says:
"Death after birth, birth after death; like a whirling firebrand, there is no rest. It is because of birth and death...
Because there is no rest, one is oppressed by old age and illness, and encounters the likes of loved ones and enemies;
since there is no means of liberation, it is said that "suffering is not severed. To be deeply attached to the five desires and so forth precisely clarifies the meaning of suffering being unsevered.
As for why the sentient beings of the six realms find their suffering unsevered, it is because deep attachment to the five desires serves as its very foundation. As it is said:
As for the *mṛgī* (yak): it serves as an extreme illustration of the harm caused by desire. This animal is the name of a beast from the southwestern tribes.

By nature, it is fond of its tail; when lying down, it turns its head toward its tail. Because the head is turned toward the tail, the eyes are obstructed by the tail. Thus, it is said that "greedy attachment blinds oneself.

Because one blinds oneself, one becomes like one who is blind or like one who is in darkness (blindness refers to having no pupils in the eyes; being in darkness refers to having no light in the eyes).

[The Buddha] said: "Even if one were to watch for it and kill it, one would see nothing at all. To take this as a metaphor means that sentient beings who are attached to desire follow after desire with their minds;
their wisdom is obscured by desire, and thus they are like those who are intoxicated or deluded.
They wound the Dharma-body and harm the life of wisdom, yet remain unaware of it—no different from that yak. The Buddha is like a guide who is able to...
It leads those on the path of delusion; therefore, it is called "Great Power. The Dharma is like a correct road, capable of leading one away from perilous paths;

therefore, it is called "Severing Suffering. Sentient beings are blinded by their attachment to desire and thus do not seek it. If they do not seek the Buddha, they easily become confused by false teachers;
if they do not seek the Dharma, they easily fall into false paths. Consequently, they descend into the dense forest of wrong views, clinging to them firmly and refusing to relinquish them.
Because these powerful [afflictions] are difficult to uproot, it is said that they have "penetrated deeply.

Due to this deep penetration of wrong views, one may engage in futile and unbeneficial ascetic practices—such as plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose with smoke, smearing ashes on the body, or going naked—in the desire to escape all suffering.

This constitutes "using suffering to abandon suffering," and for this reason, suffering is not severed. According to the ancient masters, in this regard, by means of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*)...

Commentary: Although I now venture to draw a comparison, they are largely the same with minor differences. For instance, the sentient beings of the six realms correspond to the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the defilement of beings).
The continuous succession of birth and death corresponds to the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (the defilement of lifespan), as it was previously stated that "it constantly increases from lifetime to lifetime.

Deep attachment to the five desires corresponds to the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of afflictions), because greed and desire are the root of all afflictions. To enter deeply into false views [corresponds to the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*].
This refers to the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). Taken collectively, these four defilements constitute the accumulation that is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*).

The reason this sequence differs from the previous one is that the five defilements arise with a force like that of interlocking hooks and chains; they act as causes for one another, and thus their order is not fixed.

The final two lines conclude the meaning of "eliciting" (gan). It is precisely because the five turbidities of sentient beings revolve and circulate without ceasing that the Tathāgata manifests auspicious signs of the holy and enters the mundane world to benefit all things. Therefore, it is said: "For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to great compassion.
This concludes the section on the elicitation by the faculties of sentient beings. II. The Tathāgata’s Responsive Transformation. 1. From the Ultimate Bestowal to the Provisional Establishment.

Expedient Means (Upāya). The two assemblies demonstrate how expedient means return to the ultimate reality. The first [assembly] has three parts: first, not attaining [reality] from the ultimate; second, concealing the ultimate to establish expedient means; third, the initial [section]. The third [part] has three sections:

first, seven days of contemplation; second, the devas requesting the Dharma; third, reflecting that there is no [other] plan. The first [of these three]: [The text continues with the narrative of the Buddha’s contemplation.]
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I contemplated the tree and also walked back and forth...

[until] how can they be delivered? This is the initial general statement of his reflection. Regarding this occasion as the beginning of his transformation of others, it is designated as "the start. "Sitting" (āsana) encompasses both the agent and the object;
the agent who sits is the Buddha, and the object upon which he sits is the bodhimaṇḍa. A "maṇḍa" refers to a boundary or ground; this location is in Magadha.
The country of Gayā is not far from the Nairañjanā River. Because the Tathāgata sat here and attained enlightenment, it is called the Bodhimaṇḍa (Place of Enlightenment).
As for those who contemplate the tree, they look upward with deep reflection; as for those who walk the path, they circumambulate with heads bowed—this is the manner of such contemplation.
Regarding the contemplation of these matters during the three seven-day periods, according to the *Inga-kyo* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect), during the first seven days he contemplated...
I thought: "My Dharma is subtle and wondrous, and there is no one capable of receiving it. After reflecting for two weeks, I considered those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

After reflecting for another three weeks, I considered who should hear the Dharma first. For now, I shall provide a general indication by saying: "Thus have I heard. From "What I have [taught]" below...

To explain this matter separately: regarding the wisdom attained, speaking in terms of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), it is profoundly deep and immeasurable, such that the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) cannot surpass it;
hence it is called "subtle and foremost. The "faculties" (*indriya*) refer to the five faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

Because these are weak and inferior, they are easily impaired when encountering adverse conditions; hence they are called "dull. Those who "cling to pleasure" are those who are greedily attached to worldly pleasures. [They are] greedily attached to the world...
They delight [in worldly things]. Their eye of wisdom is blinded by delusion and craving; consequently, both the superior and middling faculties are unobtainable.
Since the superior and middling are unobtainable, only those of inferior stream remain; thus it is said: "How can such types as these be delivered?

If one were to correlate this passage specifically with the three periods of seven days, the first two lines correspond in meaning to the initial seven days of contemplation on the subtlety of my Dharma.

"There is no one capable of receiving [the teaching]" refers to the next two lines, which correspond in meaning to the twenty-eight days of contemplation for those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

"The last two lines" correspond in meaning to the twenty-one days of contemplation. As for the question, "Who should hear the Dharma first? How can they be saved?", this refers precisely to contemplating who should be saved first.

(Question: During the twenty-one days, in meaning this corresponds to the time of the *Avataṃsaka*; yet now you only speak of "contemplation. Is it that the *Avataṃsaka* teaching has not yet been expounded? Answer: It is precisely contemplation...)

"At that time" refers precisely to the period when the *Avataṃsaka* was being taught—this is what Tiantai meant by "the two aspects hanging down together" and "the two beginnings occurring simultaneously. △ Second, the request for the Dharma by the various devas.
At that time, the various Brahma Kings and the various Śakras, Lords of Devas (down to) requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma.

First, the various devas are introduced as the standard; below, they formally request with full ritual decorum. This is identical to the occasion when [the Buddha] attained Great Penetration and became a Buddha.
The manner in which the various devas request the Dharma is the same; however, in this place there are many *kāmadhātu* devas, whereas in that [other] place the ritual involves much offering.
In reality, both possess these elements, yet their manifestations differ. △ Third, the contemplation of the absence of calculation.
"I then reflected to myself: 'If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle... [they] would quickly enter nirvana. Regarding this "reflection to oneself":
it was intended to repay the request of the devas, yet it involved further reflection on the matter of delivering sentient beings.

According to the preceding account of the three seven-day periods, he had been engaged solely in such reflection. Now, when it says, "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle," it appears to follow from what preceded.
Having already offered praise, it is now further confirmed that the time for right reflection is precisely the time for the correct exposition of the *Avataṃsaka*.

As for sentient beings submerged in suffering—within the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, which are as boundless as the ocean—they are drowning therein and are unable to emerge on their own.
Since even escaping from suffering cannot be attained, how could one believe in attaining Buddhahood? Therefore, it is said that they do not believe in this Dharma.

Because they do not believe in this Dharma, they instead slander the Buddha’s teachings; this constitutes the destruction of the Dharma. Due to the causes and conditions of destroying the Dharma, one will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms.
Thus, because of their lack of faith, they plummet into the three evil paths. In this way, the teaching of the Dharma suffers loss. Not...

If he did not preach, his remaining in the world would be of no benefit; it would be better for him not to remain at all. Therefore, it is said: "It would be better not to preach the Dharma and enter nirvana quickly.
This was merely the Tathāgata’s figurative expression of deep sorrow, no different from Confucius’s lamentation over crossing the sea.

From the perspective of reality, one does not attain the ultimate. △ Second, concealing the real to manifest the provisional, in three parts: 1. Recalling the skillful means; 2. The consolation of all Buddhas; 3. Properly bestowing the provisional vehicle. First [part]: Recalling the Skillful Means The Buddha, having attained the path of the Tathāgata, has already realized the supreme, true Dharma. Yet, he observes that sentient beings have long been submerged in the ocean of birth and death, suffering from various afflictions. Therefore, he pities them and seeks to deliver them. He reflects: "If I were to preach the profound and subtle Dharma of the Tathāgata’s realization immediately, sentient beings would be unable to believe or accept it. Consequently, they would fall into the evil paths, and I would fail to fulfill my original vow. Thus, he recollects his past vows and skillfully employs expedient means to guide them. This is called "recalling the skillful means. The Consolation of All Buddhas At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions—each presiding over worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—manifest their bodies, coming from afar to appear before Śākyamuni Buddha. They praise him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni Tathāgata, you have well manifested the great power of the Tathāgatas. You have well manifested the great power of the Tathāgatas. You have well manifested the great power of the Tathāgatas. You have well manifested the great power of the Tathāgatas. Having spoken these words, they each emit rays of light from the white tuft between their eyebrows, illuminating the world-system of Sahā. From within those lights, they utter this verse of praise: "O Great Hero, you have appeared in the world, Manifesting the great power of the Tathāgatas; Having attained the path of the Tathāgata, You now preach the supreme Dharma. We have come from afar to see you, And to praise your inconceivable merit. Properly Bestowing the Provisional Vehicle At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having received the encouragement of the Buddhas of the ten directions, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, and addressed them: "World-Honored Ones, please listen to me. I shall now, for the sake of all sentient beings, preach the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s realization. However, because these sentient beings have long been submerged in the ocean of birth and death, they are attached to the five desires and find no joy in the Buddha-way. Therefore, I shall employ skillful means to guide them. Then, the World-Honored One spoke this verse: "I shall now preach the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s realization, But these sentient beings are deeply attached to the five desires; They find no joy in the Buddha-way, And thus cannot believe or accept it. Therefore, I shall employ skillful means, To lead them to enter the Buddha-way. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further explain this meaning, spoke the following verses: "The Buddhas of the ten directions, As numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Have come from afar to encourage me, Praising my inconceivable merit. I have now received their encouragement, And shall preach the supreme Dharma; For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall deliver them from suffering. Yet these beings are deeply attached to desire, And find no joy in the Buddha-way; Therefore, I shall employ skillful means, To lead them to enter the Buddha-way. Thus, the Buddha, wishing to deliver sentient beings, conceals the real and manifests the provisional. This is called "properly bestowing the provisional vehicle. First [part] concludes.
Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, [the Buddha thought: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the Three Vehicles.
Since my emergence into the world was fundamentally for the sake of delivering sentient beings, how could I bear to abandon them abruptly when they lack the capacity?

Desiring to emulate the former Buddhas by proceeding through the stages of skillful means, I therefore reflect upon the past. Having thus reflected, it was only logical that he should establish a model; hence he says, "The path I have now attained."
One should also speak of three [aspects]. △ Second, the consolation of all Buddhas:
When he was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared... (until) "but it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas."

First, there is "praise and consolation" (*praśamsā-samāśvāsa*). "Contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to recollective mindfulness (*anusmṛti*). Regarding the appearance of the Buddhas of the ten directions while recollecting the past:
this reveals that the path of each Buddha is identical. "Consolation" (*samāśvāsa*) means to comfort; "metaphor" (*upamā*) means to accord with.

This means that the Buddhas, fearing that he might abandon the provisional means (*upāya*), comfort him with their Brahma-voice and accord with him through metaphors. This is a self-narration by the Tathāgata himself; therefore—
It is said: "I am so. The Tathāgata is able to awaken to the Dharma first and is able to accord with the capacities and needs [of sentient beings];

therefore, all Buddhas praise him, saying, "Excellent! As for Śākyamuni, according to the *Shifa* (The Method of Posthumous Titles): "One whose moral virtue and learning are vast is called 'Wen' (Cultivated); one who is compassionate, kind, and loves the people is called 'Wen.
Śākyamuni possesses the virtue of benefiting both self and others, and thus he is worthy of this title. Furthermore, he is also praised as the "Foremost."
Regarding the "Teacher": because the Tathāgata, through his own supreme self-realization, skillfully responds to the various capacities of sentient beings, he is the foremost among all teachers;
thus, he attains this supreme state. This clearly elucidates the Tathāgata’s own supreme self-realization.

"Skillfully responding to the various capacities [of beings]" explains the meaning of the "Supreme First Teacher" mentioned above. From "We ourselves... onwards, he provides testimony and consolation, saying:
"It is not only you who have attained the Unsurpassed; we too have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma. It is not only you who employ skillful means;
for the sake of the various classes of beings, we too have distinguishedly expounded the Three Vehicles. However, what I have taught...
The three vehicles were originally established for those of limited wisdom who delight in the small and do not believe they can become Buddhas;
thus, through skillful means, I have distinguished and taught various provisional fruits. You must understand that although I speak of three, I am in fact teaching only the Bodhisattva path.

If you, in the future, are able to practice as I have done, then what harm could these skillful means possibly do to the ultimate truth? For now, let it be; rather than teach falsely, it would be better not to preach at all.
This refers to the thought of entering *nirvāṇa* prematurely. △ Third, the correct bestowal of the provisional vehicle has three parts: 1. The bending and straightening of the turning of thought;
2. First delivering the five men; 3. A general conclusion to prevent questioning. First:
"Śāriputra, you should know that when I heard the 'Holy Lion' [voice]... up to 'I also practice in accordance with it,' I wished to recount my former state;
therefore, I called his name again and instructed him that he should know. 'The Holy Lion' refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
'Voice' refers to the voices of consolation and encouragement of all Buddhas. 'Kalaviṅka and Brahma-like' means surpassing all."
Therefore, it is described as profound, pure, and subtle. "Namo to all Buddhas" should be recited with a tone of deep lamentation. The meaning is this:

if one does not employ skillful means (*upāya*), one violates the consoling teachings of the Buddhas; yet if one employs the vehicle of skillful means, one again violates the original intent of their transcendence from the world.
At this point of utter helplessness, he therefore invokes "Namo to all Buddhas" to briefly express his profound and difficult-to-articulate sentiments.
Having thus humbled himself, he turns his thoughts toward compliance with the Buddhas; hence it says, "He further forms this thought.
When he says, "I have emerged from a turbid world," he knows for himself that the timing must not be mistaken, and furthermore, there are the Buddhas who offer him consolation.

The analogy is that when the teaching is repeated with such earnestness, it is difficult for one’s heart to resist; in principle, it is appropriate to comply and follow. Therefore, it is said: "As the Buddhas have taught, I also act accordingly.
This collectively reveals the provisional application of means based on the ultimate reality (*tathatā*), showing that this was not done out of necessity. △ Second, first delivering the five men.
Having reflected upon this matter, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī (and there) preached to the five bhikṣus.

"Having reflected upon this matter" means that he resolved his intention by employing skillful means (*upāya*). "Proceeded to Vārāṇasī" means that he bent his body to accommodate the capacities of those to be converted;
for there were the five bhikṣus and others within his sphere of influence in the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) at Vārāṇasī. Thus, it is called Vārāṇasī.
It is located within the borders of Central India; the meaning [of its name] is translated as "the river encircling the city.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Within the borders of Central India, there is a river named Vārāṇasī. Not far from it, a royal city was established, which took its name from that river.
Regarding the phrase "all phenomena are quiescent and cannot be expressed in words": this refers to the Tathāgata’s journey to Vārāṇasī, primarily for the purpose of preaching the Dharma.
However, all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent from the outset and are free from characteristics such as verbal expression; they cannot be proclaimed through words.
Had there not been skillful means regarding this, [the Buddha] would surely have remained like a bitter gourd, tied up and left uneaten.
The Buddha was not thus; therefore, by the power of skillful means, he was able to preach for the five bhikṣus.
The five bhikṣus were: first, Aññā-Koṇḍañña; second, Vappa, who was of maternal lineage; third, Bhaddiya; fourth, Mahānāma;
and fifth, Assaji, who were of paternal lineage. When the Buddha first entered the mountains, his father the King commanded these companions to practice [austerities].
Later, unable to endure the ascetic practices, they fled to the Deer Park and each continued their cultivation.
A Different Path. After the Buddha had attained enlightenment for twenty-one days, he wished to deliver Ārāḍa Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra, but he did not succeed with them.
Consequently, he thought of the five men and deemed it appropriate that they should be delivered first; thus, he went to deliver them.

This refers to his compassion for the two sages who did not encounter the "thunderous voice," and his joy regarding the five men who were capable of following the transformation of the Dharma. △ Three: General Summary.

This concludes the section on the inquiry regarding the prevention [of obstacles]. This is called "the turning of the wheel of Dharma," which immediately brings forth the sound of *nirvāṇa* (extending to the passage: "I always speak thus").

This initial summary of the capacity of the audience and the teaching indicates that "Dharma" refers to the Four Noble Truths; for by means of these, one can destroy and extinguish the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*), thereby being conveyed to *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Because the Buddha employs this Dharma to turn [the wheel] into the minds of those with receptive capacity (*yogya*), it is called "turning.
As for the term "name," it refers to the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi-tattva-bhūmi*); therein, fundamentally, there is no wheel of Dharma to be turned.

To speak of "turning the wheel" is likewise merely a name. *Nirvāṇa* is the sound that can encompass the teaching; *Arhat* is the receptive capacity that is so encompassed. Thus, it is said: "Thereupon..."
Nirvana is not ultimate reality; "Arhat" is a provisional name. To speak of an "Arhat" or to speak of "Nirvana" is merely a matter of expedient means.
Furthermore, these names exist only because they follow upon the preceding [teachings] as a concluding summary.

This refers to how, from the time the Tathāgata first proclaimed [the Dharma] at the Deer Park, this was called the "Turning of the Wheel. From that point on, there have existed the teachings of Nirvana and the Arhat.

This is the pivotal mechanism of the Han [tradition]. Since there is already the teaching of *nirvāṇa* and the capacity for the *arhat*, this adds the categories of the Dharma Jewel and the Sangha Jewel beyond the Buddha Jewel. This is the origin of these three jewels.

From "From long ago" (*jìu*) onwards, he preempts potential objections (fearing someone might ask: "The methods of skillful means also have gradual stages; why then was *nirvāṇa* present at the very first turning of the wheel of Dharma?")...

[This is] the sound of *nirvāṇa*. (Therefore, the preceding two lines serve as a defense against this objection. It is said that from time immemorial, the Buddha has been praising and demonstrating the Dharma of *nirvāṇa* for them;
because he has accomplished it through skillful means over a long period, his first turning of the wheel of Dharma now constitutes the proclamation of the sound of *nirvāṇa*.

(Fearing that one might again object: "Even the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is not reached suddenly; why then, upon the first turning of the wheel of Dharma, do those named Arhats appear? Therefore, the following two lines serve as a defense against this. It is said:
Regarding the suffering of *paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death), their karma has been eternally exhausted.
For many kalpas, I have constantly praised them with such words; therefore, now that the Wheel of Dharma is first turned, they are immediately granted the title of Arhat. [Question]:

Regarding the three assemblies of illumination, this section’s meaning should apply to the initial, middle, and final turnings of the wheel. Why are they not all fully present here? [Answer]: Although they are not explicitly present in the text, their meaning must certainly be contained therein.

According to the subsequent text, since they are called "sons of the Buddha," it can be known that this refers to the *Madhyama-āgama*, the Vaipulya, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* (i.e., the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*). This concludes the section on "Manifesting Expedient Means from the Ultimate.

II. Returning Expedient Means to the Ultimate, in three parts: 1. The time has arrived for the capacities [of the disciples] to ripen; 2. Equally bestowing the One Vehicle; 3. Hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit. First: [The time has arrived for the capacities to ripen.]
"Śāriputra, you should know that I see these sons of the Buddha... now is precisely the time.

Since their initial faculties have already matured, and lest the provisional [teachings] remain merely provisional, and fearing that Śāriputra might not yet accord with this principle, I have thus commanded him to 'know.
Having already passed through the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā [periods], their faculties are now mature; therefore, they are addressed as 'sons of the Buddha. I shall [proceed].

Because they benefit others through the Great Dharma, it is said that "they see. The phrase "vowing to seek the Buddha-way" refers to the accomplishment of the great resolve (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) and the sense of disparaging one's former mind.
The phrase "immeasurable" generally indicates the three types of faculties (*trividha-indriya*). As previously stated:
"The various bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way are, in number, eighty thousand," and so on, down to: "We twelve hundred, and others who seek the Buddha."
This refers to those very individuals. The two phrases clearly demonstrate their earnest aspiration for enlightenment, as previously stated:
"The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth, with palms joined, gaze up in expectation," and so on, until: "All with one mind join their palms, desiring to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
Furthermore, the two phrases most vividly manifest the ripening of their faculties, as previously stated: "Having previously seen various Buddhas, their faculties are sharp and keen."
...benefit. It continues until it says: "The Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed beings such as these.
Furthermore, since it was stated above that "from time immemorial, he has praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvāṇa," the various Buddhas are none other than Śākyamuni himself.

However, because this refers to many kalpas leading up to his present life, they are called "various" [Buddhas]. Thus, it means that from many kalpas ago until his present life, the Buddha [has been teaching].

Pitying those who had receded from the Great [Vehicle] and turned toward the Small, he constantly used the provisional teaching (*upāya*) to guide them; thus it is said: "Having heard the teaching of the provisional means, I immediately... and so forth.

When it says, "The time has now arrived," and "He then formed this thought," it means that having caused them to take the provisional fruit as their assurance, he now recalls his original intention for appearing in the world.
This original intention for appearing in the world was solely for one purpose; therefore, it is said: "The reason why the Tathāgata... and so forth.

They emerge [from their state] for the sake of explaining the Buddha’s wisdom. "This time" refers to what is not the [proper] time. For example, as in the Āgamas, to be satisfied with a small attainment is "not the time.
To have the Vaipulya sūtras still outside the gate is "not the time. In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no hope for even a single meal.

It was not the [proper] time. Now, having passed a short while further, it has gradually become open and unobstructed; therefore, it is called "the time. This means that the capacity [of the disciples] has matured and the moment has finally arrived.
2. Equally Bestowing the One Vehicle. 2.1 Preventing Objections. 2.2 Properly Clarifying the Equal Bestowal. First (The objection states:
"Since it is already the time, one should have taught immediately. Why wait for three requests before teaching? What is the intention behind this? Therefore, he provides this defense:)
"Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and possessed by pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
When it says 'you should know,' it is because there is fear that they might harbor doubts. Those of dull faculties and small wisdom refer here to the śrāvakas of actual practice."
"Attachment to signs" refers to inferior ordinary beings; "arrogance" refers to those who practice with overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

Furthermore, those of dull faculties are stubbornly obstructed by the provisional teachings, while those of small wisdom take no pleasure in the Great Dharma. Attachment to signs causes stagnation within the outflows (*āsrava*), while arrogance hinders further hearing of the teaching.
Therefore, regarding this Dharma, none of them are able to believe; for this reason, it was necessary to wait for three requests.
And only then did he speak. △ Third, the explicit clarification of the equal bestowal:
"Now I rejoice and am fearless among all bodhisattvas; I directly abandon expedient means and teach only the unsurpassed path."
Since the five thousand withdrew from their seats and were expelled for their transgressions, those who departed have departed and those who repented have repented;

there has been none such as those previously described—those of dull faculties and inferior wisdom who are mere continuations of the stream. Therefore, it is said that [the assembly] rejoices and is fearless. As for the Bodhisattvas:

Their faculties are sharp and their wisdom vast; they have liberated their minds through emptiness. Thus, among this assembly, there is no need to employ expedient skillfulness in a partial manner, nor to adapt crookedly to individual capacities.
Therefore it is said: "Directly abandoning expedients, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.
Having thus equally bestowed the One Vehicle, [the section on] "The Benefits Gained from Hearing the Dharma" follows as the third part.
"When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed... they shall all likewise become Buddhas.

These first two lines formally grant permission for those of superior faculties to sever their doubts. "Bodhisattvas" implicitly refers to a class of superior-faculty disciples such as Śāriputra and others.
There are two kinds of doubt: first, proximate doubt, which refers to the initial hearing of the praise of wisdom and not knowing by what cause it arose.
For what reason? There are two types of distant doubt: first, having previously seen [the Buddha] bestow a prophecy, one does not know whether it has been lost or not;

second, these two doubts attack one another so that one cannot resolve them oneself, hence they are called a "net of doubt. Now, hearing this Dharma, both the distant and the near are severed, hence it is said they are "all removed.
The final two lines pre-emptively indicate the attainment of Buddhahood by those of middling and inferior capacities. "Arhat" is a general designation for those of middling and inferior faculties.
It is said that for those whose net of doubts has already been removed, they shall naturally attain Buddhahood.

As for those of middling or inferior capacity, such as the class of the twelve hundred arhats, although they have not yet immediately attained the removal of doubt, the Buddha possesses skillful means and will ultimately bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
"All shall likewise become Buddhas. This concludes the detailed explanation of the verses on the provisional and the ultimate aspects of self-realization.
△ Third, the concluding verses summarizing [the teaching] to reveal the identity of the Way (the "Meaning Verses").
"Regarding the ritual procedures for the Dharma-teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time... [up to] 'teaching the Dharma of non-discrimination.

The first two phrases conclude the provisional and ultimate teachings of all Buddhas. "Ritual procedure" (yishi) refers to the established rules or norms. This means that from the ultimate, the provisional is implemented.
The provisional is reconciled with the real, as this constitutes the unchanging rule throughout the three periods of time.
The following two lines conclude the self-realization of the provisional and the real; "it is also thus" means that one emulates the ritual procedures of those Buddhas.

Since one emulates the ritual procedures of those Buddhas, even though the provisional vehicle is taught, it is ultimately reconciled into only a single matter; therefore, it is called the "non-discriminative Dharma."
Thus ends the section on the verses that fully explain the analysis. △ Third, the verses praising the Dharma and exhorting faith (the supplementary verses), which have two parts:
first, the verses corresponding to the prose; second, the supplementary verses preventing objections. The first part has two sections: first, the verses praising the Dharma by means of a metaphor;

"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and distant; it is difficult to encounter them, occurring only once in a great while.
According to the "Parable of the Phantom City" (Hua-ch'eng p'in), one hundred and eighty kalpas passed by in vain without a Buddha.

Furthermore, it says, "In the past, immeasurable kalpas passed by in vain without a Buddha," which sufficiently proves the meaning of their remoteness and rarity. The "Chapter on the Sublime Adornments" (Miao-yen p'in) states:
It is difficult to encounter a Buddha, as rare as the *udumbara* flower, or like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole in a floating log.
Furthermore, an ancient verse says: "While the Buddha was in the world, I was mired in saṃsāra; now that I have obtained a human body, the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.

This sufficiently proves the meaning of the difficulty of such an encounter. The word "even" (*zhèngshǐ*) here implies "let us suppose for the sake of argument"; even if a Buddha were to appear in the world, and yet...

This is already sufficient [to demonstrate its difficulty].

Using metaphors to illustrate the person: "one who is beloved by all" illustrates that such a person is revered by the multitude;
"rare among gods and humans" illustrates that such a person is not easily found in the world; and "appearing only at certain times" illustrates that such a person is not frequently seen.
Furthermore, although these are metaphors used to illustrate the person, they actually reveal the Dharma by means of the person, in accordance with the prose section on the Dharma.
It is like the udumbara flower: appearing different while being identical in reality. △ Second, the verse encouraging faith that it is not false (the Explanatory Verse):
"Hearing the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering a single word [of this]—this is the secret essence of all Buddhas."
First, it is extremely difficult to manifest faith; those who hear the Dharma with joy do so because they believe for themselves that they shall become Buddhas.

Those who rejoice and further offer praise do so in the hope that others may hear it as well. Even a single word of praise constitutes an offering to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because through successive transmission it can ensure that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas remains uninterrupted and that their life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) endures forever.
"This person is most rare" means that because those who follow this Dharma encounter many enmities and jealousies, those who rejoice are few;

furthermore, because he speaks words of praise, it is said to be "most" rare. "Exceeding the udumbara flower" means that what has been heard and listened to thus far pertains only to self-benefit, which is already as rare as the udumbara flower;
this praise further encompasses the benefit of others, and is therefore said to "exceed" it. Moreover—

It is rarer than the udumbara flower. Although it is evident that the person capable of praising [the Buddha] is difficult to find, the reason such a person speaks words of praise is due to their joy and self-confidence;
thus, it is precisely this self-confidence that is shown to be the most difficult.
Your words directly exhort [others] to have faith. Because one who possesses self-confidence is rare, you directly urge them not to doubt. I am...
"Below. "To manifest clearly that it is not false": this manifests that the speaker is not false; for if there were falsehood, one would be ashamed to claim the title of Dharma King.
"Universally proclaiming to the great assembly": this manifests that what is spoken is not false;
for if there were falsehood, it would be difficult to proclaim it universally. "But by means of the One Vehicle alone," etc.: this correctly clarifies that which is spoken.
This refers to the matter of what has been personally taught; it uses indirect expression to clarify the meaning of its non-falsity.

"You all, Śāriputra," is an address to the great assembly as well as those who are the primary recipients of the teaching. "Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas" refers to those of lower and middle capacities, as well as those of superior faculties within the teachings.
Fearing that they might not believe this with full clarity, [the Buddha] therefore commanded them to know: "This is the wondrous Dharma. This refers specifically to what is being taught here now;
it is not like provisional teachings which are easily produced. Hence, it is called "the secret essentials of all Buddhas.

Since these are the secret heart-essentials of all Buddhas, they cannot possibly be false words. This passage uses the fact that the Buddhas keep it secret to indirectly clarify the meaning of its non-falsity. Because...
If one contemplates this, then all that has been taught is free from falsehood; every word is entirely true.

If one does not believe this, then there is nothing at all that can be trusted. This concludes the verses corresponding to the prose section. △ Second, the supplementary verses to prevent objections, in two parts.
First, the objection regarding why the various Buddhas likewise keep it secret; second, the objection regarding why the Tathāgata universally proclaims it. Regarding the first, the objection states:

"If the Buddha now proclaims it universally, this should be a principle of great public-mindedness and lack of partiality. Yet the various Buddhas keep it secret as their core essence (*hṛdaya*); for what purpose is this? Therefore, the following defense is offered:

Because in this world of the five turbidities, beings merely delight in and are attached to various desires (up to) destroying the Dharma and falling into evil realms, it is said that the Buddhas of the past and present appeared because of this turbid world, while the Buddhas of the future may encounter wicked people;

thus they conceal this Dharma as their essential core, for it is not otherwise obtained. To explain in detail: the sentient beings of the five turbidities have their five faculties stuck [in sense objects].
They are stalled amidst the five sensory objects, like flies drawn to filth; thus it is said they "cling only to various desires.
Such sentient beings know only the causes and effects of outflows (sāsrava) and lack the mind for world-transcendence; thus it is said they "do not seek the Buddha-way.

When "the future" refers to the time of future Buddhas, the sentient beings of that time will be stubborn and difficult to transform, hence they are called "wicked people. Since they are called wicked people, how could...
Because they are unable to believe and accept the Great Dharma, even though they hear the teaching of the One Vehicle, they remain confused and do not believe or accept it.
Due to this lack of faith and acceptance, they will give rise to the karmic causes and conditions of the offense of destroying the Dharma, and will inevitably fall into the evil realms without doubt.

First, the narrator provides this introductory description. "Leaping for joy" refers to a state where the mind is expansive and the spirit is at ease, such that one knows not where one is going.

"Filled with delight" refers to the emotion of one’s own conviction in becoming a Buddha, whereby all anxiety and doubt are suddenly dispelled. "Joining his palms" refers to the act of making oneself upright and solemn.
His physical action (*kāyakarman*) was refined; his gazing up at [the Buddha] was the focused application of thought toward the Sage’s countenance.

having heard the aforementioned Dharma-sounds, he realized that his own mind is the Buddha. His joy exceeded all expectations, such that he could not restrain himself.

Therefore, it is said that his heart was filled with exultation. Having long feared that he was beyond hope of salvation, he now attained what he had not expected; hence, it is said that "he obtained what he had never before.

Why is this so? From my former time following the Buddha [until] "losing the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.

...Furthermore, section two: Contemplation in Solitude.

At first, one suspects that the Buddha has private interests; for those of the Two Vehicles, weary of the mundane dust and seeking tranquility, he constantly dwells alone.
Mountain forests are places of profound stillness, and beneath trees are realms of vast isolation. When dwelling in such places and environments, one’s form and shadow console each other.
To be cast adrift and fallen into ruin is truly pitiable; compared to merely encountering external circumstances and conditions, it is even more difficult to find peace.

Therefore, whether sitting or walking, I constantly harbor this thought: that those of the Three Vehicles equally sever the afflictions of views and thoughts, and equally realize the fivefold Dharma-body.

Therefore, it is said that they "equally enter the dharma-nature. Yet, being unaware of the distinction between abiding and non-abiding, one conversely wonders why the Sage’s mind possesses partiality.
What does this mean? It is a word of wonder and doubt, implying: "I and the bodhisattvas have equally entered the dharma-nature;

"Did the Savior not have a partial heart? It is we who—bringing the fault upon ourselves—mean to say that when I was dwelling in seclusion and solitude, I initially suspected the Buddha’s mind was partial.

This is the explanation of the arising [of the meaning]. "Because" (*yin*) means "for the sake of. The intention is this:

If we were to sincerely plan for the long term and wait for the Buddha to speak of it, that which is intended for the accomplishment of *bodhi* would surely be as [described] in the various [sūtras].
The Bodhisattvas attain deliverance through the Mahāyāna; reflecting upon this, he considers that it is not a partiality of the World-Honored One.

However, the title [of the scripture] conveys a sense of regret for past errors. The intention is to say: "From the outset, the four truths were taught as skillful means according to what was appropriate.

We regret that we did not understand this meaning. When we first heard the Buddha-dharma, we failed to distinguish between the true and the false, and whenever we encountered [teachings], [we accepted them indiscriminately]."
I accepted it with faith. At that time, I contemplated only how to achieve realization quickly.
Later, unexpectedly, I became a scorched sprout and a ruined seed. Reflecting on this, is it not our own fault? △ Third, constant self-reproach.
"World-Honored One, from the past until now, throughout both day and night, I have constantly reproached myself and recounted the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.

Today’s awakening potential, when compared to that of the four disciples who claimed they had already attained *nirvāṇa*, differs by as much as heaven and earth in terms of their resolve.
Thus, the doubts and regrets of the past are finally ended. △ Second, today’s faith and understanding.
Now, having heard from the Buddha what had never been heard before (up to) being born through transformation by means of the Dharma and attaining a portion of the Buddha-Dharma:
hearing the Dharma for the first time and severing doubt. "Hearing what has never been heard before" refers to the convergence of provisional means into the ultimate reality;

"Prajñā" refers specifically to the Bodhisattva. "Doubt" means doubting that one's own portion [of the path] has been severed; "regret" means regretting one's former haste. Regarding the passage beginning with "body and mind": [The text continues: ...the body and mind are below. This means that the physical body and the mental faculty are inferior. Since these two are subject to birth and death, they are termed "inferior. "Below" indicates their position relative to the superior state of liberation. Thus, when the practitioner attains the realization of the non-arising of dharmas, the fetters of the body and mind are severed, and they no longer descend into the realms of suffering. Joyful and self-confident, with both doubt and regret severed, one feels relaxed and at ease within and without; hence it is said that "body and mind are tranquil.

From this point on, one celebrates the fulfillment of one's life, no longer harboring feelings of sorrow, resentment, suspicion, or self-reproach; hence it is said that "one attains peace and security.
"Only today do I know" refers to the reversal of what was previously unknown, as one had not participated in this matter until now.
