The verses on "Faith and Understanding Today" consist of two parts: one verse on hearing the Dharma and severing doubt, and two verses on rejoicing and gaining self-confidence.
The first part has two sections: first, the distant severance of past doubts; second, the proximate severance of preceding doubts. The first [section] is presented in detail.
Now, hearing the Buddha’s voice, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, [extending] until all is forever extinguished without remainder.
The initial cause for awakening is the description of delusion. "The Buddha’s voice" refers to the preceding extensive clarification of the provisional and the real.
It was previously stated that "this Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination," and it was also stated that "all these dharmas are for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle."
Thus, etc., all clarify that the teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is the meaning of the untainted and inconceivable.

Since the teaching of the Dharma is given according to what is appropriate and is thus difficult to conceive and discuss, we know that the Tathāgata merely transforms bodhisattvas and reveals and awakens sentient beings solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
hence it is said, "causing them to reach the site of enlightenment. This is the cause for attaining awakening today. By means of...
This present awakening describes my own past delusions; therefore, it says, "I originally adhered to false views.
To say that one "originally adhered to false views" means that before encountering the Buddha, I followed the Brahmin Śarabha and practiced the teachings of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika-dharma).
After Śarabha died, Śāriputra led his own followers of false views; thus, it says, "he was a teacher of Brahmins. Regarding "Brahmin," this refers to those of the Western Regions.
He was a follower of the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). Claiming himself to be a descendant of Brahmā, his ambition was to be reborn in the Brahma realm.
Śāriputra exhausted all his teachings, yet he sought an even more eminent teacher. On the road, he encountered the Venerable Aśvajit, who introduced him to the World-Honored One.

The World-Honored One administered medicine according to his specific ailment, preaching the Dharma of the Hīnayāna for him. Thus, he described how the World-Honored One knew his mind and uprooted his heterodoxy.
This refers to the teaching on *nirvāṇa*. Upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, they encountered it and immediately believed and accepted it; hence it is said that "all false views were eliminated.
Through contemplation and cultivation, they attained realization of the partial truth; hence it is said that "they realized the dharma of emptiness.

At that time, they did not know that this provisional cessation was not the ultimate reality, and they ultimately mistook a servant for their master; thus, they claimed for themselves that they had reached extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). This was in the past.

For years, one has clung to deluded attachments. Now, however, that delusion is overturned and transformed into awakening. Previously, one took provisional means for ultimate reality, which was like being in a drunken dream.
Now, hearing that provisional means are integrated into ultimate reality, it is like waking from a dream and sobering from intoxication; therefore, it is called "self-awakening."

Furthermore, "self-awakening" (svasaṃvedana) reveals that this is true awakening and genuine realization. If those who understand the school merely follow others with a uniformity of mind, giving rise to delusions, how could they be said to have self-awakened?
As for the phrase "when one attains Buddhahood," although it is not a definitive statement, it already indicates that there is a portion [of the potential] to become a Buddha;
it is not like what was previously said regarding the inability to expound the Unsurpassed Way in the future.
Furthermore, regarding those who possess the thirty-two marks: having attained Buddhahood, they must necessarily be adorned with these marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

This is not the same as what was said previously, that within the same single Dharma, one cannot attain this matter. Regarding the fact that the hosts of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, spirits, and so forth pay them homage:
having possessed the marks and secondary characteristics, they must necessarily have the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau gaṇāḥ*) as their attendants. This is not the same as what was said previously.
When I was walking alone in meditation, I reflected that I had lost this benefit. At that moment, it could be said that my true nature was exhausted and my delusions were ended;
it was like gold extracted from ore, or like wood turned to ash. Therefore, it is said: "Exhausted and extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
△ Second, the proximate severance of prior doubts (supplementary verse).
When the Buddha spoke among the great assembly, saying "I shall become a Buddha" (up to the point where it is said), they considered this to be the work of Māra.
Initially, based on faith, they recounted their doubts. Following the previous conclusion and exhortation to believe and understand, the text says:

"Since you have already known that the Buddhas, the teachers of the world, employ various skillful means according to what is appropriate, you should no longer harbor any doubts; let your hearts give rise to great joy."
He knew for himself that he would become a Buddha. This Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, declared that he would indeed become a Buddha.

Previously, because he had not attained Buddhahood, he harbored doubts; thus, he felt remorse, constantly reproaching himself. Now, having heard that he will attain Buddhahood, [his doubts are resolved].
Both [doubt and remorse] are severed simultaneously; thus it is said: "Upon hearing this Dharma-sound, all doubt and regret are entirely eliminated.

When first hearing the Buddha’s teaching—referring to the words praising true wisdom mentioned previously in the brief exposition—one does not immediately know the cause or condition for these words and is therefore greatly startled and filled with suspicion.
Their thought is that this might not be a Buddha, but rather a māra who has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse their minds.
"Would this cause one to fall back from the fruits of the Path? At that time, I did not dare speak it aloud;
only after gaining self-confidence until now have I revealed it. From "The Buddha [said]" onwards, he severs doubts and engenders faith.

That past and future are entirely subject to causes and conditions is an illustration used to manifest his own point through another. All of this is the Tathāgata’s detailed explanation in response to the previous request.
Therefore, it is said that this is the discourse on skillful speech. At the very moment of hearing it correctly, the mind becomes settled, like the great ocean, limpid and unmoving.
Once the Dharma has been heard, one's doubts are severed, like ice melting away before the net of right knowledge.
This briefly clarifies the intent of severing doubt and engendering faith. When the Buddha speaks of the past and so forth, he again relies upon what preceded.

This derives from the meaning of his provisional and ultimate teachings. To explain in detail: among all the Buddhas of the past, there were none who did not establish the provisional based upon the ultimate;
hence it is said they "abide in skillful means. Nor were there any who did not eventually bring the provisional back to the ultimate;

hence it is said they "also preach this Dharma. This can be understood as applying equally to the Buddhas of the present and future. This passage describes the meaning within the provisional and ultimate teachings of all Buddhas, just as it is now.

The World-Honored One and others further expound upon the meaning of the provisional and the ultimate within their own realization. Both [the acts of] generating the aspiration for enlightenment and leaving the household life are the Great Compassionate Mind of the Tathāgata;

therefore, the previous statement that he "arouses the Great Compassionate Mind for the sake of these sentient beings" already encompasses the significance of both generating the aspiration and leaving the household life.
"Attaining the Way" refers to the initial sitting at the site of enlightenment and so forth. "Turning the Dharma Wheel" refers to...
The previous journey to Vārāṇasī and so forth was also taught through skillful means; thus, his bestowal of provisional vehicles is identical to that of all Buddhas.
When the World-Honored One speaks of the "True Path," he means that although the World-Honored One employs provisional vehicles, he ultimately teaches the True Path.
This reveals that he is identical to all Buddhas in terms of reality. "Pāpīyan" (波旬), translated here as "Evil One," is an alternative name for Māra.

Yet, although he harbors an evil mind and disturbs practitioners, how could he possibly master both the provisional and the ultimate teachings in a manner exactly like the ritual protocols of the Buddhas?
Therefore, it is said that such a thing does not exist. For this reason, one certainly knows that the previous praise was [intended as]...
This is true wisdom. It was not Māra acting as a Buddha; rather, it was the World-Honored One’s essential teaching of reality.
It was because my own knowledge and understanding were narrow and inferior that I fell into a net of doubt, falsely claiming this was the work of Māra.
For a time, I nearly cast the Tathāgata’s single fragment of compassionate heart into the realm of nothingness. This occurred after Śāriputra had personally accepted and gained confidence in himself.
These are words that lay bare one's liver and pour out one's gall. The verse on having heard the Dharma and severed doubts is concluded. △ Second, the verse on rejoicing and self-confidence:
"Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle... [until] teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas."
The Buddha possesses eight qualities of voice: first, it is exceedingly beautiful; second, it is soft and supple; third, it is harmonious and pleasant; fourth, it is noble and wise;

fifth, it is not effeminate; sixth, it is without error; seventh, it is deep and far-reaching; eighth, it is inexhaustible. These are now explained in detail, skillfully conforming to the inclinations of sentient beings.
It may correspond to the second [quality], hence it is called "supple. It is profound, firm, and remote; no one can reach it.
It may correspond to the seventh, hence it is termed "profound and far-reaching. To say it is "extremely subtle" means it is the ultimate in excellence, such that it cannot be described by words;
it is also one of the eight qualities of voice, namely the most excellent sound. "Expounding and flowing forth" means proclaiming, unfolding, and relaxing [the teaching].
As for "purity," it is the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Having long suppressed this Dharma within my breast, I had not yet been able to proclaim or expound it with full ease.
Now that the time has arrived and the capacity [of beings] has matured, I shall do so with a gentle voice and profound, subtle, and wondrous words.
He expounds upon this. "Great joy" refers to the joy that exceeds the ordinary because one has gained self-confidence in attaining Buddhahood.
"Doubt" (*vicikitsā*) is one of the five dull afflictions; its nature is hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths, and its function is to obstruct the wholesome qualities of non-doubt.
"Regret" (*kaukṛtya*) is one of the indeterminate mental factors; its nature is the remorseful reflection upon actions performed, and its function is to obstruct tranquility (*śamatha*).
This constitutes karma. Now, having brought provisional means back to the ultimate reality, one realizes it through direct manifestation without doubt.

There is no provisional that is not real, and thus one does not regret what was previously done; hence it is said, "permanently exhausted. True wisdom has no fixed location and pervades all phenomena.

Because you formerly abandoned the ocean to identify with a bubble, you were certain that delusion resided within the physical body. Now, hearing the Dharma, you abide in the station of the Dharma; as for the characteristics of the world—
It is eternally abiding. Thus one knows that whether body or mind, they are all things within the wondrously luminous True Mind; therefore it is called "abiding securely.
This refers to the fact that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one is always situated therein. It is certain that such a person shall become a Buddha.

Once one abides in true wisdom, even such acts as coughing or swinging one’s arms are nothing other than Buddha-work. From this point on, by accumulating merit and virtue, one will naturally attain Buddhahood without doubt;
this is what is meant by “riding this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment. As for being honored by devas and humans:
once the Way of the Buddha has been realized, devas and humans will naturally look up to and revere one. Regarding the turning of the unsurpassed wheel: [this refers to the teaching of the Dharma].

Although all dharmas are taught, they ultimately constitute only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Since the teaching that enables this is exclusively the One Vehicle, how could there truly remain any other classes of beings among those to be converted?
Therefore, it is said that the teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas necessarily encompasses the reverence of devas and humans.
As for the statement regarding the turning of the Dharma to transform the multitudes, it is precisely because one perceives the truth of faith and is free from doubt.
However, before his awakening, Śāriputra would constantly say, "I have failed to attain this matter; I have already lost it.

How bitter and sorrowful were such words regarding loss and non-loss! Now, after his awakening, he immediately says, "I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans, and shall teach and transform bodhisattvas.
How majestic and resolute are such words! What a difference there is between the two!

This refers to the tiger cub that, upon its first birth, already possesses the spirit of devouring oxen—is this not what is meant by Śāriputra? Once Śāriputra had attained full understanding, [the Buddha spoke].
Part Two: The Tathāgata Bestows a Prediction. This has two sections: First, Revealing the Trace to Manifest the Source; Second, Formally Bestowing the Prediction. Regarding the first:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... [up to] "the Dharma for teaching bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
First, he reveals his original nature and manifested traces. When Śāriputra attained understanding, the Buddha wished to bestow upon him a prediction of enlightenment;
thus, he first caused him to recognize his own past causes and conditions, and so he addressed him. There are two reasons why he must speak this in the midst of the assembly: first, [he wishes to...]
First, it is to record Śāriputra and cause him to realize [the truth]. Second, it is because there may be doubts among the assembly; therefore, the cause for this prediction is shown.

Although the names of the two hundred trillion buddhas have not yet appeared in the text, judging by the meaning, they should refer to Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha, for the Tathāgata once practiced the bodhisattva path as "Not-Disparaging" (Adhimātra) under that buddha. This is because he sought unsurpassed bodhi.
"Ti. With a single sound, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly; thus it is said that for the sake of the unsurpassed path, he has constantly taught and transformed you.
Yet, although at that time you received this vocal prediction, you were still shrouded by ignorance and instead indulged in slander, remaining as if in the long night of delusion.
Yet, as soon as a single sound reaches the ear, the seed of Buddhahood is already received within the mind; this is itself the act of receiving instruction.
It is like a person sinking into the long night of a dream who, upon finding a precious jewel cast into the darkness, instead utters delirious words and reviles it.

Nevertheless, since the jewel is already in their breast, one cannot say they have not benefited from it. After the era of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, [the Buddha] again employed the provisional teachings to receive and guide beings.
Therefore, it is said that he was guided by skillful means. When the conditions converged and the time ripened, he now encountered the World-Honored One to receive transformation;
thus, it is said that he was born into my Dharma. From the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," the teaching is formally revealed and clarified.

When the Buddha was [the bodhisattva] Not-Disparaging (Adīnapramāda), he first universally prophesied with a single voice, and later further extended his lifespan to preach this sutra, transforming thousands of millions of beings and causing them to abide in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, it is said: "In the past, I instructed you to aspire to the Buddha-way; midway, when a brahmin begged for your eyes, you fell away from that great resolve and have not yet recovered it.
Thus it is said: "You have now completely forgotten it. Because you have completely forgotten it, you cling to the provisional as real, and thus it is said:
"You then claimed for yourselves that you had already attained nirvana. The Buddha’s intention was not to allow you to reach such a [limited] nirvana.
Therefore, it is said that he wished to cause you to recall what you had practiced. For this reason, he preached the Lotus Sūtra;
thus it is said, "For the sake of the śrāvakas, he preached this Mahāyāna," and so forth. Based on this, it follows that Śāriputra’s karmic conditions spanned many kalpas.
As for the bestowal of the prediction of future Buddhahood to those below, there is a historical precedent for it. This concludes the section on "Revealing the Trace to Manifest the Origin.
II. The Actual Bestowal of the Prediction (divided into two parts): A. Prose Exposition; B. Verse Recitation. The first part [the prose] has four sections: 1. Attaining the fruit through the cause.
2. Adornment of the primary and secondary [bodies]; 3. The principal and retinue, and the lifespan; 4. The distant and near transformative activities.
First: "Śāriputra, in a future age... [you shall become] a Buddha, a World-Honored One, a Tamer of Men, and a Teacher of Gods and Humans."

First, one must undergo the practice of causes throughout kalpas. Indeed, karmic consciousness is vast and expansive, like a great ocean a thousand fathoms deep, which cannot be exhausted by a single scoop.
The path of the Buddha is long and distant, like a multi-storied tower nine *zhang* high, which cannot be ascended by a single step.

Therefore, it is necessary to pass through immeasurable kalpas to investigate and sever [delusions], making offerings to the Buddhas to bring forth merit and honoring the Dharma to cultivate wisdom. Through this merit and wisdom...

[The path] is perfected; therefore, it is said that one is "fully endowed with the path practiced by Bodhisattvas. [Question: Previously, it was stated that "merely hearing the Dharma ensures that one will not fail to become a Buddha," whereas here it is said that one must practice causes for kalpas before being able to achieve full perfection.

Why is there such a discrepancy between the ease and difficulty of these two statements? They seem to be contradictory. [Answer: The former statement was intended for those attached to the provisional teachings who do not realize that "mind itself is Buddha.

Fearing they would claim that the Buddha-way is so distant as to be difficult to attain, they would develop deep fear and resign themselves to the belief that they lack the capacity [for enlightenment]. Therefore, the World-Honored One showed them that "merely hearing the Dharma ensures that one will not fail to become a Buddha. The present statement, however, is intended for those of wild wisdom within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) who do not understand how to cultivate based on the arising from nature (*xingqi*). Fearing they would...

This means that he holds his arms level with all Buddhas and stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the sages and worthies. Because of this, he is not ashamed of his great claims; he has suddenly cast off [the need for] further cultivation and realization. Therefore, the World-Honored One showed him that it was only after practicing the causes through kalpas that one attains Buddhahood.

If this is so, then there are distinct meanings to be drawn from both the preceding and the subsequent passages; they do not merely contradict one another, but rather function as a mutual complement. How could these words have been spoken solely for the sake of Śāriputra? "Shall attain" refers to the name he shall achieve upon fruition.

His specific title, "Flower-Light" (Huaguang), signifies that "flowers" represent the manifestation of wealth and elegance, symbolizing merit (puṇya); "light" represents brilliant illumination, symbolizing wisdom (prajñā). This is because, during the causal stage...

Because he made offerings to the Buddhas and served the Dharma, he received this title as his fruit. Furthermore, having attained Buddhahood, it is like awakening from a great dream or like the blooming of a lotus;
thus, he is named after the flower. His preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is like a lamp illuminating the night or a torch dispelling the darkness.

Therefore, it is designated by the term "light. Furthermore, the Buddha represents the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), which is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. The lotus represents the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), which is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).

The light represents the greatness of function (*karma-mahat*), which is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). As Master Tanyan’s *Preface to Amitābha* states: "To utter its name is to possess all virtues simultaneously.
Thus, one knows that the virtues of the Buddha are inexhaustible and the meanings of its names are infinite; it is solely through the essence...
When applied to the mind, all things will be encompassed without exception. △ Second, the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants, in four parts:
first, the purity of the land; second, the completeness of the two vehicles; third, the excellence of the kalpa’s name; fourth, the abundance of bodhisattvas. First:
The name of the land is Vimalā; its terrain is level and even (extending through to the description of) rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which are always laden with flowers and fruit.

The first phrase indicates the name, while the subsequent phrases manifest its characteristics. "Its terrain is level and even" means it is not like the pits, hollows, mounds, and hills of the present age, where the ground is uneven with highs and lows.
"Pure and magnificently adorned" means it is not like the impurities and filth of the present age.

It was filled with impurities such as excrement and urine. "Peaceful, secure, and prosperous" means it was not like the present age, where the eight sufferings burn one simultaneously and abundance and scarcity are inconsistent.
"Heavenly beings and humans flourished" means it was not like the present age, where the three miserable realms are overflowing.

The number of devas and humans has diminished. As for the ground being made of lapis lazuli, it is not like the earth of today, with its mountains of stone and soil and its pervasive scattering of sand and gravel.
As for the eight intersecting roads, they are not like the mountain passes of today, which are difficult to cross and where travel back and forth is obstructed.
As for the borders being lined with gold, they are not like the tracks crisscrossing today, where one encounters hardship in every direction.
As for the chariot, it is so; as for the precious trees surrounding it, they are not like the thorns and brambles of today that block the roads and obstruct one’s movement.
As for their constant flowers and fruits, they are not like those of today that flourish in spring and wither in autumn, subject to incessant and unstable change.
All such things as these are manifested through the pure mind of the Bodhisattva; that is to say, "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the three vehicles.
The Tathāgata Padmaprabha also teaches and transforms beings by means of the three vehicles (up to: "because of his original vow, he preaches the Dharma of the three vehicles;
the three vehicles deliver sentient beings"). All Buddhas follow the same track. When Śāriputra attains Buddhahood, he follows the established precedents;

hence it is said that he also teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. This is the explicit clarification. Regarding the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," [the author] anticipates a question (fearing that one might ask based on the preceding discussion: "All...")

The Buddha appeared in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages; therefore, he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Now, this land is named "Free from Defilement" (Vimalā), which should not be an evil age; yet he still transforms sentient beings through the Three Vehicles—what is the purpose of this?

Thus, the *Fangguang* (Luminous) Sūtra states: "When that Buddha appeared, although it was not an evil age... and so forth. There are two meanings for his preaching the [Three] Vehicles according to his original vow:

first, to repay kindness, and second, to gather in sentient beings. Regarding repaying kindness: Śāriputra reflected to himself that he had previously regressed from the Great Mind (bodhicitta); because of [the Buddha's] abiding...

Only through skillful means can one gradually reach the ultimate fruit. When he made the vow to attain Buddhahood, he taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles in order to repay the kindness of those who had provided him with sustenance and aid.

Regarding the gathering of sentient beings, Śāriputra reflected to himself: "Had I not encountered the provisional teachings since falling into the realms of ordinary people and external paths, I would surely have remained forever submerged in suffering.
When he made the vow to attain Buddhahood, he taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to gather in all beings.
This is because it is the birth that leads to falling [into lower realms]. All of this is inferred through the meaning [of the terms].
△ Third, the name of the eon is "Excellently Adorned. The eon is named "Great Jewel Adornment" (Mahāratnavyūha) because within that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.

The first phrase indicates the title; the second phrase poses the inquiry; and the final phrase provides the explanation. Although the Three Vehicles are all treasures, it is specifically the Bodhisattva who is designated as "Great.
This is because they serve as the wings for the Dharma-transformation, continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, and gather and transform sentient beings, being thus bound to the lineage of the Way.
The *Sāmmatīya-śāstra* states: "Those who establish their names based on the Bodhisattva are like the 'Non-Treasure' (Pu-bao) in the *Chu Shu*."
Gold and jade; yet they treasure those who are like virtuous people. △ Fourth, the Bodhisattvas fill [the land].
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless... (up to) thus do bodhisattvas fill that land.
Initially, their number was vast; they could exhaustively drink from the great oceans, yet their quantity remained inexhaustible.
They could traverse the entirety of space, yet their limits remained unfathomable; thus, they are called "immeasurable" and "boundless.

They cannot be reached by the path of the mind, nor can they be communicated through words; thus, they are called "inconceivable. Neither mathematicians nor their assistants are able to calculate them.
The dust motes of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are insufficient for comparison; thus it is said that they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is transparently pervasive in every place. From this level downward, there is obstruction according to one's partial attainment;

therefore it is said that none can know it except through the Buddha’s power of wisdom. If one wishes to descend [to the conventional], the outward manifestation is extraordinary. Treasure is taken for its reality; the flower symbolizes...

The "causal practice" (hetu-caryā) sufficiently demonstrates their progress and advancement. It is said that these bodhisattvas all proceed toward the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) by means of true causes;

therefore, they are symbolized by precious flowers supporting their feet. Regarding the phrase "these [bodhisattvas]," because their roots of virtue (*guṇamūla*) are profound and their causes are deep while their conditions are superior, it is said they are not those who have newly resolved their minds (*navotpannabodhicitta*).
Because their faculties are firm and their foundations are solid, it is said they have long planted the roots of virtue. By the Buddha...
"Practicing cultivation" reveals the profound depth of "rectifying what has been neglected," thereby explaining the meaning of the previous phrase, "having long planted the roots of virtue.

"Praised by all Buddhas" reveals the excellence of their protective mindfulness, thereby explaining the meaning of the previous phrase, "not for those who have newly resolved [for enlightenment]. Regarding "constantly practicing below":

the power of the vow is vast and deep. Those who constantly practice the Buddha-wisdom possess the vow to bring the Buddha-way to fulfillment. Because they pledge that it must be accomplished, their wisdom [is perfected].
"One must constantly practice. To possess great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*) is the vow to deliver all sentient beings;
because one pledges to deliver them universally, one must necessarily possess greatness. "To know well the gateways of the Dharma" is the vow to study the Dharma-gates;
because one pledges to study them exhaustively, one must know the gates well. "To be upright and without deceit" is the vow to sever afflictions (*kleśa*); because [one pledges to sever them]...
One must vow to sever them both together; therefore, in practice, one must eradicate their very root. When one is upright and honest, the internal and external are as one;
when one is without artifice, delusions do not arise. This is precisely how one cuts off the root of afflictions. As for the aforementioned vows, they are non-retrogressive and unyielding;
thus it is said that "one's resolve and mindfulness are firm and solid. This is like the saying: "Though space may come to an end, the power of one’s vows is inexhaustible."
Thus, the following concludes the section on fulfillment. Furthermore, this is also brought about by the power of the causes of his vows and practices prior to attaining Buddhahood.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings free from flattery and crookedness will come to be born in that land.
This sufficiently proves this point. The discussion on the adornment of the primary and secondary [receptacle and inhabitants] is concluded. Part Three.
Regarding the lifespan of the principal [Buddha] and his retinue:

Śāriputra, as for the lifespan of the Buddha Flower-Light (Puṣparāja), up to the point where the people of that land have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas and the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve minor kalpas—this is discussed solely in terms of the completion of a single period of manifestation. One must understand that this refers to the Dharma-body.
They do not fall within the reckoning of numbers. How could the Buddha Flower-Light (Huaguang) still be considered a descendant of King Lao-er?

Excepting the period when he was a prince and had not yet attained Buddhahood, if we speak only of the interval between his realization of the Way and his parinirvāṇa, it is said to comprise twelve minor kalpas.
As for the people whose lifespan is eight minor kalpas, this refers to the virtuous world of the Pure Land.
His lifespan is naturally long. If one considers that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, how could it be restricted to merely eight kalpas?
△ Fourth, the matters of distant and near transformations:
From "The Tathāgata Padmaprabha passed twelve small kalpas" (up to) "also thirty-two small kalpas."
The initial prediction was bestowed upon Jianman. Twelve kalpas having passed, it was the time when [the Buddha] was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bestowed the prediction upon Jianman so that he might continue this Way, deliver this life, and serve as an inexhaustible benefit after his passing.
The Bodhisattva named Jianman (Firmly Full) vowed that his aspirations would surely reach fulfillment and his practice would surely reach its ultimate end;

this is a designation for one who, bearing heavy responsibility upon a long path, neither perishes prematurely nor is obstructed. His address to the bhikṣus was to proclaim this before the assembly, manifesting that it was not a private transmission.
Because he had a precious lotus flower supporting his feet during the causal stage, he was given the name Huazuan Anxing (Lotus-Foot Peaceful Practice) as his fruit-name, manifesting—
Cause and effect are consistent. The mention of the three titles, such as *Tathāgata* (Thus-Come One), subsumes the remaining titles.
For example, "Tathāgata" subsumes both "Sugata" (Well-Gone) and "Unsurpassed Man, Charioteer of Men.
Because he has personally realized unsurpassed *tathatā* (suchness) and comes as a charioteer, he is able to go while not going and come while not coming; thus he is named "Tathāgata."
"Arhant" (Worthy One) subsumes both "Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct" and "Teacher of Gods and Humans";

only one who is fully perfected in both merit and wisdom, serving as a model for humans and devas, is fit to receive offerings from gods and humans. "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One) subsumes both "Knower of the World" and "Buddha";
only one whose three types of awakening are perfectly luminous and who thoroughly understands the phenomena of the three worlds is entitled to be called a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Since it encompasses all virtues, it transcends everything and also includes the World-Honored One; therefore, in the sutras, the ten titles may be listed together or briefly stated as three, yet the meaning remains no different.
"The land is also like this" means that the *pariṇāmanā* (retributive) environment of Padmaprabha is likewise no different from that of Padmottara.
"Śarīra," etc., refers to the duration of the Dharma and the number of kalpas. This is the correct [explanation].
Regarding "resembling [the Buddha] with the thirty-two marks": this is due to the gravity of Huaguang’s vows and the depth of his affinity with sentient beings.

To explain the meaning of "Correct" (Zheng) and "Semblance" (Xiang): when the Dharma first flourished, those who were able to realize it through direct perception were considered to be in the "Correct" period. As the distance from the Sage gradually increased...

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is rare; one can only rely on inference (*anumāna*) to imitate its likeness. During the Age of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits were all fully present.

During the Age of Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), there were teachings, principles, and practices, but no fruits. As for the Final Age (*paścimadharma*), there is merely empty talk resembling inference—vain and devoid of reality;
though the teachings and principles exist, both practice and fruit are entirely absent. Now, in order to manifest its extraordinary excellence, [this work is composed].

This causes them to give rise to joy and aspiration; therefore, he does not speak of the final dharma age. The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the introductory heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"Śāriputra shall become a Buddha in a future age as the Honored One of Universal Wisdom" (up to) "he shall realize the Unsurpassed Way.
The first verse-line indicates the name of the fruit he will achieve; he shall become the Honored One of Universal Wisdom.

Having attained the fruit of Buddhahood, there is no wisdom that he does not possess, and because he is honored wherever he dwells, this refers to the phrase "shall deliver. In meaning, this encompasses the three vehicles in their entirety. It should be placed below [the preceding section].

Section. The Buddha has here provided a summary verse that transcends the immediate sequence. Regarding "making offerings" and below, this is a retrospective verse on practicing causes throughout kalpas.

"The Bodhisattva practitioner" refers to the various gates of practice within provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); these are the dharmas for benefiting others. "The ten powers" and so forth refer to the various merits within ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*);
these are the dharmas for self-benefit. Thus, both benefits are fully realized, and both wisdoms are perfected. Therefore...
It is said that he realized the Unsurpassed Way. △ Second, the verse on the adornment of the primary and secondary [bodies].
After immeasurable kalpas had passed, there was a kalpa named Great Jewel Adornment (until the point where it says) "the transformation of the Buddha Flower-Light."
The first two lines [of the verse] surpassingly praise the name of the eon as "Excellence. Below that, regarding the world, it follows up by praising the adornment and purity of the land.
"Defects" (*kha*) refers to pits, hollows, and mounds; "impurities" (*dūṣika*) refers to filth, excrement, and urine. The remainder is the same as the prose section.

The reason for not versifying the phrase "endowed with the three vehicles" is that its meaning has already been seen above. Below that, regarding the land, it briefly praises the abundance of bodhisattvas. All bodhisattvas...

"Sā" signifies a multitude of numbers; it denotes firm resolve and mindfulness, and reveals that the power of one's vows is vast and profound. Its supernormal powers (abhijñā) correspond to those mentioned previously.
The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) unfold three vows: they can obstruct the six hindrances and sever the afflictions (kleśa); they can open the way for the myriad practices.

This is the gateway of training. Being able to reach the other shore is the attainment of the Buddha-way. "In the presence of countless Buddhas" refers to having seen that one's roots of virtue are profound and deep.
Because compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, benefiting both oneself and others, such a person is called a Bodhisattva who trains well.
Furthermore, those who study and are called "good" arise from their nature and practice without dwelling on signs.
Such great beings, having been transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light (Puṣparāja), will never cease to feel gratitude toward him.
This is why it is said in the prose that "such bodhisattvas fill his land. △ Third, the verses on the lifespan of the principal and the retinue.
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory... [his] lifespan lasted for eight small kalpas.
There are three reasons why all Buddhas appearing in the world necessarily rely upon the status of a king: first, to manifest that the rank of a Buddha is most supreme and unsurpassed;
second, to demonstrate that worldly wealth and nobility are not to be relied upon; and third, to [transform] sentient beings with false views.
Because he knew [the world] was not worthy of reverence, he vowed to abandon this trivial realm and aspire toward the domain of the three thousandfold world-system;
thus it is said, "he abandoned his kingdom. Because he did not cling to the flowers of empty space, but hoped to attain the bliss of true permanence, it is said, "he renounced glory.
In this single lifetime alone, causes were perfected and fruits were fulfilled; thus it is said, "in his final body. In this very body, he departed from the mundane and realized the supramundane.
This is true. Therefore, it is said that he left home and attained the Way. From this point onward, one discusses the number of kalpas he remained in the world;
this refers to what is stated in the prose section as the period "excluding his time as a prince" before he became a Buddha.

△ Fourth, the verses on the far-reaching and near transformations (the former briefly records the bestowing upon Kāśyapa and Pūrṇa; the latter supplements the distribution of the Śarīra relics; the meaning of the prose and the verses mutually complement each other).
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remains in the world (until) gods and humans universally make offerings.
The first verse concerns the duration of the kalpa during which the Dharma abides. While the True Dharma remains in the world, ten people leave the household life and ten people attain the Way.
Therefore, it is said that they "extensively deliver sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "the *śarīra* [relics] spread below":
as for their "extensive dissemination," it means that in the heavens and among humans, the *śarīra* are left behind to perform the work of the Buddha.

As for "universally making offerings," it means that stupas and temples are erected, and ritual implements are solemnly prepared to cultivate fields of merit. This concludes the verse summary of the prose section. △ Second, the conclusion on supreme joy.
All that the Buddha Flower-Light performed was exactly like this (up to the point where it says) "one should rejoice within oneself.
"Initially forming the victory" means that it is still in the process of being enacted. That which is "performed" refers to the retribution upon fruition;

all of these arise because they were produced by causes, just as has been explained here, without the slightest discrepancy. Therefore, it is said that "all matters are exactly like this. Both types of adornment are complete.
Fully equipped and transcending all classes of beings, he is therefore called the "Holy Honored One with Two Feet.

Not only is he honored throughout the nine realms, even the Buddhas themselves yield to him by one step; thus he is called the "Supreme and Peerless. He then said with joy: "That Buddha is none other than your own body;

The unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood now has hope; therefore, one should naturally give rise to joy and celebration.

Because they have confidence that they shall become Buddhas. Regarding "the upper garment": it is the most superior among garments; they remove it to offer to the Buddha to signify their lack of parsimony regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, they take this as a cause, hoping for the fruit of Buddhahood. △ Second, specifically clarifying the offerings of the devas, in two parts:
first, the narrator’s account of the offerings; second, the statements of the various devas. First:
Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and others (up to) simultaneously rained down a multitude of celestial flowers.

Initially, this collectively symbolizes merit and wisdom. Specifically, the explanation of the offerings made by Śakra, Brahmā, and others is because their offerings differ from those of the preceding assembly, and because there are subsequent words regarding these offerings.
Robes are used to adorn the body, symbolizing merit; flowers, being in full bloom, symbolize wisdom. These were employed as offerings to the Buddha.

This signifies the dedication of the merit and wisdom thus produced toward the Buddha-way. Regarding the phrase "the scattering [of flowers] below," this specifically signifies meritorious action (*puṇyakarman*).

Since the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) of such meritorious action are empty in essence and one does not dwell upon signs (*animitta*), this is represented by celestial garments abiding in space while revolving of their own accord.
"Revolving" refers to the state of circling without ceasing. Regarding the phrase "the various heavens below," this specifically signifies wisdom (*prajñā*).
Karma. The karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karman*) is entirely accomplished through the assistance of written characters; therefore, it is represented by hundreds of thousands of musical arts and the like.
That which is produced in mid-air represents the emptiness of the nature of written characters. Although the nature of written characters is empty, the karma of wisdom is nonetheless accomplished;
therefore, it is represented by the raining down of various celestial flowers. △ Second, the various devas present their words, in two parts. First, [the individual accounts]. One by one...
The exposition of the holy teaching; second, the praise and dedication.
First: He spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha [at Vārāṇasī]... [turned] the unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma."

The initial prose section: "The first turning of the wheel of Dharma" refers to the beginning of the provisional teaching (*upāya*). "Now turning the unsurpassed [wheel]" refers to the conclusion of the revelation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This also summarizes the preceding discussion of the Tathāgata’s provisional and ultimate teachings, recounting them in sequence.

From "At that time" onwards is the verse section. Within the main verses, "analytically explaining all dharmas" is as follows: the category of suffering (*duḥkha*) is divided into three and eight, while the category of origination (*samudaya*) is divided into two and five.
The Path is divided into seven categories; Cessation is divided into the remainder, such as "equality" and so forth, because their distinctions differ.

The "five aggregates" refers to the five men, namely Cūḍapanthaka and the others. As for "arising and ceasing," the Four Noble Truths consist of four types: first, the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing.
That is to say: suffering involves the shifting of the three marks; origination involves the movement of the four minds; the path involves being easily supplanted by its opposites;
and cessation involves the extinction of existence and its return to non-existence. This corresponds to the meaning of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Second is the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising: suffering has no characteristic of oppression; origination has no characteristic of conjunction; the path has no characteristic of duality; and cessation has no characteristic of arising. This corresponds to...
The initial teaching’s school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as well as a portion of the meaning within the sudden teaching—namely, the three immeasurables and the four truths—are as follows:
regarding suffering, the retributive fruits of the ten realms differ; regarding accumulation, the afflictions of the five abodes differ; regarding the path, the various *pāramitās* differ;
and regarding cessation, the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges differ. This corresponds to the final teaching and the initial teaching.

This is the meaning of one school within the *lakṣaṇa* (Dharmalakṣaṇa) tradition: the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). That is to say: regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all suchness (*tathatā*);

there is no suffering to be abandoned. Regarding origin (*samudaya*), defilements (*kleśa*) are fundamentally pure; there is no origin to be severed. Regarding the path (*mārga*), extremes and deviations are all the central way;
there is no path to be cultivated. Regarding cessation (*nirodha*), birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa; there is no cessation to be realized. This corresponds to the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding the teachings and the predominant meaning within the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*): based on this, the scope reached by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is limited solely to the boundaries of arising and ceasing;
hence, they are called "arising and ceasing. Furthermore, the five aggregates are identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), because the aggregates possess the sense of combination.
Arising and ceasing is precisely impermanence (*anityatā*). This means that having already explained the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*), one further explains the five aggregates.

This refers to the meaning of impermanence. To describe it as "sublime" (*miao*) while calling it "supreme" (*zui*) distinguishes it from the Vaipulya and Prajñā teachings; it is called sublime in contrast to what is coarse.

To describe it as "great" (*da*) while calling it "unsurpassed" (*wushang*) distinguishes it from the two provisional teachings of the beginning and the middle; it is called great in contrast to the Small Vehicle.
△ Second, the praise and dedication.
This Dharma is extremely profound and subtle; there are few who are able to believe it. (Up to:
"All [merit] is dedicated toward the Buddha-way. This first section points to the Dharma and offers praise. "This Dharma" refers to that which is now being turned.

It is "extremely profound and subtle" because only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it. It is "beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas," and for this reason, those who believe in it are few. From of old...

Since that time, he has repeatedly expounded the provisional teachings (*upāya-yāna*). There were no devas who were not present in the assembly; therefore, it is said that they have "heard them many times.

As for the profound and subtle supreme Dharma, it was never before revealed; only now, at this very moment, is it being disclosed—hence, it is said that they have "never heard it before. Below the passage on the World-Honored One, the text describes faith and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding those who rejoice (*anumodana*), this distinguishes those who are not the primary recipients of the teaching; it refers to those who follow the Dharma assembly and thereby achieve the benefit of joy.

Therefore, since those present have already received their predictions of enlightenment, even those who rejoice in this merit can likewise achieve the cause. Hence it is said: "They shall certainly become Buddhas.
Having attained Buddhahood, they will inevitably transcend the world; hence it is said: "Most honored and unsurpassed.

Being most honored and unsurpassed, that which they realize is spontaneous and beyond compare; hence it is said: "The Way is inconceivable. Since the Way is inconceivable, they will also inevitably...

The phrase "dividing the vehicle" follows the literal expression; thus it is said, "expounding according to skillful means. That this necessarily includes the words of the transformative teachings after attaining the Way precisely demonstrates the depth of his faith.
All meritorious deeds refer to the causes of outflow (*āsrava*) accumulated through the goodness of the precepts.
Either what was accumulated in the present will be experienced in the future, or what was accumulated in the past will be experienced in the present.
Generally speaking, it is therefore said that seeing the merit of the Buddha belongs to the karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karman*), because one who sees the Buddha necessarily hears the Dharma.
However, this merit and wisdom were previously subject to outflows (*sāsrava*); now, by means of these causes characterized by outflows—
They proceed toward the fruit of the unconditioned; therefore, it is said that they "dedicate [their merit] to the Buddha-way.
This is also because, by hearing even a slight cause or practicing scattered wholesome deeds, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood; thus these words are spoken.

Furthermore, although the various devas herein are included among those who rejoice, they emit breath and raise their voices, possessing a distinct kind of insight and vision, declaring with certainty: "He shall surely become a Buddha," as they dedicate [their merit].

Regarding such expressions as "the Buddha-way" and so forth, who other than those who have attained the stages of sagehood or those with profound past affinities could give rise to such true faith, taking a blade of grass and manifesting it as the body of sixteen feet? It is for this reason that among the three requests, they are judged to be of superior capacity.
Thus, the first round of the Dharma-exposition for the superior capacity is concluded. II. The second round of the exposition by means of parables.

The four [sections] concerning those of middling faculties: first, the son of the householder requests on behalf of others; second, the Tathāgata grants permission to teach; third, the actual teaching through parables;
fourth, those of middling faculties obtain benefit. First:
At that time, Śāriputra [up to] requested, "May you explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
First, he personally recounted his own realization. Having previously heard the analytical explanations, he thoroughly understood that one makes a Buddha through one's own mind;

therefore, it is said, "I no longer have any doubt or regret. Because he was free from doubt and regret, he received the Buddha’s seal of approval that he would surely attain [enlightenment]; thus it is said, "I have personally received [the prediction]."

Commentary: These [beings] below are still deluded regarding others; yet, having already realized the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*), their wisdom liberates them from the bonds of the realms. Thus, they are called "those with mastery over the mind.

Their former abiding on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) refers to the period before they had realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Since they have not yet realized no-more-learning, the Buddha commands them to investigate the truth and sever the afflictions;
hence, it is said that he "constantly teaches and transforms" them, saying: "My Dharma can bring one away from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"Those who are [in training]" refers to the teaching through the words of severing delusions (*kleśa*), for only by severing the accumulation (*samudaya*) can one depart from suffering (*duḥkha*).

"Ultimate *nirvāṇa*" refers to the teaching through the words of investigating the Truth (*tattva*), for only by cultivating the Path (*mārga*) can one realize cessation (*nirodha*). "Ultimate" carries the meaning of realization and entry.
"Those in training and those beyond training" is a designation for those who formerly dwelt on the stage of training; it means that they investigate the Truth and sever delusions at the outset.

Because it pertains to those who are in training and those beyond training, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is itself the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), meaning the false conceptualization that there is a self within the body that acts as a sovereign.
The views of existence and non-existence are the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), meaning the erroneous adherence to annihilationism or eternalism regarding the body of the five aggregates.
This "etcetera" includes all other views, up to the sixty-two kinds. All such views are rooted in the view of self.
It is the foundation. As for those who consider themselves to have attained detachment: because they follow the Buddha’s words, they know suffering and sever the origin [of suffering].

When their clinging to a self is exhausted, they personally realize that all views have vanished; because they then cling to this as the ultimate, the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna takes the emptiness of self as its essence.
As for those who claim to have attained it: because they follow the Buddha’s words, they cultivate the path and realize cessation. They cultivate...

Having attained the realization of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*), they did not understand that [the Buddha's teachings] were established through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) as provisional designations;

because they grasped them as being ultimately real, they all took what was provisional to be substantial. Now, hearing [the teaching] that "he directly abandons skillful means," it is said that this is something they have never heard before.
"All fall into doubt and confusion. If one claims that the past was correct, one suspects that the present is deceptive and false;

if one claims that the present is correct, one is bewildered by the fact that the past was merely laborious toil. Furthermore, how could one know that the reality of today is not separate from the provisional means of the past?

"Excellent! and below, [the author] acts as an intermediary to offer this petition, praising the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real, and hoping that [the Buddha] will not withhold his compassion.

Out of compassion, he addresses the World-Honored One as "Excellent! and prays that [the teaching] be expounded for the fourfold assembly. This is because even those beyond training (aśaikṣa) remain deluded;

the state of the other assemblies can thus be inferred. Furthermore, within the Chapter on the Exposition of the Dharma, it is repeatedly stated that there is only the single Buddha-vehicle and no other vehicles, and it is said, for instance, that "straightforwardly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the unsurpassed Way. Thus, the setting aside of the provisional teachings is not without purpose.

Because the fourfold assembly did not understand the underlying causes and conditions, there arose doubts regarding contradictions between the present and the past, as well as the confusion of being unable to distinguish right from wrong.
Thereupon, Śāriputra acted on their behalf to request an explanation of these causes and conditions;

for once the reasons for the previous abandonment were clarified, the distinction between right and wrong regarding the present and the past would naturally be discerned. Thus it is said that they were made to be free from doubt and regret. This accords with the Tathāgata’s subsequent summary.

The answer states: "By this cause and condition, one should know that through the power of the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas, they distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
The verse says: "By this cause and condition, if one seeks truthfully throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle whatsoever, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
All of this corresponds to [the preceding]. Śāriputra has finished his request on behalf of others. 2. The Tathāgata’s Permission to Teach.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra (up to the point where it says): "Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.
Having already established the initial discourse, the Buddha spoke again because Śāriputra possessed a mind intent on benefiting both himself and others;
thus, the Tathāgata did not avoid the reproach of being prolix. His words, "Did I not say before," etc., carry the implicit sense of censuring the inappropriateness of the question.
This means that the skillful means of teaching through causes, conditions, parables, and so forth, are all for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, one knows that the provisional is integrated into and returns to the real; it is for the purpose of setting aside the provisional teachings on causes and conditions. Have I not already said these words before?
For what reason do you again request that I explain their causes and conditions? "These various... and below, this cites the Dharma and establishes the analogy. These various...

The phrase "as has been said" (*yathoktam*) restates the preceding causes, conditions, parables, and so forth, serving as the basis for the principle of the skillful provision of the three carts below;

it is intended to convert the bodhisattvas. The phrase "all [this] is for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," etc., restates the preceding [passage], serving as the basis for the principle of bestowing the single cart equally below.

Furthermore, the character *ran* (然) has three meanings: first, it is a particle of transition, meaning that its phrasing is transformed; second, it is a sound of lamentation or sighing, meaning to express deep regret...

Because they do not awaken to it, there is a third sense of "agreement," meaning that one agrees to their request. Since he explained it a second time and they still did not understand—and as the previous [explanation] was likewise of no benefit—it is said:
"It should be made clear through a parable. The phrase "all those who possess" carries a sense of encouragement and exhortation; the intention is:
"If you are indeed people of wisdom, you should naturally attain understanding through a parable. If there is still [something you do not grasp]..."
As for those who understand [it], they will end up in the lower streams; I can do nothing for them at all. When the Tathāgata had finished granting permission to speak, △ Part Three:
The Actual Exposition of the Parable, in two sections: First, the prose; Second, the verses. The first [of these] has three parts: First, the parable; Second, the application to the Dharma;
Third, the concluding response. The first [of these] has three parts: First, the parable of the sentient beings’ capacity and response; Second, the parable of the Tathāgata...
Transformation and Response. These three analogies demonstrate that the Buddha’s words are not false. The first three consist of: first, an analogy for the Buddha who is manifested;

second, an analogy for the assembly who manifests [the response]; and third, an analogy that concludes the meaning of manifestation. Regarding the first (as stated in the "Chapter on the Dharma-Exposition": "I observe with my Buddha-eye," this refers to the meaning of the word "I").
Śāriputra, suppose there were a kingdom, city, or village (extending to) many fields, houses, and various servants.
"Suppose" (*yathā*) means: regarding "kingdom, city, or village," according to the textual structure, it should be understood as referring to all the world.
Regarding "all worlds," among the three types [of worlds], it refers here to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), namely the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).

To provide specific analogies: a kingdom represents the great thousand-fold world system; a town represents the intermediate thousand-fold world system; and a village represents the small thousand-fold world system.

This sequence from the broad to the narrow is logically consistent. As for the character *yǒu* (有), it possesses a specific connection; in terms of its meaning, it is connected to the word "long" (*zhǎng*).
The lord of a kingdom, city, or village is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who is the father of all the world. The elder is a metaphor for the Buddha;

according to ancient masters, there are ten meanings [for this comparison], which I shall now briefly summarize into three. First is "abundance," meaning that one accords well with the sentiments of others and their reputation is highly renowned;
this is a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings, as his fame pervades everywhere. Second is "exalted virtue."
Advanced in years and pure in conduct, he was honored by all. He was likened to a Buddha who has realized the ultimate and whose attachments have vanished; his virtue crowned the nine realms.

Thus, he possessed the three great riches: his granaries were full and his treasuries overflowing, providing for the state without deficiency—metaphorically representing the Buddha’s pure wisdom and perfected insight that give rise to all dharmas.
As for his advanced age, "decline" signifies having exhausted both sweetness and bitterness, thereby being free from all fears.

As for "Mastery," it refers to being thoroughly proficient in both principle and phenomena, transcending all obscurity and delusion; this is analogous to the Buddha’s virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*), wherein the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) are completely exhausted and the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*) are forever extinguished—this is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned "exalted virtue.

As for "immeasurable wealth," wealth is like the purple insignia and yellow banners, and his riches are comparable to Mount Tongling and the Golden Valley; this is analogous to the Buddha’s virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), which is vast, profound, and inexhaustible.
"Exhaustless" refers to the meaning of "great wealth" explained above. Regarding "fields, houses, and servants": fields can nourish one's life; houses provide a dwelling for the body;
servants are available for errands; and attendants are there to await and serve one's needs. These are metaphors for the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue:

they nourish the *dharmakāya*, provide a resting place for the life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*), employ compassion to bestow joy, and utilize pity to uproot suffering. This is what was explained above as being "abundant."

This is the meaning. The analogy for the Buddhas who are the objects of response has concluded. △ Second, the analogy for the assembly that is capable of responding (the "Exposition by Dharma" chapter states:
"seeing the sentient beings of the six realms"—this refers to the meaning of "sentient beings").
That house was vast and had but a single gate (up to) where thirty people resided within this dwelling.
The first metaphor refers to sentient beings in the five destinies. That "the house was vast" means that it contained five hundred dwellings;

although there were five hundred dwellings, they all belonged to the elder, and thus it is called "his house. This metaphor illustrates how the three realms, though consisting of five destinies, [are unified].

The dwelling place is likewise a realm transformed by the Buddha. That there is but a single gate—where two door-panels join to form a gate—is a metaphor for the two matters of cultivation and abandonment within the categories of good and evil;
it signifies that if one wishes to exit the triple world, it can be attained only through cultivation, and achieved only through abandonment.
That there are many people is a metaphor for the five destinies (*pañcagati*); as a household is large and its affairs manifold, each has its own specific office.

Sentient beings repay debts and settle grievances; as these manifest according to their karma, the first hundred [years] represent the heavenly realm, the next two hundred represent the human realm, and so forth—skipping over the three hundred and four hundred to represent the realms of animals and hungry ghosts—the final five hundred represent the hell realm.
That the number of years in these five realms increases progressively serves to reveal the cultivation [of merit].
Those who are good are few, while those who commit evil are many; that is to say, the three evil realms are filled, and the hosts of devas and humans diminish.
Revolving in cycles of rebirth, they do not escape the triple world; therefore, it is metaphorically said that they "dwell within" the hall and pavilion below.

This is a metaphor for sentient beings of the three vehicles. A "hall" refers to a main chamber; a "pavilion" refers to an upper story or annexed building. The vertical structure represents the tiers of the triple world.
Because the four marks of existence and the three calamities arrive suddenly, it is likened to being "rotten and old. "Rotten and old" signifies being dilapidated and decayed.
The surrounding wall is called a *qiang* (enclosure); the four sides are called *bi* (walls). The horizontal metaphor represents the boundaries of the six realms (*ṣadgati*).

Because one dies here and is born there, with the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) pressing in from all sides, it is likened to collapsing. "Collapsing" (*tuiluo*) is synonymous with falling down. The pillars represent individual karma (*bhinnakarma*);

the foundation represents collective karma (*sabhāgakarma*). Arising suddenly based on the True [Nature], deluded movement is not the True; therefore, it is likened to rotting. "Rotting" (*fubai*) is synonymous with...

"Decayed and putrid. The rafters are a metaphor for individual retribution (*vyaktavipāka*); the ridgepole is a metaphor for collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*). These are both induced by two types of karma;

because they are seen through delusion and lack reality, they are metaphorically described as "tipping and perilous. "Tipping and perilous" means slanting or leaning. "Pervading throughout its interior" is called *parivṛta*.
"Without before or after" is called *yugapat* (simultaneous). "Suddenly existing where there was nothing" is called *akasmāt* (suddenly). "Fierce flames suddenly blazing up" refers to fire.
"Arising. When halls and pavilions all burn, it is called "a burning house. Now we shall take this metaphor in reverse order; its meaning will become clear of itself.
To say that fire arises and burns the house is a metaphor for the five turbidities and the eight sufferings that oppress the triple world.

Yet these five turbidities and eight sufferings originally manifest through delusion and karma from what is ultimately non-existent, becoming ultimately existent. Therefore, they are metaphorically described as "sudden."

Nevertheless, although they arise from ultimate non-existence as ultimate existence, the six realms of rebirth also emerge simultaneously and together, without void or interval, and without before or after;
therefore, they are likened to being "surrounded and occurring at the same time. The various children collectively represent the three vehicles.
Because Mahābhijñājñānabhibhū formed a karmic connection with the Buddha, he has the sense of being a "son.

If ten [years] represent the Bodhisattvas individually, twenty represent the Pratyekabuddhas individually, and thirty represent the Śrāvakas individually, the reason the numbers of the Three Vehicles decrease as they ascend is that the superior causes are difficult to cultivate.
Furthermore, because they are all submerged together with those in the five realms of existence, the metaphor states they are "in this house."

The section on the metaphors for those who experience [the results] concludes. △ Third, the metaphors that establish the meaning of experiencing [the results] (this corresponds to the "Exposition of the Dharma" chapter where it says:

"For the sake of these sentient beings, one gives rise to a heart of great compassion," while also employing metaphors for such meanings as observing with the Buddha-eye, down to their poverty and lack of merit and wisdom).
The elder sees this great fire arising from all four sides, yet his heart feels no revulsion or distress, nor does he have the intention to seek escape.

That "the great fire arises on all four sides" means it spreads all around the four directions, rising simultaneously; this is a metaphor for the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the eight kinds of suffering (*aṣṭau duḥkhāni*), which pervade the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and the six realms of existence (*ṣad-gati*).
Thus, within the ground of the principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Buddha receives the perfuming influence [of sentient beings] and extends his illuminating grace.

Therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of the elder’s vision. The meanings of "startled" (*jing*) and "terrified" (*bu*) apply to both the dharma and the metaphor. In the metaphor, "startled" refers to the injury to the sons’ bodies, while "terrified" refers to the loss of their lives.
In the dharma, "startled" and "terrified" refer to the three vehicles; "injury" refers to the wounding of the Dharma-body, and "loss" refers to the loss of the life of wisdom.

And he forms this thought: it is like the Buddha giving rise to great compassion; by forming this thought, he intends to extinguish the fire, and by giving rise to the mind of compassion, he intends to uproot suffering.
That which is being burned is the burning house, which serves as a metaphor for the gates of the three realms.

The exit from it serves as a metaphor for cultivation and abandonment. To emerge safely represents the departure from suffering and the attainment of bliss. Thus, it speaks of the Buddha and sentient beings.
We are all equally ordinary beings; we dwell together within the three realms and equally undergo manifold sufferings.
Only the Buddha, through unremitting diligence in the practice of cultivation and abandonment, has already been able to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.

Therefore, he is likened to one who has safely emerged from a burning house. The character "而" (ér) should be construed with the preceding "雖" (suī); it means that although the father has safely emerged, [the children have not].

Yet the sons still remain within the house; this is a metaphor for how, although the Buddha has transcended suffering and attained bliss, those with the capacities of the three vehicles still wallow within the triple world—some falling back to the level of ordinary beings and becoming addicted to the five desires, while others flow into false views.
Because they are deeply attached to false dharmas, they are likened to those who delight in play and sport. "Not being aware" means not being aware that there is fire within the house;
"not knowing" means not knowing that fire has the power to burn. This is a metaphor for how those of the three vehicles are submerged in the triple world (*tridhātu*):
they do not perceive the triple world as suffering, nor do they know that suffering is of a nature that oppresses. "Not being alarmed" means not being alarmed at the loss of their bodies.

"Without fear" means not fearing the loss of life. This is a metaphor for sentient beings whose afflictions (*kleśa*) daily encroach upon them, causing them to lose their *dharmakāya* and forfeit their life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*), yet remaining tranquil and without dread.
"Fire comes to press against the body, its pain cutting to the very core": here, the body is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*.

The "self" is a metaphor for the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*); collectively, it is a metaphor for sentient beings. When a single pleasure remains unfulfilled and manifold sufferings have already arrived, they oppress the *dharmakāya* and press upon the life-force of wisdom.
This is precisely what is meant in the "Chapter on Explaining the Dharma" by the phrase "the perilous path of birth and death.

That the mind does not feel weary or distressed is a metaphor for sentient beings not contemplating escape from suffering; that there is no intention to seek liberation is a metaphor for sentient beings not contemplating [liberation].

If one seeks only pleasure and does not contemplate the departure from suffering, one will not know how to sever the origin of suffering. If one does not contemplate the attainment of pleasure, one will not know how to cultivate the path.
Thus, although the gates of cultivation and severance have been established, not only can one not escape through them, but one cannot even understand them.
Reflecting upon this, one cannot help but emerge from the ultimate truth to engage with the mundane world. This concludes the analogy regarding the sentient beings' capacity for resonance.

△ Second, the analogy of the Tathāgata’s transformative response has two parts: 1. An analogy for proceeding from the ultimate to establish the provisional; 2. An analogy for returning the provisional to the ultimate. The first part has two sub-sections: 1.

An analogy for not being able to proceed from the ultimate; 2. An analogy for concealing the ultimate to establish the provisional. The first of these has two further sub-sections: 1. An analogy... [text breaks off]

Contemplating for twenty-one days, he gave rise to two metaphors to illustrate that there was no calculation [of time]. The first (refers to the meaning in the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition: "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment," etc.).
Śāriputra, this elder reflects thus (up to): "If I take it out of the house using a small table. Reflecting in this way corresponds to the verse stating that he has already entered the burning house;

it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata manifesting signs among humanity, demonstrating the attainment of perfect enlightenment, and wishing to fulfill his original intention by employing the Great Dharma.
His body is a metaphor for supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and his hands are a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*).

Wisdom and the supernormal powers possess the merit of bearing burdens, while wisdom possesses the capacity for uplifting and extricating; therefore, they are metaphorically described as "possessing strength.
The robes, the lap-satchel, and the desk collectively symbolize the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). The merits of the Buddha-ground are immeasurable and boundless.
To speak briefly: these are called *jñānadarśana* (knowledge and vision), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*).

To provide further analogies: a *kuccha* is a Western vessel for flowers that can hold many blossoms; this is a metaphor for how knowledge and vision can contain all manner of wonders. A *pīṭha* is a small table or stand;
it must always be placed in the center, serving as a metaphor for how fearlessness can occupy the central position. A *maṇḍapa* is a desk or writing-table; it is used for... [text fragment ends].
The vastness of the space is a metaphor for the boundless power of the Ten Strengths (*daśabala*). As for those who emerge from the house:

if they have strength in their bodies, they carry [the person] out using a lap-cloth (*kośa*); if they have strength in their hands, they lift [the person] out using a small table (*mañca*). Thus, they are able to emerge from the house.

This is a metaphor for when the Tathāgata first attains perfect enlightenment and, wishing to employ the power of supernormal knowledges (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom (*jñāna*), desires to praise the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
[The Buddha] manifests the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, enabling sentient beings to realize perfect enlightenment in a single lifetime and transcend the triple world instantaneously.

△ Second, the metaphor for the absence of calculation when forming a thought (which corresponds to the meaning in the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition: "If one were to merely praise the Buddha Vehicle," etc.).
He further reflected that this house has but a single door (and so forth), until: "it might collapse and be consumed by fire.
