To "further reflect" means he knew his sons were young; thus he thought again, just as the Tathāgata knows the dullness of their faculties.
This successive reflection is as follows: there is no other exit than the single door, and being narrow, it is easy to block.

Obstruction. This is a metaphor for the fact that while one may exit the three realms only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), within this path of cultivation there are many impediments;
hence, it is "childish. Being immature and lacking discernment, one does not know the way out. Being attached to the place of play, one does not comprehend the father’s mind.
Because one does not comprehend the father’s mind, the desk and table are held empty-handed, and the satchel is carried in vain; though the hands and body possess strength, [it remains useless].
There is likewise nothing that can be done about it; hence it is said that one may fall and be consumed by fire.

This is a metaphor for those whose faculties are dull and whose wisdom is inferior, who do not know the essential way of deliverance, and who remain attached to the triple world. They do not realize the Buddha-mind. They do not realize the Buddha-mind.
Therefore, they are unable to receive the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; even though the Tathāgata possesses supernatural powers and wisdom, he can do nothing for them.
It may be that their spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is not yet mature, and they will consequently fall back into the triple world, oppressed by manifold sufferings.
This is why the Tathāgata uttered the lament: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter *nirvāṇa*. To illustrate this from a parable:

The actual [teaching] was not yet fully realized. △ Second, the parable of concealing the ultimate truth to establish provisional means (this corresponds to the meaning of the previous "Exposition of the Dharma" chapter regarding the thought:

"I recall the Buddhas of the past and the power of their skillful means," etc.; however, while the Exposition of the Dharma refers only to the Deer Park, the meaning here encompasses the three assemblies; while the Exposition of the Dharma refers only to the five śrāvakas, the text here includes the various capacities of the three vehicles; while the Exposition of the Dharma speaks only of the general name for the Wheel of Dharma, the parable here reveals the distinct characteristics of the Four Noble Truths).

Regarding these preceding and subsequent dharma-expositions and parables, which differ in their detail, brevity, concealment, and manifestation, the lecturer should rely solely on the parable to establish the meaning; there is no need to forcibly draw parallels or apply them, as this would instead cause the meaning of the parable to be obscured.

[This is] in accordance [with the sequence]. It is divided into two parts: first, using a metaphor to first demonstrate suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); second, using a metaphor to subsequently bestow the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

The first part has three sections: first, a metaphor for seeking and contemplating the means; second, a metaphor for correctly demonstrating suffering and its origin; third, a metaphor for the lack of faith due to contrary emotions. The first [section]:
"I shall speak of matters that cause fear" (up to) "lest they be burned and harmed by fire. The phrase "I shall" is a term of deliberation;
it is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge of the dullness of [the disciples'] faculties and his intention to contemplate skillful means.

"Speaking of matters that cause fear" is intended to cause them to emerge quickly; it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s intention to set forth the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) so as to cause the abandonment of the Origin (*samudaya*) and the emergence [from it].
This is the realm (*dhātu*). That the house has already burned corresponds to the fear that is about to be described; one should know this as an analogy for the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

"It is fitting to go out quickly" corresponds to the exhortation to depart swiftly; this is an analogy for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) which must be abandoned, because only by abandoning origination can one leave the realm.
If one does not leave the house, one will certainly be harmed by the fire; thus, the warning "do not let [it happen]" is an analogy for not remaining within the realm.
Then various sufferings cannot be avoided; therefore, I advise that they must not be done. These [statements] are all words of deliberation.
△ Second, using a parable to correctly demonstrate suffering and its origin:
Having formed this thought, he told his sons everything exactly as he had contemplated: "All of you, come out quickly!"
Since his preliminary deliberation was already settled, it is said, "Having formed this thought. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s firm resolution to employ skillful means (*upāya*).

"As he had contemplated, he informed all his sons" means that according to what he had previously planned, he spoke of the house being ablaze, exhorted them to depart immediately, and cautioned them against the harm of the fire—each and every detail he explained thoroughly to his sons.

This is like the Tathāgata manifesting suffering to bring about understanding, exhorting the gathering [of merit] to effect its severance, and warning that the three realms cannot be inhabited for long;
he universally addresses all sentient capacities, urging them to abandon and sever [suffering] together.

The final instruction, "You must quickly emerge," is precisely the elder’s repeated and earnest entreaty, which serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s sincere and repeated exhortations. △ Third, the metaphor of contravention.
He did not believe it.
Although his father felt pity for him and used kind words to entice and advise him, [the son] merely ran back and forth playing while looking at his father.
Despite the repeated and earnest exhortations—spoken out of affectionate concern and compassion, and intended to frighten him into coming out—all were but kind words used to entice him.
“Instruction” (*yul*) refers to the Tathāgata’s earnest exhortation and admonition—speaking of suffering and its origin. Although the father acts in this way, the son still does not believe;
this is a metaphor for how, although the Tathāgata reveals suffering and its origin, sentient beings do not accept his teaching.
“Delighting in play” is a metaphor for sentient beings being addicted to the five desires and stained by false views. Because they cling to false views, they do not...
Knowing that the Buddha is the Teacher, yet because they are mired in the five desires, they do not know that the Dharma can lead to liberation;
thus it is said they are "unwilling to believe and accept. This refers to those who do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering.

To be "unstartled" means they are not startled by the loss of their bodies; to be "fearless" means they do not fear the loss of their lives. This metaphor illustrates how sentient beings do not dread injury.

Regarding the *dharmakāya*, there is no fear of losing the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvitendriya*). There is no one who has resolved to leave; they delight in play and amusement, entirely lacking the intention to exit the house.
This is a metaphor for sentient beings who are addicted to desire and attached to the perverse, seeking no liberation.
This is what the Master Padmasambhava meant by being "handcuffed at the gate of death. Furthermore, they do not know that [the house] runs through the following text; they do not know it is on fire.

This means that when fire comes to press upon the body, one does not perceive it; this is a metaphor for sentient beings being oppressed by manifold sufferings, yet not knowing that suffering is of the nature of oppression.
"Not knowing how to abandon it" means that while dwelling in a decaying house, one does not examine it for oneself.
This is a metaphor for sentient beings who have long been submerged in the three realms (*tridhātu*), unaware that these realms are impermanent phenomena.
It is as Master Padmasambhava said: "Like flies and maggots feasting in a latrine; like cattle and sheep heading toward a slaughterhouse.

To be "unaware of what has been lost" means that while there are joys and benefits outside the gate, one loses them and fails to look back. This metaphor illustrates how sentient beings merely grasp at what is within the realm [of cyclic existence].
Regarding the joy of permanence: they do not know the truly permanent joy beyond the realms, and because of this, they lose it forever.
This is what the ancient masters meant when they said one "discards the soul-restoring incense and beats the drum of lethal poison. According to their wholesome karma, they ascend upward.

It is like galloping eastward: pursued by evil karma, one falls downward. It is like running westward: following the current up and down, there is no hope of returning to the source; thus it is metaphorically called "but" (*dàn*).
One also knows that the fruit of Buddhahood is something to be rejoiced in, yet one is resigned to having no share in it; thus it is metaphorically called "merely looking at one's father.
This metaphor first illustrates the thorough examination of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*). △ Second, the metaphor for the subsequent bestowal.

The Path that Extinguishes [Suffering] has three aspects: first, it is illustrated by the skillful means of recollective reflection; second, it is illustrated by the actual application of the path that extinguishes [suffering];

and third, it is illustrated by the cultivation and realization that fulfill one’s aspirations. Regarding the first: at that time, the elder immediately thought thus... [until] ...enabling his sons to escape this calamity.
As for the thought he forms: because the sons do not believe their father’s words, the father’s anxiety increases;

this is a metaphor for how the more sentient beings refuse the Buddha’s transformation, the more the Buddha’s compassion becomes intense. "This house has already been burned by a great fire" means that the fire has long since broken out;
it is a metaphor for how, from time immemorial, these three realms have existed, and with them, these manifold sufferings.
Because it was so oppressive, the elder entered the burning house to save his children and dwelt together with them; thus he said, "I and my children.
This is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, in order to deliver sentient beings, manifests birth within the triple world, where ordinary people and sages dwell together.
If one does not emerge at the proper time, one will surely be consumed by the flames.

Since he was unable to save his children in time to escape the burning house together with them, yet could not bear to leave them behind and depart alone, he was inevitably destined to be burned along with his children.

This is analogous to how the Tathāgata, being unable to swiftly deliver those with whom he shared past karmic conditions from the Triple World, yet could not bear to abandon those he sought to transform—even though his physical body was but six feet tall.
They, too, cannot escape being transformed by the four marks [of conditioned existence]. This is also the meaning of what Vimalakīrti said regarding "falling ill because of illness.
"One should employ skillful means" refers to preparing objects of play and delight to accord with their prior inclinations;

it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata employing the Truth of Cessation through the Three Vehicles to cast them according to their innate dispositions, thereby enabling the sons to escape this [suffering].

Regarding "harm": because one’s prior disposition accords with what is pleasing, one will inevitably seek to acquire it; by virtue of this seeking to acquire it, one is naturally able to leave the house and escape harm.
This is analogous to how the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) accords with one’s innate nature: one will inevitably aspire to realize it;

by virtue of this aspiration for realization, one is naturally able to transcend the realm and be free from suffering. The meaning of the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is implicitly included herein, because by aspiring to cessation, one must necessarily cultivate the path. This...
These [terms] are also words used for deliberation. △ Second, the analogy for correctly bestowing the Path and Cessation:
"The father, knowing that each of his sons had previously harbored their own preferences... (up to) ...I shall give you all that you desire."
The father’s knowledge of his sons is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s unerring discernment of their capacities.

Their various inclinations and habitual tendencies from previous lives are a metaphor for the predispositions cultivated through past existences. These predispositions include distinctions such as those who hear [the teachings] and those who aspire to become bodhisattvas;
therefore, they are likened to "various precious toys. These "various precious toys" implicitly refer to the three vehicles mentioned below, which correspond to the three *yānas*.
Furthermore, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the Three Vehicles is in no way a worldly thing; therefore, it is likened to a marvelous and extraordinary object.
As for those whose minds are inevitably attached to such things, because it accords with their prior inclinations, even if they momentarily forget about it, love arises upon hearing of it.

This is an analogy for the habitual tendencies of sentient beings' past natures: although they are temporarily obscured by the "intermediate state" (antarābhava), their faculties are activated upon contact.

Thus, when [the father] addresses them, saying, "I already know you are my son," he gives them whatever they desire according to their inclinations; this is analogous to the Tathāgata, who, having discerned the capacities [of beings], imparts the teaching according to what is appropriate.
As for the objects of play and enjoyment, he displays them hanging outside the gate, so that there may be further things to admire and delight in.

The objects of your pleasure and delight are like the True Bliss that exists within the Cessation Truth (nirodha-satya) beyond the realms, which the Tathāgata has pointed out from afar as something to be attained.
That which is rare and difficult to obtain does not exist within the house; it cannot be acquired with ease.
This is a metaphor for the True Bliss of the Cessation Truth, which does not exist within the realms and cannot be realized in a momentary lapse. If you do not take hold of it...

Regarding the phrase "one will surely experience sorrow and regret later": this exhorts one to strive to seize the opportunity in the present, lest one later lament not having obtained it or regret having been too slow to take it.

It is like the Tathāgata exhorting one to practice and realize the truth in a timely manner, so that one does not later find oneself empty-handed with nothing gained, leading a life in vain and dying in obscurity, only to increase one's own grief and lamentation. Such various matters as these are categorized under the "Finger" section.
Externally, he displays three chariots; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s correct demonstration of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). If one were to provide separate metaphors:
the sheep-cart, which carries light loads and travels short distances, is a metaphor for the *śrāvaka*’s Truth of Cessation, as they seek only self-benefit and are urgent in seeking realization.

The deer-cart, which carries slightly heavier loads and travels a somewhat longer distance, is a metaphor for the *pratyekabuddha*’s Truth of Cessation, as they harbor a slight inclination toward benefiting others and have few desires.

Because it reaches the highest attainment, the ox-cart carries heavy loads and travels great distances; this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), as its intention is to benefit both self and others, and its aim is the fulfillment of the fruit.
"That which can be used for play" means that one may ride upon it to travel and may sport and frolic upon it;

this is a metaphor for how, once the Truth of Cessation has been realized, one naturally possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) with total mastery, sovereignty, and unimpededness. You all, regarding this fire...
"House! You should come out quickly! This means that one must clearly understand that a house made of fire cannot be inhabited for long;
one must swiftly seek liberation. It is a metaphor for the Tathāgata showing that there is no peace within the three realms; one must urgently cultivate the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).

If one urgently cultivates the Truth of the Path, then the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) beyond the realms can be realized at will. Therefore, the metaphor says: "Whatever you desire, all shall be attained."
I give this to you: it is simply a matter of discerning a sincere resolve; I shall certainly not deceive you. Now, as for the explanation of the Three Vehicles by means of the Four Truths:

since the Truths condition the Six Perfections, their names differ while their meaning remains the same. Examining the preceding and following passages of the sutra, they accord well with the Four Truths;

I have merely established the doctrine based on the text. Furthermore, the Four Truths include those of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*).

Regarding the meanings of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and so forth, what kind of capacity would not be encompassed by them? What teaching would not include them? △ Third, the analogy of fulfilling wishes through cultivation and realization:
At that time, the sons, having heard what their father said, vied with one another to run and compete to escape from the burning house.

"Hearing what accords with their wishes" means it harmonizes with their prior inclinations; this is a metaphor for sentient beings hearing the teaching on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and casting themselves toward their innate dispositions.

"Each heart is courageous and keen" means each is valiant, vigorous, and sharp; this is a metaphor for sentient beings each giving rise to a superior resolve and advancing with diligence without retreating.
"Pushing and shoving one another" means they drive and displace each other; this is a metaphor for the three [poisons].
"Each vehicle adheres to its own view and mutually disputes right and wrong. "Racing together and running about" refers to scrambling for the road and galloping away;
this is a metaphor for the three vehicles each following their own dharma, vying with one another to advance and attain [their goals]. "Striving to exit the burning house" means...

Each desires to quickly obtain their own chariot to ride upon for play and sport; this is a metaphor for those of the three vehicles each desiring to swiftly realize their respective fruits and enjoy sovereign mastery.
If explained in terms of the stages [of the path], "hearing the teaching that accords with one's wishes" is a metaphor for the stage of generating the resolve [for awakening].
This refers to beginning from non-awakening, when the mind first arises to leave the realm and seek cessation. Because it still accords with its aspiration, the minds are each courageous and sharp;

this is a metaphor for the stage of provisions (*sambhāra-mārga*). Within the stage of provisions, the five types of settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthiti*), the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) suppress the afflictions and delusions, though they have not yet attained their immediate elimination. Because they are like being courageous and sharp, their mutual pushing and shoving serves as a metaphor for [the stage of application].

The stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): Within the stage of application, the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) suppress and eliminate the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

Because they have not yet attained immediate abandonment—acting like pushing and shoving—they rush forward together in competition; this serves as a metaphor for the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*).

Within the stage of penetration, the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) abandons the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptual views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), though they are not yet exhausted.
"Co-arising" refers to running and rushing, as they strive to escape the burning house; this is a metaphor for the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Within this stage of cultivation, one abandons the first six grades of co-arising afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and [abandons the remainder] through the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Having severed the final three grades of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the desire realm, there remain seventy-two grades of innate afflictions in the two higher realms that have not yet been exhausted.
Because one has not yet emerged from contention, one proceeds downward with security until emerging;

sitting in the open air is then used as a metaphor for the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). This shall be further analyzed in the relevant section. This is the sequence of stages for the *śrāvaka*; as for the *pratyekabuddha*...
Sādhūn, you should know this: if explained by means of the Four Noble Truths, their aspiring for and being eager for [the jewels] is a metaphor for yearning for Cessation (*nirodha*);

their pushing and shoving one another is a metaphor for abandoning Origination (*samudaya*); their racing together in competition is a metaphor for practicing the Path (*mārga*); and their vying to exit the burning house is a metaphor for being freed from Suffering (*duḥkha*).

If explained by means of the Threefold Wisdom, hearing the description of the precious playthings is a metaphor for the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); each heart being eager and vigorous is a metaphor for the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The metaphor of driving away [the oxen] and dispersing them illustrates the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). The general statement that "he preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet each according to their kind understands it differently" assigns these positions to the Dharma in relation to wisdom;
this depends solely on how individuals grasp and apply it. This concludes the metaphor for establishing provisional means based upon the ultimate reality.

II. The metaphor for returning the provisional to the ultimate has three parts: 1. The metaphor for the time having arrived and the capacities of beings having matured. 2. The metaphor for the equal bestowal of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). 3. The metaphor for... [text ends]

Gaining benefit from hearing the Dharma. This refers first to the meaning [found] in the previous section on the "Teaching of the Dharma" (the passage beginning with "I see the sons of the Buddha... those who are resolutely seeking the path of the Buddha," etc.).
At that time, the elder saw his sons and [said], "I shall grant them the wish for goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts.
This initial parable indicates that the proper time has arrived. "Secure" means they have not yet been harmed by fire. "Having emerged" means they have come out unharmed.

This metaphor illustrates that sentient beings have not yet been bound by various sufferings, but preserve their goodness and emerge from the realm of transmigration. The four directions constitute the thoroughfare.
It is said: "The four crossroads. Being still halfway along the road is called "being on the way. This is a metaphor for the Three Vehicles as the crossroads to the four virtues;
however, they have not yet reached the ultimate goal. Having arrived at a secluded, open space is called "the open ground. Not seeking to travel further is called "sitting down.

This is a metaphor for those of the Three Vehicles who have already realized partial fruits and no longer advance in their quest. "No longer having any obstructions" refers to those who wish to reach their father.
Furthermore, one may depart; there is no longer any obstruction of the burning house. This is a metaphor for those of the three vehicles who wish to realize the fruit of Buddhahood;
they may likewise cultivate it, as there is no longer any hindrance from the triple world (*tridhātu*).

If one were to determine the stages and positions according to the preceding section, "peacefully and securely emerging" corresponds in meaning to the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), because within the stage of No-More-Learning lies the fruit of Arhatship.
Having exhausted the afflictions of both conceptual and innate self-grasping, one becomes detached from the bonds of the three realms.

Like safely emerging [from a house], one realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons and abides in the *pratyekabuddha*-truth of *nirvāṇa*, like sitting in the open air. [Question: Previously, the Three Chariots were used as a metaphor for the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Since they have not yet seen the chariots, it follows that they have not yet attained the Truth of Cessation. How can you suddenly use "sitting in the open air" as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*? [Answer: The Buddha provisionally established the Three Chariots because they do not truly exist; this is precisely a metaphor for how the Three Vehicles are fundamentally non-existent and merely provisional.

[This is] the name. Now that these sons have emerged from the burning house and reached the open space, they have already obtained the three vehicles; this is a direct metaphor for the three vehicles having emerged from the triple world and attained partial truth (*pratyekabuddha-satya*), which is equivalent to having already attained *nirvāṇa*. This corresponds to what was said later:

"If one has preserved one's life and body, one may be said to have already obtained objects of play and enjoyment. "Thoroughly at ease" (*taiyan*) describes the state of self-attainment, spoken in contrast to the preceding state of alarm and fear.
Previously, seeing flames erupt from all four sides and fearing that his son would be consumed by fire, he was seized with alarm and thought, "Now I see him safe and sound, having escaped.
Sitting in the open air, he felt profoundly relieved and leaped for joy. This is a metaphor for those of the Three Vehicles who have already abided in provisional fruits;
their past roots of goodness have not been lost, and the Buddha’s mind is somewhat comforted. As it is said in the "Chapter on the Teaching of the Dharma": "Now I am joyful and fearless."
This is so. At that time, the various children below—representing those whose faculties and capacities have already matured—each said to their father:

"We do not know that the chariots were merely provisional; we wish to obtain them and will surely attain them. This metaphor illustrates how those of the three vehicles do not realize that the fruits are established as expedient means, yet they desire to seek them and will surely realize them.

The three chariots previously promised by the father represent the three vehicles previously taught. "We pray that you grant them to us at this time" represents the request for the bestowal of these teachings.
Having left the house by means of the chariots, they did not see the gift of the three vehicles; therefore, they wished for them to be granted at once.

This is a metaphor for sentient beings who, having attained the fruit and exited the realm, suddenly hear that the provisional fruits are not the ultimate truth, and thus request that [the truth] be explained immediately. As the petition of a former generation states:
"Both those in training and those beyond training each consider themselves to have attained *nirvāṇa* by being free from the view of self, as well as the views of existence and non-existence."
[They were] perplexed. Now, having heard before the World-Honored One what they had never heard before, they have all fallen into doubt and confusion.

"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly"—this refers to the meaning of seeking the carts. [Question]: Śāriputra’s request on behalf of others should pertain to the Supreme Single Vehicle (ekayāna).

Why, then, does he employ the metaphor of the three carts? [Answer]: Śāriputra’s request on behalf of others was originally intended for those of middling capacity. Speaking specifically from the perspective of those of middling capacity: although they have heard that the three vehicles are not ultimate, they do not yet know how to seek the truly real Single Vehicle.

In their minds, they sought only to obtain the three vehicles from before as the manifestation of reality; they were like the children of the elder, who, although they saw that the three carts did not exist, did not know to seek further for the great white ox-cart, because in their minds they were focused only on the three carts previously promised.

I must certainly seek to receive this gift; therefore, I again employ the parable of the three carts. You should contemplate this well. (The parable concludes with the timing having arrived and the faculties having matured. II.

The Parable of Bestowing the Equal One Vehicle (This corresponds to the meaning in the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition, regarding "among all bodhisattvas, directly abandoning the skillful means," etc.). This is divided into two parts: 1. The Parable of Directly Bestowing the One Vehicle.
The second [section] explains the reasons for the establishment and rejection of the metaphors. First:
"Śāriputra, at that time the elder bestowed gifts upon each of his sons... (until) ...and provided them with many servants to attend and guard them."
The first metaphor illustrates the essence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "At that time" refers to the moment of leaving the house and seeking the carts;

it is a metaphor for the arrival of the [right] time when the capacities [of the disciples] have matured. Because their capacities have matured, he gathers all those with such capacities and universally bestows the perfect sound (*pariṇata-svara*);

hence the metaphor says, "he gave each of his sons. Because the time had arrived, he set aside the various provisional teachings and uniquely proclaimed the One Vehicle; hence the metaphor says, "equally one great [cart]."

As for the chariot: its height and breadth—height being discussed in terms of verticality—metaphorically represents the essence of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), which stands at the forefront of all positions.
Breadth being spoken of in terms of horizontality, it metaphorically represents the essence of the One Vehicle, whose principle encompasses all wonders.

As for its adornment with various jewels—the precious materials such as gold and silver used to form these ornaments—they metaphorically represent the essence of the One Vehicle, namely the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
Because it is that which is accomplished [by this]. As the text praising his virtues says: "The Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas;
he has fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all Buddhas; he is courageous and diligent; his fame is heard everywhere;

and he has accomplished this profound and unprecedented Dharma. Regarding the phrase "surrounded by" below: it is a metaphor for the characteristics of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "Surrounded by" [refers to...]
The railings, which hold within and exclude without, are a metaphor for the various *dhāraṇī* dharma-gates; they maintain the good so it is not lost and block the evil so it does not arise.

The bells suspended on all four sides, which vibrate with sound according to the wind, are a metaphor for the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.

In his later years, he awakened to the nature of all sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "above, spreading the curtains and canopy": the *xian* (curtains) refers to the surrounding drapes, which metaphorically represent the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), capable of shielding against external challenges.
The *gai* (canopy) refers to the covering above the head, which metaphorically represents the function of the ten powers (*bala*), transcending everything.

Furthermore, by using terms such as "rare treasures" to describe these curtains and canopy—meaning they are all adorned with jewels—it serves as a metaphor for the powers and fearlessnesses, which likewise [are adorned with] the *dharma*.
It is accomplished through the merit of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Regarding "intertwined with jeweled cords": the cords are made of various jewels, interlaced and connected to one another;

this is a metaphor for the four immeasurable minds (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), which, by means of them, bring about the welfare of beings and connect one's own virtues. Regarding "hanging with flower tassels":

the flower tassels hang down on all four sides, bringing joy to those who see them; this is a metaphor for the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), which gather in sentient beings so that they obtain benefit.
This signifies joy. "Laying out a layered, elegant mat" refers to a beautiful seating arrangement laid out in successive layers, such as silken fabrics, cotton wadding, carpets, and cushions;
this is a metaphor for the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis, which are fully perfected and enjoyed without end.
"Placing a vermilion pillow" refers to a pillow with two ends, upon which one rests the head in the middle; this is a metaphor for the Middle Way.
It encompasses both of the two truths. Furthermore, these three truths do not depart from the essence of the One Vehicle;

therefore, it is metaphorically described as "placing [the cart] within. "Placing" refers to setting the cart inside. From the word "wild goose" (*jia*) downward, this serves as a metaphor for the function of the One Vehicle.

The function of the One Vehicle consists of teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*tattva*), and practice (*caryā*). Of these, the first two phrases serve as a metaphor for the teaching of the One Vehicle: "yoked with white oxen."

In this passage, the chariot drawn by oxen is a metaphor for the body [of the Dharma] being manifested through the teaching. The ox being named "white" is a metaphor for the emptiness of the nature of words and letters.
"The skin and color are full and pure" means that the skin and its pores are fully developed, which is a metaphor for there being no virtue that is not complete; the complexion is clean and pure.
This metaphor illustrates that there is no evil left unexhausted. The two phrases concerning "form and body" illustrate the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Since the principle of the One Vehicle—both in its general and specific observations—is nothing other than supremely refined and supremely good, it is metaphorically described as having "a beautiful form and body.

This means that all forms are exquisitely beautiful and the entire being is wondrously excellent. To possess great strength and vigor means one is capable of bearing heavy burdens and is capable of...
"Reaching far" (*chìyuǎn*) is a metaphor for initiating practice based on principle; it signifies that one can universally deliver sentient beings and proceed directly toward Bodhi.

The four phrases concerning "walking" are a metaphor for the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because the practice of the One Vehicle does not enter into dangerous or deviant paths, it is metaphorically described as "walking with level and upright steps.
Because the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) involves encompassing the stages and realizing awakening, it is metaphorically described as "swift."

Like the wind—this refers to the practice of self-benefit (*svārtha-caryā*). Because compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, and because [the Buddha] acts in concert with both [loving-kindness and skillful means] to uproot [suffering], it is said that he has "many attendants.

By employing others to accomplish the welfare of beings, he thereby adorns his own virtue; thus it is said that they "serve and protect him. This refers to the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha-caryā*).
This concludes the parable of the actual bestowing of the One Vehicle. II. The Parable of the Reasons for Abolishing and Establishing [the Vehicles].
Why is this so? Because this great elder (up to) "is not even exhausted," how much less so for his sons.
The phrase "Why is this so? generally interrogates the two reasons. The section beginning with "Because this" first explains the meaning of "abandoning.
Regarding "immeasurable wealth": the household wealth is so abundant that it cannot be measured; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

"Vast and profound. "Various treasuries" refers to the storehouses of manifold jewels, which serve as a metaphor for the immeasurable and unimpeded qualities, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
"All are overflowing" means they are filled within and spill over without;
this serves as a metaphor for how the essence of these various distinct virtues is complete within oneself, while their function manifests externally. And...
One who forms this thought intends to discard three and give one;
it is like the Tathāgata at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, intending to set aside the provisional and follow the ultimate. "Infinite wealth" means that one's own enjoyment is inexhaustible.
Since one's own enjoyment is inexhaustible, it should be shared equally with all sons; therefore, one should not give inferior small carts to the sons.

This is analogous to how the Tathāgata, having perfected his own realization, should cause sentient beings to attain it together with him, rather than merely granting the fruits of the provisional teachings by way of the three vehicles. The "Chapter on the Dharma Explanation" states: "Having realized for oneself..."
The supreme path, the Mahāyāna Dharma of equality. If one were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed;

such a thing is impossible. This is precisely the meaning [of what was stated above]. Now, from "this inferior" onwards, the text establishes the reason for establishing the reality [of the Buddha-nature] through a parable.
"Young children" refers to those who are immature and lack discernment. Although they are immature and lack discernment, from the perspective of the elder...
All are one's own biological children; therefore, it is said that "they are all my sons.

This is a metaphor for the fact that although the wisdom of the three vehicles is narrow and inferior, when viewed by the Tathāgata, they are equally those with whom he shared past conditions and all possess great spiritual capacity (*mahāyāna-śakti*). Regarding "love without partiality":

since they are all equally one's own biological children, the heart of loving concern should naturally be without bias or favoritism. This is a metaphor for the three vehicles, once [realized as such]...
There are those of great capacity; yet, because the Tathāgata’s compassion is impartial, it should certainly be without obstruction or limit.
The great chariots made of the seven treasures were what the elder had prepared during his ordinary life, and thus he said, "I have them.

This is a metaphor for the essence of the fruit of the One Vehicle, which was accomplished by the Tathāgata through cultivation over many kalpas and is now manifested and realized in this world. That their number is immeasurable means that, based on the original chariots, more were constructed.
They increase more and more. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata using the seal of the fruit to certify the fruit;

it is unending, link after link. "One should maintain an impartial mind" means that all are his children; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata recollecting past conditions and impartially aiding them with an equal mind.

"Giving to each one individually" means that his love is without partiality; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s compassion being without obstruction, as he records each person's future attainment of Buddhahood.
Regarding the point that there should be no distinction: because there are precious chariots, this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s self-realization of the Buddha-fruit;

one should not teach other vehicles to people. The reason for this is that it further investigates the reason why [the Buddha] is not parsimonious; although his wealth is immeasurable, [he gives it all away].
There must be a time when [the Dharma] is exhausted. Why, then, do you bestow it equally without stinginess?

This is because those who do not understand the Buddha falsely claim that the Buddha-dharma has an end, and thus mistakenly raise objections; it is inappropriate to speak of the Buddha-dharma to everyone indiscriminately.
We explain "without stinginess" (*amatsarya*) as follows: *pari* means "universally," *da* means "to give," and *kṣaya* means "exhaustion. It refers to giving universally.
Even a single kingdom could not exhaust it, let alone all its sons; how could they suffice to exhaust the father’s wealth?
It is like the Tathāgata bestowing this Buddha-dharma universally upon all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm, yet still being unable to exhaust it; how much less so for those of the three vehicles.
How could this suffice to exhaust the Buddha’s Dharma? Therefore, the Tathāgata bestows the One Vehicle equally, without any parsimony.

This concludes the analogy for the equal bestowal of the One Vehicle. 3. The Analogy for Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Benefit (This analogy corresponds to the meaning in the section on the preaching of the Dharma:
"When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of doubts is entirely removed," etc.)
At that time, the sons each mounted great vehicles, attaining what they had never experienced before and which was not what they had originally expected.

"At that time" is a metaphor for the moment when [the Buddha] equally bestows the One Vehicle. "Each mounting a great vehicle" is a metaphor for those of the three vehicles, all of whom understand and dwell securely in the true reality (*dharmatā*).
"Attaining what they had never experienced before" is a metaphor for those of the provisional teachings reaching this point.
"Having the potential to attain Buddhahood, though not what was originally expected" means that while one did not originally seek Buddhahood, the attainment exceeds what was anticipated;
the meaning of this analogy is clear from the text. This concludes the section on the Tathāgata’s transformation and response.

△ Third, the analogy for the non-falsity of the Buddha’s words (this corresponds to the previous "Exposition of the Dharma" chapter, specifically the meaning of the non-falsity of the Buddha’s words within the praise of the Dharma and exhortation to faith). This is divided into three parts: first, the Tathāgata poses a question based on the analogy; second, Śāriputra... [text continues].
Answering directly according to the question, there are three parts: [the Buddha’s] praise, approval, and seal of excellence.
First: "Śāriputra, what do you think? (up to: Could such a great jeweled chariot possibly be false?"
Regarding your statement, the meaning of the verse raises an inquiry. The phrase "This is long... cites the analogy to pose a question.
Since the Tathāgata has granted both "three" and "one," and yet declares himself to be without falsehood, this objection is raised by way of Śāriputra’s perspective.
Furthermore, it cites the matters within the analogy to pose a question; this is because one borrows the words from another's mouth to clarify what is a matter of one's own heart and mind. △
Second, Śāriputra answers directly according to the question, which has two parts: first, a general answer; second, a detailed explanation. Regarding the first:
Śāriputra said, "No, World-Honored One.

The *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna) commentary states: Generally, that which is called false and deceptive is so because it is without benefit and possesses harm. Although [the Buddha] now permits these three...
Granting one [fruit] is beneficial and without harm; therefore, I answered directly with "no.

Since you now know that the Elder has no fault of falsehood and that the Tathāgata’s words are not deceptive, I hope you will not say that because "three" are provisionally established, "one" is likewise not real, thereby severing the seeds of Buddhahood for yourself and obstructing the superior progress of others. △ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First:
The analogy allows that three [of the four] are not false, while two analogies and one [verse] are not false. Regarding the first:
it is like a householder who merely causes his children to escape the danger of fire, thereby rescuing them from that burning house.
First, the example is presented: "Merely causing one to escape the fire" refers to the situation after the elder permitted the carriage;

by merely shielding and protecting with his own body and hands, he caused him to temporarily escape the harm of the fire. This is analogous to how, after the Tathāgata bestows skillful means (*upāya*), he merely employs his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to provide empowerment and protection, causing beings to temporarily escape all sufferings. To temporarily escape all sufferings is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
"O Āyuṣmat, [their lives] may be briefly extended for a short while. Therefore, it is metaphorically said that 'their bodies and lives are preserved.

This means that once they have escaped the harm of the fire, their physical bodies and their very lives can be fully preserved. Since their bodies and lives can thus be preserved, so too can those of all the sons."
Thus, it is not that he does not rescue them from the burning house, nor is it a false claim.

For example, if the Tathāgata can already prolong the life of the Dharma-body and wisdom for sentient beings, how could it be considered empty if he does not deliver them across the triple world? Why is this so? [The following] provides the interrogation and explanation.
To preserve one’s body and life is itself to have obtained all that is delightful; for with body and life as the master of all things, where the master is, there the things are.
This is analogous to how the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom are the root of all fruits: when the root is firm, the fruits remain.
How much more so below? This further clarifies that even merely avoiding fire and such dangers is not yet a false claim.
How much more so when, by means of the skillful device of the promised chariot, he rescues them from within the burning house—how could this possibly be false?
For example, if the Tathāgata merely caused them to escape suffering, that alone would not be false;

how much more so when, employing the provisional skillful means of bestowing those [chariots], he delivers them and causes them to exit the triple world—who then could argue that this is false? Thus we know that from before...
Although the three vehicles are permitted, there is certainly no falsehood in this. △ Second, the metaphor and the reality are not at variance.
From "The World-Honored One is like the elder" up to "he does not give [the small carts]" and "desiring to benefit his children, he gives them the great chariots."
First, the example is presented. The smallest vehicle refers to toy carts for children, dogs, pigs, and so forth;
it is used as a metaphor for the tainted vehicles of humans and devas, as these are inferior even when compared to the three vehicles.

Within the parable, it is said that once the sons have emerged from the burning house, not only are the three vehicles not given to them, but even the smallest vehicle is not granted. This is still not considered false. This is the metaphor.
Once sentient beings have emerged from the triple world, they are not permitted to abide even in the three vehicles;
indeed, they are not permitted to abide even in the vehicle of humans or devas. Yet, this is not false. Why? [The text] provides an interrogation and an explanation. First, one should consider this:

"That which was intended as a skillful means to cause them to emerge" means that although the elder promised the three carts, his original intention was fundamentally a skillful means. This was merely for...
Causing the son to escape does not mean that he was actually given [the treasure];

it is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, although teaching the three vehicles, originally employs skillful means solely to enable sentient beings to escape the triple world, rather than instructing them to truly abide in provisional doctrines.
For these reasons, there is no falsehood, because his initial intention was not [to grant the treasure] as a reality, yet the son has now already escaped. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata.
First, the provisional teaching was not originally intended for them to remain [in that state], yet it was able to cause sentient beings to transcend the three realms;
therefore, although it did not bestow the vehicles of gods or humans, it was still not false. How much less so, then, the lower [teachings]? And how much more so, the manifest [teaching]?
Building upon the previous point—that even not bestowing the smallest vehicle was not false—how much more so when one uses what one possesses and bestows great chariots equally?
And thus benefits them. How could there be any falsehood in this? It would already not be false even if the Tathāgata did not bestow the vehicles of humans and devas;
how much less so when he grants what he has realized for himself—the single vehicle—equally to all?
Who then could possibly charge him with the fault of falsehood? Thus we know that today’s equal bestowal of the single vehicle is even more [beyond reproach].
"It is non-delusion. Thus, Śāriputra, having answered directly according to the question, concluded. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s praise and seal of approval:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
The repeated exclamation "Excellent! has two meanings. First, it is in the sense of praise; that is, praising him for having gained confidence in the Dharma once the parable was made clear.
Second, it is in the sense of rejoicing; that is, rejoicing that since he now understands the householder’s intention, he must also understand the Tathāgata’s intention.
The phrase "as you have said" is a term of confirmation. Even if the Tathāgata himself...

To say there is no falsehood might give rise to doubt or debate; therefore, [the Buddha] now provisionally has Śāriputra speak it out, so that with a single word it is sealed and settled, leaving the assembly at that time with nothing further to say.

The analogy is concluded. II. The Application to the Dharma (Three parts): 1. The Sentient Beings’ Response to Stimuli; 2. The Tathāgata’s Transformational Response; 3. The Non-falsity of the Buddha’s Words.

The first [of these three] has three sub-sections: 1. The Buddha who is the object of response; 2. The capacity for response; 3. [The result of the response]. [The first sub-section: The Buddha who is the object of response. [The second sub-section: The capacity for response.
The assembly of sentient beings. Regarding the meaning of the formation of the three fetters:
First, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is likewise thus (up to) his great kindness and great compassion, which are ever without weariness or indolence.
The phrase "Tathāgata" (如來句) summarizes the preceding remarks. This means that the Tathāgata’s affirmation of the three as being one is without falsehood;
he is also like that elder. Thus, it serves as the subsequent section. Following this, there is a separate synthesis:

"all worlds" corresponds to the aforementioned kingdoms, cities, and villages—the meaning of which is seen in the parable. The "father" is not merely a metaphor; it is an epithet of excellence for the Buddha. Because...
The Buddha regards the world as his own child; therefore, he is called the "Father of the World.
Just as an elder regards his country and so forth as his children, there is thus a "Great Elder" of the kingdoms, towns, and villages. "Fear" refers to the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
These two kinds of birth-and-death involve beginningless transmigration, which is terrifying and formidable. "Decay, affliction, and distress" refer to the two sufferings of old age and illness.

In old age, one draws daily closer to decay; because one’s activities are the opposite of what they once were, there is distress. In illness, one lies prostrate upon a bed and pillow; because long-standing anxiety fails to subside, there is suffering.
These two conditions—old age and illness—are the characteristics of the two pillars between birth and death, and are thus subsumed within birth and death. This is ignorance.

The "separate delusions outside the realms" have the nature of making the mind lack clarity and purity; their function is to transform into various kinds of unwholesome dharmas. They are also called the "ground of abiding ignorance.
As for the "dark obscuration," these are the "pervasive delusions within the realms," namely *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *vitarka* (thought). Their nature is to be shrouded in darkness and obstruction;
their function is to bring about the causes and effects of outflowing existence (*āsrava*). In meaning, this follows upon the four grounds of abiding afflictions. As it says:
The two preceding [stages] involve death and the five abodes; because they have reached ultimate quiescence, it is said that "they are forever exhausted without remainder.

This clarifies the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), which accords with the previous meaning of "his years having declined. "Immeasurable knowledge and vision," etc., refers to the essence and characteristics of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*);
because each is perfectly complete, it is said that "he has fully accomplished them all. "Spiritual powers and wisdom" refers to the functional application of the power of true wisdom.

Since both essence and characteristics are complete, their functional power naturally manifests; therefore, it is called "existence. This refers to the wisdom of enlightened virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*), which accords with the previously mentioned meaning of immeasurable wealth.
Regarding "skillful means and wisdom" (*upāya-prajñā*): this refers to the essence and characteristics of provisional wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since the Buddha has fully perfected the distinctions between essence and characteristics, these are designated by the term *pāramitā*. Regarding "great kindness and great compassion" (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*): this refers to provisional...
The function of the power of wisdom is to deliver sentient beings through its power, forgetting weariness even across kalpas; therefore, it is designated as "without indolence or fatigue.

This clarifies the virtue of grace, which accords with the previous meanings of fields, houses, and servants. The Buddhas who are the objects of inspiration have now concluded. △ Second, the assembly that is capable of inspiring [the Buddhas].
"Constantly seeking wholesome deeds to benefit all [beings]... until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

'Constantly seeking wholesome deeds to benefit all' means that throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata has constantly sought to cultivate goodness and eliminate evil, thereby benefiting all sentient beings so that they may leave suffering behind and obtain happiness."
According to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, he has come to this world eight thousand times; hence it is said that he "was born within the triple world.

The phrase "the dilapidated fire-hall" employs a metaphor within the Dharma to make known that the triple world is impermanent, decaying, and unstable, just like a burning house, so that one may swiftly give rise to weary detachment.
Regarding "sentient beings," according to the subsequent passage, they shall attain bodhi; this should refer to those of the past.

Regarding the conditions for forming a karmic affinity (*kalyāṇamitra-bandhana*): it is said that although the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world benefits all beings, he places primary emphasis on those with whom he shares a karmic affinity.
Thus, it is stated that he appears "to deliver those who suffer from grief, lamentation, pain, and affliction. These refer to the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

In terms of their specific characteristics: birth is suffering because one enters the prison of the womb; old age is affliction because of the decline of physical vigor; sickness is grief because of being confined to a bed; and death is... [the text continues].

"Sorrow arises from the pain of separation"; this clarifies the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Folly" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*); because one lacks the clarity of sublime awakening, it is termed folly.

Its obscuring darkness is as described previously. Regarding the "three poisons," these are greed, hatred, and delusion. Because they are the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*), they are singled out for mention;
this clarifies the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). As for the fact that both the Truths of Suffering and Origination are explained as being "fire": [it is because they burn and consume].
Suffering and its accumulation are mutually causal, like fire and fuel burning together, for they share the same nature of combustion.
To cause one to attain Bodhi is to finalize the case of the Great Penetration of King Wei-yin, thereby fulfilling the aspiration to transcend the world and save sentient beings.
If one aligns this with the preceding metaphor, "constantly seeking" means remaining permanently in the world; "merging with that family's vastness" refers to the cultivation of wholesome deeds.
Skillfully severing evil, when combined, there is but a single gate. All things are collectively encompassed within the five realms of existence.

Combined, they comprise five hundred people. "Sentient beings" refers to those with whom one forms karmic connections. Combined, they are likened to thirty children. Within this metaphor, there is further the decay and ruin of halls and pavilions.
The passage beginning with "Suddenly a fire broke out" and so forth collectively compares the three realms to a dilapidated and burning house.

Within this context, the passage beginning with "In order to deliver them and enable them to attain... lacks the full metaphorical meaning; it is merely stated elliptically to show that sentient beings belong to their past conditions.
This concludes the section on the assembly of those who can be moved [to respond]. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the meaning of being moved.
"Seeing all sentient beings [suffering] from birth, old age, sickness, and death... even when encountering great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.

Regarding "seeing all sentient beings," this refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the descent [into the world]; it denotes the observation of the capacities of beings within the realm of principle (*li-di*).

The capacities observed briefly comprise the three sufferings and, in detail, the eight sufferings. Briefly comprising the three sufferings: first, the suffering of retribution in a future life (*paścimakāla-vedanīya-karma*).

For instance, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are produced by the causes of karma from previous lives; since one now undergoes burning and boiling, these belong to retribution in a future life.
Second is the suffering of immediate retribution (*drstadharma-vedanīya*): those who experience various kinds of suffering for the sake of the five desires and material gain.
Some lose their vital essence because of form; some exhaust their spirit because of sound; some receive poison through greed for fragrance; some injure their bodies through attachment to flavor;
or some ruin their physical forms because of touch. For the sake of wealth as small as a hair, they lie amidst snow and sleep through frost;
for the sake of profit as tiny as a fly’s head, they don their robes under the stars and the moon. They even endure hunger and brave the cold, thereby losing [their lives].
Those who lose their lives are found everywhere. "The greedy" refers to those who are stained by craving and attachment toward present objects.

"The seekers" refers to those who pursue and strive for past and future objects. Thus, regarding what they have not yet obtained, they suffer from the desire to acquire it, busying themselves all day long;

once they have obtained it, they suffer from the fear of losing it, going to any lengths whatsoever. Therefore, it is said that they undergo manifold sufferings in the present. This concludes the above.

All these are karmic actions performed in the present life that are experienced in the present life; therefore, they belong to the category of "retribution in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Regarding the suffering of retribution across three lifetimes (*tribhavavedanīya*) that is experienced later:

because one has pursued objects with intense craving, the causal karma has already been established. Since the "flower-retribution" (*puṣpavipāka*) is insufficient to compensate for it, one experiences the "fruit-retribution" (*phalavipāka*) later.

In the hells, there are the sufferings of the eight cold and eight hot hells, and so forth. Among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there is the "needle-throat" (*sūcīmukha*) and the "flame-mouth" (*jvalanamukha*).
There is the suffering of the mouth and so forth. Animals endure sufferings such as being yoked with iron bits and burdened with saddles;
this refers specifically to those whose evil karma is heavy. If, however, one’s evil karma is somewhat light while wholesome karma is slightly predominant, one will be born in the heavens.
If, on the other hand, wholesome and evil karma are equal, resulting in neither ascending nor falling, one will reach the human realm. Among humans...

Suffering has many varieties. The suffering of poverty and destitution—where food does not suffice for the mouth and clothing does not cover the body—is caused by a lack of understanding regarding generosity, as well as by stinginess, greed, and envy.

The suffering of separation from the beloved—such as being separated from one's wife and children while alive, or being parted from one's parents at death—is caused by severing the ties of others' kinship and by alienating their bonds of gratitude and righteousness.

This is brought about by such things. Regarding the suffering of association with the hated: it arises from being unable to resolve enmity with enemies, having no way to avoid adversaries, and so forth;

this is caused by plundering the wealth of others and taking the lives of others. If we speak in terms of the heavens, even tainted merit cannot compare to the untainted. There is the suffering of poverty and destitution.
When the time for the exhaustion of one’s retribution arrives, the five signs of decline appear. This is the suffering of separation from the beloved.
This is separation (*viprayoga*). Asuras contend for power, waging successive battles without ceasing; this is the suffering of association with the hated (*apriyasaṃprayoga*).

All of the above are karmic actions performed in this life that will only be experienced in a future life; therefore, they belong to retribution upon rebirth (*upapattivedanīya-karma*). To explain the eight sufferings in full detail:

among the sentient beings of the five destinies, there is none who does not possess a body, which is the burning suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Furthermore, being oppressed by poverty and driven by the five desires and material gain—
Being dragged along by greed, attachment, pursuit, and so forth, when one's wishes are not fulfilled, this is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

Combined with the previously mentioned birth, old age, sickness, and death, together with the subsequent meeting with the hated and separation from the beloved, these constitute eight types [of suffering]. This corresponds to the preceding metaphor:
"The elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides. The phrase "in this way" is a concluding term that summarizes [the preceding] in brief.
There are three types of suffering, which in detail comprise the eight sufferings. When divided into their subtle aspects, their categories are truly numerous;

hence it is said, "various kinds of suffering. These sufferings are boundless, like a great ocean. Sentient beings rise and sink according to their karma and cannot emerge on their own; hence it is said, "sunk within them.
Clinging to suffering as pleasure, they wander about without remembering their way back; hence it is said, "joyfully playing. Not...

The two phrases regarding awakening can be understood by analogy with the preceding metaphor. Because they do not contemplate the severing of the origin [of suffering] or the departure from suffering, it is said that "they do not give rise to weariness.
Because they do not contemplate the cultivation of the path or the realization of cessation, it is said that "they do not seek liberation.

How is it seen that they neither give rise to weariness nor seek liberation? It is simply because one observes them within the burning house of the three realms, following their wholesome karma as they move eastward.
He gallops, following his evil karma as he flees westward. Although he encounters great suffering, he does not regard it as a calamity;
how could he know to give rise to revulsion and seek the Dharma of liberation? This corresponds to the previous analogy:

that is, being struck with great terror and forming this thought, up until the point where the mind feels no revulsion or distress and lacks the intent to seek deliverance. Thus concludes the section on the sentient beings' capacity for response.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings (up to) who seek to exit the burning house by means of a goat-drawn cart, they have cultivated the category of wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in previous lives, internalizing and habituating it within their minds; therefore, it is said that they possess the nature of wisdom within.

Those who hear the Dharma from the Buddha—specifically from a Buddha of the Lesser Vehicle—hear the teaching on the emptiness of persons. Because this teaching on emptiness accords with their prior habitual tendencies, they are able to believe in it.

"Receiving" corresponds to the previous metaphor of "fulfilling one's wishes with vigor and sharpness. "Diligent and energetic" means practicing the Way with earnestness and advancing with diligence without retreating;

"Seeking nirvāṇa for oneself" means not thinking of assisting others. Da Cheng says: "Wishing to be quick..."
Then one will not reach [the goal]; seeking it for oneself results in no greatness. This combines with the previous analogy regarding the meaning of vying to exit the burning house.

At the end, it is joined with the statement that although one desires to quickly seek it for oneself and may indeed exit the realm and realize extinction (*nirvāṇa*), one cannot attain vast greatness.
Therefore it is said: this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna. Sentient beings who seek this are no different from those sons of the elder who left the house seeking goat-carts.

The Dharma consists of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which arise in succession and depend upon one another; therefore, it is designated as "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
To know this and call it "profound" means that through both forward and reverse contemplation, one understands the causes for arising as well as the principle of non-arising.

Finally, it is combined with [the preceding]. Since it is said that one seeks "natural wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) and delights in knowing conditions alone, even if one surpasses the śrāvakas, one has not yet reached the level of a bodhisattva; therefore, this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
When sentient beings seek this, they are no different from those sons of the elder who left the house seeking the deer-cart. △ Third, the cultivation and realization of the Bodhisattva.
If there are sentient beings who, from the time they follow the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [up until] seeking the ox-cart to exit the burning house,
hear the Dharma from the Buddha— those who, from the two teachings of the beginning and the end, hear the Dharma of the Treasury of Emptiness and the Mind-Dharma, and diligently practice it;

To speak of this: seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth specifically clarifies the superior seeking of the Buddha-way.

"All-knowledge" is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is formed by the transformation of the mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness. Like a great round mirror, it clearly perceives everything;
therefore, it is named "all. "Buddha-wisdom" is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which is the transformation of the characteristics of the seventh consciousness.

It is accomplished by means of the mental complex (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) associated with the mind. One contemplates all phenomena as being entirely equal to those of all sentient beings and no different from those of a Buddha;
therefore, it is named "Buddha-wisdom. Natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is precisely the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

It is accomplished by means of the mental complex associated with the transformation of the sixth consciousness. It is well able to observe the sequence of all phenomena and further knows sentient beings.
The depths and shallowness of the faculties are explained spontaneously and respond naturally; therefore, it is named "Natural" (*svayambhū*).

The "Unlearned Wisdom" (*aśaikṣajñāna*) is precisely the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*); it is formed by transforming the mental states associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
It fulfills the tasks that ought to be performed through the power of its original vows. Its transformations are boundless and do not conform to fixed patterns; therefore, it is termed "Unlearned."
Name: Possessing the four aforementioned wisdoms is termed the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). This is also the pure *dharmadhātu* and the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
When the five wisdoms are perfected, one is able to know what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), thereby accomplishing the ten powers (*daśabala*).

At that time, the Tathāgata had this thought: [omitted] "...all shall be brought to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the initial emergence of the two "yous" (causes), the phrase "he had this thought" indicates his desire to unify them into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby fulfilling his resolve for transcendent liberation.
The phrase "I have" refers to what he has personally realized (*svasaṃvedana*); the merits of this personal realization are exceedingly profound and vast. Therefore...
It is said to be immeasurable and boundless. To speak briefly: it is called wisdom, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth, encompassing all other virtues.
Each is capable of containing and giving rise to the inexhaustible Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. This corresponds to the previous metaphor:
that the householder’s wealth is immeasurable and his various treasuries are overflowing. This is the meaning.
"All sentient beings are my children" means that although their present faculties differ, their past conditions are no different. This accords with the previous metaphor;
it establishes the sense that these young children are all equally my sons. "Equally bestow" and what follows below are the double conclusion of the two reasons.
It is precisely because the Dharma-treasury realized by the Tathāgata himself is immeasurable and boundless that he equally bestows [the Dharma] upon the Mahāyāna. Since he has equally bestowed it...

In the Mahāyāna, provisional fruits are not established. This concludes the reason for the abolition of the provisional, which accords with the previous principle that one should not provide inferior small carts to the sons. Furthermore, because all these sentient beings are the children of the Buddha.

Therefore, he does not allow [the two vehicles] to attain it alone. Previously, it was said that only Bodhisattvas could attain the extinction of the Buddha; now it is not so, hence it says "does not allow.
Furthermore, previously it was not permitted that the two vehicles could equally attain *nirvāṇa*; now it is not so, hence it says "all by means of.
As for what is called "the extinction of the Tathāgata," this refers to the non-abiding *nirvāṇa* of the fruit of Buddhahood. By means of...
Because this extinguishes the afflictions of the five abodes and delivers one from the suffering of the two deaths, it is said that "he brings them to extinction and deliverance" (*nirvāṇa*).

This concludes the explanation for establishing the reality [of the One Vehicle]. It accords with the previous principle that one should maintain an impartial mind and bestow [the teaching] upon each individual;

it is not appropriate to make distinctions. △ Second, the actual bestowing of the One Vehicle. (In the parable, the essence comes first, followed by the characteristics and then the function. Here, the characteristics come first, followed by the essence and then the function. The meaning is the same, though the sequence differs.)
These sentient beings who have escaped the triple world (up to) being able to give rise to the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss.

This is the primary characteristic of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Sentient beings of the three vehicles equally transcend the *pariccheda* (segmented existence); therefore, they are called those who have escaped the triple world.
The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth of all Buddhas do not consist merely of the four *dhyānas*, the nine attainments (*navasamāpatti*), or the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*);

they must also include the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, as well as the inconceivable realm of liberation. In terms of meaning, these are combined with what precedes, repeating the analogy of the elegantly spread mat.
In the text, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes other inexhaustible merits; in terms of meaning, these are combined with what precedes, encompassing them on all sides.
The metaphors of the railings and so forth all serve as the enjoyment of the Buddha-ground; hence they are called "recreational implements.

As for the phrase "all are," this refers to the essence of the One Vehicle. The aforementioned differentiated merits, when considered from the perspective of principle (*li*), do not transcend the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle;

when considered from the perspective of wisdom (*jñāna*), they do not transcend the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, it is said that they are all "one mark and one kind" (*ekalakṣaṇam ekajātīyam*). This is based on...

This is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which possesses immeasurable characteristics; it is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which possesses immeasurable varieties.
When combined with the preceding meaning, the metaphor of the chariot being high and wide—praised by the Sages—is due to its being accomplished through these immeasurable merits.
As it is said: "The Buddha has personally attended upon various Buddhas and has fully practiced the Dharma and so forth. Thus...
These words praised by the Sage accord in meaning with what precedes. The metaphor of being adorned with various jewels refers to the capacity to produce [the path].

The function of the One Vehicle is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*), which consists in the purification and release from the bonds of karma. The wondrous awakening to all phenomena is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*).

Reaching the ultimate through supreme realization is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*). To be able to give rise to this bliss, one must rely on the teachings to understand the principle.

Arising from principle to initiate practice; in terms of meaning, this accords with what preceded. The metaphor of "yoking white oxen," continuing through "many attendants and so forth," concludes the Tathāgata’s transformational response.
△ Third, the Buddha’s words are not false, in two parts: first, reiterating the previous metaphors;
second, applying the Dharma to correspond with them. First:
Śāriputra, it is like that elder... (up to) ...that elder is free from the fault of falsehood.

The initial mention of three and the subsequent provision of one analogy represent the foremost security; this is the supreme metaphor for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which brings about liberation from the suffering of the two deaths and the birth of the bliss of the three virtues.
Because it is the most secure among all forms of security, the final phrase mentions two [points], both of which are metaphors free from falsehood.
△ Second, the application of the analogy to the Dharma:
"The Tathāgata is likewise free from falsehood... (up to) the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, yet they are simply unable to receive it in its entirety."
The initial general synthesis has already been clarified in the analogy; there is no need for further pretexts. Therefore, it is stated directly that there is no falsehood.
Regarding the section "First, the teaching of the [three] vehicles": this was originally intended to guide sentient beings. Thus, although [the ultimate fruit] was not granted, there is no falsehood.
This synthesizes the analogy that the permission of the three vehicles is not false. As for "Not teaching the One Vehicle": this was originally intended to await the proper time.
When the time has arrived and the capacity is matured, one then acts solely with great magnanimity (*mahā-udāra*); therefore, even though [the gift] is given now, there is no falsehood.
This is the analogy of "giving what is appropriate, which is not false. Why? [The text] explains further below. First, the inquiry is raised:
