this is intended to clarify why one first employs the three inducements and subsequently employs great magnanimity. From the words "The Tathāgata... onwards, the latter meaning is first explained; it is precisely because...
The Tathāgata possesses an immeasurable treasury of Dharma, which is capable of bestowing the Mahāyāna; therefore, he later delivers them through the Great Vehicle.
The final phrase subsequently explains the preceding meaning: precisely because they were unable to receive it all at once, he first used the Three Vehicles as an introduction.
Viewed from this perspective, one sees even more clearly that the Tathāgata is free from falsehood. This concludes the application of the Dharma. △ Third, the conclusion and response.
Śāriputra, by this cause and condition, you should know that all Buddhas [up to] distinguish and preach three within the single Buddha-vehicle.
This section generally承接 (continues from) the preceding text to conclude the response to the prior request. The Tathāgata’s intention is this:

you previously requested on behalf of the assembly, seeking to hear the causes and conditions for setting aside the provisional teachings; as I have explained above, the Three Vehicles were initially established.
Originally, it was for the purpose of later returning to the One Vehicle.

For this reason, you should know that what you have previously realized is merely the skillful means and expedient devices of the Buddhas; they spoke of three within the one, which is not the ultimate Dharma.
Those who cling to these expedients as being real can likewise come to know what has been awakened. The prose section concludes. II. Verse Recitation (The heading for the verses states):
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

△ (The Section on the Proper Verses is divided into three parts: First, the proper versification of the prose; second, the extreme manifestation of the compassionate mind; third, the concluding summary and exhortation. The first [part] has three sections: first, the versification of the parable;
second, the versification of the application to the Dharma; third, the versification of the concluding response. The first two [of these] have one verse for sentient beings.

The analogy of the stimulus and response. The two verses [present] the analogy of the Tathāgata’s manifestation and response. The first three [verses consist of]: one verse on the analogy of the Buddha who is the object of the response;
two verses on the analogy of the assembly that is the subject of the stimulus; and one verse concluding with the analogy of the meaning of the stimulus. The first [is a brief verse].
For example, it is like an elder.

According to the prose section, there are the qualities of his primary and secondary rewards (*niśraya* and *upabhoga*). Now, the primary [reality] subsumes the secondary, and the person subsumes the qualities;

this is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata. When his name is mentioned, all his manifold virtues are simultaneously and fully present. △ Second, the verse on the assembly that is capable of being moved [to faith].

The Similes (a broad exposition based on their meaning). This section is divided into four parts: first, similes for the retributive environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the three realms; second, similes for the retributive bodies (*upapatti-vipāka*) of the three realms;
third, similes for the various sufferings of the three realms; and fourth, similes for the nature of oppression. Regarding the first:

according to the prose commentary (*dīrgha-pāṭha*), there are generally two points concerning the retributive environment—first, that "the house is vast," and second, that "the halls and pavilions are dilapidated," continuing until "the beams and rafters are collapsing. Now, these are combined into verse. At the end, the metaphors of "mud, mire, and crumbling" are added; since these do not have a direct corresponding text in the prose commentary, they are not mentioned as "verses" in the topical outline (*kośa*).
The following sections are all modeled after this.
There was a great house, long decayed, with winding walls and enclosures, filled everywhere with filth and impurity.
This great house is a metaphor for the Tathāgata taking the three realms as his home. The preceding verse described its vastness; here we provide a brief contemplation.
There is one gate. "Ancient" means long-standing and old; it is a metaphor for that since beginningless time there has been this ignorance (*avidyā*), and with it, this world has existed.
It is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) not solid, meaning it is not merely unstable for a brief moment. "Suddenly decaying" means suddenly encountering shaking and collapsing all at once;
it is a metaphor for how the three poisons (*triviṣa*) bring about retribution, and how the three calamities (*trividha-vipatti*) are about to arise before long and sweep everything away.
Regarding the "collapse": the "hall and chambers" refer to the aforementioned hall and pavilion. Their being "lofty and perilous" means they are towering, precarious, and vast;

this is a metaphor for the tiers of the three realms (*tridhātu*), which, like these structures, are easily toppled and ruined. This symbolizes that the three realms are accumulated through the four abodes (*catvāri nivāsāni*) and are thus subject to easy transition and change.
The pillars, foundations, beams, and rafters are as described before. "Decayed and leaning" carries the same meaning as previously explained regarding rot and instability.
The "foundation" (基) refers to the base of a wall; the "steps" (陛) refer to the tiers of a staircase. These support the house, which is falsely conceived as being indestructible.
This serves as a metaphor for the two types of attachment to phenomena—conceptual and innate—which cling to the three realms by falsely conceiving them to be substantially real.
Although one clings to false conceptualizations, their fundamental substance cannot escape being transformed by the four marks [of conditioned existence].

Therefore, they are likened to collapsing ruins. "Collapsing" (*tāi-hui*) means decay and ruin. "Walls" is the same as before. "Ruined and split apart" (*pi-che*) carries the meaning of crumbling and cracking.
Mud and plaster are used to decorate cracks; thatched roofing is used to shield against wind and rain; and rafters and eaves are used to support the thatch.
These, moreover, are places where insects dwell and birds roost below—metaphors for the physical environments upon which sentient beings with dull faculties rely.
Because their evil karma is particularly intense, these environments are easily destroyed; thus, they are described as crumbling, collapsing, and falling into disorder.

To provide an analogy: "decaying" (*tuo-luo*) refers to falling into ruin and withering away; "scatteredly falling" (*luan-zhui*) refers to falling off in a disordered manner; and "dropping out" (*cha-tuo*) refers to falling away in a jagged or uneven fashion.
The fences surrounding the four intermediate directions are called "peripheral barriers" (*zhou-zhang*); that which is winding and difficult to discern is called "curvaceous" (*qu-qu*).
This refers to the place where ghosts secretly hide and dwell below; it serves as a metaphor for the physical retribution upon which sentient beings with sharp faculties rely.
Because those false teachings entrap people, making them easy to enter but difficult to escape, they are likened to being surrounded by obstructions and winding, crooked passages.
Excrement and urine that are impure are called "various filth. To pervade everywhere without exception is called "filling and permeating.

This is a metaphor for those sentient beings with false views who propagate licentious ways and falsehoods, violating the constant order and disrupting the natural relations; such things exist everywhere.

△ Second, the metaphor for the primary retribution (*vipāka*) within the three realms (according to the prose commentary, there are two parts to the primary retribution: first, the five hundred men; second, the thirty sons. Here, the thirty sons are missing, so the metaphors of owls, crows, eagles, vultures, and the like are added to supplement them). This is divided into two parts.
First, it serves as a general metaphor for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Second, it serves as a specific metaphor for the sharp and dull faculties.
Regarding the first: there were five hundred people dwelling therein.

According to the meaning of the prose commentary, although the three vehicles (*triyāna*) were complete within them due to past conditions, they still remained submerged in the five destinies at this time; therefore, they are not distinguished [separately].
The Parable of the Thirty Offspring. △ Second, the specific parables for the sharp and dull faculties, in three parts: first, the specific parable for the five dull faculties;

second, the specific parable for the five sharp faculties; third, the summary of the two parables. Regarding the first (the five dull faculties—namely, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt—which are stubborn and indecisive regarding their objects of perception, like ignorant birds and beasts, they are thus used as metaphors), it is divided into five:
first, the parable for the latent tendency of pride; second, the parable for the latent tendency of hatred; third, the parable for the latent tendency of doubt; fourth... [text continues].

The first [of the seven latent tendencies] is an analogy for the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). The five [remaining ones] are analogies for the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*). First, regarding pride (*māna*): its nature is to exalt oneself in relation to others based on self-reliance; its function is to obstruct non-pride and to give rise to suffering.
Hawks, owls, eagles, vultures, crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons.
There are seven types of pride (*māna*): first, *māna* (pride), which is to conceive oneself as superior among those who are inferior to oneself;

second, *atimāna* (excessive pride), which is to conceive oneself as superior among those who are equal to oneself; third, *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride), which is to [conceive oneself as superior] among those who are superior to oneself...

Within the Dharma, there are seven types of pride (*māna*): first, pride of superiority, which is to insist upon one's own victory; second, pride of equality, which is to think oneself equal to those who are superior; third, pride of inferiority, which is to think oneself superior to those who are equal; fourth, pride of self (*asmimāna*), which is to know only that "I exist" while failing to recognize the existence of others;
fifth, pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*), which is to claim attainment when one has not attained it, and to claim realization when one has not realized it;

sixth, pride of insignificance (*ūnamāna*), which is to maintain a sense of inferiority while acting with arrogance toward others; and seventh, pride of error (*mithyāmāna*), which is to cling to false views and fail to respect those possessed of virtue. Now...
Among these, the *chī* (owl) is also called the *xiūliú*; it seizes the opportunity to enter another’s nest, snatching and eating the fledglings.
This represents "pride" (*māna*), which is the small overpowering the large. The *xiāo* (screech owl) is also called the *liúlí*, colloquially known as the "night-cat";

once hatched, it turns back and eats its mother. This represents "excessive pride" (*atimāna*), which is the small overpowering the large. The *diāo* and *jiù* are birds of prey; they rely on their own [strength].

The "creature with physical strength" refers to one that seizes other birds for food; this is a metaphor for *māna* (pride). The "crow" refers to the common crow (*kāka*), colloquially known as a "blackbird";
it snatches twigs to build its nest and quarrels with its own kind—this is a metaphor for *atimāna* (excessive pride). The "magpie" refers to the *māyūra-śakuni* (the joyful magpie);

though originally not an auspicious omen, its calling suddenly brings joy to people—this is a metaphor for *adhimāna* (arrogance). The "pigeon" refers to the variegated pigeon (*kapota*); its nature is extremely dull-witted.

The sparrow (*śuka*): its nest is built with a few twigs, which suffices for it; this is a metaphor for base conceit (*hīna-māna*). The pigeon (*kapota*): a species of dove. Emperor Minghuang of the Tang dynasty called it the "flying servant.

It is by nature fond of mating; when gathered in flocks, it indulges in lust without restraint. This is a metaphor for perverse conceit (*mithyā-māna*). 2. Metaphor for the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣa-anuśaya*).

(Hatred is defined as having the nature of increasing anger toward suffering and the instruments of suffering; its function is to obstruct non-hatred and to serve as the basis for unpeaceful conduct and evil deeds.)
Vipers, snakes, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes.
There are three kinds of anger: first, anger with justification, which arises only when one is provoked; second, groundless anger, which arises spontaneously without cause;
third, contentious anger, characterized by stubbornly insisting on one's own correctness. Here, "viper" (*vṛścika*) refers to the *maṇḍūka-vṛścika*, also known as a chameleon (*kṛkalāsa*).
The *vṛścika* (lizard) resembles a snake but has feet; it comes in varieties such as blue-green and black, all of which contain venom and sting humans, being no different from snakes.
The *āśīviṣa* (viper) is also a species of snake; if it stings the hand, one must cut off the hand, and if it stings the foot, one must cut off the foot—otherwise, death is certain.
These three all move stealthily and sting in the dark, injuring people without cause; they serve as metaphors for irrational anger. The *vṛścika* (scorpion) is... [text continues]
The "back-protecting insect" stings people when it touches their back, yet relies on its tail to do so; this is a metaphor for anger that is justified by reason.

The centipede is fierce and swift in its movement, while the millipede moves slowly with a continuous flow of saliva; these two differ in their speed and urgency, serving as a metaphor for anger arising from disputation.

△ Third, the simile for the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-nuśaya*). (Doubt is defined as having the nature of indecision regarding the principles of the Truths; its function is to obstruct the wholesome qualities of non-doubt.
Lizards, centipedes, mongooses, wildcats, mice, and various other malevolent insects scurry about, darting hither and thither.

There are three kinds of doubt: first, doubt regarding oneself, meaning one doubts that one is not a suitable vessel; second, doubt regarding the teacher, meaning one doubts that the teacher is not a true person;
third, doubt regarding the Dharma, meaning one doubts that the Dharma is not authentic. Herein, the *shǒugōng* (also known as the *yàn dìng*) was raised in the Han palace with vermilion cinnabar.
Its blood was taken and used with a plum-blossom seal to smear between the eyebrows of palace women; if there were illicit affairs, [the mark would change].
When [the deity] does so, the flower-seal immediately disperses; because it is able to guard the palace women against lewdness, it is named accordingly.

As for that which lies prostrate against the courtyard wall, waiting to eat flies and gnats: it has a hundred legs, resembles a centipede but is smaller, and is commonly called the "coin-dragon" (qián-lóng).
At that time, they would come and go through the walls; moreover, it was often still dark at night.

These two would both suddenly appear and suddenly disappear, moving now east and now west as if in fear, likely because they suspected they were not yet mature creatures and might be harmed by others at any moment.
This is a metaphor for one's own doubts. The *yòu* is the yellow rat; the *lí* is the fox; the *xí* is the sweet-mouthed rat;
and the *shì* is the grain-stealing rat, which steals food without being aware of its own hunger. These four are creatures of many doubts:

for instance, when a fox crosses water, it repeatedly steps forward and then retreats; when rats of this sort emerge from their burrows, they hesitate several times before acting. This is because they doubt people.
"Trapping" is a metaphor for doubting the teacher. "Various evil insects" refers to species that cannot be fully categorized, such as spiders and the like.
Moving back and forth, crisscrossing from east to west, they run about undecided because they suspect there may be danger in whichever direction they turn; this is a metaphor for doubting the Dharma.

△ Fourth, the analogy for the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). (Delusion refers to that which has the nature of being obscured and ignorant regarding all principles and phenomena; its function is to serve as the basis for all defilements.
It is like a place of excrement and urine, foul-smelling and overflowing with impurities, upon which dung beetles and various insects gather.
The place reeking of excrement and urine is a metaphor for the objects to which delusion (*moha*) clings. Among all objects to which delusion clings, none surpasses men and women;
since their bodies are the root of filth, resembling a jar painted with various colors, they are thus compared to a place reeking of excrement and urine.
Furthermore, because impure substances constantly flow from their nine orifices, they are compared to overflowing impurity. The dung beetle is also called *ayaḥ-kavaca* (iron-armored).

Regarding "insects": those that form balls of dung are various insects, including flies and maggots; they all take what is filthy to be pure, and sentient beings with deluded minds are just like this.
With their deluded minds failing to understand, they give rise to perceptions of sensual pleasure toward men and women.

Therefore, it is metaphorically said that [the dust] gathers upon it. △ Fifth, the metaphor for the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*). (Greed refers to that which has the nature of being stained by and attached to existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence; it can obstruct non-greed.)
They suffer the karma of birth;
foxes, wolves, and jackals chew upon them, trample them, and engage in strife, snatching, tearing, howling, and barking at them.
There are three types of greed: first, powerful greed, such as that of corrupt officials, tyrannical administrators, and the like, including bandits and robbers;
second, cleverly calculated greed, such as seeking wealth by attaching oneself to those in power, or taking profit by harboring thieves; and third, powerless greed.

Just as a servant might wail while begging or as one might dig through a wall to steal, so too are these fox-wolves (*vṛka*) mentioned here—wild beasts resembling dogs with large mouths and the color of foxes, hence called "fox-wolves.
They are carnivorous by nature and possess great strength, capable of seizing small children and other such beings;
this serves as a metaphor for powerful greed. The *śṛgāla* (jackal) originates from the land of Hu (Central Asia) and is also known by that name.
The "Hu dog" resembles a fox but is smaller; it travels in packs and howls at night. It moves with great agility and does not avoid tigers or wolves.

Yet it is still able to associate with them to seek food; this is a metaphor for those who are clever in scheming and greedy. As for "chewing," it refers to chewing with the mouth; as for "trampling," it refers to [trampling with the feet].
Trampling with their feet is a metaphor for their insatiable greed; they consume the goods and further seize the wealth.
"Licking" refers to licking the blood with the tongue; "gnawing" refers to biting through the bones with the teeth. They willfully plunder the families of the weak and virtuous.
It is like a corpse; though one possesses strength, skill, and strategy, and exhausts all wealth until the household is emptied, what is this different from gnawing and biting?
Words such as "needles and moxibustion" [are useless]. Those who encounter such things should be struck with alarm. It is easy to come into this world, yet people recklessly squander it at will.
They do not know how to cherish [their bodies]. Therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of "bones and flesh in disarray.

To be "in disarray" means that the bones and flesh are scattered and strewn about in all directions, like the bedding upon which a wolf lies. The phrase "by this" (*yóushì*) is a term used to connect the preceding clause with what follows.

Dogs are domestic animals; they lack the power to take [food] for themselves. They either pursue it at the place where it has been left or approach it stealthily from a dark spot—this is a metaphor for powerless greed.
As for those who "vie with one another to seize and snatch": "seizing" (bō) refers to grabbing and scattering [the food], while "snatching" (cuō) refers to crowding it together in one place;
this is a metaphor for the collective assault of the petty multitude, who will inevitably pursue even a profit as small as a fly’s head.

To have one's provisions scattered and depleted until there is barely enough to fill the belly is called "hunger. To become emaciated from long-term hunger, with skin and bone clinging together, is called "emaciation" (*karśa*).

To be busily occupied all day long, constantly suffering from insufficiency, is called "anxiety" (*saṃtrāsa*). To beg for what remains and yet find it insufficient, looking elsewhere for more, is called "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).

Having no other purpose than this, devoting oneself solely to the mouth and belly, is called "seeking food" (*bhojana-paryeṣṭi*). These terms collectively illustrate the petty person (*puruṣa-adhama*).
Flies inevitably rush toward [food], yet what they obtain is not much; they constantly suffer from insufficiency and seek it out wherever they go.
Examining their state of mind, they think only of nourishing their own mouths and bodies. Each desires to eat alone, and their mutual encroachment and plundering is called "strife" (*raṇa*).
Their mutual tearing and pulling at one another is called "seizing and dragging" (*ākaḍḍhana*). They take things in their beaks, desiring to eat them, and gather...
When sounds contain the clamor of fighting, it is called *jǎi-chí*. When one loses an object and dies for it in a struggle, letting out a piercing cry, it is called *háo-fèi*.

These terms collectively metaphorize petty people who act for the sake of profit; each desires to enrich their own household and benefit themselves. First, they engage in strife and physical assault; subsequently, they resort to litigation and appeals.
This is like those who divide profits unequally, whose fighting does not cease, and who eventually abandon their bodies to file a formal accusation.
This is precisely it. Now, although these five preceding metaphors may seem unconventional on the surface, their underlying intent is in fact earnest and profound.
By borrowing the names of insects and the forms of beasts, they serve as a warning to awaken the minds of people throughout the world.
This concern for maintaining the Way of the world is, as Mencius said, "the difference between man and the birds and beasts is but slight. It is as if [this text] were speaking from the same source.

The same principle applies. Readers should reflect upon this well. This concludes the separate analogies for the five dull faculties (pañca-dauṣṭhulya). △ Second, the separate analogies for the five sharp faculties (pañca-tīkṣṇendriya).

(The five sharp faculties refer to the views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and views regarding precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Because they are resolute and firm in their determination regarding the objects of perception and their fruits, they are like those ghostly spirits who possess supernatural power; hence they are used as analogies. This is divided into two parts: first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one;
second, the actual analogies for the five sharp faculties. First:
The state of terror and transformation within that house is such that goblins and imps are found everywhere.
The first two phrases conclude the preceding description. "Terror" refers to birds and beasts menacing human beings; "states of transformation" refers to their myriad variations and distinctions.
"Thus it is" (*iti*) is a term used to conclude the summary; it means that the description of the manifestations of terror has been completed.
The following two lines introduce what follows: they state that it is not merely thus, but that *chimei* (chi-mei) and *wangliang* (wang-liang) spirits exist everywhere.
"Chi-mei-wang-liang" is a collective name for ghosts and monsters; it serves as a general metaphor for sentient beings with wrong views.

Sentient beings with wrong views can be briefly categorized into five types, as illustrated by the following metaphors. When analyzed in detail, there are sixty-two kinds that pervade the three realms.

Therefore, it is said that they exist everywhere. Just as in this land there are various heterodox teachings, each establishing its own gateway, so too do false teachers and their demonic factions fill the realm, fanning delusions among countless ignorant men and women.
These individuals suffer the king’s law in life and fall into hell after death; the harm they inflict upon the common people is far more than that of mere *chimei* and *wangliang* spirits.

△ Second, the actual metaphors for the five types of benefit consist of five parts: first, a metaphor for wrong view; second, a metaphor for [wrong] precepts and views; third, a metaphor for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

fourth, a metaphor for the view of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and fifth, a metaphor for extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Regarding the first (wrong view): it refers to those who do not revere the Triple Gem, do not pay homage to stupas and monasteries, deny cause and effect, and devote themselves exclusively to false teachings.
The yakṣas and malevolent spirits devour human flesh... (down to) the sounds of their quarreling are most terrifying.
*Yakṣa* here translates as "swift" (*jieji*), meaning that their range of movement is swift; it is a metaphor for those with sharp faculties of wrong view, who are rapid in engaging with objects.
"Malevolent spirits" refers to those who consume the food of humans and whose nature is fierce and evil; it is a metaphor for those with wrong views who deny the existence of causes.
This is the result: it is due to the incorrectness of one's knowledge and vision. Whether a person is young or old serves as a metaphor for good causes and good results.
When old, one chews thoroughly before eating; when young, one swallows directly. Likewise, those with false views who deny the existence of good causes and good results are like this.

The various species of venomous insects and all manner of wicked birds and beasts symbolize the evil fruits. Their hatching from eggs, incubation, nursing, and birth from the womb symbolize the evil causes.
When these evil causes have matured, there is much fear of being discovered by others; therefore, they are likened to each hiding and protecting itself.

As for the *yakṣas* vying with one another, it refers to those who, driven by the urgency of hunger and thirst, scramble to seize and eat [the prey] regardless of its size—yet they are themselves mistaken.
Seeing that they deny the existence of evil causes and their corresponding evil effects, the Dharma flourishes and the teaching is established;
thus, their false views become perfected. Like one who has already eaten his fill, those who follow them are numerous, and their false views increase.

Like an evil mind that grows ever more intense, they long for self-interest and gain while slandering the teachings of others. Like the clamor of strife, those who follow such doctrines ultimately enter the Avīci Hell.
This is truly terrifying. As the ancient masters said: "Foolish men and women such as these will encounter the king's law in life and fall into Avīci Hell at death.

This is precisely what that refers to. △ Second, the parable of precepts and views (precepts and views refer to regarding what is not a cause as a cause, such as the precepts of cattle and dogs, or the practice of self-mortification).
The *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost crouches upon a mound of earth (until) he places his foot upon its neck, terrifying dogs for his own amusement.

*Kumbhāṇḍa* is translated here as "jar-shaped" (*píng xíng*), meaning that its form resembles a jar; it is a metaphor for those who rely on their own precepts and views while engaging in perverse conduct.

It is like an empty stomach that puffs up the heart; it is to sit in vain without substance. To squat with the legs tucked under is called *dunju* (crouching). A mound of earth that is not level is called a *tudwa* (mound of soil).
Likewise, one who relies on those false precepts and dwells for a time in false concentration cannot dwell truly in right concentration.
They travel by means of the void. It is said that at times they leave the ground, yet they cannot raise themselves high—only one or two feet.
They cannot reach far away. It is said that as they travel back and forth, they become dissolute and self-indulgent; they act with reckless abandon and playfulness.
Relying on such false concentration, they temporarily manifest false supernatural powers, yet they cannot raise themselves high or reach far away, nor do they attain the truth.
To be thus self-mastery is like holding one's own wrong precepts so that greed does not arise; it is like seizing a dog by its two hind legs, which prevents it from acting.
This is suppression, not eradication. It is like pinning someone down until they lose their voice; "losing one's voice" indicates that it is not a true death.
Furthermore, using applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) to further suppress the seeds is like placing a foot upon a neck—it is not the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Calculating the causes for nirvana is like taking pleasure in frightening a dog. Long ago, while I was at a local inn, I encountered a heterodox practitioner who boasted of his own practices:
fasting for seven days was called "striking the seven"; experiencing blurred vision with flowers appearing before one’s eyes was called "seeing light";
and the rising of phantom flames was called "the Gate of Heaven opening. These are all of the same sort as those who take pleasure in frightening dogs. Alas! How perverse!

The teaching has now reached the point of leading people into error. △ Third, the analogy for the view of a self (the view of a self refers to falsely reckoning the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, as a "self," and based upon them, forcibly establishing a sovereign controller, constantly giving rise to the view of a self; it is the stream of clinging to "I" and "mine").
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large (extending to) who emit great evil sounds, crying out and seeking food.
Among all views, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) predominates; therefore, they are compared to ghosts. Da Cheng says:

"To reckon a self as persisting vertically through the three periods of time is called 'long'; to reckon a self as extending horizontally throughout the five aggregates is called 'large. To reckon a self as sovereign..."

They do not cultivate wholesome dharmas; because they lack a sense of shame and remorse, they are said to be "naked. Because they are adorned with evil karma and lack the support of merit, they are said to be "black and emaciated.
Because those who conceive of a self do not transcend the three realms, it is said that they "permanently dwell therein."
He conceives of a self within his mind and speaks words proclaiming the characteristics of a self; hence it is said that he utters a great, evil cry.
Hoping that by means of this speech he might realize the fruit of the Path, he cries out seeking food; furthermore, he utters a great, evil cry.
Nowadays, men and women mingle in clamor; those who proclaim scriptures and chant verses do nothing but shout all day long and raise their voices through the night.
This is nothing other than seeking material gain to sustain their physical bodies—is this not far worse than those who cry out for food?

△ Fourth: The Analogy of Seeing-Seeing (Seeing-seeing refers to the view of grasping at views [dṛṣṭiparāmarśa]. It is reckoning what is not a fruit to be a fruit, such as the case of Udraka Rāmaputra).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles;

they see those who flow [into such states]. By means of supernormal powers attained through false concentration, they reach the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

This state is neither the same as the "having-perception" of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nor is it the same as the "non-perception" of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); it is neither existence nor non-existence, yet it is both existence and non-existence.
There is none. Therefore, their throats are likened to needles. Those whose throats are like needles are the "needle-throated" (*sūcīmukha*) among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

The *Śrāddhabhojana-sūtra* (Sutra on the Offering of Food), in the "Instructor’s Admonition," states: "The throat is like the narrow opening of a needle; not even a single grain of rice can pass through.
This refers precisely to these ghosts. △ Fifth: The Simile for Extreme Views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). [Extreme views] refer to calculating [the self] based upon the view of a self in a single body.
[They are] those who have severed [the view of] permanence and cling to one side or another.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose heads are like those of oxen (up to) those driven by hunger and thirst, crying out and running about.
The ox has two horns, neither reaching the other; this is a metaphor for those with extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) who each cling to one side, mutually asserting right and wrong.
"Eating humans and devouring dogs" is a metaphor for their adherence to annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) and eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*), whereby they utterly negate the causality of good and evil.
Within the context of evil causes and effects, the specific use of "devouring dogs" as a metaphor is because greed is a fundamental affliction (*kleśa*).
This is merely citing one case as an illustration for the rest. One whose hair is disheveled and matted possesses the appearance of a malevolent being;
likewise, the actions and movements of those with extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) are such that their depraved energy oppresses others. Those who are cruel and harmful eat humans and devour dogs;

likewise, those with extreme views reject cause and effect and have no fear of retribution for evil deeds. They act according to their own whims without restraint, just like those who are ferocious and perilous.
Those oppressed by hunger and thirst are a metaphor for those who practice emptily without attainment, lacking both meditative concentration and wisdom.
Those crying out and running about are a metaphor for when impermanence arrives; they cry out in suffering with no escape.

Although these five preceding metaphors are extremely distressing to human beings, there is no avoiding their reality. Why is this so? It is because the True Dharma is difficult to practice, while the false...
These arts are easily mastered; consequently, heterodox books and deviant teachings have come to fill the world.

Therefore, our World-Honored One, even if he were to employ the eloquence of his supramundane tongue to take the place of the axes and adzes of this world, dissecting their vitals and exposing their hidden subtleties, would ensure that they could find no place to conceal themselves before the world and future generations.
This is comparable to Mencius’s rejection of Yang Zhu and Mo Di and his expulsion of their licentious doctrines. Its...
The resolve to support the True Teaching is as one in essence. Since we disciples have become children of the Buddha, we ought to repay the Buddha’s kindness;

we must exert our utmost strength to propagate it, striving to ensure that those who have not yet entered the teaching hear of it and enter, while those who have already entered hear of it and emerge from worldly attachments.
I hope you will not let your mouths be hindered by mere tolerance, allowing them to remain submerged and stifled like eggs.
[This] nurtures [the view that] it harms the True Dharma. This concludes the separate analogies for the five benefits. △ Third, the summary of the two analogies:
"Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts... [up to] ...such immeasurable perils and terrors."
In the analogy for the sharp-facultied (tīkṣṇendriya), yakṣas and hungry ghosts (preta) are briefly mentioned; the hungry ghosts here refer specifically to those with needle-like throats.
In the analogy for the dull-facultied (mṛdvindriya), various evil birds and beasts are briefly mentioned, citing two categories each to encompass the rest.

Deprived of the support of wholesome dharmas and oppressed by evil karma, they transmigrate through the four modes of birth, just like those in the four lines concerning the urgency of hunger. This is impermanence.
They are swift; as soon as they arise, they perish, without a moment’s pause. Like those who peer through a window, all such things are harmful to people;
therefore, they are called "difficulties" (*durga*). This is a metaphor for the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the dull and the sharp, both of which bring harm to the world.

Since they already inflict harm upon the world, one must guard against them from time to time; yet, fearing still that one might be invaded by them, it is said metaphorically that there is "fear of the immeasurable.
"Immeasurable" (wúliàng) means, as it were, that one cannot escape it at all. This concludes the metaphor for the primary retribution (*pratyātmika-vedanīya*) within the three realms.
△ Third, the metaphor for the various sufferings of the three realms.
"This dilapidated old house belongs to one person" (up to) "its flames simultaneously blaze fiercely on all four sides. Regarding "the house belongs to one person":
this is a metaphor for the triple world, wherein only the Buddha is the master. As stated in the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*: "I am always here, preaching the Dharma and transforming beings.
Since it says he is "always present," it implies that he does not abandon his response to the world except for brief intervals; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.
Because he had recently departed not long ago, it is said that "after the elder had gone, fire suddenly broke out.

This is a metaphor for how, after the Tathāgata has relinquished his response to the world (*saṃsāra*), sentient beings give rise to delusions and create karma; thus, the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the eight sufferings arise spontaneously and without cause.
Although they arise spontaneously and without cause, over time they accumulate and become increasingly severe, such that the six destinies and four modes of birth [are entirely filled].
Lu Chengyi is a mass of suffering; therefore, he is likened to four sides where the flames simultaneously blaze together. △ Fourth, the analogy for the nature of oppression has three parts:
first, a brief analogy for the characteristics of the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*); second, a detailed analogy for the characteristics of the primary body (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*).
Third, the summary of the two metaphors for the environment and its inhabitants. First:
"The rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars crackle, shake, split, and break; they fall, and the walls collapse.

"Rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars" refers to the specific characteristics of the burning house, which metaphorically represent the differences in the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) within the triple world, corresponding to the respective karmic retributions of beings.

Regarding the various types of retributive results: the bursting sounds that resound and crackle are the roaring of the blazing fire, which serves as a metaphor for the sound of being oppressed by manifold sufferings, such as the howling of the wind or the trembling of the earth.

The breaking, snapping, and falling down represent the state of being scorched and shaken, serving as a metaphor for the appearance of being oppressed by manifold sufferings, such as the collapsing of mountains or the boiling of the ocean. At this time, the four modes of birth and the six...
The limits of the Path do not fail to undergo transformation along with all forms of suffering; therefore, it is further illustrated by the metaphor of walls collapsing.

△ Second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the primary retribution (sabhāga-niṣyanda) has two parts: first, a metaphor for the characteristics of the lower realms; second, a metaphor for the characteristics of the higher realms. First:
The various ghosts and spirits raise their voices and cry out loudly (until) the great and wicked beasts vie with one another to devour them.
The initial metaphor refers to the conditions of human existence. That they are called "ghosts" yet also "spirits" suggests they are not ordinary ghosts;

this metaphor represents those false teachers. When false teachers encounter suffering, they proclaim false paths in the vain hope of attaining liberation; therefore, they are likened to those who raise their voices in outcry.

They cry out loudly. The vultures and eagles represent the affliction of pride (*māna*). The *kumbhāṇḍas* represent the afflictions of precept-and-view (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) collectively represents the two types of afflictions:
the dull (*mṛdu*) and the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*). "Panic-stricken" (*zōu-zhāng*) means being utterly distraught on all sides. "Terrified" (*huáng-bù*) means fearing they will be consumed by fire.
This is a metaphor for the two types of propensities—the dull and the sharp—as they cycle back and forth through the six realms and four modes of birth.

One also recognizes that the manifold sufferings are terrifying; yet, though one knows these sufferings are terrifying, because one is unacquainted with correct cultivation, there is no means of escape.

Therefore, it is likened to being unable to exit on one's own. The "ferocious beast" below is a metaphor for the characteristics of the six heavens; the "ferocious beast" further represents the propensity of greed. Poison...
The "insects" are a metaphor for the latent tendencies of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*). No other metaphors are cited because the preceding ones subsume the subsequent ones.

These [insects] are scorched by the fire and seek to escape by boring through the walls; thus it is said they "hide and flee into holes and crevices. This serves as a metaphor for those sentient beings in the human realm who possess dull latent tendencies (*mṛdv-anuśaya*).
Driven by suffering, they briefly cultivate a small amount of merit and are reborn in the six heavens above. As for "holes and cavities," these refer to apertures and crevices in a wall;

the smaller ones are "holes" (kōng), which metaphorically represent the two heavens of the Four Great Kings and Trāyastriṃśa. The larger ones are "cavities" (xué), which metaphorically represent the Yāma, Tuṣita, and other heavens.
Although these holes and cavities lack fierce flames, they still cannot escape being scorched and baked by heat; this metaphor represents the four [lower heavens].
Although the kings of the Trāyastriṃśa and other heavens lack the extreme sufferings of the human realm, they cannot escape the five signs of decay.

Since they cannot avoid these five signs of decay, it is ultimately not a place where one can find peace for the body or establish one’s life; therefore, it is compared to a place of hiding and concealment.

Piśāca: this is translated as "eater of vital essence. It serves as a metaphor for the sharp-facultied messengers (li-shi) of the six heavens, because their infringement and destruction of the True Dharma are no different from those who devour the vital essence of humans.
Although they differ from those with dull faculties (du-shi), they have not yet transcended the six heavens;
therefore, the metaphor states that they likewise dwell therein. Because they lack genuine concentration and wisdom to adorn themselves, they are compared to those of meager merit.
Because they lack virtue, they are oppressed by subtle afflictions that torment both body and mind; thus, they are likened to being tormented by fire.
Since they lack the adornment of concentration and wisdom and are further beset by manifold sufferings, they harbor doubts regarding the Dharma and engage in mutual slander.

Just as they mutually harm one another—first slandering and then denying [the truth]—and just as those jackals who previously drank blood and ate flesh, along with the pack of dogs that had already died before them, these serve as metaphors for the two types of craving:

the craving for skillful means and the craving for power, which exist only among humans. When one is about to be reborn in the heavens, this craving is severed. As for the various great predatory beasts:
"The vying to come and devour" is a metaphor for the greed of the six heavens.

Being single-mindedly attached to celestial blessings causes the two types of greed—calculative ingenuity and powerlessness—to never again manifest in active conduct. This concludes the metaphors for the characteristics of the lower realms.
II. Metaphors for the Characteristics of the Higher Realms.
Foul-smelling smoke billows and swirls, filling all four directions; (up to: tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they wander about in agitation and run in distress.
The first six phrases take up what preceded to initiate what follows. "Foul-smelling" refers to the vapors of ghosts and animals; "smoke" refers to the remnants of fierce fires.

The term "péngbèi" (蓬[火*孛]) refers to the appearance of a dense aggregation; it serves as a metaphor for sentient beings in the human realm, whether of sharp or dull faculties, who do not exhaust their remaining suffering.

This mode of activity (*ākāra*) is clearly manifest. Since this mode of activity is so clearly manifest, even though they pass through all four modes of birth and even reach the six heavens, [the afflictions] still follow them and never depart.
Therefore, they are likened to being "filling the four directions. As for the "four directions," there is nowhere they are not present.

The metaphor of suffering pervading the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and filling them means that holes and crevices are inevitably reached; this illustrates how suffering follows the six heavens.

The centipedes and millipedes represent the latent tendencies of anger (*pratighānuśaya*) within the six heavens. Being oppressed by the manifold sufferings of these six heavens, they advance to cultivate the four *dhyānas* and seek the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) above;
thus, they are likened to being burned by fire and scrambling out of their burrows. The final six lines constitute the formal [explanation].
The higher realms are illustrated by this. The *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts illustrate the precepts and views of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Because they maintain false precepts and suppress anger so that it does not manifest, they are likened to those who eat whatever they seize. This is because those in the higher realms do not give rise to anger; such is the characteristic of the form realm.

Furthermore, the various hungry ghosts illustrate the sharp faculties of the empty realm (*ākāśadhātu*), for they are born from suffering at the summit of emptiness; thus they are illustrated [in this way].

Because their heads are ablaze with fire, they lack the food of outflow-free liberation (*anāsrava-āhāra*). Since they are deficient in the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are metaphorically described as suffering from hunger, thirst, and the torment of heat.
Having no outflow-free concentration or wisdom, they can only be led away by the牵引 (attraction) of karma. When their false concentration collapses, they once again undergo the cycle of rebirth;
thus, they are compared to those who wander about in panic and distress. This is like Udraka Rāmaputra, who was reborn below as a cow.

The worm within the jaw provides clear evidence for this meaning; it is the characteristic of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*). This concludes the detailed analogy for the characteristics of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
△ Third, the summary conclusion of the two analogies for the environment and the primary retribution.
That house is thus extremely terrifying, with manifold perils such as poison, harm, and fire.

It is bound together with creaking sounds that shatter and split; it crumbles, breaks, and collapses. Therefore, it is said, "that house is thus. If one does not exit in a timely manner, one will surely be injured;
hence, it is said, "extremely terrifying. This concludes the description of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the resultant environment), which serves as a metaphor for the three realms (*tridhātu*).
"Rest thus. If you do not emerge, you will inevitably fall. This concludes the section on birds, beasts, ghosts, and spirits, and the foul smoke of the great fire;

hence it is called "poisonous harm and the calamity of fire. If one does not emerge in a timely manner, one will certainly be harmed by them; hence it is said that "the various difficulties are not one.

This concludes the primary retribution (*vipāka*), which serves as a metaphor for sentient beings giving rise to delusions and thereby bringing about suffering; if they do not emerge, they will inevitably sink into ruin.
Thus ends the verse on the assembly of those who are moved [to seek salvation]. △ Third, the verse concluding the meaning of being moved, using a metaphor (a brief verse according to the meaning):
"At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate... (until) the elder, having heard this, entered the burning house in alarm."
Standing outside the gate is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, whose reality is ultimate and whose delusions are exhausted; he has long since departed from the gateway of cultivation and abandonment.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "He is able to emerge safely from the gate of that which is to be burned.

Furthermore, standing outside while intending to return is a metaphor for the Tathāgata relinquishing his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in other realms and being about to manifest birth in this world. Being about to manifest...
Born, he receives the legacy of the former Buddhas in preparation for his future succession to the position of Regent. Therefore, it is likened to hearing someone say, "There is a person.

This "person" refers to one previously seen, which is a metaphor for the former Buddhas of the past. "You, my sons," is a metaphor for the former Buddhas indicating those who are vessels for transformation;
these are the children with whom the Tathāgata has established a karmic connection. Although they are such children of karmic connection...
My son, you have prematurely withdrawn your great resolve and, out of attachment to the outflows (*āsrava*), have once again sunk into the midst of the three realms.
Therefore, it is likened to first entering this house for the sake of play; being young and ignorant represents the dull faculties and inferior wisdom of sentient beings.

Their joyful attachment represents sentient beings’ indulgence in desire and adherence to what is false. Because of this indulgence in desire, they do not contemplate weariness with suffering or the severing of its accumulation (*samudaya*).
Because they are attached to what is false, they do not know to aspire toward the cessation [of suffering] or cultivate the Path; this is the meaning of the verse and the prose.
Their minds feel no weariness or distress, serving as a metaphor for the lack of intent to seek liberation. "The elder, having heard it" means that upon hearing, he will surely see;

this is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, having received the entrustment of previous Buddhas, will surely observe the capacities of beings with his Buddha-eye. This is the meaning of the verse and the prose. "The elder sees this great fire."

The metaphor of [the fire] arising from the four directions refers to those who enter the burning house out of alarm; they must first be alarmed before they can be mindful, and only through mindfulness do they enter.

This illustrates how the Tathāgata, observing the capacities of sentient beings and perceiving their terror, gives rise to compassion and manifests birth. This verse summarizes the meaning of the prose: "Greatly alarmed and terrified."

And he forms such thoughts, etc., as in the parables. This concludes the section on the parable of the sentient beings’ responsive resonance. △ Second, the section on the parable of the Tathāgata’s transformative response, which is divided into two parts:
first, the verse on the parable of manifesting the provisional from the real; second, the verse on the parable of returning the provisional to the real. The first part has two sub-sections:

first, the verse on the parable of not obtaining [the truth] from the real; second, the verse on the parable of concealing the real to manifest the provisional. The first [is briefly combined with the verse].
"Only then can one provide rescue so that there is no burning harm.

"Fāng" (方) means "at this juncture"; "yí" (宜) means "it is appropriate. This refers to how, once the elder had entered the burning house, he deliberated and reflected, not yet knowing how he should effect a rescue so as to ensure there was no burning harm. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata having manifested the three realms.

During the twenty-one days following his attainment of enlightenment, he contemplated the various capacities of sentient beings, wondering how he might deliver them and cause them to escape from their manifold sufferings.
This is precisely the meaning of the "Chapter on the Teaching of the Dharma," which says: "Regarding such types as these, how can they be delivered?
The long passage continues: "One should use a garment-bag, or perhaps a small table, to carry them out from the house."

...this. "Furthermore, he further contemplates," and so forth, all of which pertain to the principle of providing appropriate relief. II. Verses on the Simile of Concealing the Ultimate and Bestowing the Expedient (2).
A. One verse on the simile of first showing suffering and its origin. B. One verse on the subsequent bestowal of the Path and Cessation.

Regarding the first (The Elder has three [qualities], but the current section lacks the "reflection on expedient means"), it is divided into two: 1. One verse correctly showing the simile of suffering and its origin. 2. One verse regarding the lack of faith due to contrary emotions.
The Parable. First (a broad verse concerning the meaning):
He exhorted his sons, describing various calamities and hardships, [saying] "up to this place of suffering and difficulty, how much more so when there is a great fire."
The initial parable illustrates the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). It corresponds to the previous verse’s statement that he "fully informed his sons of the meaning as he had contemplated it.

His exhortation to the sons, in which he speaks of various calamities and hardships, is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s instruction on the three vehicles (*triyāna*), extensively discussing the Truth of Suffering within the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
This is the general metaphor. The "evil spirits" represent wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the "poisonous insects" represent the poison of hatred (*dveṣa-viṣa*). Within the three realms—
There are many such types of people; when they do not leave one another, they constantly encounter each other—this is the suffering of association with the disliked (*apriya-saṃprayoga-duḥkha*).

The meaning of the metaphor of a "conflagration" refers to other forms of suffering. "Spreading and entangling" means that they ignite one another in succession, serving as a metaphor for birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.

Arising one from another in succession, they serve as mutual causes and conditions; this is the specific metaphor. The two lines concerning "multitudes of suffering" apply both to the dharma and the metaphor.

In the metaphor, it refers to the various sufferings within the house, namely the malevolent spirits, venomous insects, and so forth. In the dharma, it refers to the various sufferings within the realms.
This refers to the suffering of association with those one hates, and so forth. "Successive" means arriving in sequence. "Continuous" means circulating through coming and going.

"Uninterrupted" means beginning again after completion; this is the summary. From the section on the "venomous snake" below, the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) is illustrated by way of metaphor.

The preceding verse explains the meaning of "you all must quickly emerge. The venomous snakes, vipers, and so forth serve as a general metaphor for those of sharp and dull faculties within the three realms.

It refers to sentient beings driven by the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), who extensively create evil karma, lack the support of concentration and wisdom, and are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Just as those tormented by hunger and thirst, if even a single affliction (*anuśaya*) were added to oneself, one would immediately lose the Dharma-body and forfeit the life of wisdom.

This is as truly terrifying as that [fire]. The final two lines contain an admonition and encouragement to escape, stating that within the burning house, one dwells day after day with ghosts, beasts, birds, and insects, constantly suffering the pain of injury; this is already difficult enough.
One dwells within suffering; how much more so when there is further the great fire! How could one not urgently contemplate escape? This is a metaphor for the three realms.
When the sun [of the afflictions] is close to the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one is moved by the suffering of habitual defilement, which is already unbearable;
how much more so when there is further the searing torment of the eight sufferings? How could one still remain complacent and fail to seek swift escape? △
The two verses on the analogy of disbelief due to contradicting one's own feelings (abridged verse):
"Though the sons were ignorant, even upon hearing their father’s instructions, they still delighted in and clung to their play without ceasing.

These first two lines correspond to the preceding section where it was said that although the father felt compassion and exhorted them with kind words, that previous account was stated from the perspective of the father. This [verse]...

"Approximately the sons hear" means that they hear the discourse emerge from one another. The following two lines are a verse summarizing the preceding passage on how "the various sons and others delight in play and so forth";

the difference lies only in the degree of elaboration. The correspondence with the Dharma should be understood by referring to the prose (long-xing). This concludes the first section: the verse showing the metaphors for Suffering and its Origin.
△ Second, the verse on the subsequent metaphors for Bestowing the Path and Cessation, in three parts: 1. A verse on contemplating the skillful means.
The Simile. Two verses provide the simile for the path of right giving and its cessation; three verses provide the simile for the cultivation and realization according to one's wishes.
First (the commentary on the meaning): At that time, the elder had this thought... (up to) he then reflected and devised various skillful means.
The sons did not listen to their father’s words; therefore, the elder thought to himself. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who do not believe the Buddha’s words;
thus the Tathāgata reflects: "These sons are like this"—meaning he feels regret for his sons, wondering, "Why have they no self-awareness to such an extent?
This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s lament for sentient beings, wondering, "Why is their wisdom so inferior to my own, reaching such a state? The sons...
Having entered the burning house, it already distressed the father’s heart; moreover, because they did not listen to their father’s words, his sorrow and affliction increased even further.
This is a verse summarizing the meaning of the prose passage: at that time, the elder immediately had this thought regarding the house.

There is not a single thing to be enjoyed; this is a metaphor for how the three realms are entirely composed of a mass of suffering. "To be addicted" refers to the extreme depth of craving and immersion;
it is a metaphor for the ultimate state of sentient beings' delusion and inversion. Being in a state of ultimate delusion and inversion, they do not believe the Buddha’s words;

therefore, it is metaphorically described as "not accepting my teaching. Because those who do not believe the Buddha’s words will inevitably be driven by suffering, it is metaphorically said that "they are about to be harmed by fire."

This verse corresponds to the prose section. The meaning is that this house has already been consumed by a great fire, and if I and my sons do not exit in a timely manner, we will certainly be burned to death.
However, the prose version differs slightly in that it states both father and sons are burned together.
One must understand that the Dharma-body is profoundly tranquil and fundamentally cannot be burned; it is only for the sake of delivering sentient beings that it manifests a form-body.
Since it is said that the son is to be burned, the father is included as well; though they are distinct, they are nonetheless not separate.
"He then reflects" means he fears being consumed by fire. "He devises various skillful means" means he wishes to rescue and deliver them.
This verse corresponds to the prose [of the Lotus Sūtra]: "I shall now employ skillful means so that my sons may escape this calamity"—the application of this principle is clear.
△ Second, the verse on the parable of the path of right giving and the cessation [of suffering] (abbreviated verse):
"I tell my sons and others: I have various kinds of [toys] (up to) for you to play with as you please."
He spoke because he knew his sons' prior inclinations; it is like the Tathāgata, who discerns their past dispositions and then teaches.
That he calls them "precious playthings" and "wondrous jewels" is to manifest their excellence and cause [the sons] to feel joy and desire to take them up.

This is like the Tathāgata praising the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) to inspire a longing for cessation. This verse summarizes the prose passage: "The father knew the various sons' prior inclinations and preferences."
...and so on, until he addressed them, saying: "The objects of your play and delight, those rare and difficult-to-attain things"—this refers to the passage below concerning the goat carts.
By pointing out from afar that the three carts are outside, it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s remote indication of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This verse summarizes the prose section.
The meaning of these various sheep-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts being outside the gate,

[the father] teaching [the children] to come out and promising them the carts they have made so that they may take whichever they please, is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s exhortation to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
The promise that the guarantee shall not be in vain is a verse corresponding to the prose section. "You all should quickly come out from this burning house;

whatever you desire, I shall grant it to you"—the meaning of these words is entirely identical to the prose, differing only in their sequence, as the translator has altered the phrasing. △ Third, the verse on fulfilling wishes through practice.
The Verses of Meaning (which differ slightly from the prose in their inclusion or omission):
When the sons heard it said that such chariots [would be provided] until they reached the open space and were freed from all suffering and distress.

The meaning of the first four lines is the same as that of the prose, with the exception that the phrases regarding "fulfilling wishes," "courageous vigor," and "mutually pushing one another aside" have been omitted.
As for the phrase "reaching an open space," this refers to sitting in the open air. As for the phrase "being free from all suffering and hardship," this means there are no longer any obstacles;
these two lines, following the prose, should logically belong to the subsequent section, as they follow the thematic order rather than the sequence of the verse.
The verse on the analogy of establishing the provisional based upon the real is concluded. △ Second, the three verses on the analogy of returning the provisional to the real:

1. A verse on the analogy of the time having arrived and the faculties being mature; 2. A verse on the analogy of bestowing the One Vehicle equally; 3. A verse on the analogy of gaining benefit through hearing the Dharma.

Regarding the first (the prose commentary does not divide this, whereas the verse expands upon the prose), it is divided into two: 1. A verse on the analogy of the season having already arrived; 2. A verse on the faculties [having already matured].
The Mature Simile. First, [the verse] extensively explains the meaning:
"When the elder saw his children had escaped from the burning house... therefore, all you people, I am now happy."
Seeing his sons emerge from the house and stand at the crossroads is a metaphor for the Tathāgata seeing all sentient beings emerge from the realm [of saṃsāra] and attain the fruit [of liberation].
This verse corresponds to the prose section. At that time, the elder saw that his sons had safely emerged and were all at the crossroads;
this is the meaning. It does not say "sitting exposed in the open without obstruction," because that was already transcended in the preceding verse. They sat before their teacher...
[The Buddha] descended. He extensively recited the meaning of his mind being composed, joyful, and leaping with delight.
Previously, fearing that his children might be burned, he had found no peace of mind; now, seeing his children emerge from the house, he sat upon the Teacher’s seat.

This is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, in the past, feared that the various capacities of sentient beings were not yet ripe for goodness and thus remained restless; now, seeing them exit the realm and depart from suffering, he dwells securely in fearlessness. Thus...
Because the lion possesses the meaning of fearlessness, he speaks words of self-congratulation. He congratulates himself that his lineage will not be severed;

since the lineage is not severed, the family estate has one upon whom to rely. Thus he says, "I am now happy. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata congratulating himself on having found one who can perpetuate and flourish the Dharma.
Since the Dharma has been entrusted to such a person, this Way has one upon whom it can depend; thus the Buddha also says he rejoices.
"Fear" refers to [the fear of] birth; "birth" refers to the initial arising, which is a metaphor for the first formation of a karmic connection.

"Nurturing" refers to rearing and nourishing, which is a metaphor for the intermediate period of teaching and transformation that has already spanned many kalpas; therefore, it is compared to being "extremely difficult. "Foolish and small, lacking knowledge" is a metaphor for having dull faculties and inferior wisdom in the past.

Because of these dull faculties and inferior wisdom, one falls back into the three realms of existence (trāya), and is thus metaphorically described as "entering a perilous house" where there are venomous insects.

Anger is metaphorically compared to *chimei* (goblins and specters). "Many" refers to encountering them frequently from time to time; "fearsome" refers to being constantly harmed by them—this further illustrates the suffering of association with the loathed (*apriya-saṃprayoga-duḥkha*).
The fierce flames of a great fire collectively illustrate the remaining types of suffering, which pervade all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).

It pervades the six realms of existence; thus it is likened to flames arising from all four sides. Their delight in play and sport is likened to the minds of sentient beings, which do not give rise to weariness and do not seek liberation.
Saving them so they may escape their distress is likened to the Tathāgata having already established skillful means to entice them toward transcendence.
This elder’s own explanation of his joy is likened to the Tathāgata himself manifesting his own bliss.
Regarding the source of fearlessness: "Therefore, O people, I am now happy. This was the elder calling out to his attendants to confirm that his happiness was not false.
It is like the Tathāgata, now before this assembly, confirming and manifesting that his joy and fearlessness are not deceptive.
As the Chapter on Teaching According to the Dharma says: "Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom are attached to..."
Those who are conceited and arrogant cannot believe in this Dharma; "now I rejoice and am fearless" refers to this.
△ Second, the verse on the metaphor of the faculties being fully matured (extensive verse).
At that time, the sons knew their father was sitting at ease; [the text continues] "Now is precisely the right time, please deign to bestow it upon us.
Having realized for themselves that they were free from suffering, they then knew the Tathāgata’s fearlessness; thus it is metaphorically said that "they knew their father was sitting at ease.

Upon hearing the teaching of the Buddha's wisdom, they lost their former abodes; thus it is metaphorically said that "they all went to where their father was. The twelve thousand [disciples] harbored doubts, while Śāriputra...

They requested three times; thus the parable says they spoke to their father, saying: "Although we have heard that the provisional vehicles are not the ultimate truth, we did not know how to further seek the true reality.
We therefore still seek instruction by means of the three vehicles. Thus the parable says: "We pray you will grant us the three kinds of precious chariots.
Based on what was previously said, it appears there were three vehicles; hence the parable says: "Just as previously promised to your children..."

"Come forth! I shall provide the three vehicles according to your desires. Now that you have emerged from the boundary, having suddenly heard that what was previously realized was not true, I pray that the Buddha will strive to reveal the reality.
Therefore, the metaphor says: 'Now is precisely the time. I only entreat you to bestow them upon us. This section is more extensive than the prose;
while the literary flow differs slightly, it should be understood through its underlying meaning rather than by assigning each line one-to-one with the prose during the recitation of the verse.

The analogy for the ripening of the faculties concludes. △ Second, the verse on the analogy of bestowing the One Vehicle equally (the prose commentary is divided into two parts; the present section lacks the reasons for rejecting [other vehicles] and establishing [this one].
Although the remainder is largely the same, the phrasing is slightly more concise, thus it belongs to the abbreviated verses).
The elder, being immensely wealthy with many treasuries, bestows these marvelous chariots and other items upon his sons.
The initial metaphor represents the essence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The verse [describes] the meaning of the single great chariot adorned with various jewels;
the treasuries of gold, silver, and so forth collectively represent the merit produced by causes. By means of this merit, the essence of the fruit is accomplished, as follows:
A chariot made of various jewels has already been formed as its essential body; it is further adorned with virtues, just as one would decorate and embellish [an object].

The reason for not mentioning its height and breadth is that these are subsumed within the "Great Meaning" (mahārtha). The reason for not mentioning that each is bestowed individually is that this is reserved for what follows. Below, "surrounding" (parivāra)...

This illustrates the characteristics of the One Vehicle (ekayāna). It corresponds to the meaning previously explained regarding the surrounding railings, up to the placement of the red pillows and so forth.

"Golden cords" refers to the aforementioned jeweled cords; alternatively, it may mean that various jewels are strung together with golden cords. Thus, the terms appear interchangeably in the preceding and following sections.
"Net" refers to the aforementioned canopy; the former provides the name, while this describes its appearance, as the canopy possesses the characteristic of a net.

Regarding the previous mention of "adorned with various jewels" and the present mention of "pearls," it is because pearls are the primary element joined together, while the other jewels serve as various supplementary ornaments.
The two phrases concerning "golden flowers" refer to the aforementioned hanging garlands of flowers.
It is merely a difference between opening and closing. "Various colors" refers to the binding of the cords for the bells and the flower tassels with many different hues.
"Adorned with various ornaments" refers to the binding of the railings and lattices above, decorated with a variety of inlaid embellishments.

"Surrounded on all sides" is a metaphor for the body being endowed with all the marks (lakṣaṇas), where these marks adorn the single entity. These two lines are supplementary verses. "Soft silk and cotton wool."
The finest and most subtle of silk and cotton floss serves as a metaphor for the various dhyānas and liberations;

it is not the provisional teachings of the mundane truth, which are coarse and superficial. Since these are neither provisional nor mundane, they constitute the realm in which the Tathāgata dwells; therefore, the metaphor is employed.
It is used as a mattress and bedding. Since mattresses and bedding are implements for sitting and reclining, "fine wool" refers to extremely fine white wool.

It serves as a metaphor for the samādhi and right reception (samāpatti) of the Buddha-ground; it is not something for worldly enjoyment. Therefore, it is compared to what is both superior and exquisite.
It is not easily obtained; therefore, it is likened to being worth a thousand billion. It does not accept other sensations;
therefore, it is likened to being fresh, white, and pure. It is used for its essential substance; therefore, it is likened to covering the top.

These six preceding phrases correspond to the previously mentioned "double-layered soft mat," merely expanding upon what was briefly stated. According to the prose commentary, there is further the arrangement of the *dan* (red/matting).
The phrase "resting upon" (*zhèn*) is an abbreviation of a verse. The section beginning with "There is a great... serves as a metaphor for the function of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

It reiterates the meaning previously expressed by the lines "yoked with white oxen," up to "attendants and guards. That the white oxen are fat and strong corresponds to the previous description of their skin being full and pure;
this is a metaphor for the teaching of the One Vehicle. Their great strength and beautiful appearance are metaphors for the principle of the One Vehicle. [They] yoke the precious chariot... must...
Walking level and moving swiftly is a metaphor for the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "Leading from the front" and "following from behind" refers to the attendants and guides.
The final two lines are a recapitulative verse (*anugīti*) regarding the distribution of gifts to each son; while the prose exposition (*gadya*) precedes, the verse (*śloka*) alters its form.
△ Third, the recapitulative verse on the parable of hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit (the "meaning-verse").
At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness (up to the point of) sporting and delighting with sovereign ease and without hindrance.
They attained what they had never experienced before, which was not what they had originally expected; therefore, they leaped for gladness.

The prose section clarifies the intent of their joy and exultation, while the verses express the manifestations of that joy and exultation. Relying upon this One Vehicle, they shall achieve the perfection of eternal bliss.

This is the land of my purity. Like riding this precious chariot, one travels through the four quarters, eternally enjoying the bliss of the Dharma, moving spontaneously through both mundane and supramundane realms with playful joy, sovereign and unimpeded. This is according to the prose section.
Below this, there are further metaphors from the Buddha’s words to demonstrate that they are not false; however, because other doubts have already been severed, they are not set in verse.

The explanation of the metaphors in verse is concluded. II. The Verse on the Application of the Dharma (Dharmasaṃgraha) has two parts: 1. The verse on the sentient beings who respond with spiritual capacity (*indriya*). 2. The verse on the Tathāgata who responds with transformation and response (*nirmāṇa-pratibimba*).

The first part [the verse on the sentient beings] has three sections: 1. The verse on the Buddhas who are responded to. 2. The verse on the assembly of beings who respond. 3. The verse on... [text fragment].
The summary of the meaning [of the preceding] is as follows. The initial verse states:
"I, Śāriputra, am likewise the most honored among the assembly of sages and the father of the world.
My wisdom and abandonment are ultimate; I am revered by all the true ones, and thus I am called the 'most honored among the assembly of sages. My compassion is vast and great. The myriad...
All classes alike receive its benefits; therefore, he is called the Father of the World. Regarding the verses (*gāthā*) and the prose (*dīrgha-pada*):

the Tathāgata is the father of all worlds, for his meaning encompasses the three virtues of Buddhahood—enlightenment (*buddhatva*), the severance of afflictions (*prahāṇa*), and compassion (*anugraha*).

This is because, as the verses and metaphors are already concise, the application of the Dharma (*dharmayukti*) is likewise concise. △ Second, the verses on the assembly that is capable of being inspired (the "Meaning Verses").
"All sentient beings are my children" (up to) "such fires blaze forth without ceasing. Regarding the statement that all sentient beings are my children, there are two [categories].
