The Bodhisattvas dwell here, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings. Their practice of trade and exchange is likened to that of merchants;

this serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas from other lands who come here to assist in transformation and establish karmic connections. Since those from both this land and other lands all gather together, they are said to be "extremely numerous.

Nevertheless, although this section is complete with both principal and retinue, and is fully equipped with both wisdom and the Dharma, as well as both the capacity of the audience and the teaching, it remains [incomplete].
This may only be understood as signifying that his Way is profound and his virtue is weighty, and that all conditions are fully prepared;

it must not yet be hastily taken to mean that he is expounding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for the metaphor of expounding the *Avataṃsaka* still lies in the future. This metaphor represents the Buddha having just completed his initial attainment of enlightenment.

II. The metaphor of deeply contemplating the capacities of those to be transformed (three parts): 1. The metaphor of the arising of the capacity within the Buddha-land. 2. The metaphor of the Buddha... [text fragment]
The triggering of the mechanism: three metaphors illustrate the proximity of the mechanism to the site of awakening. First:
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities until he eventually reached the city where his father resided.
"At that time" refers to the period when he had already attained great wealth; it is analogous to the time when the Tathāgata manifested his birth and attained enlightenment.
"Passing through kingdoms and towns" refers back to the preceding description of his gradual wandering.

It means that as he wandered gradually—whether traveling through various villages or passing through kingdoms and towns—the natural pull of his innate disposition led him at last to the city where his father resided.

This is a metaphor for sentient beings practicing the path in successive stages. Whether they give rise to the contemplation of the "stilled mind" (*sthāpanā*) and so forth, it is like traveling through various villages;

or whether they attain fruits such as that of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), it is like passing through various kingdoms and cities. Their past conditions drawing them along, they come to be born within the triple world, which is like arriving at the city where their father resides.
△ Second, the metaphor for the Buddha contemplating the capacities of beings and responding to their calls.
The father constantly thought of his son with whom he had been separated, yet he remained serene and joyful, free from further anxiety.

The initial parable was intended to illustrate the contemplation of the conditions for the Way. "The father constantly thought of his son" refers to the period after he had left home to achieve wealth;

he constantly remembered his deceased son. This is analogous to how, after the Tathāgata manifested birth and attained enlightenment, during the three weeks that followed, he constantly contemplated the means of conversion.
This is the pivot. As for our parting from you: initially, because I had business to attend to while abroad, it caused you to flee.
This is a metaphor for when the Tathāgata, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, responded to conditions in other realms, causing sentient beings to regress and fall.

Having regressed and fallen, they experienced all five paths of rebirth; thus, they were again led toward the provisional vehicles (upāya-yāna). Therefore, this is illustrated by the fifty-plus years.

"More than fifty years" refers to the length of time the son has been wandering away; it is a metaphor for sentient beings who have fallen back and already traversed the five realms of existence, as well as those of the provisional vehicles.
"Never having spoken of such matters to others" means that because they have not heard [the truth], there would be no benefit in speaking of it;
it is a metaphor for sentient beings who do not contemplate turning toward the Great [Vehicle]. For this reason, the Buddha likewise did not reveal his original nature to them.

The great capacity [of the son] remains unmoved; manifesting it would be of no benefit. "But he reflects within himself, harboring regret and resentment" means that he regrets that his own household laws were not strict and resents that his son wandered abroad and forgot to return.

This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata constantly contemplating the great capacity [of sentient beings], regretting that his past teachings were not profound enough, and resentting that sentient beings have fallen into decline and do not return. "Reflecting upon himself" and below serves as a metaphor for this contemplation.

The reason for this device is that he thought to himself: "One who is aged and infirm is unable to remain for long. This is like the Tathāgata’s vehicle, which appears temporarily by depending on conditions;
when those conditions are exhausted, it ceases to exist. As for "having much wealth," one with great wealth has heirs who look toward him for inheritance.
This is like a Tathāgata who has perfected all virtues; though the Way continues and the storehouses are overflowing, it must be one with the capacity [to receive] who can inherit them.
Without an heir, these cannot be entrusted to anyone else. This is a metaphor for the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata:
such a capacity can transmit them, but they are not bestowed upon those lacking the capacity. Once [the master] passes away, his wealth and property will be dispersed and lost.

This means that if one does not obtain a true heir, after his death the wealth will belong to the five families; even if there is an unrelated *mínglíng* (a foster child), he shall receive but a small portion.

Hence it is said: "There is no one to whom the legacy may be entrusted. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata failing to encounter a great-capacity recipient (*mahā-yogin*); after his extinction, the Dharma will be invaded by Māra.
Even if there are disciples of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), they shall obtain only partial emptiness (*prādeśika-śūnyatā*). How could such persons be entrusted with the Buddha-way?
Therefore, it is with earnestness that one who constantly remembers his son hopes for his return;

this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s profound contemplation of the capacities of those to be transformed, hoping they will return to their source. Hoping they will return to their source, he unconsciously engages in successive reflections;
thus it is said, "He further thought: 'If I obtain my son, the lineage will not be severed; if I entrust the wealth to him, the family estate will have a guardian.'"

Therefore, one is composed and joyful, free from further anxiety or worry. This is analogous to a Tathāgata who, having attained the great capacity [of a disciple], bestows upon them the merits of the Buddha-ground;
such a person will naturally delight in being the bearer and upholder of this transmission, and will no longer have the concern that the Way might fall into ruin or decline.
△ Third, an analogy for the capacity approaching the site of enlightenment.
"World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened to come upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate.
'At that time' refers to when the father was reflecting; it is like the Tathāgata’s time of contemplation.

A common laborer takes wages according to his strength, yet what he obtains is not much; this is called 'hiring out. It is a metaphor for the two vehicles before they have encountered the Buddha. Each [of them]...
Practicing heterodox paths is merely a vain exertion of effort; what is realized therein is but little. To walk straight ahead is called "unfolding" (*zhan*);
to turn back and run is called "revolving" (*zhuan*). This is a metaphor for sentient beings who, while correctly practicing heterodox paths, suddenly attain the realization of turning back.

Because they have turned back, their former karmic conditions draw them near, and by chance they approach the site of enlightenment; thus it is likened to encountering one's father’s house. As for "standing still," it means not daring to enter directly.

Regarding "by the side of the gate": one does not dare to face the gate directly. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who, though close to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), cannot enter directly into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Facing Śākyamuni directly, they still abide on the partial and deviant ground of ordinary worldlings. This concludes the profound contemplation of those to be converted.

△ Second, the three analogies for the discord between the capacity [of the listener] and the teaching, divided into two parts: first, an analogy for the teaching being at odds with the capacity; second, an analogy for the capacity being at odds with the teaching. Regarding the first:
"From afar he saw his father seated upon a lion throne... (omitted)... adorned in every way, with a majesty and virtue that were exceptionally sublime."
First is the primary metaphor. "Seeing his father from afar" means that because he was stationed outside the gate, he could not observe him closely;

this is a metaphor for how those of the Two Vehicles, having formerly dwelt among ordinary people and outsiders, were unable to truly perceive the essence of the *saṃbhogakāya*, but could only know it through inference.

"Squatting" refers to a haughty posture, representing the majestic authority of a teacher; this is a metaphor for Vairocana abiding in fearlessness and manifesting the characteristics of the Great *Avataṃsaka*. The "jeweled stand" supports...
As for the feet: they have pedestals made of jewels to support the two feet so that dust shall not defile them.
This is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, through profound samādhi, maintains the merit and wisdom he has cultivated, such that nothing can destroy them. O Brahmins!
Pure conduct and lofty integrity are like the Lord of the World who is Perfectly Awakened; the noble lineage of the Kṣatriyas is like the Lord of the world of sentient beings;
and the householder, though lacking formal rank yet possessing virtue, is like the Lord of the world of non-sentient things. These are the various Lords of the World.
Each realizes a single virtue of Vairocana, thereby assisting in the manifestation of the profound transformation; thus they are metaphorically described as reverently surrounding him.

The pearl necklaces symbolize the various marks and minor signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*); since each mark and each minor sign is accomplished through immeasurable merit, they are metaphorically described as being worth ten million.
None of these fail to adorn that retributive body (*vipākakāya*) to demonstrate its majesty.

Therefore, it is used as a metaphor for adorning the body. Regarding the officials, citizens, and servants mentioned previously, they represent the remaining elements of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The hand is a metaphor for wisdom, and the whisk is a metaphor for eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

This refers to how, in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each of the bodhisattvas possesses distinct wisdom and employs pure, wondrous eloquence to assist the Buddha and propagate his transformational teachings; hence, the metaphor.
Standing in attendance at the left and right and covered by a jeweled canopy symbolizes the Buddha’s compassion of gathering and sustaining others;

it carries the meaning of providing shelter to give rise to goodness. Hanging various flowered banners symbolizes the Buddha’s severity in subduing; it carries the meaning of overturning and extinguishing evil.
Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground and scattering various famous flowers symbolizes that the Tathāgata, having already perfected both subduing and gathering, first bestows [these graces].
First, perfect concentration is used to purify the mind; next, perfect wisdom is bestowed to give rise to understanding. The precious objects are metaphors for the merits of the Buddha-ground;
their arrangement symbolizes clear manifestation without concealment. This is intended to enable all sentient beings to likewise attain this path.
"Taking out and putting in, receiving and giving": this means that what was previously taken out is now put back inside; what is now received is given away and departs.

It is a metaphor for those with whom the Tathāgata formerly established karmic conditions being gathered in as objects of transformation today, and those who now seek transformation being granted the establishment of great conditions.

This also signifies the meaning of transformation upon transformation without interruption. As follows, the conclusion summarizes that the physical marks and merits, as well as the primary and attendant dharma-gates, collectively adorn the retributive body;

therefore, they are likened to various kinds of ornaments. Because the Śākyamuni’s *śarīra* (exalted form) is not something the followers of the Two Vehicles can endure to behold, it is likened to majestic virtue that is uniquely sublime.
△ Second, the analogy for the faculties of sentient beings being at odds with the teaching.
The impoverished son, seeing that his father possessed great power and influence (up to the point where he had formed this thought), fled quickly away.
"The impoverished son sees that his father possesses great power and influence" means that from afar he saw his father’s various adorned powers and his majestic, preeminent authority;
this is a metaphor for sentient beings perceiving that the essence of retribution is fully endowed with wondrous adornments and has been perfected.
This refers to the supreme retribution. "To harbor fear" means to dread its power and authority and to be terrified at the prospect of being seized;

it is a metaphor for sentient beings who are timid and fearful of the fruit of Buddhahood and dread the preaching of the Great Dharma. Because they dread the preaching of the Great Dharma, they contemplate in secret and regress.

Therefore, he uses the analogy of returning out of remorse. He privately reflects thus, not daring to speak aloud, because he fears that the Buddha might not permit sentient beings to secretly contemplate regressing from the Great Vehicle.
"This may be a king, or one like a king" refers to those who do not recognize their original father or his attendants;
fearing this may be the domain of kings and great ministers, it serves as an analogy for sentient beings who [do not recognize their true nature].
He recognized his original teacher and the assembly assisting in the transformation of beings, suspecting they might be Buddhas or Bodhisattvas.

Since the ground where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves dwell is not something that those of inferior capacity and weak faculties can cultivate or realize, he compared it to a place where one obtains goods by hiring out one's labor;
it was not like going to a poor neighborhood, for he considered himself mediocre and incompetent.

It is only appropriate for one to engage in hired labor in a poor neighborhood. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who know their own faculties are dull and are thus only fit to practice within heterodox paths.
Because practicing within heterodox paths does not yield true concentration and wisdom, they are compared to a poor neighborhood.

"Exerting one's strength" means to work as a hired laborer with full effort. "Having land" means that a place [of residence] is easily obtained; this is a metaphor for exerting effort in the practice of heterodox paths.
To practice [in this way] is still to have a place of refuge. Clothing and food are metaphors for wrong concentration and wrong wisdom; they are not right concentration and right wisdom.

Because there is no need for strenuous effort, they are compared to what is easily obtained. If one dwells here for a long time, or if one is coerced into working against one's will, yet desires not to leave—fearing that official matters might pressure one and force one to labor—this is a metaphor for the mental state of sentient beings who desire not [to leave].
He retreats, fearing that [the Buddha] will instruct him with the Great Practice (mahācaryā) and ultimately cause him to engage in cultivation.

Because he cannot endure the diligent toil required for such ultimate cultivation, it is likened to having formed this thought and then running away in haste. "Running away in haste" means hurrying back toward a poor village;
this is a metaphor for being in a state of agitation and each practicing a different path. This concludes the reflection on the three-week period.

△ Second, the analogy of mindfulness without calculation (this summarizes the meaning from the "Fire House" parable: "Furthermore, one reflects that this house has but a single door, and moreover it is narrow and small," etc.).

This is divided into three parts: 1. The analogy of the teaching not conforming to the capacity; 2. The analogy of the capacity not conforming to the teaching; 3. The analogy of the temporary cessation of the great transformation.
First: At that time, the wealthy elder [sat] upon the lion throne... (until) ...at that moment, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him.
Possessing the ten thousand virtues, he was like the wealthy elder; his realization of wisdom and fearlessness was like sitting upon the throne. Upon seeing his son, he...
"Recognizing" means recognizing one's own biological son; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata knowing that sentient beings were those with whom he had established karmic connections in the past.
"The mind is greatly joyful" means that having recognized his own offspring, he rejoices that his family estate has someone to rely upon;
this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, having known their past affinities, rejoicing that the lineage of the Way has someone to depend on. "He immediately forms this thought" refers to the thought...

This fulfills his original vow. It is like the Tathāgata’s thoughts being in accord with his fundamental aspiration; as his thoughts accord with his fundamental aspiration, he wishes to bestow the merit of the Buddha-ground.
Therefore, it is metaphorically said: "The treasury of wealth and goods now has one to whom it may be entrusted.

The phrase "I have always thought of this son, yet had no means to see him" illustrates the Tathāgata’s unceasing longing for his son during the preceding seven days and nights. It is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s recollection [of his son].
In the past, while I was still living, I harbored the thought that it would never end; yet now you have suddenly come of your own accord, which greatly accords with my wishes.

I rejoice in the joy of seeing you return home today, just as the Tathāgata rejoiced during the seven days and three nights after his enlightenment. I rejoice in the delight of having found a responsive opportunity today. Although I am advanced in years, I still cherish you deeply;

I already know that I shall not be able to remain much longer, and thus... [my home]... (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an incomplete thought regarding the speaker's impending departure.)

Karma is difficult to forget. This is illustrated by the fact that although the Tathāgata already knows that when conditions are exhausted, things cease, the lineage of the Dharma constantly maintains mindfulness.
Because the lineage of the Dharma constantly maintains mindfulness, its spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) is bestowed upon the bodhisattvas; therefore, it is likened to immediately dispatching bystanders.
This is because, for the most part, those in the *Avataṃsaka* assembly are bodhisattvas who speak by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power. As, for example, Dharmamati spoke of the ten [stages].
"Abiding" refers to the passage from [the Buddha] up to Vajragarbha, who expounds the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth.

"Sending a messenger to pursue and bring him back" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s empowerment to expound [the teaching] swiftly; it signifies the principle of gathering all sentient beings and leading them toward the Great Dharma.

At that time, "the messenger runs quickly to seize him" is a metaphor for the various Bodhisattvas who, riding upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*), assist in the manifestation of the profound transformation.

It is simply because the Dharma is vast while the faculties [of the listeners] are small; thus it is difficult to harmonize with and difficult to enter. Therefore, it is said "to run" and "to seize. This is why it is said:
"Although one knows the faculties are dull, one nevertheless expresses one's original intention. △ Second, the metaphor for when the faculties do not harmonize with the teaching.
The impoverished son was startled and alarmed, crying out in resentment (up to: he became even more terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate on the ground.
"Startled and alarmed" describes the appearance of fear; "crying out in resentment" expresses the sentiment of seeking release; "crying out loudly" is the sound of startled longing.

This is a metaphor for those of small capacity who, being timid toward the Great Vow, retreat; it manifests their verbal outcry as an expression of their resolve. He entered that land to seek [his father].
His wealth is said to be "infringing. It is said that the impoverished son does not pass through, but stays briefly outside the gate before wishing to return to the poor district;

hence it is said, "I do not infringe upon you. This is a metaphor for those of small capacity who claim they have no intention of seeking the Great [Vehicle], yet still contemplate practicing heterodox paths.
Having no mind to seek the Great, they instead resent the Buddha for not discerning their capacities; thus the metaphor says: "Why do you look at me?"

"Seizing him"—the more urgently they grasp him and forcibly drag him back—metaphorically represents the Bodhisattvas each preaching their own Dharma-gate to instruct and cause [sentient beings] to practice.
In instructing them to practice, there may be a deviation from the "small mind" (the limited aspiration); therefore, it is metaphorically compared to thinking to oneself that one is without fault.

"Without fault" means there is no offense committed; this metaphor represents the small-capacity practitioner thinking to themselves that they have no vow to seek the Great [Vehicle]. This is the fundamental point.
There is no aspiration for greatness; one is merely compelled to practice according to the teachings. Therefore, it is likened to being imprisoned.
Because those of small capacity lack the power to enter the marketplace, they regard the conduct of Bodhisattvas as being like imprisonment.

This "certain death" is a metaphor for those of small capacity who say of themselves that they lack the power to enter the marketplace, fearing that even their subtle roots of goodness from past causes will be lost along with everything else.

Furthermore, "becoming even more terrified" is a metaphor for conceiving doubts and lacking faith. "Fainting and collapsing to the ground" is a metaphor for destroying the Dharma and losing one's goodness.
This is as stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "Because they destroy the Dharma and do not believe, they fall into the three evil realms.
△ Third, the metaphor of a temporary respite from the Great Transformation.
The father saw him from afar and spoke to his messenger, saying: "Go to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.
As for "the father saw him from afar," this is a metaphor for a superior body and inferior faculties; it is not the primary meaning. As for "he spoke to his messenger,"...

The metaphor of commanding companions to proclaim [the teaching] refers to speaking to those who are not kin. A great assembly cannot accommodate those of inferior capacity; therefore, the metaphor states, "This person is not needed.
Yet, even those of inferior capacity may still be guided and led; therefore, the metaphor states, "Do not force them to come.

Sprinkling cold water on the face corresponds—according to the subsequent text—to the provision of material support through giving (*dāna*). This is because the subsequent text follows in sequence with kind speech (*priyavāditā*) and beneficial action (*arthacaryā*).
...practice. Because they act together through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), giving provides for their physical needs and causes joy to arise in their minds;
thus, they do not fall into slandering the Dharma or losing their roots of goodness. Therefore, the metaphor says: "causing them to attain awakening.

Although they do not reach the point of slandering the Dharma or losing their roots of goodness, the Buddha’s intention still lies solely in preserving this seed of Buddhahood to await the proper conditions. He instructs the bodhisattvas that there is no further need to [act with urgency].
The Great Dharma was shown to him; therefore, it is metaphorically said: "Do not speak with him again. The phrase "the reason for this" introduces the inquiry.

As for why he commanded that one should not speak with him again: the passage beginning with "The father knew" provides the explanation. The father knew his son—this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom discerning the capacity [of beings].
Because the small capacity did not seek higher realization, it is metaphorically described as having a base and inferior intention, knowing itself [to be so].
"Powerful and noble" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s self-awakened majesty and distinction. This self-awakened majesty and distinction cannot be endured by those of inferior capacity;
therefore, it is likened to what a son finds difficult [to behold]. "Difficult" here means to fear and revere.

"To know with certainty that he is a son" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata using his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajñāna*) to recognize him as a being with whom he had established a karmic connection in the past. Although he knows of this past connection—
The capacity [of the beings] was such, but because the time had not yet arrived, he temporarily concealed their original cause and did not immediately reveal his true identity before the assembly;
thus, he is likened to one who does not speak to others, saying, "This is my son. This represents the Tathāgata’s intent to have the bodhisattvas briefly suspend their great transformative activity.
The messenger speaking to him is a metaphor for gathering [beings] through kind words (*priyavāda*); because of these kind words, he does not force them.

Because it is great, the analogy says: "I now release you. This does not mean that because it is great, one is forced [to practice it]; rather, it means allowing them to cultivate it as they please. Thus the analogy says:
"Go wherever you wish," meaning to turn toward the cultivation of other paths and now apply oneself to former habits. Therefore, the analogy uses the joyful son of a poor man:

having suddenly been subjected to a great restraint, he unexpectedly hears that he may cultivate as he wishes; thus the analogy speaks of "attaining what was never before attained," meaning that he does not give rise to slander.
Because they do not fall into the three miserable realms due to their transgressions against the Dharma, they are likened to rising from the ground.

Because they instead cultivate heterodox paths and continue toward deviant sects, they are likened to going to a poor village. Because they rely on heterodox concentration and wisdom to support heterodox knowledge and views, they are likened to seeking food and clothing;
yet, as they fail to obtain anything real in the end, this serves as a metaphor for failing to attain the truth. △ Second, the metaphor for concealing the reality.

The Exposition of Expedient Means (this section summarizes the meaning of the "Burning House" parable, beginning with the passage: "I shall now speak of things that cause fear," etc.). This is divided into two parts: first, the parable illustrating the guarantee of the *āgama*;

second, the parable illustrating the transmission of the teaching through *prajñā*. The first part has three sub-sections: first, the parable illustrating the conversion and guidance by the person of expedient means; second, the parable illustrating the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma.
The three similes guarantee the attainment of the lesser fruits. First:
At that time, the elder was about to entice his son [to return]; when the father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at him.

The first analogy refers to the Buddha’s instruction regarding those of expedient capacity (*upāyika-pudgala*). Because past conditions do not permit their sudden abandonment, he intends to transform and guide them through a gradual sequence;
thus, it is said they are "about to be enticed. Since the Great Dharma cannot be bestowed abruptly, he intends to lead them through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*);
thus, it is said he "establishes expedients. The two persons represent the two types of those with expedient capacity: the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha. This is because of them...
They were originally bodhisattvas, but the Buddha commanded them to remain hidden within while manifesting outwardly, as if on a secret mission. It is later stated:

"Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior dharmas and fears great wisdom, for this reason the bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth. This sufficiently proves the point.
Their haggard appearance and complexion serve as a metaphor for being entangled by afflictions and karma, signifying a state devoid of any means of self-sustenance. They possess nothing...
"Venerable majesty" (*vaideha*) is a metaphor for the oppression of birth and death, possessing the aspect of suffering that is to be feared;

this refers to the provisional person who, while secretly maintaining [the truth] within, manifests it outwardly, demonstrating the existence of suffering and its origination (*duḥkha-samudaya*). As it says later: "He demonstrates to the assembly the presence of the three poisons and further manifests the aspect of false views;
yet, with few desires, he is weary of birth and death, and in reality purifies his own Buddha-field. This sufficiently proves this meaning. You may go there.

They are like those who, following the Tathāgata’s teaching, gather people through skillful means (*upāya*). There are three types of skillful means: first, physical action; second, verbal action; and third, mental action.

"Approaching them" refers to going there in person, which is a metaphor for physical action. "Speaking slowly" refers to skillfully instructing according to their dispositions, which is a metaphor for verbal action.
Mental action is as follows [described] below. "There is a place where this is practiced" is a metaphor for investigation (*vicaya*).
This is the true method for severing delusions. Within the method of analytical severance, there exists real cause and effect;
it is not like the practices of heterodox paths, which yield nothing despite one's efforts. Therefore, the analogy says: "I shall give you double your price. "Price" (*zhí*) here refers to value.

If the impoverished son consents, this metaphorizes a person of lesser capacity who is able to follow and practice according to the teaching. "The one who will employ him in the future" metaphorizes the person of expedient means. That is to say—

One should teach according to the capacity [of the student]. Teaching according to the capacity inevitably involves bending one's own will to follow that of another; this is precisely the practice of the mind.

If one asks, "What do you wish to do?"—this is a metaphor for a person of small capacity posing a question. If one replies, "What do you wish to cultivate? and then says, "I am hiring you to remove dung"—this is a metaphor for the provisional teacher.
One should then instruct them in the severing of *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-kleśa* (afflictions of cultivation), for these afflictions are defiling.

The "defiled mind" is like excrement and filth. The statement that "the two of us shall also work together with you" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata commanding various influential persons to gather [beings] through "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) and thereby sustain them; it shows that by appearing to share the same task, he secretly binds their hearts as if they were working together.
The phrase "at that time, the two [sons]" below is a metaphor for receiving the command to gather and transform [beings]. "Immediately seeking the impoverished son" is a metaphor for...
Using the Dharma to seek the capacity [of the recipient], once it has been found—this is likened to the capacity receiving the Dharma. He fully recounts the aforementioned matters;

this is likened to the teaching for the purpose of severing view-delusions and thought-delusions, thereby purifying the ground of the mind. "At that time," and so forth, is likened to relying on a Buddha who appears through transformation.
"First taking the price" is likened to a person of small capacity who, being about to engage in cultivation, first examines the benefits. Once the benefits are...
Upon careful examination, he then practiced according to the teachings; thus, "seeking" is used as a metaphor for searching, and "removing filth" as a metaphor for cleansing.
"Compassion" (*mǐn*) is a metaphor for great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and "wonder" (*guài*) is a metaphor for great pity (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because they were originally sons of the Buddha but have now flowed toward heterodox paths and external views—furthermore, having abandoned the fruit of Buddhahood above while taking pleasure in inferior practices below—the Buddha beheld them and could not help but be struck with alarm and moved to tears.

It is merely that one feels pity for them and grieves for them. This concludes the analogy regarding the person of expedient means guiding and transforming others. Part Two: The Analogy for the Buddha Turning the Wheel of Dharma. This has two sections: 1. The analogy for first demonstrating suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*). 2. The analogy for subsequently bestowing the path and cessation (*mārga* and *nirodha*). The first section: [Text omitted per instructions] ... [The passage continues with the detailed analogy of the physician treating the sick child, illustrating the Buddha’s compassionate response to sentient beings. ... [End of first section] The second section: [Text omitted per instructions] ... [The passage continues with the analogy of the physician providing medicine and instructions after the child has recovered, illustrating the Buddha’s subsequent teaching of the path and cessation. ... [End of second section] [End of Part Two] [End of entire text]
Furthermore, on another day, [the father] was at a window (up to: by means of skillful expedients, he was able to draw near to his son.
The first metaphor illustrates "turning the light to observe the capacity. Since the *Āgama* already pertains to "turning the light," it is therefore illustrated by "another day.

The Buddha abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), yet he observes those of small capacity while facing toward partial emptiness; therefore, it is illustrated by "seeing from afar through a window. There is no [other meaning].
Supported by meditative concentration and wisdom, yet subject to the oppression of birth and death, they are thus likened to being emaciated and haggard.

"Excrement" is a metaphor for the coarse and heavy afflictions of views and thought; "dirt" is a metaphor for the subtle ignorance. The necessity of emerging together from all three delusions is used to illustrate the subtle by means of the coarse.

This is because it is logically necessary that [the body] exists. "Dust" refers to dust being scattered upon the body; this is a metaphor for the three delusions obstructing one's innate capacity (*gotra*).

Because these delusions obstruct the innate capacity, the *dharmakāya* becomes defiled; therefore, it is compared to filth and impurity. "Immediately shedding [it]" is a metaphor for concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior.
The *saṃbhogakāya* (Sāmbhogikakāya) is a supreme and wondrous body, adorned with supreme and wondrous marks; therefore, it is compared to [the act of shedding].
The *kaṇṭhikā* (necklace) is a mark of supreme excellence, further adorned with ornaments of supreme excellence; therefore, it is compared to soft clothing.
Because [the Buddha] conceals this supreme excellence to accommodate those of inferior capacity, he is compared to one who has just removed his garments.
Śākyamuni’s humble body is adorned with humble marks; therefore, it is compared to something coarse and tattered. These humble marks are, in turn, [further...]
Because they delight in what is base and inferior, he uses the metaphor of a soiled garment. To accommodate those of limited capacity, he manifests this base and inferior appearance;
thus, he employs the metaphor of wearing it once more. His final body demonstrates that he is sustained by the same karmic bonds as others;

therefore, he is compared to a body covered in dust and soil. His right hand is a metaphor for expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), because expedient wisdom possesses the quality of being skillful in its application.
The metaphor of the chamber-pot represents the thirty-four moments of mind; for these thirty-four moments of mind constitute the means by which a Lesser Buddha (*hīnayāna-buddha*) severs the fetters.

The description of being "afraid" serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who, in order to accommodate those of lesser capacity, manifests as if he were terrified of birth and death—this is precisely what is meant by the saying, "Out of love for one's child, one does not notice their ugliness.

The passage beginning with "He speaks to all... serves as a metaphor for correctly demonstrating suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), while provisionally manifesting the practice of the Path (*pratipad*).
They practice together; as the Tathāgata demonstrates, they demonstrate together. Therefore, he uses the analogy of addressing the laborers.
Since the "laborers" already include those who were secretly sent away, [he says], "Work diligently," which is an analogy for the Tathāgata’s teaching to sever the origin [of suffering].
Because diligent work is no different from the previous task of removing filth, [he says], "Do not be indolent," which is an analogy for the Tathāgata.
He instructs him by making him aware of suffering: that through negligence he will be driven away and must again endure the toil of wandering.
This is a metaphor for how, if one does not diligently practice, one will continue to fall into birth and death and be oppressed by manifold sufferings.

As for "by means of skillful means, he is able to draw near to his son," there are four such skillful means from before: first, releasing him without speaking; second, sending people to search for and hire him back.

Third, [the analogy of] casting off a precious garment to wear tattered rags; fourth, [the analogy of] exerting effort to establish precepts and attain cessation. Here, we take the latter two, as they constitute the proximate expedient means (*upāya*).

If one discusses the progression from the remote to the proximate, all four meanings are encompassed. Generally speaking, when the inferior corresponds to the inferior, the relationship between teacher and disciple is no longer at variance;
therefore, it is likened to attaining proximity through expedient means. Second, the analogy for the subsequent bestowal of the Path and Cessation.
Later, he again addressed him, saying: "Ho! Man! [and so on, until] "...there are also aged and infirm servants; if you need them, I shall provide them.

This refers to the two truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*), which follow the truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*) respectively. Therefore, it is illustrated by the phrase "later, he again addressed him.

The word "ho" (*dū*) is used both as a phonetic character and as a metaphorical term. Depending on its high or low pitch, it is explained as having three meanings. First, the meaning of manifesting majesty; this is the high [pitch].

[The word] *shēng* (sound) has two meanings: first, the sense of "calling out," which is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*); second, the sense of "consoling," which is pronounced in a low tone. Here, we take the latter two [meanings].
Since the expedient skill (*quánqiǎo*) has already been demonstrated, there is no reason for a display of intimidation.

This may be understood by analogy with the previous examples of speaking slowly to manifest a state of exhaustion, fear, and so forth. "You must always act in this way; do not go elsewhere again" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Always adhere to the cultivation of the True Dharma; do not continue as before by flowing into the paths of heterodoxy.

I shall increase your price—this is a metaphorical indication to cause you to aspire toward cessation (*nirodha*). By means of the four fruits, I augment your practice accordingly; thus, the word "increase" (*jia*) is employed.

Whatever else you require, I provide a metaphorical indication of the Path (*mārga*) so that you may cultivate it; "require" (*xu*) here means "to employ. This collectively illustrates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) of both the primary and auxiliary paths for the purpose of cultivation.
Because it is essential: the basin has the sense of containing and supporting, which metaphorically represents how precepts can support meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Rice and flour have the sense of providing nourishment, which metaphorically represents how meditative concentration can provide nourishment for wisdom (*prajñā*). Salt and vinegar have the sense of harmonizing, which metaphorically represents how wisdom can harmonize meditative concentration.

This is the "Right Path. The term "belonging to" (*shǔ*) signifies a category; it serves as a metaphor for the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). This is because all thirty-seven factors are...

Because they are subsumed under the categories of the three trainings, do not harbor doubts or difficulties within yourself. This means that according to the Tathāgata’s teaching, when there is doubt one should seek its resolution;
when there is difficulty one should seek its clarification. Do not harbor internal suspicions, and do not fear or find obstacles in yourself. [This applies even to] an old, decrepit servant.
This is like those who have studied first: they must provide what is needed for others, which is like responding to all requests.

Furthermore, "there are also those" means that one should not doubt or find it difficult [to seek help], saying: "Even if you yourselves have not yet attained definitive understanding from the Buddha, there are still those who have studied first whom you may consult.
If you truly have something to seek, they will surely respond to you; why then should you doubt or find it difficult?"
Ah! This concludes the parable of the Buddha turning the wheel of Dharma. △ Third, the parable of assuring the attainment of the lesser fruits:
"Be at ease; I am like your father" (extending to) "I further grant you a name and call you my son."
"Be at peace with your own mind. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s teaching on the cultivation and realization of the settled mind.
"I am like your father" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s indication that there is a semblance of past affinity; he is fundamentally the father who established this connection.

The reason for using the word "like" (yu) is that the time has not yet arrived, and thus his true nature as the father is not immediately revealed. Because there is a semblance of past affinity, he protects and keeps you in mind. Do not... [text ends]
One will surely fear falling again; therefore, it is illustrated by saying, "Do not worry anymore.
To say "do not worry anymore" is because the previous statement that he is "like a father" corresponds to this internal logic: do not worry further about wandering about.
What follows below is an inquiry and explanation: why is it that I call myself "like a father"? It is because my age is advanced.
There is the principle of being the elder; thus, you are like a father. You are young and strong, possessing the principle of being the younger generation; you are truly like a son.
This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, whose realization is ultimate and whose delusions are exhausted, who may be called the "first awakened one" (prathamabuddha).

The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), rich in the power of study and severance, are truly the "later awakened ones. When you work, you never engage in deception, indolence, anger, resentment, or complaints; this demonstrates that the son trusts his father.
"Father" is a metaphor for the faith of those of the Two Vehicles in the Buddha. To provide a specific correspondence: "acting constantly" is a metaphor for the time of ordinary cultivation;

"deception" is a metaphor for overweening pride (*abhimāna*), because there is a sense of deluding oneself by claiming to have attained what one has not yet attained; and "laziness" is a metaphor for humans and devas.

Because they are attached to pleasure and do not practice, there is the sense of indolence; the "hostile resentment" (dveṣa) is a metaphor for non-Buddhists (tīrthika), because they delight in what is false and evil, thus possessing the sense of hostile resentment.
The two vehicles and the Buddha trust one another in their mental natures and are entirely free from these faults;
therefore, it is compared to being "non-existent. The statement "I do not see you at all" who possess these various evils clarifies the father’s knowledge of his son; this is the metaphor.

The Buddha knows the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). As these two vehicles investigate the truth and sever delusions with earnest diligence, the Buddha already knows that they differ from those who possess overweening pride (*abhimāna*) and those who follow the common flow of ordinary worldlings (*bāhya*).
Therefore, he uses the metaphor of "not seeing" to describe them. Those who act otherwise represent the aforementioned overweening pride and ordinary worldlings.
"From this day forward, like the son born [to the father]" means that once the son has placed his trust in the father, the father—

Furthermore, because he knows his children, he is no different from their biological father. By this analogy, once the followers of the two vehicles have placed their faith in the Buddha as one worthy of refuge, and the Buddha further recognizes that those of the two vehicles are capable of being instructed and admonished, he is thus like a Bodhisattva who has long since established a great karmic connection.
There is no difference in how they are viewed. At that time, the elder further bestowed upon him a new name;

this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata replacing the common, worldly appellations of outsiders and bestowing upon him the title of "Hearer" (śrāvaka). Although he was granted the title of Hearer, he still belonged to the category of "name-only" arhats and was not yet a true son of the Buddha;
therefore, he is metaphorically called a "son. As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "Then there was..."

The sound of *nirvāṇa* and those such as the *arhats* are examples of this. This concludes the section on the analogy for the guarantee of the *Āgamas*. II. The analogy for the transmission of the *Prajñāpāramitā* has three parts: 1. The analogy for the *Vaipulya* sūtras within the middle period; 2. The analogy for the Buddha’s command to transmit the teaching;

3. The analogy for receiving the command but not yet accepting it. First: The *nirvāṇa* sound refers to the *Arhat* and others. This concludes the analogy for the guarantee of the *Āgama*. △ Second, the analogy for the transmission of the *Prajñā* [Pāramitā] has three parts: first, the analogy for the *Vaipulya* sūtras during the intermediate period; second, the analogy for the Buddha’s command to transmit the teaching;
third, the analogy for receiving the command but not yet accepting it. First:

At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter (until: "yet the place where he stayed remained as it was"), this refers to the period when one realizes the small fruit by means of the metaphorical assurance. Regarding the phrase "although he rejoices at this encounter," there are two meanings for "encounter":

first, "favorable encounter" (*en-yu*), meaning that [the father] writes his name and gives him the name of a son; he rejoices in the profundity of the elder’s favor. Second, "chance encounter" (*ji-yu*), meaning that he runs...
The galloping horse finds its master; one rejoices in the extraordinary nature of one's own encounter. This is likened to the Tathāgata’s skillful establishment of provisional fruits.

The profundity of such gracious favor is like the extraordinary encounter of those who practice the two vehicles with frantic diligence when they meet a Buddha. This applies to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas alike.

All were filled with joy and exultation. However, because they should have advanced but did not advance, they are likened to those who, though told to stay, do not participate in the household affairs.

Calling themselves "hired laborers" (guest-workers) is a metaphor for the Two Vehicles who do not cultivate the Great Practice and cling to provisional teachings, failing to fulfill the duties of a son;
calling themselves "lowly persons" is a metaphor for the Two Vehicles who do not resolve upon the Great Mind.
He has settled for himself a minor path. Because he dwells in that which he ought not to dwell, he is compared to one who "still" [does so].
The phrase "for this reason" should be understood as connecting what precedes with what follows. The Vaipulya sūtras first correspond to the Āgamas and later correspond to the Prajñāpāramitā;
therefore, he is compared to one who, for twenty years, was constantly made to remove refuse, so that [the father] would know his son’s inferior resolve and his delight in menial tasks.

He constantly causes the filth and impurities to be cleansed and removed, so that they do not accumulate again. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s knowledge that those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) take pleasure in minor practices;
he constantly causes them to purify and treat their views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), so that they do not arise again.

"After this time" is a metaphor for the end of the Vaipulya period and the beginning of the Prajñāpāramitā period. At this time, the followers of the two vehicles come to embody faith in the Buddha and may return [to him].

He can rely [on this] and has no further need for other seeking. The Buddha likewise trusts the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) in body and mind; they are capable of being taught and admonished, and he still hopes they will proceed forward.

Therefore, it is metaphorically said that because their minds trust one another in essence, there is no difficulty in entering or exiting—just as at times one might temporarily enter one's father's house.
Sometimes he leaves the grass hut; this is a metaphor for how those of the Two Vehicles sometimes meet with the Mahāyāna. Sometimes they follow their minor path and accept rebukes.
When meeting together and hearing the Great [Vehicle], they do not regard it as strange; when accepting rebukes while remaining in the minor [vehicle], they do not regard it as shameful.
Therefore, he again uses the metaphor of "absence of difficulty. One who has no difficulty does not consider coming and going to be a matter of concern. This is because...
Coming and going are not taken as a matter of concern; one does not envy the father’s mansion, nor does one abandon the thatched hut. Thus, what one dwells in remains in its original place.

This is a metaphor for the Two Vehicles who, upon hearing the Great [Vehicle], do not differ from it in their response: they do not envy the Buddha Vehicle, they do not feel shame when rebuked, and they do not abandon the Small Path.
Therefore, what they abide in remains within the provisional fruit. This is because the Vaipulya (fangděng) is considered a common assembly for the Three Vehicles. Thus [it is said].
Thus it is said. △ Second, the metaphor for the Buddha’s command to propagate the teaching:
"At that time, the World-Honored One [said], 'The elder is ill... you should apply yourself with diligence and ensure nothing is lost.'"

The initial parable extends up to the *Prajñāpāramitā* period. Since the Tathāgata had dwelt in the world for a long time, the assembly became arrogant and self-indulgent, pressing the Buddha to relinquish his response to the world;
therefore, he was likened to an elder who is ill. Following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he turned the wheel at the Twin Trees.

Therefore, he was likened to one whose death would soon be imminent. [Question: Before the Buddha had announced his extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), how could he suddenly be likened to one whose death would soon be imminent?

[The questioner] asks: "In the light, eighteen thousand Buddhas all manifest the signs of parinirvāṇa. Mañjuśrī also cited the example of Dīpaṃkara, who likewise performed the ritual of proclaiming his extinction. Since those Buddhas were thus, how could the present Buddha alone be otherwise? Furthermore, human life undergoes the successive shifts of the four marks [of existence]; meeting must inevitably lead to separation.

Thus, although he has not yet proclaimed his extinction, it may still be inferred and spoken of. [The Buddha] concludes his discourse and, through metaphor, formally commands the transmission of the teaching:
"I now possess much gold, silver, and precious jewels" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). The merits of the Buddha-ground...
Virtue is embodied within wisdom and its function manifests externally; therefore, it is likened to a granary overflowing with stores. Regarding the phrase "the amount therein":
"amount" (duōshǎo) means "how much" (ruògān). Since there is a certain amount, that which should be taken from it to give to others [is likewise determined].
One must not fail to examine this with clarity; therefore, it is taught that one should know it all. This is illustrated by the fact that the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom are limitless.
All those who should be instructed as bodhisattvas are individually entrusted to the followers of the two vehicles, so that they may take them up clearly and remember them.
It must be that the Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas is entrusted to those of the Two Vehicles; this is done to foster in them the aspiration for the Great Vehicle.
Thus, it is said, "My mind toward you is such as this. Within this metaphor, "my mind" refers to the father’s expectation of the son.
"One should embody this meaning" means that since the father already expects this of the son, the son should internalize the father’s heart and regard it as his own concern.

The analogy is that since the Buddha expects them to aspire to the Great [Vehicle], those of the Two Vehicles should immediately internalize the Buddha’s intent, turning their limited minds toward the Great.
Thus, the meaning of the phrase "to be no different from me and you" can be understood as an inquiry that initiates this point. Now, "I and you are indeed not different."
"The father's wealth is the son's wealth" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata showing that the merits of the Buddha-ground belong to each [son] individually.
Since these belong to each individually, one must also properly protect and maintain them so as not to let them be severed.

Therefore, it is metaphorically said that one should apply diligent effort so as not to let them leak away or be lost. Judging from this single section, it is evident that the *Lotus Sūtra* is not merely a record of the beginning.
When one attains Buddhahood, it is precisely at the time of entrusting the wealth of Prajñā that one receives the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

Because the time has not yet arrived, one is unable to have self-confidence; thus, one merely considers the teachings on the Bodhisattva-dharma to be the very manifestation of the Tathāgata, which is revealed point by point.
The followers of the Two Vehicles have missed the mark at every turn. △ Third, the metaphor of accepting the command but not taking [the treasure]:
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instruction (until) his inferior mind had still not been abandoned.

"Receiving the instructions and so forth" serves as a metaphor for the followers of the Two Vehicles hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and fully comprehending the merits of the Buddha-ground, yet having no desire for even a single meal;
this metaphor illustrates that although the followers of the Two Vehicles have received the instructions, they do not give rise to a single thought of delight.

Since they lack such delight, the fruit of partial truth has not shifted, and their resolve to remain entangled in emptiness is not easily changed; therefore, it is metaphorically described as "remaining as before."

The original place; the lower mind has not yet been relinquished. This concludes the analogy of establishing the provisional from the ultimate. △ Second, the analogy of returning the provisional to the ultimate, in three parts:

first, the analogy of the time having arrived and the faculties being matured; second, the analogy of the equal bestowing of the One Vehicle; third, the analogy of hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit.
First (this summarizes the meaning from the "Parable of the Burning House," namely: at that time, the elder saw that his sons had safely emerged).

After a short while had passed, the father knew that his sons' minds had gradually become open and settled, that they had achieved great aspirations, and that they now despised their former inclinations.

“World-Honored One, because of these three kinds of suffering, we have been deluded and ignorant, taking pleasure in and clinging to the Lesser Dharma.

At the time of transformation and decay, it leads to sorrow and suffering. Third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which arises from neutral sensations (*adukkham-asukha-vedanā*);

"Having attained this, the mind is filled with great joy... [it] shall have a share of the Tathāgata’s treasure-store of knowledge and vision.

Regarding "having attained this": it means that having already attained nirvāṇa through the *āgama*, when compared to previously following heterodox paths where one practiced in vain without gain, the difference is more than a hundredfold; therefore, one rejoices greatly and feels self-sufficient.

This concludes the section on "From the Real, the Expedient is Established. II. Reconciling the Expedient with the Real (in three parts). First: Time.
When their faculties have matured, [the Buddha] bestows the One Vehicle upon them in two ways: first, by hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit;
second, by directly conferring it. Regarding the first: "Now we finally know that the World-Honored One, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom... the Buddha then preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for me."
Now, referring to the beginning of the sutra, it is as stated in the parable: "After a short time had passed.

It says that on the occasion of the *Prajñāpāramitā* assembly, the Tathāgata merely directed the teaching toward the bodhisattvas, appearing as if he were deeply withholding [the truth] from those like us. Now, however, our faculties have matured.
Only now do we realize that the Buddha has no stinginess; this is what is meant by the metaphorical phrase, "gradually becoming unimpeded and at ease.
The following section investigates and explains the meaning of knowing that the Buddha is without stinginess. It says:

"At the beginning of this present sutra, when we heard the Buddha extol his wisdom—which reveals the provisional as the ultimate—we reflected back upon ourselves and realized that we have truly been the Buddha’s sons all along. However..."
"We were inclined toward and delighted in the lesser Dharma; therefore, you merely directed us to teach others and did not immediately explain the Great [Dharma] to us.
Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma] in the past, the Buddha would have directly explained it to us. From this, we know the Buddha."
"I have no stinginess. This corresponds to the preceding metaphor. "Having accomplished a great resolve" refers to the meaning of disparaging one's former mind.
△ Second, the equal bestowal of the One Vehicle:
Within this sutra, it is said that there is only the One Vehicle (up to the point where it says), yet in reality, the Buddha teaches and transforms beings through the Mahāyāna.

Building upon the previous point that the Buddha is without parsimony, and because the faculties of the two vehicles have now matured, the Tathāgata, within this sutra, teaches only the One Vehicle through both doctrine and parable. This accords with the preceding metaphor:
"Whatever wealth and property I possess is all yours; what was previously brought in and spent out is known by you alone. Even in the parable, it is thus.

There are many texts; the Dharma follows brevity. Regarding the passage beginning with "And in the past," it appears that the four sons, through their present realization, fulfilled the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras—which had previously been incomplete—by means of the *Vaipulya*.

The intention of the four sons was this: when viewed from the perspective of the present teaching of the One Vehicle, it is not merely a case of the *Prajñāpāramitā* being transmitted as an instruction;
rather, it is the Buddha who, by the power of skillful means, has preached the wisdom of the Tathāgata for them.
He then proceeded to disparage the śrāvakas before the Bodhisattvas, likening them to the lame, the turtles, and the crippled donkeys;

he reviled those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle as being withered sprouts and rotten seeds. According to the Buddha’s original intent, this was truly meant to stimulate us and was also a means of teaching through the Mahāyāna.
As for what was said previously—that he "abandoned" [the śrāvakas]—this was not a true abandonment, just as the Tathāgata does not [truly abandon anyone].
This is merely my humble instruction. △ Third, the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma:
"Therefore, we say that although originally there was no mind... [up to] ...all that ought to be attained has already been attained."
Therefore, these two characters universally承接 (receive and continue) the preceding meaning.
That is to say, because this Āgama is self-sufficient and Prajñā does not delight in it, we stated in the previous analogy that fundamentally there was no mind seeking anything.
This is taking the text of the analogy as the text of the application (*upanaya*). Furthermore, because within this sūtra only one [truth] is taught...
Because one mounts it, it may now be called the great treasure of the Dharma King, arriving spontaneously.

This constitutes both the text of the application (*yōga*) and the text of the metaphor (*upamāna*). The final two lines express one's own joy at having obtained such a marvel; they correspond to the preceding metaphor.
Upon hearing these words from his father, he was immediately filled with great joy, attaining a meaning such as he had never experienced before. The prose section concludes.

△ Second, the two verses that explain the metaphors through illustration. First, one verse on the metaphor of sentient beings’ capacity for resonance;
second, one verse on the metaphor of the Tathāgata’s transformative response. The first (briefly explained).
For example, it is like a young boy who, being immature and ignorant, wanders through various countries for more than fifty years.
The phrase "for more than fifty years" also serves as a metaphor for the days spent practicing the Hinayana. This corresponds to what is described in the long prose version:
"Racing about in the four directions to seek food and clothing, he gradually traveled on until he encountered his own native land. II. Verse on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation and Response.

There are two metaphors. The first verse is the metaphor of manifesting expedient means from the ultimate reality (*tattva*). The second verse is the metaphor of returning to the ultimate reality after having gathered the expedient means. The first of these two has two parts: the first verse is the metaphor of not attaining [the goal] despite relying on the ultimate reality;

the second verse is the metaphor of concealing the ultimate reality to manifest expedient means. The first of these two has three parts: the first verse is the metaphor of the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way.

The second verse is the metaphor of contemplating for twenty-one days. The third verse is the metaphor of forming a thought yet having no calculated plan. The fourth verse is the metaphor of the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way.

The first [section] consists of two verses on the analogy of the father’s deep concern for his children; the second consists of three verses on the analogy of the discord between the capacities of beings and the teaching.
Regarding the first: "His father, filled with anxiety, searched in the four directions... (until)... because of various circumstances, many people were coming and going."
The first analogy illustrates the generation of the path to enlightenment (extensive verse). Sentient beings fall away from the great resolve;

fearing they would lose their roots of goodness and descend into suffering, the Buddha uses the metaphor of a father’s anxious concern. As for "searching in all four directions," in terms of location, this refers to every single place.

Seeking those of great capacity, he employs the Four Noble Truths as the Dharma to guide them; searching for those with whom he has a karmic affinity, when he grows weary, they first come to take refuge in him.
This is like the Tathāgata, who, failing to find those of great capacity, first prepares his own path.

This verse explains the prose section regarding the meaning of "the father coming first. As for "stopping suddenly at a single city," it means that having reached the halfway point, he again searches [for others].
He obtained [a son] and suddenly stopped, dwelling temporarily in a city. This is a metaphor for when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path;
again seeking a person of great capacity (mahā-yogya), he could not find one, so he suddenly relied upon the Middle Way and manifested birth within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

This verse summarizes the prose section concerning the meaning of failing to find a son and halting in a city. "Building a house" refers to the thorough cultivation of new karma. This is the metaphor.
After the Tathāgata manifested birth, he again cultivated the causes to bring about the fruit. Once the fruit was attained, his realm of self-enjoyment is not shared with those of the two vehicles;

therefore, it is likened to his own enjoyment of the five desires. His family being "immensely wealthy" (jùfù) is a metaphor for the complete perfection of all conditions upon the attainment of the fruit.
"Immensely" (jù) means great. The phrase "many various... and below is a brief verse illustrating the merits of the Buddha-ground.

The mention of *śaṅkha* (conch) and *musāragalva* (agate) is expanded, while *pravāḍa* (coral), *aśmagarbha* (amber), and *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli), as well as the description of overflowing treasuries, are omitted.
This is because the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) are immeasurable and boundless; they appear and disappear, open and close, such that there is neither what can be nor what cannot be.

Therefore, the metaphors employed are likewise not uniform. Regarding the section on elephants and horses: these metaphorically represent the retinue and companions who follow the Dharma. This further consists of two parts.
Meaning. First, the verse properly summarizes the prose. From "elephants and horses" up to "fields and estates," these serve as metaphors for the dharma-gates of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

These are expanded beyond the prose; the addition of "litters, carriages, fields, and estates" reflects the fact that the distinctions among the dharma-gates of the various stages are not uniform, and thus the metaphors are also applied with varying degrees of expansion and contraction.
"Servants and subjects" still metaphorically represent the bodhisattvas of the various stages. "Having no ministers or officials" refers to [the stage of] *pudgala*.

Because it is subsumed within the middle [section], the three phrases regarding entering and exiting follow the meaning of the prose (*dīrgha-paṅkti*). There is no place where this does not exist; this is the sense of "extremely many.

Regarding the phrase "ten million" (*koṭi*) and below, the verse concludes with a supplement. In the *Avataṃsaka*, the primary and attendant [elements] are layered upon one another, assisting in the unfolding of the profound transformation.

Therefore, the metaphor says "surrounded and venerated by ten million billion hosts. The "King" represents the Buddhas of the ten directions; since their Dharma-bodies are identical, [the metaphor applies].
Because their lives are intimately connected through wisdom, he uses "affectionate remembrance" as a metaphor for them.

Because the ministers and nobles represent the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who collectively assist in the Buddha’s transformation of beings and jointly praise his sublime teachings, he uses "reverent esteem" as a metaphor for them. Due to these various conditions, the multitude of those coming and going is vast;
based on the two aforementioned conditions—the King’s affection and the ministers’ esteem—he concludes by describing the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings surrounding him.
This is illustrated by the fact that the Tathāgata is both rejoiced in by all Buddhas and revered by all Bodhisattvas.
Due to these two conditions, the Buddhas transmit the lamp of the Dharma to propagate the teaching, while the Bodhisattvas act as regents for the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Whether they depart afar upon receiving an edict or return from afar in obedience to a command, the principal and their retinue are layered upon one another, inexhaustible and inexhaustible like the multitude itself.

The verse on the analogy of the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way is concluded. △ Second, the verses on the analogy of profound contemplation regarding the capacities of those to be converted, in three parts:

1. A verse on the analogy of the Buddha contemplating the striking of the capacity; 2. A verse on the analogy of the capacity arising in the Buddha-land; 3. A verse on the analogy of the capacity approaching the site of enlightenment.
The first [part] is omitted as it was already treated in an interlinear verse.
"Being wealthy and noble, they possess such great power and influence (up to: 'how shall they deal with the goods in their treasuries?').
Since they have realized the fruit of the Path and all conditions are fully prepared, they are compared to the wealthy and noble. Their merit and wisdom are revered by the assembly like a vast ocean;
their majestic radiance is brilliant and blazing like the solar orb; thus, they are compared to those possessing great power and influence.

As for the aged and decrepit, they are a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s ultimate wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), which appears temporarily in response to conditions but does not remain long in the world.
Because he cannot remain long in the world, he increasingly contemplates the need for someone to whom to transmit the Way; hence the metaphor:
"He grows ever more anxious and mindful of his son. "Night and day he thinks only of death" means that whether rising early or sleeping late, he thinks only that the time of death is approaching.
"Not long" means that the Tathāgata reflects day and night that when the conditions for his work are exhausted, he shall return to perfect nirvana.
"The foolish son has abandoned me for over fifty years" expresses the Tathāgata’s sorrow and resentment that sentient beings have fallen into ruin and forgotten their way back.
That they have fallen and forgotten their way is due to the lack of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom.
There is no one worthy of being entrusted [with the teaching]. Therefore, it is compared to the various goods within a treasury. "What should be done? What should be done?

refers to reflecting repeatedly, yet not knowing whom to entrust with it. However, since this section belongs to the summary verses (*uddāna*), it is not necessary to allocate each point one-to-one with the prose commentary.
△ Second, the verse on the simile of sentient beings being born in the Buddha-land (a retrospective verse that expands upon the meaning).
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing (until) he gradually traveled and arrived at the city where his father resided.
Since this belongs to the subsequent verse, the two characters "at that time" (爾時) should not be construed as immediately following the preceding text;

rather, they refer to the period when his father was staying there, serving as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth within the triple world. When the Tathāgata manifests birth within the triple world, he...
In previous lives, they still sought even a small measure of concentration and wisdom within the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; thus, this is likened to seeking food and clothing.

Alternatively, attaining the stages of entering the stream (*srotāpanna-pratipannaka*) and so forth is like traveling from one village to another, while attaining the fruits of the stream-enterer and so forth is like traveling from one country to another.
This verse explains the meaning of the prose passage concerning wandering through various settlements and passing through countries and towns. There is...

At that time, he practices with diligence without ceasing. He attains a small measure of concentration and wisdom; yet, as if having gained something, there are times when, encountering adverse conditions, he regresses and loses it, completely discarding his previous efforts.
Alternatively, as if gaining nothing at all, he lacks the merit to sustain himself and becomes emaciated from hunger.
He is constantly entangled by the habitual tendencies of afflictions, like sores and scabs breaking out on his body. These successive stages serve as metaphors for [the various levels of practice].
"Past lives" (宿世) refers to advancing step by step. Advancing step by step, one follows the Buddha’s descent into birth to become a sentient being ready for deliverance;

thus, it is metaphorically described as "reaching the city where the father resides. This verse corresponds to the prose section, carrying the meaning: "he eventually arrived at the city where his father was staying.
