The Instructional Parable. First (a brief verse summarizing the meaning):
At that time, the householder, within his gate... [down to] ...recorded the assets being brought in and sent out in written contracts and ledgers.
The Buddha, through the power of his wisdom and abandonment, realizes and enters the one true Dharma-realm;

thus it is metaphorically said that within its gate, he spreads true compassion according to the Dharma-realm, leaving no birth unsheltered. Thus it is metaphorically said that he unfurls a great jeweled canopy.
Relying on the Dharma-realm, he gives rise to supreme wisdom, whereby no obstacle remains unsubdued; thus it is metaphorically said that he occupies the lion throne. By means of this...
The "sons" signify the meaning of fearlessness. As for the "retinue," they are the long-haired *brāhmaṇas*, *kṣatriyas*, and householders;

because they have formed kinship by receiving benefits, they are called the "retinue. This is a metaphor for the lords of the three worlds, each realizing a single virtue of Vairocana and thus collectively becoming the retinue of the Tathāgata’s *dharmatā*. The "various people" are the officials and commoners of the long passages.

The servants and attendants may be understood according to the prose section of the sūtra. As for those who calculate gold, silver, and precious objects, these are metaphors for the various bodhisattvas who discern the virtues of the Buddha.
By discerning the Buddha’s virtues, they bestow the Dharma and thereby accomplish benefit; thus the metaphor says: "They disburse and receive property, bestowing the Dharma to accomplish benefit.
Because they rely on causes to record the fruits [of their actions], the metaphor says: "They record them in deeds and contracts (*śrāva*). Contract...

"Commentary" refers to works such as formal contracts; however, since this section belongs to the category of "Brief Verses on the Meaning of the Compact," it need not be strictly correlated [with the preceding prose].
△ Second, the verse illustrating how the capacity of the recipient contradicts the teaching.
The impoverished son sees his father as wealthy, noble, and majestic... (up to) he asks about a poor neighborhood, wishing to go there to work for hire.
"Wealthy, noble, and majestic" refers to the preceding verse; he possesses great power and influence.

His wealth and nobility arise from his power, and his power stems from his majesty—these constitute two phrases. This corresponds to the preceding thought: "This might be a king, or perhaps a prince."
The two lines beginning with "startled and terrified" (*jīngbù*) versify the preceding [passage]: "he harbored fear and regret for having come here.
The six lines beginning with "concealing himself" (*fùzì*) versify the preceding [passage]: "if he were to stay here long, he might be subjected to oppression," up to "he fled in haste.
The above [sections] correspond to the prose (*chángxíng*). The final two lines have no text in the prose; they are supplemented by the verse (*jiéyǒng*) to illustrate that.
He requests instruction from a heterodox school, desiring to practice the way of a divergent path. The verse on the parable of the three-week contemplation concludes.

△ Second, the verse on the parable of forming thoughts without a plan (following the prose section, which is divided into three parts; here, the "temporary rest" of the great transformation is omitted, and the remaining two are also abbreviated, as they belong to the abbreviated verses).
Part Two: 1. A verse on the parable of the teaching not conforming to the capacity; 2. A verse on the parable of the capacity not conforming to the teaching. First:
At that time, the elder was on the lion throne... [he] immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him.
"To recognize him silently" means to perceive with the mind without speaking with the mouth; it is analogous to the Tathāgata at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Although this does not involve the disclosure of the origin and manifestation of the fundamental [nature], it is already recognized as the fundamental [nature] for those who are to be transformed; the rest is the same as the prose section.
The Dharma should also be understood accordingly. However, in the prose section there is further the phrase: "At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him."
The verse is merely an abridgment. △ Second, the verse on the metaphor of the teaching not meeting the capacity:
"The impoverished son was startled and cried out; bewildered and distressed, he fell to the ground... (up to) 'Of what use are these clothes and food to bring me to such a state?'"

The first line of the verse summarizes the preceding account of the impoverished son’s alarm and distress, his cries of lamentation, and his calling out; these meanings should likewise be understood by analogy.

The phrase "confused and fainting, he falls to the ground" serves as a metaphor for the destruction of the Dharma and the loss of goodness. The section beginning with "This man... explains the reason for his confusion and fainting:
the impoverished son thinks to himself, "Observing this man’s violent persistence toward me, it is certain that I shall be put to death. He reflects on his original arrival...
"For the sake of seeking a mere pittance of food and clothing, I reflect upon it even now: what use was there in seeking such trifles that they led me to this point of certain death?
My remorse has reached such a state that, overcome by confusion and distress, I have fallen to the ground.

This is a metaphor for those of limited capacity; having been sustained by the Great Dharma, they fear they will lack the power to enter the marketplace and thus lose their roots of goodness. From themselves—
I reflect that when I first came to the site of enlightenment, my original intent was merely to seek a small measure of concentration and wisdom. Yet, as I ponder this further, I ask myself:
why must I have come to such a place—a ground where one loses one's roots of goodness? When I think of this, I cannot help but feel that I have violated the Dharma.
Thus, the good [qualities] are lost. In the prose (long xing), the reason is presented first and the state of confusion and distress is explained afterwards;

in the verse (gē sòng), the state of confusion and distress is explained first and the reason is presented afterwards. This is merely a variation in literary style, yet the underlying meaning remains no different.
Furthermore, regarding the "poor son" (qióng zǐ), the prose includes further phrases such as "I have not offended you," which are now omitted for brevity.

The verse on the analogy of not obtaining [the fruit] from reality concludes. △ Second, the two verses on the analogy of concealing the real and manifesting the provisional. First, the verse on the analogy of the *āgama* guarantee.
Second, the verse on the analogy of the *prajñā* transmission. The first [section] has three parts: first, the verse on the analogy of the provisional person’s gathering and transforming;
second, the verse on the analogy of the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma; third, the verse on the analogy of guaranteeing the minor fruits. The first [part]:
The elder knows his son is foolish and narrow-minded (up to) "to remove filth and purify the rooms.

This initial metaphor illustrates the Buddha’s instruction to the provisional person (the verse on the meaning). "The elder knows his son" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata observing the capacities [of beings] with precision.

"Foolish and narrow-minded" is a metaphor for those of small capacity who lack correct knowledge and vision. Lacking correct knowledge and vision, they do not understand the profundity of the One Vehicle.
As for the meaning: since he did not know his original teacher, he was compared to one who does not believe my words and does not believe that this person is his father.
Regarding "the other person," Da Cheng says: these are the two individuals mentioned. What is currently heard as the *yāna* of conditions (*pratyaya-yāna*) is merely a remnant of the Mahāyāna.

"One with a missing eye" refers to one who has a single eye that is squinting and small; this is a metaphor for wisdom that indicates partiality and deviation. "The short and ugly" refers to being short, stunted, and base;
this is a metaphor for the body indicating its segmented nature. Since these segments are impermanent and lack adornment, the short and ugly are used as a metaphor for them.
The remainder is the same as the prose section. Only the transitions between the expanded and abbreviated versions differ slightly; there is no need for exhaustive detail.

Regarding the phrase "I shall double your price," this should have been present according to the prose version as a metaphor for receiving the command to gather and transform [sentient beings]. It may have been omitted by error during the transcription, and it would be excellent to supplement it when lecturing.
Regarding the section on the "poor son," this is a metaphor based on the Buddha’s response to the needs of those to be transformed (a summary verse). He accords with their inclinations and wishes.
Because he receives transformation according to [the disciples' capacities], he is likened to one who joyfully follows those who come.

Because he relies on the teaching to sever delusions and purify all defiled minds, he is likened to one who removes filth to clean the house; this corresponds to what is said in the prose: "First taking the price, and then immediately removing the filth.
The meaning of the father’s pity and wonder is omitted in the verse for brevity. △ Second, the verse on the metaphor of the Buddha turning the wheel of Dharma.
Two [verses]. One verse first shows the metaphors for suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); two verses follow, providing the metaphors for the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding the first: "The elder constantly saw his son from the window... [and] used skillful means to approach him and tell him to work diligently."

The first analogy concerns the turning of the light to observe the capacities of sentient beings (a verse on the meaning). "Foolish and inferior" is a metaphor for having small wisdom and dull faculties.
Having small wisdom leads to timidity in hearing the Great Dharma; having dull faculties leads to the aspiration to practice minor paths. Therefore, it is compared to taking pleasure in base matters.

While the prose commentary mentions only "seeing the son," the present text adds "thinking of the son. This is because one necessarily thinks of what one sees; thus, it serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s observation.

The sentient being will inevitably give rise to compassion. Thereupon, [the text] provides a metaphor for concealing superiority and manifesting inferiority (a summarized verse). The initial passage regarding "removing the neck-ornament" is missing; this is because the metaphor for concealing superiority has been omitted.
Although the metaphor for manifesting inferiority—such as "wearing tattered clothes"—is preserved, the wording is likewise abbreviated.

Following "expedient means," there is a metaphor for correctly demonstrating suffering and its origin (a summarized verse). The phrase "expedient means" summarizes the preceding section on employing expedient means.
Therefore, he is able to approach his son; "approach" (*fu*) here means to draw near. He speaks these words and phrases, praising those who labor:
"Work diligently and do not cease. Although the sequence of the phrasing differs, the meaning may be understood by referring to the prose (*dīrgha-pada*).
△ Second, the verse following the parable of bestowing the path and cessation (abbreviated verse).
"Having increased your wages and provided oil for anointing your feet... [up to] ...with such harsh words as 'you must work diligently.

The phrase "having increased your wages" is a metaphorical teaching intended to inspire a longing for cessation (*nirodha*). The "providing of oil for anointing the feet" and so forth are metaphors for the teaching on the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*).

Regarding the "oil for anointing the feet," it specifically serves as a metaphor for the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), because the faculties and powers are established within all paths.
This category can prevent the Path from being cut short or obstructed; it is like applying oil to the feet so that they do not become chapped and cracked.
"Food and drink" refers to long-grained rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and so forth; collectively, these serve as metaphors for the three trainings of the outflows (anāsrava-śikṣā).

They also encompass the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). "Straw mats" and "rush mats"—these two are both used for sitting.
The bedding represents the four dhyānas, the nine meditative attainments (*navasamāpatti*), and so forth; these constitute the sphere of abiding for those of the Hīnayāna.

The phrase "such as this" refers to what has been explained above. The aforementioned instructions to work diligently, the demonstration of increased value, and the permission to use foot-unguents and the like are all the words of the elder’s earnest exhortations. These earnest exhortations are nothing other than his hope [that the son will accept].
Because of his diligent labor, it is said, "You should work diligently. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s own earnest instructions;
he teaches that one should practice with vigor. This reiterates the meaning of the preceding prose: "You should always do this; do not go elsewhere."
The verse on the parable of the Buddha turning the Wheel of Dharma concludes. △ Third, the verse on the parable of the assurance of attaining the lesser fruits (abridged verse).
Furthermore, with gentle words: "If you are like my own children..."
In accordance with those of lesser capacity, provisional fruits are established; therefore, they are illustrated by soft words.
"If" (若) means "just as" (猶), in the sense of "like a son," as seen in the prose section. This concludes the illustration of the *Āgama* as a guarantee. II.
Verse on the Illustration of the Transmission of the Prajñāpāramitā (The prose is divided into three parts; the verses are abbreviated and do not follow the same subdivisions).
The elder possesses wisdom and gradually causes [the sons] to enter and exit; [this continues until they] reflect upon their own poverty, thinking, "I have no such things.
In the first parable, the *vaipulya* sūtras are used. The elder possessing wisdom is a metaphor for the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

"Gradually causing them to enter and exit" means that upon entering, they perceive the father and attend to his household affairs; upon exiting, they continue to clear away various filth. This is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*).
At times he advances to hear the Great Dharma; at times he retreats to maintain the practices of the Small [Vehicle].
This verse explains the prose passage regarding the meaning of "constantly making him remove filth" for twenty years. It refers to the period that has passed.

After these twenty years have elapsed—namely, the time when the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings intersect—this verse explains the prose passage regarding the meaning of "after this has passed. He then takes charge of the household affairs.
After twenty years, their father-son bond will have reached full harmony; at times they will act as one with the father, managing the affairs of the household.

This is analogous to how, after the period of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sutras, the conditions between teacher and disciple ripen, and at times they act as one with the Buddha, assisting in the propagation of the Dharma transformation of the Mahāyāna.
This verse corresponds to the prose section. "The mind's characteristics are fundamentally trustworthy" means that there is no difficulty in entering or emerging [from the state].
The remaining text before and after this is omitted from the verse for brevity. "Showing him" refers to the Buddha’s command to propagate the teaching;

following the preceding passage where those of the two vehicles have already joined the Buddha in promoting the great transformation, the Buddha then reveals the merits of the Buddha-ground to them. Therefore, the metaphor says: "showing him."

"Gold, silver, pearls, and crystal"—this verse from the prose section means that he says to the impoverished son: "I now possess much gold, silver, and precious jewels, and my storehouses are overflowing," and so forth.
Although he displays the merits of the Buddha-ground, he merely causes the bodhisattvas to transmit the teaching and does not yet grant them the attainment of Buddhahood;
therefore, the metaphor states: "All matters of income and expenditure are made to be carried out [by them]."

"Know it. Regarding the phrase "cause [them] to know," this does not mean immediate delivery. It means that you must fully understand the meaning of what is to be taken and given within the prose commentary of this verse, including its various details.
"Still remaining outside" is a metaphor for receiving the command but not yet taking [the fruit];

it refers to the wisdom and abandonment of the Hīnayāna, which still remain provisional and expedient. Therefore, the metaphor says "still remaining outside the gate," and is not compared to the Tathāgata, who is inside the gate.
This serves as a metaphor. The truth of partial emptiness merely covers the birth-and-death of the limited stage; therefore, the metaphor says, "dwelling in a thatched hut.
A "thatched hut" is a hut made by binding grass together to provide a slight shelter from wind and rain; it is not like the Tathāgata’s use of the "great jeweled canopy" as a metaphor.
This verse corresponds to the prose section, yet its meaning is that the place of residence remains in its original location. [He] reflects within himself:
The impoverished son thought to himself: "As for the work of a pauper, it is the task of removing filth. For the task of removing filth, one is only worthy of receiving a day’s wage.
How could gold, silver, and precious jewels rightfully belong to me? Therefore, he said, 'I have no such things.

This is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who know only to sever and eliminate the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and realize the small fruit; as for the merits of the Buddha-ground, [they are beyond them].
"Awakening has no parts. This verse corresponds to the prose commentary (*dīrgha-pada*). It also implies the meaning that even the inferior mind has not yet been abandoned.

According to the prose, there is further content above this: namely, the meanings of receiving instructions and taking charge of the various objects, which are also omitted from the verse for brevity.
The analogy of establishing the provisional based on the real is concluded. △ Second, the three-part analogy of returning the provisional to the real: First, the verse.

The first [section] consists of three verses on the parable of the time having arrived and the capacity being matured; the second consists of two verses on the parable of bestowing the One Vehicle equally; and the third consists of three verses on the parable of obtaining benefit upon hearing the Dharma.
Regarding the first (the brief verses):
the father knew that his son’s mind had gradually become expansive.
At the beginning of this section of the prose commentary, there was previously a metaphor regarding the passage of a short time; now there should likewise be one.

This is because it is the beginning of the *Lotus Sūtra*, not a previous period. Since the teaching has reached its destination and the capacities of the disciples have matured—the great capacity having slightly stirred and the inferior capacity having slightly diminished—the metaphor states: "The father knows his son’s mind" and "gradually becomes vast. "Vast" here means far-reaching.
Being distant from it, they do not abide in the minor vehicles; being great, they possess the aspiration for the Buddha-vehicle.

This is also due to the power of the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) in its censure and the *Prajñāpāramitā* (bōrě) in its purging. Therefore, it is metaphorically said that they have "gradually" [attained it]. This refers to what is stated in the prose:
"Having accomplished the great aspiration, they despise their former minds. II. Verses on the Parable of Bestowing the One Vehicle Equally (Abridged Verses).
When he wished to bestow his wealth and possessions, he immediately gathered his kinsmen (and so forth) and entrusted them all to him, allowing him to use them as he pleased.
The initial metaphor of assembling the multitude to bear witness signifies that the son’s mind has already become vast and expansive.

Furthermore, the realization that it is near the time of his own end and his desire to bestow his wealth signify that the faculties and capacities of sentient beings have already matured, and that the Tathāgata’s work of transformation is about to be completed, as he wishes to transmit [the teaching].
The Buddha’s prediction was intended to ensure that this Way would continue. The remainder follows the prose section. Below this, the parable reveals the trace to manifest the fundamental.
Within the text, the phrase "the son who has come" serves as a general metaphor for the Āgama, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras taken together.

In the Āgamas, the superior is concealed and the inferior is manifested, as the Buddha condescends to those of lesser capacity; this is like the first twenty years. In the Vaipulya sūtras, both the Great and the Small Vehicles are discussed together, with earlier and later teachings following one another;
this is like the [period] from the twentieth year onward. In the Prajñāpāramitā, the teaching was transmitted by the Buddha’s disciples, through which they secretly received great benefit;

this is like the remainder of the twentieth year. Now, having reached the time of the bestowal of predictions in the Lotus Sūtra, it is therefore metaphorically said: "Twenty years have already passed."
This refers to more than twenty years having already passed. Regarding "wandering everywhere in search," in terms of place, it means seeking those of great capacity in every location;
in terms of the Dharma, it means using the Four Noble Truths to guide and lead, searching for those with whom there is a karmic affinity. As the *Changxun* (Long Practice) says:
"Filled with anxiety, he searches for him. This refers to the previous passage stating that he "searched in all four directions," which carries this same meaning.

"He has finally come here" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata manifesting birth within the triple world; it corresponds to the previous passage stating, "His father had previously arrived and was staying in a certain city.

The section beginning with "All those who are mine... is a metaphor for bestowing upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). The "house" metaphor encompasses both the treasure storehouse and the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The merit thus obtained—wherein the term "people" (rénmín) encompasses both the common folk and their servants—is a metaphor for humans, devas, and all the worthy sages (*ārya*).

Because the Tathāgata bestows it upon them and grants them predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), it is said to be "entrusted entirely to you. This is the meaning of the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* as cited in the long prose section.

"At will" (*zì*) means "according to one's inclination," referring to the realization of the merits of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) according to one's own resolve. [This applies to] the worthies of the Three Vehicles.
"Sages, you may deliver [beings] at will; you may serve the various devas at will; you may issue commands at will. All these shall come forth into the world for their enjoyment.
Therefore, they are illustrated by the metaphor of being used as one pleases. △ Third, the verse on the metaphor of obtaining benefit from hearing the Dharma (a verse of meaning).
"Son, consider that in the past you were poor and your aspirations were base and inferior—[up to the point where] you experienced great joy at having attained what you had never before possessed.
Had you been poor, you would not have sought a mansion; had your aspirations been base, you would have had no hope for precious treasures.
Yet, suddenly obtaining such great wealth, how could you not feel immense joy, as if you had acquired something never before seen? Furthermore, within this, there are two kinds of wealth..."

The character [for "treasure"] resembles that for "precious jewels. It should be changed to the two characters for "people" (rénmín), so as to correspond with the preceding section on "houses, people, and property" (shèzhái rénmín).
Furthermore, "precious jewels" may refer to the seven treasures and eight riches, while "property" (cáiwù) refers to money and material goods.
In general, because the merits of the Buddha-ground are immeasurable and boundless, they may be expanded or condensed at will within these metaphors:

sometimes it is simply called a "granary" or a "treasury"; sometimes it includes both "precious jewels"; sometimes it further includes "wealth and goods"; and sometimes it specifies "gold, silver, lapis lazuli," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is entirely acceptable to refer to this collectively as the "Treasury of Jewels. The explanation by means of parables has now concluded.

△ Third, the verses that apply the Dharma to the specific case (the prose section is divided into two parts; here, the response of sentient beings' faculties is missing, and only the Tathāgata’s transformative response is versified, likewise based solely on the underlying meaning).

This is divided into two sections: first, verses on the provisional from the real; second, verses on returning the provisional to the real. The first of these has two parts: first, the direct versification of the prose; second, the supplementary verses.
Revealing the delusion: the first two [sections]. One verse concerns failing to attain the reality; two verses concern concealing the real and establishing the provisional. Regarding the first:
"The Buddha likewise knew that I delighted in the small [vehicle], and never spoke the words: 'You shall become a Buddha.'"

The first sentence provides a general summary by way of an allegory. It states that the Tathāgata, in order to connect with past conditions, initially established provisional fruits through skillful means, and finally directly revealed the Buddha-vehicle.
This is exactly like an elder who, in order to entice his children, first writes characters and names them, and finally hands over the family estate.
Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha is also like this. Regarding the passage beginning with "He knows me," this is the specific meaning of the current section. It states:
At the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Tathāgata, knowing that we delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, likewise temporarily suspended his Great Transformation;
he did not yet say, "You shall become Buddhas. This is as it is said: "This person is not needed; do not force him to come. The long prose section states:
"Because of the three sufferings, we even came to delight in and cling to the Lesser Dharma"; this refers to what is here called "knowing that we delight in the Lesser."

Although the capacities [of the audience] and the teachings emerge alternately, their convergence upon the principle is no different. △ Second, the verse on concealing the real and manifesting the provisional has two parts:
first, the verse on the guarantee of the Āgamas; second, the verse on the turning of the teaching in the Prajñāpāramitā. Regarding the first:
It is said that we have attained all the outflows-free states (*anāsrava*) and have become disciples of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) śrāvakas.

Since the *Avataṃsaka* does not yet speak of becoming a Buddha, one must necessarily wait for the gradual guidance of the Āgamas; thus it says, "it is said. "It is said" refers to what was taught during the period of the Āgamas.

Because they have severed the accumulation [of suffering] (*samudaya*) and departed from suffering (*duḥkha*), it says, "they have attained all the outflows-free states. Because they have cultivated the path (*mārga*) and realized cessation (*nirodha*).

Therefore, it is said that they have "accomplished the Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*). Because he gave his son the name "Maker of Syllables" (*Akṣarapraṇetṛ*), he became a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

The prose section refers to the initial stage of practice; thus it says, "It causes me to contemplate and clear away the filth of conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*). This section, however, refers to those who have already attained realization;
thus it says, "And so we speak," and "We have obtained all the untainted [dharmas]" (*anāsrava*). The analogy states: "Furthermore, with gentle words... If...

"Just as my son is such. △ Second, the verse on the transmission of the Prajñāpāramitā (the prose section is divided into three; the middle scripture, the Vaipulya, is currently missing). This is divided into two parts.
The first verse concerns the Buddha’s command to transmit the teaching; the second verse concerns receiving the command but not accepting it. Regarding the first:
the Buddha commanded us, saying, "Proclaim the supreme path; those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood."
The Supreme Path is the dharma for attaining Buddhahood; those who cultivate it will perfect their merit over vast eons, and those who practice it will realize the ultimate fruit in the future.
Therefore, it is said that they "shall attain Buddhahood. This corresponds to the meaning of the gold, silver, and crystal within the parable.
The long prose section states: "The World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, speaks of the Tathāgata..."
"Wisdom" has the same meaning as in the preceding passage. △ Second, the verse on receiving the command but not taking [the offerings]:
"I, following the Buddha's teaching, act for the sake of the great bodhisattvas... (up to) ...thinking thus, I do not give rise to joy."
First, receiving the command, they shall practice accordingly; the preceding verses are spoken by us.

Furthermore, it is because of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that he reveals and expounds the meaning for the sake of all bodhisattvas. Regarding the passage beginning with "All Buddhas," the bodhisattvas obtain benefit.
These two subsequent sections contain no prose text and are supplemented by the verses. At that time, the phrase "all Buddhas" consists of auxiliary particles and refers to the original Buddha.
[This is] what was said. "All those below" [the bodhisattvas] cannot attain the secret and profound treasury.

Because they are the ones capable of receiving it, [the Buddha] spoke only for the sake of the bodhisattvas, expounding the actual reality and the most profound merits. Not being suitable vessels, these essentials were not transmitted to us;

thus, he did not preach this true essence for our sakes. However, since the Tathāgata has now commanded us to turn the teaching, how could we fail to speak? We shall do so only by means of indirect [expedient means].
Chang’s "pervasive penetration" cannot be readily grasped and accepted; to claim it is "not being taught" is precisely like asking for the city of Chang'an while standing inside the Han-yuan Hall.
As for the passage below, "the mind does not hope to attain," there are three meanings: first, citing a metaphor to provide a direct application.

This can be understood. From the phrase "We [think]... onwards, the text correctly clarifies the non-acceptance [of the path]. It follows the preceding verse to explain that they themselves lack the sense of aspiration [for further progress].
Because they have extinguished internal causes and abandoned the fruit of fragmented existence (*pariccheda-phala*), it says, "we have internally attained extinction.

Because they have realized the limited truth and abide in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it says, "they consider themselves sufficient. They merely know how to sever the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) and abandon suffering (*duḥkha*), and cultivate the path.

They realize cessation; therefore it is said, "one only understands this matter. They do not contemplate turning from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle to adorn their lands and undergo transformational birth;
therefore it is said, "there is no other matter. Because there is no other matter, if they were to hear of adorning lands and transformational birth, they would feel as if they were being imprisoned.
Therefore, it is said that there is no joy or delight at all. This refers to what was stated in the extended parable: "having no hope for even a single meal.
The following section explains the meaning of "not grasping. Building upon the preceding reason why there is no joy or delight whatsoever: why is this so?
It is because those of the Two Vehicles merely contemplate the three gates of liberation. As for the statement that "all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent," it means:

To thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without self is the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). That which is neither arising nor ceasing is without the characteristics of beginning or end;
that which is neither large nor small is without the characteristics of superiority or inferiority—this is the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

That which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) means there are no delusions to be severed; that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) means there is no reality to be realized—this is the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Reflecting in this way, one realizes that above there is no Buddha-way to be accomplished, and below there are no sentient beings to be delivered.
For this reason, one does not give rise to joy or delight. This verse summarizes the preceding prose. Yet, I did not know the true meaning of being a "Son of the Buddha.
Having finished summarizing the prose: II. Supplemental Verses Clarifying Delusion (in four parts). 1. Clarifying the Firmness of Grasping and Delusion.

Second, it reveals that cause and effect are illusory; third, it reveals the failure to repay the Buddha’s kindness; fourth, it reveals the failure to fulfill the Buddha’s intention. Regarding the first:
"For a long night, we [have been] regarding the Buddha’s wisdom... yet we ourselves have claimed that our own dharma is ultimate."
In this context, "the long night" refers to the period of the Prajñāpāramitā teachings.

Because the Prajñā was transmitted from the Buddha, yet its true essential meaning was not understood—just as one performing labor during a long night may be skillful without being aware of it—they remained unaware. It is because they were unaware [of this].
Therefore, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, they are without craving and without attachment. Because they lack craving and attachment, they do not give rise to the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle];
hence it is said that they have no further vows or aspirations. Because they lack such vows and aspirations, they do not move from their thoughts of returning to the Small [Vehicle];
hence it is said that they consider themselves to have reached the ultimate. This clearly demonstrates the meaning of firm and stubborn delusion at the time when Prajñā is manifested. △ Two.
This reveals that cause and effect are illusory.
We have practiced the dharma of emptiness throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], until we now abide in the nirvāṇa with remainder in our final body.
Here, "the long night" refers to the period of the Āgamas; for during the Āgama period, one practiced the Hīnayāna and did not know [the Mahāyāna].
The meaning of "reality" (tattva) is also like performing labor through the long night: though it be clumsy and crude, one does not realize it oneself.

Because one does not realize it oneself, one merely contemplates the principle of the selflessness of persons; therefore, it is said that one practices the dharma of emptiness. By thoroughly understanding the selflessness of persons, [one realizes reality].
There is no agent, and there is no recipient. Therefore it is said: "One attains liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the three realms.
Having been liberated from the afflictions of suffering, one does not undergo further existence; only the remaining physical substrate persists. Therefore it is said: "Abiding in the final body."
Having already dwelt in the final body, there still remains a residual basis; therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa with remainder.

One must understand that even the "nirvāṇa without remainder" of the Hīnayāna is not yet true extinction, let alone that which has a remainder. Thus, both cause and effect belong to the realm of delusion.
Ultimately, there is no basis whatsoever to rely upon. △ Third, revealing how one has failed the Buddha’s grace:
If the teachings received from the Buddha result in attaining the Way without fail, then one has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
Building upon what was stated above, they remained within the state of having a remainder [of defilements], unaware that it was illusory. They presumed that the Buddha’s teaching was merely this;
thinking, "Since we have already grasped the Buddha’s mind and attained the path to Nirvana, we have thereby repaid the Buddha’s kindness."
However, they did not know that those whom the Buddha taught were originally intended to achieve unsurpassed bodhi and would inevitably attain Buddhahood;
it was only now that they realized this was how to repay the Buddha’s kindness, and thus understood for the first time that they had previously betrayed the Buddha’s benevolence.
△ Fourth, revealing the betrayal of the Buddha’s intent.
Although we are among the sons of the Buddhas (up to) we have no aspiration or delight for this Dharma at all.
Based on the preceding [text], we say that because we have already repaid the Buddha's kindness, therefore, although we have reached the time of the Prajñāpāramitā...
Having received the Tathāgata’s command, we have preached the Dharma for the sake of the sons of the Buddha, causing them to seek the path of Buddhahood;
yet, regarding this very Dharma, we ourselves have forever lacked any aspiration or delight.

Now we realize that the Buddha’s command to turn the wheel of teaching was precisely intended to awaken within us a heart of aspiration and delight. We who formerly betrayed the Buddha’s intention have only now begun to understand. (Verse)
From the conclusion of the section on the exercise of skillful means. △ Second, the verse on returning the provisional to the real, in two parts: first, the direct versification of the prose;
second, the supplementary verse clarifying the realization. First:
"The Teacher, seeing that [the sons] had abandoned him, observed my mind... [until] like that impoverished son who obtained immeasurable treasure."
First, regarding the occasion for the verse: when the time had arrived and the faculties were matured, [the Buddha] bestowed the One Vehicle equally.
Furthermore, there are two meanings. First, following the previous metaphor: because we lacked aspiration and delight, the Guide abandoned us. This was because the Tathāgata...

He observes my own mind and knows that I delight in the small [vehicle]. To protect those of inferior capacity and to await the conditions for the Great [Vehicle], he does not initially urge me to advance and seek the Buddha-way, but rather explains that within the Buddha-dharma there are further true benefits, as in that parable.
The great wealthy householder, knowing his son’s disposition to be base and inferior, did not initially tell him that he was to obtain a treasure trove;
rather, through the power of skillful means, he caused him to take possession of the property.

He treated him with extreme gentleness to subdue his stubborn heart, and only after that, having gathered a multitude of people, did he entrust him with all the wealth. This is the gradual method of the two *dīpa*s.
It is unimpeded and expansive. Regarding the delivery of the family estate, the meaning of the two parables is as follows: from "The Buddha likewise" below, the Dharma is applied in correspondence.
The phrase "The Buddha is also thus" may be understood as a general synthesis. That the Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles turn the teaching is indeed a rare occurrence.
Because the Buddha does not teach them himself, he causes it to be so; this is his manifestation. This is why the Tathāgata manifests what is rare.
Regarding the phrase "having a matter [to address]": it is because [the Buddha] knew that my mind delighted in the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).

Thus, first employing the power of skillful means (upāya), he caused me to teach others, gradually taming my narrow mind and subduing my attachment to provisional teachings, so as to bring my faculties (indriya) to maturity.

This corresponds to what is meant in the parable by the phrase "gradually expanding [the mind] to vastness. This verse summarizes the meaning of the prose section concerning the arrival of the time when the faculties have matured.
This refers to the teaching of great wisdom; that is, pointing to the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra and bestowing the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. It corresponds to what is said in the parable:
"The house, its people, and all else are entirely entrusted to him. This verse summarizes the meaning of the prose section regarding the equal bestowal of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Because the prose is concise and difficult to distinguish, I have combined it with the verse. From "We... onwards, the verse describes the benefit gained from hearing the Dharma.
Where the long prose says, "He preached that there was originally no mind, yet there is something to be sought," this [verse] says, "Not what was previously hoped for.

Where the long prose says, "The great treasure of the Dharma King arrives spontaneously," this says, "Now one attains it for oneself. It is like that impoverished son who obtains [the treasure]. Without...

"Measuring the Jewels": the phrasing differs while the meaning remains the same. This concludes the verses corresponding to the prose section. △ Second, the supplementary verses clarifying the realization, in four parts:
first, clarifying the firmness of faith and understanding; second, clarifying the reality of cause and effect; third, clarifying the profound awareness of the Buddha’s grace.
Fourth, manifesting a profound understanding of the Buddha’s intent. First:
“World-Honored One, I have now attained the Way and attained the fruit... (omitted)... I have now attained the untainted, unsurpassed, great fruit.
Initially, he personally believed that he had become a Buddha; now, with his own mouth addressing the World-Honored One, the four sons declared: “I may now be said to have attained Bodhi.”
The Way leads to the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. How is this known? It is because we have now heard this Dharma being taught;

regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) that is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), we have attained clear faith without doubt and have gained the pure eye and ear of wisdom. We who are of inferior capacity—
They attained the fruit through their own realization. The four sons spoke again: "In the past, we were obstructed by the tenets of provisional schools, as if dwelling in the long night.
We thought that upholding the Buddha’s pure precepts would ultimately yield no real fruit; only today do we dare say that we have obtained their retribution.
How is this known? Because in the past, while dwelling in the long night, we did not depart from the Dharma of the Dharma King."
In the interim, he maintained the pure precepts of the Buddha; this was precisely his long cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

For this reason, he has now received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that he shall attain the exhaustion of delusions and the ultimate truth—the vast fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and unsurpassed state, endowed with all virtues.
This is what is meant by: "As for what a son of the Buddha ought to obtain, he has already obtained it all. △ Second, revealing the reality of cause and effect.
"We who are now truly śrāvakas... (up to) ...should universally receive offerings therein. This first reveals the reality of causal practice.
It means that although we were formerly called "śrāvakas," our "voice" (*śrā-*) was limited to the Four Truths alone, and our "hearing" (*-vaka*) was limited to ourselves alone;
thus, it was a provisional name and not real. Now, however, we are truly śrāvakas. How is this seen? For...
"From this day forward, we shall be able to cause all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way. Below this, the true nature of the fruit-virtue is revealed.
The term "Arhat" contains three meanings; according to the present text, it is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (*ārhant*).
Although they were previously called "Worthy of Offerings," this was applicable only to those who could respond to compliance but not to opposition, and only applicable to...
Excellent. Yet he should not be regarded as a Māra; his provisional manifestation was not the ultimate truth. Now, this one is truly the Arhat.
How is this known? Because from this day forward, throughout all worlds—whether among devas or humans—[he shall be so recognized].
Whether it be Māra or Brahmā, [the Buddha] is universally worthy of receiving offerings among them all. △ Third, revealing a profound understanding of the Buddha’s kindness:
"The Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One, through such rare occurrences... even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, could not be repaid."
First, the section beginning with "The World-Honored One" generally demonstrates that the Buddha’s kindness is difficult to repay.

This refers back to the preceding text, which states that in the past, upon first attaining the minor fruit [of Arhatship], one thought they had already repaid the Buddha’s kindness; yet viewed from the present perspective, the World-Honored One’s kindness is vast.
How is this seen? It is said that the World-Honored One, at the outset in the *Āgamas*, through a rare occurrence, graciously bestowed his compassion and caused [beings] to...

We had previously guaranteed us the teaching of exclusive emptiness; subsequently, during the Vaipulya period, you used rare and wondrous events to provide indirect instruction and transformation, allowing our minds to find peace whether advancing or retreating.
Later, during the Prajñāpāramitā period, you bestowed benefits through mysterious transmission via rare and wondrous events, enabling us to receive the Buddha’s teachings and pass them on ourselves.
Such was your gradual and skillful guidance, a grace that remained constant from beginning to end—how could we possibly repay it? Even if...
"Even after immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay the Buddha’s kindness? That which was perceived in the past is only now understood.
Furthermore, the reason why the three assemblies are all described as witnessing a rare and marvelous event is that [the Buddha] conceals his superior excellence within his inferior form.
Regarding the soles of his hands and feet, there is a separate clarification of the signs of the difficulty of repaying his kindness, which contains two further meanings."
First, a brief explanation: providing service with one's hands and feet, such as performing manual labor and servitude;

prostrating with the head, such as reverently paying visits; and all forms of offerings, such as the four requisites for sustenance—all such things are finite matters, whereas the Buddha’s grace is inexhaustible; therefore, none of these can fully repay it. From "If, however," below...
Detailed Explanation. The first four lines concern offerings of body and mind. Furthermore, the following section concerns the four types of material offerings.
Regarding "ox-head" (gośīrṣa) [sandalwood], below it says "stūpa and temple offerings. As for ox-head sandalwood, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that it originates from Mount Vimala;
if used to anoint the body, fire cannot burn it. Alternatively, it is so named because its shape resembles an ox's head. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
In the northern continent there is a mountain named High Mountain (*Giri*), shaped like the head of an ox; because sandalwood grows therein, it is so named.
The final four lines summarize that [the Buddha] cannot be repaid. Such matters as these are used for making offerings, and such offerings may be called ultimate.
Yet, even over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still cannot repay [the Buddha]. This is because the Buddha is, by nature...
There is no self, nor is there any phenomenon; both the receiver and that which is received are unobtainable, and therefore cannot repay [the debt].
Ultimately, how could one possibly repay it? Now, taking the verse from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as an explanation, it says:

"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. With this profound resolve, I offer myself to every atom of the lands; this is what is called..."
Repaying the Buddha’s kindness. △ Fourth, manifesting a profound understanding of the Buddha’s intent:
"The Buddhas possess rare, immeasurable, and boundless [qualities]... (up to) ...teaching the three vehicles according to what is appropriate within the path of the One Vehicle."

First, a general clarification: the Buddha’s intention is rare and extraordinary. The opening phrase also distantly inherits from the preceding text, stating that on the occasion of the *Prajñāpāramitā* assembly in the past, he commanded me to turn the teaching; this was indeed a manifestation of a rare event.
Viewed from the present perspective, the rare events of all Buddhas do not exceed those [of the past]. How is this seen? It is because sentient beings are immeasurable, as...
When there are immeasurable sentient beings, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable spiritual powers; when sentient beings are infinite, the Tathāgata possesses infinite spiritual powers;
when sentient beings are inconceivable, the Tathāgata possesses inconceivable spiritual powers.
All of these arise from the Tathāgata as manifestations intended for the sake of delivering sentient beings. This was not known in the past, but now...
Only now do we begin to understand. Regarding "the outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) and below: this separately clarifies the marks of rarity, which further contains two meanings.

First, the brief explanation of the "outflow-free and unconditioned" (*anāsrava-asamskrta*): when delusions are exhausted and reality is fully realized, it reveals that the fruit of spiritual virtue has reached its ultimate limit.

"The King of all dharmas" means possessing mastery over all phenomena; this reveals that his divine function is infinite. Because his divine function is infinite, he is able to [act] for those who are inferior.
The Two Vehicles endure this untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) matter and do not strive to speak of it quickly;

furthermore, they are able to speak appropriately for the sake of ordinary beings who grasp at signs (*nimitta-grāhin*), according to their capacities for that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This is the rare quality of all Buddhas, of which we have already seen a general outline. From the words "All Buddhas" [onward], it is explained in detail. This is identical to the section in the General Exposition.

The phrase "all concerning the Buddhas" is used to manifest that the path of every Buddha is identical. Among all phenomena, those who have attained supreme mastery may expound the teachings at will, without any obstruction.
Furthermore, these two phrases provide a detailed clarification of the meaning of being a "King of All Phenomena.
"Knowing all sentient beings" refers to the capacities of humans and devas; regarding the capacities of humans and devas, [it concerns] the precepts.
Regarding the dharmas of wholesome meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), preferences differ; hence it is said there are "various desires and pleasures.
As for their "resolute power" (*adhimukti-bala*), this refers to the fact that within these various desires and pleasures, one's orientation and mental strength likewise differ.

Regarding "according to what one is capable of," this means that once one has understood those desires and pleasures as well as one's own resolute power, one [applies oneself] to the dharmas of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wholesome meditative concentration accordingly.

Regarding whatever Dharma they are capable of receiving, he guides them by means of that very Dharma. However, because the faculties of humans and devas are inferior, it is difficult to clarify the truth through direct speech;
therefore, he teaches the Dharma by means of immeasurable parables. This explains in detail the meaning of teaching according to what is appropriate for ordinary beings who grasp at signs.
Following the various sentient beings, he points to the capacities of the Three Vehicles. The Three Vehicles...

The capacities [of sentient beings] differ according to their roots of goodness from past lives. The Buddha is able to teach in accordance with these capacities; therefore, it is said that he "follows" them.
Regarding those who are matured and those who are not yet matured: among the various types of roots of goodness, there are those that have been deeply cultivated and are thus already matured.
There are those who have practiced superficially and whose faculties are not yet matured; the Buddha is able to observe them according to the proper time, and thus it is said that he "knows.

Having deliberated in various ways and distinguished them through knowledge, he examines the capacities of beings by means of the Dharma. Regarding the teaching of the three vehicles within the single vehicle path as appropriate to their needs, he bestows the Dharma according to their capacities.
This provides a detailed clarification of the meaning of being able to act for the sake of those of inferior capacity and enduring such matters.
The Exposition of the Four Sons’ Faith and Understanding is concluded.

△ Second, the opening of the Tathāgata Seal (the chapter title states):
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Chapter Five, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
It is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" because it receives its designation through the metaphor of medicinal herbs, and the chapter is named by means of this parable. Text.

Within this [chapter] there are both the Dharma and the parable; yet the title of the chapter uses only the name of the parable because the meaning of the Dharma is difficult to clarify, whereas employing a parable makes it easy to understand.
To explain its meaning: "grass" serves as a general term for all plants, while "medicine" is taken for its efficacy in curing illness.

Furthermore, while all ordinary grasses can cure illnesses, this discussion is based on those whose efficacy is particularly superior, for those whose efficacy is weak or inferior cannot be called "medicines.
According to the subsequent verse, medicinal herbs are of three types: first, small herbs.

This is illustrated by the capacities of humans and devas. Humans and devas can cure the ten evil deeds as well as the sufferings of the three miserable realms; therefore, they are likened to small grasses.

Among these, the medium grasses illustrate the two vehicles of the Lesser Teaching; the two vehicles can cure the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), as well as the suffering of the limited分段 [segmentation] existence.
Therefore, they are compared to middle and superior grasses. The three types of superior grasses represent the Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching).

Because these Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching can cure their respective portions of ignorance and their respective portions of *pariṇāmika-nirvāṇa* (transformation-death), they are compared to superior grasses. Within [the category of] superior grasses, there are further small trees and large trees;
these represent the Bodhisattvas of the Final, Sudden, and Perfect teachings. These will be discussed again in the relevant passages. For now, this chapter title alone...

Regarding the "Designation of the Medicinal Herbs": because the teachings for humans and devas are of a minor, initial stage and belong to the provisional vehicle (*upāya-yāna*), this sutra brings these provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*), thereby demonstrating the emphasis on the partial.
However, the reason the Tathāgata preached the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" immediately after the four sons’ faith and understanding is that it also possesses five meanings.
First, it serves as a seal (*mudrā*) to certify that what has been taught is not erroneous, as the text says: "Excellent! (*sādhu*).

"Excellent, Kāśyapa! You have well spoken regarding the true merits of the Tathāgata. Second, in order to reveal that what has been said does not exhaust the full extent [of those merits], as the text says:
'The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits.'"
Even if you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you could not exhaustively describe this.
Third, it is to demonstrate that there is no difference in the single sound [of the Buddha], as the text says: "Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the trichiliocosm;
at one time they rain down equally, their moisture universally nourishing all. Fourth, it is to demonstrate that the various capacities of sentient beings differ from one another, as the text says...
It is said: "Small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves—even among all trees, large and small, each receives [nourishment] according to its superior, middling, or inferior capacity.
Fifth is the teaching by means of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). As the verse says: "The practice you engage in is the path of the bodhisattva;
by training and studying gradually, you shall all become Buddhas. This is the general statement of the instruction.

The vocalization follows the mechanism; the rhythmic beat accords with the teaching. The four disciples’ faith and understanding, having already known the sequence of the three periods, are further illuminated by the Tathāgata’s seal of approval as his single voice reveals its perfect fusion. Thus, the interaction between teacher and disciple encompasses the entirety of the Dharma.

This is what is meant by "beating the drum and playing the lute; meeting, both are masters of the assembly. [The Sūtra is divided into two parts: First, the prose exposition (*gadya*); second, the verse recitation (*gāthā*).

The first part of the third section has three points: first, the seal that indicates the aggregates; second, the formal opening; and third, the conclusion consisting of praise, consolation, and exhortation.
Regarding the first: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] "...could not be fully exhausted even by speaking for immeasurable billions of kalpas."
The initial "Praise of the Seal of Excellence" (śubha-mudrā) is spoken to address Kāśyapa and the other sons; this is because, as their understanding is identical, the seal is likewise the same seal.
Since both the exposition of the provisional and the exposition of the real are equally excellent, he repeatedly says "Excellent! (sādhu) to praise them.
He addresses Kāśyapa alone because he is the eldest in years and seniority, serving as the leader of the assembly; it is from the perspective of the Real that the Provisional is established.
The provisional ultimately returns to the real; these are all the Tathāgata’s true achievements and his true virtuous deeds, and are thus called "merit and virtue" (*guṇa*).

In terms of the teaching, it proceeds from the provisional toward the real, fully exhausting the Buddha’s intention. In terms of the capacities of beings, it proceeds from delusion toward awakening, thoroughly comprehending their fundamental dispositions.
These are all the grand rhetoric and elegant eloquence of the four disciples, characterized by refined thought and skillful metaphors; therefore, they are called "well-spoken" (*suvyākhyāta*). (5)

The connections between the joints are clear; one may thus understand that the doctrinal system of this single dispensation is perfectly intact and without error. Therefore, it is said: "It is truly as you have stated.
Regarding the passage "The Tathāgata, moreover... and so forth, this points to his virtues and delineates his aggregates.

When it says, "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits," it means that while sentient beings are immeasurable, the functional power, virtues, and deeds of the Tathāgata are likewise immeasurable.
Sentient beings are boundless; the Tathāgata’s power, virtues, and deeds are likewise boundless. Sentient beings are incalculable;
the Tathāgata’s power, virtues, and deeds are likewise incalculable. Thus, the merits of the Tathāgata cannot be exhausted by the single analogy of the impoverished son alone;
even if one were to expound them with all one's might for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they could not be fully described.
Nor can they be fully exhausted. It is said that while the void may be measured and the wind may be bound, no one is able to exhaustively describe the merits of the Buddha.

△ Second, the formal opening and revealing (kai meaning to open what has not yet been reached; qi meaning to reveal the remaining depths). This refers to what was spoken to the four sons in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Xinyue pin): they only received a portion according to their own capacity.

Above, they did not reach the level of the Bodhisattvas; below, they did not reach the level of humans and devas. Furthermore, they only knew the sequence of the single dispensation—that the provisional comes first and the real follows—and had not yet attained understanding of how a single sound yields diverse interpretations, nor the perfection of all dharmas.

"Rong. Now, each point shall be unfolded and revealed so that the Buddha’s virtues may be deeply understood. second, elucidating through metaphors; third, applying the Dharma to correspond with them. The first [part] is called "establishing the specific tenet" because its doctrine differs from the preceding chapter.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas (up to: he reveals all wisdom to all sentient beings.
First, he cuts off doubt and gives rise to faith. The Tathāgata’s intention is this: "I am the Dharma King; I have mastery over the Dharma.

I release and gather, and through the perfect integration of the sequential stages, I expound according to my will. There is nothing that is permissible or impermissible. Furthermore, as for whatever he may say:

All of these are for the purpose of truly delivering sentient beings; there is nothing false or deceptive in them. Now, I wish to further present the Perfect Sound (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*) and establish a distinct school of thought.
I hope you will not suspect this to be contradictory and thereby give rise to various forms of disbelief; this is my earnest hope. [End of section one.]
To establish the fundamental tenet: regarding "all dharmas," this refers collectively to the teachings for humans and devas, the five levels of teaching, and so forth.
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: you merely know that the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma of the Four Truths for you, the śrāvakas;
however, in reality, the Tathāgata, through both true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and skillful means (*upāya*), [teaches] all dharmas for humans and devas, the five levels of teaching, and so forth.
At the time of cutting [the hair], a single sound was expounded all at once; this is the first instance of that which you could not exhaustively explain even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.
Furthermore, you only know that for you śrāvakas and others, the Tathāgata brings provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality;
yet in truth, the various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata do not require such a convergence, for they have all already reached the state of omniscience.

The Stage of Wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*). Because all dharmas are manifested from the stage of wisdom, and because the dharmas themselves are the stage of wisdom, this is the second reason why you would be unable to exhaustively explain them even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.

[The Tathāgata] provides the following pre-emptive defense against potential objections (the objection being: "How can all dharmas be manifested all at once?"; hence he provides this defense). The Tathāgata perceives and knows all dharmas...

Regarding "the destination to which phenomena converge" and so forth: as for the destinations to which various phenomena converge, it is like how the cultivation of precepts and virtues converges toward humans and devas;
the truths and conditions converge toward the two vehicles; and the six perfections converge toward bodhisattvas, and so on. Regarding "that which is practiced with a profound mind":

it is like practicing the cultivation of precepts and virtues with a profound mind, practicing the cultivation of the truths and conditions with a profound mind, and practicing the cultivation of the six perfections with a profound mind.
One thoroughly understands each and every such category, seeing them clearly and without error; thus it is said that one has attained unimpeded penetration.

For this reason, one is able to expound upon all phenomena through wisdom and skillful means. (Furthermore, it is asked: "Even if one can expound [the teachings] instantaneously, how is it possible for all to reach the stage of wisdom?
To prevent this doubt, it says: "Furthermore, regarding the thorough and complete understanding of all phenomena," etc. Here, "all phenomena" still refers to those among humans and devas.

Regarding the five teachings and other dharmas, from their origin to their end, one thoroughly investigates them to the very source; hence it is said that they are "exhaustively and clearly understood.
Once one is able to exhaustively and clearly understand them, then all dharmas are none other than reality.
For this reason, whatever is spoken will invariably reach the state of omniscience. △ Second, the section on explaining through metaphors to clarify [the meaning] has three parts. First:

1. An analogy for the simultaneous and instantaneous proclamation [of the Dharma]. 2. An analogy for receiving benefit according to individual capacities. 3. An analogy for the identity of the teaching despite differences in capacity.
First: "Kāśyapa, it is as if in a trichiliocosm world... [down to] the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal herbs."
The reason for calling out their names again is to cause them to understand the Dharma by means of these analogies.
Regarding the "trichiliocosm," according to the subsequent combined text, it should be understood as an analogy for the world of sentient beings—namely, devas, humans, and asuras.

If they were to be treated as separate analogies, the small chiliocosm would represent asuras, the medium chiliocosm would represent humans, and the great trichiliocosm would represent devas; thus, devas, humans, and asuras are combined.
The "world of sentient beings" is like the three sets of thousands mentioned; these combined constitute a Great Trichiliocosm.

It does not include those in the evil realms because their karma is heavy and they lack the capacity to be saved. Mountains, rivers, streams, valleys, and soil are metaphors for the world of sentient beings, which refers to all bodies composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If one were to provide specific analogies: the towering height of mountains represents form (*rūpa*).

The aggregates (*skandhas*) can be seen: the river receiving the many streams is a metaphor for the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) receiving and assimilating; the winding of the mountain brooks and ravines is a metaphor for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) being crooked and tortuous;

the profound depth of the valleys and crevices is a metaphor for the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) being subtle and hidden; and the earth giving birth to all things is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*) transforming all phenomena.
All five aggregates depend upon the mind, just as mountains, rivers, brooks, valleys, and soil all depend upon the earth. Therefore, [the mind] is supreme.
Subsequently, the earth is used as a metaphor. "Herb" (*huì*) is a general term for grasses; "wood" (*mù*) is a collective designation for trees.
When both are numerous, they are called a "thicket" (*cónglín*). This serves as a general metaphor for sentient beings of diverse capacities.
These diverse capacities arise from the latent consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of sentient beings, just as those herbs and woods grow upon mountains, rivers, valleys, and the soil.

Therefore, that which is produced is used as a metaphor for this. As for "and the various medicinal herbs," this specifically serves as a metaphor for humans, devas, and the three vehicles of the Lesser and Initial [teachings];
the meaning is evident from the title of the chapter. "Species" refers to categories of seeds, serving as a metaphor for the causal seeds of sentient beings in the past.
Because the seeds are not uniform, they are likened to "various" things. As for "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), "name" refers to the characteristics of form;
it is likened to the present capacities and dispositions of sentient beings. Because these capacities and dispositions differ, they are likened to being "distinct.

"Dense clouds spreading everywhere" means that dense clouds are distributed throughout the sky; this is likened to the Buddha manifesting in the world with a body that pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. This manifestation...
Throughout the world, among the hosts of devas, humans, and asuras, it is therefore likened to pervading the trichiliocosm.
"Simultaneously raining down equally" means that within a single moment, rain falls equally and universally across the realm;
this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s instantaneous and simultaneous exposition of immeasurable Dharma gates. Having thus instantaneously and simultaneously expounded immeasurable Dharma gates...

Thus, all who are capable of receiving benefit are included; there is none for whom the opportunity is not provided. Therefore, its moisture is universally pervasive, and it is illustrated by the metaphor of the grasses, trees, groves, and various medicinal herbs.
△ Second, the metaphor of receiving benefits according to one's capacity has two parts: first, the metaphor of causing those who have not yet received to receive;

"Small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves" (up to) "each receives according to its superior, middling, or inferior capacity.
These first six phrases refer back to the medicinal herbs mentioned above; they state that among the various medicinal herbs, there are those with small roots and small stems.
The "small branches and small leaves" are a metaphor for the spiritual capacities of humans and devas;

because their roots of faith, stems of precepts, branches of concentration, and leaves of wisdom—these four factors—are all small, they correspond to what is later referred to as the "lesser medicinal herbs.

The "middling roots and middling stems," etc., should be understood by analogy. Regarding the phrase "all trees," this follows the pattern of the aforementioned medicinal herbs; it indicates that the reference is not limited solely to medicinal herbs.

Within this, there are differences and distinctions; that is, the trees themselves also vary in size. Those that are small provide a meager shade, serving as a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas of the Final and Sudden Teachings.

Because they possess both obstruction and illumination, their shading and covering of sentient beings still have limitations—this is what is meant by the later passage, "This is called a small tree. As for those that are large, their shade is vast; this serves as a metaphor for...
The Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) simultaneously employ both concealment and illumination to shelter and protect sentient beings without limit;

this is what is referred to in the subsequent text as "this is called the great tree. Regarding the categories of superior, middling, and inferior, these are discussed in relation to the sequence of grasses and trees:
for example, the great tree is termed "superior," the small tree is termed "middling," and the tall grass is termed "inferior"; alternatively, the small tree may be termed [inferior].
"Superior. Superior grasses are called "middle," and middle grasses are called "inferior" and so forth. Generally speaking, each receives moisture according to its own capacity;
thus it is said that according to the superior, middle, and inferior [capacities], each has what it receives. This is a metaphor for the various capacities of humans, devas, and the five teachings.
Each receives the benefit of the Dharma according to their respective portion of innate wisdom; there is no deficiency therein.

However, this statement refers only to those who possess the innate capacity (*gotra*) but have not previously received the benefit, and now for the first time do so. △ Second, the analogy for causing [the benefit] to increase after it has been received.
The rain from a single cloud grows flowers, fruits, and seeds according to their respective natures.
"The rain from a single cloud" refers to the water rained down by that very same cloud, which serves as a metaphor for the Dharma taught by a single Buddha.
Because the Dharma taught by a single Buddha can universally respond to the diverse capacities of sentient beings, it is said to be "according to their [natures]."

Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): "seed" refers to the seed, which is a metaphor for the causal seeds of sentient beings in the past; "nature" refers to the essential nature, which is a metaphor for the present capacities and dispositions of sentient beings.

Because the causal seeds of the past give rise to roots of goodness upon hearing the Dharma, and because the present capacities and dispositions receive benefit and cause the sprouts of the Path to grow, it is said that they "attain growth," with flowers and fruits unfolding and bearing fruit.

It should be said that "flowers bloom and fruits ripen" is a metaphor for sentient beings attaining peace and security in the present life and being reborn in good realms in the future, eventually entering the Path gradually according to their capacity.
This also refers specifically to those whose faculties are currently suited [to the teaching], who have already received benefit in the past and now further increase it;
this concludes the metaphor for receiving benefit according to one's capacity. △ Third, the metaphor for the teaching.
The capacity for the teaching is distinct.
Although they are born from the same ground and moistened by the same rain, the various grasses and trees each have their own differences.
The capacities of humans, devas, and the five teachings arise from one's own mind; since the self-mind is non-dual, it is metaphorically likened to the single ground.

The teachings produced—the Dharma of the five vehicles for humans and devas—are fundamentally the Buddha Vehicle; since the Buddha Vehicle is not different [from them], it is likened to the moisture provided by a single rain.

This illustrates that because the fundamental correct cause (正因) inherent in sentient beings is the same, the original intention of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is likewise the same, thereby manifesting the identity of the Dharma.
As for the various plants and trees, they collectively serve as a metaphor for the teachings for humans and devas and the five vehicles.

Regarding "equal capacities": the capacities of humans and devas across the five teachings are not uniform; their wisdom differs, and the benefits they obtain are unequal. Therefore, it is said that there are differences among them.
As an ancient master remarked: "The spring colors have no high or low; the flower branches are simply long or short. This is precisely the meaning here.
Having finished explaining the parable to illuminate this point, △ three: applying the Dharma to correspond [to the parable], part one: simultaneous and instantaneous exposition.

Second, benefiting others according to their capacities; third, the teaching being the same while the capacities differ. Regarding the first [of these three], although the meaning is identical to the preceding metaphorical text, the phrasing is more extensive and is thus divided into three parts:
first, manifesting the body to bestow compassion; second, extolling virtues to instruct the assembly; third, preaching the Dharma in accordance with capacities. First:
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this—[omitted]—pervading and covering the trichiliocosm.

The Buddha’s body manifests in the world like a great cloud arising and spreading across the heavens; this is the meaning of the dense clouds spreading everywhere within the analogy. The Buddha...

△ 2. Proclaiming One’s Virtues to Admonish the Multitude (Before the Buddha appeared in the world, false teachings ran rampant; even after his appearance, people did not know where to turn for refuge. Therefore, it was necessary to proclaim one’s own virtues so that the false and the correct might be clearly distinguished, and the choice between following or rejecting them could be resolved.)
Within the great assembly, he uttered these words: "[... all should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
First, he extolled his virtuous name. A "name" (hào) serves to manifest virtue; "extolling" (chēngyáng) means causing others to know one's virtue through that name.
"Those who have not yet crossed over," refers to praising compassion. "To cause those who have not yet crossed over suffering and affliction to cross over suffering and affliction;
