He establishes them in the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*). For those who have not yet realized *nirvāṇa*, he causes them to realize it;
this refers to the great compassion that bestows happiness. Regarding the passage "In this world... and so forth, it concerns the praise of knowledge and vision.

To "know [things] as they truly are" in this world and the next means knowing, for example, what causes are cultivated in this life and what fruits will be attained in future lives, exactly as I have cultivated and realized them. Truly...

By observing through the reality of causes and effects, one is able to know all things. An "all-knowing seer" refers to one who can both fully comprehend the principles of all phenomena (*dharma*) and clearly perceive their manifestations.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, its number is known;
likewise, all that appears before one—the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes..."
Wu Xuan: All understand that the fundamental source is thus. Regarding "knowing the Way" (*zhidao*): this extols the essence and function. "The Way" refers to the Buddha-way.
Initially, within the mind of ignorance, one understands without delusion; this is called "knowing.
Subsequently, when ignorance is exhausted, the perfect luminosity is revealed; this is called "opening. This luminous essence is fully present within oneself. Now...
Furthermore, after attaining Buddhahood, he expounds this Way to awaken all sentient beings; this is called "teaching.
This clarifies that its function pervades others. From the words "You all... onwards, [the text] commands the assembly to listen to the Dharma.
It states that since the Tathāgata possesses such titles of merit, such compassion, such knowledge and vision, and such essence and function, it is clearly known that he is...
Since this is a place of refuge, the teaching instructs that all should come here; and since coming here is not in vain, it is shown to be for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.
△ Third, preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of the listeners.
At that time, there were countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings (up to) being taught the Dharma according to their respective capacities.

"Sentient beings" here specifically refers to devas, humans, and asuras. Since the faculties and dispositions of devas, humans, and asuras are not uniform, when divided into subtle categories, they number thousands of myriads of koṭis.
Those who "came" did so having heard the summons; those who "listened to the Dharma" listened to the Buddha.
He preaches the Dharma. All those who should have arrived previously do so now; this is the imperial decree for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
"At that time" indicates that the Tathāgata does not miss the opportune moment. "Observing these sentient beings" indicates that the Dharma does not conflict with their capacities.

Although their faculties may be sharp or dull and their strength diligent or lax, he reveals the truth secretly through a single voice, such that there is none to whom it does not respond universally, whether high or low. Therefore, it is said:
He preaches the Dharma according to what each can bear; this corresponds to the meaning in the parable of "pouring down at once" and "the moisture universally soaking.

Having finished the simultaneous and sudden exposition, there are two parts to the second section, "Receiving Benefits According to Capacity": first, the formal application of the Dharma; second, a further reference to the preceding parable.

Regarding the first of these, there are two sub-sections: first, causing those who have not yet received it to receive it; second, causing those who have already received it to increase [their realization].
First: "Various and immeasurable [beings] are all made to rejoice and swiftly obtain excellent benefit.

Regarding "various and immeasurable," this is discussed in terms of the distinctions among those suited to the teachings. As stated in the parable, these refer to those of small faculties and small...

"Stems, small branches, small leaves, and even the various trees, both large and small"—this refers to them all. "Causing them all to rejoice" means they rejoice because they receive benefit according to their respective capacities;
the transformation is attributed to the Buddha's power, hence the term "causing. "Exceedingly obtaining excellent benefit" provides the reason for their joy:
because they receive benefit according to their respective capacities, they personally feel delighted at having obtained great and excellent benefit, and thus [joy] arises.
"Rejoice, O ears! This refers to what is meant in the parable regarding how those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities each receive [the teaching] accordingly. II.
Having received it, one causes it to increase:
"When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma... (up to) "...they gradually enter the Path according to their respective powers and abilities."

When sentient beings hear the Dharma and practice according to its teachings, they leave suffering behind and attain happiness in the present life; thus it is said that they are "peaceful and secure in this world.

This is the "flower reward" (the immediate karmic fruition). As their roots of goodness internally permeate them, they do not become deluded when passing through the barrier of death; upon changing bodies, they continue to take rebirth in favorable realms.
Therefore, it is said that one is reborn in a favorable realm. As soon as one emerges from the womb, one recognizes the true Path and is not constrained by worldly sentiments;
thus, it is said that one experiences joy through the Path, being free and unattached, and always remaining near the Buddha.

Receiving the Buddha’s guidance and inspiration, it is said that one also hears the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, one’s innate spiritual potential is awakened, and one immediately emerges [into realization].
Because one is detached from birth and death, it is said that "one is free from all obstacles"; this refers to the retributive fruit (*vipāka*).
Since one is free from obstacles, throughout successive lifetimes one does not depart from the Buddha-dharma;

thus it is said that "among all dharmas, according to the power of one's wisdom, one practices as much as possible and ultimately attains Buddhahood," which is called "gradually entering the Way"; this refers to the ultimate fruit. Now, within this...
Although the three types of retribution differ, they all belong to the category of advancing through hearing the Dharma. In terms of their meaning, they correspond to what was previously discussed;
they grow according to their respective natures (*gotra*). The analogy of flowers blooming and fruits ripening has now been fully applied to the Dharma. △ Second, reiterating the previous analogy.

Just as that great cloud rains upon all [beings] (from "reaching" to "fully receiving moisture and each attaining growth"), the first three phrases—the analogy of preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of the recipient—should have been placed after the section on "simultaneous and sudden exposition"; however, they are mentioned here for the sake of convenience.
As for those three phrases, they present the analogy of causing those who have not yet received [the teaching] to receive it, so that each may attain growth.

Long. This is the analogy of receiving [the medicine] early and then increasing its dosage; its meaning is clear. Having finished [explaining] how benefits are received according to individual capacity, section three follows:

"The Teaching is the Same, While Capacities Differ" (this is not divided within the analogy, as the textual exposition for the application to the Dharma is extensive). It consists of two parts: first, the teaching is the same; second, capacities differ. First [the teaching is the same]:
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, culminating ultimately in all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

As for the "single characteristic," it is the characteristic of the minds of sentient beings; all sentient beings are established based upon this. It is in accordance with this that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.

There is nothing that does not point toward this. This is the analogy for being produced from the same ground. "One flavor" refers to the milk-flavor of the Buddha-vehicle; all dharmas are expounded from this.
There is nothing in the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma that does not reveal and manifest this.
This is the analogy for being moistened by the same rain. What is called "below" provides the proof and explanation of the single characteristic and the single flavor.

Regarding the meaning: as for the characteristic of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*), one does not abide in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because ordinary persons cling to existence and have not yet attained liberation.

As for the characteristic of detachment (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*), one does not abide in the state of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), because those of the two vehicles incline toward emptiness and have not yet detached from non-existence.

As for the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), one does not abide in the state of a bodhisattva, because bodhisattvas grasp at the middle way and have not yet extinguished both "clinging" and "detachment. Since one abides in none of these, then...
The numinous mind is free from all dependencies; its wondrous essence is solitary and radiant. It is clear that it constitutes the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
By practicing in reliance upon this, whether one’s progress is distant or near, all shall attain Buddhahood. Thus it is said: "Ultimately reaching the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This knowledge of all modes is precisely the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). To reach this ultimate point is itself the *amṛta* (the finest essence). The *amṛta* is rooted in...
Raw milk: it is evident that its flavor is one and the same. △ Second, the distinction of capacities.
There are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata [up to] yet do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures.

The initial section correctly aligns with the preceding parable. "There are sentient beings" refers to those of the human and celestial realms who possess the capacities for the five teachings and so forth;
this aligns with the preceding parable of the various grasses and trees. "Hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

"If they uphold, read, and recite it"—not merely mastering the text but also understanding its meaning—refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Practicing according to the teaching" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Since they are already able to...
To proceed from hearing to reflection, and from reflection to cultivation, ensures that one’s efforts are not in vain; thus, there will be attained merit and virtue.
However, the differences in their depth, shallowness, loftiness, or inferiority remain unrecognized within oneself.

Because they are unrecognized, that which is deep remains naturally deep, that which is shallow remains naturally shallow, that which is lofty remains naturally lofty, and that which is inferior remains naturally inferior. This precisely accords with what was stated previously.
The text provides various metaphors for each [of these categories]. The following section raises a question to provide a counter-illustration:
"Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings," and so forth. This serves as a counter-illustration because sentient beings do not know this themselves. "Seeds" refers to past causal seeds.

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of the present mind; "essence" (*tattva*) refers to the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena; and "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the rational nature (*dharmatā*) that is realized.
However, these various types—characteristics, essence, and nature—are each distinct, as can be seen from the detailed explanation provided in sequence below.

Regarding the questions "What does one recollect? What does one contemplate? What does one cultivate?", these reveal the differences among the causal seeds; it is precisely because the causal seeds differ [that these distinctions arise].

Therefore, the objects of what is recollected, what is contemplated, and what is cultivated are likewise each different. For example, there is recollection directed toward humans and devas, and recollection directed toward the Three Vehicles;
contemplation directed toward humans and devas, and contemplation directed toward the Three Vehicles, and so forth. What is recollection? What is contemplation?
What is meant by "cultivation"? It is to reveal that the characteristics of the mind are not the same.

Precisely because the characteristics of the mind differ, the powers of recollecting, contemplating, and cultivating likewise differ accordingly; for instance, there may be slowness or urgency in recollection, and shallowness or depth in contemplation.
Cultivation may involve diligence or indolence and so forth. By what dharma does one maintain mindfulness? By what dharma does one contemplate? By what dharma does one cultivate?

These questions reveal that the essential natures (*dharmatā*) of these dharmas are distinct. Precisely because their essential natures differ, they likewise differ at the moments of right mindfulness, right contemplation, and right cultivation.
For instance, some may employ the goodness of the precepts (*śīla*), some may employ meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and some may employ the [Four] Truths (*satya*).
Regarding the conditions: whether by means of the six perfections or other dharmas, the question of "by what dharma one attains what dharma" reveals that the rational nature (li-xing) is not uniform.
This is because, as explained above, the essence of dharmas (fa-ti) differs; therefore, at the moment of realization and entry, the rational nature attained [varies accordingly].
These are also each distinct. For instance, there is the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the nature of both, and the nature of neither.
Sentient beings dwelling in various stages attain these accordingly: those dwelling in the human and celestial realms attain the nature of the conditioned;

those dwelling in the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) attain the nature of the unconditioned; those dwelling in the stages of the bodhisattvas attain the nature of both; and those observing from the stage of Buddhahood attain the nature of neither.
It is like ascending Mount Sumeru to gaze upon the surrounding peaks; therefore, it is said that one sees them as they truly are, with clear understanding and without obstruction.
To descend from this state is to become limited by individual perspectives; thus, one knows neither the other nor oneself.

Therefore, it is said that they are like the various flowers, trees, forests, and medicinal herbs, which do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures. This precisely corresponds to the opening [of the parable].

[End. △ Third, the concluding praise and consoling encouragement: (Having already opened [the teaching], there may be those who, upon hearing it, still harbor residual doubts; fearing that their own resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) is not yet perfected, they may again give rise to the sorrow of feeling utterly lost and bewildered.)

Therefore, he again concludes with a summary and offers consolation in two parts: first, resolving doubts based on the preceding discussion; second, the formal conclusion and summary. Regarding the first (the doubt is as follows):

"Although what the Buddha has taught consists of a single characteristic and a single flavor, this belongs only to a hidden revelation; thus, the benefits received differ according to individual capacities. Why not, instead, now provide an explicit teaching of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom), so that those of various capacities—humans, devas, and the followers of the three vehicles—may each attain Buddhahood? To resolve this, he says: *(Note: This section provides the structural outline and the initial portion of the commentary, including the presentation of the hypothetical objection and its introduction.)*
The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to: yet he does not immediately teach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Liberation, departure, extinction, and so forth are as before. *Nirvāṇa*—here translated as "perfect stillness" (*yuánjì*)—refers to the fact that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent. "Perfect stillness" means that all dharmas are originally tranquil.
Therefore, it is said that its characteristic is eternal quiescence (*nitya-śānta-lakṣaṇa*). According to the preceding [text], it says: "Ultimately reaching all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This refers to the aspect of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Here, it is called "ultimate nirvana with the characteristic of eternal quiescence," which refers to the aspect of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

However, abandonment is precisely the abandonment of wisdom, and wisdom is precisely the wisdom of abandonment; wisdom and abandonment are non-dual, constituting a single flavor (*ekarasa*) in the end.

Regarding those who return to emptiness: they understand above all that liberation is free from cessation; it is solely a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), ultimately and eternally quiescent, and possesses but a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
This clarifies that since difference does not exist, unity (*ekatva*) cannot be established—meaning that if so-called "one" exists, it would revert to becoming "two.
"The Buddha, having known this" means he knows the principle that even "one" cannot be established. Even "one" does not [exist].
If difference does not exist, how can it be established? Since difference does not exist, what prevents one from protecting life in accordance with conditions?

Therefore, observing the desires of the minds of sentient beings, one suddenly expounds all dharmas to protect them. For this reason, it is not as it is today, when the All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is explicitly taught.
If one is indeed such a person, then every word reveals the Truth (*satya*), and every phrase clarifies the fundamental principle (*mūla*).
What, then, is manifest and what is secret? △ Second, the formal conclusion and praise:
"You, Kāśyapa, are truly rare... [up to] ...preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know."
The address "You all" and the calling of Kāśyapa by name are intended to comfort their hearts through the aspects of faith and understanding, based on Kāśyapa and his three sons.

To praise them for their faith and understanding as being extraordinary, it is said: "It is truly rare that you are able to know the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
This has two meanings: first, knowing that [the teaching] is provisional (*upāya*), as explained in the *Śraddhā-pratipatti-parivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding).
It says: "The World-Honored One previously knew that we delighted in the Lesser Dharma, and thus He allowed us to remain as we were," and so forth.
Second, it is because He knows their reality. As the *Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta* states: "The World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," and so forth.
Those who are able to believe and accept do not merely know; they are furthermore able to have deep faith and patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).

"It is so. It has been received and not lost. This is the concluding phrase. The following serves as an inquiry: "To preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate" is something we have long been accustomed to hearing;
even if one knows this, it is not particularly rare. Why, then, is it praised as being "extremely rare"?

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddhas," the explanation is established. That preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know is also twofold.
Meaning. First, that which is provisional and not ultimate, difficult to understand and difficult to know. This is as stated in the passage where Śāriputra expresses his realization:
"However, we did not understand the skillful means spoken according to what was appropriate; when we first heard the Buddha-dharma, we immediately believed and accepted it," and so forth.

Second, that which is provisional yet is itself the ultimate, difficult to understand and difficult to know. This is as stated in the passage where the twelve thousand [disciples] raise their doubts: [text follows].
For what reason did the World-Honored One so earnestly praise skillful means, saying such things as:
"The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand; that which is spoken has a meaning and purport that are difficult to know"?
It is precisely because they were difficult to understand and difficult to know that the four sons were able to believe and accept them; therefore, he praised them as being most rare. (Prose section)
[End. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

△ (Within the actual verses, according to the prose [prose section], there are three parts; here, the first is missing. These are divided into two: 1. A verse on the formal granting of the opening; 2. A verse on the concluding praise and consolation.

Instruction. On the third day of the month: First, one verse establishes the specific thesis; second, one verse explains through metaphors to illuminate the meaning; third, one verse applies the Dharma to corroborate it.
The first [is the verse on the meaning].
The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world (up to: by means of various conditions, he causes [beings] to attain right view.

First, he severs doubt and gives rise to faith. Because the Tathāgata has truly exhausted all delusions and transcended all states of existence (*bhava*), he is called the "Dharma King who destroys existence.
Since he is called one who destroys existence and yet appears in the world, it demonstrates that this is the true means of delivering sentient beings; how much more so for...
The Kings of All Dharmas have never uttered false words to deceive the multitude. This verse and its prose commentary state that the Tathāgata is the King of All Dharmas;
whatever he speaks is entirely without falsehood. Regarding the phrase "according to the assembly" (*sui zhong*):

"sentient beings" refers to those with capacities such as humans, devas, and the five vehicles; "preaching the Dharma" refers to the teachings such as the precepts, wholesome deeds, the Truths, and Dependent Origination. Although it is said...

According to various desires, [the teachings] are in fact expounded simultaneously and instantaneously. This verse is the prose commentary on all phenomena, expounding them through wisdom and skillful means.
"Zūnzhòng" (respectful) is synonymous with "zhēnzhòng" (cherished); it refers to the aforementioned simultaneous and instantaneous exposition.
Although possessing the Buddha-wisdom, this was merely a subtle revelation through a single sound, rather than the explicit teaching as it is now. Thus says the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, I hold this Dharma in high esteem; it is profoundly deep and far-reaching. For a long time, I have kept this essential teaching in silence among all dharmas, not being in haste to proclaim it openly.
This is because if those with wisdom hear it, they will be able to believe and understand, which would certainly be excellent.
However, were there to be those without wisdom who harbor doubt or regret, they would suffer eternal loss. Would this not be a grave error? It is for this reason that I have remained silent.

Kāśyapa, you should know that the reason the Tathāgata teaches according to the capacity of beings is so that those who are already prepared may achieve immediate and sudden realization without obstruction;
even for those who are not yet suitable vessels, they may still enter the path gradually by means of favorable conditions. Therefore, it is said: "By means of various conditions."
This causes them to attain right view. This verse is a summary of the prose section. Regarding the Dharma taught therein, it all reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
To preempt potential objections, these points are omitted from the verse because they have already been explained in the prose; thus, there should be no further doubt. Part Two:
Verses Explaining Metaphors to Elucidate the Meaning. This has three sections: 1. A verse on the metaphor of simultaneous and instantaneous manifestation. 2. [The second section...]

The first verse is a simile for benefiting others according to their individual capacities. The three verses [that follow] are similes for the uniformity of the teaching and the diversity of the capacities. First:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud... [extending through] the various plants, trees, and medicinal herbs, both large and small."

The first analogy illustrates the manifestation of the body and the bestowal of compassion (in brief verse). Following the prose section, it first cites the three thousandfold world system, with its mountains, rivers, valleys, and so forth, as metaphors;
these are not versified here because the subsequent text contains a recapitulative verse. Thus, the clouds arise in the world.
The preceding verse states that "dense clouds spread everywhere," covering all things; the preceding verse further states they "pervade the three thousandfold world-system.

The meaning may be understood by referring to the prose commentary. Regarding the phrase "Clouds of Wisdom" (*huiyun*) below: this is a metaphor for proclaiming virtues to the assembly (a supplementary verse). "Wisdom" (*hui*) means beauty; it refers to clouds of exquisite beauty.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous body. Because this subtle and wondrous body internally contains the wisdom of the teachings, it is likened to being imbued with moisture.
This is based on the prose section [of the sūtra], which states: "I cause those who have not crossed over to cross over; I cause those who have not understood to understand," and so forth, up to:
"I am the all-knowing one, the all-seeing one. This completes the metaphor. It is like the vital energy of yin and yang.
When the elements strike one another and produce light, it is called lightning; this serves as a metaphor for the time when the Way of resonance and mutual response intersects.
When the Buddha emits light of the same essence—that light of the same essence pervades the entire Dharma-realm—it is therefore likened to a brilliant radiance.

This signifies the Tathāgata’s intention to first cause the assembly to see him by means of light before he issues his summons. When the vital energies of Yin and Yang strike one another, they produce sound.

It is called "thunder. This is a metaphor for the time when the path of resonance and response intersects. The Buddha emits unimpeded sounds; these unimpeded sounds universally awaken all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is likened to a distant rumble. This represents the Tathāgata’s intention to summon the multitude to return, using sound as a summons to let them know.
The rumbling of thunder serves to manifest the falling of rain; likewise, the Tathāgata’s sounding of the summons serves as... [the falling of the rain of Dharma].

It is shown as the teaching of the Dharma. It is for the purpose of demonstrating the teaching of the Dharma, so that the assembly may gather with joy; therefore, it is metaphorically described as causing the assembly to be delighted.
This is according to the prose section of the Dharma: "You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here."

This refers to the meaning of going forth for the sake of hearing the Dharma; it supplements the preceding metaphor. "The sunlight descends" and so forth serves as a metaphor for preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings (the first four lines belong to the supplementary verse).
The blazing intensity of the sunlight and the scorching heat of the great earth serve as metaphors for the flourishing of false views and the burning afflictions within the mind.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, false views are subdued and the ground of the mind becomes cool and refreshing; thus, it is compared to the sun being eclipsed so that the earth becomes cool.

This is based on the prose section [of the sutra], which conveys the meaning of how, at that time, countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma. This completes the analogy. "Āi-dài" (靉靆) refers to clouds.
The residual vapor is a metaphor for the Buddha’s transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) that manifest according to the various types of beings.

Because these transformation bodies descend to accord with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, they are compared to this hanging down and spreading forth. Although it is like something one could grasp or hold, its dense mass is fundamentally empty and cannot be grasped;

it merely hangs down and spreads below, appearing as if it could be grasped or held. This metaphor illustrates that the Buddha’s transformation body is not a substantial existence and cannot be personally clung to.
"Near" means that [the Buddha] condescends to accord with the capacities [of beings], appearing as if he were approachable and accessible;

this relies on the meaning in the prose section where the Tathāgata, at that time, observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of these sentient beings and the nature of their diligence or indolence—this completes the analogy.

(The two lines concerning "the rain" are a verse summarizing the meaning): "The rain is everywhere equal" is a metaphor for the immeasurable Dharma-gates being expounded all at once and instantaneously.
Descending simultaneously from all four directions, this is a metaphor for the four kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) pouring forth all at once;

this refers to what is stated in the prose as "simultaneously raining down equally. The phrase "flowing and drenching immeasurably" means that the nature of water flows and drenches throughout the entire extent of the earth, serving as a metaphor for how the Tathāgata’s Dharma and meaning permeate and saturate the very limits of the mind-ground throughout the whole land.

"Thoroughly moistening" refers to the total pervasion of all lands; it is a metaphor for sufficiency and saturation. It signifies that sentient beings receive this Dharma rain, whereby the field of consciousness is nourished and moistened.
Mountains and rivers still serve as metaphors for form and sensation, as seen in the long prose section. "Precipitous valleys" refers to mountain torrents.

A mountain torrent represents the most perilous aspect of a valley; by analogy with the main text, this should be understood as a metaphor for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). "Deep and secluded" refers to the valley itself;

since a valley is a deep and secluded place within a mountain range, by analogy with the main text, this should be understood as a metaphor for the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Regarding the fact that [the order of] the five aggregates here does not follow the usual sequence: it is because the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is fundamentally intended to clarify the mind; therefore, he first uses the boundless flow of water as a metaphor.
The analogy: Even if one’s mental ground (*cittabhūmi*) is not yet clear, it can still provide nourishment to the field of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Therefore, it is followed by the analogy of the entire land being thoroughly saturated. When the field of consciousness is nourished, all four aggregates (*skandha*) shall likewise receive benefit.

Hence, it is subsequently compared to mountains, rivers, steep valleys, and secluded depths (the meaning of the following two lines and a half of the verse). Grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, and various plants—both large and small—rely upon [the rain].
The earth, mountains, rivers, and steep, secluded valleys all arise from it; yet once the rain has fallen with thorough penetration, that which arises naturally receives its moisture.
This is a metaphor for sentient beings’ latent minds receiving the Dharma: their capacities and natures naturally receive benefit.

This corresponds to what is said in the long prose section regarding "the moisture universally soaking the herbs, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal plants. The verse speaks of this simultaneity.

The parable of the sudden exposition is concluded. △ Second, the verse on the parable of receiving benefits according to individual capacity, in two parts: first, the verse on causing those who have not yet received [benefits] to receive them;
second, the verse on causing those who have already received them to increase [their realization]. First:

The various grains, sprouts, and crops, as well as the sweet *śrīparṇī* and *drākṣā* grapes—down to the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—all receive moisture according to their respective capacities.

This initial metaphor illustrates how even scattered wholesome roots (*vicitra-kuśalamūla*) receive benefit (supplementing the verse). These scattered wholesome roots are subtle causes, as elucidated in the "Chapter on Past Buddhas" within the "Expedient Means" chapter;
by analogy, they are not limited to merely a hundred types. Therefore, they are illustrated by the metaphor of the "hundred grains" and so forth. Hundred grains.
Regarding this, the *Liwulun* states: "Grain" (*liáng*) is a general term for millet and panicled millet; "rice" (*dào*) is a general term for non-glutinous and glutinous rice;
"beans" (*shū*) is a general term for various legumes. Each of these three categories contains twenty varieties, totaling sixty.

The fruits of vegetables and herbs each also contain twenty varieties, which together constitute the "hundred grains" (*bǎi gù*). Sugarcane and grapes are well known. It is said that all of these are beneficial substances.
Therefore, it is compared to "goodness. The Buddha employs the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings to fulfill their wishes as they desire;
thus, it is compared to the moisture of rain, which leaves nothing unfulfilled. The two lines concerning "dry land" illustrate the benefit received by icchantikas (as a supplementary verse).

Because icchantikas have long opposed the rain of the Dharma and fail to produce roots of goodness, they are compared to dry land. The Buddha possesses the method for transforming the depraved and subduing...

Because it rests upon them, it is likened to a universal drenching. Because hearing the Dharma causes them to turn their minds and give rise to the roots of goodness of the five vehicles, it is likened to medicinal herbs and trees.

Because they practice with diligence and cultivate with courageous non-retrogression, it is likened to flourishing growth. The descent of the clouds is a metaphor for the five vehicles receiving benefit;
the rain that issues from the clouds pervades the entire world. That the water is originally of one flavor is a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching.
The method for delivering sentient beings is fundamentally based on the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Therefore, the prose section establishes a separate chapter on the "Principal Tenet," stating:
"The Dharma he expounds all reaches the ground of omniscience (sarvajñatā-bhūmi). Grasses and trees serve as a metaphor for the capacities of the five vehicles;
since these capacities each have their own distinct groupings, they are likened to a forest. Those who receive the moisture according to their respective portions refers to, for example:

Just as grass and trees receive moisture differently according to the size of their respective portions, so too do those with the capacities of the five vehicles receive benefits individually according to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
As stated in the prose section: "those with small roots, small stalks, small branches, and small leaves;

those with middling roots, middling stalks, middling branches, and middling leaves; and so on, up to those who follow the superior, middling, and inferior [capacities], each having their own [share]."
This refers to "receiving. △ Second, the verse on the analogy of causing [the received] to increase (an explanatory verse):
"All trees—superior, middling, and inferior, etc.—[possess] roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and radiant colors."
"All" refers collectively to medicinal herbs, while "various trees" specifically indicates tree species; taken together, it should be said: "all medicinal herbs and various trees.
This serves as a metaphor for humans, devas, and those of the Small, Initial, and Three Vehicles, as well as the Bodhisattvas of the Final, Sudden, and Perfect Teachings.

This is because the meaning has reached its full depth while the literal expression has not yet done so. Regarding the terms "superior, middling, and inferior," these correspond respectively to the three types of grasses and two types of trees;

the application of the Dharma should be understood accordingly. "According to their size, each attains growth" refers to the three grasses and two trees, each according to its own nature, whether large or small, all attaining growth.
"Roots, stems, branches, and leaves" refers to the three grasses and two trees, each following its own essential character, whether large or small, all attaining growth.

Long. Just as from roots and stems the short grows into the long, the fine becomes coarse, and from branches and leaves the few become many—the small grows into the great—this is a metaphor for the capacities of humans, devas, and the five teachings, according to their respective faculties.

Because faith and precepts further increase faith and precepts, and concentration and wisdom successively give rise to concentration and wisdom; thus, flowers are a metaphor for peace and security in the present life, while fruit is a metaphor for [the future].
In future lives one attains the fruit. The radiance and color are metaphors for the characteristics of the wisdom attained after the fruit.

Building upon the preceding, it is shown that not only do faith and precepts grow and meditative concentration and wisdom advance, but there is also peace and security in the present life, and the attainment of the fruit in future lives.

Furthermore, by means of the light of wisdom, they manifest signs and preach the Dharma, no different from myself now. This verse summarizes the meaning of the prose passage regarding "the rain falling from a single cloud."

According to their respective spiritual dispositions (*gotra*), they attain growth; this is the meaning of the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruits. This concludes the verse on the analogy of receiving benefits according to one's capacity.
△ Third, the verse on the analogy of the teaching being identical while the capacities differ (explanatory verse).
Wherever the single rain reaches, all things obtain freshness and luster; though the moisture is one, each grows and flourishes.
The Buddha, through the Dharma of the One Vehicle, expounds immeasurable Dharma-gates to universally benefit all capacities;
thus it is likened to the reach of the single rain. When all capacities receive this Dharma-rain, each becomes courageous and diligent, as if newly renewed.

Because they are moistened, they are all said to attain a fresh luster. "Physical form and characteristics" (tǐxiàng) refer to the external and are used as a metaphor for present conditions (*nimita*).
"Nature and disposition" (xìngfèn) refer to the internal and are used as a metaphor for past causal seeds (*hetu-bīja*). These causal seeds and conditions may be great or small;

if they are great, one responds with greatness, and if they are small, one responds with smallness. Therefore, the metaphor states: "according to their physical form and characteristics, and the magnitude of their nature and disposition."

Regarding "that which moistens is one": following from the above, although [the rain] can accord with their physical forms and natures—be they large or small—in investigating the reason why it is able to moisten them, it is found to be nothing other than rain of a single flavor.
This serves as a metaphor for how the Dharma, though proclaimed according to capacities and faculties, is ultimately of one essence.
As for the Buddha’s original intent, it is solely the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as expressed in the prose section by the phrase "moistened by a single rain.
The reason the verse does not mention "growing on a single ground" is that the nature of the mind (*cittatva*) is one and thus easily understood.
That they each flourish and grow differently—referring to the three types of grasses and two types of trees—is a metaphor for the diverse capacities of sentient beings receiving [the teaching].
The benefits are each distinct. This refers to what is stated in the prose: "All grasses and trees each have their own differences. The explanation by means of the analogy is now complete.

△ Third, the verses that apply the Dharma to illustrate the three points: first, one verse on the simultaneous and instantaneous manifestation; second, two verses on receiving benefit according to individual capacities;
third, one verse on the identity of the teaching and the diversity of capacities. The first of these has three parts: first, one verse on manifesting the body to bestow compassion.
The first two verses extol his virtues and address the assembly; the third verse praises his capacity and describes his teaching of the Dharma. The first (briefly stated):
The Buddha likewise appears in the world like a great cloud that universally covers all.
The first two lines correctly apply the Dharma [to the analogy]. The latter two lines restate the metaphorical text. The prose section states: "The Tathāgata is also like this;
he appears in the world," which corresponds to the meaning of the aforementioned first two lines. It further states:
"Like a great cloud arising, even pervading the trichiliocosm," which corresponds to the meaning of the aforementioned latter two lines. △ Second, the verse of praise.
The Virtuous One summons the assembly:
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings (up to: constantly acting as a causal condition for the Mahāyāna.

First, the source of the manifestation of virtue (supplementary verse): Appearing in the world takes the salvation of sentient beings as its task; saving sentient beings takes the exposition of reality as its task.
Fundamentally, I wish to expound the truth; fearing that divergent explanations might cause confusion, I shall hereafter extol my own virtues. This is the reason for praising these virtues.
From the words "The Great Sage" (*da shèng*) downward, the long prose is formally versified. Furthermore, there are two meanings: first, the extolling of his virtuous titles.

(Excerpted Verse) Because he has realized the true principle, he calls himself the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*); because he is not a worldly false teacher, he calls himself the World-Honored One (*bhagavat*).
Desiring that the multitude come to take refuge in him, he designates his title based on his virtues; thus, amidst the assembly, he proclaims:

"I am the Tathāgata, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings. Among the ten titles, the first three constitute the framework, the next six constitute the details, and the final one serves as a summary.
This section provides a summary of the headings and details. Here, I shall cite the opening of each heading and detail as a model for the rest. Thus it says: "The Tathāgata, the one with two feet.
"The one with two feet" refers to the one who has perfected both knowledge (*vidyā*) and conduct (*caraṇa*). This appears below in the *Gāthā on the Praise of Compassion*.

The Buddha appears in the world, his compassion universally covering all; thus it is said he is "like a great cloud. His Dharma rain falls evenly, causing those who suffer to leave suffering behind and attain happiness;
thus it is said he "saturates and moistens the withered. Because sentient beings have long dwelt amidst manifold sufferings, they lack the means to save themselves;
their roots of goodness do not sprout, like grass that has already dried. The sprouts of the Path do not grow, like wood that has already become parched.

The meaning of the verse is explained in the prose: those who have not attained peace are made to attain peace; those who have not attained cessation are made to attain cessation.
