"Peaceful bliss" is no different: it refers both to the worldly bliss of humans and devas, as well as the two types of supramundane bliss of nirvāṇa.

According to the prose commentary (*chángxíng*), there are further praises of "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*) and praises of the two meanings of "essence and function" (*tǐ-yòng*), but these have all been omitted here.

When the various heavens are mentioned, the command for the assembly to listen to the Dharma is proclaimed at length; this includes both devas and humans, as well as asuras, though the text does not manifest them all simultaneously.

This is for the sake of following the sequence of the verses. As for the instruction to listen with a single-minded focus, it is because there is a fear that the mind might give rise to hesitation and fail to comply with the words.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; those who see, hear, and rejoice in this will not have done so in vain.
Therefore, he teaches that all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One;
even his self-designation as the "Unsurpassed Honored One" reveals his intention to inspire others toward excellence by showing that he is the World-Honored One to whom none can equal.

Furthermore, it shows that there is no other person worthy of being beheld besides him, and it demonstrates that he appears in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. Thus, it reveals that there is no one else [to be relied upon] apart from him.
This is the place where peace is attained; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata personally clarifies the teaching so that one may reach and behold him.

"Amṛta" (sweet dew) refers to the medicine of immortality, which serves as a metaphor for the Dharma’s ability to give rise to goodness. "Pure Meaning" (*śubhārtha*) is a designation for being free from defilement.
This reveals that the Dharma can extinguish evil; the extinction of evil and the arising of goodness constitute matters of peace and security.

Desiring that all may attain this together, it is said, "for the sake of the great assembly. Though many provisional gateways are shown according to the capacities of beings, the clarity of the fundamental principle is in fact without duality;
thus it is said, "its Dharma is of one single flavor. As for liberation (*vimukti*), it is sovereign freedom from bondage; it is the function of the essence itself, which is *nirvāṇa*.
Nirvana is quiescent extinction and unconditioned; it is the essence of liberation itself.
Essence and function are mutually identical, merging into a single flavor—this is what is called the Dharma of Great Sovereignty and Great Tranquility.
Because the Buddha, with a single sound, suddenly expounds immeasurable Dharma-gates, it is called the "Wondrous Sound. These immeasurable Dharma-gates do not depart from liberation and nirvana.
Therefore, this meaning is stated: if one attains the root, one should naturally become a Buddha in this very moment;
yet if one obtains the branches, one may likewise enter the Way by relying on conditions. Thus it is said: "Constantly act as a cause and condition for the Mahāyāna.

This is the Tathāgata’s own clarification of the matter of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, desiring that all shall come to take refuge. The Long Discourse says: "You gods and humans..."
"The assembly of asuras should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma"—this refers precisely to this meaning.
△ Third, the verse on teaching according to the capacity (an extensive verse based on the meaning).
I contemplate all things as universally equal... (up to) ...equally raining down the rain of Dharma without weariness.

According to the beginning of this section in the prose version (*chángxíng*), there is a passage stating that "countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings came to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma";
this text should also be present here, though it has been omitted by the translator. The Tathāgata’s compassionate eye is without...
[Objection: Sentient beings and the Buddha-nature are non-dual; therefore, it is said, "I observe that all are universally equal.
Because they are equal, who is distant and who is near? What is hostile and what is kin? Therefore, it is said that there is no sense of "self" and "other," nor any mind of love or hatred.
Because there is no attachment, one does not speak excessively out of private partiality; therefore it is said, "I have no greedy clinging.
Because there is no aversion, one does not speak sparingly out of private rejection; therefore it is said, "Nor is there any limitation or obstruction.
Since these two faults are absent, at all times a single voice is expounded instantaneously; therefore it is said, "Always for the sake of all, speaking with equality."
The Dharma: Because he teaches the Dharma with equanimity, he speaks in this same manner for one person as he does for many;
from the beginning, he does not vary the detail or brevity based on the number of listeners, for he always acts for the sake of all.
Just as he speaks at one time, so he continues to expound the Dharma constantly, never withdrawing or deferring due to other matters.
Whether walking or coming, sitting or standing—whatever activity they may engage in—they always speak in this manner.
They never grow weary or fatigued due to movement or stillness. According to this, all sentient beings alike receive the rain of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that they "satisfy the world," like rain that universally moistens all. "Noble and humble" refers to those with rank and those without;

"high and low" refers to those dwelling in positions of honor and those dwelling in inferior stations—this refers to the assembly of devas and humans. Those who uphold the precepts obtain happiness, while those who violate the precepts fall into suffering—this refers to the assembly of the virtuous and the evil.
The two assemblies of the ordained are able to maintain dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), whereas the two assemblies of the laity do not [fully maintain] such deportment.

[They are] complete. These are the fourfold assembly. Those with right view have already taken refuge in the True Dharma; those with false views still revere heterodox teachings—these are the internal and external assemblies.
Those of sharp faculties are able to cultivate the Mahāyāna; those of dull faculties remain stuck in the Lesser Path—these are the great and small assemblies.
Thus, within these assemblies there are six pairs, and when their capacities are divided, they form twelve types. [The following is] the prose section.

These are all subsumed under the categories of sharp and dull faculties. Therefore, it is said that at that time, the Tathāgata observes that among these sentient beings, within each of the six pairs [of faculties], the former are sharp while the latter are dull. Regarding the "equal raining of the Dharma rain":

he expounds it instantaneously with a single voice, universally responding to those of high and low capacity without weariness; this is because, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he forgets himself from beginning to end.

[The Buddha] was weary. As the *Dīrgha-āgama* states: "He preached the Dharma according to what [the beings] were capable of receiving. This concludes the verse on the simultaneous and instantaneous exposition. II.

Verse on Receiving Benefits According to Capabilities (divided into two parts): 1. Verse on causing those who have not yet received [benefit] to receive it. 2. Verse on causing those who have already received it to increase [their realization].
The first part (an extensive verse based on the meaning).
"Of all sentient beings who hear my Dharma... (up to) "...just as those grasses and trees each receive nourishment differently.
This first section provides a general indication of the benefits received. "All sentient beings" refers collectively to all capacities, including the noble and the humble, the high and the low;

this is what is meant by the "various and immeasurable" mentioned in the prose. Regarding "those who hear my Dharma": "Dharma" here refers to the teaching tailored to specific capacities. "Hear" means...
"Will certainly give rise to joy" refers to what is stated in the prose: "causing all to be filled with delight.
"According to the capacity for what is received" means that according to their intellectual power, what they receive differs. "Abiding in the various stages" means abiding in various distinct stages;
this refers to what is stated in the prose: "swiftly obtaining excellent benefit. "Or situated in the lower [stages]" refers to the sequential and individual combinations of persons.
The people and the devas of the heavens—those of the wheel-turning lineage become kings of men, and those of the Śakra-Brahmā lineage become kings of gods.
Although these beings can temporarily escape the evil realms, they still endure the suffering of birth and death; they are like small herbs that merely treat seasonal ailments.
No. Because they treat serious illnesses, they are called "small medicinal herbs. This combines humans and devas with the "small" category.

Knowing there is no [self] below refers to the Small Vehicle of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*). Śrāvakas realize the principle of the emptiness of birth through the wisdom of the emptiness of birth; hence it is said they "know the untainted dharmas" (*anāsravadharma*).
Relying on these untainted dharmas, they realize the untainted fruit; hence it is said they "are able to attain nirvāṇa," giving rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
And "the wise" refers to the functions realized upon the fruits of the śrāvaka stage; this is explained in the commentary on the passage in the *Dṛṣṭānta-parivarta* where the Dharma is applied.

The pratyekabuddha delights in solitude and sublime tranquility; thus it is said they dwell alone in mountain forests, seeking spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said they constantly practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Because they deeply understand the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of all phenomena, it is said they attain the realization of a pratyekabuddha. If one follows the meaning [of the text] in its proper order...

The text states: "It should say 'attaining the realization of a pratyekabuddha'; this is merely an inverted expression. Although these two [vehicles] are able to exhaustively sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), they still leave behind the *parināmika-śarīra* (the transformation body).
This is like medium-grade medicinal herbs that can treat severe illnesses but cannot cure long-term chronic ailments; therefore, they are called "medium medicinal herbs.
This combines the two vehicles of the Small Teaching with the medium-grade herbs. Regarding the three phrases on seeking the world, these refer to the Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching.

“Sā. This distinguishes [them] from those of the Two Vehicles who take little as sufficient; thus it says, “seeking the state of the World-Honored One, I shall become a Buddha,” which marks the initial arousal of the Mahāyāna vow.
“Practicing diligence and meditative concentration” marks the initial establishment of Mahāyāna practice.
Since Mahāyāna practice values non-retrogression, it is described in terms of diligence and meditative concentration. Although this assembly is able...

It counteracts partiality and deficiency; yet, there remains a degree of attachment to the Dharma according to one's capacity. Just as the aforementioned herbs can treat chronic illnesses, they do not exhaust the root of the disease;
therefore, they are called "superior medicinal herbs. This identifies the Bodhisattvas of the Initial Teaching with the aforementioned herbs.
Furthermore, as for those below, the Bodhisattvas of the Final and Sudden Teachings deeply clarify the ultimate reality in the Final Teaching and are not deluded by other vehicles; therefore—

To speak of "devoting one's whole heart to the Buddha-way" refers to self-benefit. To realize that śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas devoid of nature shall all attain Buddhahood, and thus to constantly practice compassion, refers to benefiting others.

In the Sudden Teaching, it is said that when not a single thought arises, the true nature is revealed alone; hence it is said, "One knows for oneself that one becomes a Buddha. This is taught without relying on the gradual progression of stages.

Therefore, it is said that they are "decisive and without doubt. Although these two possess the meaning of benefiting others, they consist only of negation and illumination, and thus still have limitations;

they are like the shade of a small tree, which is slight and narrow. Hence, it is said, "this is called a small tree. This identifies the *zhongdun* (gradual-instantaneous) Bodhisattva with the small tree.
As for those who "abide below," these are the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), whose nature is perfectly interfused and unimpeded.
The wondrous function is inconceivable: bodies, lands, atoms, and body hairs mutually encompass one another;
neither requiring deliberate effort nor involving laborious application, they manifest spontaneously. Thus it is said that he "abides in supernatural powers. Whatever he speaks, [is thus].
They have all reached the ground of wisdom. Seeing and hearing serve as the seeds; they transcend the eight difficulties and the stages of the ten grounds.
With understanding and practice embodied, they perfect the fruit of kalpas in a single lifetime. Where there is delusion, it is immediately shattered; there is no birth that is not saved.

Thus it is said that they turn the non-retrogressive wheel, delivering immeasurable billions and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. These multitudes are the mutual fusion of concealment and illumination, manifesting in response to conditions.
It leaves no trace. Just as the shade of a great tree is vast and extensive, it is therefore called a "great tree.
This identifies the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) with the great tree. The Buddha’s level gaze concludes by clarifying their distinctiveness:

the Tathāgata teaches all dharmas with an impartial mind, and because all dharmas are equal, it is said that he is like a rain of a single flavor. Sentient beings, however, [respond] according to their diverse natures...

One receives a single dharma, yet that single dharma is also diverse; therefore it is said, "like those grasses and trees," which each receive their nourishment differently. "Receiving" (稟) is synonymous with "accepting" (受).

This verse concludes the section on causing those who have not yet received [the teaching] to receive it. △ Second, the verse on causing those who have already received it to increase [their practice].
The Buddha used this analogy as a skillful means to provide instruction (up to the point where it says): "This is called a great tree that attains growth.

First, he refuted errors and encouraged progress (supplementary verse). Because the preceding passage stated that according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, there may be those who cling to difference and become confused about sameness;
thus, they might give rise to the sorrow of harboring delusion and being cut off from the [Buddha’s] portion. Furthermore, because the preceding passage stated that the Buddha is impartial...

Thus it is said. Just as with a rain of a single flavor, there may be those who, fearing attachment to sameness while being deluded regarding difference, give rise to the view of "considering a little to be sufficient.

Therefore, the first six phrases serve to preclude this. The intent is that by means of this analogy, the Buddha skillfully reveals to you all that the Tathāgata’s various expressions originally expound only a single Dharma, and in reality, there is no differentiation.

"Distinct. This refutes the error of clinging to difference while being deluded about sameness, and simultaneously makes it known that the ground upon which you yourselves abide is, within the Buddha’s wisdom and insight, like a single drop in the ocean;
in truth, you have not yet reached the ultimate. This refutes the error of clinging to sameness while being deluded about difference.
Once these two errors have been refuted, those who harbor delusions and remain separated from the goal should certainly exert themselves with diligence until they attain it.
Those who consider a little to be sufficient should likewise strive to seek more; therefore, the next four lines exhort them. The intent is this:
although your portion of the Buddha’s wisdom may be but a single drop in the ocean, my raining down of the Dharma-rain is originally intended to fill the entire world.
Furthermore, you must not disparage yourselves as mere withered sprouts or rotten seeds because of that one drop. Moreover, the Tathāgata...
Although various words and phrases may be used to expound a single Dharma, that single-flavored Dharma must likewise be practiced according to one's own capacity;
furthermore, one must not, because of praise for this single Dharma, become like the River God or the frog in the well.

As it says below, "As with those [beings]," which precisely accords with the preceding metaphor (a broad verse summarizing the meaning). Furthermore, there are three meanings. The first, which reiterates the preceding metaphor, can be understood. All...
The Buddha descends and unifies them through the Dharma, causing all those in the world—here, "the world" refers to the world of sentient beings—to universally attain fullness.
"Fullness" means ultimate perfection; it signifies that they are unified so as to gradually increase, flourish, and become excellent.
The final two lines explain the meaning of "universally attaining fullness," which is what is meant by the term "manifestation" in the prose section.
"May the world be at peace; may they be reborn in favorable realms; and so forth, until—according to their respective capacities—they gradually attain entry into the Path.

Regarding the passage "The Śrāvakas, etc.," three examples are cited (based on the previous verse concerning those who have not yet received [the teaching], which mentions "three types of grass and two types of trees" treated both individually and collectively; here, only the middle-sized grass and the small and large trees are combined).

The intention is that since they grow together when conditions for growth arise, this can be understood by analogy. Furthermore, there are three meanings: first, the combination with the growth of medicinal herbs. Having already...

They uphold the dharmas that take the Truths as their object; hence they are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Constantly harboring the aspiration to proceed toward quiescence, they are said to dwell in mountain forests.
Having already accomplished what was to be done in the present life, they are said to abide in their final bodies. This is their own specific stage.

As for those who hear the Dharma, they advance to hear the Initial Teaching of the Six Pāramitās. Those who have attained the fruit turn their minds and transform themselves into Mahāyāna practitioners.
This is progressive advancement. Based on this, humans and devas may also be transformed into Lesser Sages; likewise, the Initial Teaching may be transformed into the Final and Sudden Teachings.
Just as those of medium or inferior capacity can be transformed into superior levels, so too can those of the smallest capacity be transformed into the medium level.
Even the small grasses can grow into trees; therefore, it is said, "These are called medicinal herbs.
That they "each attain growth" means that the intent applies to both the small grasses and the large grasses—taking one as an example for the other—to collectively synthesize them with the whole.

As for "if those below," this refers to the growth of the small trees. The Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) consists of single-minded devotion to the Buddha-way and the constant practice of compassion. The Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao)...
Knowing for oneself that one will become a Buddha, with certainty and without doubt, is thus called "firm wisdom. This is the stage of self-benefit (*svārtha*).

When this is transformed into the Perfect [Teaching], one deeply understands that the three realms are like an illusion; exercising great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one turns the wheel of non-retrogression.
Thus it is said, "thoroughly penetrating the three realms. Using this to benefit others truly serves as the adornment of the fruit of Buddhahood; hence it is said, "seeking the supreme."
This refers to spiritual progress. To express this through a metaphor: it is like a small tree that gradually grows into a great tree;

therefore, it is said, "this is called a small tree that attains growth. Furthermore, there is the "lower" [category], which corresponds to the growth of a great tree—the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

By means of the illusion-like samādhi, one gives rise to the supernatural powers of playful mastery; hence it is said that there are further those who dwell in dhyāna and attain the power of supernatural faculties.

This refers to the stage of self-perfection (*svabhūmi*). When they turn toward Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and hear the teaching on the Vajra Path, they are able to empty the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
Therefore it is said: "He hears that all dharmas are empty. Because he hears that dharmas are empty, he knows for himself that he will attain Buddhahood before long;

therefore it is said: "His heart is filled with great joy. Because his heart is joyful, light shines forth to make it known throughout the ten directions; therefore it is said: "He emits countless rays of light."

Those who receive this light all give rise to the bodhicitta; therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings are delivered. This is the stage of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*). To speak by way of analogy:
it is like a great tree that has grown until it reaches the clouds. Therefore, it is called a "great tree" because it has attained such growth.
According to what was stated previously—that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is like the rising of a great cloud—it is now equated with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The Buddha is likened to a tree that towers above the clouds; thus, from beginning to end, the principles are perfectly established. The section on "Verses on Receiving Benefit According to Capabilities" concludes.
△ Third, Verses on the Identity of the Teaching and the Diversity of Capabilities (a brief summary according to the meaning).
"In this way, the Dharma taught by Kāśyapa Buddha [extends] until it moistens the flowers of humanity, each attaining its fruit.
'In this way, Kāśyapa' means: 'It is just as I have taught,' O Kāśyapa; you should know this. This is the concluding address that summarizes what has preceded.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is fundamentally but a single vehicle (ekayāna); therefore, it is said, "it is like a great cloud," because—
The rain of the single flavor falls, and the Dharma covers those of the five vehicles; each receives benefit according to their capacity.
Just as rain moistens grasses and trees, causing flowers to bloom immediately, it is said that it "moistens the flowers of humanity. These flowers gradually grow and increasingly ripen.
Just as grasses and trees that have already blossomed further bear fruit, it is said that they "each attain the formation of fruit. As stated in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Longer Commentary):
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor; this refers to what is called "the Dharma preached by the Buddha.

It is likened to a great cloud that rains with water of a single flavor. The *Da-changxing* (Longer Version) states: "There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s Dharma, obtain merit of which they themselves are not consciously aware.
This refers to the moisture nourishing the flowers of humanity so that each attains its fruit. While the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.

The remainder is omitted from the verses. The verses on the actual teaching and its opening are now concluded. △ Second, the verses on the concluding praise and consolation (this section of the "Verses on Meaning" is divided into two parts):

first, one verse that承接 (takes up) the preceding [discussion] to resolve doubts; second, verses that formally conclude with praise. Regarding the first: [A doubt arises: "If the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like rain of a single flavor,"...
"Why are there various different explanations using causes, conditions, and parables, rather than simply proclaiming the One Vehicle today as is done now? To this, the commentary explains:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that these various causes and conditions (up to 'this is my skillful means') apply to all Buddhas as well."
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: through causes, conditions, and parables, he has generally revealed the Buddha-way.

Although these are explained differently, how could they hinder the single flavor? As for why it was not revealed explicitly today, it was because I employed the power of skillful means to protect the capacities and circumstances [of beings]. Not only am I thus now, but all Buddhas are likewise. Nevertheless...
In this section, the presentation of doubts and the resolution of those doubts differ somewhat from the prose (*dīrgha-paṅkti*), as each follows the natural flow of the preceding meaning.
△ Second, the verse concludes with a formal eulogy.
Now I shall explain for you the most ultimate reality (yāvad... krameṇa śikṣamāṇāḥ sarve bhaviṣyanti buddhāḥ).
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: you have already been able to understand and know the various teachings of the Buddhas given according to their suitability.
Now, for you Śrāvakas, I shall explain the most ultimate reality. What is meant by the most ultimate reality? First:
You should know that all the assembly of śrāvakas have not attained parinirvāṇa; for what was spoken according to their needs is provisional and not ultimate.
Second, you should know that the practice you all engage in is the bodhisattva path; for what was spoken according to their needs is itself provisional yet ultimate.
As for why those who are already bodhisattvas do not attain Buddhahood, it is solely because they are unwilling to cultivate [the path].
It is only through one's own neglect that [the potential] is lost. If you practice and study gradually from this point forward, you shall all attain Buddhahood. Should you not exert yourselves?
Thus ends the seal of authorization by the Tathāgata.
△ Third: Bestowing the Prediction of Enlightenment (The Title reads:
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Six: "The Chapter on the Prediction").
This chapter, from beginning to end, speaks entirely of the matter of bestowing predictions; therefore, it is titled "Bestowing Predictions. [Section Heading]
The commentary states: The Sanskrit term *vyākaraṇa* is translated here as "prediction" (*jùjì*). The *Saṃmitīya-śāstra* says: "A prediction is a prophetic utterance.
The *Dàchéng shìyì* (Great Vehicle Exegesis) states: "Prophetic" (*chàn*) means "verification"; that is, a prediction given in the present life is to be verified in the future.

I, the humble writer, consider that the character for "bestowal" (*shòu*) refers to the teaching, while the character for "record" (*jì*) refers to the capacity [of the recipient]. This means that the Buddha, by means of the adornments of the eons and lands...
He bestowed these matters one by one, causing his sons to engrave them in their hearts so that they might realize them as proof in the future.
What is commonly referred to as "sacred speech" (*āgama*) is called "bestowal" (*śāsana*); when the fruit accords with the cause, it is termed "recording" (*vyākaraṇa*).

There are five distinct meanings within this chapter: first, to demonstrate that although the principle is realized instantaneously, practice must necessarily be gradual, as in the bestowing of predictions upon the four sons.
1. It contains the statement that causes are practiced throughout kalpas; 2.

it demonstrates that by practicing and training gradually, all shall attain Buddhahood, as in the bestowal of predictions upon the four sons, wherein they all possess the names of the resultant qualities; 3.

it clarifies the excellence of the resultant qualities so as to inspire aspiration and acceptance, as in the bestowal of predictions upon the four sons, which fully reveals the superiority of the adornments of the kalpa and the land; 4. [The fourth point].

To clarify that realization arises through the mind, one must record the practice and realization, just as the three sons requested a record, saying that they would only eat the royal meal after receiving the king's instructions.
Fifth, to manifest the profundity of the cause and the excellence of the conditions, this serves to attract those of inferior faculties.
As the verse at the end of this chapter states: "My disciples, endowed with majestic power, numbering five hundred, shall all receive their predictions.
Furthermore, I shall now explain the karmic conditions from past lives concerning myself and you; listen well.
Because it possesses these five meanings, it is called the "Chapter on Predictions. As for the matter of predictions, they are likewise given in accordance with conditions.

This is a provisional designation. Within the reality of the *bhūtakoṭi*, such things do not exist at all. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: "As there is no arising or ceasing, one knows there is no prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
The *Saṃghāṭasūtra* says: "I vow never to hear the name of 'prediction'. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Prediction is a dharma of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That we now specifically speak of "bestowing a prediction" is because it is a matter of mind sealing mind; there is neither bestower nor recipient, yet we forcibly apply the term "bestowal."
This is a record of names. (The sūtra text is divided into two parts: First, the bestowal of the prediction upon Kāśyapa; second, the bestowal of the predictions upon the three sons.

The first [section] has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first [of these] has three parts: first, attaining the fruit through the cause; second, the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma; third, the adornment of the primary and secondary [environments]. The first [part]:

At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken these verses (up to the point where) the land was named Radiant Virtue and the eon was named Great Adornment—having first undergone the cultivation of causes throughout the eon—declared:
"As for undertaking this matter, it truly depends on the individual’s own resolve. To entrust the family inheritance, it must be certified by all;
therefore, he necessarily addresses the great assembly, proclaiming these words: 'I pay my respects and behold...'"
"The various Buddhas and so forth" refers to the practice of self-benefit. "Extensively proclaiming the phrases of the Buddhas" refers to the practice of benefiting others.
Now, Kāśyapa, even for a person such as this, who possesses such understanding, it is still necessary to practice the causes through kalpas in this manner.
How could one dare to abruptly abandon such cultivation? At the very least, one shall attain the realization of the fruit and be fully endowed with the two benefits. First.
Having fulfilled his life's purpose, it is said that in his final body he attained Buddhahood.
As for his specific title "Radiant One" (Prabhāsa), during his causal stage he continued the light by using purple-gold to paint the image of a Buddha;

from that time onward, his body has always been perfectly full as a mass of purple-gold light. He currently manifests as an Arhat named Pīṭhaka (Drinking Light), and his future fruit-title shall likewise be...
This does not contradict the causal stage. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s wisdom dispels ignorance and delusion just as sunlight dispels darkness;

therefore, it is designated by the term "Radiance" (*Prabhā*). "Land" (*kṣetra*) pertains to geography; because this land produces many wise persons, it is named "Virtue of Radiance" (*Prabhāśrī*). "Eon" (*kalpa*) pertains to celestial time;
because during this time both the primary and secondary realms are exceptionally sublime, it is named "Great Adornment" (*Mahāvyūha*). These [terms]...
This is also due to what was induced by his vows and practices prior to attaining Buddhahood. △ Second, the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma:
the Buddha’s lifespan lasts for twelve small kalpas (up to) the period of the Semblance Dharma, which also remains for twenty small kalpas.

Dacheng said: "The body of the Pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing. That the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve kalpas is merely a manifestation according to the power of his great compassionate vows.
That the teachings of the True and Semblance Dharma decline after twenty kalpas is merely a matter of flourishing and waning in accordance with the karmic responses of sentient beings.
The Buddha-body of the nature of reality remains inherently unchanged throughout this interval."
△ Third, the adornment of the environment and the body.
The realm is magnificently adorned and free from all impurities and evils (up to: although there are Māras and their followers, they all protect the Buddha-dharma).

First is the adornment of the environmental retribution (*niṣyanda-vipāka*). Because one cultivates pure conduct to adorn the merit of the resultant state, one accordingly brings about the magnificent adornment of the realm.
"Free from all impurities and evils" refers to the two phrases concerning tiles and rubble; these are the characteristics of impurity and evil.

Because he gives rise to an impartial mind to deliver sentient beings, his land is felt to be level and even, without elevations or depressions; "pits, hollows, and mounds" are precisely the characteristics of unevenness.
The four phrases concerning *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli) have their meaning seen in the passage on Śāriputra’s prediction. [He] scatters various jewels...
As for the phrase "Flowers: Universally Pure," this is also brought about by the fact that, based on the ground, the Great Dharma was extensively proclaimed;
through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it was scattered upon the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to attain purity. As for the description of that land below:

its primary retribution is adorned, the Three Vehicles are complete, and those of superior goodness assemble there. Those born there have a method for attaining the correct path and are free from demonic obstacles.

Thus, one is freed from all afflictions and disturbances; for those who give birth [to this teaching], the Path of Righteousness is easy to practice. When the Māras protect the Dharma, they possess the power to crush the heterodox;

for those who give birth [to this teaching], evil views will be transformed through their influence. This, too, is the result of preaching the Dharma according to the conditions of the ground to save sentient beings, and of assisting the Buddha to propagate his transformation.
The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
[The Main Verse Section is divided into three parts: 1. A verse on attaining the fruit through the causes of practice. 2. A verse on the adornment of the primary and secondary [realms].
3. A verse on the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma. First (the verse on the meaning):
He addressed the bhikṣus: "By means of my Buddha-eye... I have attained Buddhahood in this final body.
The first verse concerns the cultivation of causes throughout kalpas. The phrase "seeing with the Buddha-eye" reveals that what is seen is unerring.

The phrase "passing through incalculable kalpas" reveals the long duration of cultivating the causes. The subsequent passage beginning with "in a future life" precisely clarifies these incalculable kalpas.
This refers to the deeds performed therein. To behold the various Buddhas and offer them worship constitutes the fulfillment of merit (*puṇya-pāda*).

To cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom constitutes the fulfillment of wisdom (*jñāna-pāda*). Furthermore, regarding the term "pure cultivation" (*viśuddha-brahmacarya*) within the context of pure conduct, it means to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings with a pure mind;
this is what is meant in the *Dīrgha Āgama* by the "extensive proclamation of the immeasurable great Dharma of all Buddhas."

...Furthermore, "making offerings" below means that one shall attain the realization of the fruit. The four lines on "making offerings" conclude the preceding passage on the sufficiency of merit and wisdom;
it means that after having made offerings to the Buddha, one simultaneously cultivates supreme wisdom therein.

That one attains Buddhahood in the final body is because the cause is perfected and the fruit naturally becomes full. △ Second, the verse on the adornment of the primary and secondary [realms] (this verse anticipates and supplements [the following]).
[Verse]. Its land is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground... [up to] ...such that even with the divine eye one could not count it.

The first verse concerns the adornment of the *pratyaya-bhājana* (the external environment). The phrase "its land is pure" corresponds to the detailed prose description of the adornments of the realm. There is no [further elaboration].
It signifies the eradication of all defilements and evils. Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, truly worthy of the description "far removed from dust and free from defilement.

It abounds with various jeweled trees, providing a place for strolling and elegant repose; moreover, they are arranged along the sides of the paths in orderly rows, intersecting according to principle.
Golden cords demarcate the roads, so that those who travel upon them do not lose their way. Therefore, all who are born in this land and behold such a scene cannot help but rejoice.
Filled with deep emotion, he thereupon gave rise to the bodhicitta. As for "constantly emitting fine incense," it means that celestial incense is wafted forth from time to time without interruption.
As for "scattering various famous flowers," it means that celestial blossoms are constantly showered everywhere; moreover, they are endowed with all manner of wonders and marvels.
It is regarded as an adornment; how much more so, then, that his land is level and even, without mounds or pits.
This is certainly brought about by past causes, yet it is truly realized through the present mind. As it is said: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure."
"When the mind is level, the world is level. From "All the bodhisattvas" below, the verse praises the adornment of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
The first two lines praise the bodhisattvas of that land, numbering in the immeasurable thousands of billions. The four lines beginning with "their minds" are not present in the prose section;

they are added as a supplementary verse based on the underlying meaning. When the mind is harmonious and supple, one constantly accords with the capacities of others; when spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) are great, one responds perfectly and without restriction.
By upholding the Mahāyāna, one shall never again regress. Based on this, these individuals belong to the eighth bhūmi and above, distinguishing them from those in the stages prior to the bhūmis.
As for "those with outflows exhausted" (anāsrava), their fetters as a disciple have been severed, distinguishing them from those still in training (śaikṣa).

As for "those in their final body," the fetters of the fruit still remain, distinguishing them from those who have entered the quiescence of the śrāvaka vehicle. From this point onward, they turn away from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, becoming capable of succeeding to the legacy of the Dharma King.

Therefore, he is called a son of the Dharma King. Based on this, he is a manifestation of great power (*mahopāya*), and is not to be compared with those who follow the path of a śrāvaka through actual practice.
Furthermore, he is "incalculable," meaning that his name cannot be reckoned or counted, even by a bodhisattva.
He is "beyond the reach of the divine eye," meaning that the divine eyes of the lesser sages (*hīnayāna-ārya*) cannot enumerate or know his number. As stated in the prose section:
The assembly of śrāvakas is likewise incalculable. According to the prose section (*gadya*), there is further text concerning the absence of demonic interference (*mārakarman*) and so forth;

that it is not fully included here is because, given the superior virtue of those bodhisattvas and the excellence of the śrāvakas’ resolve, demonic interference has subsided, and thus it need not be explicitly stated as it can be understood by implication.
△ Third, the verse on the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma (a retrospective verse combined with a supplementary verse).
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas... [up to] the World-Honored One Radiant Light; such are the details.
The first part is a verse summarizing the lifespan, while the final two lines are a supplementary verse providing a general conclusion.

This means that by summarizing the aforementioned matters concerning the primary and secondary [rewards], it causes [beings] to give rise to joy. Having finished bestowing the prediction upon Kāśyapa, △ second, the bestowal of predictions upon the three sons has two parts.
First, the three disciples request that [the teaching] be recorded; second, the Tathāgata grants it. Regarding the first two [sections]: first, the sūtra-author describes the ritual setting;
second, they speak verses to present their request. First:
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and so forth... gazing up at the Honored Countenance, they did not for a moment turn their eyes away.

The four disciples presented their respective understandings and realizations equally, yet the Tathāgata alone bestowed a prediction upon Kāśyapa; therefore, Maudgalyāyana and the others were all struck with trepidation.
"Trepidation" refers to an appearance of being startled, fearful, and unsettled. "Joining palms and gazing up" describes the manner of requesting a prediction.
"That his eyes did not for a moment leave [the Buddha]" indicates the intensity of his longing for a prediction, as he feared that the Tathāgata might still neglect him.

△ Second, the exposition of verses to present the request, in five parts: first, the introductory verse; second, the formal request; third, the presentation of a simile; fourth, the application to the Dharma.
The fivefold invitation. First:
they speak the verse with a unified voice.
Although their voices may not necessarily be identical, because their intent is the same, they speak together; thus it is called "unified. Second: the formal invitation.
The Great Hero and Fierce World-Honored One, the Dharma King of all Śākyas... [until] removing heat and attaining coolness.
He enters the burning house directly and powerfully draws out sentient beings; thus he is called the Great Hero and Fierce World-Honored One.

Originally born of the Śākya clan, he now holds the seal of the Dharma; thus he is called the Dharma King of all Śākyas. Whether teaching through the Dharma or through parables, it all proceeds from his profound compassion and diligent care.
Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] takes pity on us, teaching both the provisional and the ultimate, and there is nothing therein that does not instruct us toward the attainment of Buddhahood;
hence, it is said that he bestows the voice of the Buddha. Fearing that the Tathāgata would ultimately not believe us and would never grant us a prediction of enlightenment, it is said:
"If you know my heart and grant me this prediction, then even a rotten seed attaining Buddhahood is no less than encountering rain during a severe drought"; thus, it is like nectar.
Sprinkling the mind; removing heat and bringing coolness. △ Third, the explanation of the analogy:
It is like coming from a land of famine and suddenly encountering the meal of a great king (until) only then daring to eat.

Previously, they practiced the Lesser Path and did not obtain the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma; thus, they are likened to those who have come from a land of famine—a "land of famine" meaning a country where there is no food.

Now, hearing the Great Dharma and being permitted that Śrāvakas may attain Buddhahood, they are likened to those who suddenly encounter a king’s meal—a "king’s meal" meaning a meal bestowed by the king. Because they have not received a prediction (vyākaraṇa) by name, they do not dare to accept it.
One must engrave this upon one's heart and prepare it oneself; therefore, the analogy says that the mind is still filled with doubt and fear, and one does not yet dare to eat.

Only after receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Tathāgata can one gain self-confidence. Because one attains the fruit by relying on the cause, the analogy says that once one receives the king’s command, one then dares to eat.
△ Fourth, the application to the Dharma.
"We are also like this; whenever we contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna [until] we finally attain joyful peace and happiness.

The first four lines correspond to the previous passage on coming from a land of famine. The two lines beginning with "Although we hear" correspond to the previous passage on suddenly encountering the king’s banquet.

The two phrases beginning with "My mind... correspond to the previous passage: "My mind was still filled with doubt and fear, and I did not dare to eat immediately. The two phrases beginning with "If I were granted... correspond to the previous passage:
"If I had received the King’s instruction, only then would I have dared to eat. Regarding the phrase "Swiftly at peace and happy," this happiness is not mere pleasure;
it refers to the joy of confident self-assurance, meaning that one has resolved the matter within one's own heart. △ Fifth, the conclusion of the request.

The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, constantly desires to bring peace to the world; we pray that you grant us a prediction [of our future enlightenment], just as one who is hungry must be taught what to eat.

Since you constantly desire to bring peace to the world, how could you bear to sit idly by while we tremble with fear? We must certainly seek a prediction, for only then will it accord with the principle of bringing peace to the world.
It is like when one is hungry: one must be instructed on what to eat before it accords with the meaning of being granted a meal. Thus the three sons concluded their request for a prediction.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s conferral of prophecies (three parts): 1. The prophecy for Subhūti; 2. The prophecy for Mañjuśrī; 3. The prophecy for Maudgalyāyana.

Regarding the first two [Subhūti and Mañjuśrī], there are two sections: 1. Prose; 2. Verses. Regarding the first [the prose], there are four parts: 1. Attaining the fruit based on the cause; 2. Adornment of the primary and secondary [marks];
3. The lifespan of the Buddha-dharma; 4. Supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma. First [attaining the fruit based on the cause]:
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts of the great disciples. [From "throughout kalpas" to] "the kalpa is named Possessing Jewels and the land is named Jewel-Born.
Having first passed through the causal practices of those kalpas, the great disciples sought a prediction of their future enlightenment in their hearts;

thus their countenances were trembling with awe and their speech was earnest and sincere. The World-Honored One, observing their countenances and hearing their words, was able to know their thoughts. Niyuta.

"Ta" (He) is also translated as "myriad billions" (*wan-yi*), which corresponds to the number *hai* among the ten great numbers. The rest is the same as before. At the very end, one shall attain the realization of the fruit.

The name of the cause is "Born of Emptiness" (*Kong-sheng*), while the name of the fruit is "Names and Characteristics" (*Ming-xiang*); this reveals the principle that true emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence.
The eon is named "Possessing Jewels" (*You-bao*), meaning that based upon these various names and characteristics, the Dharma-jewel is established. The land is named...

"Ratnasambhava" means that based upon the jewels of all phenomena (*dharmaratna*), various wise persons are born. Just as "heavenly time" and "geographical terrain" are named according to their respective causes, [so too is this name].
△ Second, the adornment of the primary and secondary [bodies].
That land is level and even, with crystal for its ground... [extending] for countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.

First, regarding the adornments of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment): "Crystal" (*sphaṭika*)—here translated as "water-jade"—and "lapis lazuli" (*vaiḍūrya*), though not of one kind, both convey the meaning of being pure and stainless.

Having completed the bestowal of the prediction upon Śūnyatā-janman (空生), section two: the bestowal of the prediction upon Maṇḍitaka (文飾). This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [prose] has three parts: first, attaining the fruit through the causal practice;

second, the adornment of the primary and secondary [bodies]; third, the duration of the Buddha-dharma and lifespan. The first of these two [attaining the fruit through causal practice] has two parts: first, practicing the causes throughout kalpas; second, the future realization of the fruit. The first [practicing the causes throughout kalpas]: *The Flower Ornament Sutra: The Ten Stages* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra Daśabhūmika-parivarta) Translated by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin Dynasty At that time, the Bodhisattva Maṇḍitaka, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha Akṣobhya, attained a profound understanding of the nature of all phenomena. He perceived that all dharmas are ultimately empty and quiescent, free from conceptual proliferation, and that they do not arise nor cease. He realized that the nature of all dharmas is like space—ungraspable and without obstruction—and that the essence of all dharmas is the single mark of non-arising. He understood that the various distinctions among dharmas are merely provisional designations, established according to conditions, yet ultimately devoid of inherent existence. He saw that the mind, the mental factors, and all conditioned phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, and reflections; they appear due to the power of habitual tendencies but have no true reality. He contemplated that the realm of sentient beings is boundless, yet their fundamental nature is pure and equal to the Buddha-realm. He resolved to cultivate the path for immeasurable eons, dedicating every thought toward the attainment of supreme, perfect enlightenment. He practiced the six perfections with unflagging vigor: he gave away his body, wealth, and kingdom without attachment; he observed the precepts purely, even at the cost of his life; he cultivated patience, enduring all insults and hardships with a mind as firm as a mountain; he exerted himself with tireless energy, never retreating in the face of suffering; he practiced meditative concentration, entering into the samādhis of the ten directions; and he perfected wisdom, penetrating the profound mysteries of all dharmas. Throughout his journey, he honored and served all Buddhas, planting roots of goodness under them. He skillfully employed the four means of attraction to gather and transform sentient beings, leading them to abandon evil and embrace the good. He traversed the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting various bodies according to the needs of beings, always acting in accordance with the Dharma. His conduct was perfectly harmonious with the Way, and his vows were vast and inexhaustible. Having fulfilled these practices over countless kalpas, he finally attained the stage of a Bodhisattva who is irreversible from supreme enlightenment. [End of first part] [The following sections would follow the structure outlined above.]
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus... [up to] twenty-two trillion Buddhas were likewise so.
As for those who made offerings and served them, it was not merely that the four requisites were fully provided; they also personally attended to them with their own hands and feet.
The number of those who made offerings to the Buddha did not equal the multitude of Subhūti, because he was able to bring matters from beginning to end and pay full homage with complete courtesy;

thus, though few, he could match the many. As for those who, out of reverence and respect, erected stupas after his passing, this precisely fulfills the meaning of bringing matters from beginning to end and paying full homage with complete courtesy. That they were a thousand *yojanas* high symbolized that they were to be gazed upon by all ten directions.
It measures five hundred [yojanas] in length and breadth, symbolizing the taking of refuge in the Five Vehicles. Those who gaze upon it obtain the benefit of the seven treasures of the noble Dharma;
thus, it is represented as being composed of the seven precious gems. Those who take refuge obtain the adornment of immeasurable merit; thus, it is represented by various flowers and necklaces.
Through making offerings and prostrating, one is able to give rise to the mind of precept, concentration, and wisdom; thus, by...

These are represented by unguents, powdered incense, and burning incense. Although the Tathāgata’s two gates of conversion—through attraction and through subduing—persist even after his parinirvāṇa, they are still able to provide shelter for sentient beings and overturn their evil views; thus, these are represented by silk canopies, banners, and streamers.

Furthermore, making offerings to twenty-two trillion Buddhas illustrates the completion of what was begun previously, fulfilling both the beginning and the end. Because he paid homage and performed every ritual with utmost reverence, it says, "it was likewise."
It is so. △ Second, attaining the realization of the fruit.
Having made offerings to these Buddhas, one is fully endowed with the Bodhisattva path (up to) "Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.

The first two phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce the following. From "One shall attain" onwards, the text properly clarifies the attainment of the fruit. Because of this excellent discourse, it is adorned.
To adorn the holy teachings is called "ornamentation" (*vibhūṣaṇa*). Using superior gold to adorn the body of the Dharma is termed "Golden Light" (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*).
The principles of cause and effect are likewise analogous. *Jambudvīpa* is the name of a tree; when its fruit falls into water and touches stone, it turns into gold.
When placed among ordinary gold, the ordinary gold loses its luster. Therefore, the ancient masters translated the term based on this meaning as "superior" (*jaya*).

"Gold. The Buddha uses this name to signify that the merit of the fruition (*phala-guṇa*) is supreme, as it transcends all things. Furthermore, refined gold that has been smelted a hundred times represents the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);
its unchanging luster and color represent the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Because wisdom and abandonment are ultimate, it is called "Jambūnada Golden Light.
As for the absence of a name for the land or eon, there is likely a textual omission or error. This concludes the section on attaining the fruit through the practice of causes. Part Two.

To sit idly at ease and wish to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom—is this not difficult? One must first attain [the stages]; one must first realize the fruits. *Tamālapatra*. This...
"Cloud-nature is stainless" means that its essential nature is free from defilement; it is the most excellent of sandalwoods.

The Buddha uses this name because the fragrant wind of his virtue and wisdom permeates all things. [This concludes the section on] the names of the kalpas, lands, and titles.
According to the *Da Cheng shi* (Great Commentary), this Buddha gathers the world through his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and teaches sentient beings;

because their minds are joyful and they submit with sincerity, the eon is named "Fulfillment of Joy" (*Priyapūrṇa*) and the land is named "Delightful Intent" (*Manoratha*). △ Second, the adornment of the lifespan.
The ground of that land is level and made of crystal (extending until: "the semblance Dharma will also remain for forty minor kalpas").

First, regarding the adornments of the environment (*pratyaya-vibhūṣaṇa*): according to the previous passage on the three predictions, it was referred to as "jewel flowers" (*ratna-puṣpa*) or "wondrous flowers" (*vicitra-puṣpa*);
here it is called "pearl flowers" (*muktā-puṣpa*). This is either because pearls were strung together to form flowers, or because they are both jewels and wondrous.

(The section on the formal verses is divided into two: first, the formal verses corresponding to the prose; second, the promise to reveal the causes and conditions. The first [section] has two parts:

This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana—[up to]—is called the fragrance of *tāmāla-candana*.
The first verse praises his cultivation of causes throughout kalpas. Regarding "golden *kṣetra*": it means using pure gold for the *kṣetra*-pole (the flagstaff). Regarding "long banner":

△ Second, the verses adorn the lifespan.
That Buddha’s lifespan lasts twenty-four kalpas (up to) forty minor kalpas; the period of the Semblance Dharma is likewise.

First, the lifespan of the Tathāgata (is treated as a *cūḍaka-gāthā*). The adornment of the *pariṇāmanika-saṃbhoga* (retributive environment) is omitted and not versified. From "常爲下" (*nityam adhas*) onwards is the primary retribution (*pratyātmika-saṃbhoga*).

The "Adornment" (a concluding verse): The fact that there are śrāvakas of great majestic power reveals them to be provisional manifestations; the fact that all bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive reveals them to be at profound stages.
Following the passage on the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the verse concludes the formal exposition on the lifespans of the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
△ Second, the promise to reveal the causes and conditions.
"My disciples are endowed with majestic power (up to: I shall now speak; listen well!

It is the intention of the Tathāgata that among my disciples, those who are endowed with majestic power like that of a Bodhisattva and are worthy of receiving a prediction of enlightenment are not limited to you four alone;
there are further five hundred such as will all receive predictions. Thus he showed.

Because in future ages you shall all attain Buddhahood; for it is because you and I have been bound by the conditions of teacher and disciple since past lives that I have not yet openly proclaimed this for forty years, as the time had not yet arrived.
Now I perceive that the season has come for you, and I shall therefore instruct and expound it for you. You all—

You should also listen with a sincere heart; then you will gain self-confidence that you shall attain Buddhahood without doubt. The first cycle of teachings through parables for those of medium capacity is hereby concluded.

△ Third, the cycle of teachings on causes and conditions for those of inferior capacity, in two parts: 1. The Buddha’s exposition of causes and conditions. 2. The inferior capacity attaining [realization].
[The] Benefit. [The title of the first chapter states:
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, Chapter Seven, "The Parable of the Phantom City.

That which exists suddenly where there was previously nothing is called a "phantom" (*hua*). That which wards off wrongdoing and resists enemies is called a "city" (*cheng*). This is a metaphor for the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle; it is not the ultimate reality.

This is merely a provisional assumption, intended to guard against dogmatic views and obstructive thoughts. If one discusses this chapter, it was originally proclaimed for those of inferior faculties as an exposition of causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

The reason the title specifically designates the "Transformation City" (*nirmita-nagara*) is that once the Transformation City is established, it connects with the preceding causes and conditions so they do not fall away;
subsequently, through the gradual possession of the Eight Treasures, it connects with sentient beings to benefit their lives. Thus, the Transformation City is truly indispensable.
However, as for the Tathāgata’s teaching of this chapter again after the Chapter on Prophecy, there are five distinct reasons.
First, it is to manifest that this Dharma has existed for a long time and did not only come into being now; thus the text says:
"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," and so forth. Second, it is to manifest that attaining Buddhahood is not easy.

This is for the purpose of admonishing wild wisdom (*kudṛṣṭi*). As the text says: "That Buddha, having originally sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and defeated the armies of Māra, was on the verge of attaining *bodhi*;
yet even after ten kalpas, the Buddha-dharma still did not manifest before him," and so forth.

Third, it is to reveal that he has been transforming sentient beings over many lifetimes, as the conditions of the assembly have now ripened. As the text says: "Each one of these sixteen bodhisattvas has transformed [beings]."
Six hundred trillion nayutas of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, have been born together with this Bodhisattva in every successive life.
Fourth, this is to manifest that they attain liberation both far and near, so that the multitude may gain self-confidence. As the text says:
Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—these are you, monks, and those future śrāvaka disciples after my parinirvāṇa.
Fifth, this is to reveal that they did not dwell in the illusory city but immediately reached the place of treasure;
thus the text says: "What you have yet to accomplish remains unfinished; the stage upon which you now abide is close to the Buddha-wisdom."
It is so. One must understand that although the causes and conditions herein were taught for those of inferior capacity, the five hundred disciples who followed were by no means ordinary people.
If we, in this regard, can indeed believe with sincere conviction and without doubt, [we shall attain realization].
Inscribe this in your heart and practice it yourself. Although this occurs after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how could it not be the remaining dust of Jñānavijaya?

△ (The scripture is divided into two parts: first, a general indication of the time; second, a detailed narrative from beginning to end. The first part has two sections: first, the prose; second, the verses.

The first section has three parts: first, indicating the time to show its remoteness; second, setting forth a hypothetical number; third, concluding with a reference to prevent further questioning. The first [part]:)
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In the distant past, until his parinirvāṇa, it has been exceedingly long.
The Buddha’s address to the bhikṣus is intended to clarify the causal conditions (*nidāna*). This serves to explain the meaning of what was previously promised.
"In the distant past" points to the time when the initial connection [with the Dharma] was established. "Immeasurable and boundless," and so forth, expresses the extreme length of that time.

Regarding the name of the Buddha, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū: "Abhijñā" (thorough penetration) means being able to reach the ultimate reality; this refers to self-awakening. "Jñāna" (wisdom) means being able to shatter ignorance and darkness;
this refers to awakening others. To say it is "great" (*mahā*) and his wisdom "surpasses" (*abhibhū*) means that he penetrates all with a single penetration and shatters all with a single shattering;
this refers to the perfection of awakening. Furthermore, "Great Penetration" means there is no dharma that he does not [penetrate].

Regarding "Pervasive" and "Victorious in Wisdom": it is not that wisdom is incomplete; rather, it is precisely because wisdom is not incomplete that there is no phenomenon through which one does not pass.
Because there is no phenomenon through which one does not pass, wisdom is not incomplete. This is a designation based on the mutual dependence of object and wisdom.

Regarding the name of the country and the eon, according to the *Sāramati-śāstra* (The Meaning of the Correct Measure): because the six directions were harmonious and flourishing at that time, the country was named "Good City" (*Supura*).
The talent of the people in that land was exceptionally flourishing; therefore, the kalpa was named "Great Characteristics" (Mahālakṣaṇa).
As for the fact that the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha occurred an exceedingly long time ago, it is as explained below. The specific highlighting of this point serves two purposes:

first, to demonstrate that the sons [of the Buddha] have deep causes and did not suddenly receive their predictions; second, to demonstrate that this Dharma has existed for a long time and did not begin only now. In total, it is for these reasons.
This leads those of inferior faculties to give rise to true faith. II. The Provisional Establishment of Numbers:
"For example, [if one were to take] a trichiliocosm... (up to) would one know its number or not? 'No, World-Honored One.'"
A trichiliocosm is the transformation realm of a single Buddha; if one were to use the soil of this world as ink, the vastness of that ink could be known.
A thousand lands are the transformation realms of a thousand Buddhas; if one were to place a single dot beyond this, the sparsity of those dots could be known.
If one were to exhaust the ink of all the soil of the world with the most sparse of dots, then the lands traversed would be at their limit.
The limits of quantity are certainly not known by mathematicians and the like; therefore, the Tathāgata intentionally posed the question, yet the assembly answered directly with "No.
Regarding the term "earth-element" (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) therein, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "It is the earth-great-element (*mahābhūta*). The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"What is meant by 'great element'? It answers: "That which is great and is an element; it can decrease and it can increase."
The capacity to diminish and the capacity to augment constitute the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*). Furthermore, the phrase "if one were to say" has the sense of "supposing that.
To say that the earth element serves as ink—though such a person does not actually exist—is merely a hypothetical assumption made specifically to demonstrate the abundance of the ink.
△ Third, the conclusion which anticipates and addresses potential questions.
"O bhikṣus, regarding the lands through which this person has passed—observing them over such a vast expanse of time as if it were today—the initial calculation was by the number of finger-joints.
This person then marked the people of those lands; he marked the places traversed by the dust particles.
Once the places traversed by the dust particles have been marked, they are beyond the reach of calculation, let alone the marking itself."
They were not counted. All were wiped away until they became dust, and each particle of dust was reckoned as one kalpa;
thus, the vast duration of these kalpas can be known. Yet the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha exceeded even this number.
This is what is meant by "extremely long ago" and "far, far away. From the words "I [recall]" below, he anticipates a potential doubt (the question being:).

As stated above, that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa occurred so very long ago that the matter belongs to the realm of profound obscurity; I fear it is beyond the scope of the mind’s capacity to measure. I do not yet know upon what basis the Tathāgata spoke thus. Therefore, this [text] provides a defense, saying: ) [End of quote].
By virtue of the power of my Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, that which cannot be measured by those far or near, I observe as if it were today, though it be from long ago.
What is there to find strange? And what is there to find marvelous? The prose section concludes.
