Thus, regarding the marking and non-marking of these various lands (up to) the thorough penetration of immeasurable eons:
the first verse concludes by indicating the number of fingers (as per the *geya* style), which may be understood according to the prose (*gadya*).

From "The Tathāgata’s" onwards, the verse preempts potential questions (the intent of the question remains consistent with the prose): the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not restricted by objective spheres, nor is it limited by temporal divisions.

"Limit. Therefore, it is called "unobstructed. This refers to the knower. Among those who are known, the mention of the Śrāvakas being "lengthened out" is for the sake of the subsequent six hundred trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are to be subdued.

The mention of the Bodhisattvas being "lengthened out" is for the sake of the subsequent sixteen princes who are to be subdued. As in the phrase "seeing," the character "see" (見) is read as "county" (縣). [This concludes] the long prose section.

This refers to what is like the present day. When he calls out to the bhikṣus and instructs them on what they should know, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the Buddha’s wisdom is capable of knowing the meaning.
The Buddha’s wisdom is called "pure" because its essence is free from afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, it is called "sublime" because its function transcends thought. Precisely because its essence is free from afflictions, it is termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*); because its function is severed [from conceptualization]...
It is inconceivable; therefore, it is called "unimpeded. Because it is untainted and unimpeded, one is able to penetrate immeasurable kalpas.

This concludes the general exposition of the time. II. A detailed narration of the beginning and the end, in two parts: 1. Prose (long xing). 2. Verse (jie song). The first part [the prose] has two sections: 1.

A formal narration of the causes and conditions. 2. A further clarification of the methods of transformation. The first of these [the causes and conditions] has three sections: 1. The reason for establishing karmic connections. 2. ... [text continues] ...

Regarding the matters of establishing karmic affinity (*karmapratyaya*): there are three [sections] concerning the attainment of deliverance by those far and near; the first two [sections] consist of: 1. the Buddha of Wisdom opening the provisional (*upāya*) teachings; 2.

the Buddha of Wisdom manifesting the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). The first four [sub-sections] consist of: 1. the Buddha of Wisdom attaining enlightenment; 2. the request to turn the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*); 3. accepting the request and bestowing the provisional teachings.

Fourth, the assurance of hearing the Dharma, consisting of three initial points: first, the prediction of attainment after ten intermediate kalpas; second, the offerings presented by the devas; third, the arrival of the time for the realization of the Way. Regarding the first:
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, [saying] "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... yet the teachings of the Buddhas still did not appear before him."
First, the mention of the Buddha’s lifespan is for the sake of providing a basis for the matter at hand. The original reference concerns the period before he attained Buddhahood.
Although it was before he had attained Buddhahood, the phrase "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) must refer to the final moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samāyikabodhi).

During that final moment, internally the eight consciousnesses are purified, and externally the four māras are subdued; hence it says, "having already destroyed the army of Māra. Once the army of Māra has been destroyed, the path of the Buddha...

It is about to be accomplished; therefore, it is said that "he is on the verge of attaining bodhi. The term "on the verge" (chui) means "about to" (jiang). This refers to being about to attain it but not yet having attained it.
Since he is about to attain it but has not yet done so, his understanding of the Buddha-dharma remains like a fine gauze curtain; thus, it is said that [the dharmas] do not manifest before him.
As for the period from one kalpa to ten kalpas, this refers to the final duration traversed. By analogy with a long journey, it is the final stage of the path.
At that time, what was but a single *kṣaṇa* has now passed as ten *kalpas*. This is because the Buddha’s lifespan is so long that everything [associated with it] is likewise prolonged;
furthermore, it is to demonstrate that the Buddha-way is not easily attained and to serve as a warning against reckless wisdom (*prajñā*).

As for sitting cross-legged with body and mind unmoving, this refers to abiding in the *vajra-samādhi*. It is because residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) have not been exhausted and the sublime realization has not yet reached perfection.
Therefore it is said: "Yet the various Buddha-dharmas still do not appear before him. △ Second, the devas present offerings.
At that time, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven first [prepared for] that Buddha... (up to) ...it was likewise so even until his parinirvāṇa.
First, the throne was prepared in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Knowing that the Buddha was about to attain enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, they prepared the seat beforehand.
It was named "Lion" (*siṃha*) to signify fearlessness. Its height of one *yojana* reveals the dimensions of the seat.
The fact that the Buddha sat upon it clarifies the purpose of preparing the seat: that he would attain *bodhi*, and so forth. This refers to the moment he rose from his seat.
"Suitable" (適) means "beginning. This refers to the fact that the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have prepared a high seat many yojanas in height;
how could this be in vain? It is surely because the Buddha will sit upon it. That the Buddha sits here does not occur within ten kalpas, but rather after ten intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa).
Only when he is about to attain Bodhi will he first sit upon this seat. At that time, all those below—
The Brahmā gods rained down flowers because they knew that the Buddha was about to attain buddhahood upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimanda); thus, they rained down various celestial flowers.

They are called "various" because their types and categories were not uniform. Regarding the phrase "a hundred yojanas on each side," this refers to the area extending one hundred yojanas from the seat of enlightenment in each of the four directions.
The withered flowers were blown away and new ones were rained down again; this signifies...

This explains the meaning of non-abiding progress. Regarding the fulfillment of ten minor kalpas: as for the time when flowers rained down and offerings were made to the Buddha, the intent behind the raining of flowers is this:
it is said that the aforementioned Brahma kings, having fulfilled ten kalpas while the rain of flowers continued without ceasing, could this not have been unconditioned?
It was surely for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha; and in making offerings to the Buddha, they held him in profound reverence.
Because that place was so, even after he had attained enlightenment and until his parinirvāṇa, this flower constantly rained down to adorn the ground.
Regarding the Four Kings below: the Four Kings beat drums as an offering to the Buddha.

The constant beating of the celestial drum signifies that the Buddha-way is about to be accomplished and that its single sound is about to resound. Regarding the others below: other devas perform music; other devas...
"Furthermore," refers to those beyond the Śakras, Brahmās, and Four Heavenly Kings—namely, the Yāma, Tuṣita, and other heavens.

"Performing celestial music" symbolizes that the multitude of the deaf awaits the thunderclap; it signifies that the meanings of all teachings shall now be expounded. △ Third, the time has arrived and the Way is perfected.
O Bhikṣus, when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had passed ten intermediate kalpas since his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it was the time when the Vajra-samādhi was perfected.
His residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were exhausted, and his wondrous realization was finally complete;
thus it is said that the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before him. Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena, he is therefore named [Tathāgata].
Anuttara, etc. After the Buddha attained enlightenment through wisdom. △ Second, the request to turn the wheel of Dharma, in two parts:

first, the Prince’s request for the Dharma; second, the Brahma King’s request for the Dharma. The first [part] has three sections: first, the arrival of the retinue; second, the praise of the Buddha with verses.
The Three Princes’ Petition. First:
When that Buddha had not yet left the household life, he had sixteen sons... [who] made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised him.

Regarding the "one son of Śākyamuni," the "eight sons of Dīpaṃkara," and the "sixteen sons of Jñānabuddhi": while they share the commonality of being sons, they differ according to their respective conditions.
As for the father named Jñānavijaya and the son named Jñānaskandha: it is by accumulating [wisdom] that one may reach the state of victory.
The son resembles his father. No other names are mentioned because once one name is given, it is sufficient for establishing credibility.
Each possesses various rare and exquisite objects of play and enjoyment, exhausting all that the ears and eyes desire and encompassing everything produced in the world;
there is nothing not prepared, and all that is beautiful is gathered therein. Upon hearing that his father had attained the Way, he believed and emerged.
Beneficial to the world, they abandoned their treasures and departed. Realizing that worldly pleasures are not true, they esteemed honor lightly and valued the Way (Dharma) highly;

they approached their fathers and drew near to the Buddha. As stated in the introductory section (*nidāna*), "Furthermore, various kings were seen going to the place where the Buddha was, inquiring about the Unsurpassed Way."
"He then abandoned his pleasant land, his palace, ministers, and concubines; this is precisely what is meant by 'of such a kind.
As for 'the various mothers,' it is because the sixteen princes were not born of a single mother, and furthermore, because each prince had different birth mothers and foster mothers.
As for 'weeping and wailing,' it refers to the affection for one's own flesh and blood, which is difficult to sever and difficult to relinquish—the pain of such feelings of longing."
It collapses within the vital organs; the traces of this tragedy manifest and disperse through all the apertures.

As for those who follow in the funeral procession, they love their child and, moreover, draw near to their lord to achieve the Way; thus, the ancestral king is surrounded and followed by his ministers and the people.

The father cannot take the place of the son; what is practiced above is emulated below. The two characters "all" (*xián*) and "desire" (*yù*) are used here to comprehensively summarize the intentions of the multitude.

It speaks of sons, mothers, ancestors, kings, as well as ministers and subjects, some of whom abandoned precious possessions to depart, some who wept as they saw them off, and others who arrived surrounding [the Buddha].
Although each had their own motives, their ultimate focus was centered upon the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that they all desire to draw near, making offerings, and paying respect, and so forth. △ Second, the recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha:
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha, and [continued] until: "I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One."
The initial section describes the ritual protocol and presents the verse. Regarding the phrase "bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet," this signifies the utmost reverence.

According to current accounts, eight years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he returned to his home country to preach the Dharma for his father, the King. The King, leading all the ministers and subjects of the realm, went a great distance to welcome and behold the Buddha.

Overwhelmed by the Buddha’s majestic virtue, they bowed in prostration without even realizing it. The Buddha, however, did not accept his father’s prostration and withdrew his body until it was no longer visible.
Having completed the prostrations, he then manifests his body. Based on this, even a Buddha of Wisdom (Jñāna-buddha) should likewise not receive prostrations from a father;

however, this is not a matter of immediate concern, and thus it is not discussed here. As for circumambulating the Buddha, one circles to the right, expressing the intention to follow the Buddha’s travels throughout life after life.
Once finished, one may circumambulate three times, seven times, or up to an infinite number of times.
This concludes [the preceding section]. "With a single mind" means to hold one's intention upright. "Joining the palms" means to solemnify one’s person.
"Gazing up" means to contemplate their virtues. "Reciting verses" means to speak words of praise. These correspond to the meanings of making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising.
In the phrase "Great Majesty" (*mahātejas*), it is precisely through this praise that his majesty is manifested as the severity of subjugation; this refers to his virtue.
The compassion of his manifest guidance and bestowal is such that neither [of these two types of compassion] can surpass it; therefore, it is called "Great.

Possessing these two greatnesses, he serves as the refuge for all beings and is thus titled "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān). To deliver sentient beings, he cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva for immeasurable billions of years.
When the bodhisattva practices were fulfilled, the fruit of Bodhi was perfected; hence it is said: "Thereupon, he attained Buddhahood. Thus it is.
"It is as it is now. "One whose vows are already fulfilled" means that since the Buddha-way has been realized, all great vows have been brought to perfection.

"Excellent" (Sādhu) is a term of praise. Having praised him as "excellent," one further calls him "the supreme auspiciousness" because the Tathāgata, with his practice complete and his fruit perfected, and all his vows fulfilled, is the most auspicious person. These are the words of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, within the final adamantine path, where delusion is exhausted and reality reaches its ultimate limit, he praised this as being most rare:

that one remains seated for ten minor kalpas is rare in terms of the duration; that the body, hands, feet, and so forth remain in meditative concentration is rare in terms of the stability of the power of samādhi.
"Body" refers generally to the entire person, while "hands and feet" specifically refer to the four limbs. This is sustained by the power of concentration.
Because it is maintained, it remains still and unmoving; this is external quiescence (*śama*). "Its mind" refers to the mind of the *vajra-samādhi*.
"Serene and tranquil" (*dàn-pà*) carries the meaning of placid stillness. Cheng Da says: "It is like the moon brightening the autumn sky, its cold radiance boundless. This is precisely what is meant.
There has never been one who was distracted. At such a time, one cannot but proceed; how could there be distraction? This is inner stillness.
As for "ultimately and eternally extinguished": delusive hopes are severed, and since there is no delusion that is not exhausted, it is called "ultimate.
It is like wood turned to ash, where the grain of the wood can never reappear; this is called "eternal extinction. One dwells peacefully in the untainted (*anāsrava*).

As for the Dharma: it is the realization of the sublime and rare; there is nothing true that it does not realize, and thus it is called "abiding securely. It is like gold extracted from ore, which never returns to the state of ore;
hence it is called the "outflow-free Dharma" (*anāsrava-dharma*). From "Now," below, [the text expresses] celebration and joy: "Now I behold the World-Honored One."

"To peacefully attain the Buddha-way" means that by personally beholding the Tathāgata, one attains the dharma of the peace of *nirvāṇa* amidst the unstable dharmas of birth and death, and achieves the path of the Bodhisattva’s perfect enlightenment amidst the lack of awakening caused by ignorance.
"We have obtained a great benefit" means that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is as difficult as the blooming of the *udumbara* flower; now that we have already attained it...

To see [the Buddha] is to obtain great and wholesome benefit. Were it not for profound causes from past lives, one would surely have to plant great seeds in the present to encounter such a marvelous opportunity.
How could one not proclaim one’s congratulations with one's own mouth and feel great joy in one's heart?

The passage beginning with "Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering" provides a detailed explanation of the reasons for this celebration. This is because, prior to the appearance of the Buddha, all sentient beings...

Sentient beings are constantly oppressed and afflicted by manifold sufferings. Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, he shall cause them to be free from suffering; therefore, there is rejoicing.
Furthermore, because they are obstructed by afflictions, they are like the blind or those in darkness. Moreover, before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was no true guide.
Now that they have encountered this Guide, they shall sever the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya); therefore, there is rejoicing. Furthermore, as for sentient beings...
Previously, they did not recognize the factors of the primary and auxiliary paths that can exhaust all suffering, and thus they constantly practiced blindly.

Now, because they recognize the path to the exhaustion of suffering, they rejoice. Furthermore, sentient beings were unaware of the two kinds of nirvana, which can bring about liberation and toward which one may aspire.
Now, because they know the dharma of liberation, they rejoice. Moreover, before the Buddha appeared in the world...

At that time, sentient beings were like those submerged in a long night, extensively creating dark karma and increasing their presence in the evil realms, thereby causing the hosts of devas to diminish.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, it is as if a lamp has been obtained in the long night; therefore, there is cause for rejoicing. Furthermore, because of sentient beings...
"Using suffering to abandon suffering, one passes from darkness into darkness, perpetually obstructed by false views;
such a person never hears the names of the Buddhas, much less is able to see them. Now, having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, you have suddenly emerged from the path of darkness;
therefore, I rejoice. Furthermore, that which the Buddha has now attained is the supreme Dharma of nirvāṇa and peace."
The path of enlightenment, free from outflows, has been personally witnessed by me and the devas; therefore, we have attained the greatest benefit.
This is the source from which this joy arises. For this reason, we all prostrate ourselves and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
"Prostrating" (kai-shou) means to bring one's head to the ground and remain there without rising. "Taking refuge" (gui-ming) means to surrender one's life.
The Buddha would not drive them away. This was also because, upon seeing the excellence of the Buddha’s virtues, they were so overcome with joy that they could hardly speak;
they could do nothing but prostrate themselves and take refuge. △ Third, the princes’ request, in two parts: first, a brief presentation of their request;
second, an extensive exposition in verse. First:
At that time, the sixteen princes, having praised the Buddha with verses, [proceeded] out of compassion and for the benefit of all devas and humans.
First, they connect the preceding to the subsequent; all together they speak as follows.

As for the devas and humans who do not know how to leave suffering behind, yet the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to instruct them in leaving suffering, this will bring great peace and security to those devas and humans.
The people do not know how to sever the origin [of suffering], yet the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, guiding them by means of severing the origin; this is a source of great compassion.
The devas and humans do not know how to cultivate the path to realize cessation, yet the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, instructing them to cultivate the path to realize cessation;
this is a source of great benefit. Since this is so, why be parsimonious or stubborn and not speak? △
Second, the detailed explanation of the verses.
The verses are recited again: "The Hero of the World has no equal... (up to) "...shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.

Regarding the first line, "As he realized and sought, he showed," the *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna) commentary states: "He stands preeminent beyond the six realms; therefore, he is called the 'Hero of the World' (*lokanātha*). No [equal].
Regarding "equal in peer": among the Four Heavenly Kings, none can equal his merit; among the Ten Sages, none can surpass his wisdom. Regarding "adorned by a hundred blessings":

because he cultivated a hundred blessings as the cause, he attained the marks of physical adornment as the fruit. Since the blessings were cultivated by himself, the adornments are likewise possessed by himself.
Regarding "attaining unsurpassed wisdom": his own realization of noble wisdom is ultimate. May he act for the sake of the world.
"Please speak" means to request that this wisdom be expounded so as to awaken others. "Deliver me and the multitude" is a request made for the sake of both self and others.
Since the faculties and capacities of self and others differ, one prays that the Buddha will accord with them; thus it says, "discriminately reveal.
When the time arrives and the faculties have matured, there is the expectation that he will still preach the One Vehicle; thus it says, "cause them to attain this wisdom. Thus it is.

Thus, there are no capacities that are not reached, and all who possess the conditions enter [the path]. Therefore it is said: "We have attained Buddhahood; so it is for all sentient beings. Regarding the passage "The World-Honored One," etc.:
as for "knowing the request to turn [the wheel]," it means knowing what is being contemplated. Whether one contemplates the Lesser Vehicle or the Great Vehicle, the Tathāgata is able to know it all.
He also knows those who practice the path—whether they practice the path of the Truths (*satya*) or the path of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Or...
The Tathāgata is also able to know those who practice the path of the six perfections. Furthermore, regarding the power of knowledge:

whether one possesses the power of knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñānabala*) or the power of knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñānabala*), the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this;

it is the knowledge of the capacities of the three vehicles. Regarding inclinations: some delight in being born in the heavens, while others delight in being among humans. Regarding those who cultivate merit: some have previously...

They have cultivated celestial merit, or perhaps cultivated human merit; they possess past karma—either having practiced the wholesome karma of the precepts in previous lives, or having practiced the karma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in previous lives.
This is the knowledge of the capacities of humans and devas. Having known the three vehicles and also knowing the realms of humans and devas, one is without error in each instance;
this is called "knowing them all. According to the capacities thus known, one gradually induces and guides them, never skipping over stages.
...the faults thereof, as well as the transgressions of interrupting [the teaching]. Therefore, it is said that one "should turn the unsurpassed wheel.

The Prince’s request for the Dharma concludes. II. The Brahma King’s Request for the Dharma has two parts: 1. The Buddha of Wisdom Manifests Auspicious Omens; 2. The Various Devas Come to Request the Dharma. The first part:

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "From the time the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [attained enlightenment] until his light pervaded the world, surpassing the radiance of all the devas, it reached down to the dark and obscure realms.
All the worlds of the Buddhas are collectively produced by the ignorance of sentient beings.
When a Tathāgata attains the Way, he is able to shatter the ignorance of both himself and others; therefore, he manifests this through the six kinds of earth tremors. In that land..."
The intermediate realm of profound darkness refers to within the Iron Ring Mountains, in the Avīci Hell.

Although it is in this place, it nonetheless exists within one's own treasury of radiance; however, because it is obstructed by the karmic power of sentient beings, the majestic light of the sun and moon cannot illuminate it.
Being situated therein together, they likewise cannot see one another. Now, having received [the grace of] the Tathāgata...
"O Jñānaprabha, come! Having shattered the power of all karmic forces, the Great Treasury of Radiance (Mahāprabhāsa-garbha) is revealed;

therefore, it is said that 'all became brilliantly illuminated' and each was able to see one another. These words are expressions of astonishment and wonder. It means that while they had previously been unable to see one another at all, they suddenly saw each other;
thus, they marveled at how this could have occurred so abruptly. Furthermore, from below up to the Brahma-heaven, [the earth shook] in six ways.
As for "shaking and trembling": although it surpasses that of the human realm, it is still encompassed by the world; therefore, it moves together with the world.
Regarding "the great light shines universally, filling the entire world": the Buddha’s light is unimpeded, such that even beneath overturned basins there is nowhere it does not reach.
The light of the heavens is obstructive and not pervasive, and thus it cannot compare to the Buddha’s light; hence it is said to be "superior. △ Two.
The five occasions when the devas came to extend invitations: first, they came from the east; second, they came from the southeast;

third, they came from the south; fourth, this serves as an illustration for the other six directions; fifth, they came from above. Regarding the first five [sections]: first, the deities received the light and deliberated together;

second, they prepared offerings through diligent search; third, they beheld the Buddha and presented their offerings; fourth, they formally requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma; fifth, he accepted their invitation by remaining silent.
The first two [sections]: 1. Receiving the light and forming a thought; 2. Deliberating on the cause. Regarding the first:
At that time, five hundred myriads of koṭis from the eastern direction... [up to] "by what cause and condition has this sign appeared?"
The Buddha’s light surpasses the light of the heavens; thus it is said to be twice as bright as his usual radiance. Such a phenomenon has never occurred before.
Since there must be a cause for what exists, he reflected upon what causes and conditions had brought about this manifestation. △ Second, the collective deliberation on the underlying reason.
At that time, the Brahma Kings each went to one another and illuminated the ten directions.
"Each went to one another" means they went together to a single place. "Discussed this matter together" refers to deliberating upon the causes and conditions for emitting light.
"Named 'Savior of All'" is a name derived from his altruistic activity, revealing that he occupies a profound stage.
"The Superior One" refers to one who manifests residence in a celestial station. Since this has never occurred before, do not regard it as an ordinary event;
therefore, he exhorts them, saying, "Each of you should together seek [this]. "The Greatly Virtuous Deva" (*Mahāpuṇya-deva*) points to the Honored One who is next in succession to Buddhahood.

The two characters "wei" (為) and "zi" (字) are words used when harboring doubt, meaning that it may be the Greatly Virtuous Deva who is born, or it may be a Buddha appearing in the world; in short, it must certainly be so.

It is extraordinary that such a great radiance should appear, illuminating the ten directions. After they had finished deliberating together under the influence of this light, [the second section follows:
II. Fully Preparing Offerings and Conducting a Search.
At that time, five million billion lands (extending to... all went together toward the western direction to investigate this sign.
Because their heavenly merit was so preeminent, their palaces followed them; thus it says they "went together.

As for those who filled their robes with flowers, they knew there was an extraordinary person and had prepared offerings in advance. The Heavenly King of the East, seeing the light coming from the west, therefore went to [meet it].
He searched toward the west. △ Third, seeing the Buddha and making offerings:
"I see the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... (up to) now I offer this to the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will compassionately accept it."

Upon first seeing the Buddha and his assembly, they immediately descended and each offered worship. As for those who scattered flowers over the Buddha, the flowers formed canopies that covered him above;
their extreme abundance and height were such that they were compared to Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, regarding the trees used in the offering:
the tree is that upon which the Buddha relies, and people revere it because of the person [who dwells within]. As a poem says: [Insert relevant verse here]

This reflects the sentiment of the *Gāndī-stotra*: "The lush and flourishing sweet pear tree—do not prune it, do not cut it down. As for the measurement of the tree, it is described as being like Mount Sumeru in height;

this is intended to manifest the meaning of the non-obstruction between the vast and the narrow. That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) cannot reach that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*); thus, one abandons the light to seek the heavy.
Therefore, I offer this palace to the Buddha and make this humble request that the Buddha accept it. Reflecting upon my own long submersion in the outflows (*āsrava*), I seek the Buddha’s compassion;
desiring to aspire toward the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*), I seek the Buddha’s benefit. I pray that you will deign to accept and dwell within it.
The Tathāgata accepts and dwells within it precisely because he seeks to show compassion and bring benefit. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower;
therefore, it is praised as something marvelous and difficult to encounter. His powers, fearlessnesses, and other qualities are such that there is not one that is not fully perfected.

Therefore, he is praised as one endowed with immeasurable virtues and as a "Savior and Protector. To save means to cause beings to leave suffering behind; to protect means to enable them to attain happiness.

This is a general praise of the Tathāgata’s virtues of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). Being endowed with great loving-kindness and compassion, he is able to save and protect;

thus, he is called the Great Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). His pity for the world signifies the meaning of his great compassion being capable of saving them. Thus, all universally receive his bounty.
"Benefit" (*yi*) signifies the meaning of Great Compassion being able to protect [beings]. He describes his own origins as being remote, hence he says "five hundred million.
He describes his sincerity in making offerings, hence he says "he abandons the joy of deep dhyāna.

His meritorious karma from previous lives was extraordinary, hence he caused palaces to appear, magnificently adorned, which he used to offer to the Buddha. His wish that the Buddha accept them is because he desires to relinquish [them].
The fruit of outflows (*sāsrava*) is transformed into the cause of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). △ Fourth, the formal request for the turning of the Dharma:
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse (up to the point of "delivering sentient beings from suffering and affliction").
The path to nirvana for sentient beings has long been blocked and cut off. We pray that the Buddha will deliver us; thus we seek to have this path opened.

With self-benefit through the two feet [of walking], he teaches the Dharma to transform others; with great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) he bestows happiness, and with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) he uproots suffering.

When a Buddha appears and teaches the Dharma, he can cause them to leave the false paths and recognize the correct path. Therefore it is said: "Now a Buddha has appeared in the world for the sake of the multitudes."

The opening line of the verse generally praises the perfection of his wisdom and abandonment, which are honored by the world; therefore, he is difficult to behold.
Having cultivated the causes through vast eons, he was able to destroy his own afflictions to achieve the Way and preach the Dharma, and furthermore, he was able to destroy the afflictions of others.

Therefore, he is called "the Destroyer of Afflictions. Previously it was said that [he appeared] after one hundred and eighty kalpas, and elsewhere it was said that more than one hundred thousand kalpas had passed;

now it is said that one hundred and thirty kalpas have passed. This is because the Buddha’s body manifests or remains hidden according to the capacities of sentient beings, and thus what is perceived differs in various regions.

That one should obtain even a single vision corresponds to the previous statement regarding his being difficult to see; this is a praise of his rarity in terms of his virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Regarding the meaning of "existence": before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was no Dharma-milk to nourish the life of wisdom; thus, they are called "hungry and thirsty sentient beings.
Once the Buddha appeared in the world, he spread the clouds of compassion to moisten all conscious beings; thus, it is said that "the rain of Dharma fills them completely.
Because there was no Buddha for one hundred and thirty kalpas, it is said, "something never seen before. Since the Buddha is the Omniscient One, he is so titled.
"Immeasurable wisdom is as rare as the appearance of an udumbara flower; now that I have encountered it, I rejoice at this extraordinary fortune.
This praises the rarity of the meaning [of the teaching] by way of his wisdom and virtue. His palace, graced by the light, was more magnificent than usual;
not daring to remain there himself, he requested compassionate acceptance [of his offering]. △ Fourth, the formal request for the turning of the Dharma-wheel.

The meaning of "rain" (u) refers to moistening the roots of goodness so that they increase according to their respective capacities and gradually attain entry into the Way.

from the southwest up to the nadir, it was likewise so.

Having first received the light, they conceived this thought and immediately descended together to deliberate on the cause. Śikhin—here translated as "Crest" (*dīngjì*)—realized [the truth].

The "Supreme Vehicle" refers to those who manifest their residence in celestial positions. That their "radiance, renown, and majestic virtue" are "twofold compared to the ordinary" is because they surpass the common.
As for the phrase "that which was previously," it means not only that [the author] has not seen it, but moreover has never even heard of it. △ Second, the comprehensive search for offerings.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (down to) together proceeded to the lower direction to investigate this sign.
