Seeing the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū (down to) "we and all sentient beings shall together attain the Buddha-way."
Upon first seeing the Buddha and his assembly, the various inferiors each offered worship and made this vow: "Please deign to accept [this offering].

Furthermore, there are five meanings [to this]. First is the formal request for a place of acceptance. According to the present account of the time when the Buddha attained enlightenment, the Four Heavenly Kings each presented a bowl, vowing that the Buddha would accept them.
By means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the Tathāgata merged them into a single bowl, which he then accepted.
According to this, the various Brahma palaces may likewise be merged into one, and [the merit] received simultaneously;
therefore, all take the place of reception as their vow. The passage beginning with "At that time" praises the Buddha’s compassion.

"How excellent it is to see the Buddhas" is a self-congratulation on having attained the vision of the Buddha; because seeing that which is difficult to see is achieved, it is called "excellent. All these are aids.
Regarding the terminology: because the Buddha, with a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), rescues and delivers sentient beings, he is called the "Holy Honored One who Saves the World.
The three realms are termed "prisons" because one is bound by retributions for past causes, making it difficult to escape.

To urge sentient beings to depart [from them] means to exhort them toward the supramundane path so that they may be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra. This praises the Tathāgata’s great compassion in his deliverance and salvation.
This is virtue. The Buddha is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom and possesses great compassion that benefits humans and devas;

therefore, he is honored as the Universal Wisdom Honored One of Heaven and Humanity. As for "the multitudes of sprouts," the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ, just as the sprouts of the three types of grass and two types of trees are each distinct.
Regarding the "gate of ambrosia," ambrosia is established within this gate; to open it is to rise from death.
"Returning to life" is a metaphor for the teaching that elucidates the principle of nature (*dharmatā*). To expound upon it is to extinguish evil and give rise to good;

because it extinguishes evil and gives rise to good, it is able to extensively deliver all beings. This praises the Tathāgata’s virtue of great compassion and benefit. Regarding the passage "In the past... and below:

it celebrates one's own encounter [with the Buddha], contrasting the time when the Buddha was absent and one’s life passed in vain with the previous one hundred and eighty kalpas. One hundred and three... [text fragment].
Ten kalpas and so forth are even more remote; therefore, it is called "immeasurable kalpas. When a Buddha dwells in the world, it is like the sunlight shining everywhere.

Thus, when a Buddha has not yet appeared, the ten directions are shrouded in darkness. Because of this darkness, sentient beings know only how to commit evil, and consequently, the evil realms increase.
According to the text of the *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the asuras are also included [among those who receive the prediction].
Thus, they are also numerous in the evil realms. Because they do not know how to perform wholesome deeds, the hosts of devas gradually diminish.

This is because, once their celestial merit is exhausted, they mostly fall into the evil realms upon death. Even if they should happen to be born in the human realm, it may be a time when no Buddha has appeared;
consequently, they cannot hear the Dharma from a Buddha. Failing to hear the Dharma, they have no means by which to reform their faults.
Because one does not cultivate oneself anew, it is said that one constantly practices unwholesome deeds.
Due to this, one’s natural lifespan is cut short and the nature of consciousness is deluded and confused; consequently, both physical vitality and wisdom diminish.
Regarding past karmic offenses, when the present physical vitality and wisdom have both diminished, one’s movements will feel unpleasant, and all undertakings will always be...
This leads to suffering. Furthermore, due to the causal conditions of past karmic offenses, the retribution is unfailing;
not only does one no longer obtain happiness, but even the very perception of obtaining happiness ceases to exist. Thus it is said that one has "lost both happiness and the perception of happiness.
Because of this loss of happiness and its perception, one is constantly oppressed by manifold sufferings and yearns for liberation, which leads one to mistakenly enter into the wrong path.

They see [these things] and cling to them tenaciously without relinquishing them; thus, it is said they "dwell" [in them]. Because they do not seek the Dharma for severing suffering, they do not recognize virtuous conduct.
Because they do not seek the Buddha of Great Power, they do not receive the Buddha’s transformation. Consequently, they revolve through the three miserable realms with no prospect of escape;
thus, it is said they "constantly fall into evil paths. This refers to sentient beings when the Tathāgata had not yet appeared in the world.
Wandering on and off in this manner, they are thus pitiable and worthy of compassion. The Buddha can analyze good and evil and distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox;
therefore, he is called the Eye of the World. From immeasurable kalpas until the present day, he has appeared after a long period of time.
His appearance is not without cause; thus it is said that out of pity for sentient beings, he manifests in the world. Although he appears in the world...

...without being bound by the world; thus it is said that he transcends [the mundane] and achieves awakening. This is a source of great joy and celebration, a marvel never before seen. Reversing the previous explanation, there are six meanings:
first, because the darkness has ceased due to the appearance of a Buddha in the world; second, because the evil realms have diminished while the wholesome realms have increased;
third, because those who practice in accordance with the Dharma excel in both form and wisdom; fourth, because of [the cessation of] transgressions...
Because karma ceases and merit and happiness arise; because the fifth [evil] view is destroyed and virtuous conduct is established;
and because the sixth [evil path] is severed through the Buddha’s transformation—since the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, sentient beings gradually cease the wheel of suffering.
This is truly something to be rejoiced in and delighted at. We, the lowly ones, hereby express our sincerity and conclude our vows, following the previous example.
[The Buddha] knows. The final four lines dedicate [the merit] to sentient beings.

Observing the words here that it "universally reaches all" and that "all together shall attain the Way," one fears that it cannot yet be regarded as the actual practice of humans and devas. △ Fourth, the formal request for the turning of the Dharma wheel.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings [from the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*)] have practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas.

They bestow peace and security while providing happiness, and they deliver others by uprooting suffering. Both of these are established according to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, it is said, "in many ways.
"In many ways" means not just once. The Dharma is called "ambrosia" (*amṛta*) because it possesses the meaning of extinguishing evil and generating goodness.
Furthermore, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "There is a tree of ambrosia (*amṛta*). In the eighth month of autumn, dew drips upon its leaves;

if people take it, it serves as a medicine for longevity. If it enters the earth, it transforms into pearls. This is like when one hears the Dharma and it enters the mind, transforming into the seeds of Bodhi.
Striking [the drum] is a metaphor for the teaching, and the drum is a metaphor for the sound. It means that the Tathāgata’s voice of preaching the Dharma pervades everywhere.
"Urgently. This is like beating a drum to alert the multitude. For sentient beings in suffering, *nirvāṇa* cannot be bestowed precipitously;

therefore, they seek instruction on the path, desiring to reach extinction by means of that path. Thus, [the Buddha] expounds according to their capacities, such that all are thoroughly led to the truth;

hence it is called the "Great Sublime Sound. "Practiced over immeasurable kalpas" refers to the dharmas practiced as the causes of all Buddhas. The passage following "what is practiced" [describes]...
This refers to the path to nirvāṇa. According to various editions, following this section there is another section concerning "accepting an invitation in silence.
It is not included here because, as will be seen below, there is a passage regarding the general acceptance of an invitation from the assembly; thus, it was omitted to avoid redundancy.
Furthermore, one should understand that although the Brahma Kings of the ten directions are listed in sequential order, at that time—

In reality, there is no sequence of before and after. It is simply that the Wisdom-Buddha and the emanated Buddhas emit light simultaneously, and the Brahma-kings of the ten directions search for him at the same time;

thus, they see the Buddha appear and make offerings, and they request him to turn the Wheel of Dharma—all of these occurring at once. However, because words cannot be expressed all at once, they are described and listed in succession.
If one were to represent this as a symbolic teaching (*dharmaparyāya*), the Brahma-kings of the ten directions symbolize the six [faculties] of sentient beings.
The four bodies of the faculties: the six faculties and their four bodies each possess spiritual luminosity and cognitive awareness;
this is precisely the Buddha’s light shining universally. However, because sentient beings do not know the source of this light, they are unable to see the Buddha.
The passage in the text that asks, "By what causes and conditions does he manifest these marks? represents the most critical point for a practitioner to apply their mind. And as for the verse:
"What is the cause of this? We should each seek it together," they said. This is the most critical point for a practitioner of the Right Training (*śaikṣa*) to advance.
As for searching eastward and westward, or searching southward and northward, this precisely reveals that this segment of luminosity is vibrant and active, having no fixed location:
looking east, it is west; observing south, it becomes north. Recognizing its falling within this is the key.
Thus, the Wisdom-Buddha does not depart from one's own mind; yet the six sense organs and the four limbs all understand and request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
A single thought unmoving is itself the silent acceptance of this request. Those who set their minds upon this Way must not treat it with negligence.

Having finished requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. △ Third, accepting the invitation and employing provisional means, in two parts: first, generally accepting the requests of the assembly;
second, employing provisional means for the sake of those with specific capacities. First: At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [up to] ...and the request of the sixteen princes.
The Tathāgata appears in the world fundamentally to deliver sentient beings. To request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma accords precisely with the Buddha’s own mind;

therefore, the Buddha accepts this request. II. Bestowing Expedient Means according to Capabilities, in two parts: 1. Turning the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths; 2. Turning the Wheel of Dependent Origination.
First [Turning the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths]:
"Immediately he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects... [up to] 'this is the cessation of suffering' and 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is the initial heading and praise. "Immediately" means at the very moment of accepting the invitation, without waiting for many days;
it is analogous to how the present Buddha, having contemplated this matter, immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī and so forth. "Three revolutions" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
The Dharma makes three turnings. As it is said: "This is suffering; its nature is oppression," etc., is called the turning that indicates characteristics (*lakṣaṇānvayaparivarta*).

"This is suffering; you should know it," etc., is called the turning that exhorts practice (*anuśāsanīparivarta*). "This is suffering; I have known it," etc., is called the turning that establishes realization (*sākṣātkriyāparivarta*).
Regarding the twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra*), there are three turnings for each Truth (*satya*); one turning can establish one aspect. Thus, there are four [turnings per Truth].
Because they are combined with the Truths, they are called the "Twelvefold Path of Practice. By relying on this path of practice, one subdues delusions and reaches the Truth;
therefore, it is called a "Wheel" (*cakra*). As for the phrase "if a śramaṇa, etc.," it means that this is the ritual procedure of previous Buddhas, which only a Buddha can know and turn.
If one is a śramaṇa, he does no more than propagate the teaching according to the instructions; likewise, a brāhmaṇa also does no more than [rely upon them].

Regarding the instruction on cultivation: even the devas, Māras, Brahmās, and other worldly non-Buddhists do not know how to rely upon the teaching for cultivation, let alone how they could turn [the wheel].
Therefore, it is said in general that they cannot sever [suffering]; this refers to the "lower.
To explain "turning" means to point out the names and categories of the Four Noble Truths as the dharma that is turned. As for "suffering," it consists of birth, old age, [and so forth].

Suffering (*duḥkha*) has birth, aging, sickness, and death as its essence; because it oppresses both body and mind, it is called suffering. Accumulation (*samudaya*) has the afflictions (*kleśa*) of views and thoughts as its essence;
because it summons and brings about the fruit of suffering, it is called the accumulation of suffering. Cessation (*nirodha*) has the *nirvāṇa* of partial emptiness as its essence.

Because it can extinguish all sufferings, it is called "the cessation of suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha*). As for the "path" (*mārga*), its essence consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that assist toward correctness;

because it can realize the cessation that is free from suffering, it is called "the path to the cessation of suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha-mārga*). Furthermore, regarding these Four Noble Truths, the latter three are also established by taking the truth of suffering as their object;
therefore, they are all named in connection with suffering. △ Second, turning the wheel of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

And the detailed exposition of the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (up to): "With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

First is the forward contemplation of the process of evolution (*pravṛtti*). Regarding the "detailed exposition," since the factors of dependent origination are not distinct [from the Four Noble Truths], it is an extensive explanation of the aforementioned Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
From ignorance (*avidyā*) to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), there are twelve links that arise in succession and depend upon one another;
therefore, they are called the twelve causal conditions (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*). Ignorance is the affliction of the past.
Because of this affliction, one lacks clear comprehension regarding phenomena and principles; hence it is named "ignorance. With this ignorance as a condition, one performs various [karmic actions].

Because it is karmic activity (*saṃskāra*), it is said that "ignorance conditions activity. These two links belong to the past cause and are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Because karma drags consciousness (*vijñāna*) along as it enters the womb, it is said that "activity conditions consciousness. Because consciousness grasps and maintains [the embryo], it undergoes a transformation every seven days to form the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the womb;
thus, it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). "Name" refers to sensation, perception, mental formations, and so forth.
One discerns the four aggregates (skandhas). Within the womb, they still lack practical utility and exist as mere names. "Form" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha);
from the moment of conception until the fifth week, the various sense organs and physical forms arise, and the four limbs become distinct; therefore, it is called "form.
As name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increases, by the seventh week the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana) are fully developed; hence it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six [faculties]."

They enter, because the sense-faculties possess the meaning of entering their objects; thus the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are accomplished. When the moon is full, one emerges from the womb and encounters external objects;

hence it is said that "the six entrances condition contact" (*ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ*). From the habitual practice of contact, sensation (*vedanā*) arises, which perceives the characteristics of the disagreeable, the agreeable, and the neutral.
Therefore it is said: "Contact conditions feeling. Feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the experience of sensation; that is, the sense of undergoing [an object].

These five factors belong to the present fruit and are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering. Because of the experience of sensation, the mind gives rise to craving and attachment toward desirable objects;

therefore it is said: "Feeling conditions craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Because the fire of craving blazes intensely, one pursues [the object] without relinquishing it; therefore it is said: "Craving conditions grasping" (*upādāna*). Due to grasping...

Arising and proceeding, one creates various karmas which serve as the cause for all states of existence (*bhava*). Therefore, it is said that "clinging conditions existence" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*).
Of these three links, the first two belong to afflictions (*kleśa*) and are identical to past ignorance (*avidyā*); the latter one belongs to karma and is identical to past formations (*saṃskāra*).

Both are present causes and are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). By means of these causes, fruits are induced, and one will give rise to the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), once again receiving the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, it is said that "with conditions there is birth. The five aggregates (skandhas) are a provisional combination that will soon change and decay;

thus, it is said that "birth conditions aging, death, and so forth," including sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. These are also matters within aging and death, for aging inevitably entails sorrow and suffering, while death inevitably entails lamentation and affliction.
These two links belong to the future fruit and are likewise subsumed under the Truth of Suffering. Furthermore, these ten...
Regarding the two causes and conditions: according to the *Avataṃsaka* and the ancient masters, there are further meanings; however, to avoid prolixity, they are not recorded here.

This [section] on the Tathāgata extensively elaborates upon the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), serving as the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti*). From "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) downward, it is the contemplation of the reverse order of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Regarding "observing in reverse": one observes in reverse order from old age and death back to ignorance.
As the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "Due to the existence of what does old age and death exist? From what further condition does such old age and death arise?

The first two phrases constitute the knowledge that infers the cause, and the latter two phrases constitute the knowledge that examines the cause. By inferring and examining across the three periods of time, these together constitute six types of knowledge.
Having completed this investigation, one knows that old age and death exist because of birth; this is called the knowledge of abiding phenomena (*sthiti-dharma-jñāna*).

Thereafter, one again uses seven types of knowledge to contemplate the cause of the branch of birth. In this manner, one proceeds by successive retrogressive contemplation until reaching the branch of formations (*saṃskāra*), which exists because of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Together, these constitute seventy-seven knowledges; as for ignorance itself, it has no further cause and thus requires no further contemplation. One need only—
Arousing a courageous mind and exerting firm strength, one cuts off and extinguishes ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, through a successive causal chain, they are extinguished;

hence it is said that with the extinction of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are extinguished, and so on, until with the extinction of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are extinguished.

Now, this section concerns the contemplation in reverse order (*pratiloma*), which enables the analytical investigation and abiding in wisdom; this is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). As for the [contemplation] in forward order...

Cessation (*nirodha*). It can manifest the principle of non-arising; this is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). Thus, the Tathāgata extensively elaborates upon the two truths of the Path and Cessation as the gate of returning to cessation.
Having concluded the bestowing of provisional means in response to the request, [Section] Four: Assurance through Hearing the Dharma.

The Buddha, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans—[extending] to those who are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—first and foremost makes a vow (such as when the present Buddha first converted the five bhikṣus). "The great assembly of devas and humans" is a general description of the sentient beings present in the gathering;
"six hundred billion," etc., specifically points to the assembly that has made the vow. Because the Buddha’s wisdom and conditions are superior, he is the foremost.
At the initial attainment of deliverance, there were six million billion nayutas in number. "All dharmas" refers here to the six sense-objects of the world.
Humans, being solely addicted to and defiled by these six sense-objects, give rise to various outflows (*āsrava*), thereby causing their minds to suffer bondage.
One cannot attain liberation. Now, having heard the Dharma of the Truths as conditions, one knows that sensation is suffering; therefore, one does not accept anything at all.
Because of this non-acceptance, the mind is no longer bound by the outflows (*āsrava*), which is called attaining liberation.

The nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) progress gradually, becoming deeper and more profound, and as they become deeper and more profound, they become more subtle and wondrous; hence they are called "profound and wondrous meditative concentration. The three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six...

It penetrates the eight liberations. A brief explanation is found in the preceding text; a detailed account is as explained in the *Sammitīya-nikāya-śāstra*. Regarding the second [category], "the lower":

this refers to the subsequent stage of assurance (such as the present Buddha continuing to deliver twelve hundred disciples). The second, third, and fourth all refer to the *Āgamas*, for the *Āgamas* were taught in four assemblies.
From this point onward, it refers to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā, because during the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā, or...

He spoke of both the Great and the Small Vehicles. There were those who received benefit from the Small Vehicle; thus, the assembly of *śrāvakas* became immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and innumerable.
He did not mention the *pratyekabuddhas* because their realization is equal to that of the *śrāvakas*, and they are therefore subsumed within the category of *śrāvakas*.
The Buddha of Wisdom has finished revealing the provisional teachings. II. The Buddha of Wisdom Manifests [the Real].
There are four actual sections: first, the Prince’s request; second, the following of him into the homeless life; third, the arrival of the time to reveal the truth;

and fourth, the attainment of benefit upon hearing the Dharma. Regarding the first (although he had previously requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned, the Buddha knew that the time had not yet arrived and thus taught only the Hīnayāna; now that the Hīnayāna has been perfected, it is necessary to request again in order to open the gateway to the Mahāyāna).

At that time, the sixteen princes—all of whom were youths (up to) whose deep resolve was realized through the Buddha’s self-attestation—first established the capacity for awakening to reveal their original nature.
At an age when their innate truth had not yet been lost, they left the mundane world to enter the Way; hence it is said, "the youths renounced the household life.
However, as the matter of their renunciation occurred at the very beginning and was not previously mentioned, it is recounted here. From below...

The same applies to those who have left the household life. A *śrāmaṇera* (novice) is here translated as "one who rests from cruelty" (*xi ci*), meaning that they cease all evil and constantly practice kindness and compassion.
Generally speaking, there are three types: first, those whose form is that of a *śrāmaṇera*, referring to those who, though having received tonsure, have not yet received the categories of precepts;
second, those whose dharma is that of a *śrāmaṇera*, referring to those who study the same disciplinary codes and receive the transmission of the precepts. Furthermore...

There are three types: first, the *kāka-vāyasa-śrāmaṇera* (crow-shaker novice), referring to those aged seven to thirteen, who are able to drive away crows and other birds for the sake of the Saṃgha and protect places such as the kitchen;

second, the *dharmārha-śrāmaṇera* (fit-for-the-dharma novice), referring to those aged fourteen to nineteen, who are able to serve their teachers, perform manual labor, and cultivate meditation and recitation, being thus in accord with the dharma of renunciation; third, [the *pravrajita-śrāmaṇera* (renunciant novice)].
The "name śrāmaṇera" refers to those aged twenty or above who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), as they still retain the name of a śrāmaṇera.
These three types all receive the ten precepts and are collectively designated as having identical dharma.

The "bodhisattva śrāmaṇera" refers to those who, before receiving full ordination, first generated the great resolve; these are now bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, because they possess the aspiration directed toward the lower [vehicles].

Because of the meaning of "knowledge and vision," the two phrases regarding the faculties clarify the excellence of the present capacity. "Having already made offerings" and so forth clarify the profundity of the past foundation.
Alternatively, these may also be Great Beings of the Dharma-body who act as responsive retinues for the Wisdom-Buddhas, utilizing this to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-lands.
"Both [the disciples] spoke below" refers to requesting the Dharma and expressing their circumstances. This is...

The phrase "all those immeasurable ones" refers to the assembly previously mentioned as having attained assurance. Although this assembly belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, they all possess the potential for the Mahāyāna;
therefore, they are called "Virtuous Ones" (Bhadanta). The phrase "all have already accomplished" indicates that their minor fruits [of the śrāvaka path] are already perfected.
Since their minor fruits are already perfected, there is no further occasion to teach the minor Dharma; thus it says, "For our sake, you should preach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Ti. This is the request for the Dharma. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, they shall not fail the Buddha’s intention; hence it is said, "We all practice and study together.
That we all practice and study together is not merely a matter of empty words; hence it is said, "Our aspiration and vow—this is what we keep in mind, this is where our attention rests.
Because our profound resolve has been firmly established for some time, it is said, "The Buddha himself knows us by witness. To "know by witness" means to realize through direct experience.
"Verifying this through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, one comes to a clear understanding of the present; this is my petition. Thus concluded the Prince’s request. 2.
Following [the Prince] into the Monastic Life:
At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, [those who] also sought to leave the household life were immediately granted permission by the King.
"The retinue he led" refers to the aforementioned hundred great ministers, as well as the remaining hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of people.
Among them were eighty trillion individuals who, upon seeing the prince leave the household life, suddenly conceived the desire to emulate him;

they, too, sought to renounce the world. Generally speaking, there are four ways to distinguish those who leave the household life: first, those whose bodies join the ranks of the Dharma-fellows, while their minds...

1. Still feeling attachment: the body has departed but the mind has not. This refers to those who, though they have left their wives, children, and possessions behind, do not give rise to craving or defilement toward them;

this is called "the body has departed, but the mind has not. 2. Not departing from the body but departing from the mind: this refers to those whose bodies remain among the assembly of Dharma companions, yet whose minds harbor no lingering attachment;

this is called "both body and mind have departed. 3. Neither departing from the body nor departing from the mind: this refers to those who feel deep craving and defilement for their wives, children, and possessions; this is called "neither body nor mind has departed. Now...

This belongs to the third category. As for the King’s immediate granting of permission: although he acted as a companion to his son in this worldly matter, it was nonetheless in accordance with the intention of the sages who delight in leading people toward goodness.
However, since this assembly had followed the Prince in leaving the household life, the karmic affinity (*dharmapratyaya*) should properly reside with the Prince;

alternatively, they may have been a group of followers from whom he formed connections later on. For these reasons, they are specifically mentioned here. △ Third, the time arrives and [the narrative] is revealed.
Truly so.
At that time, that Buddha accepted the request of the śrāmaṇera (up to) they all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered [the teachings].
From the initial stage until the faculties were matured—having already accepted the request and further passed twenty thousand kalpas—he then preached the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
"If" refers to tuning the faculties and awaiting the proper time. Thereupon, he preached the sutra for the assembly;

the sutra he preached was no different from the present one, which is why it is called "this Mahāyāna," etc. Regarding the phrase "preaching this," those present received and upheld it according to their capacities.
"Receiving" means accepting it without contradiction; "upholding" means maintaining it without loss. "Reciting with fluency" means that "fluency" (*tong*) refers to a thorough mastery of its meaning.
"Benefit" refers to the thorough mastery of the text. This corresponds to what was previously stated: "Having heard this, we all together practice and study it.
△ Fourth, the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma:
When this sutra was being preached, sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras (up to) ten million billion kinds [of beings] all gave rise to doubt and confusion.

The sixteen bodhisattvas possess faculties that are fundamentally equal and correct; therefore, it is said that they all "believe and accept. Among the assembly of śrāvakas, however, the capacities of their faculties vary;
therefore, it is said that they "also have faith and understanding. Yet, "faith and acceptance" (śraddhā-pratigraha) differs from "faith and understanding" (adhimukti).

"Faith and acceptance" means to find the principle acceptable and to internalize it deeply within the mind. "Faith and understanding" means to find the words acceptable and to have a slight comprehension of them.
The meaning is as follows: because one has faith in the Buddha’s words, "following this sutra" refers to faithful understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*).
As for "other sentient beings," these include those of fixed nature who are *śrāvakas*, ordinary persons who dwell in signs, or the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride;

because there are such various distinctions, it is said they are of "thousands of millions of kinds. That they all give rise to doubt and confusion is due to the faults of having a fixed nature and so forth.

This is because they were obstructed. (Question: The outline states that they "obtained benefit from hearing the Dharma," yet the sutra says they "all gave rise to doubt and confusion. Is this not a discrepancy between the sutra and the outline? Answer: There are two kinds of benefit.

First, immediate benefit, which refers to those who believe, understand, and accept it. Second, remote benefit, which refers to those who harbor doubt and confusion. If these people had not harbored doubt and confusion, by what means would the Prince have had the opportunity to lecture again to establish a karmic connection? By what means would they have heard the Dharma today and attained deliverance? Based on this, even those who harbor doubt and confusion all serve as remote causes for Buddhahood;
can this not be called a benefit? The section on the reasons for establishing karmic connections is concluded. △ Second, the matters regarding the establishment of karmic connections, in three parts.
1. The Buddha enters meditative absorption; 2. The two princes lecture in his stead; 3. Emerging from absorption, he praises and exhorts them. First:
"The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand *kalpas* (until) he dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*."
Regarding the initial time and occasion for preaching the sutra: the "eight thousand kalpas" is also spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings (*yǒu jī*).

In reality, it has been preached throughout the dust-motes of worlds and across all lands, continuing without cessation until this day. From the phrase "Having preached this... onwards, it describes entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The Buddha knew that among the assembly of those harboring doubts, the karmic capacity (*jī*) resided with the Prince; therefore, he immediately entered his quiet chamber. There is no state in which the Buddha is not in concentration; he merely manifested the power of expedient means (*upāya*) by showing himself as having transcended words.
Therefore, it is said that he "dwells" [in samādhi]. As for the eighty-four thousand kalpas, this refers to the duration of his dwelling in meditative concentration;
it was merely a time set aside to form a karmic connection with the prince. △ Second, the Prince’s Re-exposition.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras [up to] gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This was the first instance of the "covered lecture" (*fùjiǎng*) for establishing karmic affinity. "Silent" (*jìrán*) means that body and mind are unmoving. Then, Zhìfú entered the room.
He remained behind to form a karmic connection with the prince; the prince silently understood his intention, which is why it is said that he "knew.
As for each ascending to the Dharma seat: the Buddha’s intent must not be contravened. Regarding the eighty-four thousand *kalpas* spent for the sake of the fourfold assembly:
the timing and opportunity must not be missed. "Extensively expounding" refers to unfolding the text; "discriminating" refers to explaining its meaning.
According to the Prince’s intention, there was nothing other than his desire to dispel the doubts of the multitude and thereby establish conditions for the future.

Each and every one of the six hundred trillion beings who gathered to form these conditions were precisely those same people who had previously harbored doubts. As for "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening":
he showed them the benefit of attaining Buddhahood, taught them so that they might joyfully accept it with faith, and thus served as their intermediate recipient [of the Dharma].
The conditions for their deliverance serve as the cause for attaining Buddhahood in the future. △ Third, emerging from samādhi to praise and exhort:
After the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had passed eighty-four thousand kalpas... [up to] ...the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

First, he praises what is rare and marvelous. Having known that the task of establishing karmic connections with those beings was complete, he arose from samādhi. Desiring to strengthen the faith of the assembly of listeners, he felt it necessary to proclaim this universally.
Since their spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is superior and their roots [of merit] are profound, benefiting both self and others, it is said to be "most rare and marvelous.

This is the general praise. The phrase "those whose faculties are keen and penetrating" is the specific praise for their superior capacity. The phrase "who have already made offerings," and so forth, [is the praise for their deep roots].

The first praises the profundity of the source; receiving and upholding the phrases of the Buddha’s wisdom praises self-benefit. Revealing [the Dharma] to sentient beings and so forth praises the benefit of others.
The former states that all should together receive and uphold it, reciting it until it is thoroughly mastered; the latter further states that one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them.
This causes them to resolve upon *bodhicitta*; this is precisely the meaning of self-benefit and benefiting others herein.
"You all," and so forth, is an exhortation for the assembly to draw near, which further contains two meanings. First is the formal exhortation. "Repeatedly" (*saṃkhyāta*) means constantly.
Being constantly near [the teacher] signifies diligence for the sake of the Dharma; furthermore, making offerings signifies reaching the ultimate for the sake of the Dharma. Therefore...

The following is an interpretive commentary. The Buddha feared that those of the three vehicles within the provisional teachings might think that because this was preached by a prince in disguise, it was not the word of the Buddha and would therefore not necessarily be beneficial.
Thus, he explained that those who can believe it without disparaging it shall attain *bodhi*.

The matters concerning the formation of karmic connections are concluded. △ Third, the four categories of those who attain liberation according to distance [from the present]: 1. Those whose number is not yet exhausted in the interim;
2. Those who attain liberation up to the present; 3. Those who have not yet finished even now; 4. Those who will attain liberation in the future. First:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas—up to the present time, these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have not yet come to an end.
Because these sixteen bodhisattvas do not forget the supreme path of wisdom, they constantly preach this sutra to transform sentient beings."

He constantly recalled the instructions of Mahābhijñājñāna; therefore, he was accompanied by him in every lifetime. Furthermore, regarding being accompanied in every lifetime, Da Cheng (Dacheng) said:

"Where there is no affinity, there will surely be no gathering; where there is affinity, there will surely be no separation. Because they heard the Dharma from him, all were able to believe and understand it;
for this reason, their causal roots became ever deeper. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they were able to encounter various Buddhas; thus, their affinities became even more profound.
Because [the number] is superior, it refers to forty trillion Buddhas. Since the sutra has not yet been fully revealed, one may reasonably remain in doubt as to which specific Buddha is meant.

As for those who have not yet reached completion today, this refers to those with whom [the Buddha] formed karmic connections in the past; among them, those who encountered the Buddhas in the interim and whose conditions were ready to ripen, have indeed ripened.

Those who were to be liberated have been liberated; yet, as for those who have reached maturity and are ready for liberation, they are still not all finished. △ Second, the attainment of deliverance up to the present, in two parts:
first, the prince attains Buddhahood; second, he returns to deliver that multitude. First:
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you... [up to] "...attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This first section provides a general heading for his attainment of Buddhahood and his preaching of the Dharma. Because the prince’s practice was perfected, he attained the fruit of Bodhi;
because his preaching of the Dharma saved sentient beings and his transformative conditions were profound, there were bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who served as his retinue. The second part [below].
The names of the directions are listed separately. Among them, there are eight directions and sixteen names.
The ancient masters interpreted these by taking the meaning of the hexagrams (*gua*). This was in accordance with the spiritual capacities of those in this region.

Although I have now slightly altered the phrasing, I still employ that same interpretation, both to guide those who prefer such methods and to cause them to receive the seed of the Buddha. As for the East: it belongs to the position of *Zhen* (Thunder) and serves as...
The meaning of "movement" (*āśva*). *Āśva* here means "immovable. This signifies that while manifesting movement, one realizes the principle of immovability.

Having realized the principle of immovability, one responds perfectly to the various capacities of sentient beings; because their hearts are gladdened and they submit with sincerity, the land is named "Joyful" (*Abhirati*).
As for "the summit of Mount Sumeru," it means that this Buddha, having realized the principle of immovability, stands loftily above all things, like Mount Sumeru.
Majestic and immovable, its summit towers above all other peaks. To the southeast lies the position of *Xun*, which signifies flexibility and compliance.
Only when a person abides in flexibility and compliance can they subdue all others; therefore, both Buddhas are named after the lion.
One represents fearlessness in preaching the Dharma, while the other represents fearlessness in manifesting physical forms; thus, they are distinguished by their voices and appearances.

The South belongs to the position of *li* (the fire element). It is characterized by emptiness and luminosity. The Buddha realizes the principle of empty luminosity and responds universally to the capacities of all sentient beings, yet his essence remains free from dwelling or attachment;
therefore, it is called "abiding in space. To say "abiding in space" refers to an abiding that is itself non-abiding.
As for "constant cessation," it means that the principle of self-realization is supremely void and supremely luminous, capable of containing all things.

The verses consist of [the Buddha] of Wisdom opening up the provisional (upāya): two verses on the Buddha of Wisdom revealing the ultimate reality (bhūta). The first four [sections] are as follows: one verse on the Buddha of Wisdom attaining enlightenment;
two verses on the request to turn the wheel of Dharma; three verses on accepting the request and bestowing the provisional; and four verses on hearing the Dharma and attaining assurance.
Regarding the first [section], there were originally three prose passages, which are now included here in an abbreviated verse form.

The first four lines of the verse, from "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas" up to "their hearts were filled with exultation," praise the period of ten kalpas leading up to his imminent attainment of Buddhahood. The following eight lines praise the offerings presented by the various devas;

the absence therein of the Trāyastriṃśa devas arranging the seats is due to the brevity of the verse. The final four lines praise the arrival of the time when he attained the Way; this is self-evident.
△ Second, the two verses requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma. First, one verse on the prince’s request for the Dharma; second, one verse on the Brahma King’s request for the Dharma.

Regarding the first (which, according to the prose commentary, consists of three parts, but here lacks the verses praising the Buddha; only the two preceding and following meanings are briefly summarized, without further subdivision).
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, together with their retinues... (up to) "fill me and all others.
The first four lines praise the fullness of the retinue. From "head and face" downward, these praise the princes' formal request.
Within this, the upper two lines constitute the ritual of the request, while the lower two lines constitute the words of the request. △ Second, the Brahma King.

The request for the Dharma consists of two parts: one verse on the Buddha manifesting auspicious signs through wisdom, and two verses on the deities coming to make their request. Regarding the first (the brief verse):

"The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter; appearing but once in a vast expanse of time, he manifests as an Awakened One to enlighten all sentient beings, causing all things to tremble."
That which is difficult to encounter is easily missed; when the time appears, many do not recognize it. Therefore, one must awaken.
As for the method of awakening, nothing but a great transformation can alert the mind; thus, there must be a shaking.

According to the prose (*pāṭha*), there is further the meaning of light illuminating all, but here in the verse it is abbreviated. △ Second, the verse on the request of the various devas (abbreviated verse), in two parts.
First, a separate verse concerning the eastern direction; second, a combined verse concerning the nine directions. Regarding the first:
[The Buddha traveled through] five hundred myriads of kotis of lands in the eastern worlds (up to) accepting the invitation and sitting silently.

The first verse concerns the shared deliberation under the light; it briefly records the words of their collective consultation. The two lines concerning the Brahmās describe the ritual of presenting offerings, which has been sought out in detail;
however, the specific procedure for the offering is missing. The two lines concerning the scattering of flowers describe seeing the Buddha and making offerings;

although the phrase "seeing the Buddha" is implicit, its meaning must certainly be present. The two lines concerning the invitation to the Buddha describe the formal request for him to turn the Wheel of Dharma, followed by praise in verse.
This follows the prose section and should be placed within the passage on seeing the Buddha and making offerings. It is as stated in the text for the eastern direction:
"The World-Honored One is most rare; it is difficult to encounter him. He possesses immeasurable merit and is able to rescue and protect all beings," and so forth.
The two lines beginning with "The Buddha knows" verse-ify his silent acceptance of the invitation. △ Second, the combined verses for the nine directions.
The same applies to the three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir (up to:

"turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma"). These words of requesting the Dharma are an abridgment of the extensive prose. The verses of the Heavenly Kings of the Nine Directions summarize the meaning and chant them in verse.

Having finished chanting the request to turn the wheel of Dharma: △ Third, the verses on accepting the request and employing skillful means (the prose section is divided into two; this belongs to the brief verses and is not further subdivided).
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepted the invitation of those people...

[up to] "you should all know that all exist through the condition of arising. This means that just as ignorance serves as the productive condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations serve as the productive condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth—this verse refers to the gate of forward evolution (*pravṛtti-mukha*). This evolution proceeds without ceasing, like a wheel.

Because it revolves without ceasing, it is designated by the term "suffering" (ādīnava). As for the instruction that one "should know," once one knows the reason for its arising, one then knows the reason for its cessation;
this verse pertains to the gateway of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*). △ Fourth, the verse on the assurance of hearing the Dharma (abbreviated verse).
When this Dharma was proclaimed and circulated, even six million *billion* *nayutas* [of people] could not reach its limit.
The first verse refers to the initial guarantee; "one *nayuta*" is a large number, equivalent to ten billion. The second verse below refers to the subsequent guarantee.
From "after this" onwards, it includes the third and fourth [guarantees], extending even to the time of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.

Thus it is said. The verse on the Buddha of Wisdom’s completion of the provisional teaching is finished. △ Second, the verse on the Buddha of Wisdom’s revelation of the ultimate truth (the prose commentary has four sections;

here, the second and fourth are missing). It is divided into two parts: first, the verse on the Prince’s request; second, the verse on the revelation of the ultimate truth when the time has come. The first is a brief verse.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras (up to: "the wisdom-eye is foremost and pure").
Their attendants—those who followed and accompanied them from among the eighty trillion people previously led by them—all were destined to attain Buddhahood.
Having heard the Dharma, they believed and accepted it; they did not fail the Buddha’s intention. [This concludes] the verse on our having heard it.

The meaning of all practicing and studying together. "May we obtain the eye of wisdom," etc., is a verse summarizing the preceding meaning of our aspiration for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and so forth.
Regarding "the foremost purity": because all three vehicles possess the eye of wisdom, yet only the Buddha is the most pure.
2. A brief verse on the arrival of the time to reveal the reality.
The Buddha knew the conduct of the youth in his past lives (extending to the verse "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges").

This "conduct in past lives" should belong to the practice of a Bodhisattva, because the preceding text contains the meaning that he had already made offerings to various Buddhas and had purely cultivated the Brahma-faring.
Regarding the "immeasurable causes and conditions" and "various parables," these are [taught] through many expedient means.
"Instruction and guidance" embodies the Tathāgata’s tireless intention to teach others. The six *pāramitās* represent one's own cultivation to reach the other shore;
the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) represent the ability to deliver sentient beings and transform others.
These are all the true Dharma and the path of the Bodhisattva. One should explain these during the period of the Vaipulya Prajñā, for by means of the Vaipulya Prajñā...
Although he preached the Dharma of ultimate truth, the path of the Bodhisattva still involved the taming of faculties and the protection of the senses;
it was not a direct revelation. Therefore, the words of "discrimination" were set aside, as in the Extended Version: "After twenty thousand kalpas.

This refers to events occurring within those twenty thousand kalpas. When he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the time had arrived and the faculties were matured, so that the provisional was brought back to the real.

[This is] the teaching; for there is no room for silence. Although the verses of the Ganges-sand [Sūtra] are more numerous than those of the present sūtra, the Dharma has no fixed form, adapting to the capacities and times of beings.
This concludes the section on the verses regarding the occasion for forming karmic connections. △ Second, the verses on the matter of forming karmic connections (the prose commentary has three parts;
here, the second—Emerging from Samādhi and Praising—is missing). This is divided into two: first, verses on the Wisdom Buddha entering samādhi; second, verses on the Prince’s secret recitation.
First (the summary verse):
After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber and sat with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
△ Second, the verse on the prince’s re-exposition (the interpretive verse).
These śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha’s meditation had not yet ended (up to "as many as the sands of the Ganges").

The first eight lines praise the closing lecture and the establishment of karmic connections; the latter four lines praise the assembly for whom the connections were established. The section on the matter of establishing karmic connections is concluded.
△ Third, the verse on those who attain deliverance from afar and near (the prose commentary has four parts, but the latter two are now missing). Second, one verse on those in between.
It is not exhausted. From these two verses until now, they have attained deliverance. First (the brief verse):
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in various Buddha-fields wherever they may be.
Although it is said that he was always with his teacher, there were times when he had already attained liberation and times when he had not;

this refers to what is described in the long prose as "encountering forty trillion Buddhas," which does not yet include those up to the present. △ Second, the verse on attaining deliverance up to the present (abbreviated verse).
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras fully practice the Buddha-way (up to) gradually teaching them through the Buddha-way.
The first four lines praise the prince’s attainment of Buddhahood and his full practice of the Buddha-way:

throughout birth after birth, he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, accomplishing his own perfection by benefiting others. The latter four lines praise his returning to deliver those multitudes. This concludes the verse.

The formal narration of the causes and conditions is concluded. △ Second, the verses further clarify the ritual of transformation in three parts: first, the verse restates the fundamental principle and introduces a metaphor;
second, the verse correctly clarifies the meaning through the metaphor; third, the verse applies the Dharma to correspond with it. First:
I have previously taught this for you during the sixteen [assemblies] (up to: "do not harbor fear or alarm").

The first four lines are a verse summarizing the principle of employing provisional means (*upāya-kauśalya*) (a summary verse based on the meaning). The employment of provisional means is fundamentally intended to reveal the ultimate reality;

therefore, it is said that they are "led toward the Buddha-wisdom. The latter four lines are a verse summarizing the principle of revealing the ultimate reality (a summary verse based on the meaning). Revealing the ultimate reality is fundamentally based upon the original cause.

Therefore, the teaching strictly exhorts you not to be startled or afraid. △ Second, the verse clarifies the two points through parables: first, a verse on the metaphor of sentient beings’ responsive capacity;
second, a verse on the metaphor of the Tathāgata’s transformative response. First (the commentary on the meaning of the verse):
For example, it is like a perilous and evil road that is remote and desolate, teeming with venomous beasts, extending for five hundred *yojanas*.
"Remote and desolate" refers to a region where no humans dwell; this is a metaphor for the absence of the Buddha’s transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) in one's surroundings.

The long stretch of venomous beasts, water, and grass: the venomous beasts are a metaphor for false knowledge and false views, because they can destroy right faith. The water and grass are a metaphor for... [text fragment ends].

Right concentration and right wisdom, because they can support understanding and practice; the rest is the same as the prose section. △ Second, the verses on the analogy of the Tathāgata’s transformation and response have two parts:
first, a verse on the analogy of establishing provisional means based on the ultimate reality; second, a verse on the analogy of returning to the ultimate reality from the provisional means.
The first two [verses]. One verse is a simile for not obtaining the reality; two verses are a simile for concealing the real and establishing the provisional.
First (the prose commentary): At that time there was a guide, possessed of strong memory and wisdom... [up to] ...desiring to turn back from here.

The initial metaphor establishes the attainment of the Way and the preaching of the Dharma; "possessing strong memory and wisdom" and so forth praise the meaning of being "intelligent, wise, and far-sighted.
Furthermore, "one whose mind is resolute" necessarily implies one who knows both the open and the obstructed, which also praises the phrase "skillfully knowing the perilous path."

The principle may be understood by analogy. "Rescuing those in peril from distress" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata manifesting his dwelling within the afflictions of birth and death, attaining enlightenment, and preaching the Dharma;
it corresponds to the prose section stating that he leads the multitude, desiring to help them cross over these difficulties.

The phrase "the multitude" and what follows is a metaphor for the difficulty of entering the Great Teaching; its meaning may be understood by analogy with the prose. △ Second, the verse on concealing the ultimate and manifesting the provisional.
The *Dṛṣṭānta* (Metaphor; including both *Geya* and *Udgīti*).

The passage beginning with "The Guide had this thought: 'These people are truly pitiable... up to "they claim to have already attained deliverance" constitutes the initial *Geya* on the metaphor of recollecting skillful means.
The prose section following "The Guide had this thought... may be understood through the extended *Geya*.
One should contemplate the expedient means and so forth at that time to supplement the remaining meaning of the verse; this shall be pondered.

"One should employ the power of supernatural transformations to manifest a great city" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s intention to utilize provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to skillfully establish provisional fruits.

This is because provisional wisdom is applied by responding to and adapting to the capacities of beings; therefore, it is compared to supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*). Since these provisional fruits are not ultimate, they merely serve as a temporary support for those of lesser capacity.
Therefore, it is likened to a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*). The house serves as a metaphor for the principle of partial emptiness (*pradeśa-śūnyatā*).

This is because partial emptiness exists within *nirvāṇa* as that upon which the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) relies, just as a house exists within a city wall as that which provides a basis for material form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, since it is not the true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is compared to adornments. As for the surrounding gardens and groves, they represent [the objects of] wandering...

The "place of pleasure" is a metaphor for the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which provide clear illumination and serve as the place where those of the two vehicles sport with mastery.

The "canals and bathing pools" are places for washing and bathing; they are a metaphor for the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), serving as the place where those of the two vehicles bathe their bodies and minds.
The "repeated gates" are a metaphor for the three gates of samādhi. The "pavilions" are a metaphor for the path of the Arhat. The "A... [is incomplete].
The path of the Arhat transcends the three realms; therefore, it is metaphorically described as being placed on high. "Men and women" refers to those belonging to the class of servants and laborers;

this metaphor signifies the exhaustion of afflictions through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the realization of principle through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as these are utilized by the two vehicles.

Furthermore, since wisdom corresponds to its fruit, it is metaphorically described as being "filled. However, from this point upward, all belong to the metaphors for the skillful means of recollection and contemplation.
This is followed by the verse below, which provides a metaphor for the correct application of the provisional vehicle (*upāyayāna*).

"Having performed such transformations" refers to the aforementioned manifestations of city walls, palaces, houses, and so forth, each having been fully conjured. This corresponds to the preceding verse:

"Having formed this thought, he conjured a city three hundred *yojana*s away, comforting the multitude and telling them not to fear," which serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s words of exhortation. This concludes the preceding verse.
He addressed the multitude, saying: "Do not be afraid; do as you wish. [The passage] concludes with verses on the analogy of descending to the level of ordinary people.

The meaning of these verses, which serve as a guarantee for hearing the Dharma, may be understood by referring to the prose commentary. This concludes the verses on the analogy of establishing provisional means based upon the ultimate reality. II.
Verses on the Analogy of Returning Provisional Means to Ultimate Reality (Explanatory Verses).

The Guide, knowing that [the people] had rested, gathered the assembly and addressed them: "[We shall] together proceed to the place of treasure. The first line of verse corresponds to the preceding passage:
"At that time, the Guide knew that this multitude... until they were no longer weary. The three lines of the assembly correspond to the preceding passage:
"He immediately extinguished the conjured city. The four lines beginning with "I see" correspond to the preceding passage: "The great city mentioned earlier."

"What I have manifested through transformation. These two lines of yours now [refer to] the preceding verse: "You all go and come; the place of treasure is near. This concludes the section that uses metaphors to clarify the meaning.

△ Third, the section using the Dharma to provide a formal application (based on the prose commentary, there were two parts; here, the latter is missing, and the former metaphor is restated, applying it directly to the Dharma).

This further divides into two: first, a verse on the manifestation of provisional means from the ultimate reality; second, a verse on returning provisional means to the ultimate reality. The first of these further divides into two, the first of which is as follows:
The verse states that [the truth] cannot be attained from reality. Two verses conceal the ultimate to establish the provisional. The first (summarizing the meaning in brief):
"I, likewise, am the guide for all... [from] the perilous paths of affliction."

The first two lines praise the accomplishment of enlightenment and the preaching of the Dharma; it is said that one must necessarily attain enlightenment and preach the Dharma in order to become a Teacher.

"Seeing all... and so forth praises the difficulty of entering the Great Teaching. Those who "slacken and abandon the path midway" correspond to the meaning in the prose section of not wishing to see the Buddha and not wishing to draw near him.
"Unable to deliver sentient beings," and so forth, corresponds to the prose section where he [the Bodhisattva] thinks as follows:

[The Buddha] reflected: "The path to Buddhahood is long and distant; it is through enduring suffering for a long time that its fulfillment is achieved. 2. Verse on Concealing the Ultimate and Manifesting the Expedient (Explanatory Verse):
"Therefore, by the power of expedient means, for the sake of providing rest, I spoke of Nirvana, saying: 'Your suffering is extinguished, and all that was to be done has been accomplished.'"

The first two lines [of the verse] represent the application of provisional means according to the capacities of sentient beings; the latter two lines grant a guarantee. This concludes the section on "Applying Provisional Means Based on the Real.
△ Second, the verse on "Returning the Provisional to the Real" (an extensive verse based on the meaning).
"Having known that they have reached nirvāṇa and all attained arhatship" refers to the first two lines [of the verse].
"Then [the Tathāgata] leads them into the Buddha-wisdom" refers to the following eight lines.
"The Tathāgata at that time immediately preached for them: 'What you have accomplished is not yet complete'" refers to the preceding six lines.
The preceding verse states that the stage upon which you currently abide is close to the Buddha’s wisdom; you should examine and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not ultimate.
The final four lines of the verse state that it is solely through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
This must refer to the words of all Buddhas, in order to manifest that the path of each Buddha is identical.
The glossary reads "ru" (如) as the character itself. This also combines with the meaning of the preceding metaphor. The Buddha’s exposition on causes and conditions is concluded.
*Fahua Zhizhang Shu*, Scroll Three, Phonetic Glossary.

*Jiá* (the first character is pronounced *jié*, meaning "to permeate" or "to moisten thoroughly"). *Gēng-nuò* (the first character is pronounced *gēng*, the second is pronounced *nuò*; rice that is not glutinous is called *gēng*, while that which is glutinous is called *nuò*).

*Yín* (rhyme with *rèn*, pronounced *shěn*): a chronic ailment within the abdomen. *Wò* (rhyme with *yǐ*, pronounced *wò*): to hold; when applied externally it means to grasp, when applied internally it means to clench.
*Fahua Zhizhang Shu*, Fascicle Four.

proofread for characters by his dharma-heir disciple, Mingyuan.

△ Second, the benefits obtained by those of duller faculties, in two parts: 1. The prediction received by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); 2. The prediction received by those still in training (*śaikṣa*). The first [is titled in the chapter heading]:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eight: "The Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples."
The five hundred disciples—namely, the three Kāśyapas mentioned later in the text, as well as Cunda, Svāgata, and others—"received" (shou) means they took it upon themselves;
that is, they personally recognized their past causes and accepted the prediction of their future Buddhahood. It does not mean that [the Buddha] bestowed it upon them.
Regarding this bestowal [of predictions], the emphasis lies on the capacity of the recipient, as it manifests their actual ability to have self-confidence.

According to the text, there were one thousand two hundred people, including Pūrṇa, who received these predictions; yet in the present title, only five hundred are mentioned because they represent the primary recipients.
As for Pūrṇa, he was one who concealed his inner realization while manifesting outwardly, whereas the rest of the assembly was represented by Kāśyapa.
Commentary: It is not primarily intended for those of limited capacity; therefore, it is not mentioned. According to this, there are also five distinct meanings to this section:
first, to manifest that the Buddha’s virtues are inexhaustible. As the text says: "We are unable to proclaim the Buddha’s merits with our words. This is it.
Second, it is to reveal that those of inferior faculties do not possess the ultimate truth; the text says: "My disciples are thus; they employ skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
Third, it is to reveal that the Seal of the Mind (cittamudrā) penetrates universally from afar; the text says:
"Those who are not in this assembly—you should proclaim and explain [the Dharma] for them. Fourth, it is to reveal one's own past causes and conditions; the text says: "The All-Knowing One..."
The vow remains intact; this is what is meant by "not losing it. Fifth, it is to manifest self-confidence free from doubt. As the text says:
"I now know for certain that I am truly a bodhisattva," and so forth. In sum, the three karmas of the Tathāgata are sublime;

whatever he ordains never goes in vain. Therefore, following the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), the *Pañcaśatānām vyākaraṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred) follows.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [was able] to know our deep-seated original vows. First, the narrator describes the realization:
"Hearing this wisdom" refers to grasping the meaning of the two previous cycles of the Dharma and the parable—the convergence of the provisional back into the real.
"Expedient means according to suitability," etc., refers to grasping the two previous cycles of the Dharma and the parable—the issuing of the provisional from the real.
Regarding the meaning: furthermore, hearing "the bestowal of predictions" summarizes the meaning of the five people receiving their predictions from the preceding two cycles of Dharma and parable.
Furthermore, hearing "past lives and so forth" summarizes the meaning of the prior establishment of conditions through the re-explanation in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter.

Furthermore, hearing "all Buddhas and so forth" summarizes the meanings of the phantom city and the destruction of the city within the Parable of the Phantom City; for it is by means of the phantom city and the destruction of the city [that the purpose is fulfilled].

All these are metaphors for the Tathāgata’s sovereign power of supernatural penetrations (*ṛddhi*). "That which has not yet occurred" refers to past causes and conditions that have not been previously explained.
"Purity of mind" means that former doubts have now been severed. "Leaping for joy" means experiencing the bliss of realization and being unable to contain oneself.

Immediately following this, [the assembly] prostrated from below, paid homage, and made a request with mindfulness; their understanding was equal to that of the four disciples, as they desired to have something [further] explained.
[He] presented [this]. Thereupon, he rose from his seat and went before the Buddha; among the assembly of sages, none were able to offer a word in response.

Thus, he simply prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side. "Withdrew" (què) means to retreat. As for "gazing up at the Honored Countenance": it refers to looking up at the face of the Venerable One.
"Longing for the prediction and awaiting its bestowal" refers to the heart’s reception and spiritual realization of the Buddha’s compassionate intent, never for a moment averting one’s gaze.
"Wishing that he might bear witness and know" refers to the thought that it is most marvelous;

"marveling at the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom acting according to what is appropriate" praises the Tathāgata’s power of the Dharma for universal salvation, which accords with the world and so forth—this is the true provisional wisdom.

The meaning of "according to what is appropriate" refers to uprooting sentient beings and so forth. The meaning of the power of the True Dharma universally rescuing them refers to the knowledge of expedient means, which is precisely skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Its ability to uproot various attachments is the power of the Dharma. It is said that the Buddha can preach in accordance with the various dispositions of the world;
this is like raindrops falling upon all things, where both the great and the small are equally moistened—it is nothing extraordinary.

Is this not extraordinary wisdom? Sentient beings are greedily attached everywhere; the Buddha is able to weigh their conditions and rescue them, just as a wildfire consumes a vast wilderness, leaving nothing—neither the great nor the minute—unconsumed.
Is this not a rare occurrence? As the "Expedient Means" chapter says: "He extensively expounds his verbal teachings."
"By means of countless skillful expedients, he guides sentient beings, causing them to abandon all attachments. As stated in the *Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta*:

"He is able, for the sake of those who are inferior, to endure such matters; for ordinary people who grasp at signs, he teaches according to what is appropriate. All of this conveys this same meaning.
Regarding the Buddha’s merits and so forth, when Pūrṇa wished to praise the Buddha’s virtues, his thought was that he himself was incapable of doing so—this is the sense of the "poor son."

The first analogy: the four sons spoke in unison, extolling the Buddha’s virtues to the utmost. They maintained that even if the Tathāgata were to speak for an infinite duration, he could not exhaustively describe them;
how much less so could my own wisdom and eloquence compare? Even if I wished to proclaim them, it would be like attempting to measure the void with a ruler or to fathom the ocean with a bushel.
Therefore, it is said that words cannot express them; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and those like him can do so.

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra reflects that the Buddha’s wisdom is able to discern the intent of his own mind. His "deep mind" refers to the true faith manifest before him, which is not the superficiality of the past;
therefore, it is called "deep. His "original vow" refers to his distant vows of the past, not something first initiated now.
Therefore, it is called the "Root. By granting himself alone the status of one capable of knowing [the Buddha's virtues], his intention was:

"Although my wisdom and eloquence fall short, I am unable to fully extol the Buddha’s merits; nevertheless, my present profound resolve and my past original vows have long been within the Sage’s discerning gaze, and he should not reject me for my lack of fluency. Thus concluded Pūrṇa’s request. △ Second, the Tathāgata grants...
The prophecy consists of two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections: first, praising his merits; second, formally bestowing the prophecy. Regarding the first:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... [up to] ...no one is able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
He addressed the bhikṣus, asking whether they had seen him or not. This was because he wished for them to truly see Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and not to regard him merely as a śrāvaka.
Among all his sons who were able to preach the Dharma, Pūrṇa was the most excellent;
therefore, it is said that among those who preach the Dharma, he is the foremost. Regarding the phrase "constantly praised," the *Āgama Sūtras* state: "Within my Buddha-dharma..."
"Puṇyamānīputra is foremost among those who are well able to expound extensively and analyze the principles of meaning.
The word "also" (亦) is a term used to extend the preceding description; it indicates that he is not only praised for his ability to speak, but also for his ability to practice.
"Various merits" refers to practicing according to what has been taught, specifically such matters as diligent protection and maintenance mentioned below, as in the *Āgama* contemplation.
"Merely practicing" refers to diligent application. "Receiving the censure of the Vaipulya [sūtras] without retreating" refers to upholding and protecting [the Dharma].
Regarding what is meant by "upholding and protecting": it is to prevent practitioners of the Śrāvaka vehicle who follow the literal meaning from destroying the Dharma.

Furthermore, "transmitting the teaching from the Buddha" as in the *Prajñāpāramitā* refers to assisting in its proclamation. "Showing, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening" means that one transmits the teaching to Bodhisattvas, demonstrating how to achieve [enlightenment].
The benefit of the Buddha is to teach and cause others to rejoice. Furthermore, whatever the Tathāgata has taught—beginning, middle, and end—is all called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Pūrṇa was able to discern it from beginning to end; this constitutes a complete exposition.

By borrowing words to manifest the principle and relying on the principle to enter the Way, he brings benefit to those who practice together. "Those who practice together" refers here to the followers of the Two Vehicles. The second...
