even those with minor causes of scattered goodness shall all attain Buddhahood, and thus they may also be called "Brahman. "Shedding" (捨除) means to exhaustively eliminate. "Exhaustive" (盡窮) means to reach the limit.
This refers to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s magnificent prose and elegant verses, his extraordinary skill in debate, and his possession of versatile talent as he maneuvers [his arguments].

Regarding the pivot of killing and bringing to life, with the exception of the Buddha alone, even one whose wisdom resembles that of Śāriputra—though his questions arise like clouds—would be unable to exhaust its expressions when seeking to fathom its words.
Judging by this, his wisdom surpasses all sages and his eloquence equals that of the Sublime Sage;
yet, in the preceding text, he still considered himself unable to proclaim the Buddha’s merits. This was for one reason: he perceived...

The Buddha’s virtues are inexhaustible; fundamentally, they cannot be fully proclaimed. For the time being, to provide practical guidance for those of inferior capacity, he has provisionally displayed these ritual manifestations.
How could this be truly inferior to the four sons? The section on praising his merits concludes. II. Properly Bestowing the Prediction (Vyākaraṇa). This has three parts: 1.
Attaining the fruit through the causal practices; 2. The adornment of the primary and secondary realms; 3. A summary of the merits. The first of these has three [subsections].
First, his past causes were profound; second, his future practices were fulfilled; third, he shall attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the protection and assistance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and so forth, these reveal the matters of the Original Ground as being no different from those of the present.

This distinguishes him from those who merely engage in empty verbalism; he had attained the four kinds of unimpeded mastery (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
"Equality" (etc. refers to the unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*) by which one transforms and teaches bodhisattvas based on what has been clearly understood.

Although it is called "unimpeded eloquence," it is here termed "wisdom" because eloquence is issued from wisdom; since there is eloquence only when there is wisdom. "Thoroughly" (*śanaiḥ*) means to examine the suitability of the faculties [of the listeners].

"Passing through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas [until] the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans.

Regarding "passing through immeasurable *saṃkhyeya* [kalpas]," this refers generally from the time of ninety billion past Buddhas until the point when he shall fully complete the bodhisattva path; it concerns the cause by which he will attain *bodhi* in this land.

Because one practices this path within it and because the conditions for it reside herein, the Buddha is titled "Dharmaprabhāsa" (Light of the Dharma). This title has two meanings: first, that there is no dharma regarding which he is not clearly enlightened;
second, that he uses the great light of the Dharma to shatter the darkness of sentient beings. It is also named after his self-awakening and his awakening of others.

First, the adornment of the environment; second, the adornment of the primary retribution. Regarding the first:
that Buddha, with [a land as vast as] the trichiliocosms equal to the sands of the Ganges River... (up to) humans and devas interfacing so that they may see one another.
Since those with whom he formed karmic connections during his causal stage were numerous, the reward lands (*vipākabhūmi*) in the resultant stage are naturally vast.

Therefore, although he attained Buddhahood in this land, there is no impediment to taking the sands of the universe as his realm. As for the ground being composed of the seven treasures, it is that which is evoked by the adornment of the minds of sentient beings through the Dharma-treasure during the causal stage.
Regarding the ground being as level as the palm of a hand: the Buddha’s palm is flat and even, unlike the palms of worldly people.
Some say that beneath the sea there is a stone named "The Palm," upon which not even a single speck of dust is uneven;

the earth is level as this stone because it was moved by the response to a mind that levels the ground to save all beings. As for mountains and hills, these are places of high elevation; as for streams and ravines, these are areas of low depression.
All of these are responses to an uneven state of mind within the ground of the heart. By leveling the ground through a mind of equanimity to save all beings, [the earth becomes level].
Therefore, the land of retribution does not possess these features. This is why the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara leveled the ground to await the Buddha, to which the Buddha replied:
"O Benevolent One, you should level the mind; for when the mind is level, the world is level.

As for the seven-jeweled terraces and pavilions filling the space, they arise because sentient beings are moved by the Dharma-treasure and dwell therein. The palaces of the various devas are situated near the void.

"Emptiness" reveals the reach of the Buddha's teaching. That "the heavens above bestow their protection and humans and devas meet, so that both may see one another" reveals the mutual penetration of the Buddha-way;
it shows that the principles of humans and devas are one. As the *Da Cheng* says: "The Way of Heaven is perfected by humans;
what humans have not yet begun is not other than Heaven, and what Heaven has not yet begun is not other than humans. Yet, Pūrṇa [Maitrāyaṇīputra], regarding this Sahā world...
This defiled land has been transformed into pure realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; compared to that of Śākyamuni, it is truly extraordinary.

Yet, the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment was granted to those of inferior capacity. Alas! Regarding the matters of the fundamental and the manifested, there are indeed aspects that cannot be fathomed by thought.

There are no evil realms (*durgati*), nor are there women... (up to) the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the three knowledges (*trividyā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
First, as for "sentient beings being purely virtuous; there are no evil realms, nor are there women": because they are born by transformation (*upapāduka*) on the causal ground, [they are made thus].

They practice wholesome dharmas and are constantly cultivating the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Since they are not moved by the influence of women and do not arise from a womb, it is said that all sentient beings are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Sexual desire is the foremost of all evils; since it is said that none exist [there], it can be known that sentient beings are purely wholesome.

It is obtained and moreover is great. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When the breath of desire is coarse and turbid, one cannot give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrously luminous *Jāmbūnada-golden-light-aggregate*.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers who, because of his attachment to desire, suddenly lost his divine feet.
According to this, those who emit light from their bodies and possess mastery over flight do so entirely because they have attained freedom from desire.

As for those who are universally golden-hued and so forth, possessing the dignified bearing of presiding over assemblies and preaching the Dharma while naturally adorning themselves—it is not [due to anything other than these causes].
It is fashioned and adorned with beauty. Based on this, the sentient beings of that land are all capable of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above and delivering sentient beings below.
As Vimalakīrti said, "The profound mind is the pure land"; it is for sentient beings who are fully endowed with merit.
Those who come to be born in that land are surely what is meant by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. As for those who "constantly partake of two kinds of food":

their transformation bodies are light and pure, and thus they do not rely on solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Hearing the Dharma with joy can assist one's nature and nourish its source; this is called the food of Dharma-joy (*dharma-prīty-āhāra*).

Abiding in meditative concentration with a sense of sublime ease can sustain the spirit and harmonize the vital breath; this is called the food of dhyāna-delight (*dhyāna-prīty-āhāra*). Alas! The multitudes of the Sahā world...
Birth. A lifetime of toil is for nothing but the sake of the mouth; boundless karma of killing arises entirely from the faculty of the tongue.

By means of calculation and reckoning, it is shown that the Śrāvakas are innumerable—those who possess the supernormal powers, the clear knowledges (*vidyā*), and liberation.

This excludes those who do not come, as they cannot be compared [to the former]. According to this, those born in that land are said to "meet with the superior beings," which is no different from the Land of Ultimate Bliss itself.

The *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states that his mother followed her husband far away, and after a long time she became pregnant.

As her delivery drew near, she longed to return home, but gave birth to her son while on the way. She subsequently gave birth to another son, making two children in total; thus, they were distinguished as the elder and the younger.

It is further said that according to the customs of the Western Regions, when a woman is about to give birth, she must return to her mother’s home; because she gives birth twice on the road, it is named accordingly.

Responding to conditions to deliver sentient beings is the public duty of the sages and worthies; it cannot be otherwise, just as one cannot be free in matters of official business. There is no... [end of fragment].
The priceless jewel is a metaphor for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is not possessed by other vehicles; therefore, it is likened to something of incalculable value.

"Tying it on" is a metaphor for the closing lecture (*punaḥkathana*) and the establishment of karmic connections (*bandhana*). Through this closing lecture and the establishment of karmic connections, one causes [beings] to resolve upon the aspiration for omniscience.

At that time, the knowledge of all modes is already stored within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), just as the precious jewel is tied inside the lining of a garment. "Giving it and departing" refers to...

The metaphor of having finished forming karmic connections in this land and being destined for another direction represents the fact that although one has received great benefit at that time, one is still shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of this obscuration by ignorance, one lacks faith and understanding regarding all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*);
thus, one is compared to being unaware and unconscious. "Having arisen" represents the internal permeation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Ignorance is slightly diminished; yet, although ignorance is slightly diminished, one continues to drift and sink according to karma.
Therefore, this is illustrated by the metaphor of wandering. "Arriving in another country" is a metaphor for drifting and sinking according to karma, wandering through the five realms of existence.
Wandering through the five realms, oppressed by manifold sufferings, one enters the dense forest of false views, desiring to seek even a small measure of concentration and wisdom and practicing them.
All such fruitless ascetic practices are likened to the diligent seeking of food and clothing;
their extreme hardship is likened to having previously followed heterodox paths where one practiced in vain without gain.

That which is "obtained in small measure" is likened to attaining the partial truth within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Having attained this partial truth, one considers it to be ultimate; therefore, it is metaphorically described as "then."
He considers this sufficient. This was the manner of those in former years who grasped at the provisional as real. △ Second, the parable of now attaining great benefit:
Later, while meeting with his kinsmen and friends, he encounters [the jewel] (extending to: "he shall always be able to act as he wishes, lacking nothing").

"As for 'later on,' this is a metaphor for the present high assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Since the time has arrived and the conditions have ripened, the capacity of the disciples and the teaching are in accord;

therefore, it is said metaphorically that one 'meets him by chance. This serves as a contrast to the forty years prior, when although [the disciples] entered the gate and received instruction, the Great and Small Vehicles were vastly different—what is called 'meeting yet not meeting,' meaning they had not yet truly met him. The phrase "and spoke these words," etc., is a metaphor.
The Tathāgata’s discourse on returning from the provisional to the ultimate is intended to awaken those who are heedless. The exclamation "Alas! is a word of admonition; the phrase "What is it for?
expresses a sense of urgency. It means: "How can you, a magnificent man of honor, be so preoccupied with mere food and clothing as to drift about until you have come to such a state?
This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata awakening the followers of the Two Vehicles and stimulating those of the provisional teachings, revealing that they inherently possess the Great [Vehicle].

As for this condition: you truly deserve to be called a dragon or an elephant. Why then do you allow yourself to drift and wander through successive lives with only meager concentration and wisdom, ultimately falling into the Lesser Vehicle?
When I previously wished to bring you peace and happiness, it was like my former practice of giving expository lectures to establish karmic connections;

my original intent was to cause you to resolve upon the Great Mind, so that you might forever leave behind the suffering of birth and death and ultimately attain the bliss of Nirvana. As for the five desires:
These are metaphors for the five supreme and wondrous sensual pleasures that transcend the world: the form adorned with the marks and signs [of a Buddha]; the sound of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
the fragrance of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the flavor of the unsurpassed One Vehicle; and the touch of awakening to the self-nature of phenomena.

All of these are the enjoyments of the Buddha-ground, just as in the case of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. The statement that "on such and such a year, month, and day, a pearl was tied inside the robe" is a metaphor for when the formal lecture was being given;
it means that by causing one to generate the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) has already been received into the field of consciousness.
That it exists now, yet you do not know it, is a metaphor for the Tathāgata pointing out [the truth] to those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*). All...
Your wisdom and vows remain intact and have not been lost; it is only because you are firmly obstructed by provisional teachings that you do not recognize this yourself.
Because of this ignorance, you merely refine and cultivate yourself within the teachings of the Hīnayāna to seek your own benefit.
Therefore, I liken your diligent toil and distress to seeking one's livelihood through such means—like wearing a pearl while begging for alms—and thus I reprimand you as being extremely [foolish].
It is delusion. The Two Vehicles forget the Great and grasp at the Small; the Tathāgata’s reproach of them is likewise so. "To trade" means to exchange this for that;

"must" (xu) means to employ. "Teaching to use jewels to trade for what is needed, which can always be as one wishes," is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, having revealed the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), teaches [beings] to use this to deliver sentient beings and to perfect their own virtues, thereby fulfilling Buddhahood.
As for the fruit, its enjoyment will be inexhaustible. This concludes the explanation through the use of analogies. Part Three: Applying the Dharma to the Case [in Two Sections]:
1. The former realization of the small fruit; 2. The present attainment of great benefit. First [The former realization of the small fruit]:
The Buddha was also like this when he was a bodhisattva; his vow for all-knowledge remained intact and was not lost.

While he was a bodhisattva, at a great assembly of the Great Penetrating Wisdom, he entered the home of a close kinsman and friend in accordance with the Dharma’s meaning, causing them to resolve upon the mind of wisdom.

Having planted the seeds of wisdom within the field of consciousness, it was as if a pearl were tied inside their garment according to the Dharma’s meaning, yet they forgot it and were unaware of it due to [their negligence].
Enveloped by ignorance, it is as if one is intoxicated and lying down, unaware of the truth. Having attained the state of an Arhat, one has realized the partial emptiness of the Lesser Fruit;
thus, it is appropriate that one feels there is something gained. Believing oneself to have reached extinction (*nirvāṇa*), one does not realize that what has been realized is not ultimate;

thus, it is appropriate that one considers this sufficient. The two phrases concerning "sustenance" (*jīvitapariṣkāra*) further explain the meaning of believing oneself to have reached extinction. This is because:

Formerly, while following other paths, it was difficult to acquire the means of livelihood and right wisdom. Now that we have encountered the Buddha-dharma, we consider ourselves satisfied with what little we have obtained.
Although we are satisfied with this meager attainment, we claim to be beyond the reach of the knowledge of all modes; yet, such is our former great resolve.
The seeds in the field of consciousness are indestructible; therefore, it is said that all the vows for omniscience remain intact and are not lost.
Since they have never been lost, one ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, yet one instead considers one's own limited wisdom sufficient.
This is what the preceding text meant by "only now do I realize this," which is like being a person of no wisdom. △ Second, attaining great benefit now.
"Now the World-Honored One has awakened us" (up to) "we have attained great joy, such as we have never experienced before.
This refers to the present assembly. Former karmic conditions have drawn them together until they meet here; friends from the past and future have converged and encountered one another.
"Awakened" means to alert and cause them to realize. This corresponds to the previous exclamation, "Alas! (takkhaṇa). By comparison—

The Master possesses the full demeanor of a dragon-elephant (nāga-hastin) and is worthy of the title of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). Since what he has attained is not yet ultimate, it is inappropriate for him to take formal realization as his goal.

As for his clothing and food, why does he act in such a manner? May he, for the sake of those who have long planted the roots of goodness for Buddhahood, point far ahead toward the Great Penetrating One (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) and the covered lecture hall, causing them to resolve upon the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and planting the seeds within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

To summarize what was previously stated: in the past, when I wished to enable you to attain peace and happiness—even up to the priceless jewel—I tied it within the lining of your robe and skillfully manifested *nirvāṇa*.
This was because you obscured yourselves by delighting in the small; it was a provisional teaching established in accordance with your capacities. To summarize the present:

although I am now manifest before you, you do not know this and believe that I have truly passed into extinction. Relying upon that [belief], you have undergone refinement through cultivation and practice.
I sought it for my own benefit; combined with my previous diligent toil and distress, I sought only my own livelihood.

Now I realize this, which conversely reveals that I was ignorant in former years—combined with my previous state, I was truly foolish. That I have received the prediction of the fruit must surely have been bestowed by the Tathāgata;
combined with his previous exhortation to trade, I felt no joy, yet now I rejoice that my enjoyment shall never be exhausted. Combined with... [the text ends here].
The preceding prose section on the fulfillment of wishes is concluded. II. Verse Recitation (the introductory title states):
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
△ (The Main Verses, divided into three parts: 1. One verse expressing joy and self-reproach; 2. Two verses explaining through parables; 3.
Three verses applying the Dharma to the analogy. First (the verse on the meaning):
When we heard the voice of the unsurpassed and peaceful prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), (up to: "we considered ourselves sufficient.
The first two phrases should be read as a single sentence. It means that the Tathāgata bestowed the prediction, causing us to attain the unsurpassed peace;
because he instructed us directly and personally, we were able to hear it. Since the Buddha is the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*), he is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).

Regarding "The Buddha of Wisdom" and "Those Who Repent Their Own Transgressions," the *Dacheng* (Great Vehicle) commentary states: "There are four kinds of transgressions: namely, forgetting one's original vow;

fearing the Mahāyāna; delighting in the Lesser Dharma; and being satisfied with meager attainment. However, the preceding prose section belongs to the narrative framework established by the sūtra compiler.
What follows is the self-accusation of the five hundred [bodhisattvas], which is not in verse form like the preceding prose. Indeed, the prose section is based upon this.
This is an introduction. Regarding the "attainment of a small portion of nirvāṇa" within the immeasurable treasure of the Buddha: this refers to the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Within the treasury of the Buddha’s merits, it is like a mere grain of dust. Foolish people lacking wisdom often consider a small attainment to be sufficient.
The five hundred disciples each thought, "I am also like this," and thus it is called "like" (*tathā*). However, this too was only known after their awakening;
this corresponds to what is said in the prose section: "Only now do I know it. II. Verses on the Parable to Elucidate the Meaning, in two parts: A.
Verses on the Parable of Formerly Realizing the Lesser Fruit. B. Verses on the Parable of Now Attaining the Great Benefit. First:
For example, it is like a poor man who goes to the house of a kinsman and finds there a priceless jewel.

Having formerly been an ordinary person of low station, he is now permitted to participate in this sublime assembly, just as the poor man arrived at his kinsman’s home. Thus it is with all the Buddha-dharmas.

It is primordially and spontaneously present, like a family that is exceedingly wealthy. Relying upon that Buddha-dharma, one lectures for the sake of the assembly, like providing a full array of delicacies;

this causes the mind of wisdom to arise and plants seeds in the field of consciousness. Like a pearl tied within one's clothing, it is clearly known to be effortless, yet it secretly bestows great benefit while awaiting the appropriate conditions.
It is as if one silently gives and then departs; yet, when shrouded by the seal of ignorance, [it remains unperceived].
Faith is not yet understood; it is like lying down and remaining unaware. When great goodness internally perfumes the mind, ignorance is slightly diminished, like rising and wandering about.
Yet, as one continues to drift and wander, one falls into false views, like seeking food in a foreign land through fruitless ascetic practices.
To practice in vain without attainment is like the hardship of seeking a livelihood. To enter the Buddha-dharma and immediately realize a small fruit is like being satisfied with a meager portion;
one has no aspiration for the Great Dharmas, just as one who does not desire fine things.

Although one passes through the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, one remains as before, harboring delusions that have not been dispelled—just like one who fails to realize there is a pearl within their garment, remaining entirely as they were.
Proceed. There is no need for a detailed distribution. △ Second, the verse on the simile of obtaining great benefit now (summarized by way of meaning):
"The kinsman who gave him the jewel later saw this poor man... indulging himself in the five desires."
The first two lines [of the verse] commemorate the previous [passage]: "Later, while meeting with a close friend... The lines on bitter urgency commemorate the previous [passage]:
"Alas, O man! Why do you labor for the sake of food and clothing? up to "...in this manner," which indicates the [previous] statement. The lines commemorating "I formerly desired to have...
up to "...the jewel tied inside his garment" follow the section on the poor man. The lines commemorating "the necessities for trade" are merely a summary of what preceded.
The exhortation by friends and relatives is like the Tathāgata bestowing a prophecy; this refers to the joy upon seeing the jewel, which serves as an analogy for the disciple receiving the prophecy.
Although the preceding and succeeding parts reflect one another, their meaning is no different. The explanation of the verses illustrating the metaphors is complete.

△ Third, the verses that apply the Dharma to the illustration have two parts: first, a verse on the former realization of the small fruit; second, a verse on the present attainment of great benefit. The first:
(Explanatory Verse).
We, likewise, O Bhagavān, throughout the long night... [until] ...self-sufficient and seeking nothing else.

The first line of the verse repeats that the Buddhas of the past were likewise; this is because the capacities of beings and the teachings emerge in mutual correspondence. Throughout the long night, O Bhagavān...
The long discourse states: "When he was a bodhisattva, he took it upon himself to deliver sentient beings; thus he remained for a long time in birth and death, as if in a long night.
The two lines beginning with "constantly pitying" commemorate his previous teaching and transformation of us, causing us to give rise to the mind of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "wishing and planting seeds": it means that once this mind is aroused, the seeds are planted within the field of consciousness (*vijñānabīja*).
The two lines beginning with "we" commemorate the previous state of seeking and then forgetting, being neither aware nor knowing;

the two lines beginning with "attaining a little" commemorate the previous attainment of the path of Arhatship, up to the point of considering a small gain sufficient. 2. Verses on the Great Benefit Now Attained (a brief versification according to the meaning).
"Now the Buddha has awakened me, saying that [my] extinction was not real" (up to) "body and mind are filled with universal joy.
These first two lines are a verse summarizing the previous passage: "Now the World-Honored One has awakened us," and so forth, up to "that which you have attained."
This is not ultimate extinction. The two phrases regarding "attaining Buddhahood" manifest that he has already established the great vow.

The preceding [verses] eulogize how he long ago caused you all to plant roots of merit for Buddhahood; the subsequent four phrases eulogize how he now realizes, "These are truly Bodhisattvas," up to the point of "experiencing immense joy at having attained what was never before.
While the meaning is the same, the phrasing differs. This is called the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

"Decisive" (*niyata*) means that the fruit accords with the cause; it is so called because it is definitively not in vain. The section on the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) receiving the prediction is concluded.
△ Second, the learned (*śaikṣa*) receiving the prediction (the title of the chapter states):
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
"Those in training and those beyond training" refers to those who are still in the stage of learning, such as those in the three fruits and four stages of approach.

Because they are practitioners who have begun their study by investigating reality and severing delusions, although they remain in the stage of learning, they do not find satisfaction in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is because they witness those beyond training receiving their prophecy.
He suddenly gave rise to the aspiration to emulate [the Buddha], and thus he too received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Someone may ask:

"Rāhula had already realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), while Ānanda still retained residual fetters (*saṃyojana*); why, then, are both referred to as 'those in training and those beyond training' (*śaikṣāśaikṣa*) in the title?

It is because this chapter is specifically intended to grant predictions to these two thousand disciples. As for these two individuals, they were merely introduced as examples to lead others toward actual practice. Therefore...
The title does not provide a separate heading. If one were to clarify the five meanings individually: first, it is to show that every individual has a share in this path;
as the text says: "We, too, should have a share in this. Second, it is to show that the attainment of Buddhahood results from the combined support of both learning and cultivation;
for example, Ānanda is placed first because of his extensive learning, while Rāhula is placed second because of his secret conduct.
It is so. Third, it is to manifest the profound foundation, in order to sever doubts and give rise to faith; as the text says:

"At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas," and so forth. Fourth, it is to manifest those still in training (*śaikṣa*), whose karma has already been redirected toward the Great Vehicle;
as the text says: "Their intentions were supple, tranquil, and pure," and so forth. Fifth, it is to manifest the three cycles [of teaching].
Because its capacity is universally pervasive, even those who are still training (śaikṣa) and those who have completed their training (aśaikṣa) receive predictions of enlightenment.

Generally speaking, the Buddha-nature is equal for all; whether one attains it or fails to do so depends on the individual. Provided one possesses the sincere resolve, there is no principle that can be violated.

Therefore, following the "Chapter on the Predictions for the Five Hundred Disciples," the "Chapter on the Predictions for Those Still Training and Those Who Have Completed Their Training" follows. (The scriptural text is divided into two parts; the first is as follows:)

The Request for Prediction. Part Two: The Tathāgata Bestows Predictions. This section has two parts: first, the request for prediction by the two sons; second, the request for prediction by the two thousand disciples.
Regarding the first: At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought... [up to] "...my own vows are fulfilled and the expectations of the assembly are satisfied."
First, reflecting upon my original aspiration, I have often contemplated this, referring to the period after the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings. My intention was this:
when we were formerly at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, we saw various bodhisattvas receive the prediction of their future buddhahood;
every time, I would constantly reflect, "If we were likewise to receive such a prediction like those bodhisattvas, would it not be a source of great joy and self-satisfaction?"
At heart, he immediately descended and, assuming the proper decorum, made a piteous plea. For Ānanda and the others had long harbored the aspiration to receive the prediction of future Buddhahood;
now seeing that those beyond training (aśaikṣas) had received their predictions, they were like one who encounters peach and plum trees and is reminded of the spring in his old garden.
Therefore, he immediately rose from his seat and approached the Buddha to present his request.

His intention was that, since they were fellow disciples who had entered the same gate, and they had already received their predictions, he too ought to do so. Thus he said, "We, too, should have a share in this;
in a single lifetime we shall cultivate the causes and realize the fruit, having no other reliance but entirely depending upon the Buddha’s empowerment. Therefore he said, "Only the Tathāgata, I..."
"...the one to whom all turn for refuge. Furthermore, from "I, moreover," onwards, he cites the aspirations of others to conclude his request. This again has two meanings.

First, he cites what the assembly aspires to, meaning: "Whether among devas, humans, or asuras, there is no one who beholds us two who does not know our lineage, recognize our worthiness and ability, and honor, cherish, revere, and befriend us—this is because of Ānanda."
He has constantly served as an attendant; moreover, by the power of his retentive memory (*dhāraṇī*), he protects and upholds the treasury of the Dharma.

Rāhula manifested birth into the Buddha’s family and exclusively excels in the excellence of esoteric practice. As the Son of the Buddha, one is most venerable toward the Dharma, while the other is most intimate toward the Buddha.
These are no ordinary individuals; there is no room for them to be ranked or disparaged. If they were not disciples of the Buddha—
This constitutes the formal request for the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). His intention was:

"Since I am already held in high esteem by the assembly and the Buddha is my ultimate refuge, if I am indeed granted a prediction, my own aspirations will be fulfilled and the expectations of the multitude will be satisfied.
I pray that you do not abandon me in vain, thereby failing the hopes of both myself and others. 2. The Two Thousand Request for a Prediction.
At that time, the śrāvaka disciples, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), [proceeded] until Rāhula, who stood to one side with his aspirations fulfilled.

Rising to approach the Buddha, they performed the ritual for requesting a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). As for "joining their palms with single-minded devotion," this is the earnestness in seeking a prediction;

as for "gazing up at the World-Honored One," this is the sincerity in hoping for a prediction. However, at that time, the two thousand [disciples'] words of request were not necessarily identical in every detail.
The two sons’ aspiration for a prediction was no different from that of the two sons themselves;

thus it is said, "Just as Ānanda and Rāhula wished," for the compiler of the sutra avoided prolixity and intended for this to be understood by analogy with what precedes. As for "standing to one side":
With longing and eager anticipation, I prostrate myself to await your compassionate instruction—what is called "the bright moon tonight, gazed upon by all.

Thus ends the request for a prediction from those still in training. II. The Tathāgata Bestows Predictions (in three parts): 1. Bestowing the prediction upon Ānanda; 2. Bestowing the prediction upon Rāhula; 3.
Bestowing predictions upon two thousand others. The first two [sections] consist of: A. The actual bestowal of the prediction; B. Revealing the original [cause] to resolve doubts.
The first two [sections]. One: prose; two: verse. The first four [sub-sections]: one, the time of attaining the fruit; two, the adornment of the environment and its inhabitants;
three, the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma; four, the renown of the fruit. First.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda... [up to] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This was the first bestowal of a fruit-name; he was titled "Ocean and Mountain Wisdom" (*Sāgaragiri-prajñā*). This means his wisdom was as lofty and profound as a mountain or an ocean.
Thus, an ancient master explained: "Majestic like Mount Sumeru, such that no other peaks can reach it; deep like..."

The great ocean is vast and unfathomable. It is further said that the "King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers" refers to one whose wisdom is like a mountain or an ocean, and who further employs sovereign supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to manifest forms and preach the Dharma, being as sovereign as a king.

This is likely the result of Ānanda’s mastery of much learning (*bahuśruta*) and his power of retention (*dhāraṇī*), through which he protected the treasury of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "should offer below," it indicates...
As for the duration of time: from this point onward, he further made offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas; the length of that period can be known.

At the abode of each and every Buddha, he protected and upheld the treasury of the Dharma; the depth of those causes can be known. Having practiced such causes for so long a time, he finally attained accomplishment;
thus, it can be known that his Bodhi was not easily achieved. Based on this, one should not rely on one's own heavenly [status].

Truly, even those who are inclined toward slight weariness [with the world] and advance in their practice can thereby know what they have realized. △ Second, the adornment of the environment and its inhabitants:
[The teaching of] twenty quadrillion *Ganges* [sands of worlds]... until the eon named "Pervasive Wondrous Sound."
First, regarding the adornment of the primary retribution: even when counting the number of bodhisattvas by the measure of the sands of the Ganges, they still amount to twenty quadrillion.

How much more so when each and every one is led to attain Bodhi? Thus, it can be known that as the transformative influence spreads and worldly customs become beautiful, the people will abound in superior goodness.
Furthermore, this is brought about by the profound and vast karmic conditions formed through the protection and upholding of the Dharma-treasury. The name of the country is...
Below, the secondary environment (niṣyanda-vipāka) is adorned. His wisdom is like mountains and seas; he preaches the Dharma to universally deliver all beings.

Therefore, the country is named Constantly Erecting the Victorious Banner (*Nityotthitavijayadhvaja*), for the banner symbolizes the meaning of universal deliverance. When sentient beings hear the Dharma, their mental ground becomes pure;
thus, the land manifests lapis lazuli as its soil, for when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. His supernormal powers are sovereign, and his preaching of the Dharma is unimpeded.
Therefore, the kalpa is named "Pervasive Wondrous Sound. Furthermore, the faculties of sentient beings are pure; when the water flows or the wind moves, all constitute wondrous sound.

Now, that both the land and the kalpa are named after the preaching of the Dharma is because, during the causal stage, the treasury of the Dharma was compiled, and in the resultant stage, the heavens, times, and lands are all in accord with it. △ Third, the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma.
The lifespan of that Buddha was immeasurable thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of years (up to) the period of the Semblance Dharma remaining in the world being twice that of the True Dharma.
Although the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and equal [to these numbers], it manifests according to the capacities of beings; nevertheless, it can only be known through the wisdom of a Buddha.

From this point downward, the more one analyzes, the more confused it becomes; therefore, it is said that calculation and estimation cannot know it. The True Dharma is twice [the duration of the Semblance Dharma].

Regarding "The Semblance Dharma is twice as long as the True Dharma": if one discusses the Way, it becomes increasingly decadent as time passes; if one discusses the duration of time, it becomes increasingly long as it grows more decadent.
Such is the natural course of affairs. △ Fourth, fame and renown based on the fruits [of realization].
Ānanda, this is because the Buddha King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain and Sea Wisdom (up to the point mentioned) praised him together with others and extolled his merits;
he called him by name and informed him so that he might know his own excellence and give rise to joy, thereby enabling him to protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma during the causal stage.
To ensure that the wisdom-life of all Buddhas remains uninterrupted, the fruition is thus endowed with all meritorious qualities and praised by all Buddhas without end.
This concludes the prose section. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.

(The section of the formal verses is divided into four parts: First, a verse on the timing of attaining the fruit; second, a verse on the adornment of the primary and secondary [realms]; third, a verse on the renown of the fruit;
fourth, a verse on the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma. Part One.
"I now speak within the Saṃgha concerning Ānanda, the upholder of the Dharma" (up to) "the Buddha Sovereign of Autonomous Supernatural Powers.
The first four lines are a transposed verse (*chāu-sòng*) indicating the temporal setting; the final two lines are a retrospective verse (*chuī-sòng*) bestowing the name of the resultant fruit.
△ Second, the verse on the adornment of the primary and secondary [realms].
That land is pure and is named "Ever-Erect Exalted Banner," where it transforms and guides bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The first two lines [of the verse] are an anticipatory praise (*caokong*) of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment), while the latter two lines are a retrospective praise (*zhuisong*) of the *sambhoga-vipāka* (the physical body).
△ Third, a praise of the renown attained in fruition (anticipatory praise, treated briefly).
The Buddha possesses great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*), and his renown fills the ten directions.
Among the Buddha’s merits, the two methods of "subduing" (*saṃgraha*) and "gathering" (*vinaya*) are briefly cited here to encompass the rest;

therefore, it is said that he has great majestic power and his fame pervades the ten directions. This is praised by all Buddhas themselves; the meaning is the same as in the long prose section, though the phrasing differs slightly.
△ Four verses on the lifespan of the Buddha-dharma.
"His life-span is immeasurable because he has compassion for sentient beings" (up to) "planting the causes and conditions for the path of the Buddha.
The first four lines are a retrospective verse on the lifespan. The phrase "because he has compassion for sentient beings" reveals that his life-span is immeasurable; it is not...
I merely envy those who have lived for a long time. The final four lines supplement the verse by describing its benefits. Regarding "countless sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges":
since the Buddha-dharma has remained in the world for a long duration, sentient beings who undergo transformation naturally become more numerous; thus, within the Buddha-dharma...
Regarding those who plant the conditions for the Buddha-way: because their permeation by the Buddha-dharma has already become profound, they will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood in the future;
thus, the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) is completed. II. Revealing the Original Nature to Resolve Doubts (three parts): 1. The Bodhisattva at the Initial Stage harbors doubt. 2.
The Tathāgata reveals the original nature to resolve the doubt. 3. Ānanda recognizes his own original cause. First: [The Bodhisattva at the Initial Stage harbors doubt.]

At that time, among those in the assembly, there were bodhisattvas who had newly resolved [to attain enlightenment]... until the śrāvakas received such predictions. "Newly resolved" refers to beginners;
"great bodhisattvas" refers to those in deep stages. Those in deep stages have long since received their predictions, whereas beginners have only recently entered the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, they made the thought that they did not hear it. Since they did not hear the bodhisattvas receiving their predictions, they also did not know of the śrāvakas' [attainment].
Having heard of his true virtues, yet seeing only a lame turtle and a crippled donkey, he suddenly finds himself being trampled by a dragon-elephant;
for this reason, he wonders and doubts, asking, "By what causes and conditions... etc. △ Second, the Tathāgata reveals the original [cause] to resolve the doubt.

At that time, the World-Honored One knew the minds of the bodhisattvas; because their original vows were such that they had attained this prediction, their initial resolve was identical to that of the Buddha.
Yet, doubt remained within their hearts and hesitation manifested outwardly. Therefore, the Buddha, knowing this, addressed them.

This is intended to resolve their doubts. Regarding the "King of Emptiness" (*Śūnyarāja*): according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, he was a Buddha encountered by Śākyamuni during the intermediate period of his three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Based on this, the time when [the King of Emptiness] first resolved to attain enlightenment already belongs to the realm of manifestation;
Ānanda may be understood by this same principle. Below the section on Ānanda: their practices were each different, yet they attained Buddhahood for the purpose of saving sentient beings.

Fundamentally, to save sentient beings, one takes extensive learning as the requisite. Desiring to perform the task well, one first sharpens the tool; thus, Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning.
To attain the fruit, cultivation is essential; in cultivation, diligence is the backbone.

One prioritizes what is difficult and subsequently reaps the reward; thus, the World-Honored One was always diligent and energetic. Therefore, the following section demonstrates the attainment of the fruit.
Regarding speed and slowness: because the World-Honored One took the power of diligence as his means, he made the attainment of the fruit his primary task; thus, he had already realized Bodhi.
Because Ānanda took the power of extensive learning as his means, he made the salvation of sentient beings his core concern;

thus, he continues to protect the treasury of the Dharma, as well as those who will protect the treasury of the Dharma in the future, maintaining the life of wisdom so that it shall not be severed, and teaching and perfecting bodhisattvas so that they may succeed him.
This causes the lineage of the Buddha to flourish so that it may be perpetuated. An ancient master’s commentary states: "Above, there is the merit of succession;
below, there is the virtue of accomplishment. The final two lines conclude the discussion and resolve doubts. Regarding the phrase "the original vow was thus":
this demonstrates that extensive learning is not inferior, as it fulfills a long-standing vow. Therefore, one who attains such a record does so because their causal conditions are profound and grave.
Having made this vow, he obtained a most excellent prediction. This new development caused doubt to arise, much like the small quail laughing at the Great Peng;
how could it have known that the one who charts a course of ninety thousand *li* toward the south has indeed a profound reason for doing so?
△ Third, Ānanda recognizes his own original cause.
Ānanda personally heard his own prediction (upadeśa) before the Buddha, [extending] to the protection and upholding of all the Buddhas' teachings.

Upon first hearing the prediction, he was filled with joy; for long his heart had hoped to attain Buddhahood, fearing only that he might not succeed. Now that he has heard it directly before him, he is overjoyed.

Therefore, it is said that his vows were fulfilled and his heart was filled with great joy. Furthermore, "his heart was filled with great joy" refers to celebrating the certain attainment of the Buddha-way;
"attaining what had never been attained before" refers to knowing the extraordinary excellence of the land’s adornments.

From this point downward, he obtained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives and attained mastery over the treasury of the Dharma; these are the deeds of the Venerable One in the past, [revealed] because he manifested his traces here. [The text] is interrupted.

For a moment, [his memory] was temporarily lost. Now, through hearing and recording [the teaching], he rejoices; because his mind is pure, he further attains the recollection of past lives, and thus it is said that "he immediately recalls.

Furthermore, regarding "recognizing his original vow": although this is due to the Buddha’s teaching, it also arises from the power of his past lives, whereby he gains self-confidence free from doubt.
From "At that time" onwards, the power of his vows is further clarified. "Most rare" praises the power of the Buddha-dharma.
It is sublime; it is capable of generating wisdom. When I say "me," I am attributing this merit to the Buddha, expressing my intention not to presume upon it myself.
The immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, such as those now heard, are distinguished from the limited scope of the two vehicles' knowledge of past lives.
It is not impure. These two phrases of mine are words of self-confidence and self-assurance. Their meaning is this: the Buddha-way is fundamentally inseparable from human beings;
it is only because of one's own doubts and alienation that one cannot abide in it peacefully.

Now that I have heard the prediction and regained my memory of past lives, I know with certainty that I shall become a Buddha. From this moment on, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I shall never be apart from it.
Therefore, it is said that he "abides securely in the Buddha-way. The two phrases concerning skillful means (*upāya*) precisely clarify the meaning of the power of his vow (*praṇidhāna-bala*).
The intent is this: although protecting the Dharma was his original vow, he had already forgotten it after passing through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Now that he has been reminded by the Buddha, how could he dare suddenly violate his past cause? Thus, he clarifies the power of his vow and continues to serve the Buddha through his former skillful means.
Protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma. Having finished bestowing the prediction upon Ānanda, [the text proceeds] in two parts:

1. Bestowing the prediction upon Rāhula in prose; 2. Repeating the verses according to their meaning. The first part has two sections: 1. The fruit-name and causal practice; 2. The primary and secondary aspects of the Buddha-dharma.
First: At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula... [omitted] ...always acting as the eldest son of all Buddhas, just as he is now.

Because he cultivated secret practices (*guhyacaryā*), and by relying on those secret practices he perfected his virtues, as a result he was moved by precious flowers; he walked treading upon these precious flowers.
Therefore, it is taken as the name. It is likely intended to manifest the subtle and secret practices of the causal stage by means of the precious flowers of the fruition stage.

That he constantly serves as the eldest son of all Buddhas signifies his role in managing the "inherited troubles" of his father and upholding the Way of the Buddha; this is the intent behind Mañjuśrī being considered the eldest son, like Samantabhadra.
△ Second, the Dharma of the Buddha’s environment and its inhabitants.
This is the adornment of the Buddha-land of the Buddha Dabao Hua (Flower of Seven Jewels), extending up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because during the causal stage they practiced secret conduct and extensively heard the teachings, constantly supporting and assisting one another, the *dharmakāya* and *rūpakāya* of the resultant stage—the Buddha-dharma—are likewise like the ocean and mountains, without any difference.
Furthermore, his being the eldest son of this Buddha signifies that practice arises based on wisdom.

This constitutes the meaning of the perfection of conduct and wisdom. After this point, those who shall attain Bodhi are, in essence, those in the stage of the "Mountain and Sea" (Sāndhāna) as a candidate for Buddhahood (*upapatti-sthāna*).
The prose section on the bestowal of predictions is concluded. II. Reiteration in Verse according to the Meaning (The introductory verse states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
[The following is the formal verse:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son... (up to) in order to seek the unsurpassed Way."
"Receiving the Dharma" refers specifically to this very day, for it is on this day that one receives the teachings of the mind.
"Immeasurable billions of Buddhas" refers to the number [of Buddhas] equal to the dust motes of ten worlds mentioned in the prose section; the phrasing has merely been altered.

"Secret practice" means manifesting as a śrāvaka while secretly practicing the path of transformation, using outward traces to conceal the fundamental reality; therefore, only a Buddha can know it. He manifests as a long-lived being.

"Son," [the Buddha said], "to manifest this to sentient beings and others is the matter of the secret practice of the Way of Transformation. The two phrases concerning "immeasurable" clarify the merits manifested;
it means that the Venerable One harmonizes with the light and blends with the dust, secretly manifesting the merits of the Buddha-ground.
According to the capacities and suitability of beings, these are immeasurable—billions, trillions, and even incalculable. Regarding all Buddhas, the Venerable One...
The Dharma has long been clearly understood; even in moments of haste or adversity, it has never been neglected. Therefore, it is said that he "dwells securely in the Buddha-Dharma.

From his inherent nature, he gives rise to cultivation, secretly practicing the path of transformation. By means of these illusory causes, he brings the illusory fruit to perfection. Therefore, it is said that he "seeks the unsurpassed Way.
Having finished bestowing the prediction upon Rāhula, [the text proceeds to] △ Three: Bestowing Predictions upon Two Thousand Disciples, Part One: Examining and Determining the Capabilities.
It is appropriate. Second, the actual bestowing of the prophecy; third, the joy upon receiving the prophecy. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One saw two thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training... not only did he see them thus.

Those who were still in training and those beyond training personally witnessed their fellow students receiving the prediction of enlightenment; moved by this internal realization, it manifested externally, and thus the World-Honored One beheld them.
"Gentle" means following the true Dharma and turning away from provisional attachments. "Tranquil" means suddenly forgetting the narrow mind and accomplishing the great resolve.
"Pure" means concentrating the spirit and focusing the thoughts, maintaining an open heart to listen attentively. "Beholding the Buddha" means listening with yearning thirst.
I stand waiting with bated breath, respectfully awaiting your imperial decree. This is precisely a moment of "frustration and yearning," when one is ready to be enlightened and inspired.
Desiring to observe his demeanor to discern the depth of his realization, he asked whether such a person was present;
observing that his blinking and raising of eyebrows were vastly different from the ordinary, he replied, "Yes, I have seen him. △ Second, the main body.
The bestowal of the prediction consists of two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
Regarding the first: "Ānanda, these people shall make offerings [until] the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma are all equal."

Making offerings to the Buddhas and so forth clarifies the causes cultivated throughout kalpas; that which is hidden within while manifested without, assisting the Buddha to propagate his transformation, all carries the meaning of protecting and upholding the Dharma-treasury.

That the Buddhas of the ten directions attain Buddhahood and so forth is the attainment of the fruit based upon causes; it is because they protected the Dharma-treasury [that they attained this fruit].

By cultivating various meritorious virtues, the fruit is the attainment of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) that adorn the Dharma-body; therefore, they are all equally named "Precious Marks" (*Ratnalakṣaṇa*).

As for their lifespan, their primary and secondary supports (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), and both the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpa-dharma*), these are all entirely equal because their causal practices were without difference. II.
Verse Summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses (the following being the actual verses):
"These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me... gradually entering into nirvāṇa."

The initial verses correspond to the prose commentary, which may be understood according to what has been explained above. From "All" onwards, the verses supplement the account of the transformative deeds.

Regarding the necessity of employing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to save sentient beings, there are two meanings: first, because those who are difficult to transform can be transformed [by them], as in the cases of Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra.

First, they transform deviant minds into those of wondrous adornment; second, because they are able to reach what is difficult to reach, such as the manifestations of various physical bodies in different lands by Samantaghoṣa and Avalokiteśvara.
As for their renown being universal, it is because their supernatural powers universally deliver beings and their grace extends widely.
Regarding their gradual entry into nirvāṇa: although the attainment of Buddhahood occurs at one time, the entry into nirvāṇa is nonetheless divided.

The preceding and following sections are distinguished because the responses to conditions are each distinct. Having completed the bestowal of the predictions, △ Third, Rejoicing upon Receiving the Predictions:
At that time, the two thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), [their hearts] were filled with joy, as if they had been sprinkled with nectar.
His mind was supple; hearing the Buddha’s voice of prophecy was like the transformation brought by a timely rain, which is why it is said that he was "joyful and leaping with delight.
Regarding "the lamp of wisdom shines": this praises the Tathāgata for using the light of wisdom to penetrate and illuminate the mental capacities of beings, just as the brightness of a lamp.
Regarding "his heart is filled": he rejoices that his own *dharmaprīti* (joy in the Dharma) is sufficient and his vows are fulfilled; such joy is inexhaustible.
This refers to one's own excellence. Though one calls oneself a withered sprout or a ruined seed, one gives rise once more to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā);
therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of being sprinkled with ambrosia (*amṛta*). For ambrosia is the medicine of immortality; even the dead are sprinkled with it and restored to life.

The above constitutes one complete cycle on causes and conditions, summarizing the preceding text and extensively clarifying the provisional and the real, thereby concluding the section on severing doubt and engendering faith.

△ Third, the supreme manifestation of the sutra’s merit: regarding the propagation of the Dharma through others (while the present-day recipient of benefit surely relies upon the direct discourse of the Perfectly Awakened One, those in the final age who receive his grace depend entirely upon...)

The fourth section concerns the entrustment of the teaching. Desiring to borrow others to propagate the sutra, one must speak with utmost clarity to manifest the benefits. From the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" onwards, up to the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," all of this pertains to this meaning.

[This section has] three parts: first, manifesting excellence to recruit people; second, testifying to the benefits and making vows; third, requesting instruction on the proper method. The first two [parts] consist of: first, manifesting excellence and clarifying the benefits.
Second, recruiting people to propagate the sutra. First (the title of the chapter says):
"The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher. There are two types of dharma-preachers:
first, those who practice according to the teaching and take the Dharma as their teacher, such as those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it.

Those who provide offerings are of two kinds: first, those who rely on the teachings to propagate them; second, those who serve the Dharma Master, such as those who explain the text for others or transcribe it.
This chapter, from beginning to end, serves to clarify these points; therefore, it is named accordingly.

Furthermore, the reason the Tathāgata opens this chapter after the conclusion of the three cycles of teaching is that, according to the distinct meanings of the scriptural text, there are five [reasons].
First, it is to manifest that the scope of the teaching is universal, for it is sufficient yet not exhaustive of those previously mentioned.

As the text records extensively regarding the present and provides prophetic declarations regarding the future, this precisely suffices for the remaining capacities of the three prior cycles and for the assembly not yet reached.
Second, it is to manifest the excellence of the upholders, so as to inspire joy; as the text describes their receiving, upholding, and reciting [the teaching].
Reciting, explaining, and transcribing [this sutra], and so forth, will inevitably lead one to attain Buddhahood;

this is intended to inspire joy upon hearing it, thereby inciting the intention to uphold, recite, and study it. Third, it is to manifest the profound depth of this sutra and to entrust it with the instruction to be cherished, as the text says:
"This sutra is the secret essence of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or bestowed recklessly."
This is precisely to ensure that those who propagate the sutra understand what is to be cherished and do not transmit it recklessly.

Fourth, it is to manifest the vastness of its benefits so that they may know how to follow them; as the text says: "Upon hearing this sutra, one is then able to practice the bodhisattva path well," and so forth.
This is precisely to ensure that those who have resolved their minds to attain enlightenment follow the established path and maintain the track, not daring to overstep or deviate.
Furthermore, the fifth [point] clarifies the excellence of the conditions for protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*), so that one may practice the Path without obstruction.

As shown in the text by providing "methods and rules" (*fanggui*) and granting "protection and maintenance," it is intended to allow those who propagate the sutra to practice the Path with a settled mind, without fearing hindrance or stagnation.
Moreover, the *Dacheng* (Great Commentary) states: "The three rounds of bestowing predictions have already established them as Dharma Kings; yet the position of a Dharma King has not yet..."
There are those who attain realization not through a Dharma Master; therefore, following the Bestowal of Prophecy, the "Dharma Master" chapter follows next.
Now, the Dharma King is the sovereign holder of the lineage of the Way, while the Dharma Master is a tributary stream of that lineage.
The sovereign holder is like the ocean, and the tributary streams are like rivers. Without the great ocean, the flowing rivers would have nowhere to return; without the rivers...

If [the Dharma] were to flow away, then even the great ocean could be exhausted. Therefore, the station of the Dharma King and Dharma Master is fixed, and the Way of Śākyamuni shall continue in an unbroken lineage without end. [The scriptural text is divided into two parts: First, manifesting excellence by way of the person; second, manifesting excellence by way of the Dharma. The first part has two sections: first, concluding the previous section and initiating the subsequent one; second, the actual manifestation of its extraordinary excellence. The first [of these two]: [The text continues: "The Buddha told Ānanda: 'If you wish to know the lifespan of the Tathāgata, it is like the sands of the Ganges River. This is the section on concluding the previous and initiating the subsequent. It is said that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is as immeasurable as the sands of the Ganges. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s lifespan is not subject to birth and death. Since he is free from birth and death, his lifespan is immeasurable. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of all sentient beings. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s nature is identical to the nature of all sentient beings. Since the natures are identical, there is no distinction between long and short. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of empty space. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s body is the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is coextensive with empty space. Since they are coextensive, there is no limit to their duration. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the wisdom of the realm of phenomena, and the realm of phenomena is eternally abiding. Since it is eternally abiding, there is no exhaustion. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the minds of all sentient beings. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s mind is the mind of all sentient beings, and the minds of all sentient beings are originally unborn. Since they are originally unborn, there is no arising or ceasing. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the future. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s vow is a vow for the future, and the future is boundless. Since it is boundless, there is no end. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the past. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s practice is a practice of the past, and the past is inexhaustible. Since it is inexhaustible, there is no exhaustion. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the present. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s teaching is the teaching of the present, and the present is non-abiding. Since it is non-abiding, there is no coming or going. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the three times. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s body is the body of the three times, and the three times are indivisible. Since they are indivisible, there is no distinction. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s merit is the merit of the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are beyond calculation. Since they are beyond calculation, there is no measure. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *anabhilāpya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s name is the name of the *anabhilāpya* kalpas, and the *anabhilāpya* kalpas are ineffable. Since they are ineffable, there is no speech. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *aparimita* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s light is the light of the *aparimita* kalpas, and the *aparimita* kalpas are limitless. Since they are limitless, there is no boundary. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *acintya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the wisdom of the *acintya* kalpas, and the *acintya* kalpas are inconceivable. Since they are inconceivable, there is no thought. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *anantaka* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s power is the power of the *anantaka* kalpas, and the *anantaka* kalpas are infinite. Since they are infinite, there is no end. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *asīmā* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s realm is the realm of the *asīmā* kalpas, and the *asīmā* kalpas have no boundaries. Since they have no boundaries, there is no obstruction. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *avyaya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s essence is the essence of the *avyaya* kalpas, and the *avyaya* kalpas are indestructible. Since they are indestructible, there is no decay. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *nitya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s nature is the nature of the *nitya* kalpas, and the *nitya* kalpas are eternal. Since they are eternal, there is no change. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *dhruva* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s stability is the stability of the *dhruva* kalpas, and the *dhruva* kalpas are firm. Since they are firm, there is no falling. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *śiva* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s peace is the peace of the *śiva* kalpas, and the *śiva* kalpas are quiescent. Since they are quiescent, there is no agitation. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *sukha* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s bliss is the bliss of the *sukha* kalpas, and the *sukha* kalpas are joyful. Since they are joyful, there is no suffering. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *subha* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s purity is the purity of the *subha* kalpas, and the *subha* kalpas are immaculate. Since they are immaculate, there is no defilement. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *praśānta* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s tranquility is the tranquility of the *praśānta* kalpas, and the *praśānta* kalpas are profoundly still. Since they are profoundly still, there is no movement. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *anālaya* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s non-attachment is the non-attachment of the *anālaya* kalpas, and the *anālaya* kalpas are without a basis. Since they are without a basis, there is no dwelling. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *anābhoga* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s effortlessness is the effortlessness of the *anābhoga* kalpas, and the *anābhoga* kalpas are without striving. Since they are without striving, there is no exertion. Moreover, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *asambheda* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s non-differentiation is the non-differentiation of the *asambheda* kalpas, and the *asambheda* kalpas are undivided. Since they are undivided, there is no separation. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is equal to the lifespan of the *avikalpa* kalpas. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s non-conceptualization is the non-conceptualization of the *avikalpa* kalpas,
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, [bestowed] the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This first extensive record concludes the preceding section. The World-Honored One spoke directly to Bhaiṣajyarāja, yet his intention was directed toward the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas];

hence it is said, "on account of Bhaiṣajyarāja," he addressed the eighty thousand. This chapter takes the bodhisattvas as its primary audience (*adhimukta*), for herein the extensive record is suspended [for them].

The record, as well as the subsequent sections concerning the distinctions between subject and object and so forth, are all instances where the effort required far exceeds the power [of the teaching], and the matters presented are difficult to believe.

This is because there is no one other than a Bodhisattva who can provide sufficient testimony. Furthermore, as he was about to recruit people [for the task], he showed that they bore the responsibility for protective mindfulness;

thus, he addressed the Bodhisattvas. His statement that it must be due to the King of Medicine (Bhaiṣajyarāja) was intended to manifest the benefits of the sutra and to demonstrate the merit of its universal salvation.

Therefore, furthermore, as the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) is the embodiment of the Dharma King, he reveals this so that those who propagate the sutra may know what the Dharma is. By calling out his name and causing him to be seen, he teaches the intent of attaining realization.
[The Buddha] discusses the traces of the eight classes of beings who occupy the rank of ordinary persons; even those seeking the three vehicles are still at the stage of the initial resolve.
All of these belong to the three cycles of preaching, during which there was no leisure to bestow predictions upon them. Such are the various categories of this kind.

This refers collectively to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who all hear the wondrous Dharma; that each has it pass through their ears establishes the causal conditions for enlightenment.
To say "not even a single verse or a single phrase" is to speak of the extreme meagerness of what they have heard. "Rejoicing" means to follow with joy and not give rise to opposition or slander.

"A single thought-moment" refers to a fleeting arousal of the aspiration for awakening that has not yet become enduring. Yet all such individuals are granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that they shall attain Bodhi.
As for the term "提" (ti): first, it serves to manifest the extraordinary excellence of the Dharma-power; second, it serves to manifest the equality of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
That is to say, a single phrase that permeates the spirit provides all with the means to reach the other shore. All who possess a mind shall become Buddhas.

From the words "The Buddha said" onwards, following the prediction of future events, those who hear this sutra after the extinction [of the Buddha] will not be born in an age when a Buddha is present; they shall instead rely solely upon the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
As for those who received [the prediction] at the periphery: since they were neither taught by ear nor instructed face-to-face, why were they all likewise granted predictions?
It is because, as this sutra states, even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were still many who harbored resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa!

Therefore, even those who hear but a single verse or a single phrase, or even those who rejoice for but a single moment, can all infuse their own Buddha-seeds and lead others to come and study. Who would say...
"Are they not among those destined to attain Buddhahood in the future? This concludes the section on concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent.

**II. The Main Exposition of the Extraordinary Excellence.** This has two parts: 1. Prose; 2. Verse. The first [part] has three sections: 1. Illustrating the extraordinary excellence by way of comparison; 2. Measuring the extraordinary excellence; 3.

Exhorting one to make offerings to and uphold the person [who possesses it]. The first of these two [sections] has two parts: 1. Illustrating the superiority of the person who extensively upholds [the teaching] by way of comparison; 2. Illustrating the superiority... [of the person who extensively upholds].

Explaining the superiority of the person: the first two [sections]. First, the person who extensively upholds [the teaching] is extolled; second, the few are used as a contrast to reveal [the greatness of the many].
Regarding the first: "If there be another person who receives, upholds, reads, and recites... (up to) they will certainly attain Buddhahood in a future age."

The initial mention of "a person" serves to indicate their practice. "If there should be another person" connects directly to the preceding text, still referring to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
"One who receives and maintains" means to receive and bear it in mind; "one who reads and recites" means to open the text for reading and chant it;

"one who explains" means to provide commentaries and deliver lectures; "one who transcribes" means to set it down in writing so that it may circulate; "even a single verse" is used here to represent the meaning in its entirety.
"Little Zhou, as for those who venerate [the teachings] as they would the Buddha: observe the ultimate extent of their reverence for the Dharma.

'Flowers and incense' refers to famous blossoms and sublime perfumes, arranged in rows to be displayed for all to behold. 'Necklaces' refers to precious garlands woven together, displayed to show their beauty.
'Powdered incense' refers to various fragrances ground into a fine powder, placed within to prevent insects and moths. 'Anointed incense' refers to using [fragrant substances]..."

Add water. Smear the ground to signify solemn purity. Regarding the burning of incense: blend fragrant substances to form the wicks; their combustion signifies the principle of uninterrupted continuity.
Regarding the silk canopy: use silk and cotton to form a parasol; its erection signifies the merit of providing shelter and protection. Regarding the banners and streamers:
they flutter to the left and right to signify the subduing of heterodoxy and the upholding of the orthodox. Regarding the vestments: they provide shielding and protection from above and below.

"Turning away from the dust of the mundane and uniting with awakening" refers to the musicians; "singing and chanting" refers to the Dharma-gates. "Joining the palms" means crossing the hands at the chest.
"Reverence" means being respectful and deferential. This is not merely manifesting outward ritual forms, but also manifesting the inner mind.
From the passage on Bhaisajyaraja downwards, the original and bright virtue is revealed. "Having made offerings to ten trillion Buddhas" means that the Buddha [manifested]...
This is a judgment based on their conduct; it is not that such people are incapable of this. One who has accomplished the great vow has already reached the stage of non-retrogression.
One who "takes pity on sentient beings" cultivates the causes through the exercise of compassion. This refers to the fact that their original roots were profound in the past.
If someone asks, "Which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in the future? and wishes to know those individuals, one should examine the practices they have undertaken.
Therefore, one should show that such a person will certainly attain Buddhahood; for by inferring the fruit from the cause, it is determined to be not in vain.
This speaks of the gravity of their future merit. △ Second, illustrating by means of the small.

Why is this?
