[The passage from] "If a son of good family" [up to] "how much more so for one who can fully receive, uphold, and provide various offerings" constitutes the opening phrase that raises the inquiry regarding the fact that one who extensively upholds [the teaching] as described above will certainly attain Buddhahood.

The section beginning with "If a son of good family" below uses the case of one who upholds only a small portion, such as the following, to serve as a comparative illustration. It says "even down to a single phrase," though it does not reach even one [verse].

Verse: Furthermore, although one may receive [the teachings] in great quantity, if one is able to uphold, recite, and even join their palms in reverent salutation, they must not be viewed with indifference.
Such a person is one whom all the worlds should honor and revere, for they are able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings;
therefore, one should honor them with the same offerings one offers to a Tathāgata.

"Such a person" means that this individual will attain Buddhahood before long. "One should know" indicates that they are worthy of being looked upon and worthy of offerings, thereby instructing one to understand the reason for this.

"This great bodhisattva who has accomplished enlightenment" clearly explains that he will attain Buddhahood before long, thus clarifying the meaning of the preceding passage regarding how he should be honored with the offerings due to a Buddha. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he vows to be born [in this world].
"Those here" clearly explains their ability to serve as a basis of reliance, thereby interpreting the meaning of "those who should be venerated" mentioned in the preceding text.

Regarding "extensively expounding and analyzing": even a single sentence of a sūtra, if one receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, can enable others to grasp the Dharma and give rise to understanding;
this itself constitutes extensive exposition and analysis. One should be able to receive and maintain them all.
"Various offerings" refers to what was explained in the preceding section. To state it fully, one should say:
"To be able to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe—even down to a single verse—[and provide] various offerings. This is an abbreviated expression for the sake of brevity.
The reason for making this comparison is that even the receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting of a single phrase of the sutra from this section is still [meritorious].

If one practices the cause while carrying the fruit, and extensively expounds and analyzes [the teaching], how much more so for those who, as previously categorized, are able to receive and uphold it in its entirety, even providing various kinds of offerings;
this requires no further mention. It should be shown that such a person will attain Buddhahood in the future;

their faith is not in vain. This concludes the section on manifesting the superiority of those who extensively uphold [the teaching]. △ Second, manifesting the superiority of those who extensively explain [the teaching].
There are two ways in which such a person excels: first, by providing a comprehensive description of the person; second, by using a brief illustration to reveal their excellence. Regarding the first:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person, having personally renounced [their own welfare]... shall appear in an evil age and extensively expound this sūtra."

"This person" refers to the individual previously illustrated. Although the preceding analysis has already illustrated and clarified this figure, it only established that he will attain Buddhahood in the future;
it did not yet state that he is fundamentally a Buddha from the beginning. Now, wishing to express this, [the text] calls him "Bhaiṣajyarāja."
This is taught so that one may understand: pure karma is the cause of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), and pure retribution is the fruit of Bodhi.

It is said that such a person does not fail to deliver sentient beings because their Brahma-faring is already perfected, nor do they fail to manifest their traces because they have already realized Bodhi;
therefore, it is said that they "forsake" [the world] for the sake of saving beings. If the Buddha were to pass into extinction, sentient beings would be left without reliance.

Therefore, one should feel especially compassionate [toward them]. In an evil age, the various defilements are difficult to purify; thus, one must provide urgent relief. Regarding the urgent relief of an evil age, nothing compares to expounding and preaching this sutra.

For this reason, it alone is emphasized and extensively elaborated upon. This does not mean that other practices such as receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting are not to be performed concurrently;
it is simply that they cannot all be fully accomplished at once due to the urgency of the situation. 2. Illustrating by means of a small example.
"If it is so for a son or daughter of good family [up to] 'how much more so when they extensively expound it for the great assembly'":

this follows from the preceding text. It is because there may be sentient beings in the final age who do not believe those who widely propagate this sutra that [the Buddha] states here that even one who expounds it but little is originally a Buddha, thereby using the case of the minor practitioner to illustrate the greater. "Privately for a single person" means...

Because there were difficulties among the assembly, he was unable to speak; even regarding "not even a single phrase," it means that because difficult circumstances pressed upon him, he could not speak much.
Yet, although this person was unable to speak before the great multitude, his mind for the Dharma remained unchanging in the face of such adversity.
Were it not for having received the entrustment at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and never forgetting his vow, one would not have been able to act as he did.
Therefore, it is said: "One should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata. An "emissary" refers to one who is commissioned to carry out tasks;

this points to the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances. These Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances have secretly received the entrustment of Vulture Peak and act as the Buddha’s representatives to proclaim his teachings.

Therefore, it is said that they are "sent by the Tathāgata" and "perform the work of the Tathāgata. The phrase "expounding extensively among the assembly" refers to what was stated in the preceding section.

The reason for making this comparison is to say that even if one were to secretly expound a single phrase for a single person here, it would still be being sent by the Tathāgata and performing the work of the Tathāgata;
how much more so, then, regarding what was said in the preceding section concerning [expounding] within the great assembly?
"One who extensively preaches this for others—is he not indeed the Buddha himself? It is truly no falsehood that he has abandoned his own pure karmic retribution to manifest birth in an evil age.
How much more so when the excellence [of this teaching] has been fully revealed! II. Comparing the Excellence.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are wicked people—those who do not recognize cause and effect, those who do not believe in sin and merit—who with an unwholesome mind truly desire to harm the Buddha, it is not that they lack intent. Their transgression is exceedingly grave.
"One kalpa" is used to distinguish this from a short duration. "Those present before him" refers to those currently in his presence.
This excludes those who constantly revile [the Buddha] with malice; it distinguishes this from those who do so only occasionally.

As for the statement that "the offense is still relatively light," this is because the Buddha regards enemies and kin with equality, such that neither slander nor praise can affect him. It is like the dog of Shun barking at Yao:
Yao was certainly not diminished by it, and the dog was likewise not to be blamed. Furthermore, the phrase "the offense is still relatively light" merely serves as a comparison to what follows below.

This is intended to manifest the superiority of those who uphold [the Dharma]; do not, however, take this to mean that the Buddha can truly be reviled, thereby committing the offense of an *ānantarya* crime.

Even one who utters an evil word unintentionally, whose words are produced by chance rather than being selected with an unwholesome mind, yet for an entire eon slanders those who recite and study, defaming them behind their backs and speaking falsely to their faces—[such a person incurs great retribution].
[The Buddha] rebuked him, saying: "This is not like those who manifest before the Buddhas and constantly revile them, whose sins are exceedingly grave.

For one who recites the sutras is entrusted with the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas; if such a person regresses and feels regret even once in a lifetime, they can cause the life-force of the Buddhas' wisdom to be severed.
This is just as a son who cuts off his father's food, thereby causing the father’s death. Although he has not committed patricide, it is tantamount to patricide."
This is a transgression; it cannot be excused. Based on this, those who read the sutras are superior to the Buddha.

Those who read them should certainly know to exert themselves, and those who disparage them should likewise know to refrain from doing so. The comparison of their relative excellence is concluded. △ Third, exhorting the offering and support of those who uphold [the Dharma].
“Bhaiṣajyarāja, for those who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra... up to the attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
First, the person is identified and exhorted to make offerings. Since the fruit of Buddhahood is adorned with myriad virtues, one who reads this sūtra shall realize those myriad virtues;
therefore it is said that the Buddha’s adornment is one’s own adornment. This sūtra is the entire body of the Tathāgata. One who reads this sūtra [is as if] riding upon...”
Regarding this cultivation and realization, it is said that they "bear what is upon their shoulders. As for the places they reach, one should turn toward them and pay homage;

wherever such persons arrive, it is as if the Buddha himself is present. Therefore, with single-minded palms joined, one should offer worship, respect, and so forth, hoping that they will joyfully preach the Dharma so that one may hear it even for a brief moment.
Among the beings of the human realm, who do not possess celestial jewels, one should only...

The above constitutes the offering for making offerings. As for the various devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whose merit is somewhat superior, they should hold celestial jewels and scatter them.
As for the various devas of the higher realms, whose merit is most superior, they should further offer them by gathering celestial jewels into heaps.
This is done collectively to exhaust all that they possess, in order to manifest their utmost reverence. Below, [the text] interrogates why this is so.

Explanation of the Encouragement. It was stated previously that those who hear even a single verse or a single line of this sutra and rejoice for even a single moment are all granted a prediction of enlightenment;
therefore, it is said that by hearing it for a brief instant, one immediately attains ultimate Bodhi. This is why they are described as "those worthy of veneration and offerings.
The prose section concludes. II. Verse Recitation (The heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
(The Main Verse Section has three parts: 1. A verse exhorting offerings to the upholder; 2. A verse illustrating superiority by contrast; 3. A verse comparing and measuring superiority.
First [the section on the meaning, presented as an interlinear verse].)
If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way to achieve spontaneous wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna)—up to—and to make offerings to those who uphold it:
the "Buddha-way" refers to unsurpassed bodhi; "spontaneous wisdom" refers to the wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna). The meaning is seen in the *Upamā-parivarta*.
It says that all sentient beings who wish to realize unsurpassed bodhi and dwell securely in the Buddha-way do so by means of wondrous observation.
Regarding the discernment of wisdom: those who preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings must diligently make offerings to those who uphold the sutras.

This is because they rely on the merit of the latter’s reception and maintenance [of the teachings] to support the power of one’s own hearing and cultivation (*śruta-vāsanā*). As for "attaining swiftly," it means without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
"All-seeds" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), for this wisdom is capable of containing all seeds of wisdom. This clarifies [the point].

It comprehends all things, for it is like a great round mirror. It is said that if all sentient beings desire to contemplate this and swiftly attain the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) such that all is clearly understood, they must personally uphold this sutra and make offerings to those who uphold it.
This is because, having relied upon the power of the sutra for refinement and polishing, one must further rely on the assistance of virtuous friends for cleansing; only then can one proceed swiftly.

This completes [the preceding section]. △ Second, the verses that illustrate the excellence by way of comparison, which has two parts: first, one verse that illustrates the excellence of the person who extensively upholds [the teaching];

second, one verse that illustrates the excellence of the person who extensively explains [the teaching]. The first part (concerning the meaning) is summarized in brief verses without further subdivision.
"If there are those who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*... (up to) "...out of compassion for the masses, they have been born here.

The first four lines of the verse cite those who extensively uphold [the teaching]. "Those who can receive and uphold" refers to those who, at the maximum, uphold the entire sūtra, and at the minimum, a single verse;
among these, they read, recite, receive, uphold, explain, and transcribe it, mastering each part thoroughly. They are the envoys of the Buddha.
Thus, having established oneself through practice, one manifests birth out of great compassion for the sake of pitying the multitudes;
this refers to what is stated in the prose regarding those who will certainly attain Buddhahood in future ages. The final four lines employ the method of "using the few to illustrate the many":
"all" refers to ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*). It means that if there are any who can uphold [this teaching], it refers to as little as even a single verse. As for "abandoning the pure land,"...

This refers to those who have already realized the fruit of Buddhahood and do not abide in the land of the Dharma-nature, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, they "reverse the direction of the boat of mercy" and again manifest bodies that dwell in the same realm as us.

If even those who merely uphold [the teachings] are of such a nature, how much more so those who extensively uphold them as described above? They are what are called the "messengers of the Buddha," who take pity on sentient beings.

This is indeed credible. △ Second, the verse that uses an analogy to reveal the superiority of those who provide extensive explanations (an extensive verse based on meaning). This has two parts: first, a verse citing those who provide extensive explanations;
second, a verse using a small measure to illustrate [the greatness of] the extensive. The first part:
It should be known that such a person is born according to their own will (up to) making offerings to those who preach the Dharma.

It should be known that this person differs slightly from the one mentioned in the preceding prose passage. The preceding prose passage refers to the person being illustrated, whereas this refers to the person doing the illustrating;
this is for the sake of following the convenience of the meaning of the respective preceding texts. Regarding "born according to their own will":
Riding upon his vows, he responds to the needs of beings; this is distinct from being led by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of past deeds.

Based on this, a single phrase of the sutra is intended merely to provide a temporary, brief teaching for those of dull faculties; in reality, it enables one to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in an evil age.
Yet, preaching the Dharma in an evil age is already a difficult task; that one can now do so extensively is truly extraordinary.
Difficult. Therefore, one should make offerings to them with celestial flowers, celestial incense, and so forth. △ Second, the verse uses the few to illustrate the many:
"Those who, after my parinirvāṇa, in the evil age, can uphold this sutra... shall walk in the world of the Tathāgata."
Within this context, there are two types of analogies used for illustration. The first analogy illustrates that one ought to offer worship:

if even those who merely uphold [this teaching] should join their palms in prostration and offer various kinds of offerings, hoping to hear it for even a brief moment, how much more so for those mentioned previously who extensively expound it in the degenerate age—should they not honor them with celestial flowers, celestial incense, and the like?
Yes. If this is so even for those who merely receive and uphold [the teaching], they are still sent by the Tathāgata to perform the Tathāgata’s work;
how much more so for those previously mentioned who extensively expound it in the evil age—are they not indeed those who manifest through their own sovereign will?
This concludes the verses illustrating the excellence through comparison. △ Third, the verses comparing and measuring the excellence, in two parts.
First, the verse corresponds to the prose commentary; second, the verse supplements two meanings. Regarding the first:
"If, throughout an entire kalpa, one constantly harbors an unwholesome mind... (up to) its transgression exceeds even that."

Regarding "making facial expressions": this refers to such acts as knitting the brows, frowning, and gesticulating with hands and feet. The long discourse states that such offenses are still relatively light;
however, the present statement that one incurs immeasurable and grave retribution each has its own intended meaning.

If one compares the offense of reviling the Buddha with the offense of disparaging those who uphold the sutras, the former is relatively light; yet if compared with reviling all other people, [the former is far more serious].
This is extremely grave. "Speaking evil words for a brief moment" refers to the slander added for a short time;
this is what is meant by the aforementioned "a single evil word. △ Second, supplementing the two meanings with a verse.
There are those who seek the Buddha-way and, throughout an eon... [until] "I have now attained great benefit.
The first eight lines compare and praise the merit of upholding [this teaching]. As stated in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*:

"Whether with a joyful heart one chants verses praising the Buddha’s virtues, or even produces but a single small sound, all such persons have already attained the Buddha-way; how much more so for one who does so now seeking the Buddha-way."
The time passed for as long as one kalpa. With palms joined before him, he offered countless verses in praise. As for the merit thereby obtained, how could it possibly be measured?

Yet, because the Buddha is free from the mark of self and does not take delight in praise, he finds joy only in transmitting the Buddha’s teachings and continuing the Buddha’s wisdom-life; thus, he extols the upholding of this sutra, for its merit exceeds [all else].
This is because they ensure that the Tathāgata’s vocal teaching does not fall into decline and that the life-force of wisdom remains forever present.

The final eight lines weigh the benefits of making offerings and upholding the Dharma: while the renunciation of five-sensory objects over many kalpas may be called great, the acquisition of even a moment’s hearing of this One Vehicle may be called small;
thus it is said that one should rejoice within oneself for having attained the Great [Vehicle].

Regarding "excellent benefit": through the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), one obtains tainted merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*); by hearing the Dharma, one attains the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Since the One Vehicle is untainted (*anāsrava*), when compared to the benefits and merit of the tainted, it is therefore "great.

Now, although these two meanings are intended as praise for those who uphold [the Dharma] and exhort them to seek the Dharma, they are also used here to manifest the excellence of the person who upholds it. This is explained in terms of the person.

The section on victory concludes. △ Second, manifesting superiority by way of the Dharma, in two parts: first, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, the actual manifestation of its excellence.
The first (a standalone verse):
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost.

This is because it brings to completion the excellence of the preceding [teachings] and initiates the superiority of the subsequent Dharma. For forty years, the various sūtras I have preached would not have achieved the opening and unification [of the teachings] through the Lotus Sūtra;
otherwise, humans and devas would have remained forever submerged in outflows, and those of the three vehicles would have remained eternally stalled.

This is the provisional teaching; therefore, this is promoted as the foremost. △ Second, the actual manifestation of its superiority has two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section.

The former has three sub-sections: first, a brief manifestation of its superiority; second, an elucidation of its superiority through analogies; third, the granting of protection for the practice of the Dharma.
The first three [points]: first, faith is difficult; second, the person is honored; third, the station is noble. Regarding the first:
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja (up to) "there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy, how much more so after my parinirvāṇa."

First, the difficulty of clarifying the meaning has already been explained; this refers to the period prior to the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Now, the explanation shall encompass the *Anantamukha-sūtra*; this will be discussed.
As for the "class of *Nirvāṇa* sūtras," although they grant that sentient beings attain Buddhahood, they have never explicitly bestowed a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* also speaks only for the sake of bodhisattvas. As for the *Prajñā...* [text ends].
If one considers the preceding [teachings], they all belong to expedient means adapted to specific capacities;

however, this present sutra has already abandoned such expedients and encompasses all types of capacities, moreover clearly bestowing predictions upon each and every one. Therefore, it is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.
From the section on "Bhaiṣajyarāja" onwards, there is an injunction to cherish and respect the meaning of the secret heart-essence of all Buddhas. Relying on...

This contains [all teachings] and is produced from this; therefore, it is called the "Secret Essential Treasury. This Secret Essential Treasury must not be transmitted to those who are not suitable vessels;
hence, it says, "it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others," just as a national seal would be given to a commoner.
I fear it would be of no benefit. As for "guarding and protecting," it means to cherish and mindfully protect; to cherish and mindfully protect. Do not expound it at an improper time.

Therefore, it is said that from the distant past until now, it has never been openly taught. That it has never been openly taught does not mean that there has been no profound, secret transmission of great benefit;
it is not a matter of total silence. From this point downward, the text further explains the intent of the admonition, stating that while the Tathāgata was in the world...
Regarding the excellence of the three karmas: when this sutra was being preached, there were still many who possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and withdrew out of resentment and jealousy;
how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) have declined? If one wishes to propagate this Dharma, how can one avoid contradiction and slander?
This is why the Tathāgata cautioned against bestowing [this teaching] recklessly. △ Second, the Honored Ones.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... [up to]... it is as if the Tathāgata were personally stroking their head with his hand.
Buddhas transmit this to one another; they use the robe as a sign of faith, saying: "Although this person has not yet attained Buddhahood, there is no doubt that they will attain it in the future.
Therefore, they are covered by the Buddha-robe. "Protection" refers to the secret empowerment of supernatural power; "mindfulness" refers to being gathered in by a compassionate heart.

[The Buddha] conferred [the teaching], saying: "This person transmits and upholds the Noble Path; their life-vein is thus connected with that of the Buddhas, and they are therefore protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.
This sutra is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; that this person can endure it and transmit it shows they possess great power of faith.
As previously stated, one should know that such a person is a Great Bodhisattva. Regarding this sutra, many people...

Regarding resentment and jealousy: if such a person is able to endure hardships and propagate [the teaching] widely, they possess the power of aspiration, which is as previously described—namely, having compassion for sentient beings and wishing to be born in this world. This sutra is the secret essence of the Buddha;
if such a person can receive and proclaim it, they possess the power of roots of goodness, as previously stated: "One should know that this person has already..."
This refers to one who has made offerings to ten trillion buddhas. "Dwelling with the Buddha" (fó sù) means staying in the chamber of nirvana.

"Rubbing the head" (mó dǐng) signifies the intimacy of receiving a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). To say that such a person shall depart from saṃsāra and will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood means they already abide in nirvana and have long since received their prediction;
hence it is said that they dwell together with the Buddha and have their heads rubbed by the Buddha. △ Three.
Regarding the "nobility of the location": wherever the *Bhaiṣajyarāja* [Sūtra] is preached or read—up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This first section clearly elucidates the nobility of the location. As for the phrase "wherever," it refers to any place whatsoever, whether it be a remote borderland or a desolate ruin; whether it is preached or...

"Reading," and so forth, collectively refers to the places where [the Dharma] is transmitted and maintained, as well as the locations where the sutra scrolls reside—that is, the grounds upon which this sutra is enshrined.

"In all such cases, one should erect a stupa" means that one should revere those places as one would revere the Buddha. "Making them exceedingly high and wide" and so forth is done to honor the matter and manifest one's sincere devotion.
"There is no need to further install relics" is because these are places for transmission and maintenance, as well as sites of offering.
This refers to the locations where the sūtras were taught. To explain below why this is so, he raises a question to establish the point:
Why is it that at the two aforementioned locations one should erect a stūpa even though the *śarīra* (relics) are not enshrined there?

It is precisely because the Tathāgata’s entire body (*kṛtsna-kāya*) is already present therein. This "entire body" is none other than the *dharmakāya*. While various sūtras analytically expound the ultimate truth, [this location embodies it directly].

There are certain parts of the body; this sutra fully reveals the true reality (*dharmatā*), and is therefore called the "entire body. Since the entire body is present, it is no different from the Buddha;
thus, one should make offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise it. To see a stupa and perform prostrations and offerings is to perform prostrations and offerings to all Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said: "One should know that these [who do so] are all close to Bodhi. Now, regarding the three [sections] above this...
Section. This is collectively intended to manifest the extraordinary excellence of the Dharma. It is because the Dharma is supreme that faith is difficult;

because faith is difficult, the person is honored; and because the person is honored, their station is noble. The detailed manifestation of this excellence is complete. II. Clarifying Excellence through Similes (in four parts):
1. Establishing the Fundamental Tenet; 2. Explaining the Simile to Elucidate the Meaning; 3. Applying the Dharma to Correlate with the Simile; 4. Reinforcing Faith through Two Gates.
First: "Many people, whether householders or renunciants... [attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This first section establishes the fundamental tenet. "Many people" refers to those spoken of forty years prior. Forty years ago.

There are many who, without departing from the secular world, immediately give rise to the great mind; there are also those who shave their hair and don the dyed robes before giving rise to the great mind.
Therefore, it is said that both laypeople and monastics practice the path of the Bodhisattva. Although they practice the path of the Bodhisattva, [the distinction remains].
This refers only to those taught through the provisional and gradual teachings, such as those delivered in the various assemblies since the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) period.

Those delivered in these various assemblies, had they not encountered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, would not have been free from stagnation within the stages of practice; thus, it would have taken kalpas for them to achieve accomplishment. Therefore, it is said:
"If one is unable to see, hear, read, or recite [this sutra], this person has not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path. This...
This sutra is a teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) Dharma-gate; by hearing it, one may suddenly transcend and realize perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said that to hear this sutra constitutes practicing the path of a Bodhisattva well. The phrase "Those who have" and so forth further explains its meaning:
as stated above, those who practice the path well or do not practice it well—specifically, those who see, hear, believe, understand, receive, and uphold [the sutra]—shall attain proximity to Bodhi.
"Ti-erh. "Bodhi" means to attain proximity; it signifies the meaning of directly and suddenly transcending to perfect realization. This refers to what is called:
"When not a single thought arises, one is immediately named Buddha. It is also like the stages of attaining enlightenment and verifying awakening upon the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
△ Second, the illustration is explained to clarify the point.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst, requires water [until] his mind becomes certain that water must be near.
"A person" refers to a traveler on a journey, oppressed by the heat and distressed by hunger and thirst; thus it is said he is "parched with thirst and requires water.
This is a metaphor for those, whether lay or ordained, who have long been parched by ignorance and destitute due to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and who desire [liberation].

Subhūti’s water is used for the purpose of explanation. "Dug into high ground" is a metaphor for the forty years prior [to the Lotus Sūtra], when one practiced the bodhisattva path based on provisional and gradual teachings.
"Still seeing dry earth" is a metaphor for not yet having reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as one was still obstructed by the rigidity of provisional doctrines.

Being obstructed by provisional doctrines means that one has not yet escaped being entangled in the stages and positions of practice; thus, it is difficult to achieve accomplishment even after passing through kalpas. Therefore...
This is illustrated by the metaphor that the water is still far off; it means that one has not yet skillfully practiced the Bodhisattva path.
When one exerts effort without ceasing and subsequently perceives moist soil, this is a metaphor for the arrival of Prajñā (wisdom).

Having already received the purifying power of this wisdom, the obstructions of provisional teachings have gradually lightened, and as the water of Bodhi-wisdom is about to permeate [the mind], one thus gradually reaches the mud; this is a metaphor for what is attained now.
Upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one realizes that the provisional and the real are mutually identical, like water and earth combining to form mud.
One’s mind becomes certain, knowing that water must be near; this is a metaphor for now having heard this Dharma and suddenly transcending to perfect realization.
This refers to those who practice the bodhisattva path with skillful means. △ Third, the application of the Dharma:
"The Bodhisattva is also like this" (up to) "this sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true aspect."

The initial "correctly corresponding" (*samyak-saṃprayukta*) refers to the preceding analogy. "Not having heard or understood," and so forth, means that practicing through expedient and gradual means corresponds to digging into high ground;
one should know that such people correspond to those whose provisional teachings firmly obscure the ultimate reality, which is like seeing that the water is still far off.

"If one obtains hearing and understanding," and so forth, means that when the time arrives, one gains admittance to the sublime assembly; this corresponds to seeing moisture and reaching the mud. It is certain.
"Knowing that one has attained proximity, etc. means that when one has self-confidence in becoming a Buddha without doubt, one should know that the water [of enlightenment] must be near.
The analysis of the meaning follows the above. As for the following section, it raises a question to provide an explanation. It says:

"As stated above, whether or not one has heard and understood this sutra is the reason why there is a distinction between far and near regarding Bodhi. Why is this? Precisely because all Bodhisattvas..."
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi all belongs to this sutra. "Belongs" (shu) means "to rely upon" (yi).
This means that the bodhi of all bodhisattvas emerges by relying upon this sutra. Below this, the text provides a further explanation of the term.

It states that all bodhisattvas, by using the provisional gateways of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), keep the reality closed off; therefore, their bodhi remains far distant. This sutra, however, opens the gateway of skillful means.
It reveals the true aspect [of reality]. Therefore, one knows that one has drawn near to Bodhi; this is because all [who do so] belong to this sutra.
△ Fourth, the two sections for strengthening faith: 1. Praising the sutra to clarify the capacity; 2. Pointing out faults to exclude those who are not [qualified]. First:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* treasury is profound, firm, and far-reaching (extending to) the accomplishment of bodhisattvas, for which it provides revelation.
As the perfect teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it subsumes all other scriptures as its retinue; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*).
"Profound and firm" means extremely deep and solid, such that heterodox schools cannot enter it and celestial Māras cannot destroy it. "Far-reaching" means subtle, remote, and suspended...
It is remote; no ordinary eye can peer into it, and no provisional wisdom can reach it. Thus, it is that which only a Buddha can realize and only a Buddha can know;
therefore, it is said that no one can arrive there. If no one can arrive there, what benefit would it be for the Buddha to speak of it now?
It is solely for the sake of instructing bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and bringing to fulfillment those bodhisattvas who have long practiced, that he provides this guidance.
Instruction: It can be seen that only Bodhisattvas are the proper recipients (*yogya*) for this sutra.
This is explained by way of the "Gate of Praise" (*praśaṃsā-mukha*) to demonstrate the intent of providing encouragement. △ Second, identifying errors and excluding those who do not qualify.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [from "should be known" to] "are those of overweening pride," are startled and doubtful;
those who do not dare to accept it; or those who are terrified and fear losing what they hold—such as these are not long-practicing bodhisattvas.
Therefore, it is said that these are those who have newly resolved their minds. True śrāvakas, by principle, should abandon the provisional and follow the real.
They are struck with alarm, doubt, and fear; they are not true śrāvakas. Therefore, it is said that they possess "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).

This is according to the method of censure and rebuke, intended to demonstrate the meaning of startling and exhorting them. The explanation by way of analogy regarding their excellence is concluded. △ Third, the permission to protect the practice of the Dharma, in two parts:
1. Showing the proper method; 2. Granting the permission for protection. First [Showing the proper method]:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are sons or daughters of good family who extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra—this is the initial inquiry.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, people will be mostly depraved and evil; it will be difficult for them even to place their trust in the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle."
To expound upon the four aggregates for the sake of those with desire is truly no easy task; therefore, he asks how one ought to explain them.

To say "one ought to explain" is to distinguish this from mere hearsay or idle talk—insufficient for those of the conditioned world—and implies that one must necessarily possess deep accumulation and profound cultivation.
This is like that [story] of him who, having nurtured his strength for ninety thousand *li* against the wind, then took up his great wings and plotted his course toward the south.

This is "excellence in humility. It indicates three things: the chamber, the robes, and the seat; these possess both a phenomenal (factual) and a noumenal (principle-based) aspect. For now, let us discuss them according to their phenomenal aspect.

As for the Tathāgata’s chamber, it refers to the place where a portrait of the Buddha is enshrined and offerings are made. That one must enter this [chamber] signifies that they act as a representative of the Buddha to proclaim and spread the Dharma.
Nowadays, at lecture halls, images and the like must necessarily be installed above. As for the Tathāgata’s robe, it is the robe by which the thousand Buddhas conferred predictions;
one must certainly wear this to manifest that there is a fundamental basis for this transmission of the teachings.

Just as lecturers today wear the *kāṣāya* and so forth, the Tathāgata’s seat consists of various kinds of adorned seats; one must certainly sit upon these to manifest that this is the [Tathāgata’s]...
The Buddha is no different from the ritual protocols used today, such as sitting loftily upon a lion throne; it is exactly like this.
When discussing matters, one must reach such a conclusion before one may preach this sutra. The theoretical basis follows below. From "The Tathāgata" onwards, the meaning is explained.
The word *śālā* has two meanings: first, a place of reliance; second, a shelter. As for the mention of great kindness and great compassion, since they are for the sake of the multitude...
It is a dwelling because it serves as a basis for birth and can provide shelter for sentient beings; thus, it is a "house. Clothing also has two meanings:
first, adornment, and second, protection. It is said that gentleness can adorn one's own virtues, while patience can protect against difficult circumstances.
Therefore, this is the robe. The seat also has two meanings: first, majesty; second, receptivity.
It is called a "seat" because by declaring that all phenomena are empty, one is both able to receive all dharmas and able to preach the Dharma with fearlessness. Thus says Da Cheng.
Benefiting sentient beings takes compassion as its priority; engaging with the phenomenal world takes patience as its foundation; preaching the Dharma takes non-attachment as its basis.
Based on this, the three items—the room, the robe, and the seat—are truly the fixed and unalterable methods for propagating the sutras in the final age.
"Abiding securely" concludes the demonstration. Regarding the phrase "within these": it refers to the midst of these three dharmas. "Without indolence" means...
This is the mind of diligence. However, one must abide securely in three dharmas to be able to transform beings throughout the entirety of the dust-filled worlds.
Only when one practices diligence without slackening can one employ it across the three periods of time. By saving sentient beings in this manner, there are none who are not saved;
by practicing the Way in this manner, there is no path that is not traversed. Therefore, he was able to extensively expound this for all the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Sūtra. △ Second, the promise to protect and uphold:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I shall dispatch emanated persons to other lands... (until) I shall further explain it for them, so that they may attain fulfillment."

"First, he dispatched people to protect from within. Regarding 'I [reside] in other lands': this means that when conditions have ripened in other lands, he travels there to perform his transformative work (*saṃdarśana*).
Although he performs his transformative work there, he must also provide remote protection and sustenance; therefore, he dispatches transformed beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).

These 'transformed beings' refer to various Bodhisattvas who manifest as ordinary people, blending their light with the dust of the world and secretly winning over the hearts of the masses; hence it is said, 'for the purpose of gathering.'"
Regarding the phrase "the audience, such as the manifested bhikṣus," this refers to bodhisattvas who manifest as the fourfold assembly.
Internally they remain secret while externally they appear [as ordinary beings], leading those of genuine practice forward; thus it is said that they "listen to their preaching of the Dharma.

The phrase "these manifested persons" generally refers to all those manifested above—the individuals and the fourfold assembly—who hear the Dharma, believe and accept it, and follow it without opposition. This is stated in order to exclude other assemblies.

They harbor doubts and slander, thereby establishing a path of deceptive flattery. If one were to preach in a lowly manner, sending others to provide external protection while remaining in a secluded place, it would easily invite difficult circumstances;
therefore, the Eight Divisions [of Spirits] are sent to listen to the Dharma to serve as a retinue for external protection.

Although [the Buddha] manifests his body to bestow teachings in an inferior state, and although his transformation bodies may reside in other lands, his Dharma-body does not depart from its proper location, responding to and harmonizing with beings.
The Way intersects with us, allowing us to behold it from time to time. Yet, when for even a single thought-moment one becomes clouded or distracted, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before one;

thus, one comes to forget the *jù* (phrases) and *dú* (readings). A *jù* refers to a place where both the text and the meaning are concluded; a *dú* refers to a place where the text is concluded but the meaning is not.
When for a single thought-moment the mind becomes clear and pure, words and principles leap forth within the heart; this is precisely the Buddha speaking again for one’s sake. It is complete.
As for "the feet" (verses): the punctuation is clear, the phrasing is unerring, and the meaning is not obscure. The prose section concludes.
△ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[The Main Verse Section is divided into three parts: 1. A verse on the indirect manifestation of its excellence. 2. A verse clarifying its excellence through parables. 3. A verse granting permission to protect the practice of the Dharma.

Regarding the first [which, according to the prose, originally had three sections but now lacks the latter two; it concerns only the single point of the difficulty of faith and is the most concise in its phrasing, thus belonging to the category of abbreviated verses]:
Those who wish to abandon all forms of indolence should listen to this sutra; for this sutra is difficult to encounter, and those who can hear it and accept it with faith are likewise rare.

"Indolence" here refers to those of the Lesser Vehicle, the Śrāvakas. Because they do not give rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, they are designated as indolent.
This sutra is able to rouse those who linger [in complacency] and cause them to set aside provisional teachings; therefore, it is admonished thus.
Listen! Having shown that it is difficult to hear, he further clarifies that it is difficult to believe, so as to cause those who propagate the Dharma to know what to cherish and value.
This refers to the prose statement that it "must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others. II.

Verses illustrating the excellence through parables (following the prose, this is divided into four parts; here, the first and last are missing, as they belong to the abbreviated verses). 2. One verse explaining the parable to reveal its meaning. 2. [The second part].
The verse applies the teaching to the analogy. First:
"As when a person thirsty for water digs in high ground... [until] they know for certain that water is near.
The meaning follows the prose commentary. Second: The verse applies the teaching to the analogy.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these... are near to the Buddha’s wisdom.

These "such persons" still refer to the śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna; because they have not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and cannot suddenly transcend to achieve perfect realization, they remain very far from the Buddha’s wisdom.
When this sutra says [the Dharma] is "profound," it means that which is unknown to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Therefore, "resolutely determining the Śrāvaka teachings" means that once one has heard this sutra, one definitively understands that the teachings of the Śrāvakas are skillful means and not the ultimate reality. That it is "the king among all sutras" still refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
for this is the perfectly complete and supreme teaching, its principle surpassing all other scriptures, just as a worldly king is not subject to his ministers.

Because they are capable of reaching it. "Having heard" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Reflecting with discernment" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). When the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is further added, one may then ascend to Bodhi.
Therefore, it is said: "One should know that such a person is near to the Buddha-wisdom. (According to the prose section, these people should refer to bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings;

however, because the phrase "śrāvakas who have attained definitive understanding" appears here, the reference is specifically to śrāvakas. This is because both the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings and the śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle have not yet received the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening and unification [of the three vehicles] and thus collectively belong to the category of "thirsty men. Hence, the prose section...)

Verse (the two persons take turns reciting). This concludes the section explaining the excellence through verses and metaphors. △ Third, the verses on permitting the practice of protection, in two parts:
first, one verse showing the proper method; second, two verses permitting the maintenance [of the precepts]. First:

If a person says that one who should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber according to this sutra [up to] "preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings," there is no introductory verse to raise the topic;
it is first indicated [by the prose]. The three modes of conduct are in accordance with the Dharma. Being solemnly present as the Dharma King, he possesses mastery over the Dharma;

therefore, he is able to dwell among the assembly without fear. The rest may be understood. From "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*) onwards, the explanation of the meaning follows the *Dīrgha-āgama* (Long Discourses).

[The section on] Practice. This [phrase], "dwelling herein," concludes and indicates [the meaning]; it is a summary verse (gāthā) that expands upon the sense [of the prose]. The long prose says, "abiding therein," while this [verse] says, "dwelling herein and preaching the Dharma"; their meaning is one and the same.
Regarding "enduring difficulties while preaching the sūtra," this refers to the mind of non-indolence in the long prose.
For it is not possible for one who does not possess great diligence (*mahāvīrya*) to endure being reviled, cut, beaten, or struck. As for "recalling the Buddha and being patient," it means:
One should endure all hardships by recollecting the Buddha’s benevolent virtues. The "thousands of millions of lands" refers to the horizontal pervasiveness of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body);
although it manifests physical forms, it is seen that there is no body, and yet it is able to endure all manner of difficult matters—hence it is called the "pure and firm body.
The "immeasurable hundreds of millions of kalpas" refers to the vertical exhaustion of time through the *nirmāṇakāya*; as for its preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, this reveals...
Having bestowed kindness upon the multitude, he reveals to them the meaning of what they should keep in mind. This means:

"I have already long ago realized Bodhi, yet I still manifest my body in countless ways across thousands of millions of billions of lands, preaching the Dharma for immeasurable eons for the sake of you sentient beings of the final age."

How much more so for you, Dharma masters of the final age! Since you are still far removed from the Buddha’s Bodhi, should you not contemplate the Buddha’s grace and virtue, and exert all your strength to endure all hardships?
This is the Tathāgata using himself as an example to encourage others. Part Two: Verses on the Promise to Protect and Sustain.
This has two sections: first, the direct verses corresponding to the prose; second, the revelation of benefits and the exhortation to practice. First:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who can preach this sutra... [they shall] act as an assembly for hearing the Dharma.
The initial verse dispatches people to provide internal protection—namely, pure men and women—which corresponds to the prose section on *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*.
Because they do not depart from worldly life yet are able to cultivate pure conduct, the prose says "to listen to their preaching," whereas here it says:

Making offerings to the Dharma Master is, in essence, making offerings to the hearing of the Dharma; both serve to guide sentient beings and assemble them to listen to the Dharma—their meanings emerge interchangeably.
This verse transcends [the literal] to explain the meaning of transforming the fourfold assembly. Regarding those who wish to inflict harm:

although their malicious intent has already been stirred, the harmful act has not yet been committed. Regarding "transforming people": it refers to various Bodhisattvas and others who manifest in the form of their peers.
"Such a person. "The protectors" refers to those who dispel evil intentions and transform others toward goodness so that they may listen to the Dharma;

this is a verse summarizing the meaning of dispatching emanated beings. As for "if one preaches below," this is a verse on manifesting the body to bestow teachings (a transposed verse based on the meaning).

If the person preaching the Dharma remains alone in a secluded place, it is feared that their support will not be substantial and they will be insufficient to "plot southward" (i.e., achieve great success). It is silent, devoid of human sound.
Those who read and recite this sutra must first sharpen their tools if they wish to perform their task well. The body of the Tathāgata manifests by virtue of his vows;
it is not born of desire or attachment, and therefore possesses pure radiance. "Chapters" (zhang) are formed by linking verses, while "sentences" (ju) are formed by linking readings.
The term "long passage" (changxing) refers to the reading of these sentences. Their meanings reflect one another. "Penetrating" (tong) means to achieve thorough understanding.
Regarding its meaning: "benefit" refers to thoroughly mastering the text. If a person can act in this way, they are one who possesses virtue;

for they are able to proclaim [the teachings] on behalf of the Buddha, thereby possessing the virtues of a Dharma-preacher. Having possessed the virtues of a Dharma-preacher, their voice and spirit communicate with those of the Buddha.
Thereafter, whether they explain or recite, the Buddha manifests his body from time to time; thus, they all attain [realization].
[This] is seen. From "If a person" onwards, the verse dispels [the notion of] external protection (a subsequent verse). Both the phrasing and the meaning are identical to the prose.
△ Second, revealing the benefits and concluding with an exhortation.
This person delights in preaching the Dharma with unhindered discernment (up to the point of) attaining the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The first two phrases clarify that they have personally attained the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*); the phrase "all Buddhas" reveals the merit of the secret empowerment of the various sages.
Preaching the Dharma in this manner will necessarily accord with the capacities of beings; hence it is said, "it can cause the multitude to rejoice. One should draw near to such a Dharma Master.

This means that by not lingering in minor paths, one is able to swiftly attain the state of a bodhisattva. Those who follow and study under a teacher are able to practice the Mahāyāna, and thus they are able to see Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Based on this, those who resolve their minds to practice the Way and aspire to see the Buddhas [should do so].
Regarding this Dharma Master, you must not let the opportunity pass by simply because he is before your eyes. This concludes the section on "Manifesting Excellence and Clarifying Benefits.
△ Second, Recruiting People to Propagate the Sutra (the title of the chapter is as follows):
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
As for the stupa being named after its jewels, it is because it is composed of the seven treasures and further adorned with various kinds of precious objects.

According to the Āgamas, four places are prescribed for the erection of stupas: namely, the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, [and the place where he entered parinirvāṇa].
The place where the wheel [of Dharma] was turned; the place where he entered parinirvāṇa; the present stupa is, in fact, the stupa of the former Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa.

If one discusses the correct meaning of this chapter, it was originally intended for the purpose of summoning people to the proclamation of his passing; yet, the summoning for the proclamation of his passing was instead triggered by the sight of the stupa.
Therefore, the chapter is titled "Seeing the Stupa. Furthermore, there are five distinct meanings of this chapter: first, for the sake of the three... [text fragment ends].

The Buddha preached the Dharma and universally predicted their attainment of Buddhahood. Desiring to have Much-Treasure (Prabhūtaratna) serve as a witness to prove that what he had spoken was not false, a great voice issued from within the stupa, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!
and so forth, declaring that all that has been spoken is indeed true. Second, in the chapter on the Dharma-preacher, having already shown the essential practice, [the text] now seeks to clarify...
Having practiced causes throughout kalpas, one relies entirely on the sustaining power of vows;

thus it is like the case of Prabhūtaratna, who, though having entered parinirvāṇa long ago, emerged from the earth upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* being preached, precisely because of his vow-power. Third, regarding the three faculties' realization and attainment of the whole body:
wishing to employ the gathering of the divided bodies as a provisional means to enable them to obtain the function of that very body, it is as follows:
It is as stated: "The three thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems, even when contained within a single portion of a manifested body of the Tathāgata, cannot yet fully accommodate them.
Fourth, it is so that when the multitude of sages attain Buddhahood, they all rely upon a pure land;

for fear that they might suspect the Sahā world to be defiled and evil, [the Buddha] wishes to demonstrate that the defiled and the pure are identical. Thus, without leaving the Sahā world, he transforms the pure lands in three ways. Now...

This refers to such acts as transporting the various devas and humans and placing them in other lands. Fifth is the attainment of Buddhahood by the multitude of sages, all of whom possess long lifespans;
fearing that people might doubt that Śākyamuni undergoes extinction, he wishes to demonstrate that birth and extinction are non-dual.

This is exemplified by the fact that when Prabhūtaratna shared his seat, he was "extinguished yet not extinguished," and when Śākyamuni took his seat, he was "born yet not born. Now, regarding these five...
The meaning [of this passage] is as follows: the first three [sections] provide a preliminary indication of the provisions (*sambhāra*), while the latter two clear the way in advance.
One who grasps this intent will find that the Dharma Master need not fear a lack of support; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* can then be practiced both horizontally and vertically.

Therefore, at the end, the Buddha proclaims his extinction and recruits someone to bring its meaning to completion. [The Sūtra text is divided into three parts: First, the testimony of Prabhūtaratna; second, the gathering of the emanated bodies; third...

Regarding the solicitation of donors for the entry [of relics] into the stupa, there are three points: first, the manifestation of a seven-jeweled stupa; second, the sounding of a voice as a witness; third, the inquiry into its origins through question and answer. First:
At that time, before the Buddha, a stupa made of the seven treasures appeared (and so forth, until) he made offerings to the precious stupa, honoring, respecting, and praising it.
Initially, it surged upward and remained suspended in the air. The Buddha represents ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); the stupa represents the true nature (*dharmatā*).

This indicates that for those of the three vehicles and others, their minds open to awakening and understanding; moment by moment, ultimate wisdom emits light, and from time to time, the true nature manifests before them.

Therefore, the stupa is placed before the Buddha to symbolize this. As for the stupa being composed of the seven treasures: although the principle of the true nature is inherently complete within one's own nature, [it is manifested through these means].
It is also because it is manifested by the seven noble treasures of wealth—faith, precepts, learning, renunciation, and so forth.

That it is five hundred *yojanas* high symbolizes that the true nature (*dharmatā*) vertically pervades the five destinies. That its length and breadth are two hundred and fifty *yojanas* symbolizes that the true nature horizontally traverses the three vehicles.
As for the statement regarding sentient beings of the three vehicles, when compared to the sentient beings of the five destinies, they are merely...
Therefore, it is represented by two hundred and fifty *yojanas*. As for its emergence from the earth:
the stupa was originally manifest and complete, but had previously been covered by the great earth; now it breaks through the earth and emerges.

This symbolizes that the true aspect (*dharmatā*) is inherently and primordially manifest, yet had previously been obscured by provisional teachings; now, having shattered the provisional, it is revealed. Thus, it abides in mid-air.
This refers to a physical stūpa residing within formless space, symbolizing that while ultimate reality (dharmatā) appears with marks, it ultimately returns to emptiness.
Regarding the "adornment with various precious objects," this means that upon the body of the stūpa, various jewels are set and decorated;
this symbolizes that within the essence of ultimate reality, the adornments are naturally possessed as the infinite virtues of its nature. Five.
"Ten thousand adornments, most excellent. Regarding the "five thousand railings," these refer to the horizontal crossbars and vertical balusters atop the stupa, numbering five thousand layers.

This signifies that within the essence of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), all dharma-gates of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) are comprehensively subsumed. Within each of the five stages, ten factors are present;
these tens mutually possess one another to form a hundred, and these hundreds mutually possess one another to form a thousand. Thus, for the time being, [it is expressed] by means of five.
A thousand railings represent this; in reality, they are inexhaustible, like the net of Indra (*indrajāla*).

As for the "thousands of millions of niches," there are niches surrounding each [pillar], totaling thousands of millions when counted; these represent the inexhaustible skillful means (*upāya*) within the various Dharma-gates for gathering sentient beings.
Briefly, to correspond to the differences in the mental activities of the ten types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one thousand [niches] are established.
"Ten thousand words" and "innumerable banners and streamers used as adornments" refers to the fact that outside each niche chamber, each is adorned with banners and streamers;
this symbolizes the skillful means of gathering sentient beings, all of which are preceded by the two gates of subduing (*kośa*) and attracting (*saṃgraha*).
"Hanging jeweled necklaces" refers to the fact that above each niche chamber there is a canopy, with jeweled necklaces interlaced and draped down.
The canopy symbolizes the skillful means for gathering [beings]; all are taken as methods of transformation through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
As for the "billions of jeweled bells suspended above it," this refers to the jeweled bells suspended from the necklaces; they symbolize, among the four means of integration, [the method of giving].
Each responds to the capacities of beings through various and diverse modes of speech and sound.

These diverse modes of speech and sound are supported by the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), producing true morality, concentration, and wisdom that universally benefit all. Therefore, fragrance issues forth from its four faces.

This signifies that they pervade the entire world. As for those various banners and canopies, atop each of the countless standards and pennants there is a precious canopy, signifying the sheltering protection of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).
When practicing compassion, all phenomena converge upon compassion; therefore, this is represented by their being composed of the seven treasures.
Their height reaching as far as the palaces of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*)—the palaces of the Four Great Kings correspond to the human realm—[signifies...]
At the juncture where heaven and earth meet, it manifests that compassion reaches upward to the heavens and downward to humanity; there are none to whom it does not reach.
This is spoken in reference to the wholesome realms (sugati). "Thirty-three" refers to the vast multitude of offerings made to the Thirty-three Heavens and others.

Regarding "each person raises offerings": by seeing the stupa, one knows for certain that there is a Buddha. This signifies that within the essence of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the self-nature Buddha is inherently present;
therefore, all sentient beings ought to respect it. △ Second, the manifestation of sound as testimony.
At that time, a great sound issued forth from within the jeweled stupa (up to): "That which has been spoken is all true.

The sound issuing from the stupa was intended to serve as a witness for the Buddhas of the past. By briefly clarifying the provisional and the real, the Tathāgata aroused the true doubts of the assembled multitude;
by extensively clarifying the provisional and the real, he gave rise to true faith in those whose capacities were suited to the teaching. Both [purposes] were fulfilled.
It is utterly excellent; therefore, he speaks "Excellent! twice to praise it. "Equal Great Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas as explained in the section on the brief clarification.
Because this is possessed equally by both ordinary beings and Buddhas, it is called "equal.

This is what is meant in the Chapter on the Dharma-Teaching by the phrase "the unsurpassed path realized by oneself" and "the equal dharma of the Mahāyāna," as found in the *Banzhou Sanmei Jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra).
What is called "the equality of this Dharma, wherein there is no high or low," refers precisely to this.

It is termed "the teaching for Bodhisattvas" because it is something unknown to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* specifically refers to what was extensively expounded during the three stages [of the Lotus assembly];
it had not been revealed for forty years prior. Therefore, it is called "that which is protected and remembered by the Buddha."
The "Great Assembly" refers to those spoken for; the three faculties are universally encompassed, without exclusion or selection.
The repetition of the phrase "Thus it is" serves to seal the meaning that both the extensive and abbreviated teachings are free from falsehood.

Having thus established this seal, fearing that there might still be doubt or deliberation, he proclaims "Śākyamuni World-Honored One" to testify that all that has been spoken is indeed true. 3. Questioning.

Answer: There are three parts: first, the fourfold assembly’s wonder and admiration; second, their joyful desire to inquire and question; third, the Tathāgata’s gracious response. Regarding the first:
at that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stūpa... [they] stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
The earth is not the place where a stūpa is enshrined; empty space is not the locus where a stūpa dwells. Now we see the stūpa emerge from the earth and abide in mid-air;

we know for certain that this is an auspicious omen of a different age. Furthermore, we hear a great sound being emitted, which corroborates the previous teaching and further confirms our prior understanding.
Having examined it, we find it to be truly real and not false; thus it is said that all have attained the joy of the Dharma. Although...
I attained the joy of the Dharma; yet, because there was a stupa within the earth, I could ultimately not understand the reason for its abiding in the air.

Furthermore, since the stupa contained only the physical form of the Buddha, for the voice to emerge as if from a human mouth was something that left me both joyful and astonished, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence. I wished to express my gratitude for having attained the Dharma.
To express this benefit and to further manifest his feelings of wonder and astonishment, he rose from his seat, performed the formal gestures (*vidhi*), and withdrew to stand aside.
△ Second, the inquiry with joyful eloquence:
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) who again produced these sounds therein.
The Bodhisattva possesses the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and teaches others without weariness; therefore, he is named for his eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

This chapter emphasizes the circulation [of the teaching] and values eloquence above all else; thus, it is addressed to those who are appropriately suited to receive it. As previously stated, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy and wonder.
The phrase "the eight classes of beings harboring doubts in their hearts" refers to the mutual reflections among the assembly.

As for their addressing the Buddha, they wished to inquire into the reason for the appearance of the stūpa and the cause of its emitting sound, in order to resolve the doubts of the gathered multitude. It was already suspicious that a precious stūpa had emerged from the earth;
furthermore, its uttering of sound was even more difficult to comprehend. Although it was known to be within the realm of the Buddha, [the assembly remained perplexed].
Since it was difficult for the minds of the assembly to find peace, [the Buddha] therefore inquired with such questions as "By what causes and conditions... etc.

△ Third, the Tathāgata’s response, which has three parts: first, the power of vows within the causal stage; second, the final instructions after attaining the fruit; third, addressing them by name to conclude the answer. First:
At that time, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa (up to the point where he) acted as a witness and praised him, saying, "Excellent.
Regarding the "entire body" (*sarvakāya*): this distinguishes it from the *śarīra* (relics); it refers to the physical body that remained in the world during his lifetime.

Regarding "of the past": this distinguishes it from the present. Regarding "in the east": this distinguishes it from this land; because it is the farthest from here, it is called "immeasurable tens of millions."
[Regarding] "Billion" and so forth: *Da Cheng* (Great Vehicle) states that the land is named "Jeweled Purity" because it is composed of the seven treasures and is free from all defilements.
The Buddha is titled "Many Treasures" because he bestows the inexhaustible wealth of merit and Dharma. When he was practicing the path of a bodhisattva...
Those who make great vows do so out of a desire to repay the grace of the Dharma and with the resolve never to forget it.

Even after [the Buddha's] passing, they continue to listen to the Dharma throughout the ten directions at stūpas and temples, acting as witnesses and praising those who do good; this is primarily for the purpose of guiding and introducing future students.
This causes firm and upright faith to arise, thereby continuing the wisdom-life of all Buddhas. This is the first cause for the emergence of the sound from the surging stūpa.
△ Second, the posthumous bequest following the fruition.
When that Buddha had attained enlightenment and was approaching his parinirvāṇa, [he] praised them, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
Although the construction of stupas is a matter for both devas and humans, the administration and regulation thereof rests with the bhikṣus.

Therefore, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, he addressed the bhikṣus: "Do not forget your former vows; you should take these stupas to the ten directions to listen to the sutras and perform [meritorious deeds]."

[He] testified to this. Therefore, he entrusted [the relics] with the intent that they be enshrined in their entirety, and that a great stūpa should be erected. "Supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the powers attained after fruition;
"power of aspiration" (*praṇidhāna-bala*) refers to the power of the vow made during the causal stage. If one possesses only the power of aspiration but lacks supernormal powers, one is unable to go.

If one possesses only supernormal powers but lacks the power of aspiration, one is able to go but has no desire to do so. Thus, Prabhūtaratna [was able to appear] by means of the union of supernormal power and aspiration.
Because of this support, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, wherever the sutras are preached, that jeweled stupa invariably emerges to bear witness.
This is the second cause for the emergence of the stupas and the sounding of their voices. △ Third, the conclusion by calling out the name.
Mahāpratibhāna, the stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna [has appeared]... [and] praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
Being about to conclude his response, he addressed Mahāpratibhāna by name, for he was the host of the assembly. The Tathāgata’s intention was this:
"You asked by what causes and conditions this jeweled stūpa exists; as I have explained above, it is now the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has arrived."
Finally, he left his final testament. Regarding the stupa for his entire body, you asked by what causes and conditions the earth surged forth and emitted a voice.

As I have explained above, it was due to the power of that Buddha’s vows during his causal stage; because [the assembly] heard him preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the earth surged forth to praise him as "excellent.
Thus concludes the section on the manifestation of the earth and the testimony of Prabhūtaratna. II. The Gathering of the Emanated Bodies. 1. The Reasons for the Gathering.

Second, the explicit explanation of the gathering of the clouds; third, the dispatching of messengers to communicate the desire [to teach]. Regarding the first of these two: first, Śākyamuni responds to the vow for eloquent exposition;
second, the emanated bodies respond to Śākyamuni’s invitation. Regarding the first of these: [The section on] Śākyamuni responding to the vow for eloquent exposition.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna [thought]: "Those who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions should now be assembled.
First, he wished to see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna; however, the realm of the Tathāgata was not something that Pratibhāna could advance to inquire about by his own power.

Therefore, it is said that he addressed the Buddha by means of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). This is the discussion of this matter. If one were to represent this as a symbolic teaching (*dharmanirukti*), by means of oneself...
The Buddha of the True Nature cannot be realized through the samādhi of mere words; it must rely on the power of actual wisdom to be in accord with it.
Those who wish to see this Buddha-body, though they have heard the Buddha’s teaching, must personally behold it so that their doubts may be completely exhausted.
From "The Buddha said" onwards, he demonstrates the power of the vow of Prabhūtaratna, whose vow was made with profound and heavy words.
It may be moved, yet it cannot be shifted. However, since Many Treasures has come before the Buddha to hear the sutra, he is unwilling to lightly reveal his body;
he insists that all the emanations of that Buddha must assemble before appearing. This is likely because he fears the assembly might harbor thoughts of levity.
If this is interpreted as a symbolic teaching (*dharmaparyāya*), it means that one who wishes to see [the Buddha]...
The Buddha of the True Nature must exert the power of his perfect wisdom; only then can this be nearly achieved. Regarding "the Great Bliss" below:
he fulfills his vow by gathering his manifested bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Those who should now be gathered fulfill the distant vow of Prabhūtaratna and the proximate vow of Delightful Preaching.
△ Second, the manifested bodies respond to Śākyamuni’s request.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...and to make offerings to the jeweled stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
First, Mahāpratibhāna requested that the emanated bodies be assembled; now he sees the Buddha’s body present here, and he has also heard that the emanated bodies are in the ten directions.
A sense of rare wonder arose; thus, he also wished to see them. He saw them presently here preaching the Dharma, and he also heard them preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
A mind of deep respect arose, so he further wished to pay homage and make offerings. At that time, light was emitted from below [the brow] to invite the Buddhas from afar.
The white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) is located between the two eyebrows, symbolizing the wisdom of the Middle Way and the virtue of the Dharmakāya. The white tuft of hair is like crystal.

The crystal tube represents the wisdom of true emptiness and the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). The emission of light that universally illumines the *dharmadhātu* represents the wisdom of wondrous existence and the virtue of *prajñā*.

The introductory section represents the convergence of provisional means toward the ultimate reality and the bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood, thereby manifesting the complete essence of the three virtues.
Within this, it represents the subsumption of differences into unity and the recruitment of persons to propagate the Dharma, thereby revealing the three types of wisdom.
The Great Function. One who grasps this intent will find that the magnificent texts of the seven volumes are all but mere fishing weirs and rabbit snares.
The Buddha’s light shines forth, illuminating the ten directions simultaneously; yet, because words cannot manifest [the truth] all at once, it is first explained by way of the eastern direction.
According to the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, regarding the transformation bodies manifested by Śākyamuni in the east, even down to the pulverization of the great trichiliocosm...
Even the motes of dust therein cannot be counted; what is now described as "five hundred million *koṭis*," etc., is likewise merely a count of that which is uncountable.
That the ground is made of *vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli) manifests the purity of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution).

Rows of jewel-trees are provided for pleasure and contemplation, and precious garments are spread upon the ground for sitting and reclining; thus it is said that the jewel-trees and precious garments serve as adornments. The Bodhisattvas...
