"Filled" indicates that the primary retribution is purely wholesome. Precious canopies hang from the heavens to provide shade and protection;
precious nets are suspended in the void to serve as a barrier and defense. Therefore, it is said that "precious canopies are spread everywhere, and precious nets are draped above.

Regarding "the Buddhas preaching the Dharma," this refers to the primary teacher of the transformation preaching the Dharma with a perfect, resonant voice that pervades the ten lands instantaneously and completely; hence it is so called.

With a great and wondrous voice, the Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma manifests transformed companions to assist in its proclamation. As principal and retinue are layered upon one another, they sing in unison throughout the ten directions;

thus it is said that [the sound] pervades all lands. In the south, west, north, and other directions, the light illuminates the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the principal and the retinue, no differently than here;
hence it is said, "it is likewise so. From the words "At that time" onwards, the emanated bodies take leave of the assembly and desire to depart.
"Come. Each addressed the bodhisattvas, intending to depart from their respective assemblies because they had received the light; this expressed their desire to take leave of those crowds.

In accordance with the intent of the light’s illumination and out of sincere compassion and delight in preaching, it was said: "I shall now go to the Sahā world, to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides.
This demonstrated the intention to go in order to request his appearance; thus, it says, "and to make offerings to Prabhūtaratna."
Regarding the Tathāgata’s Jewel Stūpa, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "This and that are of one essence; fundamentally, there is neither self nor other.

That he addressed those who were to go was a provisional response according to their capacities, merely establishing the distinction between host and guest. This concludes the section on the reasons for the gathering like clouds.

II. The Main Exposition of the Gathering Like Clouds. This has two parts: A. Brief Gathering; B. Extensive Gathering. Part A (Brief Gathering) has three sections: 1. Brief Transformation of a Single Land; 2. ... [text continues] ... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The Buddhas have briefly gathered together; the three fetters are briefly not yet exhausted. First:
at that time, the Sahā world immediately transformed into purity (until) all devas and humans were moved and placed in other lands.
Regarding the transformation of the Sahā world into a pure realm, there are three meanings. First, it is due to the power of the pure karma of the assembly at that time.
Since their previous actions were all categorized as outflowing (*sāsrava*) and impure, they perceived the Sahā world as defiled and evil;
since their subsequent actions were all categorized as non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) and pure karma, they perceive it as pure and adorned. Second, [it is due to] the Buddhas...

First, by virtue of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): because the Buddhas desire to greatly benefit the assembly in this gathering, they pre-emptively purify the land through their supernormal powers prior to the future. Second, by virtue of Śākyamuni’s power of skillful means (*upāya*):

because the Tathāgata considers that the members of the assembly have not yet forgotten the distinction between the defiled and the pure, he employs the power of skillful means to demonstrate that defilement and purity are non-dual.
2. Regarding "the ground is made of lapis lazuli, adorned with jeweled trees": this distinguishes it from the previous [world], which was boundless dust and earth with thorns covering the wilds.
Regarding "golden cords demarcate the eightfold paths": this distinguishes it from the previous [world], where tracks crisscrossed haphazardly, making passage difficult and impassable.
Regarding "there are no villages, hamlets, or cities": this distinguishes it from the previous [world] inhabited by people.
The land is vast yet the space is narrow; the five destinies dwell intermingled, and there are neither great oceans nor rivers, mountains, streams, forests, or marshes.
This distinguishes it from the previous descriptions of pits, hollows, mounds, and uneven elevations, as well as from the great marshes.

"Burning great precious incense and scattering celestial flowers upon the ground" distinguishes it from the previous scenes where smoke rose from the borders of war and the dust of campaigns obscured everything, or where jeweled nets [hung in the air].
Covering it above and suspending various precious bells: this is not like the past, when yellow winds obscured the sun and red sands roared through the air.
Observe that the impure land of the past is none other than today’s pure land; today’s pure land is precisely the impure land of the past.
To the ultimate degree, what is illusory and what is real? One must simply know that it is neither pure nor impure, but merely a transformation.

Do not disparage their minds; rather, only those who remain in this assembly are permitted to do so, because this assembly turns its back on dust and accords with awakening, making it fit to enter the realm of the Buddhas.
As for the displacement of the devas and humans, it is because they turn their backs on awakening and accord with dust, thereby generating inherent obstruction.
Thus, their being placed in other lands does not mean they are actually moved to other lands; it simply means that although they have eyes, they do not see.
It is like that which faces one across a thousand *li*. If one interprets this as a symbolic representation (*pratibimba*), then Sahā is the dwelling place of Śākyamuni;
it symbolizes the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and entering the dharma-realm of principle (*li-fajie*).

Its transformation into a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*) represents the Buddha’s knowledge and vision entering the dharma-realm of phenomena (*shi-fajie*). [Question: Sahā is a defiled land; why does it represent principle? Why is its transformation into a pure land, on the contrary, said to represent phenomena? [Answer: It does not change into principle; rather, following conditions (*pratyaya*), it constitutes phenomena.

The relationship between the signifier and the signified is extremely clear in principle. Some may place the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*) first and the noumenal dharma-realm second; this is likely because they are speaking from the perspective of the stage of delusion, describing the process of entering the noumenon by way of the phenomena. Here, however, we speak from the perspective after awakening, where one relies on the noumenon to engage with phenomena;
therefore, it is arranged in this order). △ Second, the brief collection of all Buddhas.
At that time, each of the Buddhas brought a great bodhisattva and sat cross-legged upon their respective seats.
They had come solely to witness the event; there was no need for a vast multitude, so each Buddha was accompanied by only one attendant.
As for "each arriving beneath a tree," this means one Buddha per tree. As for "each having a teacher’s seat," this means one Buddha per seat. However—
Each tree corresponds naturally to a Buddha. Furthermore, each tree is adorned in succession with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits;

for each Buddha, a seat is spontaneously manifested. Moreover, these seats are embellished with various kinds of great jewels—all of which are unobstructed realms manifested through the inconceivable power of all Buddhas. As for those seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*):

They approach from afar, manifesting the etiquette of taking a brief rest. If this is interpreted as a symbolic teaching (*dharmaparyāya*), it signifies that the Buddhas have gathered in brief to demonstrate their Buddha-knowledge and vision;
having already entered the realm of non-obstruction regarding phenomena, the power and function of their wisdom are somewhat superior to what preceded.
△ Third, the conclusion of the summary, which is not exhaustive.
In this manner, as they successively multiplied until filling the trichiliocosm, the emanated bodies in a single direction were still not exhausted.
The *Sammitīya-nikāya-śāstra* states: "The manifestations of the Buddhas consist of only one Buddha with one attendant, one tree, and one seat; the space they occupy is not vast.
Even if they filled the Sahā world-system, they would still not exhaust a single direction. This sufficiently demonstrates the vastness of their responsive transformations. (Abridged)

The summary is concluded. △ Second, the extensive gathering has three parts: 1. The extensive transformation of the eight directions; 2. The extensive gathering of all Buddhas; 3. The conclusion on the extensive pervasion.
Regarding the first two [parts], there are two sections: 1. Further transforming the eight directions; 2. Further transforming beyond the directions. Regarding the first:

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate [the assembly]—until the celestial jewel-flowers were spread across the ground—first transformed one land to accommodate the emanations of a single direction;
yet even this was not sufficient. Now, wishing to accommodate those of the ten directions, he must transform further.
The passage beginning with "two hundred myriads of koṭis" clarifies the magnitude of the transformation. There was no ground remaining.
Regarding "the hells and so forth," there are two meanings: first, that the assembly is pure and perceives all phenomena as being like [empty] space;
second, that those in the evil realms have heavy karma and are far removed from the sphere of the Buddhas.
To transfer the devas and humans to these same states—namely, the Mucilinda, which means "stone," and the Mahāmucilinda, which means "great stone"—refers to the world-system.
All large and small stones are mountains. The Cakravāḍa Mountains encircle the small chiliocosm;
the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains encircle the great trichiliocosm; these are the mountains that mark the boundaries and divisions of all worlds.

Sumeru—also called Sumeru—is translated here as "Wondrous High" (Miaogao), for it is composed of wondrous jewels and rises as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; it stands at the center of the four continents.

Mount Sumeru is the great sovereign mountain at the center. As for the "kings of mountains," this refers collectively to the seven layers of golden mountains situated beyond Mount Sumeru at the edge of the seven layers of fragrant water seas.

These are known as Yugandhara (Holding the Pair), Īṣādhara (Holding the Axle), Kālaparvata (Carrying Wood), Sudarśana (Good to Behold), Aśvakarṇa (Horse Ear), Vinataka (Elephant Trunk), and Nimindhara (Fish Mouth). Furthermore, above these mountains, there are others such as the Cakravāḍa (Iron Ring) mountains. Thus it is said:
Where there are divisions between worlds, such as Mount Sumeru and the like, there are distinctions between this and that world;
where there are mountains such as Mucilinda and the like, there are differences in their heights and depths;

furthermore, where there are rivers, seas, and so forth, there are changes of ebb and flow, or the shifting of lands and waters. Since none of these now exist, it is said that they are universally one single realm. (From the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*)
"The level ground with a canopy of interlaced precious jewels" refers to a canopy formed by the interlacing of various jewels to shield against the open air.
"Hanging various banners and canopies" refers to unfurling banners and setting up canopies to adorn the boundaries of the kingdom. The rest is all as explained above.

If one were to interpret this as a symbolic representation of the Dharma, it further transforms the eight directions to symbolize the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, entering into the non-duality of principle and phenomena.
This obstructs the Dharma-realm. △ Second, the further transformation beyond the directions:
Śākyamuni Buddha, for the sake of all Buddhas who will come... [until] heavenly jewel flowers are spread everywhere upon the ground.
Since the eight directions have already been transformed previously, they are capable of providing space; however, it is still not yet possible for them to serve as seats.

Now, for the sake of future seating, it is necessary to further transform the areas beyond the directions. Nevertheless, although this is so, it is truly intended to symbolize the Dharma; were it otherwise, [it would not be so].

Even the chamber of Vimalakīrti could accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones; how much more so, then, could the wondrous realm of ultimate perfection fail to surpass that which is merely "small" and inconceivable?
The remainder of the text follows the above. If one were to interpret this as a symbolic representation of the Dharma:

The further transformations beyond the mundane realm manifest the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is the entry into the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
Having completed the extensive transformations throughout the eight directions. △ Second, the vast assembly of all Buddhas.
At that time, those emanated by Śākyamuni from the east (up to) all assembled and sat in the eight directions.
As for the mention of the eastern direction specifically, it refers to the remainder of the previous brief assembly.

Those who came to the assembly after hearing the Dharma preached were those who, wherever they had traveled, performed Buddha-work according to conditions. Yet, even among the remainder of those gathered from one direction, there were still hundreds.
There are as many as ten million billion nayutas of Ganges sands; how much more so for the successive Buddhas of the ten directions, all of whom have gathered here.

Thus, the primary figures and their retinues are layered upon one another, infinitely and inexhaustibly. To contemplate this with a serene mind is like beholding a single, solemn painting of the Flower Treasury World (*Avataṃsaka*).
If one were to interpret this as a symbolic representation of the Dharma, it signifies that while the east was not yet fully assembled, it has now already arrived.
Awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one enters into the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*).

As the function of wisdom becomes increasingly superior, until all Buddhas of the ten directions gather together, this signifies entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the perfect realization of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*).
Thus, the functional application of wisdom is inexhaustible, truly inexhaustible. △ Third, the conclusion on the universal pervasiveness.
At that time, in each and every direction, four million billion [Buddha-lands] (extending to) were filled with all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The phrase "four million billion" and so forth refers to the two sets of transformed lands. "All the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas" refers to the emanated bodies gathered from the ten directions.
The lands are vast enough to contain the Buddhas without being cramped; the Buddhas dwell in the lands without being diminished. Therefore, it is said:
They fill it completely. This concludes the explicit description of the gathering of clouds. △ Third, the dispatch of messengers to convey the desire [to see the Buddha].
At that time, each of the Buddhas was beneath a jewel tree... (up to) ...the Buddhas dispatching their messengers was likewise so.
Although all Buddhas and each Buddha are of one essence, since they have already manifested as divided bodies to appear in the world, they act like guests and hosts in the mundane realm;
thus, each staying beneath a tree, they dispatch messengers to inquire after one another’s well-being. "Inquiring after well-being" means asking about their daily life and health.

"Bringing flowers" is a modest way of expressing the purpose of the visit. "Cupped hands" refers to holding both hands together in a gesture of reverence. As for what was told to them, it was to inform them that...
How does one inquire after [the Buddha’s] well-being? How does one make offerings? It is by practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "as my words say," this means instructing others to inquire after him individually using the very same words I have spoken.

As for the Buddha being without the conditions for illness and without sorrow or affliction, yet inquiring whether he has "little illness and little affliction," it is because sentient beings do not accept his teaching that he appears to have illness and affliction. This is the Dharma.

The body is truly eternal; there is nothing that is not peaceful and blissful. When asked about peace and bliss through physical vigor, it is because their former fundamental aspirations were not fulfilled that they find no joy.
Furthermore, when asking about the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, one intends this for their leaders as well as their companions.
Since the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas have already transcended the three realms, when one further asks about their security and well-being, it is because—
"In the past, you were bound and stalled at the stage of practice; because delusion was not yet dispelled, you lacked peace and stability.
By this "precious flower," he gives him the flower he has gathered in his palm. By "scattering it as an offering to the Buddha," he instructs him to perform offerings according to the Dharma.
By saying these words, he commands that [the teaching] be transmitted to Śākyamuni Buddha. "That certain Buddha... [refers to the recipient].

1. Opening the stupa and taking one’s seat; 2. Receiving the assembly in mid-air; 3. Praying for and recruiting a person to assist.
The first section has four parts: 1. The World-Honored One opens the stupa; 2. The fourfold assembly offers worship; 3. Prabhūtaratna shares his seat; 4. Śākyamuni takes his seat. Part One.

Desiring to repay the request for eloquent exposition, and because the stupa was suspended in the air and he now wished to open it, [he acted].

One must rise from one's seat and dwell in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If this were to be expressed through symbolic dharma (*dharmanirukti*), it would mean that since the preceding explanations of the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūtārtha*) all belong to the realm of relative opposition and both involve attachment, now that the provisional has been integrated into the real, even the real does not abide; ultimately, one returns to the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Therefore, rising from the seat and dwelling in emptiness serves as its symbolic expression. The fourfold assembly, knowing in their hearts that the stupa was opened, all gave rise to [faith].

Out of longing and reverence, they all rose and stood with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. The Tathāgata, whose wisdom reflects the minds of the multitude, briefly manifested his supernatural power;
thus, with his right hand, he opened the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa. It was as if a severed bolt had been removed.

He marveled that the Dharma had never before been heard; because this matter was unprecedented, his heart gave rise to yearning and reverence, and so he scattered flowers over Prabhūtaratna.
Because the Dharma had never before existed, his mind harbored gratitude, and so he scattered flowers over Śākyamuni. △ Third, Prabhūtaratna shares his seat.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, Prabhūtaratna Buddha [said to Śākyamuni Buddha]: "Śākyamuni Buddha, you may take this seat.

Free from views of arising and ceasing, he profoundly embodied the intention of Prabhūtaratna; thus he entered the stūpa and sat cross-legged.
Having opened the stūpa and taken his seat, [the second section follows]: "Receiving the Assembly into the Void."

"Good sons, each of you should contemplate this carefully; this is a difficult matter, and you must make great vows.
As for instructing them to "contemplate this carefully," it is because he fears that if they respond to the call in haste, they may have a beginning but no end.

First, regarding the difficulty of writing it down: while one endowed with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) might be able to grasp empty space and travel about, that is not yet considered difficult;

That would be difficult; yet, compared to what follows, even reading this [text] is difficult. To place the great earth upon one's toe-nail and ascend to the Brahma Heaven is not difficult because it is a matter of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

However, to read this sutra in an evil age, even for a brief moment, is difficult because it is the cause for the Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*). For such supernatural powers are what the Hīnayāna prizes, whereas the Buddha—

The Way is not a great vessel that can easily be sustained; this is how the distinction between what is difficult and what is not difficult arises. △ Third, the comparison of the difficulty of preaching and listening:
Suppose one were to carry dry grass through the conflagration at the end of a kalpa (until) being questioned on its meaning and intent—this would indeed be difficult.
At first, the comparison was said to be difficult. However, the conflagration at the end of a kalpa arises only in accordance with one's karma;

those who have no karma to follow can carry grass without it burning. Therefore, it is said that this is not yet considered difficult. This sutra is not something that can be heard due to the presence of obstacles.

If even a single person has such obstacles, it is difficult to uphold, explain, or cause others to hear it; therefore, it is said that this is indeed difficult. "If one upholds... and so forth, the comparison follows.
It is not difficult to listen to the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates, for each is a medicine administered according to the specific ailment.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures all adapt the Dharma to the capacities of beings; they are easy to hear and enter, and their efficacy is easily realized.

Thus, all attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Since the faculties respond to the transformation and the teaching can be applied, it is said that this is not yet difficult. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
People are for the most part corrupt and evil. Even upon hearing this sutra, the world abounds in resentment and jealousy; how much less could they inquire into its meaning and intent?

Were it not for those with great karmic conditions from past lives, one could not be thus. Therefore, it is said that this is difficult. △ Fourth, the comparison regarding the difficulty of upholding and maintaining [the teaching].
If a person preaches the Dharma—ranging from ten million billion [teachings] up to such a sūtra as this—it is indeed difficult.
Among all sentient beings, there are none who do not delight in the Hīnayāna and revere supernatural powers; since they delight in these things, they are easy to reach.
If one honors [these practices], they are easily possessed; thus, although it may seem that such benefits are difficult to achieve, they are not actually so.
"Serving" (feng) means serving them for one's own cultivation; "upholding" (chi) means upholding them to teach others. To serve them for one's own cultivation requires a perfectly sharp faculty;
to uphold them to teach others requires a great vow, lest one surely fall back. Therefore, it is said that these are difficult. However, regarding the four sections mentioned above:

Through successive deliberations, this is all intended to provide insight for the propagation of the sutras in the final age. Yet, the Dharma masters who propagate the sutras suffer primarily from not knowing its difficulties.
If they were to anticipate these difficulties beforehand, their great vows would arise first and their diligence would lead the way;
donning the armor of patience and grasping the bow of wisdom, even if they enter the dense forest of false views or the realm of Māra and his celestial armies, [they would remain unshaken].
The realms of staffs, clubs, tiles, and stones; the domains of foul abuse and physical blows—these too are not what he concerns himself with.

To praise his merit and compare his hardships would be endless. △ Third, praising the teaching and extolling the faculty [of the audience], in two parts: first, praising the teaching as transcending the multitudes;
second, extolling the faculty as extraordinary. First:
"For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands... whoever is able to uphold this, they uphold the body of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: for the sake of the Buddha-way, I have sought people throughout immeasurable lands.
From the time I first attained enlightenment until this very day, I have extensively expounded all the various sūtras, and within them, I have thoroughly investigated their meanings and principles.
Profound and deep; as for the excellence of its power, nothing surpasses this. Therefore, it is said that this sutra is the foremost.
*Dacheng* (Great Achievement) says: "It is the key to all scriptures. This sutra is the mother of all Buddhas and the source from which the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas arise.
Hence it is said: "If there is one who can uphold it, they uphold the Buddha-body. *Dacheng* says: "A thousand..."
The Gate of Life of the Sages is based upon this. △ Second, the excellence of the manifestation of the mechanism:
"All sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa... (up to)... all devas and humans should make offerings."

The first [section] is able to evoke all Buddhas; the second exhorts them to speak their vows and demonstrates the difficulties of upholding [this teaching], repeatedly and earnestly admonishing that, in general, the propagation of this sutra is not easy.
It also serves to use this as a means to manifest the excellence of those who uphold it, even for a brief moment. Regarding those who uphold it temporarily:
Even if one upholds it for but a short time, all Buddhas behold this together; therefore it is said, "I am filled with joy, and so too are all Buddhas.
From the passage "In this way" onwards, [this teaching] can rival all other practices. Precisely because it can rival all other practices, it is called "that which is praised by all Buddhas.
This sutra is like a burden of a thousand scriptures; though one carries it for but a moment, it is already no small matter.
This is possible for those who are courageous; therefore, it is said that this constitutes valor. This sutra is like a mountain ten thousand fathoms high;
once one has resolved to ascend it, it is no longer within the ambition of those who would retreat or yield;
therefore, it is said that this constitutes diligence. This sutra is like a vajra sword; though wielded but momentarily, it can sever the sevenfold non-virtues; therefore, it is said:
This is called upholding the precepts. This sutra is like the great Vairambha wind; it stirs with a mere moment’s motion, sufficient to shake off the dust of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said that those who practice *dhūta* (also called *duṭṭha*, translated here as "shaking off") [attain their goal]. This sutra is like the grain of the *cakra* tree:
though it enters the belly for a brief time, before long it pierces through and emerges. Thus, it brings about swift attainment.
The Buddha-way is able to benefit both oneself and others from below. One who reads and upholds this sutra is capable of continuing the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom;
therefore, it is said that such a person is a true child of the Buddha. Being clearly realized of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), they are fully worthy of being the refuge for all wholesome deeds;

therefore, it is said that they "dwell on the ground of pure goodness. "Pure" (*chun*) means ultimate, and it also carries the sense of abundance and richness. This above has been explained in terms of self-benefit.
Being able to understand its meaning, one can then preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; therefore, it is called "the eye of the world.
"The world of fear" refers to the turbid and evil age. During this turbid and evil age, people are mostly stubborn, violent, and cruel; for this reason, it is named "fear."
At this time, one who is able to preach even for a brief moment is sent by the Tathāgata and performs the work of the Tathāgata;
therefore, they should be honored. This preceding section, spoken in terms of benefiting others, concludes the exalted recruitment of persons.
△ Second, the realization of benefits and the making of vows, which has two parts: first, demonstrating the realization of benefits; second, accepting responsibility and making vows.
Regarding the first (the title of the chapter states): *The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twelve: Devadatta*.

Devadatta is also named Tiāodá (調達). This is translated as "Heavenly Heat" (*Deva-datta*), because when he was first born, the minds of the assembly of humans, devas, and others were all struck with agitation and heat.
He is also called "Heaven-Conferred" (*Deva-datta*), because King Śuklodana had no sons and prayed to the heavens for an heir.
Because he falsely claimed to have been granted [powers] by the gods, he was the younger cousin of the Buddha and the biological elder brother of Ānanda.
Throughout successive lifetimes, he acted as an adversary to the Buddha; yet, it was precisely through his practice of unwholesome paths that he brought the Buddha’s virtues to fulfillment.

As for this chapter, it also includes the activities of Mañjuśrī in propagating the Dharma; however, following the principle of omitting the latter to prioritize the former, we shall treat it solely under the name of Upatiṣya (Da-da).
This is the chapter on "Renown. Furthermore, there are five distinct meanings to this chapter: First, to demonstrate that worldly wealth and status are not to be relied upon;
for example, when the Buddha was formerly a king, he relinquished his royal throne and so forth for the sake of the Dharma.
Second, to subdue the arrogance of sentient beings and cause them to become humble and open-minded; for example, as when a rishi came and said to the king, "I have... [and so forth].
1. To teach the *Saddharma* (Sublime Dharma), as in the passage: "If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you," and so forth. 2.
To cause those who are in opposition to perceive things as favorable, by forming the thought of accomplishment (*siddhi*), as when the Tathāgata himself said:

"It was through the spiritual friend Rāhula that I became fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*," and so forth. 3. To shatter the inferior minds of the assembly of nuns and cause them to give rise to true faith.

Therefore, it is as in the case where the dragon girl suddenly transformed her female body into a male one and immediately went to the Immaculate World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south to attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and so forth.
Fifth, it is to demonstrate the two benefits of the sudden and the gradual, in order to preclude two kinds of errors.
This is as in the case where Śākyamuni’s gradual cultivation did not cling to principle, while the dragon girl’s sudden realization did not stagnate in phenomena, and so forth. (Sūtra Text)

This is divided into two parts: first, citing the case of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra to demonstrate gradual benefit; second, citing the case of Mañjuśrī’s propagation of the Dharma to demonstrate sudden benefit.
The first part has three sections: first, a remote citation of the original cause; second, a summary that confirms the realization of benefit; third, the merit of hearing and believing.
The first two [sections]: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first three [sections]: first, the king abandons his kingdom to seek the Dharma;
second, the rishi requests a vow and expounds it for him; third, the king attends upon him for the sake of the Dharma. First:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas... [up to] "...I shall serve as his messenger for the rest of my life.
This initial section provides a general outline regarding the Dharma. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he sought the Dharma without excusing himself on the grounds of the long duration of time;

therefore, it says, "without weariness or fatigue. In the section beginning with "In many [lifetimes]," he generally recounts his vows and practices, constantly acting as a king and aspiring to seek Bodhi.
This means that one does not find contentment in what is tainted (*sāsrava*), but takes only the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the goal.
Even if the kalpa-stone were to be worn away, this resolve would not change; therefore, it is said that the mind does not regress.

Regarding the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*, the specific mention of "diligently practicing giving" is because the meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses all six. Thus, the mind is free from stinginess regarding elephants, horses, and the seven treasures.
As for "giving away wealth and property," it means not being stingy even with one's kingdom, cities, wife, children, slaves, or servants; this refers to the giving of material things (*āmiṣa-dāna*).
Furthermore, "not being stingy even with one's head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, or feet" refers to the giving of one's person and life (*kāyajīvita-dāna*).
These collectively manifest all forms of possible giving; hence it is said, "not sparing one’s body or life. This is because these are what people value most highly.
As for this, he did not even begrudge his own body or life; everything else can be understood from this. "At that time, the world was declining" clearly indicates the actual events:

it was an age when human life spanned immeasurable years, a period of the "Good Age. The reason for specifically noting this is to provide a contrast for the limit of one thousand years mentioned later in the sutra.
"Renouncing the throne" means suddenly casting aside the wealth of the four seas; "entrusting the administration to the crown prince" means...

"Entrusting the authority over the myriad affairs of state to him forever. Based on this, those who are greedily attached to worldly pleasures and lack the heart of wisdom should know to exert themselves.
[The phrase] "beating the drum to assemble the multitude" means that one must gather the assembly to proclaim the decree;

this is to demonstrate the intention that it is solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma, without discriminating against the person. "Provisioning" refers to the four types of requisites. "Running messengers" refers to listening.
He was employed as a messenger. Yet this king, regarding the Dharma as his lifeblood, set aside his body and forgot his own self-interest for the sake of the Way.
He humbled himself to accept the dignity of the Nine-Five Throne [the Emperor] and willingly performed the service of a slave.
Based on this, those in the present age who harbor ulterior motives in their pursuits ought to feel shame. 2. The Immortal Requests a Vow and Explains It.
At that time, there was a rishi who came and said to the king: "If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim [the teaching] for you.

Regarding the phrase "if you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you," Da Cheng (Daosheng) says: "When one guides people through the Way, one must ensure they listen to their words and follow their instructions;
it is not merely a matter of assuming a title to purchase favor. Furthermore, one tests whether the person has ulterior motives—for instance, if they rely on their power."
To rely on one's noble status is insufficient for attaining the Way. That a common man becomes a teacher for a hundred generations—can this not be called a transcendent immortal?
△ Third, King Gaozu served as his attendant for the sake of the Dharma.
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness (up to the point where it says) he served him with diligent devotion so that nothing was lacking.
That he leaped for gladness upon hearing the words is because [the seer] possessed the Dharma. That he immediately followed the seer is because he did not disregard his word.
That he provided what was required refers to the four requisites; he provided each one individually, such as gathering fruit, drawing water, and so forth.
First, as a servant, there was nothing he would not obey or perform; even using his own body as a bed or seat, his body and mind never grew weary.

This collectively demonstrates that he underwent extreme toil and suffering, accepting it all with joy and without refusal. As for "serving at the proper time," it means acting without fail according to the occasion.
As for "passing a thousand years," it means continuing without ceasing through both cold and heat. This was not done to seek the fame of asceticism, but was truly intended—
Seeking the unsurpassed Way, he said, "For the sake of the Dharma, I shall serve you with diligent devotion, hoping that you will joyfully preach the Dharma for me, so that I may lack nothing.
This is what is meant by "honoring these sons of the Buddha," in the hope of hearing [the teaching] even for a brief moment.
Yet, although the hermit was austere in his integrity and resolute in his aspirations, he alone was able to humble the heart of the king; and this king—
Valuing the Way and forgetting worldly concerns, he was thus able to humble his most august person. Without this king, there would have been no way to perceive the loftiness of the immortal;

without the immortal, there would have been no way to realize the greatness of the king. Only the king and the immortal may serve as a model for the transmission of the Dharma throughout ten thousand generations.
The prose section concludes. △ Second, the Verse Recitation (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
[The Main Verses are divided into two parts: 1. Verses on the Meaning corresponding to the Prose Exposition. 2. A Conclusion, Verification, and Exhortation. The first part has three sections: 1.
Verses on the King Abandoning His Kingdom to Seek the Dharma. 2. Verses on the Rishi Requesting a Vow and Preaching for Him. 3. Verses on the King Following [the Rishi] for the Sake of the Dharma.
Attendant: First, I recall that in past kalpas, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, [I was willing to] become a slave (up to this point).
The first two lines of the verse summarize the dedication for the sake of the Dharma; the following two lines generally describe the vows and practices, characterized by non-attachment.

Regarding the five desires, one will certainly be able to resolve to attain Buddhahood because of practicing extensive acts of giving. The final four lines of the verse correctly clarify the original event.
While the prose says "beating a drum," this [verse] says "striking a bell"; these two actions together serve to assemble the multitude.

These appear interchangeably in the preceding and following sections. "To serve as a slave" means to provide services and run errands. △ Second, the verse on the seer requesting a boon and the subsequent explanation:
At that time, the seer Asita came and addressed the Great King (up to) "I shall explain it for you."
*Asita*, here translated as "Incomparable" (*Abhūta*), refers to one whose person and Dharma are both incomparable. "One who is able to practice" means practicing according to the teachings;
that is, practicing in accordance with the meaning of the prose section. △ Third: A verse on the king attending upon the Dharma.
At that time, when the king heard the words of the seer, his heart was filled with great joy (up to the point where) his body and mind were free from weariness.
Da Cheng [the Great Commentary] states: "The fruit of trees is called *guǒ* (fruit), such as peach and plum; the fruit of plants is called *luò* (gourd), such as melon and bottle-gourd."
"Respecting according to the season" means that firewood, fruits, melons, and so forth, each should be offered at its appropriate time. The rest is self-evident.
This concludes the prose commentary on the verse of meaning. △ Second, the conclusion of the proof and the exhortation (supplementary verse).
I have diligently sought the Great Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; it is for this reason that I now speak it for you.
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: in the past, I universally sought the Great Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, not for my own sake nor out of desire for pleasure;
therefore, although I was a great king, I was still able to apply myself with diligence and vigor.
I sought and obtained this Dharma. Because I practiced the Dharma in this manner, I have ultimately attained the fruit of Buddhahood today.
This was my own practice; I now proclaim it for your sake. If you are able to act as I have done, you too may swiftly realize the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
[The section on] the remote exposition of the original cause is concluded. II. The Conclusion and Corroboration of the Realization.
The second [section] on further benefits has two parts: first, correlating the past and the present; second, establishing the progressive benefit. Regarding the first:
the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "At that time, the king... (up to)... at that time, the rishi was none other than Devadatta now."
The King is my own self; this demonstrates that the Buddha-way is not easily accomplished. The Immortal is Rādha; this demonstrates that even one who harms the Buddha truly has no evil intent.
One follows and one opposes, yet together they serve to drum forth and propagate the wondrous Dharma, merely to guide and receive sentient beings.

Regarding the thought of further cultivation: thus, concerning Yaśodaśarman and Śākyamuni, those who gradually achieve benefit do so by means of these two proofs: first, Śākyamuni’s attainment of enlightenment; second, Yaśodaśarman’s receiving of a prediction. First:
It is because of the spiritual friend Devadatta (up to) all because of the spiritual friend Devadatta.
In the past, Devadatta was a rishi who was able to humble the Buddha’s pride and was able to bring about the Buddha’s virtuous deeds.
Therefore, the Buddha referred to him as a "spiritual friend. "Complete" means "perfect. Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are called...

The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are: first, immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which can bestow happiness upon all beings; second, immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*), which can extract suffering from all beings;

third, immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which rejoices when others are freed from suffering and attain happiness; and fourth, immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*), which regards others without hatred or attachment.

As for the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*): first is integration through giving (*dāna*), which means that for sentient beings who delight in material wealth, one provides gifts of material goods.

1. Gathering those who delight in the Dharma by means of the gift of the Dharma; 2. Gathering through kind speech (*priyavāditā*), which means that with a virtuous and gentle mind, one accords with all beings, offering consolation and exhortation to inspire their affection and attachment; 3.

Gathering through beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), which means that one brings about the welfare of all beings by initiating actions of the three karmas so that they may be transformed; 4. Gathering through common purpose (*samānārthatā*), which means clearly perceiving—
For sentient beings, he divides his form and disperses his shadow, harmonizing his light while engaging in the same activities, secretly binding their minds together.

"Supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the six kinds of supernormal powers, which are also the ten powers of the *Avataṃsaka*. "Power of the Path" refers to the power of the primary and auxiliary paths, which is also the adamantine power of the path.
The remainder is as seen in the preceding text. The above clarifies the fulfillment of merit; yet it is not merely the fulfillment of merit.
It was through this that he was honed and tempered; it is now, as a fruition, that he teaches and transforms others, continuing to bask in the merit of his deeds. Thus it is said:
"He attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment and extensively delivered sentient beings—all because of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) Upagupta.

Yet, although Upagupta had been a foe of the Buddha in previous lives, the Buddha still addressed him by the title of "spiritual friend. Based on this, all those who act in opposition to me should likewise...

One should form the perception of him as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). △ Second, the attainment of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) by many: 1. The name of the Buddha and the name of the realm; 2. His dwelling in the world and his teaching; 3. The benefits after his parinirvāṇa. First: [The Name of the Buddha and the Name of the Realm] ... He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta [attained] a world named Heavenly Path (*Deva-mārga*).
As for his title as a Heavenly King (*Deva-rāja*), it was obtained by means of protecting sentient beings.

Indeed, his manifesting himself as an enemy of the Buddha during the causal stage and his manifesting entry into hell were all for the sake of protecting sentient beings, so as not to allow them to give rise to evil. The name of the world is..."

Regarding the Way of Heaven (Tian Dao): because the sentient beings of this realm have long been subject to his transformation and teaching, such that it has permeated their very bones and marrow, they are able to continue the Way of the Heavenly King Buddha.
Thus, although Raudrākṣa is called a provisional manifestation, because he harmed the Buddha, he could not escape the suffering of hell;
yet, although he is called an evil man, because he taught the Buddha, he subsequently received the prophecy of the Heavenly King. Based on this...
Those who harbor difficulties with the Buddha should naturally feel a chill in their hearts; yet those whose evil intentions are not yet like those of Devadatta—how can they fail to exert themselves?
△ Second, dwelling in the world to teach and transform.
At that time, the Buddha Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas (until they attained the patience of non-arising and reached the stage of non-retrogression).
According to the teachings, one cycle of increase and decrease constitutes a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute an intermediate kalpa (*madhyakalpa*).

Each of the four periods—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, totaling a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). The present text refers to "twenty" [intermediate kalpas].
An intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) should be understood as one of the five great kalpas (*mahākalpa*).
"Extensively for the sake of sentient beings" refers to those with the capacities of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). "Expounding the wondrous Dharma" refers to the teachings of the three vehicles.

These teachings of the three vehicles are collectively termed "wondrous" because whatever is taught therein reaches the ground of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*). One thereby attains the benefits of the three vehicles, such as that of an Arhat.
The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) leading to the stage of non-retrogression corresponds in meaning to the seventh and eighth stages (*bhūmi*).

As the text of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* on the eighth stage states: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has skillfully cultivated the wisdom of expedient means within the seventh stage, and even enters into the nature of all phenomena as being like space, this is called attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Having accomplished this patience..."
At that time, they enter the eighth stage, the Immovable Bhūmi. △ Third, the benefits after the parinirvāṇa:
From the time after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, until they resolve their minds on Bodhi and reach the stage of non-retrogression.

First, the measure of the True Dharma; below this, the size of the stūpas for the entire body and the śarīra relics; below this, the various heavens; below "immeasurable," the offerings made out of gratitude to the stūpa;
and according to the Dharma, the realization of the fruits—this concludes the summary of the benefits realized through the assembly. △ Third, the merit of hearing and believing.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In future ages... if one renounces their kingdom as a king and, with faith and reverence free from doubt, has no mind of greed;
if one seeks a boon from a rishi and, with faith and reverence free from doubt, has no mind of anger;
and if one acts for the sake of the Dharma as a king and, with faith and reverence free from doubt, has no mind of delusion."
As for the mind: since the three poisons have been extinguished, there is no retribution of the three miserable realms.

Because one believed and revered [the Buddha] without doubt when he attained Buddhahood, one was able to be born before the Buddha. Because one believed and revered without doubt while [the Buddha] propagated the sutras, one constantly hears this sutra.
Because one did not doubt that Dàduō was truly an evil person, one was born among humans and devas to receive happiness. Because one did not doubt Dàduō...
He ought to have entered hell; therefore, he was instead caused to be born miraculously within a lotus flower.

This was likely because Devadatta’s evil reputation was long established, and had he been suddenly prophesied to attain Buddhahood, it would have easily invited suspicion and slander. Thus, it is said that the merit of hearing and believing [the Dharma] is such as this.
Furthermore, by means of this, he sought to manifest the equality of enemies and kin, thereby severing all views of hatred and attachment.

The section on Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s mastery of the sūtras to demonstrate gradual benefit is concluded. △ Second, the section on Mañjuśrī’s propagation of the Dharma to demonstrate sudden benefit has three parts: 1. The meeting of the two masters; 2. Questions and answers to verify the benefit; 3. The assembly’s faith and acceptance. First: The meeting of the two masters. The second part, "Questions and Answers to Verify the Benefit," has four sections: 1. Mañjuśrī questions the Elder; 2. The Elder explains his own realization; 3. Mañjuśrī praises the Elder; 4. The Elder expresses his gratitude. First: Mañjuśrī questions the Elder. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the great city of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the Elder Subhūti and say to him: 'The Buddha invites you to come. At that time, the venerable Ānanda received the Buddha’s instruction and went to where the Elder Subhūti was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Elder’s feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Elder Subhūti: "The Buddha invites you to come. At that time, the Elder Subhūti said to the venerable Ānanda: "Wait for me a moment, Ānanda. I must first attend to my duties within the monastery before I can go to see the Buddha. Then the venerable Ānanda returned to the place where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have already delivered the Buddha’s invitation to the Elder Subhūti. The fact that the flowers are like chariot wheels represents that when practice is perfected and wisdom is realized, one is able to transcend the great ocean of birth and death by oneself.

Therefore, emerging from the ocean symbolizes this. Dwelling in the midst of empty space symbolizes that, having already emerged from birth and death, one dwells securely in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Reaching Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa symbolizes that although one dwells in the emptiness of meaning, even emptiness does not abide.
Descending from the lotus flower signifies that although one attains realization by relying on practice, one does not cling even to that practice.
Because of this non-abiding and non-attachment, one accords with the Buddha’s realm—the awakened wisdom in which arising and ceasing are non-dual; thus, one arrives before the Buddha.

The Bodhisattva Jñānakośa said: "I see that Śākyamuni Tathāgata [from his initial resolve] until his attainment of perfect enlightenment in a mere moment.
