Virtue. All such [practices] are for the supreme pursuit of the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that one "seeks the path to bodhi.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, there has been not the slightest interruption; therefore, it is said that one "has never ceased. The phrase "trichiliocosm" refers to the places where he practiced and transformed beings in the past.
The places of his practice and transformation did not stop at the trichiliocosm alone; however, for the time being, we shall take the Sahā world as our focus.

Regarding the discussion of realms: setting aside other realms for the moment, if one observes closely within this Sahā world, even down to something as minute as a mustard seed within the trichiliocosm, every single spot is where the Tathāgata sacrificed his body and life while he was a bodhisattva.
Therefore, it is said that there is no place that is not such a site. All of these were for the sake of delivering sentient beings of the lower realms; hence, it is said:
"For the sake of sentient beings. This refers to the final body (*carama-bhava*). Within this final body, the causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled;
therefore, it is said that "the path to Bodhi is accomplished. Although the accomplishment of the Way occurs at the very end, the accumulation of causes dates back to the past.
Because the present exists by virtue of the past, it is said that "only after [that] is it accomplished. The phrase "is accomplished" specifically indicates the act of achieving realization.
The Way is not easily understood. Failing to believe in what is below, one instead doubts previous words.

Having personally witnessed the difficulty of Śākyamuni’s path, yet hearing for the first time of the ease of the Dragon Girl’s attainment, it is no less than the difference between sailing with a favorable wind and tide versus an ant’s laborious climb up a high mountain;

thus, they do not believe. However, one must also know that the lack of faith on the part of Jñānakūṭa was actually the Great Being’s skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in the transformation of beings. Śākyamuni...
This is the practice of causes; it is also the Tathāgata’s skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
To claim that a bird a thousand years old cannot equal a phoenix born this morning is yet another instance of being deceived by the tongue of Zhijie. △ Second, the Dragon Girl speaks a verse.
While their discourse was not yet concluded, the Dragon King’s Daughter appeared, [saying]: "I shall propagate the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering sentient beings.
That she suddenly manifested while the discourse was still unfinished is precisely like the ritual of master and disciple chanting in response to one another to complete a musical performance;
her offering of prostrations and the recitation of verses of praise were intended to manifest immediate benefit and thereby resolve the doubts of Prajñākūṭa.
The first two lines of the verse praise the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*. In Sanskrit, this is called *Vairocana*, which here means "Full Purity.

This refers to the profound realization that both sin and merit are empty, thereby attaining perfect purity; this corresponds to the first line of the verse, representing the self-recompense body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
It is also called "Universal Radiance," referring to the radiance of the physical marks that shines throughout the ten directions;
this corresponds to the second line of the verse. This refers to the *parabhāva* (the fruit of others' merit). The phrase "subtle and wondrous" praises the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*.

The Sanskrit term is Vairocana, which means "pervading all places. This signifies pervading even the most minute particles and encompassing all wonders. Although it pervades the most minute particles, [it remains...]
It universally encompasses all wonders and is pervasively pure, leaving no room for anything else; thus it is called the "subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body.
The three phrases concerning the possession of marks praise the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya*. In Sanskrit, Śākyamuni means "Able Benevolent One" (*Śākya*) and "Tranquil Silence" (*Muni*).

"Able Benevolent One" refers to one who is able to manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), benefiting the people and loving all things; this is what is meant by "possessing the marks" in the verse.

This is because they accord with the excellence of meaning. As for "silent and still," the essence of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is fundamentally quiescent, and its marks and signs are likewise silent;

yet, they serve to adorn the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) in order to guide and attract those who are ignorant. This refers to the sense of "using [marks and signs] to adorn the Dharma-body" within the verse. Thus, the three bodies are perfectly interfused.
Being unimpeded in responding to the capacities of beings, he inspires the veneration of devas and humans and the reverence of dragons and spirits.

"Veneration" means to hold him upon the crown of one's head and gaze up at him with admiration; "reverence" means to pay homage with devout respect. Thus, all who possess breath and vitality know him as their honored parent;
therefore it is said that among all classes of beings, there are none who do not revere and follow him. This is the Way of the Tathāgata that moves devas and humans through the Dharma.

"It is so. Furthermore, regarding the accounts of attaining *bodhi* and so forth, this reflects the Dragon Girl’s own conviction in her ability to become a Buddha and her resolve to deliver sentient beings.
Her thought was: "I observe that the Way of the Tathāgata moves both devas and humans; I know with certainty that if I were to become a Buddha, I too would be like this.
Moreover, I have heard our Original Teacher grant me the promise of attaining *bodhi* instantaneously—how fortunate I am!"
[He said: "However, as this matter is difficult to believe, may only the Buddha bear witness to me and protect me with His mindfulness.
Until I attain Buddhahood, I shall likewise expound the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering beings; I most resolutely vow never to betray the grace of the Buddha nor the grace of my teacher.
Having finished speaking the verse to testify to his benefit, [the section] "Second, manifesting the body to testify to the benefit" has two parts. First, Śāriputra...
They did not believe it. Then the two dragon girls manifested their bodies.
First, Śāriputra spoke to the dragon girl, saying: "How can a female body so swiftly attain Buddhahood?"

At first, he spoke bluntly of the difficulty of belief, intending to say: "Based on your words, 'I have heard that one attains bodhi' and 'the Buddha shall bear witness,' you stand there self-assured, claiming you will soon attain the Unsurpassed Way.

You imagine that we, with our status as great men and our preeminent excellence, having fortunately heard this Dharma for years, must still wait many kalpas to achieve enlightenment; how much more so for someone like you?"
This is like a woman offering herself as collateral. To view the fruit of Buddhahood as so easy is for grand words to wound the reality; this matter is truly difficult to believe.
Below, the text raises a challenge and provides an explanation, which further contains two points. First, regarding the inability to achieve it:

the female body is the root of craving and desire, and is therefore called "defiled. A vessel of the Dharma must be one who practices pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and is therefore said to be "not [a woman]."
This is because, by virtue of not being such [a vessel], they are incapable of receiving the Dharma; hence it is said: "How could they possibly attain unsurpassed Bodhi?

Below this, regarding the failure to believe in the swift accomplishment of the Buddha-way, there are two further meanings. First, the Buddha-way is remote and difficult: "remote" (*xuán*) means vast and far-reaching.
This refers to the journey from cause to fruit, which passes through five hundred *yojanas*; thus it is called "remote and vast. Second, the difficulty of death.

The perfections (*pāramitās*) are difficult to exhaust even at the fifth stage; therefore, one must pass through immeasurable *kalpas*, accumulating practices and fulfilling the perfections—this refers to the events occurring throughout those immeasurable *kalpas*.

Only then does one achieve completion, because the fruit is first fulfilled once the causes are perfected. This is the first reason why Śāriputra did not believe that such swift accomplishment was possible.
Furthermore, as for the passage concerning the woman: women have heavy obstructions, which do not cease [as easily as men's].
Because of what was stated previously, the word "furthermore" (*you*) is employed. Regarding the five obstacles (*pañca-āvaraṇa*), according to the *Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsasamādhi-sūtra*:

If one purely cultivates the four dhyānas, one becomes a Brahmā King; if one is licentious and unrestrained, one receives a female body. If one is courageous, vigorous, and has few desires, one becomes Śakra;

if one is coquettish, unrestrained, and full of affectations, one receives a female body. If one is endowed with the ten wholesome dharmas, one becomes a Māra King (that is, Maheśvara). [The text then continues with] the disparagement...

Losing the true teaching results in receiving a female body; out of compassion for sentient beings, one acts as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). Because of excessive anger and jealousy, one receives a female body;
by fulfilling the practices of a Bodhisattva, one can become a Buddha. Failing to cultivate pure conduct leads to receiving a female body.
In all these cases, the former acts as the obstacle and the latter is that which is obstructed. Now, Śāriputra has spoken briefly, referring only to that which is obstructed. Based on this:
Thus, if one wishes to attain Buddhahood, it is best to resolve upon this path from now on;
one must wait until the female form is transformed into a male, and only after accumulating practices and fulfilling the perfections over immeasurable eons can one hope for success.

This is the second reason why Śāriputra did not believe in such rapid attainment. Based on these two points, he concludes his objection by asking: "How could a woman's body so quickly attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha. △ Second, the Dragon Girl manifests her body in two parts: first, offering a jewel as a symbolic manifestation; second, manifesting her attainment of Buddhahood. First:
At that time, the Dragon Girl had a precious jewel... (until) "my attaining Buddhahood shall be even swifter than this."

At first, he offered the jewel with the intention that: "Since Zhizhi is the noble heir of Prabhūtaratna and Śāriputra is the foremost disciple of Śākyamuni, if even these two sages harbor doubts, one can well imagine the state of the rest of the assembly. If I were to rely on words to argue my case, they would ultimately never believe me."
Therefore, it is presented solely by way of offering a precious jewel to manifest this meaning. The precious jewel symbolizes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Its value of three thousand signifies that one who attains this knowledge can take the great trichiliocosm to achieve Buddhahood.

Offering it to the Buddha symbolizes the Dragon Girl’s sudden realization and her upward alignment with the fruit of Buddhahood. The Buddha’s immediate acceptance of it symbolizes the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*).
The Seal. Having received the Buddha’s seal of certification, one who understands this meaning will turn from the female state below and attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there is another layer of kōan. Following the passage on the Dragon Girl, the dialogue proceeds according to the facts. When asked, "Is it not so?

the Dragon Girl, confident in her own attainment of Buddhahood, wished to use this to demonstrate its swiftness. When the answer was given, "It is exceedingly swift," the two worthies did not understand her intent.
The essential meaning is this: to address the matter directly by revealing its true nature—namely, that what is right is indeed right, and what is wrong is truly wrong.

By responding swiftly beneath your words, I instruct you to "observe me," thereby causing you to establish proof of the reality [of my teaching] and demonstrating that the attainment of Buddhahood is not a mere empty claim.
By instructing you to observe through spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), I cause you to deeply examine the subtle, demonstrating that sudden enlightenment is not a fabrication.
This is an illusory transformation. By receiving the jewel, she becomes a Buddha; since the attainment of Buddhahood resides within herself, it is said to be even swifter than this.
△ Second, manifesting the body to attain Buddhahood:
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl (up to) preaching the wondrous Dharma to all sentient beings.
That the entire assembly saw [this] clearly and distinctly was because there was no concealment;
due to the excellence of the causes and conditions, the karmic obstacles were suddenly transformed, and thus he was able to suddenly change into a male.

Furthermore, the reason for this sudden transformation into a male was to eliminate the body of a woman, which is not a vessel for the Dharma, as well as the lingering doubt regarding the five obstacles. A single jewel accords with the nature of reality, such that the myriad practices are simultaneously perfected.

Thus, she was able to fulfill the practices of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, her fulfillment of the bodhisattva practices was intended to dispel the doubts raised by Śāriputra regarding the accumulation of merit over kalpas, as well as the doubt raised by Jñānakūṭa concerning the Buddha’s own example. As for the "Southern Region," it is a land of empty luminosity;
"Stainless" refers to an area of purity. Regarding the statement that she "immediately departed," this is because a person can be both female and male, and likewise, a region...
The dark may become bright, and the realms may likewise be defiled or purified. Thus, attachments to such dualities as male and female, light and darkness, or defilement and purity are all untenable.
Sitting upon the precious lotus flower is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body); attaining perfect enlightenment is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body);
and the thirty-two marks and so forth are the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). The preceding verse praised the Buddha by means of these [attributes]; now, however, by means of these...

Self-attestation: The Dragon Girl may indeed be called a great man (*mahāsattva*). Furthermore, regarding the passage "she immediately went to the south," etc., it was for the purpose of removing Śāriputra’s doubt as to how one could so quickly attain Buddhahood, as well as the doubts of Prajñākūṭa who did not believe that enlightenment could be achieved in such a brief moment.
To universally expound the wondrous Dharma for the sake of the ten directions is the fulfillment of her vow after attaining the Way; this precisely corresponds to the preceding text: "I..."

The discourse on expounding the Mahāyāna and delivering sentient beings from suffering—comprising the questions, answers, and proofs of its benefits—is concluded. △ Third, the assembly’s faithful acceptance:
At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all members of the assembly in the Sahā world [up to] silently accepted it with faith.

First, they extend their respectful salutations from afar. Having personally witnessed the attainment of Buddhahood, they believe that this Dharma is efficacious; thus, their hearts are filled with great joy.

Having personally witnessed the preaching of the Dharma, they look toward true compassion reaching even to distant places; therefore, they all offer respectful salutations from afar. "Immeasurable" and below.

Both lands receive benefit. As for the "immeasurable sentient beings," those who possess the capacity of the roots of wisdom from past lives may, upon hearing the Dharma, attain realization and immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
Their merit is perfected in a single instant, and they receive their prediction of enlightenment in the present—just like the Dragon Girl who suddenly attained it in one moment.
Regarding the "sixfold earthquake," this symbolizes the simultaneous and sudden shattering of the ignorance of the six stages within both lands.

This refers to receiving benefit. Within this context of receiving benefit, the stages of hearing the Dharma and attaining realization are omitted; it simply describes the long-term arousal of the bodhicitta, which is presented in contrast to the other land.
From the passage beginning with "Zhiji" (Jñānakuṭa) downward: at that time, the assembly remained silent. Jñānakuṭa witnessed these events with his own eyes.

Xin accepted his argument, while Śāriputra examined its subtleties with wisdom until his arguments were exhausted. If even these two sages were thus reduced to silence, the rest of the assembly may be inferred;
therefore, they all remained silent without speaking, receiving it with deep faith and acceptance.

According to the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the youth Sudhana traveled extensively through one hundred and ten cities, all of which were said to be in the south; those he encountered numbered fifty...
The three types of superior friends are not limited to a single category; thus, an ancient master explained their significance as follows:
"To clarify what is correct is to reach the furthest reaches of the South. To benefit me is to be my friend; therefore, all people are my friends.

Now, in this chapter, the Tathāgata refers to Sudhana as a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra), and the dragon girl goes to the South to attain Buddhahood. This is also consistent with the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (Gandavyūha) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Is this not so? The demonstration of signs and the conclusion of the benefits of testimony are complete.
△ Second, the undertaking and making of vows (as titled in the chapter heading):
The Thirteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Chapter on Upholding."
"Upholding" (*dhāraṇā*) has two meanings: first, to receive and maintain; second, to transmit and maintain. The text says:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall receive, maintain, read, recite, and expound this sutra. This refers to receiving and maintaining. It further says:

"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions and enable sentient beings to copy this sutra and so forth. This refers to transmitting and maintaining.

This refers to "upholding" (dhāraṇī). Furthermore, "reverently upholding" (parigraha) also encompasses "transmitting and upholding," and "transmitting and upholding" likewise encompasses "reverently upholding.
This is because self-benefit and benefiting others are always mutually dependent; therefore, this chapter is titled simply "Upholding. If explained separately, it also possesses five meanings.
First, it serves as a recruitment for the jeweled stupa. The Tathāgata was deeply concerned with the propagation of the sutra; this chapter [addresses] the multitude...
The Worthy Ones (Bhadra) made this vow to comfort the Buddha’s mind, as the text says: "We only pray that the World-Honored One will not worry," and so forth.
Second, from the beginning of the "Dharma-Teacher" chapter, the supreme excellence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is revealed again and again;
this chapter exhorts one to propagate the sutra with diligence, thereby clarifying one's own deep faith, as the text says: "We ourselves also vow... and so forth.

"In other lands" refers to the extensive exposition of this sutra and others of its kind. Third, regarding the three cycles of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), they did not extend to the assembly of nuns.
The Dharma Master recorded them extensively but did not state their names; this chapter provides the additional predictions to fulfill the aspirations of the nun assembly.
As the text says: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: 'For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with a face of sorrow? You..."
The Master’s intention was likely this: "I shall not mention your names or bestow predictions upon you.
Fourth, it was for the sake of newly predicted śrāvakas who were unable to propagate the sutra in the Sahā world; he wished to expand their resolve by entrusting them to non-regressive bodhisattvas.
As the text says: "At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas, and so forth."
Furthermore, fifth are the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas. They know that the Buddha repeatedly bestows his favor like a blue lotus, and they take it upon themselves as their own responsibility.

Out of reverence for the Buddha’s intent, they take it as their own task to propagate the sutra. Thus, as the text says: "At that time, the various bodhisattvas, respectfully complying with the Buddha’s intent...
even went before the Buddha and uttered the lion’s roar," and so forth. In summary, although the Dharma was spoken by the Buddha, the Way...

It is propagated among humanity. The various worthies each occupy a particular path, serving as ferries and bridges for the final age, so that this culture may perpetually flourish through kalpas of dust and sand, enabling all who possess discernment to collectively forge karmic ties with the Dharma. This is the reason why the "Chapter on Upholding" is expounded. (The scripture is divided into four parts:
1. The Bodhisattvas’ Vow; 2. The Śrāvakas’ Vow; 3. The Bhikṣuṇī Assembly’s Vow; 4. The Vow of Non-retrogression.
The first is the vow.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja (up to) made various offerings, not sparing even his own body or life.

He was the first to make the vow to propagate the sutra. Since the essence of making a vow lies in universal salvation, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja is placed at the forefront for the purpose of propagating the sutra.

One must rely upon eloquence; therefore, *pratisaṃvid* (joyful speech) is placed second. As for seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, one must further cultivate the myriad practices and adorn oneself with the myriad virtues;
therefore, twenty thousand bodhisattvas are taken as retinue. Desiring to give rise to great vows, one first comforts the Buddha’s mind;
thus it is said: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will not worry about this," and so forth, up to "upholding, maintaining, reading, and reciting."

Those who cultivate themselves through the Dharma are those who preach this sutra; they transform the world through the Dharma. This refers to both maintaining the teaching for oneself and transmitting it to others.

Regarding the subsequent passage on "evil": in an evil age where one endures hardships without fear, the time since the Sage has passed is remote, and sentient beings have become increasingly corrupt and wicked;
thus it is said that roots of goodness grow ever scarcer. People know only how to polish their empty reputations, but do not strive for true cultivation or reality.
Because they have realized this, it is said that many harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*), falsely claiming to have attained the Way in order to solicit the respect of others;
thus it is said they "crave gain and offerings. Once greed arises, anger and delusion follow in its wake; thus it is said they "increase the unwholesome roots.

By giving rise to delusions and creating karma, they are bound eternally to birth and death; thus it is said they are "far removed from liberation. Seeking nothing beyond the mundane world, they will surely give rise to slander upon hearing [the teaching].
Therefore, it is said that they are difficult to teach and transform. Although they are difficult to teach and transform, one does not abandon them despite the hardships;
thus, it is said that one "arouses the power of great patience. Why is this power of patience called "great"?

It is because one not only endures insults without retaliation, but furthermore desires to bring them to ultimate liberation—just as Nāgārjuna did for those of arrogant pride. Regarding "not sparing body or life," it means that one knows only [the Dharma].
Regarding the Dharma, even if it should lead to the loss of body and life, one does not begrudge them; thus, the Bodhisattva completes his vow.
△ Second, the vows of the Śrāvakas, which has two parts: first, the vows of those beyond training (aśaikṣa); second, the vows of those still in training (śaikṣa). First:
At that time, five hundred arhats among the assembly [up to] went to other lands to extensively preach this sutra.
These newly ordained śrāvakas were unable to equal the bodhisattvas in making their vows in a uniform manner; therefore, it says, "they also made their own vows.
Because their power of the Path was not yet sufficient, they deeply feared the Sahā world, finding it difficult to transform and teach its inhabitants; hence it says, "in other [lands]."
The Land. △ Second, the aspiration made by those in training (*śaikṣa*):
Furthermore, there were eight thousand persons, both in training and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)... [up to] ...because their minds were turbid with anger, deceitful, crooked, and insincere.

The initial vow was made while he was in another land. The following passage provides the evidence and offers an explanation for its fulfillment. In this Sahā world, beings are for the most part stubborn, violent, and cruel;
they are difficult to harmonize and difficult to subdue. Therefore, it is said that "many people are depraved and evil," falsely claiming to have attained the Way or its fruits.

Having unwarrantedly received respectful offerings, they are said to harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Failing to apply themselves to authentic cultivation and realization, their merit and wisdom diminish;
thus it is said that their virtues are shallow and thin. Internally harboring a heart of envy and malice, they externally manifest an air of excessive courtesy.
Therefore, it is said that they are turbid with anger and crooked with flattery, seeking gain and offerings with single-minded greed and deceiving the world;
thus it is said, "because their minds are not sincere. This is why those in training (śaikṣa) aspire to be above others—it is not without reason.
The vows of the Śrāvakas are concluded. △ Third, the vows of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, in three parts: 1. Mahāprajāpatī’s increased prediction; 2. Yaśodharā...
Supplementary Note: III. The Joyful Aspiration. First:
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt... [until] ...attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Initially, Mahāprajāpatī hoped for a prediction [of her future enlightenment] for six thousand people who were her kinswomen. Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment was the manner in which she sought that prediction;
she thought to herself, "Our virtue is equal to that of the śrāvakas, yet our lineage is superior to that of the dragon girl."
Since he had already been specifically named and given a prophecy of attaining Buddhahood in the presence of others, [the Bodhisattva] thought, "Why should I not do likewise?
For this reason, he was filled with resentment and frustration, gazing up at him without ceasing. Furthermore, his gazing without ceasing was a look of sorrowful countenance.

From the phrase "At that time" onwards, it shows the initial general promise; his looking with a sorrowful countenance was precisely because [the Buddha] had not yet granted him a name and bestowed upon him the prophecy.
Commentary: The Tathāgata observed his countenance and knew the depths of his heart; therefore, he asked why he looked with such sorrow, as if he were concerned for us.
Regarding the general explanation of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) for śrāvakas, it is as stated in the extensive text of the *Dharmabhāṇaka-vyākaraṇa*: [text follows].

Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and those who seek the path of the Buddha—such classes of beings as these, if they hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha, or even for a single moment rejoice in it, I bestow upon them all the same prediction of enlightenment.
From "Now you" onwards, I shall further clarify this; if you wish to know, you should understand the cause of practice.
Regarding the details of his attainment of the fruit and its full extent: in future ages and so forth, he is recorded by his causal practice;

that he shall attain Buddhahood and so forth, he is recorded by his resultant name. Because he served as a Great Dharma Master during the stage of the cause and established affinities through the Dharma, those who saw him in the state of fruition were filled with joy;
thus he was named Sarvadarśanapriya (Joyfully Seen by All). As he successively received these predictions, his names should likewise correspond accordingly.
This is because, in their causal stage, both were Dharma masters. △ Second, Yaśodharā’s increased prediction:
At that time, Rāhula’s mother Yaśodharā... [until] the Buddha’s lifespan shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
At first, Yaśodharā thought: "Although I am not the leader of the nuns, I have already surpassed six thousand;

it would be logical for my name to be mentioned separately when the prophecy is bestowed. Thus, she harbored this thought regarding the omission of her name. However, if one discusses this matter, what matters most is one's own acceptance.
What connection is there between whether something is said or not? It is simply because women are attached to signs (*nimitta*); even after attaining the Way, they remain so.

This is because there remain residual habits (*vāsanā*). From "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata grants her a prophecy. Regarding the "Good Land": its people are preeminent in virtue and goodness, and it is free from all evils and corruptions.
This is due to her having served as a Dharma Master in a previous cause, thereby eliciting the adornment and purification of a Buddha-field.

Because she was a Buddha’s consort in a previous cause, she utilized her exquisite beauty for the sake of cultivation; as a result, she realized True Suchness (*tathatā*) and employed radiant marks to adorn her body. Therefore, she is so named.
"Endowed with ten million marks of radiance; the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Regarding this, Da Cheng (Dacheng) says:

"Since it is called a 'Land of Virtue,' benevolent people succeed one another, and their allotted lifespans are long; therefore, according to their capacities, their lifespans are such that their dwelling in the world is also eternal.
△ Third, the joyful making of vows.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī [reached] other lands and widely proclaimed this sutra.
It was initially due to the prediction concerning Ānanda; "along with her retinue" refers to the six thousand people. Immediately below, a verse is spoken to clarify this:
for those who have not yet emerged from the path of delusion, she causes them to emerge from the path of delusion; therefore, she is called the World-Honored One’s Teacher. Not yet...
"Those who have escaped from suffering and affliction cause others to escape from suffering and affliction; therefore, it is said that they bring peace and security to devas and humans.

In the preceding passage, Mahāprajāpatī looked on with sorrow, her mind deeply unsettled; Yaśodharā was likewise filled with a void in her heart. Thus it is said: "Having heard this prophecy, our minds are peaceful and fully satisfied.
From "All these bhikṣus... onwards, the verse expresses their aspiration; having already made their vows, they now wish to repay the Buddha's kindness and thus make this vow.
Regarding the propagation of the sutra: [The nun] perceived her own strength to be meager and felt she could not endure the evil age; thus she said, "I am able [to propagate it] in other regions.

There are two kinds of practice: first, the primary practice; second, the auxiliary practice. The text states: "One who wishes to expound this sutra should abide securely in four dharmas.

Here, expounding the sutra refers to the primary practice, while the four dharmas refer to the auxiliary practice. There are likewise two aspects to peace and bliss: first, that which brings peace and bliss;
second, that which is brought to peace and bliss. The text states: "One who wishes to attain tranquility and expound this sutra should..."

To draw near to these four dharmas—namely, the primary practice (*maula-caryā*) which is itself the state of peace and bliss, and the auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-caryā*) which enable one to abide in peace and bliss—since the text encompasses both the primary and the auxiliary, and the meaning includes both the agent and the object, it is not convenient to designate them separately. Therefore, they are directly named after the "Peaceful and Blissful Practice" (*Anrakugyō*).
If one were to extend this reasoning and seek the underlying meaning, there should also be five [categories], the first being for the purpose of introducing the preceding chapter.
First, this chapter demonstrates practice, as it shows that practice and vows support one another. Second, it is for the sake of enduring difficulties in propagating the sutra;
while those in deep stages may already be capable, this requests the display of the proper methods for the benefit of those who have newly conceived the aspiration.

Third, it is because he wishes to strengthen the faith of the assembly, causing them to uphold the four dharmas by using the analogy of the crest-jewel, thereby demonstrating the supreme veneration accorded to this sutra. Fourth, it is to manifest...

To demonstrate the upholding of the sutra, it is shown that its retribution brings forth flowers and fruits, and that dreams provide auspicious omens; this is to let people know that the benefits are not in vain.

Fifth, because even Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom still had concerns regarding the upholding of the sutra, he demonstrated the four practices to show how wisdom and practice mutually accomplish one another.

Generally speaking, while enduring hardships to propagate the sutra is commendable, it is no match for the excellence of propagating it without such hardships. Thus, if one can truly rely upon these means and ends...
Cultivating both the primary and auxiliary practices, one remains unimpeded amidst worldly afflictions and maintains constant composure amidst the profusion of sensory splendors.

Being thus at peace and joyful, what difficulty could there be that is not endurable? Therefore, following the Chapter on Upholding, the text demonstrates the "Peaceful and Joyful Practices" (Anrakugyō).

They should maintain an even mind toward both the one who does not enter the pratyekabuddha path and the one who enters the pratyekabuddha path. Furthermore, they should not harbor thoughts of aversion toward those who do not enter the path of the bodhisattva, nor should they harbor thoughts of attachment toward those who enter the path of the bodhisattva. They should maintain an even mind toward both the one who does not enter the bodhisattva path and the one who enters the bodhisattva path. Moreover, they should not harbor thoughts of aversion toward those who do not dwell in the ultimate reality, nor should they harbor thoughts of attachment toward those who dwell in the ultimate reality. They should maintain an even mind toward both the one who does not dwell in the ultimate reality and the one who dwells in the ultimate reality. They should maintain an even mind toward both the one who does not realize nirvāṇa and the one who realizes nirvāṇa. Mañjuśrī, what is meant by “Bodhisattva” (up to) “without being impetuous, and the mind is not startled”?
What is the meaning of these phrases? The introductory statement serves as a general inquiry. From “If a Bodhi-” onwards is the formal explanation of the practice of the matter.

“Abiding” means that even in moments of haste or distress, one does not deviate from [the path]. “Patience” means being able to endure all forms of humiliation; being able to endure all forms of humiliation, there is no further...
Because it is free from grasping and rejecting, or hatred and attachment, it is designated as "earth" (*bhūmi*).

This is because earth can support and carry all things, and while it is performing this very function of supporting and carrying, it is devoid of any grasping, rejecting, hatred, or attachment. The *Yāojie* (Essential Explanation) states: "The place of practice must abide in patience."
Although the six perfections are each suited for their respective times and uses, in facing hardships, nothing surpasses patience (*kṣānti*).
It is precisely because one is able to be patient that one can be supple amidst the rigid so that things cannot crush one; one can be compliant amidst adversity so that things cannot harm one;

one can be discerning in affairs so that what is enacted is not violent; and one can observe the subtle so that what is encountered does not cause alarm. This, then, is the magnification [of patience].

Regarding those who benefit sentient beings through the Dharma, one must not fail to regard this as a realm that must inevitably be traversed. △ Second, the section on practicing the sphere of conduct:
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma, there is nothing to be practiced... (up to) ...this is called the sphere of conduct of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Building upon the above, although one dwells in patience, if one clings to the notion that there is an insult to be endured, then the dharma of patience becomes something practiced as a personal possession.
By extension, the six perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth, would all become obstructions within the mind.
Since liberation alone can bring true peace and happiness, one must not engage in any activity whatsoever regarding all phenomena.
Yet, while one is indeed engaged in practice, how can one avoid engaging? Therefore, one must contemplate all phenomena.
All are the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*). Having observed that all phenomena are the true mark, there is naturally no longer any duality of subject and object;
what, then, could be practiced? This is precisely where the Tathāgata unties the adhesions and removes the bonds for the sake of sentient beings.
Once the adhesions are untied and the bonds removed, one does not engage in discrimination. If one takes this very non-discrimination to be the ultimate...
Thus, to take this non-discriminative dharma as one's own practice, becoming uniformly submerged in emptiness and stalled in quiescence, conversely constitutes a great illness.
Therefore, one must not only abandon this non-discriminative dharma but also refrain from stubbornly clinging to it, instead seeking to practice that which is essential.
Only when it is thus will existence and emptiness not obstruct one another, and principle and phenomena be perfectly integrated. One acts all day long yet there is no acting;
there is no acting, yet all day long there is acting. What is called "great liberation" and "great bliss" is none other than this.

This is the name and phrase; it serves as a summary in words. The explanation of the "places of practice" (*caryā*) is now complete. △ Second, the explanation of the "near places" (*upaniṣad*) has two parts: first, the practice of the matters of the near place;
second, the practice of the principles of the near place. Regarding the first, there are four sections. First: not approaching conditions that obstruct what is correct.
Second, do not associate with those who are unsuitable vessels. Third, do not associate with causes that give rise to suspicion. Fourth, always associate with objects that discipline the mind.
Regarding the first:
what is called the sphere of association for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? (Up to: he teaches the Dharma to them without any expectation of reward.
One should not associate with kings and the like, for they can obstruct right mindfulness. The *Dacheng* (Great Vehicle) commentary states:
"I fear that secular masters might surreptitiously seize power and position to indulge in arrogance and luxury, or take up offerings to pander to favor and gain.
Once this occurs, they will become negligent in their conduct, becoming coarse and vulgar; wagging their tails to beg for pity, they act as if they were commoners wiping away spit."
Being thus occupied, what mind could one have for the Path? This is why it is said that these things obstruct right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

Although it is said they obstruct right mindfulness, in truth they also obstruct oneself. For example, the Tathāgata did not abandon the sixteen kings; many ancient worthies relied upon rulers to practice the Way.
Moreover, the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings and great ministers, and most wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*) were followers of the Dharma.

The Great Being of the Body possesses the mechanism of expansion and contraction; its value lies in its vitality. I hope you will not become mired in words and lose the true meaning, thereby missing the mark right before your face.
[The mention of] "not approaching non-Buddhists" and so forth is because they can obstruct correct speech. As for these various non-Buddhists:
In the Western Regions, there are many varieties; here, five types will be briefly set forth below, while the remainder are subsumed by their general meaning.
The *Brahmins* (梵志) are also called "Pure Lineage" (*Vamśa*); they falsely reckon themselves to have descended from the birth of Brahmā, and they are devoted to serving Brahmā.

The *Nirgranthas* (尼犍), which means "Freed from Bonds," falsely reckon that beneficial asceticism can liberate one from fetters. Worldly literature and the like are as follows—[the fourfold division].
Regarding the Vedic scriptures, the *Jñānaprasthāna-sūtra* states: "The first person was named Brahmā, who composed one Veda (translated here as 'Treatise on Wisdom').
The next person was named Śukra, who divided that one into four: [1] Recitation (*svādhyāya*), [2] Sacrifice (*yajña*), [3] Chanting (*gāna*), and [4] Exorcism (*śānti*).
What is now called secular literature consists of the categories of sacrifice and exorcism; it praises and extols non-Buddhist texts."
These refer to various forms of recitation and chanting. *Lokāyata* is translated here as "malicious rejoinder," meaning that based on various evil views, one provides improper responses.
*Pratilokāyata* is translated here as "malicious interrogation," meaning that based on various evil views, one poses improper inquiries.
All such individuals wander outside the Path; they are unacquainted with the True Dharma and associate with those who follow it.
Consequently, they focus exclusively on seeking out flaws, and their discussions are characterized by nothing but contradiction; this is why it is said that they obstruct the correct teaching.

Dàchéng (Dacheng) quotes the *Kēzhù* (Commentary on the Sections), saying: "Although there are now prohibitions, if one wishes to ward off external insults, it does not hinder one from studying and understanding [them], provided one does not forget or abandon the fundamental school, nor indulge single-mindedly in them. I, the fool, say: if one wishes to transform those [outsiders], [one must study them].

One may also draw near [to such beings], as did Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra when they manifested birth in the family of King Susaṃbhava, or as did Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara who did not abandon the assembly of brahmins;
however, this is because such matters do not pertain to those at a shallow stage of practice, and thus one should not associate with those who engage in violence or games.
Because they obstruct right livelihood, "vicious games" refers to violent and dangerous amusements, such as boxing and wrestling, which are the very essence of vicious and perilous play.
"Nara"—in full, Nārāyaṇa—means "Firm" (Sthira) in this language; it is also an epithet for a strongman.
"Various transformations" refers to dressing up as deities or ghosts, smearing the body or appearing naked, and performing on a banner-pole.
Tossing things upside down; conjuring illusions of people and objects—these all concern matters of human life and offer no benefit to the nature and principle (xìnglǐ) of reality.
To be intimate with them leads to being entangled in calamities; to draw near them invites derision from bystanders.

Therefore, it is said that they obstruct one’s primary practice (zhèngyè). One does not associate with *caṇḍālas* and the like because they can hinder the correct discipline (*zhènglǜ*). *Caṇḍāla* is translated here as...

Butchers are also called *yanzhi* (rigid banners). This means they carry out their trade under a banner of severity; when good people see them, they avoid them because of their lowly status and will not travel with them.
They raise pigs, sheep, and other animals, selling them alive in the market for profit, or taking their meat to satisfy their own appetites.
Hunters capture birds and beasts, while fishermen catch aquatic creatures.
Those who catch fish and snakes with nets; those with various evil vows (akuśala-saṃvara); and the sixteen types of occupations involving transport: first, the butcher; second, the executioner;
third, the pig and sheep farmer; fourth, the poultry and dog keeper; fifth, the fisherman; sixth, the hunter; seventh, the bird-catcher.
8. Catching snakes; 9. Chanting spells over dragons; 10. Committing robbery; 11. Pursuing robbers;
12. A prison official; 13. A house of prostitution; 14. A tavern; 15. A laundry and dyeing shop; 16. An oil-pressing workshop.

Now, among these, the *caṇḍāla* corresponds to items one and two; the phrase regarding "raising pigs" corresponds to items three and four; and the phrase regarding "hunting" [corresponds to item five].
These refer specifically to the [offenses of] the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth; the remaining [categories] are subsumed under various other characters.

Now, these sixteen [offenses] fully encompass [the prohibitions against] sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying, and it is precisely these that constitute the first section of the *Vinaya*. This is why they are said to obstruct the *Vinaya*. Regarding "when the time comes":

this refers to when external circumstances happen to arise, distinguishing them from cases where there is no intent of disrespect. Regarding "the one who preaches the Dharma": this refers to one who skillfully employs expedient means (*upāya*).

To turn back their evil thoughts. Regarding "having no expectations": it is because one fears that if they think the Dharma is being taught for the sake of profit, they will instead give rise to a lack of faith.
Furthermore, it is because their wealth and profit all originate from lust, killing, theft, and falsehood.
△ Second, not associating with those who are unsuitable vessels.
Furthermore, one should not associate with or treat as close friends those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka—up to and including the five kinds of impotent persons.

Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka are not great vessels; to associate with or draw near to them not only fails to benefit oneself, but will also cause their own superior resolve to decline and lead them to a sense of complacency.
This applies equally to offering them greetings and inquiries; therefore, [one should avoid them] in all such matters.
It is improper [to do so]. As for those with whom one does not dwell together, he briefly refutes their excessive pride.

As for preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate, he gradually guides their stagnant emotions. As for having no expectations, it is because he fears being ridiculed for speaking of emptiness with every word.
At every step one encounters existence; yet you contradict what has been taught and do not believe it.
A female body is capable of giving rise to thoughts of desire and is thus not a vessel for the Dharma.

To preach the Dharma to a woman is censured in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, let alone to preach while being attached to her and giving rise to the signs of desire. This defiles the holy words and binds oneself.
One must be cautious indeed. Furthermore, those whom one does not wish to see are encountered only when there is no other choice;
these include young girls (*kṣudra-kanyā*) and maidens (*kumārikā*). A "maiden" refers to a girl who is unmarried. If she has married but lost her husband, she is called a widow (*vidhavā*).
Now, young girls and maidens are generally protected by their parents, whereas widows are more easily [approached].
Because one would incur the resentment of outsiders and, even when conversing with them, how could one avoid slander? Therefore, it is prohibited by means of the precept against [sexual intercourse].
Regarding the five kinds of impotent men (*paṇḍaka*): first is the *jāta*, meaning one who is born without male organs; second is the *kṛtta*, meaning one whose virility has been removed by a blade;
third is the *īrṣyaka*, meaning one who only arouses desire upon seeing another engaged in sexual activity; fourth is the *pakṣa*, meaning one who... [encounters a man]... [text fragmentary].

The "transformed woman" (biàn nǚ) refers to one who encounters a woman and transforms into a man. The fifth is the "half" (bàn), meaning one who is capable as a man for half the month and incapable for the other half.
Since these individuals have been granted such vulgar and debased forms, they are not proper vessels; furthermore, they are equal to women and base men.

To draw near to them is disrespectful, while to distance oneself from them leads to resentment. It is sufficient simply not to be intimate with them. △ Third, the section on "Causing [Harm] by Not Drawing Near."

The reasons for disliking this are not limited to entering the homes of others; even when there is a proper cause (up to the point where) a *śrāmaṇera* or a young boy does not wish to share a teacher,
one who enters the homes of others alone— having neither an *upādhyāya* nor an *ācārya*— fears that he may lose his composure or encounter misfortune.

This is like a magical illusion; therefore, it is improper. As for those who must enter alone due to specific causes and conditions—whether by the power of a donor’s vow or by the assignment of a preceptor—they should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.
This is to counteract the faults of distraction, such as looking left and right. When preaching the Dharma, dignity is paramount;
to expose one's teeth or chest increases defilement and invites slander. To do so while claiming it is for one’s own benefit is mere pretension.

To benefit others while simultaneously leading oneself into ruin is likewise improper; one should not even maintain close intimacy with those engaged in such matters for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
How can those who today pursue fame and profit, claiming me as their mother or sister, feel no shame?
Young disciples who do not recognize the exigencies of the times and are unacquainted with the rules of discipline will easily give rise to affliction if they are kept.
To share the same teacher would conversely diminish one's virtue and practice; therefore, this too is not preferred.
Although each of these prohibitions has its specific purpose, they are collectively essential for avoiding suspicion. △ Fourth, constantly remain near objects that restrain the mind.
"Always delighting in sitting in meditation in a secluded place" (up to) "this is called the first stage of intimacy.
"Always delighting" does not mean being fixed in one state; it simply means not forgetting this mind. Sitting in meditation cuts off distraction; a secluded place cuts off clamor;
gathering the mind cuts off false conditions. If one does not forget these, then the objective realm will be difficult to disturb. This is [the meaning].
Therefore, those who propagate the Dharma and benefit sentient beings must not fail to take this as the sphere in which they may achieve their goals. This concludes the section on names;
furthermore, it ties the matters discussed to the immediate context. Having finished the section on immediate matters and conduct, △ Second, the section on immediate matters and practice.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] this is called the second station of intimacy for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Regarding the word "furthermore" (*punar aparaṃ*): it carries the sense of a gradual progression toward greater depth, which shall now be explained.

As for the statement that one previously did not draw near to anything—like fleeing from a shadow in the midday sun—and now withdraws the mind in a secluded place, like seeking the shade to extinguish [the heat]: although one approaches [the shade],...

The shadow vanishes, yet its reflection remains as before when facing the sun. Therefore, one must observe that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, just like when one correctly faces the midday sun and realizes that the shadow is an illusion.
This is called "truly not approaching" [the duality of true and false]; it is the true gathering of the mind.
Now, having observed the emptiness of phenomena, every phenomenon accords with the primordial truth, just as once one has realized the illusory nature of shadows, every shadow is likewise [realized].

Because it accords with the fundamental substance, it is called the "suchness" (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa). Since phenomena are already such as they truly are, one ought not to engage in inverted or deluded conceptualizations regarding them.
Furthermore, just as a shadow accords with its substance, one ought not to engage in false and erroneous discrimination regarding the shadow.

Therefore it is said that there is no inversion. Since one does not engage in inverted false conceptualization, one does not perceive the movement of ordinary beings, the decline and retreat of the two vehicles, or the advancement and progression of bodhisattvas. It is like reflections upon a surface:

if one is free from discrimination, one does not see the flickering of chaotic reflections, the shrinking of small reflections, or the expanding of large reflections. Therefore it is said: "immovable and non-retrogressive."
It does not turn. Based on this, the nine realms do not exist; all phenomena are fundamentally empty, being only the single true essence, vast and profound beyond measure.
Therefore it is said that, like space, it has no intrinsic nature. This clarifies its inconceivability. Since it is like space and lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be expressed in words;
therefore it is said that the path of language is cut off. Since the path of language is cut off, it is not...
One might say that [dharmas] arise from the past, emerge toward the future, and manifest in the present; therefore, it is said they are "unborn, unemerging, and unarising.

Since they cannot be apprehended across the three periods of time, one should not speak of them as having distinct names or characteristics; therefore, it is said they are "nameless and characteristic-less.
To be nameless and characteristic-less does not mean that existence is negated to assert non-existence; therefore, it is said they "truly do not exist at all."
Since it truly possesses nothing at all, one cannot speak of its dimensions or boundaries; therefore, it is called "immeasurable" and "boundless.
Since it is immeasurable and boundless, one cannot say that there is any further dharma that acts as an obstruction, nor what constitutes a hindrance to dharmas;
therefore, it is called "unobstructed" and "without hindrance. This clarifies that it is inconceivable. Since it is inconceivable, the Buddha said:
What is being said? It is merely that all phenomena exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions, arising from inverted conceptualization.

Subject and object are distinct, and thus the cycle of transmigration arises. Therefore, the Buddha expounded various Dharma-gates to cause beings to encounter conditions and enter into reality, to overturn the perverse and return to the correct, to sever subject and object, and to still the cycle of transmigration. This clarifies that which is inconceivable yet is being discussed.
Thus it is. Since the Buddha has deliberated from within the inconceivable, the Bodhisattvas who propagate the sutra must likewise contemplate within the unthinkable.
Therefore, it is said: "One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of dharmas. This clarifies contemplating that which is unthinkable.
Because one contemplates that which is unthinkable, every thought-moment accords with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Even though there be a vast deluge...
One does not drown; one is not burned by the great fire. This is precisely what is called the Dharma of Great Liberation and the Practice of Great Bliss;
therefore, it is named the second proximate stage (*upaniṣad*). The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the introductory title of the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[The Section of the Proper Verses is divided into two: 1. The proper verses on the prose section. 2. Manifesting the benefits and concluding the response. The first [section] has two parts: 1. A verse summarizing the two locations. 2.
A verse specifically explaining the practice of proximity. The first [part]:

If there are bodhisattvas who, in the future evil age, [from "should enter" to] "the spheres of practice and the spheres of association," possess a mind free from fear, it is because they ride upon the power of their vows.
△ Second, the verse analysis of the spheres of practice and association (following the prose commentary which treats these two spheres separately, here they are combined into verse).
This is divided into two parts: first, the combined verse on the matters of the two spheres of practice; second, the combined verse on the principles of the two spheres.

Practice. This section consists of two verses on the practice regarding the two matters of what to avoid (in this context, avoiding the non-proximate subsumes approaching the proximate; by knowing what is not to be approached, one knows why it is approached;

by knowing why it is approached, the mind attains settled vision and can naturally abide in patience, thereby understanding how to practice). It is divided into three parts: first, a verse on the conditions that hinder the correct path if not avoided; second, a verse on not associating with those who are unsuitable vessels;
third, a verse on avoiding the reputation of being suspected [of misconduct]. (This is a brief summary of the meaning.)
First: "Always avoid kings and princes... (up to)... and *caṇḍālas*, non-Buddhists, and brahmins. Regarding "always avoid":
it means constantly maintaining a mind of detachment; this is the sense of not drawing near throughout one's life. As for "kings" and so forth:
Vicious and dangerous games can obstruct right mindfulness; *caṇḍālas* can obstruct right action; non-Buddhist brahmins can obstruct right discipline;
and others can obstruct right speech—the rest is abbreviated. △ Second, the verse on not associating with those who are unsuitable vessels.
Furthermore, do not associate with those who possess overweening pride (until: do not associate with them at all as close friends).
Regarding the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna: when the Buddha was in Vārāṇasī, he first preached the Hīnayāna Sūtras for Kātyāyana and others;
and again, when in Rājagṛha, he first preached the Hīnayāna Vinaya for Sunakṣatra.
Furthermore, in the Nyāya [Vinaya], it is recorded that by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, he first taught the Hinayana Abhidharma for the sake of the Vṛjiputra.
It is on this basis that Tiantai judges these to belong to the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao).

However, those with overweening pride take the non-existent to be existent, while followers of the Hinayana mostly cling to the provisional as real; both lack the great capacity [for the Mahayana] and therefore should not be approached. [This refers to those who] break the precepts.
As for the bhikṣus, there are those whose precepts (pārājika-skandhas) have been violated; as for those called "arhats" by name, their views and afflictions are still blazing.
These are all types who deceive the world and steal its reputation. As for bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter, it can be known that their natures are depraved.

Regarding those who are deeply attached to the five desires, one should point to a certain class of upāsakas who are preoccupied with fame. Although the text does not explicitly state this, based on [the context]...
The principle must be so, for it is for the sake of fulfilling the needs of the fourfold assembly. They merely seek the reputation of upholding the precepts, yet do not abandon defiled conduct;

thus it is said they are "deeply attached to the five desires. Because they are attached to the five desires, they employ various means to stifle their transgressions, doing so to manifest the outward appearance of attaining the Way;
hence it is said they "seek to manifest nirvāṇa. As for the laywomen (upāsikās), their attachment to children and kin is heavy, and for the most part...
They do not believe in the supramundane. Yet these individuals already fall short even within the Hīnayāna; how much more so in the Mahāyāna?
They are naturally unfit vessels. However, because this was absent from the prose version, I now supplement it with verses:

"Those who come with a sincere heart, who intend to reform their former errors, who have come to hear the Way, who maintain their minds in the desire to seek the Great Dharma, and who are free from fear."
One directly points out the transgression and reveals the offense, without fearing the other's resentment and without hoping for anything in return;
one merely aims to extract the nail and pull out the wedge, without seeking their deference. To speak in this manner, the other will easily follow, and oneself remains free of fault.
The cases of widows and virgins are all treated identically to the prose section above. △ Third, a verse on the causes that lead to suspicion when one does not keep a distance.
Furthermore, do not associate with butchers or those who serve as executioners (up to: "in these two places one can dwell in peace and speak with ease").
A butcher (*tāyin*) is the literal Chinese translation for *caṇḍāla*; it refers to those who slaughter today.
The raw stench of oxen, sheep, fish, and meat—mincing and slicing them—is called *huài* (minced meat). The term "chief" (*kuái*) mentioned above refers to the foremost among these executioners.
Those who currently run brothels are such persons. Hunting and similar activities are to be understood according to the above.
All these involve killing for profit and selling that meat to sustain one's own life. "Hypocrisy" (xiàn) refers to self-promotion;
to seek profit through female beauty and promote oneself to others is called "selling female beauty. These acts not only obstruct the correct discipline (*vinaya*), but furthermore constitute...
Because these are the causes for giving rise to aversion, the prose (*gadya*) is placed first, while the verse (*śloka*) follows by summarizing this point later.

The two lines concerning "viciousness" (*dāruṇatva*) can obstruct one's primary practice; since sexual misconduct and other such acts are among the worst violations of the precepts (*vinaya*), they should all, according to the prose, likewise be placed at the beginning.
Furthermore, because this could lead to suspicion, it is reiterated here in verse: "Do not preach the Dharma to a woman alone in a secluded place.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences—unless a man of intelligence is present—he incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
how much more so when preaching alone in a secluded place? It is simply improper. If he does preach...
During the Dharma session, no one shall engage in frivolous laughter; even in a place that is not secluded, one should maintain a solemn demeanor.
One should be accompanied by another bhikṣu to avoid unforeseen lapses, and by single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha to sufficiently ward off the slanders of onlookers.
Based on the three categories mentioned above, one not only knows what should be approached, but also possesses a settled vision of mind;
thus, when encountering circumstances, one is able to endure and also knows what must be practiced. Therefore, it is summarized: "This is called the sphere of practice and the sphere of proximity.
By means of these two spheres, external difficulties do not arise and internal disturbances can be controlled; hence, it is said that one can abide in peace and happiness.

The explanation concludes the combined verses on the two points regarding the practice of activities (caryā). △ Second, the combined verses on the two points regarding the practice of principles (yukti). (Explanatory Verses) Two parts:

The first [section]: The second [verse] states: "By means of the wisdom of non-arising, One does not perceive the arising of dharmas; Because one does not perceive their arising, One does not perceive their cessation. Commentary: This verse explains the practice of cessation. "By means of the wisdom of non-arising" refers to the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of all phenomena. "One does not perceive the arising of dharmas" means that because all phenomena are empty, they do not truly arise. "Because one does not perceive their arising" means that since there is no arising, there is also no cessation. This is because arising and cessation are mutually dependent; if arising is unattainable, cessation is likewise unattainable. Thus, through this wisdom, one transcends the dualistic views of arising and ceasing, which constitutes the practice of cessation. This is called the "practice of cessation" because it involves the cessation of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of arising and ceasing. This is the meaning of the practice of cessation. The second [section], explaining the practice of activity, follows. The third [verse] states: "By means of the wisdom of non-ceasing, One does not perceive the cessation of dharmas; Because one does not perceive their cessation, One does not perceive their arising. "One does not perceive the cessation of dharmas" means that because all phenomena are empty, they do not truly cease. "Because one does not perceive their cessation" means that since there is no cessation, there is also no arising. This is because arising and cessation are mutually dependent; if cessation is unattainable, arising is likewise unattainable. Thus, through this wisdom, one transcends the dualistic views of cessation and arising, which constitutes the practice of activity. This is called the "practice of activity" because it involves the manifestation of the great compassionate activities for the benefit of sentient beings. This is the meaning of the practice of activity. The third [verse] concludes. The fourth [verse] states: "By means of the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing, One does not perceive the arising or cessation of dharmas; Because one does not perceive their arising or cessation, One does not perceive the attainment of nirvāṇa. "By means of the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing" refers to the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of both arising and ceasing. Furthermore, the various minor kings are metaphors for the Māras of the three realms—namely, the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and so forth.

It is said that these Māras, such as those of the five aggregates and afflictions, seize and hold sentient beings, preventing them from turning away from defilement to unite with awakening, or from reversing delusion to return to the truth;

The exercise of authority and the mobilization of various troops is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, during the period of transformative illumination, preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to encourage and exhort the assemblies of the Three Vehicles.

He masters the three supernormal knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and so forth, enabling the followers of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) to act with unimpeded freedom; this is the exercise of provisional means (*upāya*).

At first, it cannot be obtained from the perspective of ultimate reality. The phrase "Tathāgata" is a provisional expression that synthesizes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, it is said that he "attains the land of the Dharma. This corresponds to the meaning of a powerful Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). He himself abides in the *dharmatā*.

Each of these bodhisattvas is a leader who guides the great assembly; thus we know that among those who arrived gradually in succession, with the exception of their own retinues, all served as guides, whereas those who emerged simultaneously were the foremost among the leaders.

Therefore, the phrase "most excellent" and so forth is placed below the word "great. With palms joined in salutation, he inquires: "The Dharma-body is truly eternal;

it is fundamentally free from illness and affliction. Wherever it goes, there is no lack of peace and joy. To inquire whether one has little illness and little affliction, and whether one practices with peace and joy, is to accord with worldly etiquette.
When one easily receives the teaching, the life of wisdom does not cease; when one is not weary, one is capable [of enduring].
"Patience abides for a long time. All of these are inquiries concerning this critical juncture. From "At that time" onwards, verses are spoken as a reiteration to transform and guide sentient beings;

"that is, the characters of the prose section" refers to [the term] *xing* (practice); "attaining freedom from weariness" refers to the two characters *anle* (peace and happiness) in the prose section;
the rest may be understood by analogy. △ Second, responding to the inquiry.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... [until] "shall hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom.

This is the initial general response. The Tathāgata’s intention is as follows: regarding what you have asked concerning "myself" and "sentient beings," I am indeed all of them, and the sentient beings to be transformed are likewise so. Therefore, he responds generally by stating "thus" twice. All.

"Excellent, excellent. This may be understood from the separate response. As for "therefore," it serves as an interrogation and an explanation. Among the four responses, the single explanation is easy to traverse; for if it is easy to traverse, there is no weariness;
if there is no weariness, one will be at peace, free from illness and affliction.

Regarding those who receive transformation through successive lifetimes, as the Buddha’s record concerning Śāriputra states: "In the past, I constantly taught [him] in the presence of twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas."
To transform you. Furthermore, as it says in the "Chapter on the Transformed City": "At that time, the sentient beings who were transformed were born together with the Bodhisattva in every lifetime.
This refers to the Buddhas of the past, specifically Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, as well as all those encountered in the intervening periods whom he honored and respected;
this demonstrates that his accumulation of practice was already profound. "Those who planted various roots of goodness" demonstrates the greatness of the conditions [for his awakening].
It is already accomplished. These sentient beings have all suddenly realized the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra]; therefore it is said:
"From first seeing my body, up until entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This refers to what is called "entering the initial goodness" at the beginning of the day.

As for those who previously practiced the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), although they formed the great vow in the past, they subsequently habituated themselves to the Lesser Vehicle in the interim. Such persons, in...
In the *Avataṃsaka*, [the senses] are closed to sight and severed from hearing; thus it is said they are "removed. However, this "removal" does not mean they are lost forever;

rather, it simply means that because they are incapable of hearing the Great [Vehicle], they must still await provisional guidance. This refers to those who, at the time of midday, enter the stage of the "good within" (*antarakalyāṇa*).

Those who hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom are precisely those who, in the present, return from the provisional to the real (*prajñapti* to *tattva*), and thereby attain faith and understanding.

He attains Buddhahood; this refers to what is called "the excellence of the latter part of the day" and "entering into the goodness of the latter period. Having finished the inquiries and responses, △ Second, the mutual praise between teacher and disciple.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse. (Up to: "They are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.

Regarding the first bodhisattva’s praise of the Buddha, where he repeatedly says "Excellent" (*sādhu*), Chengguan states: "This praises his practice of both the provisional and the ultimate (*upāya* and *dharmatā*) together."

Bestowing equal benefit upon both the great and the small, he practices both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously; seeing no such thing as a "difficult practice," he is thus called the Great Hero, the World-Honored One.
Bestowing equal benefit upon both the great and the small, he sees no sentient being who is difficult to transform; thus it is said that sentient beings are easy to deliver.

Since sentient beings are easy to deliver, he naturally does not remain obstructed by the present moment, further seeking the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi). Therefore, it is said: "He is able to answer all questions."
The Buddha’s wisdom is profoundly deep. This "profoundly deep wisdom" refers to what will later be discussed extensively regarding the span of his life (*āyus-pramāṇa*).

This extensive discussion of the span of life concerns matters within the sphere of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is the realm personally realized by the Tathāgata and is not easily accessible.
Although it is not easily accessible, one must nonetheless accord with the Buddha’s words and strive diligently in cultivation and study; therefore, it is said: "hearing."
"Having already practiced with faith—this foremost of bodhisattvas—foreknows that there is someone capable of inquiring about the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
As for our words 'we rejoice,' they contain an air of humility; the meaning is: if indeed there is one capable of inquiring, although I am not quick-witted..."
One should likewise follow along with joy; one must never be like those who, upon seeing a precipice, retreat.

When the Buddha, having descended, praised the Bodhisattvas by repeating "Excellent! (*sādhu*), he was praising their ability to discern the occasion and the Dharma, as well as their capacity to follow and rejoice.
The words "Good sons" and so forth are the Tathāgata’s own explanation of the intent behind that praise. This is consistent with the subsequent passage concerning rejoicing in this sutra.
Emerging from the assembly, they passed the teaching on from one to another until it reached the fiftieth person; yet their merit was still immeasurable.
How much more so for those who personally developed a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata—how could their merit possibly be conceived?
This is why the Tathāgata spoke repeatedly, saying "Excellent! to praise them. [The section on] the many thousands emerging from the earth concludes. △ Three: The Dedication.
The brief response consists of three parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s reflection; second, Maitreya’s inquiry into the cause; third, the Tathāgata’s brief reply. Regarding the first:
at that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and eight thousand [beings as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges (up to) joined their palms in worship and paid their respects to the Tathāgata.
"Since ancient times" refers to the period from the Āgamas onward through the various assemblies of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.
"Neither seen nor heard" means not only that their faces were not seen, but also that their names were not heard.
Since they had neither been seen nor heard of, their sudden emergence from the earth was already suspicious; yet they joined their palms in greeting with such a serene and joyful air.
The bond between teacher and disciple overflowed from his words; this is why these bodhisattvas reflected upon it repeatedly and could not let go of it.
△ Second, Maitreya’s Deduction of the Cause, in three parts: 1. Stating the intention and presenting the verse; 2. Questioning the three locations individually;
3. Seeking a definitive resolution in general. First:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned him in verse.
Knowing the doubts in the minds of the assembly and wishing to resolve them for himself as well—to benefit both self and others—he questioned him in verse.

△ Second, the specific questioning of the three locations, in three parts: first, questioning the place from which [the Buddha] came; second, questioning the place where he realized the fruit; third, questioning the place where he cultivated the causes.
First: An immeasurable assembly of many thousands of millions of bodhisattvas (up to) has gathered for what cause and condition?

This is an assembly that no one has ever seen before; therefore, I pray that the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings will explain it. Furthermore, this ground is not a place where such an assembly dwells. Therefore...

Question: From where have you come? Being separated by such a great distance above and below, it is difficult to hear the Buddha’s words; therefore, one asks by what causes and conditions this assembly has gathered.
△ Second, the question regarding the place of realizing the fruit.
"Vast-bodied, with great supernormal powers and inconceivable wisdom" (up to) "from where have they come?

The intention of the questioner is as follows: These bodhisattvas possess physical forms identical to those of a Buddha; their bodies may indeed be called vast. They can extend a single day into an eon;
their supernormal powers may indeed be called great. That they know there is one capable of questioning them—their wisdom may indeed be called [inconceivable].
It is inconceivable! Moreover, observing that his resolve is firm and steadfast, he will surely be able to vow to propagate this Dharma.

Possessing great forbearance, he will surely be able to aspire to enter this degenerate age. As one whom sentient beings delight to behold, he will surely be able to establish transformations according to the various regions.
From what Dharma have such supreme fruits and extraordinary virtues come? This is why we— [The text ends here.]
