This question was asked because [the Bodhisattvas] did not know. △ Third, the inquiry regarding the place of cultivating the causes, in two parts: first, citing the number to manifest its vastness;
second, the actual inquiry into that place. First:
"Each and every Bodhisattva’s retinue they bring along... even they cannot fully know."
The first part provides a general indication. "Ganges sands" refers to the sand within a single Ganges River;
since there are more above and less below, the word "etc. (or "and so forth") is placed to encompass them all. Alternatively, the latter section separately cites the first eight lines among them:
these refer to the assembly that previously surged forth simultaneously, while the final twenty lines refer to the assembly that previously arrived gradually in succession.
There are slight variations in appearance and disappearance compared to what precedes it; this can be understood through the mind. "Thus, below," concludes the summary.

Regarding "counting by means of tally-sticks (*śalākā*)," it refers to methods such as those used during the half-monthly *poṣadha*, where the number of monks is calculated using tally-sticks. △ Second, the formal inquiry regarding the location.

Regarding this assembly of bodhisattvas of great majesty and diligence (up to the point of asking), "What Buddha-way do you practice and cultivate?"—the benefits of hearing and reflecting are not without a teacher; therefore, he asks, "Who preaches the Dharma for you? A journey of a thousand li does not depart from the first step;
therefore, he asks, "From whom did you first resolve to attain enlightenment? To preach the Dharma and benefit living beings, there must necessarily be a lineage of transmission; therefore, he asks.
What is the Dharma of which Buddha that you praise? [This] relies upon the sūtras; it is not without transmission and reception. Therefore, when receiving and upholding [the teachings], one asks:
whose sūtra is being practiced? As for knowledge and vision, they should be broad; one must travel through a hundred cities to gain comprehensive experience. As for cultivation, it should be concise;
the Way values a single, straight line as its standard. Therefore, one asks: what is the Way of which Buddha that you cultivate?—thus spoke the ancient masters.
It is said: "The Master sings whose song? To whom does he succeed in the ancestral wind? This is precisely that meaning. The separate inquiries regarding the three points are concluded.
△ Third, a general request for resolution.
Thus, regarding the great power of the supernatural knowledges and wisdom of these bodhisattvas (up to): "I only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
First, they request the resolution of their own doubts. "I pray that you will speak of the name of the land" means they seek an answer as to where they have come from.

"I pray that you will speak of the causes and conditions" means they seek an answer regarding the cultivation of causes and the attainment of fruits—the causal conditions from beginning to end. From "Now, here below" onwards, they request the resolution [of further doubts].
He was doubtful; this can be known. Maitreya has finished deducing the causes. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s brief response, in two parts: first, the attendants of the emanation-bodies wait to hear;
second, the Tathāgata properly answers Maitreya. The first part has two sections: first, the attendants each question their own teacher;
second, the teachers instruct them to wait and hear. The first section: [The text continues with the specific content of the questions and instructions.]
At that time, as for where the various Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni and the great assembly of bodhisattvas have come from, the meaning is clear and can be understood from the text.
△ Second, the teaching of the Original Teacher awaits hearing.
At that time, each of the Buddhas addressed their respective attendants... [omitted] ... "You yourselves shall hear it through this.

Because they knew there were those who would inquire, they told them to wait for a moment. Having thus indicated the person who would ask, they further announced the Buddha’s prediction concerning those who would subsequently become Buddhas; this was to show that such matters can be known only by a Buddha, and only by a Buddha.
Those who dwell [in the stages] below this level are not only unable to know, but they are also unable to ask questions.
Since the Buddha has already answered them, there is no need for further explanation; therefore, he tells them that you yourselves shall hear it through this.
The attendants of the emanated bodies wait until the discourse is finished. II. The Tathāgata’s Proper Response to Maitreya. 1. Admonition to Listen. 2. [The Main Response].
The direct answer consists of two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. First [the prose]:
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [up to] ...the sword of the majestic and powerful might of all Buddhas."
Because Maitreya’s single question benefits both himself and others, [the Buddha] praises it by repeating "Excellent!
This "great matter" refers to the matter within the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

The matter within the ground of the reality-limit cannot be measured by a single person, nor can it be realized through a distracted mind; therefore, he instructs that they should all together be of one mind. Furthermore...
He instructs them to don the armor of diligence and to resolve with firm intent. He exhorts them that upon hearing [the teaching], they must believe; having believed, they must practice.
They must not harbor doubt upon hearing it, nor allow such doubt to lead to regression. Through diligence, one shall not be indolent; through firmness, one shall not be defeated.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is collectively directed toward what is to be explained hereafter, by means of the principle of the *bhūtakoṭi*.
The "Ground" (bhūmi) refers to the realm of the profound wisdom of all Buddhas.

"Mastery of supernormal powers" specifically indicates the meaning of the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, because manifesting birth and manifesting extinction are the unimpeded miraculous transformations of the Tathāgata. "Fierce prowess" [refers to this].

This also refers to the merit of discernment. That, within a single moment, one can cause such a multitude of sentient beings to sever delusions and realize the truth—just like cutting silk and dyeing it—is what constitutes "leaping forth" (*visphūrjana*) and what constitutes "majestic power" (*vīrya*).
Through the leaping forth of the lion, one can destroy false lions; through majestic power and great might, one can embrace true lions and bring them into accord with the Tathāgata.
It is similar in meaning to [the statement that] "it can cause the severance of delusions and the realization of the Truth. △ Second, the Verse Summary (a summary of the meaning).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, said: "[From here until] 'In this way, I shall now speak; you all should listen with a single mind.'"

He instructs them with diligence and single-mindedness; he shows that one who wishes to speak of this matter must do so because this matter is profoundly deep, and cannot be realized by those who are indolent or distracted in mind. He admonishes them not to harbor doubt;
he shows that the Buddha’s wisdom is subtle and profound, for anyone who even slightly lapses into doubt or regret will inevitably fall back. He instructs them to emerge...

Abiding in faith and patience, he shows those who have not yet heard how to hear what they have not heard. In hearing what they have not heard, one does not prize mere faith in the Buddha’s words, but values deeply patient endurance of the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*).
Only through this deep patient endurance of the sublime Dharma can one receive this secret that has not been transmitted.
Fearing that others might suspect it to be absurd and dreading their inability to grasp its loftiness and distance, he provides consolation lest there be any hindrance.
Because they are advancing in their practice, he permits them to be comforted and exhorts them not to harbor doubt or fear.
That the Buddha has no words that are not true clarifies that there is no need for uncertainty. That his wisdom is fundamentally immeasurable clarifies that there is no need for alarm or dread.
However, because this matter is the very realm in which the Tathāgata himself dwells, it is called "the foremost dharma attained."

This is the foremost Dharma; it is not within the cognitive domain of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others, and is therefore described as "profoundly deep and beyond conceptual discrimination. Based on this, only a Buddha can know it, and only a Buddha can teach it;
only Maitreya can inquire about it, and only Maitreya can listen to it. Therefore, he indicates it by saying, "Now I shall speak," and instructs you all.
"Listen with a single mind. The instruction to listen is concluded. △ Second, the actual response, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [part] has three sections:

first, the answer regarding the place where the cause is cultivated; second, the answer regarding the place from which one comes; third, the answer regarding the place where the fruit is realized. First [the place where the cause is cultivated].
At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken these verses, [proceeded] until he had tamed their minds and caused them to resolve upon the path.

The initial section, from "Ānanda" downward, serves to conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent. The section beginning with "I" (the name of the Buddha) is the direct answer to the question asked.
It teaches and guides, answering the previous inquiry as to who preached the Dharma and provided instruction, thereby causing them to resolve upon the path.
In response to the question of from whom they first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, the other questions are not answered because they may be understood by analogy.
△ Second, the answer regarding their place of origin:
"These bodhisattvas all [reside] in this Sahā world... (up to) contemplate, discern, and maintain right mindfulness."
Regarding those who dwell in the void beneath this Sahā world, [the text] answers the previous question as to where they have come from.
As for the phrase "in various sūtras and so forth," it clarifies that their dwelling is not a mere residence; rather, they borrow that space to cultivate contemplation in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding "reciting and chanting until one is proficient," the sūtra serves as the basis for contemplation; if one is not proficient, contemplation will be difficult.

Because they have been accomplished. "Contemplation" (思惟) refers to contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). "Discrimination" (分別) refers to discriminating the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

it is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*). "Right mindfulness" (正憶念) refers to right mindfulness of the middle truth; it is the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*).

Once these three contemplations are perfected, all things are without obstruction. Therefore, as soon as a single sound is uttered, many thousands gather together. This also answers the previous question: "By what [means]?"
This is the question concerning the gathering of causes and conditions. △ Third, the answer regarding the stage of realizing the fruit:
"Ajita, these sons of good family... (up to) ...with single-minded diligence seek supreme wisdom."
An ancient worthy once said: "The affliction of man lies in his desire to be a teacher to others. A virtuous elder of antiquity said:

"To speak for ten *zhang* does not equal practicing for one *chi*. Therefore, when Bodhisattvas do not delight in being among the masses and frequently speaking much, but instead always delight in solitary places, it is because they practice alone, apart from the crowd, so that their passions may easily be exhausted. When they are diligent and tireless, they value practice over speech.

The Way is easy to accomplish; yet when the five desires are arrayed before one, it is extremely difficult to penetrate and escape them. Therefore, one does not abide in the realms of humans or devas.
When the three truths are illuminated simultaneously, they reach the ultimate state of perfect fusion. Thus, one always delights in profound wisdom that is unimpeded.
One who constantly delights in the teachings of all Buddhas does not consider minor attainments sufficient. One who earnestly seeks supreme wisdom does not settle for shallow understanding.

[Answer: "It is so. Regarding the previous question as to where the one of massive body and great supernatural powers has come from, the answer now given concerning the place of origin is that the cause itself is taken as the place.
This concludes the prose section. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

(The section on the formal verses is divided into two parts: 1. The formal verses corresponding to the prose; 2. A brief exposition for clarification. The first part has three sections: 1. A verse answering the place where the cause is cultivated;
2. A verse answering the place where the fruit is realized; 3. A verse answering the place from which one comes. The first [is the verse on the meaning].)
"Ānanda, you should know that these great bodhisattvas... [omitted] ...caused them to resolve upon the Great Way. The long prose version says:
"He taught, transformed, and guided them, causing them to resolve upon the Way. This [verse] says: "All were transformed by me, causing them to resolve upon the Way.
The meaning is the same. II. Verse Response on the Place of Realizing the Fruit (a thematic summary in verse).
"These are my sons who rely upon this world" (up to) "for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way. They have long relied upon the Tathāgata;
because the Dharma-transformation has issued from his mouth, they are truly my sons. Although it is said that they rely upon this world, they nevertheless constantly practice *dhūta* austerities.
As it says in the *Dīrgha-āgama*: "They do not rely upon or dwell among humans or devas. This refers to their resolve.
"Delighting in secluded places," and so forth, means to dwell alone apart from the multitude and practice diligently, not delighting in much talk but regarding speech lightly and practice seriously.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "Not delighting in being among the multitude and engaging in much talk, but always delighting in secluded places and practicing with diligence," and so on. The *Dīrgha Āgama* further states:
They also constantly delight in the Dharma of all Buddhas. The phrase "these sons" refers to those who study my Way and Dharma;
this is because the Way of each Buddha is the same—the Way of Śākyamuni is itself the Way of all Buddhas.
The long passage states, "With single-minded diligence, they seek supreme wisdom," which here means "diligently practicing day and night to seek the Buddha-way"; the meaning is no different.
△ Three verses in response concerning the place of origin (a summary verse).
Residing in the space below the Sahā world... until... his mind is free from fear.

The first two lines directly answer the question regarding the location. "One whose resolve and mindfulness are firm" refers to not receding or being cowed in one's own practice or in transforming others.
"Diligently seeking wisdom" means practicing the three contemplations simultaneously. "Fearlessly preaching the Dharma" results from being thoroughly proficient in the scriptures;
thus, while differing in form from the prose section, they are identical in meaning. This concludes the formal verse corresponding to the prose. △ Second, the brief [summary].
To clarify the refutation:
I sat beneath the Bodhi tree in the city of Gayā (up to) and taught these various assemblies.
Initially, the trace concealed the fundamental; the name "Gayā Mountain" refers to a location approximately twenty *li* from the site of enlightenment, as the city is situated nearby.

This mountain is named after the mountain itself. Regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the turning of the unsurpassed wheel, this should be understood as referring to the time of the initial illumination, namely the *Avataṃsaka* assembly.
It was there that he performed his teaching and transformation for those who had first resolved their minds toward awakening.
This is discussed here based on his more recent traces; since it concerns these recent traces, Maitreya should understand this, especially as Maitreya was a preeminent friend within the *Avataṃsaka*.
Why is it that not a single person among them is unrecognized? Therefore, it is said that this is a realm where concealment and manifestation are unimpeded.
Those who all abide in non-retrogression are at the stage of the eighth bhūmi or above. Those who are destined to attain Buddhahood are such that their fruition is not far from Bodhi.

However, according to the *Avataṃsaka*, one who resolves their mind [on enlightenment] draws near to the rank of a Buddha in a single lifetime. Were it not for profound causes, how could one possibly reach such a state? Thus it is said.
This refers precisely to "covering the fundamental with the derivative. Now, below, I shall shatter the derivative to reveal the fundamental. When I say, "I now speak words of truth;
you all should believe with one mind," this reveals that what was previously explained still retained expedient means and was thus easier to believe;
this is the meaning of "shattering the derivative. When I say, "From long ago I have taught and transformed these multitudes," this reveals—
Long ago, even before the kalpa of a speck of dust, he had already received transformation and had already resolved his mind [for enlightenment].

This clarifies the meaning of the "original" (the fundamental state). [Question]: Above it was said that he resolved his mind at Gayā, yet here it is said that he has been transforming beings for a vast duration. How are these two accounts to be reconciled? [Answer]: There are two meanings here. First, the gradual; second, the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). Regarding the gradual:

this means that after undergoing transformation over these many kalpas, his great faculties have already matured. If one were to say he resolved his mind only at Gayā, it would merely represent a single manifestation of his descent into the world. Fearing that [beings] might fall into the calculation of naturalism held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), he specifically manifested this appearance. Regarding the perfect fusion, there are again two meanings. First, extending [the lifespan] by more than forty...

Regarding years: one refers to extending a *rajas-kalpa* (dust-point eon) into more than forty years; the second refers to condensing a *rajas-kalpa* into more than forty years. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Infinite past eons are placed within the future and the present; infinite future eons are turned back and placed within the past."

This is also the meaning [of the previous passage]. The abbreviated response by means of inferring the cause is concluded. △ Fourth, raising doubts to provoke discussion, which has two parts: first, the Bodhisattva raises the doubt; second, Maitreya provides the clarification. First [the Bodhisattva raises the doubt]:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because the signs of decay were only slightly apparent and not yet fully manifest, he conceived doubts and perplexity in his mind.

Since the teacher and disciples did not conform to the norm, and the old and young violated the proper order, he marveled at this unprecedented occurrence. "To conceive such a thought" refers to the thought of doubt and wonder.
Since the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, barely more than forty years have passed;
thus it is said that "in a short time," the bodhisattvas he has transformed all dwell on the stage of non-retrogression, and thus it is said that "he causes them to abide in Bodhi.

If this were so, the Teacher would lack the merit of long-term transformation, while the disciples would possess the realization of many kalpas. This is why Maitreya and the others gave rise to doubt in their minds.
And they marveled at what had never occurred before. △ Second, Maitreya’s refutation, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first [part] has three sections:
first, refuting through adherence to the traces; second, elucidating by means of an analogy; third, applying the Dharma to correspond. The first [of these three] has two parts:
first, refuting by adhering to the Buddha’s traces; second, engaging in debate by adhering to the traces of the assembly. The first [of these two]: [The text continues with the specific arguments.]
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Initially, he took the site of the Buddha’s footprint near Gayā City to be close; it was approximately twenty *li* from the Bodhimanda, hence it is said to be 'not far.

'From this time onward' refers to the period from his attainment of the Way until the present day. The *Śāsana-yāna* (Teaching Vehicle) states: 'The *Āgama* [is ten...]"* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the full passage as per the instruction to provide only the translation.*
Second, regarding the eight years of the Vaipulya [sūtras] and the twenty-two years of the Prajñāpāramitā teachings:

since the present sūtra follows after the Prajñāpāramitā, it states, "more than forty years have passed. From the words "The World-Honored One" onwards, there is a counter-objection to the Buddha’s words;
the intent is to say that even with such a multitude of disciples taught to achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even by the power and merit of the Buddha, it must still...

Having long undergone many kalpas, he has performed great Buddha-works; yet we do not know how the World-Honored One, in such a short time, performs such great Buddha-works, being able to use the power of a Buddha and the merit of a Buddha to transform such a multitude and cause them to achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
This is a counter-objection that challenges the Buddha’s words as being excessive. △ Second, the attachment.
The various traces have led to much debate.
World-Honored One, this assembly of great bodhisattvas—World-Honored One, such a matter is difficult for the world to believe.
Initially, one holds that the traces are distant; even if someone were to enumerate them, these [beings] have existed for a long time.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) reveals the long duration of his causal practices. The section beginning with "The World-Honored One" addresses the difficulty of believing [this account].

The underlying intent is as follows: for a single person to transform such a vast multitude of beings already borders on the extraordinary; how much more so when it is claimed that in a short period of time he could accomplish such far-reaching causes?
This makes one feel even more like a fish out of water. Therefore, it is said: "Matters such as these are difficult for the world to believe. This is an objection based on appearances.
[End. △ Second, the illustration is presented to clarify the meaning.
"Suppose there were a person with handsome features and black hair... [up to] "...that we were born from him is difficult to believe.
"Handsome features and black hair" refers to the appearance of youth; this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s recent manifestation. "Twenty-five years old" refers to his age.
At the age of vigorous maturity, his cultivation of the Way had not yet long been accomplished.

Judging by the previous analogy of Maitreya’s inference, the Tathāgata replied that [the youth] had first resolved his mind under him and was thus one whom he had transformed; therefore, he used the metaphor of a hundred-year-old man, saying, "He is my son."
"One who is a hundred years old" refers to a lifespan that transcends the world; it is a metaphor for having traveled a great distance from the multitude of traces.

According to the previous account of the emerging multitude, they inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being; their presence is harmonious, embodying the relationship between teacher and disciple.

Therefore, the metaphor also points to the youth, saying, "This is my father," meaning he is the one who gave me life and nurtured me—distinguishing him from those of a different surname, such as the *mínglíng* (adoption), and identifying him as the source from which my very being and body originated.
"Raised" (*yù*) refers to the multitude who have emerged from the earth; they do not resemble the shadows and echoes from other directions.

They appear as if they have personally resolved their minds to cultivate goodness and rely directly upon the Buddha. That this matter is difficult to believe is because it contradicts the common course of things—wherein the father is young and the son is old.
Within the Dharma, the teacher is near while the disciples are distant; it is likewise so. △ Third, applying the Dharma to the analogy, in two parts: first, correlating the "young father."
The Parable of the Old Man. Second, the parable of the entire world’s lack of faith.
First: “The Buddha was likewise; since attaining the Way... [it has been] most rare for all the world.”
Not long after attaining the Way, he possesses the same physical beauty and black hair as before, being twenty-five years of age;

yet this great assembly is the same as those hundred-year-olds mentioned previously. This clearly illustrates that the duration of his traces [in the world] spans immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
To practice diligently for the sake of the Way demonstrates the steadfastness of one’s resolve.

To be skillful in entering, emerging from, and abiding in [meditative states], even attaining great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), demonstrates the profundity of one’s concentration (*samādhi*). Cessation of objective conditions is called "entering"; contemplation of principle is called "abiding."

When responding to the capacity of the practitioner, the cessation of conditions is manifested; yet when ceasing conditions, it does not obstruct contemplating the principle as it responds to that capacity.

When responding to the capacity, it does not obstruct the cessation of conditions or the contemplation of the principle. It is the same when contemplating the principle. Therefore, it is called "skillful.

This is discussed in terms of vertical progression within a single samādhi. If discussed in terms of horizontal breadth across multiple samādhis, it means that at one time, immeasurable hundreds [of conditions] are suddenly ceased.

Simultaneously and instantaneously observing trillions of conditions, and simultaneously and instantaneously responding to the infinite hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of diverse capacities of sentient beings—therefore, it is called "skillful. One who has attained great supernormal powers (mahābhijñā) is so named because of this.
This is similar to the previous examples, such as extending days to constitute eons (*kalpa*). Furthermore, this also arises from profound *samādhi*.
Indeed, it is the vast and wondrous function of the unimpeded dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *samādhis*.

It encompasses the long cultivation of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), up to and including skill in question-and-answer, while also clarifying the excellence of that practice. This has been cultivated throughout successive eons.

Regarding practice: not perceiving that there is any practice to be cultivated is called the "Brahma-faring. Clearly knowing there is nothing to cultivate does not preclude training in the successive stages;
thus it is said one is "skillful" and "adroit in question and answer," where questions arise like clouds and answers flow like water from a jar.
There is not the slightest thing that is not extended, and no difficulty that is not resolved. This, however, results from being well-able to cultivate the wholesome.

For since the Dharma-gates are harmoniously integrated, natural wisdom and eloquence are unimpeded. To call one a "jewel among men" and a rarity in the world serves to clarify the importance of such a person.
There are two meanings of "jewel": first, it brings joy; second, it is held in high esteem. Thus it is said:
The Bodhisattva propagates the Dharma to benefit sentient beings; he is able to bring joy to others and is always held in high esteem by them. This is something extremely rare in the world:

his Way is profound and his virtue is weighty, and he is seen but rarely. [Question: Previously it was said that he does not delight in being among the multitude and does not engage in much speaking. Now it is said that he is skillful in question and answer. Are these not contradictory? [Answer:

His skill in question and answer arises because the conditions and capacities of those present press upon him; it is not that he is consistently inclined toward much speaking. Furthermore, movement and stillness fundamentally do not obstruct one another. Thus, what harm is there in his being silent while speaking, or speaking while silent?
[The Buddha] spoke [thus], yet now you wish for me to keep my mouth shut and remain tongue-tied, so that I say nothing at all? △ Second, the combined illustration of the world’s lack of faith:
"Today the World-Honored One has just said that when he attained the Way of the Buddha... (up to) "...having heard this matter, they likewise do not give rise to doubt."
First, to establish the Buddha’s words as definitive: the term "just now" (*fang yun*) means that it was spoken at this very moment.
The passage beginning with "The World-Honored One" (*shizun*) reveals that the matter is difficult to believe. The phrase "only those who are able" (*neng*) implies a sense of disbelief.

Although such disbelief is implied, because the Buddha’s words are taught according to what is appropriate for each person, there is nothing that is either acceptable or unacceptable; the Buddha’s speech is without falsehood and is necessarily true. The Buddha knows all.

He has attained thorough understanding and his speech is free from error; yet he does not dare to believe [everything]. Although he does not dare to believe [everything], because the matter contradicts the relevant sūtras, he cannot fully believe it either.

Thus it is said: "Although one may have faith that the Buddha’s various provisional teachings, even up to what the Buddha himself knows, are all thoroughly understood"—this appears to be a state where one seems to believe but has not yet truly believed, and thus one has not yet reached the point of violating the Dharma and incurring [retribution].
As for the offense: although the resolution and explanation may still be deferred, the character should properly be written as "nài" (奈何).

When new ideas first enter the Buddha-dharma, one does not know the realm of the Tathāgata; how much more so after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata? Upon hearing this, how could one not harbor doubts?

Therefore it is said: "Some do not believe or accept it. Because they do not believe or accept it, they will inevitably give rise to the karmic offense of destroying the Dharma, leading to their downfall in the future.
This is the reason why Maitreya specifically presents this petition: it is precisely because he perceives that this matter is difficult to believe, and yet its rectification must not be delayed.
"Venerable Sir" (*veyyākarohi*) and below constitute a general request for a definitive resolution. "Venerable Sir" (*veyyākarohi*) is an exclamation of anticipation;
it means that one who wishes to seek a resolution first utters this sound of expectation, hoping that the Buddha will grant him his attention. It is a common expression among people of the world.

[The] prose [section] concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the title of the verses states): "Often there are such [cases]. First, one seeks to remove our own doubts, desiring to truly reach the ground free from doubt.
Next, one seeks to remove the doubts of those in the future, so that there shall certainly be no transgression of destroying the Dharma.
Thus ends the prose section. △ Second, the verse summary. (The title of the verses states:)
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
[The Main Verse Section is divided into three parts: 1. One verse on the refutation of clinging to traces. 2. One verse illustrating through analogy. 3. One verse applying the Dharma accordingly.
Regarding the first [which, following the prose section, is divided into two; here they are interwoven and combined into verses rather than being treated separately]:
The Buddha formerly left the Śākya clan for the vicinity of Gayā... [up to] "explaining through suchness and discrimination.
The first verse maintains that the Buddha’s traces are near. The *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna) commentary states: "The Śākya clan" indicates his lineage;
he was a descendant of King Siṃhahanu and the crown prince of King Śuddhodana. The phrase "these various [traces]" and below maintains that the traces of the assembly are distant.

(The prose section follows after the refutation and belongs to the *udāna* verses. The first two lines clarify the great number [of bodhisattvas]. The phrase "for a long time" reveals the profundity of their causal practice.
"Abiding in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)" refers to the practice of benefiting others. "Bodhisattvas who have well-trained themselves" refers to the practice of self-benefit.

Because they engage with the mundane world without hindering the cultivation of the Real, it is said that they are "unstained by worldly dharmas. Thus, benefiting others does not obstruct self-benefit.
Therefore it is said: "Like a lotus in water. Emerging from beneath the earth, he presented his verses to resolve the doubts of those who found him difficult to believe.

As they stood before him with reverence, he appeared exactly like a teacher and his disciples; yet, regarding their long-standing or recent differences in status, these were ultimately inconceivable and beyond discussion, leaving the entire assembly in bewilderment.
Therefore, it is asked: "How can this be trusted? The verse below provides a rebuttal to the Buddha’s statement (the prose commentary precedes the verses and belongs to the subsequent summary).
It is extremely close and exceedingly numerous; this is a counter-objection that challenges the Buddha’s words as being contrary to reality.

The final two lines—“I pray you will resolve the doubts of the assembly” (which are absent from the prose section and belong to the supplementary verse)—state that because the matter may not be real, one seeks its true and accurate discernment.
△ Second, the verse cites a metaphor to clarify the point.
For example, it is like a person in their youth whose age is only twenty-five (up to) something that the whole world does not believe.
White hair and wrinkled faces are metaphors for the signs of long-term cultivation. The rest follows the prose. △ Third, the verses apply the Dharma to illustrate two points:
first, one verse applies the metaphor of the father being young and the son being old; second, two verses apply the metaphor of what the whole world does not believe. First:
(Explanatory Verse).
The World-Honored One likewise attained the Way not long ago; [the phrase] "descending to dwell in the space below" constitutes the first two lines.
"The father being young" corresponds to the elder [son], while "these various ones below" corresponds to the younger [son]. The line "firm in resolve" clarifies the depth of his determination.

Having resolved to attain Buddhahood, one does not fear long-lasting suffering; thus it is said that there is no timidity. From the phrase "without [limit]," its remote traces are clarified. The long prose states:
"For immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas," while the verse omits this for brevity. Yet, through the four lines [of the verse], [the meaning is conveyed].
This clarifies the excellence of his practice. By practicing the bodhisattva path, his dharma-gates become harmoniously integrated;
being skillful in question and answer, his wisdom and eloquence are unimpeded. He penetrates all difficulties and extends even the most subtle points. Thus, his mind is free from fear;
even when encountering opposition, he recollects the Buddha without resentment. Therefore, it is said that his patience is absolute. These two lines concerning "uprightness" clarify the person.

"Important. The long discourse states that he is a "jewel among men," precisely because of his upright majesty and virtue. The long discourse states that he is "rare in the world," precisely because he is praised by all Buddhas.

He is "skilled in the three phrases," which clarifies the profundity of his concentration (*samādhi*). Relying on profound concentration to preach the Dharma, his teaching accords with the capacities of his audience and is thoroughly authentic;
thus, he is said to be "skilled. Having left behind crowds of people to cultivate dhyāna, his object of focus and wisdom—*ālambana* and *jñāna*—[are in harmony].
This further clarifies the meaning; thus it is said "always delights. The final two lines clarify that he dwells in stillness (not present in the prose section, belonging to the supplementary verse).

Regarding "dwelling in the space below for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way," this shows that his dwelling is not in vain; rather, it is because by relying on such a quiet place, the Way is easily accomplished.
△ Second, the verse summarizing the metaphor of the world’s lack of faith (an explanatory verse).
"We have heard this matter from the Buddha and are without doubt [until] we abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
According to the prose section (*dīrgha-pada*), there are three meanings; here, following the fixed words of the Buddha, there are only two. First, it reveals that the matter is difficult to believe.
Those who have no doubt regarding this matter merely follow the Buddha’s words; they have not yet truly reached the stage of being beyond doubt.
Future sentient beings, not knowing the realm of the Tathāgata, will all harbor doubts upon first hearing this Dharma.
Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will expound it for them so that they may attain understanding. This is because by giving rise to doubt and lacking faith, [they will fail to realize the truth].

One would immediately fall into the evil realms. I pray that you will now descend [to us] to provide a general resolution so that we may understand. This concludes the brief clarification of the fundamental and the manifested, which was intended to shake off attachments and resolve doubts.

△ Second, the extensive elucidation of the original and the trace, which consists of two parts: first, the extensive elucidation of the original and the trace; second, the severing of doubts and the engendering of faith.
Regarding the first (the title of the chapter states):
The Sixteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "On the Lifespan of the Tathāgata":

"Tathā" (Thus) refers to the essence being eternally unchanging, which is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmakāya*); "Āgata" (Come) refers to the function being able to accord with conditions, which is the Reward and Transformation bodies (*saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*).

Although it does not change while acceding to conditions, the Dharma-nature is itself the Reward and Transformation bodies; although it accedes to conditions while remaining unchanged, the Dharma-nature is itself the Reward and Transformation bodies.
The *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are themselves the *dharmatā*. It is neither "coming" nor "suchness," yet it is both "suchness" and "coming";
therefore, it is called the Tathāgata. An ancient master said: "The *dharmakāya* has no beginning and no end. However, according to this very sūtra, there is indeed a beginning, as it says:

"Since my attaining Buddhahood, a very long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable. Since this statement refers specifically to the period since his attaining Buddhahood, [it does not contradict the nature of the *dharmakāya*].
This is because it has not yet been accomplished and is therefore not manifest. Furthermore, it is said that the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) has a beginning but no end;
however, according to this present sutra, it also has an end, as it says: "The lifespan I achieved while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not exhausted even now.

Since it merely states that it is "still not exhausted," it follows that there will ultimately be an exhaustion. Moreover, it is said that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) has both a beginning and [an end].

End. According to the present sutra as well, both [the beginning and the end] are absent. As it says: "By the power of skillful means (*upāya*), there is the manifestation of extinction and non-extinction.
Since this speaks generally of the manifestation of skillful means, it follows that from beginning to end, all is provisional (*upāya*).

This chapter is titled as such because it fully reveals the lifespan of the three bodies (*trikāya*) from start to finish. Regarding the five distinct meanings: first, for those who cling to the traces...

1. To resolve the objection that [the Buddha-land] is remote from its origin, it is shown that the wondrous function of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) exists, so that one may know how to apply it. 2.

For those who cling to the idea that the true nature is inherently complete, it is shown that the Dharma-body has a beginning, so that one may know that cultivation and realization are not non-existent. 3.

For those who cling to the idea that the fruit is without distinction, it is shown that the reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) has an end, so that one may know that causal practices should be extensive. 4. Fourth...

First, for those who cling to the Buddha as having birth, it is shown that transformation-birth (*nirmāṇa-jāti*) is not ultimate, so that they may know that although there is birth, there is no birth.

Fifth, for those who cling to the Buddha as having cessation, it is shown that transformation-cessation (*nirmāṇa-nirodha*) is not real, so that they may know that although there is cessation, there is no cessation.

Generally speaking, if one is deluded regarding the wondrous function, then the manifestations of response and transformation will not be extensive; if one denies cultivation and realization, then the *dharmatā*...

It is not perfect. If one’s practice is not broad, then the retribution of reality will easily be exhausted; if one’s attachment to birth and death is firm, then the non-arising [of phenomena] will be difficult to realize.
This is the reason for the teaching of the "Chapter on Lifespan. (The scriptural text is divided into two parts: first, the admonition, entrustment, and request for the teaching;
second, the actual exposition in detail. First:)

At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly... [until] "we should faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. This was the Tathāgata’s initial exhortation and entrustment.
Desiring to reveal the realm of the Buddha, he feared that [the audience] might give rise to alarm or doubt; therefore, he exhorted them that they should believe and understand.
"Sincere words" (*cintya-vāk*) are words of earnest devotion; "truthful words" (*satya-vāk*) are words of careful verification and reality. As it is said: "to incline one's heart."

"To vomit forth one's gall" means to be without falsehood or error. "The ultimate admonition in three ways" refers to the earnest instructions and commands intended to inspire a sense of absolute faith and understanding.

At that time, the Bodhisattvas requested the teaching; not knowing the realm of the Buddha, they harbored doubts regarding both the present and the future, and thus addressed him, saying, "We only pray that you will explain it.
"To believe and receive" means to accept with patient conviction (*kṣānti*), transmitting it from one to another.

"I have heard" refers to both the present and the future. That he did not stop at three and proceeded to four is because he made a fervent request, expressing his intention that the Buddha would certainly speak without hesitation. Part Two: The Actual Exposition, which is twofold. First, the prose section.
There are two verses in total; the first two clarify the following: first, the vastness of the lifespan; second, the non-falsity of the manifested parinirvāṇa.

The first [section] has three parts: first, the formal explanation of the vastness; second, the comparison by means of analogy; third, the preemptive resolution of potential objections. First [the formal explanation of the vastness]:

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas [had been practicing] for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, first cautioned them to listen to the Dharma.
Although they requested three times without ceasing, their earnestness was pitiable; therefore, he cautioned them to "listen attentively.
To caution them to "listen attentively" implies his intention to grant them the teaching. They abide fundamentally in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is not the realm of the śrāvakas.

Because it is the realm of the Pratyekabuddhas, it is called "secret. Because its traces manifest as responsive transformations, constantly displaying unimpeded and sovereign wondrous functions, it is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the phrase "all those below," this refers to the various attachments to traces.
Within the world, it specifically points to the "good paths" because those in the evil paths cannot see the Buddha and thus lack such attachments. It does not point to the Three Vehicles because...
Maitreya still clings to this; there is no need to mention others. Thus, all [such views] are called "clinging to the traces while remaining ignorant of the source.

However, from the passage beginning with "But [he who] is skillful... onward, the reality of the source is revealed as it truly is. When it says "I am real," it reveals that the proximate traces are not real. The phrase "attaining Buddhahood, etc. [refers to the realization of the source].
"Manifesting realization after many kalpas over a long duration" reveals that within the essence of the fundamental [nature], there is the intention to break through the traces [of the provisional].

△ Second, the comparison by means of analogies has three parts: first, posing the question regarding the number by means of an analogy; second, answering with "not knowing"; third, calculating by repeating the numbers.
First: For example, [if there were] five hundred thousand *koṭī-nayuta-asamkhyeya* [of them], could one conceive of, calculate, or know their number?
*Nayuta* here means ten billion; *asamkhyeya* here means incalculable. Now, by means of these five hundred thousand...
Counting by hundreds of billions of nayutas, and calculating such nayutas as asaṃkhyeyas,
and calculating such asaṃkhyeyas as the number of worlds— those worlds may indeed be said to be many. Furthermore,
were one to grind these worlds into fine dust, even if those particles were scattered everywhere, it would still be difficult to exhaust them.

If one were to exhaustively traverse all these lands, let alone those exceeding five hundred thousand million *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* worlds to the east, and then drop a single mote of dust, the vast distance between motes would be evident.

Continuing in this manner, traveling eastward and dropping such dust-motes until every such mote has been exhausted, the number of lands traversed would be beyond the reach of thought or calculation. Thus it was asked.

Why is this so? If one examines whether it can be known through investigation, it is clearly understood that it is inconceivable and beyond calculation; therefore, it is made to be verified by oneself.
△ Second, answering by means of not knowing.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others together addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "Such worlds as these are immeasurable and boundless. First, he directly answered that he did not know;
that which cannot be known by calculation is beyond the reach of multiplication and division;

that which is not within the scope of mental power is difficult for intellectual consciousness to attain. From "All those below" onwards, he explains by way of persons to clarify this: the wisdom of the two vehicles is still partial.
Therefore, its limit is unknown. Because the wisdom of non-retrogression has not yet reached its ultimate, it is likewise something that cannot be fathomed.
From the words "The World-Honored One" downwards, the conclusion regarding its boundless measure can be understood. △ Third, the comparative calculation by repeated enumeration.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas (up to the point where it says): "I have guided and benefited sentient beings in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands.

If one were to fold worlds together to form a single mote of dust and use that to calculate the number of kalpas, what was previously stated—that 'since I truly attained Buddhahood, an immeasurable and boundless [time has passed]'—was not yet clear.
Therefore, he said: 'Now I shall declare this clearly. This is based on the previous analogy of placing motes of dust."
This land is already beyond what can be known through calculation; how much more so for those that are layered upon one another and those that do not manifest?
To take a single mote of dust and calculate it as one kalpa, the number of kalpas would be inexhaustible.

When I attained Buddhahood, having calculated the duration of my long career to clarify the manifestation of transformation, from the time the Dharma-body and Reward-body were first perfected until now—right up to this point.
The time that has passed from then until today, when compared to the aforementioned *rajas-kalpas*, still leaves a vast difference;
therefore, it is said that "it has further exceeded this by hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions," which clarifies the magnitude of the elapsed time.

"I have always been here, preaching the Dharma and transforming beings" means that arising from the Truth (*dharmatā*) to manifest as a response (*nirmāṇa*), one benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, as described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.

As for what has been explained elsewhere regarding those who guide and benefit sentient beings by dividing their forms and dispersing their shadows to respond to conditions throughout the ten directions—such as the category of the emanated bodies that gather like clouds—the analogies and comparisons have now concluded. △ Third, preventing and subduing difficulties, part four.
First, to prevent the difficulty that there might be other Buddhas within this realm; second, to prevent the difficulty that [the Dharma] would not be heard in other places regarding Śākyamuni;

third, to prevent the difficulty that his own statement that he had attained enlightenment not long ago would be contradicted; fourth, to prevent the difficulty that both the present and the past would collectively constitute false speech. Regarding the first [difficulty, it is said]:

Since it is said that [the Buddha] is eternally present in Sahā, there should be no other Buddhas arising or passing away during that interval. For what reason, then, is it said that Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world during that interval, and furthermore, that they entered *nirvāṇa*? To this, the following defense is offered:
"O sons of good family, throughout this interval... [up to] ...all these are distinguished through skillful means.

The word "equal" (*等*, *děng*) includes Kāśyapa. Based on this, it follows that the prediction of Dīpaṃkara and Kāśyapa’s status as the successor are both merely teachings given through skillful means.
II. Preventing the objection that [the Buddha] is not heard of in other places (The objection states: "If it is said that he also guides and benefits sentient beings in other lands...")

If that were so, there should be a Śākyamuni in every world throughout the ten directions, with their respective lifespans, parinirvāṇas, and activities such as preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings. Why is it that, despite examining all ears and eyes and traversing through various kalpas and lands, one has never heard of such things? Therefore, this [text] provides a defense [for this view].
"O sons of good family, if there are sentient beings... [up to] "...able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.

The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) encompasses the meanings of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Since each of these possesses degrees of superiority and inferiority, they are distinguished as sharp or dull.
Based on this, names, ages, and so forth throughout the worlds of the ten directions all manifest differently according to the faculties [of beings]. Although in every place...
He preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, yet they do not realize that he is a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of a single Buddha. 3.

Preventing the objection that his attainment of Buddhahood was not long ago. (The objection states: "If it is said that since attaining Buddhahood he has further passed through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, why does he usually say of himself, 'I left home at a young age and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'?
Therefore, this [passage] serves as a defense.)
"Good sons, it is because the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings [as they are]—from those who delight in the small to those who lead them into the Buddha-way—that he speaks thus.

Those who 'delight in the small' have faculties that are narrow and inferior, capable only of responding to an inferior manifestation. Those whose 'virtue is meager' have shallow merit and do not behold the sublime, extraordinary body.
Those whose 'defilements are heavy' have deep-seated stains of transgression that have long obstructed their *dharmatā*. For such people as these, [the Tathāgata] conceals..."
This reveals the fundamental reality through its traces; therefore, it is said that I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. To understand the Buddha’s intention:

it was primarily to demonstrate that there is cultivation and realization, thereby inspiring a superior resolve. Thus, he spoke of "expedient means" (*upāya*) to teach and transform others, leading them into the Buddha-way.

He made such statements for this purpose. 4. Preventing the Objection that Past and Present Statements Collectively Constitute Falsehood. (The objection states: "In the past, you spoke of both self and others... )

Since these belong to the realm of expedient means (*upāya*), how could they possibly be the ultimate truth when presented now as being for oneself and others? To reason by analogy, the sutras preached in both the past and the present would all become false teachings. How, then, can you be called a Dharma King who speaks the words of truth? Therefore, this [text] warns: ( ) *Note: The original text contains an ellipsis marker.*
"Good sons, from the time the Tathāgata first preached the sūtras until now, the Buddha-work he has performed has never for a moment ceased.

His initial and correct subduing of difficulties was entirely for the sake of delivering sentient beings; this is the reason why he manifested without falsehood. Sometimes he spoke of his own person."
"Sometimes it refers to another's body," as when it is said that Śākyamuni has recently attained [enlightenment] while Dīpaṃkara truly existed;

this points to the words concerning the concealment of the original [state] in the past. "Sometimes it reveals one's own body, or sometimes it reveals another's body," as when it is shown that my own body is eternally present while Dīpaṃkara does not exist.
"Sometimes it reveals one's own affairs, or sometimes it reveals another's affairs," as when it is shown that Śākyamuni possesses cultivation and [attainment].
The realization was originally for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings. That Dīpaṃkara had birth and extinction belongs entirely to provisional and discriminative discourse.

This refers to today’s words that "break the traces," which actually conceal the fundamental source in order to manifest the traces; the intent of breaking the traces is to reveal the fundamental source.
There is no contradiction with the original intent, as it is beneficial for sentient beings; therefore, it is said that "all that is spoken is real and not false.

The following section further explains why it is not false: "knowing and seeing the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are" means that one personally realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and contemplates phenomena in accordance with that limit of reality.
By contemplating phenomena in accordance with reality, one thoroughly understands that delusory appearances are fundamentally empty. Therefore...
It is said that there is neither birth-and-death nor cessation. Since birth-and-death does not exist, one does not see anyone remaining stagnant within birth-and-death as a human or a deva;
nor does one see anyone transcending birth-and-death as one of the three vehicles. This is called the non-establishment of the realm of beings (*sattva-dhātu*).
Since the realm of beings is not established, even the Buddha does not exist. Therefore, there are no Buddhas dwelling in the world, nor—
Nirvana. This is called the simultaneous emptiness of both birth and Buddha. Because the Buddha is empty, the Buddha-realm is not real; because birth is empty, the realm of birth is not false.
Because the realm of birth is not false, although it differs from the eternal suchness; because the Buddha-realm is not real, although it is like the eternal yet different.
Since these two natures mutually negate one another, it is said that they are "neither like nor different. To perceive the three realms in this manner is called [true seeing].

Because one sees according to reality, it is said that "one does not see the three realms as the three realms. Such a matter that accords with principle is realized only by the Buddha at the ultimate level;
therefore, it is said that "clear vision is without error. Based on this, he now demonstrates [the truth] for himself and for others.
All of these are for the purpose of delivering sentient beings in accordance with principle; therefore, there is nothing in vain. Why was it not so in the past? Thus it is said:

"Because sentient beings possess various kinds of natures (*prakṛti*), etc. "Nature" refers to the nature of their faculties (*indriya-prakṛti*). "Desire" refers to their inclinations and wishes (*chanda*). "Conduct" refers to the karmic actions they perform.
"Recollection and conceptual discrimination" refers to the arising of various retrospective memories and anticipations in relation to objects of the past, future, and present.
Perception (*saṃjñā*), discrimination, and equal mindfulness—likewise, the inclinations, dispositions, and modes of mindfulness are each different; therefore, they are all described in various ways.
To cause the arising of goodness means to gradually guide and lead [beings] according to their respective inclinations, dispositions, and modes of mindfulness.
By means of the roots of goodness for attaining Buddhahood in the future, he has, through these causes, conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, preached the Dharma in various ways.
For forty years, the Buddha-work he has performed has never been suspended for even a moment.

Based on this, it is clear that his past teachings—whether concerning himself or others—were all intended to guide and transform beings according to their capacities, and thus were not in vain. This clarifies the length of his lifespan.

The section on the past concludes. △ Second, clarifying that the present extinction is not in vain, in two parts: 1. Following the previous to initiate the subsequent; 2. Clarifying through both Dharma and analogy.
First: "Thus, since I attained Buddhahood... (up to) "...the Tathāgata uses these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings."

First, regarding the permanence of the Dharma-life: it is as previously stated. This is sufficient to know that since my attainment of Buddhahood, a very long time has passed—indeed, a very long time.
For now, this is spoken in terms of the Dharmakāya; the lifespan of the Dharmakāya does not fall within the scope of numerical calculation.
Therefore, although immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have elapsed, it remains eternally present and undying until now. [The section] "All virtues... and below follows.
The retributive lifespan has not yet ended. Because the Bodhisattva’s causal practices are vast and extensive, the measure of his reward-body is infinite;

therefore, it is said that the lifespan he has accomplished is still not exhausted. "Furthermore, doubling the aforementioned number" means that the remaining quantity is twice as much as the amount already passed.
However, below this point, the transformational lifespan is temporarily extinguished. Question: Regarding the dharma-lifespan...
[The Buddha] abides eternally; his retributive lifespan is not yet exhausted. For what reason, then, does he proclaim in the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter that he shall enter extinction?
Answer: This is not a true extinction. His proclamation that he shall enter extinction is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) to teach and transform sentient beings;
it is also the Tathāgata’s sense of being compelled by necessity. △ Second, the combined explanation through Dharma and parable, in three parts: First, the explanation by Dharma; second...
The analogy clarifies the three conjunctions. Regarding the first three: first, abiding in the cause involves harm; second, proclaiming cessation produces benefit;
third, the Buddha’s words are not false. First:
Why is this so? [It is because] if the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, [people would develop] the thought that he is difficult to encounter and a heart of reverence.
This phrase serves as an inquiry: why does the Tathāgata, though not actually entering extinction, proclaim his own extinction, claiming it is a skillful means (*upāya*) to deliver sentient beings?

The passage beginning with "If the Buddha... provides the explanation: those who lacked roots of goodness in past lives and possess little merit and wisdom in the present life [would fail to see him].
Such a person is called one of meager merit. Relying upon the Tathāgata, they do not know how to cultivate merit or wisdom;
this is called not planting roots of goodness. Because their merit is scant, they place themselves in poverty and lowliness; because their wisdom and virtue are scant, [they remain so].

As before, they remain greedily attached to the five desires. Consequently, they give rise to deep recollection regarding past objects, pre-conceive anticipatory thoughts regarding future objects, and momentarily form deluded perceptions regarding present objects. Their mental consciousness becomes entangled and difficult to liberate;
thus it is said that they have entered the net of recollective thought and deluded perception. Because this state is constant, they do not consider it rare.

Therefore, they are arrogant and self-indulgent; because they do not extinguish these traits, there will be times when they draw near [to the Buddha]. Consequently, they become weary, lax, and indolent.

Because they are weary, lax, and indolent, they do not conceive the thought that [the opportunity] is difficult to encounter. Because they are arrogant and self-indulgent, they do not give rise to a heart of reverence.
This is what is meant by "those who do not plant roots of goodness. △ Second, proclaiming extinction to produce benefit.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means (upāya), [extending] until: "Although the Tathāgata does not truly pass away, he speaks of parinirvāṇa.
First, he shows that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, desiring to cause [beings] to plant various roots of goodness.

He uses provisional words as an exhortation; thus he says, "Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means. This is for the sake of those who have entered the gate, to encourage the remaining multitude; hence he addresses them as such.
The multitude of my disciples must be taught what they ought to know: the two phrases of all Buddhas are precisely the words of the Tathāgata’s exhortation. The meaning is this:
a human body is difficult to obtain, like tossing a mustard seed onto the point of a needle; a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like a blind turtle encountering a floating log.
"You all must not fail to exert yourselves! This is why I speak thus; it is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s exhortation and admonition.
It is because those of meager merit, encountering a Buddha, do not know how to plant roots of goodness.

If they miss this present life, then even if they pass through immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas, whether they will see a Buddha or not remains uncertain."
Therefore, these words regarding the difficulty of encountering [the Buddha] were spoken in order to admonish them. Those of inferior capacity, upon hearing these words, plant seeds of goodness.
Hearing such speech, they realize for themselves that it is not easy to meet a Buddha; thus, they conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter.
Fearing they might miss this opportunity and not know when they might see him again, they harbor a heart of longing and devotion, approaching him frequently.

He relinquished [his life]. Therefore, it is said that he "thirsted with longing for the Buddha. From this point on, he extensively cultivated merit and wisdom; therefore, it is said that he "planted roots of goodness.

Consequently, below, he announces his extinction so that they may know it. Because they hear for the first time that such a one is difficult to encounter, they immediately realize they have planted roots of goodness;

how much more so when he further demonstrates his imminent extinction—would this not cause their hearts to tremble? For this reason, the Tathāgata does not pass into extinction, yet speaks of extinction. △ Three: The Buddha.
My words are not false.
Furthermore, good son, such is the nature of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas: for the sake of delivering sentient beings, all that they say is true and not false.
Following the skillful means of the Buddhas to deliver beings—how could there be anything false? The explanation of the Dharma is concluded. △ Second, the clarification by way of analogy.

Three [sections]. First, an analogy for how remaining in the cause results in harm; second, an analogy for how proclaiming extinction produces benefit; third, an analogy for how the Buddha’s words are not false.

Regarding the first analogy—how remaining in the cause results in harm (this section is longer than the corresponding Dharma-text)—it is divided into four parts: first, an analogy for how abandoning the response leads to suffering;
second, an analogy for going to respond to seek salvation; third, an analogy for remaining long to bestow the teaching; fourth, an analogy for how weariness and indolence result in harm. First.
For example, it is like a skilled physician, wise and discerning, who—[omitting intermediate text]—when the medicine takes effect, [the patient] becomes distressed and rolls upon the ground.

This "skilled physician" is one who thoroughly examines the source of the illness, skillfully prepares prescriptions and medicines, can raise the dead and restore life, and excels at prolonging years and increasing longevity.
Taking this as a metaphor for the Buddha means that the Tathāgata thoroughly examines the mental capacities of sentient beings and skillfully establishes the gates of the Dharma to bring them forth.
The Two Vehicles sever [wrong] views, restore the roots of goodness in icchantikas, prolong the years of the Bodhisattvas' Dharma-body, and increase the lifespan of the Buddhas' wisdom-life;

this is similar in meaning to that skilled physician. Regarding "one whose wisdom is sharp and penetrating": "wisdom" (智) refers to the clarity of the essence of knowledge, while "insight" (慧) refers to the penetration of its function.
This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s true wisdom being luminous and pure, and his provisional wisdom being boundless and practiced with proficiency.
Regarding "prescriptions and medicines": this refers to one who clearly understands medical arts and is thoroughly practiced in the natures of medicinal substances.

This is analogous to the Tathāgata’s ability to penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and his ability to recognize the various gateways of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*).

These various gateways of the Dharma can eliminate derivative afflictions (*kleśa*), while the true reality of the One Vehicle can exhaust fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, it is compared to skillfully treating all manner of illnesses for all sentient beings. All sentient beings...
All who are born possess a mind; all who possess a mind shall surely become Buddhas.

Since they are all sons of the Buddha and all capable of continuing his lineage, he uses the metaphor of having many children to illustrate this. Da Cheng (Dacheng) says: "The number ten represents Bodhisattvas;

twenty represents those of the Two Vehicles; and the number one hundred represents the ten classes of sentient beings. This is because those who practice the Mahāyāna are few, while those who practice the Hīnayāna are many."
Those who [accept] are many, while those who are transformed are few; those who do not accept are many. Therefore, they are used as metaphors in sequence.

Those with matters and conditions serve as a metaphor for the mutual attraction of responsive capacities (*mārga*) in other directions. Those who travel far to reach other lands serve as a metaphor for abandoning this world to respond to beings there.
As for the sons who later drink the poison of others, this serves as a metaphor for sentient beings [encountering the Buddha] after the Tathāgata has ceased his response.
"Subsequently, he associates with false teachers, receives false teachings, and when the medicine takes effect, he becomes dazed and confused, rolling about on the ground.

This is a metaphor for sentient beings who, having received false teachings, have their minds permeated by false views; they become ignorant and deranged, and their roots of goodness are on the verge of extinction.
Their "rolling about on the ground" represents the state of being on the brink of death. 2. The Metaphor of Seeking Rescue through Response.
At that time, his father returns home and [arrives] wishing to be rescued and healed, and to be granted a renewed lifespan.

The initial metaphor represents the Tathāgata responding to the call; for the Tathāgata takes the triple world as his home. The passage beginning with "the sons" represents sentient beings seeking rescue.
Those of meager virtue and heavy defilements are deluded regarding their past causes, just as those individuals may have lost their original minds.
Those whose virtue is profound and whose defilements are thin do not obscure their past causes; they are like those who "do not lose" [the way].

Although there may be cases of obscuration and non-obscuration, once one has accepted false teachings, one has already distanced oneself from the Buddha; therefore, he uses the metaphor of seeing one's father from afar.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, his three karmas are preeminent; among those who see him or hear him, there are none who do not rejoice and exult with joy.
They pay homage and offer praise; thus, they are all filled with great joy. "Bowing and kneeling to inquire after one's well-being" is a metaphor for [the disciples] bidding farewell.
"May you return in peace and safety" is the very phrase used when inquiring after someone’s welfare; it serves as a metaphor for sentient beings’ words of praise for the Buddha.

Since the Tathāgata does not revolve within saṃsāra nor remain stagnant in nirvāṇa, yet is still able to manifest birth in accordance with conditions, this is precisely the meaning of "returning in peace and safety. I...
The phrase "deluded and foolish" refers to sentient beings who, like those who have mistakenly ingested poison, claim to be ignorant and practice in a confused manner;
their plea for rescue and treatment, and for the granting of further life, is a metaphor for sentient beings seeking to uproot false views and increase their roots of goodness.
This represents sentient beings seeing the Buddha for the first time, turning away from heterodoxy and returning to the true meaning. △ Third, the metaphor of long abiding.
The Bestowal of the Teaching:
When the Father sees his children suffering in such a manner, [he acts] so that their suffering may be swiftly removed and they no longer face manifold afflictions.

Sentient beings lose their goodness and fall into suffering; the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, observes them as a mirror reflects an image. Therefore, it is metaphorically said that "the father sees his children."
Suffering is thus. Regarding those who seek excellent medicinal herbs according to various medical prescriptions (*sūtra-vaidya-vidhi*):

the "prescriptions" are what were transmitted by former physicians, while the "medicinal herbs" are the specific items within those prescriptions. This is analogous to how the Tathāgata, relying on the One Vehicle’s true reality (*ekayāna-bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) and wondrous Dharma bestowed by previous Buddhas, has expounded countless distinct Dharma-gates that accord with the capacities and timing of sentient beings. These are the distinct Dharmas.
Within this text, the meanings and principles are fully and exhaustively provided; thus it is likened to color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor being entirely complete.
"Pounding with a mortar and crushing" and "sifting through a strainer" are metaphors for the Tathāgata analyzing [the teachings] with his own wisdom and conveying them with his own eloquence.
"Mixing to form a powder" and "combining to form pills" are metaphors for the Tathāgata manifesting them as scattered flowers and threading them together.
The phrase "to provide chapters and sentences for you, so that you may don [the armor]" is intended to show the hope that they will eliminate poison and return to life;

it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata employing the Dharma to suit the capacities of beings, desiring to cause them to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness. The subsequent statement, "yet he speaks these words," and so forth, is a metaphor for the Tathāgata urging them to practice in accordance with the teachings.
By practicing in accordance with the teachings, one is naturally able to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness; therefore, it is said that suffering is swiftly eliminated.
It is vexing; there is no longer any comparison for its manifold afflictions. △ Fourth, the analogy for the harm caused by weariness and indolence:
Among those sons, those who have not lost their minds [regarding the previous medicine] find this fine-colored, fragrant medicine to be unpalatable.

"One who does not lose their mind" is a metaphor for a person of profound virtue and thin defilements. Because such a person possesses profound virtue and thin defilements, they are naturally able to practice in accordance with the teachings;
hence the metaphor says, "one immediately takes it. By practicing in accordance with the teachings, they are naturally able to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness.

Therefore, the analogy states that the illness has been completely eliminated and healed. As for those who have lost their minds, this is a metaphor for people whose virtue is meager and whose defilements are heavy.
Because they possess little virtue and heavy defilements, they merely know how to request the Dharma according to custom; thus, the analogy says:

"Although they joyfully seek it and request the Dharma according to custom, they cannot practice in accordance with the teachings. Therefore, the analogy says: "They are given medicine but do not take it. Thus, the word "equal" (or "same") refers to...

This explains why the elder refused to take the medicine: it is a metaphor for sentient beings who are deeply attached to false views, deluded regarding their past causes, and do not believe the Buddha’s words;
therefore, they are unwilling to practice. This refers to what was stated in the preceding text: "They immediately give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence.
This concludes the section on the metaphor of dwelling in existence which brings harm. II. The Metaphor of Proclaiming Extinction to Produce Benefit.

(This differs slightly from the section on the Dharma. In the section on the Dharma, the discussion is limited to the proclamation of extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Here, the metaphor of "showing extinction" is also included. Since showing extinction still pertains to subsequent matters, it is omitted and not mentioned in the section on the Dharma.)
The father thought to himself, "This son is to be pitied" (up to the point where he) immediately returns home so that everyone may see him.

The initial parable of proclaiming his death was intended to make [the son] know that, having encountered the medicine, he would rather choose death than take it; therefore, the father thought, "He is to be pitied."
When sentient beings hear the Dharma but do not accept it, the Tathāgata’s great compassion and pity for them is likewise.
Those "poisoned by venom" are a metaphor for sentient beings defiled by false teachings. Being defiled by false teachings, they instead harbor doubts toward the True Dharma;

therefore, it is said that their minds are all "inverted. To be inverted means to take what is beautiful for what is evil. Because they take what is beautiful for what is evil, [they are thus described].
Not taking good medicine is a metaphor for sentient beings who do not believe in the True Dharma and are unable to practice according to the teachings;

instead, they give rise to arrogance, indulgence, aversion, and indolence. "One should employ skillful means" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s contemplation and proclamation of his passing into extinction.
The statement beginning with "He then spoke these words" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s proclamation of his passing into extinction.
