"Decrepitude" is a metaphor for the end of the period of transformation having approached; "the arrival of death" is a metaphor for Nirvāṇa being imminent; "leaving behind medicine" is a metaphor for bequeathing the Dharma to save sentient beings;

and "it may be taken" is a metaphor for entrusting them to uphold it. Entrusting them to uphold it involves praising the supreme excellence of the Dharma's merit; therefore, the metaphor states: "Do not grieve that it will not cure you."
*Chāi* (差) is synonymous with *chāo* (瘥); it signifies the meaning of complete recovery. "Below this" refers to the metaphor of "extinguishing birth to bring benefit.
"Returning to another country" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata abandoning this [world] to respond to that [realm]; it refers to what is called "not extinguished yet appearing as extinguished.

"Sending a messenger back to report" is a metaphor for the Buddha commanding a manifested person (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) to come and respond; the manifested person comes and responds, demonstrating the Tathāgata.
After his passing, you should exert yourself with diligence. Therefore, it is said by way of metaphor: "Your father has already died.
Upon first seeing the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa, one may still not take it to heart; only when suddenly prompted by a transformed person does one realize it and feel remorse.

Thus, the analogy is used of hearing that one's father has passed away and feeling great distress in the mind. The phrase "recollecting the father’s compassionate rescue" is a metaphor for sentient beings reflecting deeply.
The Buddha’s grace is such that he considers those who have perished far away as if they were his own children. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who cling to cessation as being real.
Clinging to cessation as real, they realize for themselves that they are like a son who has lost his father or a guest who has lost his host; they are without rescue and without refuge.

Therefore, reflecting on their own state of being orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon, the phrase "constantly harboring a sense of sorrowful resonance" is employed both as a teaching and as a metaphor. Within the metaphor:

The pain of the father’s injury is likened to one’s own suffering; within the Dharma, it refers to grieving over the Buddha’s swift entry into parinirvāṇa and feeling the regret that one’s own spiritual cultivation has been so slow.

The mind then attains awakening, which is metaphorically like realizing that what was mistaken was actually wrong; knowing the fragrance and excellence of the medicine is metaphorically like having faith that the Dharma is the truth.

He immediately took it and consumed it. This is a metaphor for practicing according to the teachings. The toxic illness was entirely cured; this is a metaphor for all evils being completely extinguished.
When the father heard that his son had recovered, this is a metaphor for the Buddha observing that there are those with the capacity [for enlightenment]. He caused them to come and see him;

this is a metaphor for responding to and transforming beings according to their capacities—what is called "not being born, yet manifesting birth. This concludes the metaphor for the benefit of proclaiming the cessation of birth. △ Third, the metaphor for the non-falsity of the Buddha’s words.
“What do you think, sons of good family? [The Buddha asked. “...Is it not a false and vain offense? “No, World-Honored One.
Using the treatment of feigned death to save a son who was about to die is a metaphor for manifesting cessation to rescue those whose faculties are on the verge of perishing.
Because of the physician’s momentary skillful means, one comes to know the Tathāgata’s limitless expedients; repaying this kindness and virtue would leave one with no leisure at all.
Who could possibly inflict the offense of falsehood upon him? Therefore, when the Tathāgata asked whether such a thing existed or not, the assembled multitude answered directly with "No.
The illustration is now concluded. △ Third, the synthesis.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this; since my attainment of Buddhahood (up to) those who speak according to the Dharma regarding my faults of falsehood—the Dharma is the eternal Dharma.
Yet, it is not that extinction speaks of extinction. If one speaks according to the eternal Dharma, it may appear as if there were falsehood."

Now, this is a provisional means (*upāya*) for saving sentient beings; therefore, it is not so. According to the preceding parable, although there are many passages, they collectively serve to elucidate that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, and that his manifestation of extinction is not in vain. The combined text is thus: concise in words yet rich in meaning.
This concludes the prose section. II. Verse Recitation (The heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.

(The section of the formal verses is divided into two parts: first, a verse on the long duration of his lifespan; second, a verse on the non-falsity of his manifest extinction. The first part has two sections: first, a verse clearly explaining the long duration;
second, a verse preemptively addressing potential objections. The first [of these] is the verse on the meaning.)
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed [until] I constantly abide here preaching the Dharma.

First, the verse itself. "Carrying" (zài) is also a name for a numerical unit. The supplementary note states: one hundred becomes one thousand; one thousand becomes ten thousand; ten thousand becomes one hundred million (bì); one hundred million becomes one billion (zhào);

one billion becomes ten billion (jīng); ten billion becomes one hundred billion (zǐ); one hundred billion becomes one trillion (yè); one trillion becomes ten trillion (rǎng); and ten trillion becomes one hundred trillion (gōu).
From the ravines arise the gullies; from the gullies arises the level ground; from the level ground arises the "bearing" (*zài*). This "bearing" refers to the fact that the earth cannot bear it.
Although the enumeration here differs slightly from that in the long prose version, both are based on the number of "innumerables. These verses are taken for their underlying meaning.

The expression "always said" and so forth indicates that the transformative activities in the interim are uninterrupted; this is precisely the sense of "long duration. From "since then" onwards, it serves as a counter-illustration of the directions.
He then manifests extinction. This, conversely, reveals that he does not truly enter parinirvāṇa; thus, it still does not contradict the meaning of his long-term duration.

Therefore, it is said that he dwells eternally preaching the Dharma. According to the prose section, following this chapter, there is another section providing analogies and comparisons, which is not versified here.

△ Second, the verse on preemptively resolving potential objections (the text for preempting objections differs from the prose because each is established according to the specific meaning of the preceding passage).

Two [points]. First, to prevent the objection: "If it is eternally abiding (*nitya*), why not manifest it now? Would one not receive greater benefit? Why must you employ skillful means to manifest its cessation, thereby causing it to be unseen? To this, the defense states: [The second point: To prevent the objection:

"If it manifests its cessation now, why must you speak of its permanence? Regarding the first [objection], the challenge says: "Since it is eternally abiding, it should be seen as such right now. Would it not be more beneficial? Why must you use skillful means to manifest its cessation, thereby causing it to remain unseen? Thus, the defense is provided.

I always abide here through the power of my various supernormal knowledges (ṛddhi), yet I manifest the passing into extinction through the Tathāgata’s skillful means so that beings may give rise to a heart of longing and veneration.
It is not that I have completely ceased to appear; rather, by the power of my supernormal knowledge, I conceal myself from those deluded sentient beings.
This is because I desire them to extensively make offerings to the śarīra relics, and through their yearning and veneration, to plant roots of goodness.

Root [text]. △ Second, preventing the objection that since the manifestation of extinction through skillful means can accomplish benefit, why is it necessary to reveal the trace and manifest the fundamental by definitively teaching permanence? (The objection states:

"Since the manifestation of extinction through expedient means is able to bring about benefit, why must one open the trace to reveal the fundamental and definitively teach permanence? Therefore, this [text] provides the following defense:)
When sentient beings have already become convinced, their natures are upright and their minds are supple... (up to) "they merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
"Belief" means believing in his teaching; "submission" means submitting to his person. By believing in his teaching, they are free from deceitful intentions.

Therefore, it is said that through sincerity and straightforwardness, one brings others into submission; thus, there arises a mind of compliant obedience. Therefore, it is said that one must be supple.

Because of this suppleness, the mind desires to behold [the Buddha] with single-minded devotion; because of this sincerity and straightforwardness, one does not spare even body or life. These words refer to the capacity of sentient beings to respond to the Buddha’s stimulus.
When it is said, "I and the assembly of monks together emerge from Vulture Peak," this refers to the present occasion where the principal and the retinue meet in mutual interpenetration.
Speaking of permanence, skillful means, and so forth, this refers to the manifestation of the fundamental [truth] today to subvert the provisional traces.

These words indicate that the Tathāgata possesses teachings that respond to and adapt to beings. While others in other lands have faith and joy, and the Buddha further preaches the Dharma there, this assembly does not hear it;
thus, based on their previous understanding, they claim the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa. To shatter this attachment, he definitively proclaims his permanence. (Verse)

The section on the long duration of the lifespan is concluded. △ Second, the verse on the manifestation of extinction being non-illusory (Note: This does not carry forward from the preceding section nor initiate the subsequent one; it is directly divided into three parts). First, a verse explaining by way of the Dharma;
second, a verse clarifying by way of analogy; third, a verse for synthesis. Of these, the first two [consist of]: first, a combined verse on abiding, detriment, extinction, and benefit.

Second, the specific verses demonstrate that the Buddha’s words are not false. This section has two parts: first, the direct verses on the two meanings; second, the supplementary verses for resolving objections.
The first (the brief verses):
"I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction... [until] I emerge to preach the Dharma for them."
The first two lines [of the verse] praise the fact that the cause for remaining in the world involves some degree of detriment:

because the Tathāgata has long remained in the world, those of meager merit have failed to plant roots of goodness; therefore it is said, "I see sentient beings submerged in suffering," and thus he does not descend.

These lines praise the benefit produced by proclaiming his passing into extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). While the prose section concerns the proclamation of extinction, this verse concerns the demonstration of extinction; their meanings mutually clarify one another. △ Second, the supplementary verse.

Six defenses against objections (the distant versions clarify the difficulties; the near traces are easy to cling to. "Scented oil and ghee lamps illuminate the interior and brighten the exterior. Regarding "the evil age" and below, it should be understood that this verse concludes the excellence [of the teaching].

If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present (extending to: "all things are adorned with excellence").
Upholding is the general term for all practices; writing is a specific form of upholding. Since the general term is used here to represent the specific, it is called "upholding."
It is not called "scripture. The prose section refers to *rakta-candana* (red sandalwood), which here is translated as *gośīrṣa-candana* (ox-head sandalwood);

these differ only in their color and form. △ Third, the verse on the merit of saving others (the prose section has three parts; here, there are fewer, as the meaning is revealed through the combination of the dharma, the metaphor, and the application).
Part two: first, one verse citing the inferior to illustrate the superior; second, two verses providing a detailed clarification. First:
If there are those with faith and understanding who receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe [the teachings], up to practicing patience and delighting in meditative concentration.
The first verse raises the inferiority of those who merely provide material offerings (the broad verse). The prose commentary follows from this, hence it says, "Therefore, I say," and so forth.
This directly presents the matter, hence it says, "If there are those with faith and understanding," and so forth. The prose commentary simply states:
"Offerings. This clarifies the various articles of offering concurrently; flowers, incense, powdered incense, and so forth, are all such articles.
*Sumana* is fully called *sumanā*, which translates as "well-gathering the mind"; it is the name of a flower. It is yellowish-white in color and extremely fragrant.
The tree is three or four feet high; its branches hang down like a canopy. *Campaka*—translated here as "yellow flower"—is small but extremely fragrant.
*Atimuktaka*—translated here as "well-considered"—is shaped like hemp; it has red flowers and green leaves and is the most excellent among the fragrant grass-flowers.
When oil is perfumed with these three flowers and burned constantly, one obtains both fragrance and light.
Therefore, the long discourse states that there is no need to erect stupas or construct monasteries;

this precisely reveals that the merit is immeasurable, like empty space. Here it says, "merit is immeasurable, as boundless as space," which precisely reveals that it can rival the erection of stupas.
And the construction of monasteries: while the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same. Furthermore, the following verse illustrates the excellence of both [giving and morality] together.

(Omitted Verse) The three perfections of giving, morality, and patience all rely upon diligence (*vīrya*). All wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); therefore, the text omits the two perfections of diligence and wisdom.
According to the prose section following this division, there is further an explicit illustration through the application of the dharma, the metaphor, and their synthesis. Now...

Having already employed analogies for that which is illustrated (*dṛṣṭānta*), the subject to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) may now be inferred accordingly; therefore, the following section provides a detailed clarification.
△ Second, the verses provide a further detailed clarification in two parts: first, verses detailing its practice (*caryā*); second, verses detailing its virtues (*guṇa*).
The first [part] (summarizes the meaning in brief verses).
Being free from anger and harsh speech, one shows reverence to stupas and temples; (up to: the merit is immeasurable.
By being free from anger, one can bring about fearlessness. By not using harsh speech, one acts in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. Through reverence, there is nothing that is not provided.
This is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Furthermore, not being angry is the precept of mind; not being malicious is the precept of speech;

and being respectful is the precept of body—this is also the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Being humble eliminates the causes for receiving disgrace; being free from arrogance possesses the power of endurance—this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Constantly encompassing [all things] is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); reflecting and relying upon [the teachings] is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). Not becoming angry when questioned or challenged, and explaining in accordance with [the truth], is wisdom (*prajñā*).
[The word] "crosses over" [refers to] the final two lines. This concludes that practicing both [the perfections] constitutes practice; its merit is immeasurable.
△ Second, the verse provides a detailed explanation of its virtues (a broad exposition according to the meaning).
If one sees this Dharma-preacher endowed with such virtues—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—the long discourse states:

"One should know that this person has already set out for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Since it is known that they have already set out for the site of enlightenment, one should scatter flowers and robes over them, conceiving of them as being like the Buddha.
The long discourse further states: "They are close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they sit upon the path to enlightenment."
"Under a tree": since one is already close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it will not be long before one proceeds to the Tree of Enlightenment (*bodhivṛkṣa*).

Once seated beneath the Tree of Enlightenment, one attains the fruit and brings vast benefit to humans and devas. Regarding "untainted and unconditioned" (*anāsrava-asamskrta*): this refers to the meaning of attaining the fruit when one has reached the ultimate limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The long discourse states: "At the place where [the Buddha] sat, stood, or walked, a stūpa should be erected for worship. This is consistent with the present [text].
The meaning of "in the midst" and "where he dwells" is the same. The final four lines further explain the preceding meaning:
precisely because the Buddha is eternally present, one ought to erect stupas and make offerings. This concludes the separate clarification of the three kinds of merit.
*Fahua Zhizhang Shu*, Scroll Five, Phonetic Explanations: Bāojū (苞苴):

The first character is pronounced *bāo* (cut by the rhyme *jiāo*); the second is pronounced *jǔ* (cut by the rhyme *yú*). It refers to grass that can be made into mats and used to wrap objects. Háisàng (骸髒): An appearance of being stubborn or perverse. The first character is pronounced *kǔ* (cut by the rhyme *lǎng*).
Yīn (upper character: kǎng; lower character: zhèng; pronunciation: zàng). Wěi xié (upper character: wū huǐ; lower character: xiān liè; pronunciation: xuē; upper means vulgar and base;

lower means arrogant and insolent). Huì (hú duì; pronunciation: huì; means a city gate). Mǐ (mò lǐ; pronunciation: nǔ; means to press down). Hé (hé gè; pronunciation: hè; means the water is exhausted). Juàn (guī xuán; pronunciation: juàn; means fickle and impulsive). Chão (liǎo; jiāo in the third tone;
means to cut off). Jiǒu (jí yǒu; pronunciation: qiú; means crooked). Xù (xū yù; pronunciation: xù; means to exert oneself). Gǔn (gǔ běn; pronunciation: gǔn; means to roll rapidly). Shāng.

*Shīyáng* (cut with the rhyme *shāng*; the sound is *shāng*): the mourning for one who has not yet reached adulthood. *Kǎo*: (the ancient form of the character 考). *Bēi* (cut with the rhyme *pūméi*; the sound is *bēi*): the first month of pregnancy in a woman. *Zōngzhū* (upper character cut with the rhyme *zǔdōng*; the sound is *zōng*; lower character cut with the rhyme *lìjū*;

the sound is *lǚ*): Its original name is *bīngzhū*. The tree is one or two *zhàng* high; its leaves are like those of the *púshàn* (rush fan), and beneath the leaves there is hair like a mane (*zōng*), hence it is called *zōngzhū*. It is also written as *zōngzhū*, and is also named *púkuí*.

Composed by the later student of the Xianzong school, Tongli;
proofread for characters by his dharma-heir disciple, Mingyuan.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the five kinds of merit (as indicated by the chapter title):
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eighteen, "The Merit of Rejoicing.
"Following" (*sui*) means to accord with, not giving rise to a mind of opposition. "Rejoicing" (*xi*) means to feel joy, not giving rise to resentment or envy.

Reflecting thus, because there is no resentment or envy, one does not incur the fault of slandering the Dharma; because there is no opposition, one spontaneously creates the conditions for becoming "one who has the jewel tied in his garment.
Judging the result by its cause, such merit is inexhaustible, as can be seen in the text. If we discuss this chapter specifically, it possesses five kinds of merit;
however, here we omit the latter and follow the former, designating it simply by the name "Rejoicing" (*anumodana*). If explained separately...
There are two types: first, the merit of rejoicing (*anumodana*). As the verse says: "If one hears [this teaching] through successive transmission, the merit is already immeasurable;
how much more so for those who hear it for the first time at a Dharma assembly and rejoice. This refers to that. Second, the merit of hearing for a brief moment. As the verse says:
"The joy felt upon hearing it for even a moment—I shall now describe its merit: in future lives, one will be born among gods and humans and obtain a magnificent elephant."
These refer to such things as horse-drawn carriages. Third is the merit of temporary exhortation. As the verse says:

"If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one exhorts others to sit and listen to the sutra, by this causal condition of merit, one shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin.
Fourth is the merit of earnest exhortation. As the verse says: "If there is one who exhorts even a single person, leading them to listen to the Lotus Sutra, saying that this sutra is profound..."
Exquisite! It is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas. Now, I shall describe its merit: that one will be free from oral ailments in every lifetime, and so forth.

Fifth is the merit of listening with sincerity. As the verse says: "How much more so for those who listen with a single mind, explain its meaning and intent, and practice according to what has been taught;
their merit shall be beyond measure. In sum, this sutra is like a good friend.
Seeing the medicine as if it were nectar, touching it causes all illnesses to be eliminated; being moistened by it, one neither dies nor is born.

What was discussed in the preceding chapter is not yet exhaustive; therefore, it is further elaborated upon in this chapter. (The scriptural text is divided into two parts: First, Maitreya asks about rejoicing alone;
second, the Tathāgata fully elucidates the five virtues. First, the question regarding rejoicing alone:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] "...if one is able to rejoice, how much merit will they obtain?

To examine the intent of Maitreya’s question: it has been developing since the preceding chapter. This is because it was previously stated that after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one should know that this is already a sign of profound faith and understanding.
Maitreya’s thought was that the merit of sympathetic joy (anumodana) seemed to yield little fortune; yet the Buddha had ultimately granted it as a mark of profound faith and understanding.
Fearing that this might be difficult to believe, he therefore followed up with the question regarding how much merit would be obtained.

△ Second, the Tathāgata fully elucidates the five virtues (Having already clarified the merit of rejoicing, there is concern that others may not inquire further regarding the remaining four; therefore, they are fully elucidated.

This also reflects the Tathāgata’s intent to seek out those for the Dharma without shunning prolixity). Second [section], which has two parts: first, prose; second, verse. The first [prose section] has five parts:
1. the merit of rejoicing; 2. the merit of briefly listening; 3. the merit of briefly exhorting; 4. the merit of sincerely exhorting; 5. the merit of sincerely listening.
The first part has four sections: (1) each individual rejoicing and teaching others; (2) the successive transmission reaching fifty people;
(3) the evaluation of the merit of the final person; and (4) the illustration of the initial rejoicer by comparison. First:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] "good friends and spiritual mentors should expound according to their ability.

Once the fourfold assembly has entered the Buddha-dharma, they all belong to the internal teaching (insider tradition). Other scholars who preside over the hundred schools all belong to the external teaching (outsider tradition).
This statement regarding those who rejoice applies regardless of whether one is insider or outsider. It generally includes those aged twenty and above; as for the young—
"Twenty or fewer" refers to those who rejoice, regardless of whether they are many or few.
"One who hears the sutra and rejoices" means one who follows with faith and delights through understanding.
"Going forth to a place" means desiring to transmit what has been gained by teaching others. "A secluded monastery" refers to a place of tranquility; [as for] cities, towns, and streets...
"Roads and the like" refers to areas of disorder; this speaks of the place where the teaching is transmitted, regardless of whether it is still or chaotic.
"As one has heard" means to illuminate what one has attained for oneself, without arbitrary addition or subtraction. "Parents and kinsmen" refers to those closely related by blood;
"virtuous friends and spiritual teachers" encompasses those more distantly related by different surnames. This speaks of the persons to whom the teaching is transmitted, regardless of [their status].
This refers to the distinction between those who are close and those who are distant. "According to their capacity" means according to the power of their wisdom.

"Expounding" means expounding the Dharma as they have heard it. Indeed, there is no consideration of whether their wisdom is superior or inferior, nor whether their exposition is complete or deficient;
rather, simply by not being selfish toward themselves and delighting in sharing goodness with others, their resolve is already praiseworthy, and their merit is already—
Infinite. △ Second, the successive transmission up to the fiftieth person.
These individuals, having heard it, rejoiced (up to) thus transmitting it successively until the fiftieth person.
Characters have undergone three transcriptions; the forms of "pig" (*zhī*) and "boar" (*hài*) have changed.

Now that these have been transmitted through successive generations until the fiftieth generation, they differ from the original teachings received directly at the Dharma assembly—face-to-face instructions—by no less than the distance between heaven and earth.
△ Third, the comparison of the merit of the final [transmission] has three parts: first, establishing an example; second, the question-and-answer on merit; third, the formal [comparison].
Comparison: The first two [points]. First, the universal bestowal of material gifts; second, the broad benefit of the gift of Dharma.
Regarding the first: "Ajita, that fiftieth son of good family... [up to] ...palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems."

At the outset, he granted permission to speak and cautioned the assembly to listen. Desiring to compare the merit of the first [recipient] with that of the fiftieth, he cautioned them to listen well, saying:

"If you know this, you know that. If there are four or fewer, the entire assembly is designated as the "Saṃgha" for the purpose of clarifying the act of giving; this is according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
This is already called "innumerable"; how much more so when accumulated to four hundred trillion? This speaks to the extreme vastness of their multitude.
There are six destinies (*gati*) toward which sentient beings tend, yet there are only four modes of birth (*yoni*). Hence, one speaks of the "six destinies and four births.

The four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—explain the four births while encompassing the six destinies. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The egg-born arise solely from thought; the womb-born result from emotion."
Moisture corresponds through conjunction; transformation responds through separation. However, these [categories] appear to be restricted to that which has form;

therefore, below this, they are further discussed in contrast to what has form and what is formless. That which has form refers to the realms of desire and form. That which is formless refers to the sphere of infinite space.
That which possesses perception refers to the sphere of infinite consciousness. That which lacks perception refers to the sphere of nothingness. It is not...
There is the realm of perception, not the realm of non-perception, nor the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

However, as these [categories] appear to be restricted to superior rebirths, the text proceeds further below to discuss them in contrast with those who are legless, two-legged, and so forth. "Legless" refers to the class of wriggling creatures.
"Bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth" is as can be understood. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it refers to what has already been stated above and includes other things not yet mentioned;

it is used collectively to encompass all subtle categories. Therefore, the general statement "those included within the number of sentient beings" is interpreted by some as referring to those who are capable of giving.

Such a person seeks merit and seeks preeminent merit. Since preeminent merit must rely upon preeminent giving, they provide all the articles for amusement and pleasure according to each being's desires. To every single sentient being...
"Providing as much gold, silver, and so forth as would fill Jambudvīpa" means that there shall be no lack of articles for entertainment and enjoyment.
Jambudvīpa refers to the southern continent of Jambudvīpa; because there is a tree named Jambu on the southern side of Mount Sumeru, the continent takes its name from this tree.
2. The Universal Benefit of the Dharma-Gift.
This great donor practiced such giving (up to the point where he) attained mastery and was endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Although he practiced the gift of material wealth, his mind remained unsatisfied; therefore, after eighty years had passed, he formed this thought:
"Objects of pleasure serve only to sustain life before death. Since death will soon come, what will they provide for the next world? Therefore, one should [rely] upon the Buddha..."
"Guiding with the Dharma; instructing, benefiting, and gladdening" means instructing by means of supramundane benefit and teaching so that they may rejoice in hearing the Dharma.
Through rejoicing in hearing the Dharma, their outflows are exhausted and their minds are opened; thus, they suddenly transcend to the four fruits at once.

*Srotāpanna* (入流, *rùliú*) means "entering the stream," referring to the initial severance of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms and entry into the stream of the sages. *Sakṛdāgāmin* (斯陀含, *sītúhán*)...

This is called "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*): it refers to one who has already severed the first six grades of the afflictions of thought (*karma-kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and will return to the desire realm only once more before severing the remaining three grades.

This is called "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*): it refers to one who has completely severed all afflictions of thought in the desire realm and is reborn in the higher realms, never returning to the desire realm again.
This is called "Arhat" (*arhat*): it refers to one for whom both [afflictions of] views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought have been extinguished, and thus they do not undergo further birth.

"Exhausted" means that because one will never again undergo birth in a future existence, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted; this signifies the simultaneous exhaustion of both the views and the afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Regarding the nine successive concentrations (*anupūrva-vihāra-samādhi*), they progress gradually and deepen, being without obstruction or hindrance; therefore, it is said "in profound meditative concentration."

All have attained mastery over the meaning of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), as explained in the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*). Having concluded the setting of these illustrative examples, [the text proceeds to] the second section:
Question and Answer regarding Merit.
What do you think? As for this great donor—let alone enabling others to attain the fruit of Arhatship—who extensively bestows gifts to relieve the masses;

even sages still suffer from illness. This great donor was able to provide such vast wealth to so many people and further instructed them in the Buddha-dharma, leading them to realize the four fruits. His merit should naturally be [immeasurable].
Because there is no limit or measure, the Tathāgata intentionally asked, "Is it not much?
and Maitreya answered directly that it was exceedingly much, immeasurable, and boundless. If these donors and others were to further explain the preceding meaning, they would say:
"The mere bestowing of articles of pleasure is already called immeasurable; how much more so when it causes one to realize the fruits [of the path]! Therefore, it must indeed be boundless. △
Third, the comparison with the Correct [Dharma].
The Buddha told Maitreya, "I shall now speak to you clearly... (up to) that which cannot be known through calculation or analogy.
To show this with clarity is to manifest that these are words of truth. The giving of the requisites for pleasure certainly belongs to the outflows (*āsrava*).

They cause others to attain arhatship, yet these remain stuck in provisional teachings. As for the fiftieth person, although it is said that they have merely heard the verse through successive transmission, their single act of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is capable of serving as the causal seed for attaining Buddhahood.

Therefore, even the merit of the two types of giving—though [the former] may be a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or otherwise—is not equal to even one part of this. Thus, one knows that this merit is such that it cannot even be reached by calculation.
It is so. However, this meaning is extremely difficult to comprehend and believe. I shall now provide an analogy to clarify it. The merit of that material gift (*āmiṣadāna*) is like lead;
the merit of the provisional vehicles (*upāyayāna*) is like mercury; the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is like a small portion of gold.
The successive transmission from the fiftieth person is like gold that has entered an alloy; one must know that although the gold has entered [the alloy], it remains gold.
Gold is refined until it becomes increasingly pure; lead and mercury are not gold, yet they become increasingly counterfeit through repeated smelting.

Therefore, even if there is a great quantity of lead and mercury, it is not equal to a small amount of gold that has been refined into a semblance of the real. One who understands this analogy will naturally no longer harbor doubts regarding the intent of this comparison.
This concludes the final section on the comparison of merits. △ Fourth, illustrating the initial sympathetic joy by way of contrast.
Ajita, the merit of the fiftieth person in this sequence—even up to those who have heard it through successive oral transmission—is such that it cannot be compared to an *asaṃkhyeya*.
Yet, even for those who hear it through hearsay, there is no lack of error; their merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) is still immeasurable, boundless, and as vast as an *asaṃkhyeya*.
How much more so for those who hear it directly from the lips of the Teacher, face-to-face, and rejoice in it!
The merit of this naturally becomes even more supreme. Those who are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) cannot be compared to it.
This concludes the section on the merit of sympathetic joy. △ Second, the merit of listening for a moment.

Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, [offers] precious carriages and celestial palaces, or goes to a monastic dwelling for the sake of this sutra, this demonstrates the sincerity of their intent to go.

If they listen and receive it for even a brief moment, whether sitting or standing, this demonstrates the brevity of the time spent listening. By virtue of planting these seeds as causes, they will hear it once again upon returning to this world.
He then attained awakening. The Way is revered and its practitioners are honored; they are venerated by both gods and humans.
Thus, one is able to obtain excellent and most sublime elephants, horses, and chariots, even ascending to celestial palaces. △ Third, the merit of brief exhortation.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, when someone comes to a place where the Dharma is being preached—or even to the seat of a Wheel-Turning Sage King—first exhorts them [to listen], this reveals that they have temporarily given rise to right view.
As for one who offers half of their own seat to let the other sit, this indicates they possess a mind that seeks mutual benefit.
Such a person will surely become a Dharma Master in the future. Once they have become a Dharma Master, if they encounter...
When Emperors, Brahmās, or Universal Monarchs seek the Dharma, they are all able to obtain their respective seats;
this is just as when one now invites a Dharma Master, one must leave a seat vacant to await them—this is the very proof of it. △ Fourth, the sincere exhortation regarding merit.

Ānanda, if there should be another person who, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, believes and accepts his instructions—this refers to one who follows the scriptural teachings with sincerity and is exhorted to listen. Because that person is moved by such sincerity, they follow him into the assembly;
therefore it is said, "they immediately receive his teaching. As for "hearing it in an instant," it is as previously described: whether sitting or standing.
The merit of merely listening and receiving [the teaching] for a short time is as previously described;
how much more so for one who is able to encourage others—how could such a person not receive a superior reward? Therefore, below, the merit of such a person is specifically detailed and clarified.

According to the *Da Cheng* (Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra), which cites the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, a Bodhisattva possessing dhāraṇī resides on the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*). My humble opinion is that this refers to the dhāraṇī...
"Ni" means "dhāraṇī" (total retention) in this language. Since it is called "total retention," it encompasses all within one; thus, it refers exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Do not stagnate in fixed stages or positions. For this sutra belongs to the Perfect Teaching, those who hear it should naturally rely upon those of the Perfect Vehicle.

To dwell together in one place means to rely upon one another. Because they rely upon one another, they influence and permeate each other through mutual cultivation, thereby attaining sharp faculties and wisdom.
Because they possess sharp faculties and wisdom, they are endowed with the virtues of a Dharma-preacher and attain the physical marks of a Dharma-preacher.

Consequently, for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they never suffer the retribution of being mute or speech-impaired. One who is mute has unclear articulation and lacks words in their voice.
There is no foul taste in the mouth; therefore, it is said to be "not malodorous. The tongue is neither short nor knotted; therefore, it is said to be "without affliction.
That the mouth is also "without affliction" means it is free from sores or ailments. The teeth are neither black nor yellow; they are clean and white.
Furthermore, they are not sparse or missing; they are dense and complete. Nor are they uneven or crooked; they are even and upright. The lower lip is drawn in and well-proportioned; therefore—

It is said that [the lips] do not hang down; the upper lip is closely enveloped, hence they are said not to be "torn back" (*kian*). "Torn back" refers to upturned lips, while "shortened" refers to lips that are too short.
They are red, fine, and moist, hence they are said not to be "rough or coarse. No sores or afflictions arise upon them, hence they are said not to have "ulcers or rashes" (*chuang-zhen*).
A "zhěn" refers to sores appearing on the lips. Those that are "defective and ruined" mean the lips are not complete or beautiful. Those that are "crooked and slanted" mean the lips are not upright.
Those whose lips are thick and large will surely be dull-witted; those whose lips are tawny and black will surely be low-born. These [conditions] do not manifest in his form.

Because one does not cause others to feel aversion or dislike, it is said that there are "no loathsome qualities. A flat [匚@虎] (a hollow or depression) refers to a sunken nose; being "crooked" means the nose is not straight.
Because the mind is upright and the countenance is relaxed, the facial complexion is not dark. When the cheekbones are high and large, it is called "not narrow and long";
when the flesh of the cheeks is full and round, it is called "not sunken or curved. One who is free from these [defects] can inspire love and respect; therefore, it is said:
There is nothing unpleasing. This above clarifies the characteristics of being free from faults.

As for the lips, tongue, teeth, and so forth, they not only avoid the aforementioned faults, but are moreover upright, dignified, and beautiful. Regarding the nose being long, high, and straight: it not only avoids being flat or crooked.

Furthermore, as for those whose features are not crooked or distorted, but rather well-proportioned, elongated, prominent, and upright, and whose countenances are perfectly round—such individuals are not merely free from narrowness, lengthiness, or concavity;
they are also complete, full, and substantial. Those with high and long eyebrows will surely preside over literary refinement and nobility;
those with broad, level, and upright foreheads will certainly possess honor and glory. With such a physical formation, one may truly be called perfect.
Therefore, it is said that "the marks of a person are fully complete. The above clarifies the possession of virtuous characteristics.

Having already possessed the virtues of a Dharma Master and further attained the physical marks of a Dharma Master, one’s connection to the Buddha-Dharma becomes increasingly intimate and proximate; one’s faculties and wisdom become increasingly sharp and clear.

Consequently, in life after life, one sees the Buddhas and hears the Dharma, faithfully receiving their instructions. This concludes the section on the merit of sincere exhortation. △ Five: Sincere Listening.
“Merit. Ajita, you should observe this... for the sake of others, distinguishing [the teaching] and practicing according to what has been taught.

First, he exhorts them to observe the aforementioned virtues; how much more so for those below? Furthermore, he clarifies that they should listen with sincerity. “With a single mind” means listening with sincerity.
Because of the sincerity with which one listens, one is able to read, explain, and practice [the teachings]. The merit of exhorting others to listen cannot be compared to this on the same day.

The Fragrance of the Sages.

various fragrances are combined to form a powder, a pill, or an ointment; these may be worn, burned, or rubbed upon the body. In this regard—
Regarding "dwelling in the intervals" and "being able to discern them all": one who is thus capable will certainly be able to perform Buddha-work through this.

Furthermore, below [this], the Dharma Master separately knows that incense does not inherently exist in elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth; at times they may have a foul odor, yet now, by means of the purity of the faculties...
Because it is pure, there exists a distinct true fragrance. It is the same with grasses, trees, and forests; thus, one is said to discern fragrances distinctly.

Whether near or far, if one’s discrimination is unerring, one does not merely distinguish the fragrance, but can also know its nature and temperament, recognize its direction, and differentiate its species—whether it serves to benefit, to complete, or [to harm].
[This is] its application. △ Second, incense from the heavens:
Those who uphold this sutra, though dwelling here [until] they also smell the incense burned by the various devas.
First are the insentient fragrances of the devas: the Pārijātaka, here translated as "Perfectly Born," which is the King of Trees mentioned in the introductory section;

Furthermore, one smells the sentient fragrances of the devas below: the Vaijayanta Palace, which is the private palace of Śakra, together with his court ladies.
The place of recreation is that which was formerly burned by Maudgalyāyana.
The Hall of the Sublime Dharma (Dharmasabhā) is the public hall of Śakra, the place where he assembles with the various devas and deliberates on affairs on all fast days.
The various gardens, such as the Nandana Garden and others, are the places where the devas sport and play. However, the mind turns according to its objects, and fragrance follows [the senses].
At that time, the palaces, Dharma halls, gardens, and so forth of the various heavens were each distinct.

As for the "other devas," this includes those from the Four Great Kings below up to the Yāma heaven, and even the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven and others. From the Brahma worlds up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this includes all the devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Since their excellence and inferiority differ, the fragrance of their bodies also varies. Furthermore, as mentioned below... all [the devas]... [smell it].
As for the incense burned by the devas, those who smell it also come to know the intention behind the burning of that incense.
△ Third, the incense of the sages, as well as the incense of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas (up to): they likewise smell them from afar and know their locations.
The provisional sages of the Two Vehicles, knowing where [the practitioner] resides, receive and guide them;
the partially enlightened Bodhisattvas, knowing where they reside, draw near to them; and the most holy Buddhas, knowing where they reside, make offerings and serve them.
Thus, such knowledge is truly beneficial. This concludes the separate listing of the various fragrances. △ Third, the summary of its merits.
Although one hears this fragrance, from the faculty of the nose (up to) explaining it to others, one’s recollection is unerring.

Because it has been perfumed by love for a long time, that which hears nothing at all is called "impaired" (*bhraṃśa*). Although there is something heard, being unable to distinguish it is called "erroneous" (*vibhrama*).
Now, because there is fragrance and one necessarily hears it, and having heard it one can distinguish it, it is said to be "neither impaired nor erroneous. This is the discernment of recollection.

Mindfulness pertains to the faculty of mind (*manas*). Speaking for others pertains to the faculty of tongue (*jihvā*). Since these two faculties and the faculty of nose (*ghrāṇa*) function interchangeably, there is no error.

The nose-faculty of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrances or foul odors, he perceives and knows all their various kinds.
Although the preceding and following [verses] speak only of "fragrance," the inclusion here of the term "foul odor" is for the purpose of not destroying worldly conventions.

If one considers the capacity of smelling itself, both fragrance and foul odor are unattainable; in totality, they constitute a single true fragrance. △ Second, the verse enumerates the assembly individually.

Regarding incense (the prose section originally contained only three parts; now there is a supplementary verse, divided into four): 1. A verse on human incense; 2. A supplement on miscellaneous types of incense;
3. A verse on celestial incense; 4. A verse on the incense of sages. First:
From *sumanā*, *jāti*, *tamāla*, and *candana* (up to) "by smelling the fragrance, one knows their bodies.
This is a brief verse summarizing the prose. Below the section on "Great Power" (*mahānubhāva*), supplementary verses are added for the remaining fragrances.

[The Buddha] knows the location of those among the princes, ministers, and others who are capable of being transformed or who must be avoided, so that he may find the appropriate opportunity for their departure or arrival. [This concludes the section on] Treasures from the Earth.
The treasury of the Wheel-Turning King and his precious queen are enjoyed solely by the Wheel-Turning King; other people do not know of them.
Now that you can perceive them through their fragrance, what more is there to envy in the Wheel-Turning King?

Merely by hearing of his ornaments, one knows what kind of person he is, without needing to see him to observe his origins; thus, one naturally avoids the faults of losing sight of the person or losing the words [of the teaching]. △
Second, regarding miscellaneous supplementary types of fragrance:

whether the devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing miraculous transformations (up to their places of origin and their current locations), the joy of their sports and the wonders of their miraculous transformations are all the result of the devas' superior merit; one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
Then, as for heavenly blessings, there would be no cause for envy. Exquisite flowers, rare fruits, and the fragrant scent of ghee and oil are all things sought after in the human world;
once one knows where they are located, there will be no need to trouble oneself seeking what is required. When the sandalwood flower blooms, its fragrance overwhelms the eranda;
sentient beings within it ought to be overwhelmed by it, yet now, through the fragrance, they are able to perceive it—thus, the nose [is awakened].

The faculties are so perfected that they penetrate the subtlest realms. Within the Iron Ring Mountains lies the dark abyss; within the great ocean lies the dragon palace; within the earth lies the Avīci hell.

By smelling their fragrance, one knows where they are, and thus the means for their salvation and deliverance are obtained. Asuras engage in strife and contention, their anger and ferocity being particularly excessive;
they sport with their kin and are truly extreme in their dissipation. By smelling their fragrance, one can know this, and there must surely be a way to resolve it.
There are ways to warn them. If one encounters a wild elephant in the wilderness, one will surely be injured; if one meets a tiger at a narrow pass, there is no way to avoid it.
By knowing where these dangers lie, one can take precautions for the future and thus avoid their harm.
Knowing whether a fetus in the womb is male or female, and even whether it will reach fulfillment or not, is likewise sufficient to startle the ignorant and deluded, and to lead them [to virtue].
They give rise to right faith. However, one must not focus one's intent solely on this to manifest spiritual wonders.

Rather, knowing the defilements of lust, ignorance, and anger in men and women, they employ skillful means to break them apart; knowing the treasures and hoards hidden within the earth, they employ skillful means to point them out.

All of these are likewise based on seizing the opportune moment to destroy evil and following conditions to benefit others. As for various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, they recognize their value and provenance.
Although these appear to be worldly arts, within the knowledge of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), even a single one lacking would render it incomplete.

How could worldly arts possibly be considered insignificant? [Question]: "In this section, the various celestial flowers, fruits, men, women, and sentient beings seem to overlap with what was mentioned previously. What is the intention behind including them here? [Answer]: "The three preceding sections each relied upon their own respective categories; although they manifested the perfect hearing (*pariśuddha-śrotra*), they did not yet achieve ultimate universal integration.

Now, in this section, we suddenly speak of the heavens and again of the human realm; we properly discuss sentient beings and then discuss insentient things. The intent is to clarify that they are presented in a chaotic intermingling, demonstrating unimpeded discernment. Thus, the principle of the nose faculty’s perfect hearing becomes even more clearly evident."
...of these). △ Third, verses on celestial incense:
"The various flowers of the heavens, such as the *māndārava* and *mañjūṣaka* ... (up to) by smelling their fragrance, one can know them all."

The first verse describes the insentient incense of the devas. The palaces of the devas vary in height and excellence; their adornments of precious flowers differ, and thus their fragrances likewise vary.

Therefore, they are collectively described as having distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. Following this, the verse on the "Gardens of the Heavens" describes the sentient incense of the devas.
As for "the devas," this includes the Four Great Kings below and the Yāma heaven and others above, entering and emerging from meditative concentration.

This refers to the incense [used] during periods of meditative concentration and periods of distraction. "At the time of first arising and at the time of passing away" refers to the incense [used] during the times of ascending and descending.
According to the prose (*gadya*), there are further types of incense to be burned, which are omitted in this verse. △ Fourth, the verse on the incense of the sages.
The assembly of bhikṣus always exerts themselves with diligence regarding the Dharma (up to: by smelling [the fragrance], they are able to know [all things].
These bhikṣus include both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; their recitation of scriptures, cultivation of wisdom, sitting in meditation, and practice of concentration are all for their own benefit.
The bodhisattvas are firm in resolve and cannot be compared to those at the initial stage; they cultivate themselves through meditation and recitation, and also preach the Dharma.
"To act as a person" means to encompass both self-benefit and the benefit of others. "In every age, the World-Honored One" refers collectively to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

"With all reverence" indicates that the conditions for spiritual resonance fill the space before him. "Out of compassion for the multitudes, he preaches the Dharma" signifies the universal salvation of great compassion.

The final four lines concern hearing the Dharma and practicing it; these were absent from the prose section and are thus supplemented by the verse. Having finished the separate listing of the various fragrances in the verse: △
The three verses conclude by summarizing its merits:
although one who upholds this sutra has not yet attained the nose born of the bodhisattva’s untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, they first obtain this mark of the nose.
This is the "nose of wisdom" born from the arising of untainted dharmas, for it is produced through the cultivation of pure, untainted dharmas.
The merits of the nose faculty are concluded. △ Fourth, the merits of the tongue faculty, in two parts: first, a general statement of the number of merits;
second, a detailed enumeration of the various merits. First:
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a good man (up to) attains twelve hundred merits of the tongue.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration of the various virtues has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first [part] has four sections: 1.

Transforming flavors into excellence; 2. Preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of the listeners; 3. Inspiring the assembly to listen to the Dharma; 4. Attaining the protection and mindfulness of the sages. First [section]:
Whether good or foul, whether delicious or not delicious—up to the point that nothing is not as delicious as celestial nectar.
"Good" refers to exquisite food; "foul" refers to coarse food. "Delicious" refers to the most excellent food; "not delicious" refers merely to ordinary food.
That these are transformed into a supreme flavor, like celestial nectar, is because the faculty of the tongue is purified; there is something distinct [about this].
This is the true flavor. Thus, there was a person of old who spoke the verse: "The fragrance of vegetable roots is the nature of meditative concentration.

Yet, when people of the world take life and commit various evil karmas, it is almost always due to their three-inch tongue-roots. If one can now find nothing that is not delicious, then coarse food may be eaten at all times.
△ Second, preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of the listener.
If, by means of the faculty of the tongue, one causes all within the great assembly [to attain] joy and happiness—such that everyone universally attains the truth, it is called "profound" (*shen*);
such that one skillfully adapts to the various capacities of beings, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*).
That one can enter their hearts and cause them all to rejoice and be happy is precisely due to being both profound and wondrous. △ Third, causing the assembly to listen to the Dharma.
Furthermore, the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and all other devas attended upon and made offerings to him for as long as their lives lasted.
Initially, they moved the male and female members of the eight classes of beings. As for the sequence of the discourse, it proceeded from the shallow to the profound, without deviation or disorder.

Because it is easy to enter through this [method], the celestial hosts were moved to come and listen. The same applies to the other sections; thus it is said that they all came near to make offerings for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, as indicated below, the fourfold assembly, kings, and ministers—including King Kṣemadatta (the King who Scatters Grain)—were likewise moved to do so.
As for the minor wheel-turning kings, they possess wheels of silver, copper, or iron; only the golden wheel-turning king who governs the four continents is called "great.
Regarding the seven treasures: first, the wheel; second, the jewel; third, the elephant; fourth, the horse; fifth, the general; sixth, the treasurer; and seventh, the queen.
Whenever a wheel-turning king appears in the world, these naturally emerge, each possessing supreme excellence.

Because of these merits, they are called "jewels. As for the "thousand sons," these are the sons of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); it is the natural law that when a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world, he possesses a certain number of sons.
Regarding "riding in his palaces," this means that because the wheel-turning monarch’s merit is exceptionally sublime, the palaces upon which he relies are always present with him.
From this point downward, he brings about a population of noble and virtuous people. "For the duration of their lives" means throughout their entire existence.

They do not depart from him, but attend upon him, serving him at his left and right. All of this is due to the purity of the faculty of the tongue, and is what is evoked by the profound and wondrous sound.
△ Fourth, obtaining the protection and mindfulness of the sages.

Furthermore, whenever Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas—up to those who can produce the profound and wondrous sound of the Dharma—constantly delight in seeing [this person], they will at times harbor thoughts of affection for them and, toward those who preach the Dharma for them, provide distant protection and support.
By virtue of this, their wisdom increases further, such that they are able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas; their eloquence becomes even more superior, such that they are able to...
Emerging from the profound and wondrous sound of the Dharma, the prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary (the introductory heading for the verses states):

The tongue-faculty of this person is pure and shall never again experience unpleasant flavors; whatever he eats or chews all becomes nectar.
△ Second, the verse on preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of the listeners:
"With a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preaches the Dharma for the great assembly... (up to) providing various supreme offerings."
The prose version merely states that it is "profound and subtle. That it is further described here as "pure" is because it accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
△ Third, the verse on inspiring the assembly to listen to the Dharma:
"The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth... constantly come to where he is."
The first four lines praise the eight classes [of celestial beings], omitting the female members of those eight classes. The word "etc. (*ādi*) collectively includes the remaining classes.

The next eight lines praise the kings and ministers, omitting the fourfold assembly (*catur-parṣad*). Although the text does not explicitly mention ministers, they are included within the category of "retinue.
The final eight lines expand upon the previous eight classes, omitting the *bhadra* (the virtuous) and the common people. △ Fourth, the verse on obtaining the protection of the sages.

"Mindfulness" means that the Buddhas and their disciples, upon hearing the sound of one's preaching of the Dharma, constantly keep one in mind and provide protection, or at times manifest themselves before them.

"Mindfulness" refers to being mindful with affection; it means always delighting in seeing [the practitioner]. "Protection" refers to providing secret empowerment by preaching the Dharma toward [the practitioner]. "Manifestation" [refers to appearing in person].

This refers to the "manifest protection," which is absent from the prose (*gadya*) and is supplemented by the verse (*śloka*). The remainder is not versified. This concludes the merits of the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*).
△ Five: The merits of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), in two parts: first, the general indication of the number of merits; second, the detailed enumeration of the various merits. First [part].
Furthermore, if a son of good family (up to) attains eight hundred merits of the body.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration of various virtues has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [part] has two sections: first, the essence is free from defilement;
second, the function is able to manifest signs. Regarding the first:
He has attained a pure body like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings joyfully behold.
As for the old woman to the east of the city, she did not joyfully behold the Buddha, and thus the Buddha could not deliver her. Now that she joyfully beholds him, sentient beings may be delivered.
△ Second, the manifestation of signs through his power.
Because their bodies are pure, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system (up to its limits) all manifests its forms and appearances within their bodies.

Initially, they are able to manifest the six realms of ordinary beings across the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world; this is discussed in terms of the horizontal extent of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment).

Regarding "the time of birth," it refers to when the nature of consciousness first takes up residence [in a new body]. Regarding "the time of death," it refers to when the light of the eyes has already ceased. As for the nature of consciousness first taking up residence, one may receive the body of a human or a deva.
Some receive bodies in the evil realms; thus it is said that they may go up or down, or be beautiful or ugly.

Once the light of their eyes has faded, some encounter mountains of knives and trees of swords, while others encounter the lotus groves of the Pure Land; thus it is said that they are born in good or evil places.

Outside, there are the great and small Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), and inside, the great and small Mount Meru; within these spaces dwell sentient beings who are not seen by the world. All of them...
It manifests within the body of the Dharma Master. From the lower realms up to the highest, this is discussed in terms of the vertical dimension of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support).

"All" refers to the intermediate environment (*bhājana-loka*), and "sentient beings" refers to the intermediate physical bodies (*indriya-śarīra*). This means that both the environmental world and the physical bodies of sentient beings all manifest within the body of the Dharma Master.
If one follows the sound [of the teaching], it can manifest the four types of noble ones (*ārya*); yet, these four noble ones inherently possess both provisional and ultimate aspects.

The six classes of ordinary beings are likewise divided into the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is only that people do not perceive this, remaining unaware of what to cultivate, what to sever, what to abandon, and what to seek.

Now that all these are manifest, this Dharma Master, within his pure body, manifests various causes and effects for the sake of all sentient beings and performs various Buddha-works, causing all sentient beings to cultivate the wholesome, sever the unwholesome, abandon the provisional, and seek the real. At that time, the World-Honored One manifested great supernatural power before Mañjuśrī and the entire assembly.
Because he had newly emerged from the earth, he pointed to Mañjuśrī and the others as those who had long resided there.

He necessarily manifested such supernatural power before the long-residing bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings in order to demonstrate that which is undivided yet divided, and that which is divided.
Yet they do not divide; rather, by expanding their minds, they cause the newly manifested assemblies to know that the emanation of bodies is, in reality, devoid of any trace of coming or going.
The reason Mañjuśrī is necessarily placed at the head is that this meaning cannot be understood except through the spiritual power of the Tathāgata;
it is not something that can be grasped by those who practice causes while already possessing the fruit, nor by those who merely possess great wisdom. △ Second, the specific [explanation].
This has two parts: first, manifesting through physical characteristics; second, indicating through sound. Regarding the first:
extending his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world, he displayed this supernatural power for a full hundred thousand years.

The tongue is the instrument for responding to capacities; without departing from it, one reaches as far as the Brahma-world. If there are those with capacity in the Brahma-world, one may respond to them right here.
Light possesses the merit of awakening the multitudes; without departing from it, it shines universally upon the Ten Powers.
If there are multitudes in the ten directions, there is no need to go there to awaken them. All of these are instances of the principle of differentiation within non-differentiation.
It is also like this: the various Buddhas who manifest their bodies beneath trees are likewise equal in this way; that is to say, they are identical despite not meeting.
That they are identical despite not meeting means they return to being of one body. This, moreover, is the meaning of "dividing without dividing.
Within the brief moment of a manifested spirit, there are a full hundred thousand years; thus, what is contracted is extended. By means of these hundred thousand years, people—
The brief manifestation of the spirit is both prolonged and abbreviated; prolongation and abbreviation are simultaneous.
Entering the three periods of time without leaving a trace, the one and the many are without obstruction, responding to the various capacities of beings without leaving a mark.

This is the great function of the whole body, which all Buddhas of the three periods have realized, are realizing, and will realize; it is the divine mechanism for benefiting sentient beings, which Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied, are studying, and will study.

Now, as for what must be studied: those who read this sutra, if they can apply their attention to the very moments of eating and dressing, then the luster of their tongues and the radiance of their pores will appear—not only in the Buddha and his emanations, but in them as well. Part Two: Demonstrating by means of sound (3).
First, the two sounds pervade everywhere; second, they awaken sentient beings; third, they accomplish their benefit. Regarding the first:
[he withdraws his tongue] and then, withdrawing the mark of his tongue, he coughs once. (Up to this point,) these two sounds pervade the ten directions.

they do not understand how to deal with it while eating and wearing clothes. Therefore, one must cut off the dust of sensory attachments and open another expedient means. Thus it is said: "He again withdrew his tongue-organ" and "all at once he cleared his throat" (and so forth).

Those who read this sutra, being unable to extend their broad and long tongues or emit light from all their pores, must instead observe others coughing and snapping their fingers; ultimately...

The grounds of all Buddha-worlds shook in six ways (up to) all being filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before.
That the sound reaches such places and is able to cause the grounds of the Buddha-worlds to shake is also the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata, intended to awaken sentient beings.
Once awakened, each turns their mind toward mindfulness of the Buddha; thus, they are moved by the empowerment of the Buddha’s power.

Therefore, the devas, relying on the Buddha’s supernatural power, proclaimed these words from mid-air to awaken them.

He indicates the primary and secondary marks, as well as the names and the Dharma being taught. Although they have already seen these from afar, they still do not know which country it is, who the Buddha is, or what Dharma is being taught.

Because this is the teaching for Bodhisattvas, he instructs them to give rise to a profound and far-reaching mind and to cultivate sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Because this is that which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas, he instructs them...
They made offerings to the Buddha to seek his protection and to awaken all sentient beings. △ Third, the accomplishment of benefit:
Those sentient beings, having heard the voice from the void (up to) attained unimpeded penetration as if it were a single buddha-field.
Having heard the voice from space, he knew the name of the land was Sahā; therefore, he joined his palms.
Knowing the name of the Buddha was Śākyamuni, he called upon that name for refuge. He spoke "Namo" twice to express the utmost depth of his devotion and reverence.

He did not mention "prostration" because as he called the name, he was already prostrating, making it unnecessary to state it separately. With various kinds of offerings, he scattered them afar toward Sahā.
As for the word "vā" (婆): it signifies the desire to rejoice in this sutra and the intention to seek the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

As for the various objects scattered from the ten directions that transform into a jeweled canopy, they arise through the sincere resolve of sentient beings; they gather like clouds and manifest as such.
This is brought about by the Tathāgata’s mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*). This mind of loving-kindness benefits all beings and, in turn, adorns himself;
therefore, it completely covers this Buddha-field and surveys the ten directions without limit or obstruction. Thus, everything is pervaded as if it were a single buddha-land.

Furthermore, by means of his tongue-mark, the radiance of his body hairs, his clearing of the throat, and the snapping of his fingers, the Tathāgata manifests to those dwelling nearby and responds to those in the ten directions from afar. He is able to...
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he performs great Buddha-works, awakening all sentient beings and accomplishing their benefit.

Furthermore, he causes the ten directions to merge into a single realm. For one who attains this function, the distinctions between "dividing the body" and "not dividing the body" are both superfluous terms.

The natural sound reaches the Brahma-world; its resonance pervades the ten directions. His tongue covers the void, and his speech transcends spatial dimensions.
