Regarding "the power of obscurity" and so forth: [The Buddha] wished to arrive together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, and first manifested as many precious lotuses as a portent.

The reason precious lotuses serve as a portent for the bodhisattvas is that flowers are capable of bearing fruit, and bodhisattvas are those who attain Buddhahood. As for being not far from the Dharma-seat, it was for the sake of...

The omen portends that he will arrive before long. The stem signifies that his power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) sustains him; the leaves signify that the wheel of wisdom (*prajñā-cakra*) has blossomed;
the filaments signify that his manifold practices have been mutually perfected; and the pedestal signifies that his great vows are fulfilled.

Thus, although the person has not yet arrived, the signs of his virtues appear first. One who possesses wisdom can naturally recognize this. Therefore, in the following passage, Mañjuśrī asks, "Who is this?"?
Regarding the causal conditions: first, there is the question concerning the manifestation of these auspicious omens.

Da Cheng states that the reason these omens appear first in this land in the future is to serve as a precursor to the signs of the [Buddha’s] coming, and to inspire the veneration of the assembled congregation.
*Jambūnada* is translated according to its meaning as "superior gold"; the significance of this has been seen previously. *Kiṃśuka* is here called "parrot" (*yīngwǔ*); this jewel is red in color.
Because its beak was such [as described]. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The *cīnaka* tree has leaves of a red color;
the color of the jewel is like that, hence it is so named. △ Third, Mañjuśrī infers the cause.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma (up to: took *cintāmaṇi* jewels and *vaiḍūrya* jewels for its base, and *jāmbūnada* gold and *candana* sandalwood for its stalk;

it was made of *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha* gems, with *lohitamukti* pearls for its filaments, and *uragasāra* agate for its pistils, with *sphaṭika* crystal for its pericarp, and *vaidūrya* lapis lazuli for its pedestal. This was an omen of the ultimate limit (*paramārtha*), which none but one of great wisdom could fathom; thus, only Mañjuśrī was able to inquire about it. Upon seeing this lotus flower...
Although the person has already been roughly visualized, because the assembly does not yet understand, they must wait for the Buddha’s explanation;
therefore, they ask what the causal conditions are for this omen appearing first. In the question, the single character "first" (xiān) already indicates that someone will arrive later.
Furthermore, the use of the single character "shuai" (瑞) clearly shows that he was no ordinary person. How could Mañjuśrī truly have been unaware?

As for why he did not say "eighty-four thousand" but rather "a certain number" (*jiǎnrú* 若干) and so forth, it is because he asked immediately upon seeing the flower, having not yet had the leisure to enumerate its specific count.
The stalk, leaves, filaments, and pedestal are all related to the virtues of this person; therefore, each is fully detailed within the question.
[The section on] Chen. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s direct response.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [up to] "...also wishes to make offerings to and hear the Lotus Sūtra.

This refers to the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, pointing to the person who manifested the omens; he wished to come from the World of Pure Flower... [and so forth], responding to the manifestation of the auspicious signs.

Regarding the cause: the final sentence states that they "also wish to make offerings to the Dharma and also wish to listen to the Dharma. These should properly be stated separately; it is merely for the sake of brevity that the phrasing is thus combined.
Having completed the task of serving the Master’s command. △ Third, the response to the summons of Prabhūtaratna, which has two parts:
first, Prabhūtaratna accepts the invitation and calls from afar; second, Gadgadasvara and the assembly together set out. First:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī wishes to see your body. At the outset, Mañjuśrī requested that [the Buddha] bestow his transformative power;
this must surely have been due to profound causes, which led to the attainment of such supreme fruit. Therefore, he asked what roots of goodness had been planted.
"What merit has been cultivated? By what roots of goodness was such supernatural power (ṛddhi) produced?"—this asks how many Buddhas were honored in the past.
"What merit has been cultivated?"—this asks what kind of offerings were made in the past.

Although supernatural power arises from past causes, the manifestation of supernormal faculties (abhijñā) must rely on present conditions; therefore, he further asks: "In what samādhi do you currently abide?"
"I pray that you will declare its name. Those who desire to diligently practice it shall yearn for its spiritual efficacy and emulate its entry and abiding.
Only by practicing this samādhi can one see it; this indicates that those who have not yet reached its realm cannot see it even if they come.
These words clearly reveal the skillful eloquence of a master. We thus know that Mañjuśrī’s request for empowerment was not for his own sake. As for 'form and characteristics' (rūpalakṣaṇa):"
Regarding "the physical form and appearance, and the deportment": "deportment" refers to outward manifestation. "Great" refers to superior characteristics;

"small" refers to inferior forms. "Advancing" means coming forward; "stopping" means remaining there. Because Mañjuśrī was concealed, [the Buddha] pushed back [the inquiry] out of ignorance, yet spoke of both.
He wished that through his supernatural power (ṛddhi), those who see him come might realize for themselves that he has not yet practiced that samādhi. Not so.
"One can see for oneself; it is simply that one requests the Buddha’s empowerment. At that time [the passage] below: The Buddha defers to Prabhūtaratna.
He does not summon him himself but defers to Prabhūtaratna because Mañjuśrī represents faith, Prabhūtaratna represents aspiration, and Gadgadasvara represents practice;

this is to manifest that the propagation of the sutra must necessarily be complete with the three provisions (*saṃbhāra*). At that time [the passage] below: Accepting the invitation and being summoned from afar. He...
That land is located one hundred and eight million *nayuta* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds away from here; yet in the text it says, "He addressed him, saying, 'Come,'" as if they were face-to-face.
This is because the voice of Prabhūtaratna is perfect and the faculty of Gadgadasvara is pure; thus, the sense organ and its object mutually pervade one another.
It is indeed thus. As for the indication that Mañjuśrī wishes to be seen: this is because within the mind of Gadgadasvara there has long been Mañjuśrī;
hearing of his desire to see him, [Mañjuśrī] will surely not fail to arrive promptly. 2. Gadgadasvara and the assembly set out together.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land (until) hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
From his initial disappearance there until his arrival here, he vanished from that land—this single phrase serves as the opening for the following "Universal Gate" chapter.

Because his manifestation involves both presence and absence, his wondrous response appears not yet fully perfected. Consequently, during the causal stage, he offered various jeweled bowls to the Buddha.
I vow that in the future, those who possess the capacity for the Dharma shall follow me. It is for this reason that several bodhisattvas have come together from afar.
Regarding the auspicious signs encountered along the way, the reach of their divine virtue caused heaven and earth to manifest their spiritual efficacy;
thus, the earth shook in six ways and a rain of various precious flowers fell. During the causal stage, for twelve thousand years, they offered music and performance arts to the Buddhas.
"May they, in the future, be accompanied by delightful sounds. For this reason, hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
This concludes the account of how [the music] came from afar. II. Properly explaining the arrival from afar has two parts: 1. Describing the appearance and indicating the arrival.
Second, the formal protocol for the audience with the Buddha. First:
This Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the broad petals of a vast blue lotus flower... [he proceeded] to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Sahā world.
In India there is the blue lotus (*utpala*). Its petals are long and broad, with a clear distinction between the blue and white; the Buddha’s eyes resemble them.

The Bodhisattvas of today are likewise so, and thus it is said they are "like" [the Buddha]. As for the term "vast," since the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are already large, the eyes are proportionate to them;
no subtle flower can serve as a metaphor for them. This is precisely what is meant by "immediate" (*ji*). "Harmonious union" (*hehe*) has the meaning of gathering together. According to...
In various sutras, when praising the Buddha, it is simply said that his face is like the full moon.

Now, because the countenance of a Bodhisattva is so vast and expansive that a single moon cannot compare to it, he is metaphorically likened to the combined light of hundreds of thousands of millions of moons. Even though these hundreds of thousands of millions of moons are combined...
Its vastness is like that; its physical perfection is slightly inferior, hence it is said to "surpass" it. His body is of true golden color—this is the essence (*tattva*).
His adornment of merit and virtue is the cause. His majestic power, radiance, and so forth are the fruit. "Blazing" means like a fire burning intensely.

Because he is awe-inspiring when beheld from afar; because he is approachable when drawing near, his various marks are fully perfected, such that although he dwells in the stage of a cause, his wondrous marks are identical to those of a Buddha. Nārāyaṇa is the name of a celestial athlete.
Their bodies are firm and solid, incapable of being thwarted or destroyed; the physical marks of the Bodhisattvas are like this.

Previously it was said that they all set out together, but it did not specify how they set out. Now it says they "enter" among the seven treasures and so forth; this refers to their setting out by mounting a platform and traveling through space.
Regarding "respectfully surrounding," this means the principal figures and their attendants form a complete circle, facing one another with composure, rather than rushing about in haste.

Because of the exhaustion resulting from such labor, and because of the loss of the proper ritual order, those who have come here to Gṛdhrakūṭa to make offerings to the Buddha and listen to the Dharma behold Mañjuśrī and the others.
△ Second, the formal approach and audience, which has two parts: first, seeing Śākyamuni; second, seeing Prabhūtaratna. First:
Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace [and asked]: "Are you dwelling in peace, free from affliction, and able to endure for a long time?

First, he offered a necklace to the Buddha. The reason for the arrival of Gadgadasvara was to make offerings to Śākyamuni; therefore, upon arriving, he first made the offering and then spoke as follows.

On behalf of his teacher, he inquired after [the Buddha's] well-being. This followed the previous account of Gadgadasvara’s desire to come, wherein that Buddha merely cautioned him to forget all worldly attachments.
Furthermore, there are no words of inquiry regarding his well-being included [in the text], yet they must certainly have existed; it is simply that the compiler of the sutra did not record them.

In the questions, Śākyamuni is addressed first and then Prabhūtaratna; this is merely because of the distinction between host and guest. Within the questions directed at Śākyamuni, the discourse is divided into three sections.
In the first section, he is described as being externally free from sorrow and internally detached from affliction—meaning he has little illness and little...
As for affliction: movement is most appropriate, and stillness is especially suitable; this is what is meant by being light and agile in daily activities.
When the Way of the Dharma is established, demons and heretics do not arise; this is what is meant by practicing with peace and bliss. This is the rough inquiry.

In the following section, it says that if one wishes to have little illness and little affliction, one must ensure that the four great elements are in harmony. As for these four great elements: they are to be universally sustained through a heart of loving-kindness.
The earth element is precisely the mind of compassion, which universally moistens all. The water element is the mind of sympathetic joy, which rises buoyantly.
The fire element is the mind of equanimity, which abides nowhere. The wind element is the harmonization [of these states]:

that is to say, compassion does not exceed love, sympathetic joy does not exceed delight, and equanimity does not exceed patience. By means of this, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from affliction; thus it is called "sage."
To sever afflictions through wisdom and attain ease and agility in one’s daily life, one must be able to endure worldly affairs.

To be able to endure means that each matter accords with the Dharma and does not interfere with the holy mind; it is for this reason that one remains composed amidst experience, whether in motion or stillness, and everything becomes appropriate.
To attain peaceful and joyful practice, one must find sentient beings easy to deliver. To be easy to deliver means to follow the teachings.
Practice accordingly. Do not cling to the activities of Māra. For this reason, one’s vision is like that of a butcher who sees no whole ox before him; he moves with effortless ease.

This refers to the middle section of the three parts. Within these three sections, it is said that to achieve harmony among the four great elements, one must ensure that sentient beings are free from obstacles;
therefore, the question is asked whether there is no excessive greed, anger, or delusion, etc., so that worldly affairs may be managed as desired.
Patience requires that sentient beings act in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, he asks whether they are free from such things as filial impiety toward parents and lack of respect for śramaṇas.

The "five emotions" (wu qing) refers to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). To be unrestrained by the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and to have no knowledge of how to stop them is called "lack of restraint.
If one wishes for sentient beings to be easily delivered, one must abandon the activities of Māra; therefore, he asks concerning sentient beings.

"Are you able to subdue all the demonic adversaries? This is a detailed inquiry. Within the questions concerning Prabhūtaratna, first he asks whether [the Buddha] has come, and next he asks whether he will remain;
this clearly shows that [the Buddha] must certainly come. Yet, there is fear that he may not have arrived yet, or that having arrived, he might be unwilling to remain for long.
Now that the Way of Śākyamuni has found its entrustment and the vow of Prabhūtaratna is not violated, this is indeed peace and security.
With few afflictions, he realized the matter according to the Dharma; only after concluding his session did he return, which signifies his capacity for endurance and long-term residence.
△ Second, seeing Prabhūtaratna:
"World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna... [until] Mañjuśrī and the others have come here for this purpose."
When Gadgadasvara first sought to see [the Buddha], having already received a distant summons, he ought to have had a karmic affinity;
yet, arriving here and failing to obtain even a single glimpse of his face, how could he restrain himself? Thus, he requested that the World-Honored One manifest him for his sight.

As for why Gadgadasvara could not see him on his own and must wait for the Buddha’s manifestation, the *Śāstra* explains that after the body was divided and dispersed, the stupa remained closed as before; it could not be opened without the power of the Buddha.
[The Buddha] was able to reopen [the stupa]. To manifest the Dharma, practice does not arise of itself; its arising must necessarily depend upon the Truth (*tathatā*).

If it is thus, only then can it fulfill the vow. At that time [and below], the World-Honored One, on behalf of the request, understood the sentiments of Gadgadasvara and spoke to Prabhūtaratna, desiring that he once again display his wondrous form to accord with the intent of the visitor.
At that time [and below], Prabhūtaratna manifested his form; [Gadgadasvara] should now offer praise.

The time of "goodness" is precisely the time when signs are manifested. Since one is able to make offerings to the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and furthermore draw near to spiritual friends to receive benefit, he praises it by repeating "Excellent! (Sādhu).

This refers to the time when Gadgadasvara was about to arrive, speaking these words to his own teacher while making offerings to Śākyamuni and beholding Mañjuśrī and the others; yet even this is difficult to practice.
...such matters. How much more so when one abandons that Pure Light and enters far into this defiled land; this is truly most difficult.
Therefore, Many Treasures raised this [stūpa] to manifest what he praised, showing it was no empty eulogy. Thus the chapter on "The Arrival of Gadgadasvara" concludes.
II. The Tathāgata Discusses His Merits (in three parts): 1. First, discussing his roots of goodness from past lives. 2. Second, discussing his present [merits].
In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, regarding the names of the three samādhis discussed in the latter part, there are two sections: first, the inquiry of Śrīmālā;
second, the Tathāgata’s response. Regarding the first:
at that time, the Bodhisattva Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "By cultivating what merit does one possess such supernormal power?"
The flower possesses two virtues: first, its color is exquisite and beautiful; second, its fragrance is pure and fragrant.
The Bodhisattva’s physical appearance is dignified and majestic, and his moral virtue is overflowing, resembling these qualities; therefore, he was given this name.

Mañjuśrī recognized him at the mere sight of him, whereas Puṣpamitra (Hua-de), despite seeing him, still harbored doubts, and thus asked again. Furthermore, in the past, Miaoyin (Ghoṣadatta) was the Lady Jingde (Jing-de fu-ren), while Hua-de...
In the past, he was King Wondrous Adornment. Throughout successive lifetimes, they have inspired one another; therefore, he now again demonstrates this by posing the question.
△ Second, the Tathāgata provides the answer.
The Buddha told Huade Bodhisattva: "In the past, there was a Buddha [up to] who is none other than the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta).
First, he cites his original teacher: the Buddha named King Cloud-Thunder Sound (Meghadundubhisvara-rāja). His voice issues from the gate of compassion to awaken those who are deaf and blind;

thus he is metaphorically likened to a cloud and thunder. He subdues the heterodox and responds to the capacities of beings; his wisdom and eloquence are unimpeded, and thus he is sovereign like a king."

The name of the land is Manifesting All Worlds; within a single realm, there are differing perceptions, such that purity and impurity are not uniform—just as when various devas eat from the same vessel, yet the coarse and the exquisite appear differently to each. The name of the eon is Joyful Vision;

at that time, there was a Buddha dwelling in the world whom all who saw him rejoiced in. This is the Buddha whom this Gadgadasvara originally served, as well as the names of the eon and the land upon which he relied.

Furthermore, regarding "Miaoyin" (Wonderful Sound) below: next, he cites a past account (*pūrvayoga*). That person who was named Miaoyin at that time had long possessed the title of "Master of Dharma," a name not assumed for the first time now.
His music reached a hundred thousand [melodies], which may be called "Juntian" (the Music of Heaven);

how much more so when it lasted for twelve thousand years—the firmness of his power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*) can thus be known. The bowl was made of the seven treasures; it truly served as a vessel for the Dharma, all the more so since...
"Eighty-four thousand. From this, the grandeur of his offerings can be known. Because of this, he was moved by celestial music that followed him, which the Bodhisattva accompanied;

thus it says, "By these causes and conditions," and so forth. This concludes the answer to Puṣpadatta’s question regarding what roots of goodness he had planted and what merits he had cultivated to possess such supernormal power. Below the section on Puṣpadatta, the text connects the past with the present.
The wondrous voice of the past is the very same as the wondrous voice of the present; cause and effect are clearly distinguished, so there is no need for further questioning.

The preceding discussion on the roots of goodness from former lives is concluded. II. Second, the discussion of present spiritual wisdom has two parts: 1. Fully manifesting the power of the cause; 2. Detailed demonstration of the function of the fruit.
First [fully manifesting the power of the cause]:
"Flower Virtue (Huade)" refers to the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) [up to] "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
The phrase "had already made offerings to" and so forth means that prior to the time of Thunder Sound (*Meghasvara*), he had already made offerings to Buddhas and planted roots of virtue;

it was not only during the time of Thunder Sound that this was the case. Furthermore, the phrase "encountered" and so forth means that after the time of Thunder Sound, he again encountered a certain number [of Buddhas].

△ Second, a detailed exposition of the fruit and its functions, in two parts: first, a general indication; second, a specific explanation. First [the general indication].
Huade, you have merely seen the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (up to) preaching this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.

According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, Avalokiteśvara manifests his body in response to the capacities of beings; he does so either to enable them to escape their respective conditions or to increase their merit according to their capacity.
Now, Gadgadasvara specifically preaches this [sutra] for them. These two sages preach the Dharma together, yet they do so both primarily and concurrently.

They are not the same. △ Second, the specific explanation has two parts: first, the transformation of the mundane world; second, the transformation of the supramundane world. Regarding the first of these two, there are two sections:

He may manifest in the body of Brahmā or the body of Śakra (up to) transforming into a female body to preach this sūtra.
First, he manifests the bodies of the celestial hosts: Brahmā, Śakra, and Maheśvara. Regarding the "Śakra," this refers to the introductory section.

As for the "Great General of the Gods," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are eight kṣatriyas who are the mighty warriors among the gods. Vaiśravaṇa is translated here as "Much-Hearing" (Bahudhāraṇa); he is the [Lord] of the North.

Regarding the title "Heavenly King" (*devendra*), other deities are not mentioned because they can be understood by analogy. Alternatively, appearing below the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*), they manifest in the forms of human beings;
thus, the two kings may be known. A "Householder" (*gṛhapati*) refers to one who is advanced in years and of high moral standing, revered and esteemed by the multitude.

A "Layman" (*upāsaka*) refers to one who delights in discussing profound teachings and dwells in purity. An "Official" (*rājapuruṣa*) refers to one who adjudicates matters within the state and provinces, bestowing grace upon the people.
Those who assist in governance; Brahmins, meaning those whose conduct is pure and lofty, dwelling in seclusion amidst mountains and fields;

the fourfold assembly, meaning those who uphold the precepts and maintain their persons, practicing according to the Dharma; women, meaning those who have married into other families, sharing in the honor or obscurity of their husbands;

Each is distinct. Yet the supernatural powers and wisdom of the Bodhisattva can manifest accordingly;

they may manifest as devas or nāgas, or appear in the bodies of the eight classes of beings, and preach the phrases of this sutra. This applies to all the aforementioned forms, because wherever a body is manifested, the Dharma must necessarily be preached.

Regarding "in various difficult places": he manifests a body in locations of hardship. As for those "difficult places," these include the northern continent (Uttarakuru) with its long life spans, and the presence of a Buddha.
The Buddhas are equal in their subsequent [manifestations]. However, these [beings] were obstructed by difficult circumstances and were unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma;
thus, the Bodhisattva specifically manifested his body for them to rescue and liberate them from those difficult circumstances.

Although the text does not explicitly state that he "manifested his body," there is no impediment to saying so, as it has been the practice since antiquity to act among beings of different classes. This extends down to the manifestation of the form of a palace lady. Now...
The term "those who have reached [this state]" is a concise expression that includes all women subject to constraints.

While it may be said that being a woman is not inherently difficult to endure, one is restricted by one's parents in youth, held in check by one's husband in middle age, and obstructed by one's children in old age;
thus, throughout one's life, one is under constraint and lacks any share of freedom. This is especially true for those within the palace precincts.

It is difficult for one's feet to cross the threshold; were it not for the supernatural transformations and wisdom of a Bodhisattva, how could one, facing old age and death at the inner gate, behold the Supreme Person and hear the wondrous Dharma? Furthermore, these words of the sutra should also be understood as applying to the preceding context.
This is because the purpose of preaching this sutra was originally for the sake of providing salvation and relief. △ Second, the summary of divine wisdom:

First, we shall properly conclude with the divine wisdom. Now, the Dharmakāya is without marks, yet it manifests form in response to things. Prajñā is without cognition, yet it illuminates in response to conditions.

This is the meaning of "is bodhi" (is enlightenment) and below. Using this as an analogy for the rest, even if one specializes in propagating the Lotus Sūtra.
He guides and instructs according to individual capacities; hence it is said that there are "various wisdoms. He causes unsurpassed *bodhi* to be within the reach of every person;

hence it is said that he "illuminates the Sahā world. To those who should be planted as seeds, he plants them; to those who should be ripened, he ripens them; to those who should be liberated, he liberates them;
hence it is said that each "attains what they know. Yet his wondrous response does not stagnate in any single corner; how could his great transformation ever discriminate between different beings?

Therefore, it is said that throughout the *sāhasra-cūḍika* worlds of the ten directions, it is likewise so. This concludes the section on responding to and transforming the mundane world. II. Responding to and Transforming the Supramundane World.
If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a *śrāvaka*, [and so forth,] up to: "The power of his wisdom is such as this."
First, to explain the manifestation of forms individually: [The beings] fundamentally value the path of the śrāvaka and look up to those people with admiration;
they are to be delivered by means of the form of a śrāvaka. If another form were manifested, they would not even wish to see it, so how could it possibly move and transform their minds?
In order to cause them to advance toward hearing this sutra, he immediately manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them;

the forms of pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas should be understood by analogy. If they have long admired the Buddha-way and wish to see the body of a Buddha, they should be delivered by means of the Buddha-form.
If one were to manifest other forms, it would instead contradict the Great Mind; therefore, one manifests the form of a Buddha. Such phrases conclude what has already been explained above.
Furthermore, the phrase "and so forth" comprehensively includes the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]. As it is said:

for those who are to be saved by the form of a Bodhisattva in his final birth, he manifests as a Bodhisattva in his final birth; for those who are to be saved by the form of entering the womb, he manifests entering the womb.
...and so forth. To avoid excessive prolixity, these have been stated by way of abbreviation.
If, upon hearing of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one gives rise to a heart of longing and reverence, thereby planting roots of goodness, such a person is one who is to be delivered through parinirvāṇa.

Had he remained in the world, [the disciple] might instead give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, leading to weariness and indolence; therefore, he manifests parinirvāṇa. This means that although there is no actual extinction, yet...

"Extinction" (nirvāṇa) refers to this very point. "Huade" (Flower Virtue) and those below summarize spiritual wisdom (*jñāna*). The previous summary concerning the manifestation of transformation within the mundane world merely mentioned "spiritual wisdom";
this summary concerns the manifestation of transformation in the supramundane realm, and thus again employs the term "Great Word.
"The matter is such as this" points out and informs Huade as well as the rest of the assembly. This concludes the discussion on present spiritual wisdom. △ Third, the subsequent discussion.
Regarding the names of the samādhis:
at that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying [up to] "able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
First, Flower Virtue asked; Mañjuśrī had already questioned [the Buddha], yet the World-Honored One had not yet answered; therefore, Flower Virtue asked again. This is the intent.
That is to say: having heard what the Buddha spoke, [the assembly] already knew that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound had deeply planted roots of goodness and possessed such divine wisdom;
yet, although this was due to past causes, it was also supported by present conditions.

However, they did not yet know which samādhi he currently dwelt in to be able to act in such a way, and thus they still prayed for him to explain it so that they might study accordingly. From "The Buddha told them" onwards, the World-Honored One provides the answer. (3)
The name "Maitreya" differs slightly from that realized by Sudarśana. This is because they share the same samādhi, yet its functional efficacy is particularly superior.
The Tathāgata has finished discussing his merits. III. The Return of Gadgadasvara to His Country. This section has three parts: 1. The completion of beneficial deeds; 2.
Gadgadasvara’s return to his country; 3. A summary of the accomplishment before the Buddha. First: [Text continues]
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, [the assembly] also attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī.

The bodhisattvas who had come together were those who possessed the physical form but were yet minute [in their realization]. Therefore, it is because of this teaching that they are all able to realize and enter [it].

The bodhisattvas of this world had already been able to approximate [this state] in the previous chapter; now, having heard this chapter, they have thoroughly realized it without contradiction. Thus [it is said].
It is also possible. Not only will they attain these samādhis, but they will also be able to acquire the power of dhāraṇī;
regarding the words and meanings spoken by the Buddha, they will remember, receive, and uphold them without any forgetfulness, thereby circulating this Dharma.
It is for this reason that, naturally, even through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, he does not fall, and the light shines forth upon the arrival of Gadgadasvara. 2.
Gadgadasvara Returns to His Own Land.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara... [proceeding] until he arrived at the place of the Buddha Śubhavyūhapadmottara-jñāna.

The preceding section shows that both assemblies have obtained benefit, manifesting the merit of transforming others. This present section concerns making offerings to the Buddha and the stūpas, illustrating the excellence of one’s own practice.
Since the dual benefit of self and others is thus fully realized, there is nothing further to be done; therefore, one should return to one's native land.
Regarding the various countries passed through and so forth—one comes in this manner and departs in this manner—and once arrived at one's native land and so forth, it is in this manner that...
Seeing Śākyamuni, he likewise saw the King of the Constellations (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) composed and self-possessed, remaining unchanged from beginning to end.
This was further evidenced in his lack of any diminution regarding his supernormal powers and wisdom. △ Third, the description by the Buddha confirming this.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I went to the Sahā world and attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
This first section describes the deeds performed; having received the command to come, he now reports back upon his return. Furthermore, the following section describes the benefits achieved.
Thus concludes the account of Gadgadasvara’s completion of his mission and his return to his own country. 4. The Benefits Attained by the Assembly Upon Hearing This Chapter.
While this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s Coming and Going" was being preached, the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇarāja attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Forty-two thousand devaputras beheld him with their own eyes as he arrived and beheld him with their own eyes as he departed; they gazed at him with fixed, unblinking vision, not giving rise to a single thought.
Subsequently, even the marks of coming and going could no longer be apprehended; the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing shone forth with brilliant clarity.
Manifest before them. This is what is meant by attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Bodhisattva Puṣpadeva saw that his coming was without attachment and his going was without obstruction; because he was neither attached nor obstructed, he could not be said to exist. Yet, because he came and went, he could not be said to be non-existent.
Since he cannot be said to be non-existent, there is no mark of non-existence. Since he cannot be said to exist, [there is no mark of existence].
There are no marks; both marks are absent. Having wondrously realized the true mark (dharmatā), this is called attaining the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
Thus, Miaoyin, having forgotten all attachments, completed his propagation of the sūtra.
△ Section 25: The Universal Door of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s Dispelling of Phenomena through Perfect Response (The title of the chapter reads:
*The Lotus Sutra, Chapter on the Universal Door of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*, Number Twenty-Five).
According to the *Bie xing xu* (Prolegomenon to the Separate Circulation), the correct Western pronunciation is *Anabulujidishu*; this is translated here as "Contemplation" (*guan*).

Regarding Avalokiteśvara: according to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, during the time of the Buddha Ratnagarbha in the past, there was a universal monarch whose eldest crown prince made offerings to the Buddha and provided for the Sangha for three months. He then made this vow:

"If there are sentient beings undergoing the sufferings of the three miserable realms who are able to mindfully recollect me and invoke my name, may I perceive them through my divine eye and divine ear; should they not be spared from their suffering..."
"If it were suffering, I would never attain bodhi. For this reason, that Buddha was given the name Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva himself declares:

"Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the vajra-samādhi of illusory hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, whereby I achieved the thirty-two transformations."
Regarding the fourteen fearlessnesses and the four inconceivables, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained this Dharma-gate of perfect penetration.
In the midst of the great assembly, he conferred upon me the title of Avalokiteśvara; thus, in this present sutra, I seek out sounds to rescue beings from suffering.

The meaning is the same as that of the *Baihuajing* (Flower of Sorrow Sutra). If one investigates the cause by which it can save, the merit originates from "turning back to hear" (*fanwen*), which also subsumes the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
That its essence is replete with all virtues is called "Universal" (*Pu*). That its function manifests through various means is called a "Gate" (*men*).

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s attainment of true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), wherein the infinite qualities of nature are fully possessed; and according to the capacities of beings, infinite wondrous functions manifest accordingly. All [of these]...
He emerges from this. In the sutra, only his function is revealed; in the title, both his essence and function are presented together.
Combining the person with the dharma, it is titled "Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate. To clarify its specific meaning: first, it serves to dispel the conceptual marks of the preceding chapter.
In that previous chapter, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara came having received illumination and departed once his task was finished, appearing as though there were coming and going.
Regarding the characteristics: if there were truly coming and going, then the response [to prayers] would not be so universal.

To dispel this notion, this chapter is taught so that one may know that as soon as a single thought arises, all sufferings are immediately cast off; such is the spontaneous nature of resonance and response. What, then, is there to come or go?
Second, it serves to erase the traces left by the previous chapter, wherein the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound vanished from that land and appeared here.
In this regard, there appears to be a trace of appearing and disappearing. If such appearing and disappearing were real, then one would exclude the other.
To dispel this trace, this chapter is taught so that it may be known that while the emanated bodies respond everywhere, the single reality remains unmoved;

thus, they are present simultaneously throughout the ten directions—what is there to appear, and what is there to disappear? Thirdly, it is to manifest the function of uprooting suffering, following the previous chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
[Sa]. This alone clearly reveals the function of the Dharma-teaching; although it universally rescues all from difficulties, it does not explicitly clarify this point.
Now, therefore, the extraction from suffering is extensively revealed to fulfill the aforementioned function. Fourth, it is to manifest the urgency of saving the world:

whereas the previous chapter on the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound focused primarily on manifesting the body to preach the Dharma and did not mention the eradication of delusions by upholding the name, what of those sentient beings [who cannot encounter such manifestations]?
The three poisons blaze fiercely; it is truly difficult to hear the Dharma. Without skillful means, one may instead lose the benefit.

Now, this chapter—using constant mindfulness and reverence to extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion—is especially a vital and urgent necessity for saving the world. Fifth, it demonstrates the ease with which the mundane are gathered:
whereas the preceding chapter was dedicated solely to propagating the Lotus Sūtra and emphasized realization of the Truth, this one addresses the children of sentient beings.
Women’s affections are profound, while their mindfulness of the Buddha-dharma is slight. If one does not accord with worldly customs, even the truth itself will be lost.

Now, in this chapter, by means of prostration and making offerings, one gives birth to sons endowed with merit and wisdom, as well as daughters possessing auspicious marks; this is especially a skillful means for gathering in the laity.
In brief, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s compassion is vast and great, and his vows are profound and far-reaching, surpassing those of the twenty-four sages.
Having realized perfect penetration, it alone is called the "True Reality. Its merit is equal to that of sixty-two billion bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In discussing the grand efficacy of its responsive manifestations, it exhausts the ultimate limit of perfect subtlety. Thus it has been widely circulated.
This may serve as a guide. Therefore, the Venerable Zengxiu preached this chapter. (The scripture is divided into three parts: First, the prose section provides specific indications;

second, the verse section reveals the meaning through synthesis; third, the benefits gained from hearing the chapter. Regarding the first, the prose section provides specific indications (according to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, there are three kinds of superior functions of a Bodhisattva:

first, the thirty-two manifestations; second, the four fearlessnesses; and third, the four inconceivable powers. These are now also present here by implication. However, regarding the structure of the questions and answers, and the points where the textual flow is interrupted or concluded, it differs in many respects from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*).

The categories are similar. If one were to strictly follow that classification, it would obstruct the current text; yet if one were to rely entirely on this interpretation, there is fear of contradicting one's own words. Now, the classification follows the explanation of this sutra while simultaneously reconciling it with the other, so that the two sutras may correspond and both the text and its meaning are fully realized.

(2) First, the reason for the names as established through question and answer; second, the skillful means of wandering and transforming. Regarding the first: [The disciple] raises the names and requests instruction. 1. Question and Answer on the Reason for Receiving the Name 2. Question and Answer on the Skillful Means of Wandering and Transforming Regarding the first of these two: 1. The Disciple Raises the Names and Requests Instruction 2. At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat... [up to] "...for what reason is he named Avalokiteśvara? As for why the Bodhisattva is named Akṣayamati:

because from the very first moment he resolved his mind upon exhausting the realms of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), and since the realms of sentient beings are inexhaustible, the Bodhisattva’s intention is likewise inexhaustible. Thus, as the foolish praise says: "The world is boundless and turbid with dust."
Turbulent! The countless karmas of sentient beings leave them in a state of frantic haste; the river of craving has no bottom, its waves flow on and on.

For this reason, I am named Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible Intent). At the conclusion of the correct cultivation, I manifest as the one suited to the occasion (*yathābhavya*) so that the teaching may be ultimately propagated.
It is solely because this intent is inexhaustible that I bare my shoulder to facilitate service, exhausting all resources for the sake of the Path. With palms joined, I uphold the One.
This is the ritual for the earnest invitation. Avalokiteśvara is venerated throughout the Dharma-realm; his influence over the multitude of sages is like the wind that bends the grass.
His name does not manifest itself spontaneously; where there is manifestation, there must be a cause. Therefore, he asks by what causes and conditions he is named "Avalokiteśvara.

This is because the Tathāgata wishes to demonstrate his practice through his name, serving as a method for those who propagate the sutra in the final age. △ Second, the Tathāgata fully demonstrates the response.

This corresponds to the fourteen fearlessnesses in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Following the current text, it is divided into two parts: first, the direct answer concerning the reason for receiving this name; second, the extensive manifestation of the response to the invocation of the name.

The first part has three sections: first, a general indication of seeking out sounds to save beings from suffering; second, a specific demonstration of the response to the invocation of the name. The first of these [three] has three sub-sections: first, a general statement on seeking out sounds to rescue those in distress; second, a detailed exposition of the response to the invocation of the name.

The third section provides the answer regarding the causes and conditions for obtaining the name [of this samādhi]. First, it presents a general heading: "Seeking the Sound to Rescue from Suffering" (this refers to the *Lengyan jing* passage on being fearless amidst suffering and affliction).
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati... [up to] "...immediately observing their sounds, all attained liberation."
The initial suffering is described by names such as "Immeasurable Hundred Thousand" and so forth; these are numerous indefinite numbers, not implying that there are only this many sentient beings.

The *Lengyan jing zhengmo shu* (Commentary on the Correct Pulse of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) states: "Although suffering and affliction are universal, they may be categorized separately according to body and mind;
for while suffering torments the body, affliction disturbs the mind. It further states: "They are listed separately..."
Not all hardships are exhausted; they are all subsumed herein. Regarding "observing the world below" and "seeking the sound to bring about liberation":
"immediately observing their sounds" means seeking where the sound resides and then bestowing empowerment upon it. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"First, because I do not observe my own auditory organ, but rather observe the observer, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions..."

By contemplating their sounds, one immediately attains liberation. To explain the meaning: "not contemplating sound" means not being like sentient beings who single-mindedly follow after sensory objects.
"Contemplating by means of contemplation" means turning back to contemplate one's own nature from the perspective of that which contemplates.
If one can cultivate in this way oneself, one can also cause those suffering sentient beings to be moved and inspired upon hearing one's name.
Because they invoke my name, it is said, "contemplate their voices. It does not say "invoke the name," but rather "contemplate the voice.

This is because invoking the name belongs solely to the practice of recollecting through phenomena (*dharma*), whereas contemplating the voice also encompasses the maintenance of principle (*li*). This is due to the empowerment of the Bodhisattva’s power of compassion, which enables the simultaneous cultivation of both principle and phenomena;
thus, while this present sutra speaks of invoking the name with a single mind, the ancient masters have also stated that there is [this dual aspect].
There is indeed a principle to this matter. However, while practice based on phenomena may not necessarily accord with principle, practice based on principle invariably encompasses all phenomena.

Therefore, when it speaks simply of "observing sound," it simultaneously includes the act of "naming. Yet, in the practice of naming phenomena, the mind of the practitioner meets the mind of the Sage;

whereas in the practice of principle, one forgets sensory objects, and both the nature of suffering and the nature of sound become quiescent. Thus it is said that one immediately attains liberation. These two...

The reason why the sutras do not entirely agree is that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* emphasizes the exhortation to practice; thus, its "observing the sounds" refers to the resonance of the sentient beings' faculties.
This sutra, however, is solely intended to manifest the [Buddha's] power of application; thus, its "observing the sounds" refers to the response of the Sage.
There is difference within sameness; pray do not "mark the boat" [in pursuit of what has already passed]. △ Second, specifically showing the response to the invocation of the name:
"If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... (up to) all shall attain liberation from the calamity of the rākṣasas."

First, it can rescue one from the calamity of fire (this refers to the "fearlessness regarding the calamity of fire" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*). The *Lengyan Zhengmo* states: "Having realized the ultimate Dharma-realm, his majestic spiritual power is immeasurable;

therefore, those who single-mindedly invoke his name are immediately embraced by the majestic light of his great compassion and do not fall into the calamity of fire, just as when one enters the shade of a mountain, the summer heat cannot penetrate. This is the surplus power of his self-benefit added [for the sake of others].

It is through the power of compassionate vows that such a thing is possible. That sutra states: "Second, the revolving and returning of knowledge and vision enables all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.
To explain the meaning: "the revolving and returning of knowledge and vision" refers to the mutual interpenetration of the six sense faculties.
Since the Bodhisattva has already revolved the faculty of hearing back to its original nature, knowledge and vision likewise follow the hearing and revolve back to their source. Regarding this...

This refers to the reversal of the single faculty; it is the liberation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Now, seeing and cognition belong to the nature of fire and are thus interconnected with all fiery natures.

Therefore, when the activity of seeing intersects [with fire], one perceives fierce flames. Now, knowing that seeing has already been reversed, one can likewise respond to conditions by reversing those other fires as well.
Thus, it causes sentient beings not to be burned by fire. This is what the present sutra calls "awesome spiritual power" (*prabhāva*).

As for this power, it also arises from the ultimate perfection of the practice of *xuánfù* (revolving and returning). There is difference within sameness; one must understand this well. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern. (*The Record of Manifested Responses* states:

Zhū Chángshū was in Luoyang during the Yuánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty when his thatched house was overtaken by a spreading fire. Amidst a great wind, there was no possibility of escape. He single-mindedly invoked the name [of the Buddha], whereupon the wind shifted and the fire turned back toward the neighboring houses and was extinguished).

If practiced at the lower level, it can rescue one from the perils of water (this is precisely the "Fearlessness in the Peril of Water" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*). As for why the term "awesome spiritual power" (*weishén*) is not used: [it is because]...

This can be understood by reference to what precedes it. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Third, the revolving and returning of hearing and listening, which causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned.
To explain the meaning: "the revolving and returning of hearing and listening" refers precisely to the revolving of the faculty of hearing back to its original nature.
However, since the faculties of hearing and listening belong to the element of water and are interconnected with all watery natures, when the karma of hearing engages, then seeing [arises].

Regarding the great waters: now that [the practitioner] has returned to hearing and restored their nature, they are likewise able to respond to conditions and return those remaining waters to their source, thereby ensuring that sentient beings are not drowned by the great floods.

(The Biography states: "Dào Jiǒng and two others were traveling together on ice across the Yù River. When they were nearly halfway across, one man fell forward into the water, and the next sank as well. Jiǒng moved back and forth upon the surface of the water.")

One will certainly drown without doubt. If one single-mindedly recites the name, the feet will feel like treading on a board until nightfall; then, encountering a red light, one will ultimately reach the shore. "Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back into themselves, one leaves behind all sensory dusts and delusions; this can cause sentient beings such that fetters, shackles, and chains cannot bind them. To explain the meaning:

△ Fourth, the ability to escape the peril of bandits (this is the "Fearlessness in the Peril of Bandits" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*).

hence the word "immediately. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Eighth, the sounds are extinguished and hearing becomes perfect."

The power of universal compassion enables sentient beings to pass through perilous paths unrobbed by bandits. To explain the meaning: "the cessation of sound" means that the sensory object of sound is not obstructed;

"universal hearing" means that the nature of the faculty is eternally pervasive. Because it is eternally pervasive, one seeks out the location of sounds and universally generates the power of compassion.

May all sentient beings, when encountering bandits, not be plundered. (The tradition says: During the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, the monk Huida went to the northern Long Mountains to dig for licorice root.

The majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Immeasurable Intent, is as sublime as this.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, each [method] has its own specific cause, yet none departs from the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

Great! It is to be looked up to but cannot be reached. He is able to completely escape the four difficulties. △ Second, the ability to depart from the three poisons, in two parts:
first, a specific explanation of departing from the poisons; second, a summary of his spiritual powers. First [part].
If there are sentient beings who abound in lust (and so forth, up to) those who reverently contemplate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from delusion.

First, they are able to leave behind the poison of greed (that is, the "Fearlessness Regarding the Poison of Greed" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*). [Question: Difficulties such as fire and water are manifest states of suffering; it is understandable that one speaks of fear regarding them. "What fear could there be? [The Master] replied: "There are two reasons why one may speak of dread. First, poison is a cause of suffering that can summon the fruit of suffering. In its lightest form, it damages the body and ruins one's virtue; in its heaviest form, it leads to the loss of the physical frame and the end of life. Furthermore..."
In this life, it brings about unchaste wives and discord among one's kin; most grievous of all are the retributions of the copper pillars and iron beds that manifest at the moment of death.
One must personally endure the accumulated cold and solid ice of the hells from head to toe. Knowing this, one should cultivate fear and maintain constant mindfulness and reverence.
Using the power of mindfulness as an antidote to the lustful mind, pray for the sword of wisdom to sever it.

Indeed, those who can cause sentient beings to leave desire behind gather others into their own likeness by emptying all forms.

As for "many inferior [states]," one can leave the poison of hatred behind (this is the "fearlessness regarding the poison of hatred" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*). Those with much anger flare up when confronted with objects; they cannot be restrained.
At its lightest, it harms one's vital energy and brings disgrace; at its heaviest, one forgets both oneself and one’s kin, leading to being harmed by others in future lives.

They seek out flaws, thereby entering into affliction and harm, especially that which is most severe: the appearance of the signs of the mountain of knives, iron spikes, the sword-tree, the sword-wheel, and so forth, manifesting at the moment of death;
and the experiences of being dismembered, cut, hacked, crushed, pierced, and beaten—all of which they must undergo personally from head to foot.
From this, one knows to fear [anger] and constantly maintains mindfulness and reverence. Through the power of mindfulness, one subdues the mechanism of anger;

by relying on the wind of compassion, one brushes away the fever of one's own resentment. Seeking refuge through sound, one receives salvation; thus it is said that one "immediately attains freedom from anger. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Tenth, when sounds are pure and free from dust, the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, such that there is neither subject nor object. This can cause all resentment and hatred..."
Sentient beings are free from all anger and hatred. The *Zhengmai* commentary states: "The sound 'pure' (chun) means 'free from dust' (wuchen).

This means that although the sound is not destroyed, it is already free from the fault of being defiled by dust; this is the identity of mind and object. The sense organ and the sensory object merge into a single dharma."

Therefore, there is no faculty that can act as an object of opposition, nor is there any sensory field (*viṣaya*) that serves as such an object. Since there is neither the subject of opposition nor the object of opposition, one is able to bring about liberation from hatred.
This is because hatred arises from confrontation and resistance; now, since there is neither the subject nor the object of opposition, hatred has no basis to arise.
By assimilating others to oneself, one causes them to do the same. If [the practitioner] is many and of low status, they are able to abandon the poison of delusion. (This is...)

on a large scale, they invert the correct and the false. Furthermore, they will experience rebirth in a family of wrong views in future lives, their minds becoming sycophantic and crooked.
Most extreme of all, the signs of royal envoys, chief clerks, and the testimony of written documents appear before them at the moment of death.

Regarding matters such as interrogating those who employ deception, examining, and conducting judicial investigations, one should proceed through them from beginning to end. Through this, one comes to know fear and maintains constant mindfulness and reverence.

Because mindfulness manifests accordingly, it is said that one "attains freedom from delusion. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Eleventh, as the dust of the senses is eliminated and luminosity turns inward, the dharma-realm, body, and mind become like lapis lazuli—brilliantly penetrating and unimpeded.

"Obscured": being shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*). When the dust is eliminated, there is no obscuration; when the light is turned back, there is no shrouding.

Therefore, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind become crystalline, pure, and brilliantly penetrating, departing from the darkness of delusion. "Able to cause," etc., may be understood according to the above.
