To be fully endowed with the four requisites, those offerings could be called "complete. Regarding you below, in the question-and-answer concerning merit:
though a drop of rain is minute, if gathered upon the earth, it can still form a stream; though a particle of dust is exceedingly fine, [it likewise accumulates].

If even the accumulation of mere baskets would suffice to nourish a mountain, how much more so for such bodhisattvas who, relying on the names [of the teachings], uphold them and provide the four requisites in various ways throughout their entire lives?
The merit they thereby obtain should naturally be inexhaustible. Therefore, the Tathāgata intentionally posed the question, "Is it much or not?
to which the bodhisattva, responding directly to the occasion, replied that it was indeed very much. Below this, the Buddha said:
By this comparison, upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara does not equal that of the multitude of names numbering sixty-two billion *gaṅgā*-sands;
nor does even a single moment [of such practice] equal the constant [practice] of making offerings for as long as one lives. It is simply a matter of performing prostrations.
It does not equal the provision of offerings complete with the four requisites. When comparing the life-traces of these two individuals, they are as different as heaven and earth;
yet when comparing their merit and virtue, they do not differ by so much as a hair’s breadth.
This is because while the various other bodhisattvas employ different skillful means and wisdoms according to the needs of sentient beings, Avalokiteśvara alone has attained [this specific mastery].
The fundamental organ of perfect penetration universally encompasses all others. Since one organ can already match all other gates, one name can likewise equal all other designations.
It is like a small bird attaching itself to the wings of a great *garuḍa*; it may then rival the thousand flights of ordinary birds.

Or it is like tasting all waters; none surpass the single flavor of the great ocean. The difference between a perfectly round faculty and an imperfect one is such that their respective durations—whether measured by days or kalpas—are multiplied by a factor of ten million. This is the principle.

This is indeed so. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The fourteenth [attainment] is: by means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have realized, I have developed the wondrous faculty of hearing;
thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrously all-encompassing, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This enabled sentient beings to hold my name together with sixty-two billion Dharma-princes as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. II.

The merit of people is equal and without distinction. To explain the meaning: it is because Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration is uniquely designated as his fundamental faculty, for in this land, the essence of the true teaching resides in the purity of hearing sounds. Furthermore, it is because he is able to contain all and pervade everywhere.
Therefore, it is called "wondrous. This gate has already been opened; it can lead to other gates.

Because it leads to other gates, it encompasses those other gates and makes them as subtle and wondrous as itself, and likewise makes them as pervasive as itself. Hence it is said, "Thereafter, body and mind are equal," etc.
The meaning of "being able to make equal" has already been explained in the commentary on the current text. △ Third, the conclusion revealing the manifold merit.
Akṣayamati, by upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one shall obtain the benefit of merit.
This merit is untainted (anāsrava), and because it is uniquely supreme, it is called immeasurable and boundless.
Because it fully encompasses and pervades the two kinds of subtle meanings, the explanation for how the names were obtained through the question-and-answer session is concluded.

II. Question and Answer on the Expedient Means of Wandering and Transforming. This has two parts: 1. The disciple asks about wandering and transforming according to the occasion; 2. The Tathāgata provides a comprehensive exposition. Regarding the first, the response to the initial inquiry: The disciple advances the question concerning wandering and transforming.
The Tathāgata fully demonstrates the principle of resonance and response. First:
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...the power of skillful means—what are its manifestations?
As previously explained, this only revealed the merit of secret empowerment; it had not yet manifested the power of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Desiring to know this responsive transformation, he asked: "How do you roam within this Sahā world? How do you preach the Dharma for the sake of the assembly? This was because the Bodhisattva...
To traverse the world with one’s physical body, there must necessarily be the power of skillful means (*upāya*). However, not knowing what those matters are, I have therefore made this inquiry.

II. The Tathāgata Fully Demonstrates the Response and Induction. This has two parts: 1. Extensively manifesting the responsive transformations in various lands; 2. Directly answering the question regarding wandering in the Sahā world.

The first part (which corresponds to the thirty-two responses in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) states: "Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata [the following]..."

"Like an illusion, through the hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation of the Vajra Samādhi, and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata, my body manifests thirty-two transformations to enter all lands. (2) This section has two parts: first, clarifying the manifestation of responsive transformations;

second, concluding with the virtues and exhorting offerings. The first [section] has eight parts: first, the ability to respond to the three types of sages; second, the ability to respond to the six heavens.
1. Capable of responding to five types of persons; 2. Capable of responding to the fourfold assembly; 3. Capable of responding to a multitude of women; 4. Capable of responding to two youths; 5.
Capable of responding to ten classes [of beings]; 6. Capable of responding to the Mallas. First.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to) "he immediately manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for him.
At first, he was able to respond to bodhisattvas. Although the phrasing here is limited, its meaning encompasses all capacities of sentient beings;
for with the exception of the Buddha alone, those in the nine realms are all born [of this teaching]. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "If various bodhisattvas enter samādhi and advance..."
Cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*), their resolute understanding becomes fully manifest. I then manifest in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
Regarding the interpretation of "entering samādhi": this refers to seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above by relying on the power of that "turning back the hearing.
"Progressively cultivating the untainted" means gradually refining one's practice in anticipation of the state of being untainted, as it is said: "This faculty..."
The first refers to the "perfect clarity of emptiness" and so forth. "Supreme resolution manifests perfection" means that the untainted, supreme wisdom will soon become perfected;
as it is said: "First one attains the emptiness of persons, and then achieves liberation through the dharmas," and so forth.

To respond to these capacities, he manifests the body of a Buddha and teaches the Dharma of supreme advancement, enabling them to be liberated from attachment to the Dharma according to their respective stages and reach the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood.
"Should" and below refer to those capable of responding as Pratyekabuddhas; there are two such categories.

First, those who respond as Pratyekabuddhas. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If there are those in training whose tranquil, wondrous clarity manifests as supreme perfection, I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation. Second, those who respond as Pratyayabuddhas.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If there are those in training who have severed the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance of conditions, the supreme wondrous [nature] manifests..."
[The Buddha] said: "I appeared before him in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to attain liberation. To explain the meaning:
one who is a *śaikṣa* (a learner) is one who is about to realize the state of *aśaikṣa* (one beyond learning), yet has not yet realized it. Wēnlíng says: "A *Pratyekabuddha* (Solitary Realizer)..."
They appear in worlds where no Buddha is present. Observing the transformation and decay of all things, they personally realize non-arising.

Delighting in solitary tranquility, they seek natural wisdom; hence it is said that they are "tranquil, wondrous, and luminous. As for the *pratyekabuddhas*, they receive the Buddha’s teaching and awaken to the Way by observing conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Knowing that delusion regarding the supreme nature arises from the twelve links of dependent origination, they sever them; thus, beginning with the extinction of ignorance, [the rest follow].
When sorrow, grief, suffering, and affliction are extinguished, then conditions are severed and the supreme nature (paramārtha-svabhāva) manifests.

Since this nature is revealed through the severance of causes and conditions, it is called "the supreme nature upon the severance of conditions. The *Zhengmo* states: "The supreme nature is precisely the nature of the non-arising of causes and conditions."
However, as for these two categories, both are termed "supremely wondrous and manifesting perfection" because each refers to the ultimate fruit of its own respective class;
at the time when the path of cultivation is about to be exhausted, they pre-emptively manifest signs of perfection. For the sake of these two types of capacities, two types of bodies are manifested.
For their sake, he expounds the Dharma of supreme progress, causing them to leave behind birth-and-death in discrete segments; this is called liberation.

It should be understood that those below [this stage] are capable of responding as Śrāvakas; the manifest text is clear. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "If those in training attain the emptiness of the Four Truths..."

They enter cessation through the cultivation of the path, and their supreme nature manifests in perfection. Before them, I manifested in the body of a śrāvaka and preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: "those in training" refers to those who have attained the first three fruits.

"Those who have attained the emptiness of the Four Truths" refers to those who, at the outset, heard from the Buddha the Four Truths as well as the principles of emptiness and non-self; it is by virtue of this hearing that...

Because of the Dharma of the Four Truths, one knows the suffering of the three realms and cultivates the supramundane path; by partially severing the afflictions of views and thought, one partially realizes *nirvāṇa*.

Hence it is said: "Cultivating the path leads to entry into cessation. Regarding "the supreme nature manifesting its perfection," this refers to the stage of the Arhat-approacher (*arhattva-pratipannaka*), wherein the most excellent nature of cessation premanifests the aspect of full perfection. To explain this for the sake of current understanding, it may be inferred from the above. △ Second.
He is able to respond to the six heavens.
For those who should be saved by means of the body of a Brahmā King, he manifests as such; [and so on,] up to manifesting as the body of Vaiśravaṇa to preach the Dharma for them.

According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, when the mind of desire is clearly enlightened and one does not transgress the dust of desire, such that the body of desire is pure, this is precisely responding to [the needs of beings].
Those who should be delivered by the body of a Brahmā King—desiring to become a celestial lord and preside over the various heavens—are those who should be delivered by the body of Śakra.
Those who desire bodily sovereignty to travel throughout the ten directions are those who should be delivered by the body of Īśvara.
Those who desire bodily sovereignty to fly through the void are those who should be delivered by the body of Maheśvara.
Those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a Heavenly Great General are those who love to govern spirits and deities and protect their own lands.
Those who are to be delivered by means of the body of one of the Four Heavenly Kings are those who love to govern the world and protect all sentient beings.
The mention here of Vaiśravaṇa is an instance of citing one from among the Four Kings to encompass the others. This is based on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Below this, there are further beings who, out of craving, are born in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities;

those who should be delivered by means of the body of a prince of the Four Great Kings are likewise included because they are governed by the Four Great Kings. However, within this context, among the gods of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), only the Brahma King is mentioned.
Regarding the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the Buddha] manifests only above and below them; for others, he does not appear. This principle may be inferred accordingly.

As for manifesting bodies according to the class of beings to preach the Dharma for them, although it is not specified what kind of Dharma is preached, a detailed examination of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* shows that this is generally to explain the fruit based on the cause, thereby enabling their accomplishment;
it also first uses desire to draw in the mind. Below, follow this pattern. △ Third, the capacity to respond.
Regarding the five types of people:

for those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a minor king (up to) manifesting the body of a *brāhmaṇa* to preach the Dharma for them—concerning those who are to be delivered by the body of a minor king and so forth—the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings, I..."
Before him, he manifested in the form of a human king and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve fulfillment. The *Zhengmai* commentary states:
"This [king] must have been one who possessed virtue and harbored benevolence; unable to endure the chaos of the world, he made a vow to become a king of the Way in every lifetime."

He governs the states and nations through principle. For those who find delight in his present form, the Bodhisattva manifests that body for them, teaches them the causes for being born into noble status, and describes the virtues and achievements of emperors and kings, merely to perfume the seeds of their future lives. Regarding those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of an elder, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"One who loves his clan and lineage, whom the world honors and defers. The *Zhengmai Shiyi* (Correct Pulse Commentary) explains: "In India..."
The title "Elder" (長者) does not merely refer to advanced age; it is a designation for one who belongs to a prominent family of hereditary ministers and possesses both virtue and reputation.
Furthermore, this is not something attainable in the present life alone. For those who are to be delivered through the form of a lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*), the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:
They delight in discussing famous sayings and maintain themselves in purity. The *Zhengmai* commentary states: "These individuals possess virtue but hold no official rank.
They may discuss the Way and discourse on virtue to serve as models for others, or they may compose books and establish doctrines to leave instruction for future generations.
'Famous sayings' refers to canonical texts and traditions. 'Maintaining oneself in purity' means remaining in seclusion and refusing office—just like Wang Tong and Shao Yong of our own land."
Regarding those who are to be saved by means of the body of a minister: the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "Those who love to govern the land and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts.
The Wēnnéng commentary explains: "The Three Dukes, the Chancellor, the Governors of provinces, and the Prefects and Magistrates are all termed 'ministers' (*zhāiguān*)."
Regarding those who are to be delivered by means of a Brahmin body, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "They love various arts and sciences (*śāstra*) and maintain themselves through self-discipline.

To explain the meaning: "arts and sciences" refers to the combination of divination and physiognomy, as well as the calculation of the waxing and waning of celestial bodies; "self-discipline" refers to...
This refers to practices for sustaining life and protecting the body, refining the spirit, and regulating the breath; many of the Brahmins in the Western Regions (India) habitually practice these.
△ Fourth, being able to respond to the fourfold assembly:
he preaches the Dharma by manifesting in the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, if there are men or women who delight in learning and renouncing the world, upholding the various precepts and codes of discipline—those who should be delivered by means of the bodies of bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—the teacher should preach the Dharma of renunciation for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
This includes such things as extolling the maintenance of the precepts and praising the holy life (*brahmacarya*). If there are men or women who delight in maintaining [the precepts]...

Regarding the five precepts: this refers to those who should be delivered by means of the bodies of upāsakas and upāsikās, and for whom one preaches the Dharma by explaining the ways of householders—such as the teaching that one performs Buddha-work without departing from worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), or cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) without abandoning wife and children.
△ Fifth, being able to respond to the various women.
One should manifest in the form of a householder, a lay devotee, or a high official (up to) a woman to preach the Dharma;
there are four such types [of manifestations]. Those who can be categorized together are grouped as one class.
If they were expanded, the number would exceed thirty-two. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If there is a woman who establishes herself through domestic governance and cultivates her household..."
In that country, I manifested before them in the forms of a queen, a court lady, a titled wife, and a noble matron (dàjiā) to preach the Dharma for them and bring them to fulfillment.
The *Zhengmai* commentary states: "Internal governance" refers generally to all the duties of women.
A Confucian text says, "Instructions do not go beyond the inner chambers," hence it is called internal governance; it implies that the inner chambers are the source of [all order].
This is the source of transformation; thus, it pertains to the order or chaos of the family and the state. "Family" refers to those from the rank of Great Officer (*daifu*) downward;
"state" refers to those from the rank of Feudal Lord (*zhuhou*) upward. Gu Shan says: "Female ruler" refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven.

"State lady" (*guofuren*) is as described in the *Analects* regarding the wife of a lord of a state, who is called "the lord’s lady" (*junfuren*). "Ennobled lady" (*mingfu*) refers to a wife who attains honor through her husband. These are the great ladies.
For example, the wife of Cao Shishu of Fufeng during the Later Han dynasty was the daughter of Ban Biao from the same commandery; her name was Zhao, and her courtesy name was Huiji.
Emperor He summoned her to the palace several times and commanded the Empress and the ladies-in-waiting to take her as their teacher.
Among the wives of high-ranking officials mentioned here, those who possess an official edict are titled "noble ladies" (mingfu). The wives of elders generally possess great virtue and reputation.
The wife of a layman (*gṛhapati*) possesses extensive learning; the wife of a Brahmin possesses numerous arts.

These three can all serve as great mistresses, though they are not called "lady of the household" (*gṛhapatnī*) or "lady of the state" (*rājñī*). These titles should have been included according to the preceding description of the king’s person, but they were likely omitted by the translator.
△ Six: Capable of Responding to Two Children.
Those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a young boy or a young girl, [the Buddha] manifests in the body of a young boy or a young girl and preaches the Dharma for them.
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, if there are sentient beings whose male organ remains intact, they are those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a young boy.
The *Zhengmo* commentary explains: "This refers to those who have resolved to remain chaste throughout their lives and do not violate the female form. If there are those... [text truncated]
The woman delights in remaining in her body and does not seek to be violated. This means she is one who should be delivered by means of a maiden’s body.
The *Zhengmai* commentary states: “Delighting in remaining in her body” means she vows to remain a virgin forever and never to marry.
“Does not seek to be violated” means she maintains her integrity and self-restraint; even if someone were to forcibly commit an assault, she would still vow not to yield.
It is so. △ Seventh, the ability to respond to ten classes [of beings]:
he manifests whatever is appropriate—whether as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—and preaches the Dharma to them.
Regarding these eight classes [of beings], according to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, they all delight in departing from their own kind to enter into the human realm;
thus, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for them to bring them to fulfillment. This is because it is only through the human path that one can rectify the mind and thoughts to advance toward Bodhi.
As for "humans and non-humans," this term collectively includes the various assemblies not fully enumerated previously. For example:
Beyond kings, ministers, elders, and laypeople, there are others; beyond devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, there are further non-humans.
These are not mentioned separately for fear that the "wondrous response" might be thought to have omissions;
therefore, they are included here collectively to complete the number thirty-two. △ Eighth, the Capable Responding Malla.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma for them.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: In the past, there was a king whose principal queen gave birth to a thousand sons.

The king set out a thousand counting-sticks (*śalākā*) and intended to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future. Kṛtagupta drew the first stick, and so on, up to... [Vipaśyin].
When the last tally was drawn, the second wife gave birth to two sons. One vowed to become a Brahmā King and requested the thousand Buddhas to preach the Dharma;
the other vowed to become a Vajrapāṇi and protect the teachings of the thousand Buddhas.

The present statement that those who should be saved by means of the Vajradhara deity refers precisely to this latter vow to protect the Buddha’s teachings, as they belong to the class of those who delight in being Vajrapāṇis. Thus it is.
The *ṛṣabha* (powerful one) holds a *vajra* mallet in his hand; thus he is also called a *Vajradeva*. Regarding the "preaching the Dharma" for him, Daicheng says:
it means preaching the Dharma that destroys the heterodox and assists the orthodox, causing him to achieve accomplishment.
However, the thirty-two manifestations herein appear and disappear in relation to those in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*; for instance, among the celestial beings, there are the Four Heavenly Kings.
My son, those [attendants] are not present in the current sutra. Among wives, there are many female rulers and noble ladies (*guófūrén*), yet these are also omitted in the present text.

As for the Vajrapāṇi deities mentioned in this sutra, they are not listed in that [other text]. This is because the Bodhisattva’s wondrous responses are boundless and his spiritual transformations are inexhaustible;
thus, each [text] selects those that are easily believed and easily perceived to complete the number of thirty-two. In reality, each...
It is inexhaustible; whatever one speaks, it is all attained. This concludes the section on the Manifestation of Wisdom. II. Conclusion of Merits and Exhortation to Offerings:
"O Akṣayamati, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with single-mindedness... [up to] ...should make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara."

First, the summary of merits: By means of the samādhi of the ear-gate, through the effortless and wondrous power of hearing and cultivating what has been heard, the Bodhisattva naturally possesses sovereign karmic functions;
thus it is said that they "accomplish such merits. Although it is said they manifest in various forms, they are in truth only the One True Reality;
although it is said they travel through all lands, they do not depart from their current location—just as in the case of the single moon reflected in many waters.
The moon universally reflects in all waters; the moons in all waters are encompassed by the single moon. The moon does not descend, nor do the waters rise;
that the water is clear and the moon is bright is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*). Only one who understands this meaning may be taught the thirty-two manifestations.
Therefore, the following section on exhorting offerings can be understood. This concludes the extensive explanation of the various lands of responsive transformations. II. The Direct Answer.

Wandering through the Sahā world (this refers to the four inconceivables of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. That sutra further states: "I have also attained this perfect penetration (*pari-citta*) because I have cultivated and realized the unsurpassed path; furthermore, I am well able to attain the four inconceivables, which are the wondrous virtues of non-action").
Part Two: One, manifesting wondrous virtues; two, answering by way of responding to questions. The first part has three sections: one, being able to bestow fearlessness;
two, being able to elicit offerings; three, being able to cultivate offerings. The first, being able to bestow fearlessness (this is...):
The *Lengyan* [Sūtra] speaks of two kinds of inconceivable mantras for manifesting the same essence and different essences.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is universally known as the Bestower of Fearlessness.
They can dispel fear and rescue those in urgent distress; thus, they are said to be "able to bestow fearlessness.
However, when one investigates the reason why they are able to dispel and rescue, it is due to the power of the *samaya* (homogeneous) and *vi-samaya* (heterogeneous) mantras of the Bodhisattvas.
For this reason, names such as "Sahā" (Endurance World) are established based on these virtues, precisely because they manifest the capacity to bestow fearlessness.

This is merely an empty claim. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "First, because I initially attained the wondrous and subtle faculty of hearing, the essence of mind abandoned ordinary hearing, such that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned;
they became a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and can preach boundless secret divine mantras, even to the point of protecting and rescuing sentient beings."

One attains great sovereignty. To explain the meaning: "first obtaining the wondrously wondrous mind of hearing" means that the Bodhisattva first attains the mind of "hearing-in-reverse," which transcends all other gates and is thus the most wondrous among the wondrous. "The essence of the mind leaves behind hearing" means...

This means that once the hearing-mind has returned to its essence of refined purity, it leaves behind that false nature of hearing which has been accumulated within the faculties since beginningless time.
When false hearing is abandoned, seeing, awareness, cognition, and so forth, also become liberated along with hearing.

Therefore, it is said that "seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition cannot be separated. Because there is no separation, they form a single, true, perfect, and profound stillness; hence, it is called "accomplishment."
The single, perfectly interfused, pure, and enlightened awareness is "perfectly interfused" (yuanrong), and thus one and many are without obstruction;
therefore, within a single body, it can manifest countless wondrous forms. It is "pure" (qingjing), and thus this true mystery is revealed;

therefore, from within those countless wondrous forms, it can proclaim boundless secret mantras. Bestowing both compassion and majesty, and practicing both meditative concentration and wisdom, it is therefore called "rescue and protection."
Sentient beings attain great mastery. This clarifies the mantra of identical essence and form, which can bestow fearlessness amidst urgent calamities.
It is further said: "Secondly, through my hearing and reflection, I have emerged from the six sense-objects, like a sound passing through a wall."
They cannot act as obstacles. Therefore, I am able to skillfully manifest each individual form and recite each individual mantra.
These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings. To explain the meaning: "those who hear and contemplate" refers to two of the six natures.
Because they are fundamentally one body, whether mentioned individually or collectively, each fully encompasses the others; it is appropriate to use either according to the occasion.
"Transcending the six dusts" means that the six natures are perfectly tranquil and clear, remaining unfettered by sensory objects. This metaphorical meaning is easily understood.

Precisely because they are not bound by the dusts, they are able to manifest in response to conditions. "Manifesting each individual form" refers to responding to the various capacities [of sentient beings].
Each manifests [its own form]. Those who recite each individual mantra speak of them according to their respective forms.

Upon seeing these forms and hearing these mantras, all fears are completely dispelled; therefore it is said that "their forms and their mantras" are able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
This clarifies the *vidyā-mantra* of distinct form, which is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terror.

Since these two inconceivables are fully present in that sutra, how could they be absent from this one? Moreover, since the latter two [inconceivables] exist as evidence, we know they must certainly be here.
It is simply because the text abbreviates the *vidyā-mantra* that those of old failed to perceive this, resulting in the two sutras not being entirely consistent.
[End of section on] the ear. △ Second, the capacity to elicit offerings (this corresponds to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*’s refutation of stinginess and the seeking of inconceivable results).
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One... [omitted] ...out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace.”

At the outset, the practitioner raises offerings out of reverence for his character and admiration for his virtue, praying on behalf of all sentient beings; hence it is said, "Now I shall make this offering.

As for the necklaces worn upon the neck—those very ornaments adorning the body—to untie them and give them away is already extremely difficult, let alone when they are composed of various jewels, worth hundreds of thousands. Were it not for the inconceivable power of Avalokiteśvara...

Furthermore, who could abandon their own [possessions] to offer them to another, performing such an act of worship? Having already given them, fearing that they might not accept, he says, "Virtuous One, please accept this.

Now, while precious necklaces originally belong to the category of material gifts (*āmiṣadāna*), because they are dedicated in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they are identical in meaning to the Dharma-gift (*dharmadāna*).
"At that time, Avalokiteśvara did not accept" refers to the reason for his non-acceptance.
There are two reasons for this: first, because he was already in the presence of the Buddha, and since the Buddha had not commanded him to accept it, he did not dare to accept it;
second, because it was currently hanging from his neck, and to accept it in that state would be improper and unsuitable. From "Inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*) onwards, the disciple makes a formal request.
There are also two intentions behind this repeated request: first, to express his sincerity and earnest hope that the Buddha will intervene so that the gift may certainly be accepted.
Second, one gives for the sake of the multitude and receives for the sake of the multitude; this does not violate the principle. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Third, because I have cultivated the fundamentally wondrous and perfect penetration—the pure fundamental root—every world I visit causes sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures, seeking my compassion.
The Wēnnéng commentary explains: "When the fundamental root is pure, then [it is one...]"
It is entirely free from attachment; thus, it causes sentient beings to abandon all stinginess and clinging.

"Those who seek my compassion" refers to those who receive [his aid] through his compassion, whereby he performs the work of a Buddha. Based on this, that previous scripture was Avalokiteśvara’s own declaration, whereas the present scripture manifests the actual occurrence of those events.
It is precisely through the present scripture that one sees that his own words were not false. Furthermore, by means of...
In that sutra, one first comes to know that there is a cause for receiving offerings. The following sections are modeled after this.
△ Second, the ability to practice offerings (i.e., the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*’s "Offerings to the Buddha Producing the Inconceivable").
At that time, the Buddha addressed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... [up to] "...a portion to be offered to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

Initially, the World-Honored One transmitted this message, saying: "Since Ajita has already made this offering for the sake of the assembly, if you do not accept it, his vows will remain unfulfilled and his benefit will not be realized.
How could this be something a benevolent person would do? Thus, the World-Honored One exhorted him.
He accepted it out of compassion. Immediately, he descended. Avalokiteśvara accepted it out of compassion;

he did not say "I pity You, Akṣayamati," but rather said "I pity the fourfold assembly and others. This is because it was revealed that while Akṣayamati bestowed it for the sake of the assembly, Avalokiteśvara likewise accepted it for the sake of the assembly.
He divided it into portions and presented them to the two Honored Ones. Having already accepted it, and furthermore—
This is further offered to the two Honored Ones with two intentions: first, to manifest that although one accepts [offerings] for the sake of the assembly, there is fundamentally no attachment;
second, to ensure that the merit of the performed giving becomes a cause for Buddhahood. As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:
"Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, one is able to use various kinds of rare treasures to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."
Extending to all sentient beings throughout the six realms of the Dharma-realm: those who seek a wife obtain a wife; those who seek a son obtain a son;

and so on, even unto those who seek Great Nirvana obtain Great Nirvana. To explain the meaning: "I have attained the Buddha-mind" means that the merit of entering the stream has reached its ultimate limit, and wondrous awakening is identical to that of the Buddha.
"Realizing the ultimate" means that the merit of extinguishing the objective realm has reached its ultimate limit, and [wondrous awakening...].
This means attaining realization equal to that of a Buddha. Having awakened to and realized this equality with the Buddha, one does not perceive a single dharma as something to which one is attached.
Therefore, one is able to offer precious treasures and other such things to the Tathāgata. Whatever merit is produced by these acts of giving, one dedicates it to all beings;

thus it is said that its influence extends throughout the Dharma-realm. By causing the aspirations of sentient beings within the six realms to be fulfilled without exception, it is said that they "seek a wife."
One obtains a wife; one seeking a son obtains a son, and so forth. Yet now, this sutra accepts [these offerings] out of compassion for the multitudes.

Having accepted them, to transfer them [to others] is to properly make offerings to the Tathāgata and, by extension, to reach the Dharma-realm—this demonstrates the ultimate attainment of the wondrous. II.
The Response to the Question and Conclusion.
From the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Inexhaustible Intent (up to) "wandering in the Sahā world":

his sovereign spiritual power refers to the four aforementioned inconceivabilities, which manifest spontaneously and induce conduct spontaneously, rather than through contrived effort or deliberate mental application;
therefore, it is called "sovereign. This is what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by "unconditioned wondrous virtue" (*anabhisaṃskāra-guṇa*).
It is so. Although he transforms all ten directions simultaneously, the Sahā world alone is most suitable.

This is because the Sahā world has many causes for fear and its urgent calamities are especially widespread; its people are habituated to the ways of stinginess and greed, and its things lack the majesty of merit and wisdom.
When the Bodhisattva traverses it by means of the four inconceivable powers and his sovereign spiritual might, then fear can be abandoned, and the urgent...
Difficult to save, yet stinginess and greed can be broken, and merit and wisdom can be attained. The prose section, showing the specific details, concludes.

△ Second, the verse summary that reveals the combined meaning (this verse was not translated by Master Kumārajīva; later masters all maintained that it exists in the Sanskrit original, and thus it has been supplemented according to that source).
Part Two: 1. Repeatedly asking for the reason for obtaining the name; 2. Revealing the combined attainment of the name and the practice of wandering to transform others. First [part].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati [from "to" (至)] asked: "O Son of the Buddha, by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?
O World-Honored One, you who possess wondrous marks, you praise the Buddha’s adornment of ten thousand virtues.

Because he is one who has already passed through [the stages], such a person who has already passed through can naturally know the conduct and practice of those yet to come; therefore, he asks again. △ Second, the combined manifestation of how he obtained his name.
Wandering and Transforming [throughout the World] has two parts: first, revealing the reason for receiving the name; second, revealing the skillful means of wandering and transforming.
The first [section] has three parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition; third, a summary conclusion. The first [of these].
The Honored One, endowed with the wondrous marks, answered Akṣayamati in verse: [up to] "able to extinguish all suffering of existence.
The first two lines, which most clearly manifest the practices and vows, were arranged by the compiler of the sutra as a preamble. The phrase "Listen well" serves as a general admonition to attend.

The phrase "responding skillfully" reveals the breadth of the practice for transforming others. The phrase "vast and great vow" reveals the depth of the vow for transforming others. [This continues] through the kalpas.

The two phrases reveal the excellence of his own practice. It is said that the kalpas traversed during the Bodhisattva’s practice on the causal ground have already reached the inconceivable, and the Buddhas he has served have already numbered many thousands of billions; thus, his conduct may be called supreme.
The phrase "arousing the great [resolve]" reveals the purity of his own cultivated vows. "Pure" means that he aspires solely to attain Buddhahood without remainder.
This is the vow. Now, these two types of vow and practice represent the ultimate way of engaging with the world and are truly the authentic cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Fearing that the scope of [the listener's] inquiry might not reach them, I have first presented them here. The phrase "I act for" serves as the general heading.

Since the practices and vows for oneself and others cannot be fully recounted, it is said to be a "brief explanation. This means that while one's own cultivation is abbreviated, the transformation of others is explained.
It also functions through other actions. Hearing the name, one must praise it; this evokes a response through the vocal karma (*vākkarman*). Seeing the physical form, one must pay homage;

this evokes a response through the bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). Contemplating with the mind, one must reflect; this evokes a response through the mental karma (*manaskarman*). Since all three are capable of bringing about a corresponding response, they do not pass by in vain.
This is because all existing sufferings can be extinguished thereby. △ Second, the specific manifestation has two parts. First, the capacity...
One is exempt from the three calamities. Second, one is able to escape the eight difficulties. First:
even if one were to harbor a malicious intent to push another into a great pit of fire (up to: ...the waves cannot submerge them).
First, one can avoid the disaster of fire. "Even if such a thing should occur" means that even if it were to happen, by reciting the name, one immediately escapes it.

The subsequent phrases, "or drifting on water" and so forth, should be understood accordingly. The latter four lines concern escaping the disasters of wind and water; "the ocean" refers here to the disaster of water.
This includes both the wind disaster; it refers to what is described in the prose as being blown down by black winds.

While the prose passage only manifests the perils of ghosts, this verse additionally includes those of fish and dragons. Nevertheless, these also belong to the category of water-related calamities, and thus they are explained together here.
As for "the waves being unable to submerge [them]," once one has escaped the peril of water, the remaining dangers likewise remain unharmed. This verse is largely consistent with the prose.

[This section] proceeds; however, there are slight differences in the opening and closing [phrasing]. △ Second, the ability to escape the eight difficulties (*aṣṭau durgatayaḥ*). (In the prose version there are only four; here they are increased to eight to supplement the deficiencies of the prose.
Four: 1. The difficulty of enemies, bandits, and execution; 2. The difficulty of shackles, fetters, and poisons; 3. The difficulty of *rākṣasas* and fierce beasts; 4.
The difficulty of venomous insects and torrential rain. First:
Or, if one is pushed from the peak of Mount Sumeru by others (down to the point where) the sword immediately breaks it into pieces:
if one initially claims that this allows for escape from enemies and bandits, it must refer to Mount Sumeru because its summit overlooks the void of space.
Looking down upon the great ocean from above, this [state] can save; the rest may be understood accordingly. This also serves to illustrate how the difficult is made easy through comparison.
As for one who is pushed over by another, that person is not merely an enemy but a thief, because they intend to deprive one of life by pushing one down.
For a brief moment, one remains as if the sun were suspended in the sky; once the enemy-thief has departed, one is like the sun rising again. The same applies to wicked people.
Above, when Mount Kongara—the mountain capable of destroying all things—fell upon him, his own emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) should have been reduced to powder;
yet that not even a single hair was harmed clearly demonstrates the power of the Great Being’s protection.

When encountering hostile bandits who brandish swords to inflict harm, there is no possibility of escape; yet upon hearing the Holy Name, they all give rise to a compassionate heart, and by this means, one attains liberation.
They are liberated. This, too, is the reach of the Great Being’s true compassion; it transforms the violent into the benevolent, occurring spontaneously without being sought.
The final four lines, concerning the ability to escape execution, may be understood by reference to the prose section. △ Second, the difficulty of shackles, fetters, poisons, and drugs.
Or those imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, [until] it returns to the person themselves.
First, regarding "able to release from imprisonment and shackles": "imprisonment" has the meaning of binding; "releasing" has the meaning of loosening. The rest is the same as the long prose section.
Regarding "mantras and curses" below: "able to remove poisons and drugs. "Mantras and curses" refers to the cursing of ghosts and spirits to bring about misfortune or fortune.
These words were a solemn oath. Now, while even poison can harm a person, how much more so when combined with incantations and curses?

It would naturally have struck its mark a hundred times out of a hundred; yet that it instead returned upon the person who cast it reveals, on one hand, the compassion of the Great Being’s protection, and on the other, the majesty of his subduing power.
Should the person who cast it feel urgency because the curse has returned upon them, [they will surely seek refuge].
Repent; reform and uphold the Name. Then you yourself will receive salvation and be liberated, and both of you will be free from trouble.

As for those who say that this would instead lead to attachment and harm compassion—this is to grant permission to Bodhisattvas to cultivate goodness through the gate of gathering-in (*saṃgraha-vastu*), yet not to permit Bodhisattvas to transform evil through the gate of refutation (*pratikṣepa*).
This is like the playful remark of Su Shi: "Do not be like a fool who hears a dream. △ Three.
Regarding the perils of rākṣasas and fierce beasts:
should one encounter evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and so forth, [one shall] flee swiftly to boundless directions.
Because of the illumination of Wisdom-Light and the protection of Compassionate Power, rākṣasas, dragons, and ghosts dare not inflict harm. [This is the power of the] Name and Title.
As soon as [the name] was invoked, the majestic power arrived; thus, the fierce beasts broke their encirclement and fled far away. △ Fourth, the difficulty of poisonous insects and torrential rain:
"The mottled vipers, adders, and scorpions, whose poisonous breath blazes like smoke and fire... (until) they are instantly dispersed."

Vipers, pythons, vipers, and scorpions accumulate the poison of their rage until their breath is like smoke and fire; yet upon calling upon Avalokiteśvara, they receive his compassionate power and their natures naturally become tame and gentle.
Thus it is said that they turn back upon hearing the sound [of his name]. Even when a great rain pours down accompanied by thunder and lightning, [they do not harm].
To report another’s evil in an instant, yet to deliver them by invoking Avalokiteśvara with sincere devotion, is to turn the wrath of Heaven in a mere moment;

hence it is said that [the calamity] “dissipates immediately. Regarding “thunder like a drum and flashing lightning,” this means the thunder resounds like the sound of a drum being struck, and the lightning flashes like the form of a cord being pulled. This concludes the detailed explanation. △ Third, the general summary.
Sentient beings are beset by calamities and immeasurable suffering afflicts their bodies; yet the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from its pain.
To summarize: sentient beings may be constrained by poverty, or afflicted by illness, even unto immeasurable torments that oppress their bodies;
yet through the power of Avalokiteśvara’s perfect and penetrating wisdom, there is none who is not [saved].
He seeks out their voices to provide salvation; this is why he is named Avalokiteśvara. This concludes the section on explaining the reason for his manifest name. II.
Explaining the Expedient Means of His Wandering Transformation (in two parts): 1. Extensively explaining his responsive manifestations in various lands.

2. Specifically explaining his wandering within the Sahā world. First [section] (following the prose commentary: prior to this, there should have been words of the audience requesting instruction; here, however, he speaks of his own accord without waiting for a question).
"Endowed with the power of supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*) and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom" (up to) "extinguishing the flames of afflictions.
Initially, he manifests his body according to circumstances; because he brings forth superior functions through samādhi, it is said that he is "endowed with spiritual power.

Because he initiates gates of transformation based on universal penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), it is said that he "extensively cultivates the skillful means of wisdom. Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, they respond to conditions without...

"Directions. Therefore, it is said: "In the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm where [the Buddha] does not appear. "Various," and so forth, refers to the contemplation that functions to extinguish suffering.
"Various evil destinies" is a general term for the miserable paths (*durgati*). "Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals" is a specific classification of their categories.

"Birth, old age, sickness, and death" are the universal sufferings common to all sentient beings; these are matters that the prose section (*gadya*) could not fully encompass, and thus they are supplemented by the verse (*śloka*).

[One] applies [these] by means of the five contemplations, adding them subtly; therefore it is said that they are "gradually and completely extinguished. "True contemplation" and so forth correctly reveal the contemplation that is capable of extinguishing [them].
One contemplates that their nature is fundamentally true, hence it is called "true contemplation. One contemplates that their obstructions are fundamentally quiescent.
Therefore, it is called "pure contemplation" (*śubha-bhāvanā*). To eliminate adventitious obstacles and restore one’s original truth, one employs the contemplation of vast wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
To extinguish extreme suffering and bestow supreme bliss, one adds the contemplations of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

This is what is meant by the phrase "gradually causing all to be extinguished. [Question: Food can only satisfy one's own body, and suffering is summoned only by one's own karma. What does the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of contemplation have to do with sentient beings, such that he could suddenly extinguish their suffering?

Answer: This is said with reference to those who have not yet attained perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). If one has already attained perfect penetration, then one's nature is inherently all-pervasive; the internal root-body and the external vessel-world—all that exists—is entirely my wondrous clarity.

There is not a single dharma that does not revolve according to me, nor a single dharma that is not for my use. Therefore, a single verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* can empty all hells, and a single bowl of fragrant food can satisfy the entire ocean-like assembly of beings.

How much more so when a Bodhisattva employs great wisdom and true compassion to extinguish the sufferings of all beings—how could there be anything that does not vanish like snow struck by hot water, dissolving at the very thought? [The passage] beginning with "Constantly vow" refers to preaching the Dharma to shatter delusions, stating that sentient beings desire...
To destroy all delusions, one should constantly make this vow: "May I always behold the stainless, pure light.
"Light" refers to the wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva; because it emerges from obstructions and is perfectly luminous, it is called "stainless and pure.
The two lines concerning the "sun of wisdom" clarify the reason for constantly making this vow and constantly beholding [the Buddha]. This is because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is like...
The sun is able to shatter the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings. Among calamities that encompass various misfortunes, wind and fire are the most formidable;
therefore, they are singled out for mention. However, disasters such as wind and fire are all induced by the afflictions of sentient beings.

Since all forms of darkness are completely shattered, [the sun] is thus able to subdue them. "Universal Radiance" and so forth correctly manifest the meaning of wisdom being able to destroy darkness. It says:

The Bodhisattva, with the illumination of universal wisdom, shines upon all worlds. Thereafter, taking great compassion as his essence, he strikes the thunder of the precepts to awaken the multitude who are deaf.
Taking the mind of loving-kindness as clouds, he pours down nectar to extinguish the flames of affliction.
This is what is meant by "the sun of wisdom breaking the darkness. △ Second, the actual manifestation of wandering in the Sahā world.
"In the midst of litigations before officials, and within the terrors of military arrays" (up to) "therefore one should pay homage.
First, [the Buddha] can bestow fearlessness. Sentient beings are by nature prone to much strife and contention; therefore, he specifically mentions "litigation" and "military arrays.
In litigation, the mind is anxious regarding punishment; in military arrays, life is endangered by weapons. Both are truly terrifying and fearful.

This refers to the fear of worldly affairs. By recollecting Avalokiteśvara and relying upon his compassionate power, long-standing enmities are instantly dissolved; lawsuits are abandoned and encirclements are lifted.
Moved by this sacred transformation, each person repents their former intentions; thus it is said that they all retreat and disperse. However, this still pertains to a response from the hidden realm.
As for a manifest response, the *tongti* (same-substance) form-mantra contains manifold wonders within a single sound, while the *yiti* (different-substance) [form-mantra]...
Mantra. Observing the world, he manifests various teachings; manifested from a pure mind, he shatters the obstacles of others while uttering the Brahma-voice.
Responding to those who seek him, he never misses the proper time, resembling the ocean tide. Humans and devas listen with joy, while malevolent spirits tremble with fear.
Therefore, it is said that he surpasses this world. Because his manifestations are revealed through this, sentient beings in urgent distress should constantly keep him in mind.
Each thought-moment consists of four phrases. This precisely clarifies the reason why one must maintain constant mindfulness.

For if one maintains an uninterrupted succession of thoughts without giving rise to doubt, then the Pure and Holy One, Avalokiteśvara, will be able to act as a refuge amidst suffering, affliction, death, calamity, and all manner of fears.
That Avalokiteśvara is called "Pure and Holy" (淨聖) reveals that he is himself able to be free from hindrances; therefore, he is able to [bestow protection].

He acts as a refuge for sentient beings. If he is unable to save even himself, how could one expect him to bestow fearlessness upon those in the midst of suffering, affliction, and the perils of death?
The final four lines concern the possession of virtue and the accumulation of merit.

The prose section reveals his reception of offerings, while the verse clarifies his possession of virtue; it is precisely because he possesses virtue that he is able to receive offerings. This is seen in the prose...
"Compassionately accepting. The verse expresses his compassionate eye; it is precisely through viewing with compassion that he compassionately accepts.

The prose clarifies his making offerings to the Buddha; the verse praises his accumulation of merit. It is precisely because this accumulation of merit is like an ocean that one can produce rare treasures to offer to the Buddha;
furthermore, by producing rare treasures to offer to the Buddha, one further brings about an accumulation of merit like an ocean. Because of this, he is sovereign.
By his supernatural power, he wanders through the Sahā world; therefore, all sentient beings of the Sahā world should prostrate to him. The combined explanation of the verses is complete.
△ Third, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter has two parts: first, the Earth-Holding Bodhisattva’s praise; second, the resolve for enlightenment by the assembly at that time.
First. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat... (until) "one should know that the merit of such a person is not small.
Regarding the name of the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara, according to the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, there are ten meanings of "earth": first, vastness; second, multitude... [and so forth].
1. It is the basis for birth; 2. it has neither preference nor aversion; 3. it receives great rain; 4. it produces grasses and trees; 5. it is the support for seeds;
6. it produces various jewels; 7. it produces various medicines; 8. it is not moved by the wind; 9. it is not startled by the lion’s roar.
One who upholds the mind of bodhi is like this, and thus it is named after it. If the terms are combined individually, it means that one is able to give rise to the vast and great bodhi.
Because it is the mind; because it can serve as a refuge for sentient beings in saṃsāra; because it makes no discrimination among sentient beings;
because it receives the great rain of the Dharma from all Buddhas; because it causes all merits to grow; because it is that upon which the seeds of bodhi rely;
because it gives rise to the dharmas that benefit sentient beings; and because it gives rise to the remedies for afflictions.
Because he is not troubled by worldly phenomena, because he is unmoved by the eight winds of the world, and because he does not feel alarm or doubt upon hearing the teaching of the profound Dharma;

his ten virtues are like the earth, providing a foundation for the practice of perfect and wondrous realization. Therefore, [the text] hears of him and extols him, thereby awakening the minds of the assembly.
Furthermore, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, in the passage where the Bodhisattvas personally recount their attainments of perfect penetration, it says: "I recall the distant past... (This is...)
During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha in the present age, the great king of that land invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast.
At that time, I leveled the ground to await the Buddha. Vipaśyin Tathāgata touched the crown of my head and said to me, "You must level the ground of the mind;
then the ground of the world will all become level. My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the subtle particles of my own body were identical to the particles of the world.
They are equal and without distinction. The self-nature of these atoms does not touch one another; even by weapons they are not touched.
(And so on) until the dust is exhausted and wisdom is perfected, whereby the Unsurpassed Way is realized. Based on this, it is as if one were relying upon level ground.

Having attained realization of perfect penetration, he is named "Earth-Holder" (Dharaṇīdhara). Furthermore, because weapons cannot touch him, his afflictions have been eliminated and his wisdom is perfected;
for the most part, his practice corresponds with that of Avalokiteśvara. Thus, upon hearing of his conduct, it was praised.
The "karma of mastery" refers to what has been explained above, as the fourteen fearlessnesses and other such qualities are all the magnificent virtues and great powers of a Bodhisattva.
It is called "karma" because its manifestations appear in the world; it is called "sovereign" (*vaśitā*) because it is spontaneously accomplished without depending on conceptual conditions.
Such sovereign karma constitutes the power of one's own spiritual transformations and harmonious integration.
It arises from the gateway of the Universal Dharma of Perfect Penetration; hence it is called "Manifestation through the Universal Gateway. Regarding "the power of spiritual penetrations":

through the recitation [of this dharani], one can evoke the response of the sages, and the merit of its cultivation surpasses that of other gateways; therefore it is said: "One should know that such a person’s merit is not small.
△ Second, the assembly arouses the aspiration for enlightenment.
When the Buddha spoke this "Universal Gateway" chapter, [the assembly] generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the term "unequaled" (*asama*): there is no dharma of equal outflow that can be equaled to it; it is the most supreme and most excellent bodhicitta.
Having heard what the Tathāgata had spoken, and further hearing the praise of the Earth-holding One (Kṣitigarbha), they admired Avalokiteśvara.
This is the most supreme and sublime practice; it gives rise to the most supreme and sublime mind of a bodhisattva. See the worthy and strive to equal them;
rely on goodness to perfect goodness. Do not say that after Avalokiteśvara, the Universal Gate has fallen to the ground and the lion’s lute-string has ceased its resonance.
The section on the method of correct cultivation is concluded.
△ Second, the methods that assist cultivation, which are threefold: first, using divine mantras to protect against external māras; second, relying on virtuous friends to protect the internal mind;
third, grasping the essentials to fulfill the period of cultivation. First (the title of the chapter says):
The Dharani Chapter, the Twenty-sixth of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
*Dharani* here is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). This means that it encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings.

Alternatively, it is said that it prevents evil from arising and maintains goodness without loss; this is the efficacy of the meaning of "total retention of phenomena. It expels the heterodox and wards off [evil].

It is strange. Because it resembles the incantations and curses of this region, it is also called a "mantra" (zhòu). Among the five reasons for not translating, it falls under "not translated because it is secret";

among the four examples, it is a case of "translating the characters but not the pronunciation. Its essence varies according to whether it consists of many syllables, few syllables, a single syllable, or no syllables at all.
Its functions differ according to whether it serves to eliminate evil, generate goodness, protect the sutras, or cure illness. Now, as for its essence...
It consists mostly of long syllables, yet also includes some short ones. Its function is primarily to protect the sūtra, while also encompassing other meanings.

Since, from beginning to end, the main text of this chapter consists solely of mantras—even where there is incidental prose, it is likewise established for the sake of the mantra—it is therefore titled simply after the mantra.
If one clarifies its fivefold significance: first, although it demonstrates correct cultivation, it is suitable primarily for those at deep stages; for those at shallow stages, [it is] mostly...

First, because obstacles must rely upon the power of mantras; second, to demonstrate that while the extensive scriptures are broad, the secret mantras are concise, such that through the perfect interpenetration of the exoteric and esoteric, one attains results by reciting either;
third, because the True Dharma is difficult to practice while the Māras are easily inflamed, [the Buddha] spoke mantras to protect the Dharma masters and prohibit their disparagement;
fourth, because those who disturb and harass Dharma masters commit sins equal to those of the most heinous evildoers, [the Buddha] spoke mantras to prohibit such acts.

To destroy [them], so as not to allow transgressions to occur. Fifth, to listen to the Dharma with a focused mind; seeing that [beings] fall into arising and ceasing, one provides the secret, definitive interpretation to cause them to accord with non-arising.
Generally speaking, this sutra is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind, yet it is that which Māras and outsiders loathe and envy.
Its fragrance of practice is defamed, and its radiant Way is obscured by dust. If one does not hang up the precious mirror...
In lofty halls, how can one avoid being disturbed by manifold strange phenomena? Anticipating the need for protection against such violations, this chapter is therefore taught.

[Section Two of the Sūtra] 1. The Protector of the Dharma Recites the Mantra; 2. Upon Hearing the Recitation, One Attains Patience. The first [section] has three parts: 1. The Bodhisattva recites the mantra; 2.
