having already demonstrated the methods for quenching the boiling cauldron, Miaoyan converted the heterodox, and Jinshou bestowed the arts for removing the firewood.

As the *xuan* and *chi* pipes played in succession and the *qin* and *se* lutes resounded in harmony, they propagated the noble reputation of the Buddha-King, causing the present and the past to be as one day. This is...

Following the *dhāraṇī*, this chapter is expounded. (The scriptural text is divided into four parts: First, a general account of the original person; second, a detailed explanation of the past events; third, a synthesis of the ancient and the present;

fourth, the benefits gained by hearing this chapter. Regarding the first two [parts]: first, an account of the teacher and parents in the original land; second, an account of the brothers in the original land.

The first [of these] (although the title of the chapter is derived from the king, the actual substance takes the son as the primary subject; the terms "teacher" and "parents" are both used in relation to the son).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly... [up to] "the king’s queen was named Pure Virtue (*Viśuddhaguṇā*).

According to the previous *Sudhana-svara-parivarta*, the Buddhas encountered by Sudhana in those two lifetimes were: first, Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalasupratiṣṭhitaguṇaviśuddhacūḍarāja*), whose land was named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhālaṃkāra*);
the name of the kalpa is not mentioned. Second, Cloud Thunder Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*), whose land was named..."

He manifests throughout all worlds. The eon is named "Joyful Vision" (*Priyadarśana*). Although the name of this single Buddha now encompasses the names of two Buddhas, as they are not entirely identical, there is no impediment to providing distinct interpretations.
Upon careful examination of their meaning, it appears they are named according to their vocal wisdom (*ghoṣajñāna*).

There are two metaphors for "voice": first, "cloud," which metaphorically signifies containing moisture to nourish goodness; second, "thunder," which metaphorically signifies proclaiming the precepts to warn against evil.
Wisdom also has two metaphors: first, the "Constellation King," which metaphorically represents the illumination and discernment of mental capacities;
second, the "Flower," which metaphorically represents the adornment of beings' conduct. Each metaphor encompasses two aspects to manifest two virtues.

Furthermore, because wisdom possesses these two virtues—illuminating the mind and adorning conduct—the land is named "Radiant Adornment. Because sound possesses these two virtues—fostering the good and restraining evil—the eon is named...
"Joyful to Behold. The lands and eons were all named after the virtues of the Buddhas. The king was named Śuddhadarśana (Pure Vision), and his queen was named Viśuddhaguṇā (Pure Virtue).
She manifested in a female body for the sake of delivering Miaoyan; this was because her true virtue is fundamentally pure. △ Second, an account of their original ground as brothers.
He had two sons, the first named Viśuddhigarbha and the second named Viśuddhanetra. They had both fully mastered this samādhi.

Because his wisdom-aggregate possessed pure virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he was named Viśuddhigarbha; because his wisdom-illumination encompassed pure dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he was named Viśuddhanetra.

As for those who possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), it is because they develop supernatural faculties based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*); as for those who possess merit and wisdom, it is because they achieve them based on spiritual practice (*caryā*).
Because it is solemn. [The text] describes the practices cultivated over a long period by Bodhisattvas and others to clarify that merit and wisdom have their origins.

Within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, provisional wisdom is opened up as skillful means; thus, the six perfections become seven. The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
As for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), the first is called the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*); the second is...
The four right efforts; third, the four bases of power; fourth, the five faculties; fifth, the five powers;
sixth, the seven factors of enlightenment; and seventh, the eightfold noble path. When combined according to their respective numbers, they constitute thirty-seven categories.

These assist the preceding six perfections and are thus called the "auxiliaries of the path. For one who understands and penetrates them clearly, through long-term cultivation, the modes of practice become familiar.

"Quiescent. Because it illuminates all subtle distinctions without obstruction. Furthermore, it attains the "equality of bodhisattvas," clarifying that the meditative concentration attained has its source in spiritual power.
Among the seven kinds of samādhi, the first six are specific and the last one is general.
Within the specific ones, the first is called "the purity of the bodhisattva," because it eliminates hindrances according to one's capacity. The second is called "the sun."
The "Constellation" [Buddha] is so named because he illuminates principles according to their respective capacities; these two [names] seem to pertain to self-benefit.

The third is named "Pure Light," so named because he emits pure light to gather in sentient beings. The fourth is named "Pure Form," so named because he manifests pure forms to respond to the various faculties of the multitudes;
these two seem to pertain to benefiting others. The fifth is named "Pure Illumination."
He preaches the Dharma with a pure mind, for he illuminates the darkness of the world. The sixth is named "Long Adornment," because through long-term cultivation, he adorns the fruit of Buddhahood.
These two [aspects] seem to encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others; collectively, they are termed the "Great Majestic Virtue Treasury."
Possessing the six aforementioned meanings, its divine function is transcendent; demons and heretics dare not gaze upon it directly, and it is that which all humans and devas alike revere.
It possesses a majesty that inspires awe and a virtue worthy of emulation.

Furthermore, as for "thoroughly penetrating," this refers not only to being skilled in entering, abiding in, and emerging from [samādhi], but also to the fact that within a single samādhi, one thoroughly penetrates all samādhis. (According to the *Dacheng shi*)

The preface states: "In the past, during the final dharma age, there were four bhikṣus who made a pact to dwell in the mountain forests, their aspirations set upon the Buddha’s wisdom. As they lived in seclusion for many days, their clothing and provisions were completely exhausted. One among them said: 'We four are so destitute that we can no longer even preserve our own bodies.'"

"The Dharma should be entrusted to those who are stable. You three gentlemen need only devote your lives to the Way; do not worry about the court. As for me alone, I shall set aside this body and strength, vowing to provide whatever is required. Thereupon, he shook his mendicant’s staff at the city gates to seek alms and offerings.

The three men were thus able to manifest their sincerity; their merit was perfected and their task accomplished. The benefit of one lifetime shall endure through immeasurable lifetimes. As for that one man, he frequently traversed the human world and repeatedly encountered sounds and sights. Once, encountering the King’s procession with its dense throngs of chariots and horses, he gave rise to thoughts and stirred his mind, coveting that splendor.

Through the influence of his cultivated merit, he received retribution according to his thoughts, becoming a king among humans and in the heavens, always attaining the status of sovereign. When the three men attained the Way, they gathered to deliberate, saying: "We have escaped the cage of worldly bondage; our success is due to this king. Yet he remains addicted to the fruits [of his power]..."

[The Buddha] replied: "It will increase his conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*). Once he dies from this life, he shall no longer be a king; he will then sink into a pit of fire, making him truly difficult to save. Fortunately, before he suffers [this fate], he is precisely the right time for conversion.

One person said: 'This king is attached to desire and furthermore holds false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Unless one uses the hook of affection, there is no way to convert him. First, become a beautiful wife; second, become a clever son. Through the words of a wife and a child, he will surely comply. If you employ such a means of conversion, he will surely succeed in reforming his heterodoxy.

However, this matter also involves his previous lives; the cause and effect are quite similar. I simply do not know from which scripture it originates. I suspect that a great master must have seen it. I have recorded it here to await further investigation. This concludes the general summary of the individual's case. △ Two.
Detailed Explanation of the Original Events, Part Two: 1. The two sons manifesting supernatural powers for their father. 2. Miaoyan (Subhūṣita) converting from heterodoxy to the Path.

The first [section] has two parts: A. The reason for manifesting supernatural powers. B. The actual manifestation of supernatural transformations. The first [of these two] has two parts: 1. Going to hear the Buddha’s Dharma.
2. Complying with his mother’s command. The first [of these two]:

At that time, that Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha [to the point where he would] hear and accept the preaching of the Lotus Sutra, first established the Dharma for the king out of compassion for his past roots of goodness; because [the king] was about to fall before long, [the Buddha] desired to lead him.

He reflects that the multitude has long suffered and has no means of liberation; thus it is said, "and out of compassion. The terms "desiring" (*yu*) and "reaching" (*ji*) clearly manifest the sense of combining both [concern and pity].
Regarding the passage "at that time, Jìng... and below: the two sons requested their mother to go with them.

They did not inform their father but informed their mother because the mother and sons shared the same intent, whereas the father and sons did not. Furthermore, they waited for the mother to decide, after which they could inform him.
[The son] first informed his father; only then did he speak [to his mother]. △ Second, in order to comply with his mother’s command:
His mother said to her son, "Your father has placed his faith in and accepted the teachings of the non-Buddhists... (omitted)... or he might permit us to go to the place where the Buddha is."
First, the mother instructed her two sons to inform their father. Regarding the necessity of informing the father, there are two meanings:

first, to avoid going without notification, which would result in the loss of a wife’s virtue and a violation of the way of a son; second, to ensure that if he were attached to the heterodox, they might restrain him from false views and establish him in right view.
Below the passage on "Pure Treasury" (Vimalagarbha), it says the two sons harbored resentment and hesitated. "Harboring resentment" means they were the sons of the Dharma King.

It is not fitting to be born into a family that holds false views. As for "hesitation," it is feared that [the father] will not listen, which would conversely cause his aspirations to remain unfulfilled.

Within these two phrases, there is boundless pathos. In the passage beginning with "The mother said," she instructs him to manifest his divine power for the sake of his father. To be attached to the heterodox is to be on the verge of falling;

this is a matter worthy of concern. When attachment is deep, it is difficult to uproot; thus, it is necessary to manifest one's divine power. For by seeing the divine, his heterodoxy may be transformed, and his mind [will be saved].

Pure. Knowing that he was truly worthy of being relied upon, she permitted him to go. Since his path was completed and his aspirations had attained their fruit, his mother’s admonition regarding the manifestation of spiritual powers was indeed excellent.
This concludes the account of the reasons for manifesting spiritual powers. 2. The Actual Manifestation of Spiritual Transformations.
Thereupon, because the two sons were mindful of their father, they [acted] so as to cause the King, their father, to attain pure faith and understanding.

Da Cheng (Daosheng) says: "The manifestation of transformations should consist of eighteen changes. I, however, say that one need not be strictly bound by this number; it is sufficient that they accomplish benefit.
Now, examining the text at hand, there are fourteen manifestations: first, the four modes of deportment in mid-air constitute four; second, ...
1. From the upper and lower parts of the body, water and fire emerge alternately; this constitutes four [transformations]. Combined with the preceding, they form eight.

2. The three great bodies fill the void; this constitutes one. Combined with the preceding, they form nine. 3. The four [elements] manifest as large and small forms alternately; this constitutes two. Combined with the preceding, they form eleven. 4.

The five [elements] vanish into emptiness and appear upon the earth; this constitutes one. Combined with the preceding, they form twelve. 5. Earth and water alternate and become as they were; this constitutes two. Combined with the preceding...

The preceding section constitutes fourteen [verses]. The reason he is able to manifest such transformations is that the seven great elements are fundamentally all-pervasive and all phenomena have from the beginning been mutually interfused.
It is only because sentient beings are driven by external objects that they encounter contradictions at every turn;

whereas the Bodhisattva is skillfully able to transform objects, causing them to be manifested through mere thought. The final two lines conclude the reason for the manifestation of these spiritual powers. Its...
The meaning is now clear. The two sons have finished manifesting their spiritual powers for their father. **Part Two: Miaoyan Converts from Evil and Attains the Way.** This section has five parts:
1. Converting from evil and approaching the Buddha; 2. Hearing the Dharma and making offerings; 3. Receiving a prediction of enlightenment and leaving the household life;

4. Practicing and attaining the Way; 5. Cherishing the virtue and making a vow. The first part has three sub-sections: 1. Miaoyan receives transformation and converts from evil; 2. The two sons pray...
"Please urge [him] to come. Let the members of the three palaces go together to the Buddha's abode.
First, at that time, the father saw his son’s supernatural power was such that he said, "Seeing that your teacher is thus worthy, we may all go together."
When the spirit first saw the Master, it had never seen anyone like him before; recognizing that the Master was extraordinary, it asked who he was and whose disciple he was.
The two sons descended, pointed to the Master, and said to their father: "The man is truly enviable; his Dharma should also be heard."

Therefore, he mentions both the Buddha and the Dharma together. Regarding the father’s words below: "I wish to go together with you to see your teacher," etc., this shows that his wrong views have been transformed.
II. The two sons pray and urge their parents to visit [the Buddha]. 1. First, they pray at their mother’s place. 2.
Second, they urge their parents to go there at once. The first part: *Note: This is a structural outline (p'in-t'i) for a commentary on a Buddhist scripture.*
Thereupon, the two sons descended from mid-air. Why was this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter.

First, they reported to their father their faith and understanding: "Although we have not yet seen the Buddha, we already believe that he is no ordinary man; although we have not yet heard the Dharma..."
That one who has already understood this Dharma follows the supreme path; this is so even for those who have not yet seen or heard it.

If one has already heard and seen it, how could they still bury their head in the defilements and endure the cycle of birth and death? By this, we know with certainty that we, being of inferior capacity, are fit to resolve our minds toward enlightenment.
He prayed for ordination. Having been born into that family, his original purpose was to initiate roots of goodness;
now that he had fulfilled his filial duty toward his father and had nothing further to attend to, he wished to seek ordination and cultivate the Path.
From these few words, the background of the mother and son is already briefly seen. To restate this meaning: while the mother was still hesitating, he calmly requested it once more.
Furthermore, in the verse, the first two lines describe the actual act of seeking to leave the household life; the next two lines clarify the intention for leaving the household life.

The following two lines, beginning with "As [the opportunity] is rare," express the fear of missing what is difficult to encounter; the subsequent two lines, beginning with "To escape from all...", express the fear of falling back into what is difficult to recover from. "The mother" refers to the one below.
It may be known that they received their mother’s permission. △ When they went to exhort their parents for the second time, the two sons then said to their parents:
(up to) "The appearance of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter, and such a time is likewise rare."
"At the very first time of being exhorted, one must go. To "go at that time" means to proceed immediately and swiftly, without allowing even the slightest delay.

As for the subsequent section, which serves as a formal inquiry and an explanatory fulfillment, the reason for reiterating the previous analogy is that while the mother already knows, the father does not yet know.
Regarding the single-eyed turtle encountering the hole in a floating log, according to the *Āgama Sūtra*, this occurs beneath Mount Sumeru in the great ocean.
There is a one-eyed turtle and a log with a single hole. If the turtle’s head can enter the hole of the log, it may escape drowning;

yet the log drifts with the current around Mount Sumeru, and only once every three thousand years do they happen to meet. Moreover, for the one-eyed turtle to peer into that single hole is an extreme rarity.
If they miss this single opportunity, there will be no time for them to meet again. Now, these two sons have raised these two [analogies].
The analogy serves to demonstrate the difficulty of encountering a Buddha; it is precisely to show that seeing, approaching, and making offerings to him must not be delayed.

Regarding the passage "But I," etc., he again seeks to go forth into homelessness. As for "again seeking to go forth," although his mother has already granted permission, he must still inform his father.

Having accumulated profound merit in past lives and thus being born during the time of the Buddha’s Dharma, he rejoices that encountering a Buddha is no easy matter, and is fortunate to have attained this.
This encounter should not be allowed to pass in vain; therefore, it is said, "Please allow us to go forth [into the homeless life].

In the section explaining the significance of this request, the phrase "such times are also difficult to encounter" means that although one has met the era of a Buddha, this physical body is difficult to preserve. If one does not practice while still strong and healthy, what can be done once old age and decay arrive?
Having finished the two sons' prayerful entreaty and exhortation to visit the Buddha, [the third section follows: Three, the royal family and retinue together proceed to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Two. First, an account of the virtues of the royal harem; second, the actual description of their departure together. Regarding the first:
At that time, King Subhavyūha’s inner palace (up to) caused their minds to have faith, understanding, and a fondness for the Buddha-dharma.
There were eighty-four thousand women in the inner palace, though their specific associations are not made explicit.
However, since Pure Virtue (Śuddhaguṇā) is none other than Gadgadasvara, her retinue of women is identical to the aforementioned followers of Gadgadasvara.

Because these eighty-four thousand beings have been bound together by causes and conditions such that they are never separated from one another throughout birth after birth, there are two who are capable of receiving and upholding the Lotus Sutra.
The meaning is as follows: first, because the time has arrived and the faculties [of sentient beings] have matured; second, because one encounters difficulties without being cowed.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, its explanation is found in the "Chapter on Gadgadasvara. As for the *Pāpāpāya-vinivartana-samādhi*, by entering this samādhi, one clearly discerns birth and death and never again falls into the three evil realms.
Because one is able to realize this for oneself and further desires to transform others through it, it says "desires to... [and so forth].

To cause all sentient beings to be equal [to the Buddhas]: regarding those who have gathered in the Samādhi of the Assemblage of All Buddhas, when they enter this samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions all come together for the sake of preaching the Dharma. Because the Buddha preaches the Dharma, they hear it all simultaneously within their meditative concentration;
thus, they are able to fully know the secret treasury of all Buddhas. Based on this, every gate belongs to the Dharma-parishad (Dharma-kin).
Miaoyan alone adhered to heterodox teachings. His two sons could not bear this, so they used the power of skillful means to transform him and lead him to faith and understanding.
Because they did not harm the path of human relations while being able to awaken him to right faith, it is said that they were "skillfully transformed.
Their fondness for the Buddha-dharma meant they were capable of giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). △ Second, the actual account of their going together.
Thereupon, King Subhavyūha (up to) circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to stand to one side.
As for the "concubines" (*cai-nü*), this refers to those selected from the inner palace; they all possess a degree of splendor (*cai-se*).

The two sons' retinue was reduced by half compared to their mother's, hence there were only forty-two thousand [attendants]. Having finished turning away from error and approaching the Buddha, △ second, hearing the Dharma and making offerings.
At that time, that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king (up to) the accomplishment of the foremost, most subtle form.
That original Buddha preached the Dharma; that present Buddha has established the Dharma specifically to guide the king, and now he has come to pay his respects.

Therefore, he immediately preached the Dharma for him; it was not that he did not preach for others, but because he was specifically for the sake of the King, and when the causes and conditions converged, a single stroke turned [the King's mind].

Thus it is said, "The King was greatly delighted. From the passage "At that time" onwards, the husband and wife offered worship and, grateful for having attained the Dharma, they untied their necklaces and scattered them over the Buddha.
That they were in the midst of empty space symbolizes that what is given is non-abiding, arising from non-abiding.
The "Root" (Ben) establishes the stages of abiding, practice, progression, and the grounds (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it is symbolized by a four-pillared precious terrace formed through transformation.

The presence of a great precious couch represents these stages of abiding, practice, progression, and the grounds, while simultaneously manifesting the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*). This emptiness is not a nihilistic void; it must be adorned with ornaments.
Thus, it is symbolized by the spreading of various celestial robes (*devavastra*). When both principle and adornment are fully prepared, one perfectly accords with the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore—
One sees a Buddha seated in the full lotus posture, emitting great radiance. According to this, a single offering of a necklace has already transcended all stages.
That the Tathāgata bestows a prediction upon one below [this stage] is not without cause. Yet, this Buddha does not emerge from the mind, nor does he manifest from material objects;
he is not identical to the Buddha, nor is he not identical to the Buddha. Such is the Buddha; such is the seeing of the Buddha. Thus it is.
At that time, looking down, he observed the appearance and formed this thought: "This body, so dignified and extraordinary, must have been attained through superior conduct.
This foremost and most subtle form is certainly not the result of inferior intent. He marveled at its rarity, thinking that it was not without purpose or significance.

The previous passage spoke of being "capable of generating the aspiration for enlightenment" (*cittotpāda*); this current section concerns the actual generation of that aspiration. For one of perfect capacity (*paripūrṇa-pudgala*), the aspiration and the final realization are not distinct;
the former indicates the latter, and there is no contradiction between them. △ Third, receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and leaving the household life.

At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja-pūrvaguṇaviśālanetra (Cloud Thunder Sound King of Past Virtuous Wisdom) [was present], and [the youth] went forth from home to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
Initially, the Buddha carefully examined his capacity; Miaoyan joined his palms and stood before him, and the fourfold assembly all witnessed this.

The reason the Buddha questioned him again was to demonstrate that his capacity had matured, thereby enabling him to bear witness. From the words "This king" onwards, the text records his progress through cause and effect as he assists in the Buddha-way.

"Dharma" means to support and propagate the holy teachings; it refers to what was called by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra as "protecting, upholding, and assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha’s true Dharma.
"Sāla" is translated here as "firm and solid. Da Cheng (Da Cheng) says: the name of the Buddha takes the meaning of providing vast shade for all living beings;
the name of the land takes the meaning of shattering all false darkness; and the name of the eon takes the meaning of surpassing all that is noble. All of these accord [with the truth].
This is the practice of uniting with causes. By means of a single thought of pure faith, he transformed his ministers and subjects, causing them all to obtain the benefits of the Dharma;

this is the practice of broad shelter and the practice of destroying heterodoxy. Thereby, he relinquished the rank of king to attain the rank of Buddha; this is the meaning of transcending all noble status.

The merits of both the primary body and the environment can be known from this. Regarding the passage "The king below abandoned his kingdom and left home," the *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna) commentary states: "The Buddha..."

Possessing the discerning faculty that surveys the stars across the heavens, he directly points to the wondrous essence of the original nature. King [Wu] possessed the talent to perceive the whip and dance accordingly;

thus, with a single word that pierced the divine, he emerged like the finest blade from its sheath and took up the responsibility. Once a single phrase enters the spirit, all myriad conditions become a dream.
He abandoned the nobility of ten thousand chariots to don the robes of the six harmonies; he knew that the Way existed, yet he was unaware of the existence of the world. △ Four.
He practiced the path until he attained enlightenment.
After the King had left the household life, for eighty-four thousand years he [attained] the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits.

Throughout these eighty-four thousand years of practice, he never departed from the assembly of the Buddha; thus, his practice over eighty-four thousand years was characterized by the unimpeded mastery of both prolonging and shortening time.
Regarding this meaning, *Dacheng* (The Great Achievement) says: "For eighty-four thousand years, one practices the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* path; thus, one purifies the afflictions (*kleśa*).
After this period has passed, the afflictions being purified, samādhi manifests before one. One then transforms the defilements of false views into adornments."

This is for the sake of the pure adornment of merit. △ Fifth, the threefold section on cherishing virtue and making a self-vow: 1. Miaoyan cherishes the virtues of his two sons; 2. The Tathāgata seals and praises him, revealing his origins; 3. He makes a self-vow to forever leave behind false views. First: The Lotus Sutra: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan, having heard from the Buddha Śākyamuni this teaching on the Dharma-gate of the medicinal herbs, was filled with great joy and leaped up into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees. He then addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni, saying: “World-Honored One, I shall now go to the world-system called Sahā to see, pay homage to, and serve the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and to hear the Dharma. Then the Buddha Śākyamuni said to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan: “Go, son of good family! You should know that the lifespan of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna is immeasurable and incalculable. Furthermore, you should not think that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna has entered parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Son of good family, the lifespan of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna is immeasurable and incalculable; he does not enter parinirvāṇa, yet he manifests the appearance of entering parinirvāṇa. Son of good family, you should go there and, having seen the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, pay him homage and listen to the Dharma. Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan, together with five hundred bodhisattvas, set out for the Sahā world-system. Before long, they arrived at the Sahā world-system. Having arrived, they saw the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, which was made of the seven treasures, adorned with various precious jewels, and standing high and wide. They also saw the Buddha Śākyamuni seated upon the lion throne within the stupa, preaching the Dharma. Seeing this, they were filled with great joy and paid homage to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. Then the Buddha Śākyamuni, knowing the thoughts of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan and the other bodhisattvas, emitted a great light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers. All the Buddhas in those lands also emitted great light, and their lands all became visible. In each of those lands, a Buddha was seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, preaching the Lotus Sutra. Then the Buddha Śākyamuni addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan: “Son of good family, do you see these Buddhas, these World-Honored Ones? Miaoyan replied: “World-Honored One, I see them. The Buddha said: “Son of good family, these Buddhas, these World-Honored Ones, have all attained the Way under my guidance. Son of good family, you should go to these Buddhas, these World-Honored Ones, and pay them homage. Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan, together with the five hundred bodhisattvas, went before those Buddhas and paid them homage. Having paid homage, they withdrew to one side and sat down. Then the Buddha Śākyamuni addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Miaoyan: “Son of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of these Buddhas, you should uphold, read, recite, and explain this Lotus Sutra for the sake of sentient beings. Why is this? Son of good family, this Lotus Sutra is the king of all sutras, supreme and unsurpassed. It is like the moon among the stars, like the sun among the luminaries, like Mount Sumeru among the mountains, like the ocean among waters, like the diamond among jewels, like the sandalwood among fragrances, like the lion among beasts, and like the great physician among physicians. The *daśakoṭi-vartanī-dhāraṇī*. If one can further describe this meaning, exhausting all that has been attained so as to cause others to understand and awaken, it is called the *dharmasvara-upāya-dhāraṇī*. Taking these three as the foremost, they lead all the rest;

△ Third, the protection and cultivation [of practice] has two parts: first, manifesting the body to preach the Dharma; second, preventing wrongdoing by reciting mantras.
First: "World-Honored One, in the future, during the final five hundred years... (up to) "...he preaches the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.

The preceding two [sections] serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for this section; this section serves as the actual cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the preceding two. This is because the preceding two involve mental contemplation (*manasikāra*).
Having already exerted himself, and with concentration and wisdom already established, he fixed upon a period of twenty-one days to achieve success through diligent effort.

This must be said in reference to the degenerate age; for in an age of virtue, where faculties are sharp and hindrances are thin, there is no necessity to fix a specific deadline. Thus it is for those who seek [enlightenment].
As the Buddha once was a king, he beat the drum and issued a proclamation seeking all those from the four quarters who sought the Dharma.

Whether they wished to practice after having obtained it, or wished to practice after having received and upheld it, or even wished to practice after having transcribed it—their initial motivations may have differed, yet their aim was the same: the desire to practice.
The mind itself does not differ; however, the mention of "three weeks" (three times seven days) is intended to ensure that the commitment is not distant, thereby making the mind sharp and intense.

Fewer than two periods would not suffice because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) would not yet be pure, fearing that success might not be achieved. More than four periods would not be reached, as it would be unnecessary.

Time passes quickly and easily leads to indolence; for fear that such dread might arise, even if one possesses both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the delusions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are difficult to eliminate.

Therefore, one should practice with single-minded diligence. "Single-minded" means setting aside all myriad conditions and focusing exclusively on this sutra. "Diligence" means exerting oneself to the utmost of one's natural life, vowing to sever all delusions and habitual tendencies.
Once the three weeks have been completed, the power of the sutra will have become pure, and the delusions and habitual tendencies will...
Because it is empty, he again summoned Samantabhadra and immeasurable bodhisattvas to surround him.

Once this canopy has encircled them, it manifests a distinct, supreme, and wondrous body to preach the inconceivable Dharma. Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening":
it shows [the path] through sudden severance, teaches through perfect cultivation, causes one to obtain inconceivable benefit, and gives rise to vast joy. This...
This clarifies the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth), which is the benefit of entering into principle. △ Second, the recitation of mantras to ward off evil.

Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], they will be covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.
When the initial resonance first meets with the response, one sees Śākyamuni; this is because that which is expressed (the signified) is the Dharmakāya.
Just as when hearing from the Buddha, that which expresses (the signifier) is the Buddha’s own speech; thus, among all forms of offering, this is the offering of the Dharma.
"Nurturing is supreme," because all Tathāgatas revere the Dharma. One should know that from the words "the Buddha praises" below, there is a mutual response between cause and effect;

by verifying the cause through the result, one knows that [enlightenment] will certainly be attained. Therefore, the Buddha praises them, saying, "Excellent! Within the eternally quiescent light, he secretly bestows a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa);

Ritual. The covering of the body with robes is the method for transmitting the Mind. △ Second, departing from hindrances and approaching the fruit, in two parts: first, the ability to depart from the two hindrances;
second, the ability to approach the two fruits. First [the ability to depart from the two hindrances].
Such a person no longer clings to worldly pleasures (*yāvat*) and is able to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
First, they are able to abandon external obstacles. "Not craving worldly pleasures" means abandoning the obstacle of the five desires (*pañca-kāma*).

"Not delighting in non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the like" means abandoning the obstacle of false paths. "As well as various evil persons and the like" means abandoning the obstacle of wicked people. [The two types of evil...]

The term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) encompasses all sixteen types of restraint. If one were to briefly cite examples such as butchers and the like, these persons possess three phrases which explain, respectively, the three aforementioned abstentions.
This is because their minds and intentions are upright and straightforward; thus, they do not engage in false greed.
Because he possesses right mindfulness, he does not undergo false defilement; because he possesses the power of merit, he does not rely upon evil karma.
This is because all improper modes of conduct (*akuśala-saṃvara*) arise from a lack of sufficient merit, which they then employ to seek profit.
This person, moreover, is able to abandon internal obstacles. Greed, anger, and delusion are all produced by one's own mind and disturb the correct intention; therefore, they are so called.
The internal obstacles: these two phrases explain the aforementioned ability to remain detached. Because one has few desires and is content, greed and other afflictions do not arise;
because one’s pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is stainless, no defilements can invade. Thus, nothing whatsoever can cause distress. △ Second, the ability to approach the two fruits.
"Samantabhadra, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... you shall sit upon the lion Dharma-throne amidst the great assembly of devas and humans;

before long," and so forth—this refers to the proximate fruit of self-benefit. "Turning the wheel of the Dharma," and so forth—this refers to the proximate fruit of benefiting others. This concludes the section on the proximate fruits regarding the removal of obstacles.
△ Third, obtaining merit and warding off disparagement.
Samantabhadra, if in a future age one upholds, receives, reads, and recites [this sutra], such karmic retribution for transgressions shall result in being blind life after life.

Initially, one obtains blessings according to one's wishes; by receiving and reading this sutra, one can inspire offerings from humans and devas, and thus no longer craves clothing and other such things.
Thus, one’s vows are not in vain, just as in the case of Vinaya Master Xuān, who was provided with celestial food and drink. This is precisely it.
This is the verification. Those who obtain the retribution of merit in the present life may become teachers to kings, or receive the offerings of emperors, and so forth;

it is not merely that their four requisites are fully provided for. "If there are those below" refers to those who obstruct the practice of emptiness, disparage it, and do not believe in the Supreme One Vehicle.
They merely observe his movements and claim he has attained Buddhahood; thus they disparage him as a madman who acts in vain and ultimately gains nothing.
Once such a person falls back, the eyes of gods and humans are suddenly extinguished; therefore, it is recorded that such a person shall suffer this retribution: being blind life after life.
△ Fourth, praising the benefits of [correct] belief and the sins of slander.
If there are those who make offerings and offer praise (up to the point of curing) diseases such as dropsy and shortness of breath— these various grave and evil illnesses—

the person who first benefits from these offerings and praises shall obtain visible retributions in this life, such as having a complexion that is bright and white, and a mouth that emits the fragrance of a lotus.

This extends even to those whose six sense faculties have attained purity. Furthermore, as for those who disparage or mock [this teaching] out of malice—saying that those who receive and uphold this sutra are bound by the Buddha-dharma—if one speaks of their faults and evils, whether true or false, they shall all contract the disease of leprosy.
"Leprosy" (pāṇḍuroga) refers to white spots and scabies; it is the manifestation of a malignant disease upon the exterior.

Because retributive results must correspond to their causes, such things as sparse or missing teeth will inevitably provoke the laughter of others, and a foul-smelling body will easily lead to being held in contempt by others.
These retributions of lightness and derision arise according to their respective categories.
Alas! The relationship between karmic retribution and mental actions is like that between myriad forms and their underlying models; how can one not be cautious?
Ah! In this passage, "twisted and contorted" refers to the appearance of the hands and feet being unable to extend or move naturally.

"Oblique staring" refers to the eyes looking askance from the corners. "Water-bellied" refers to the disease of edema. "Shortness of breath" refers to the ailment of labored panting. These are symptoms of certain death;
yet, the patient remains entangled in illness without dying, lingering at the bedside for a hundred days. Though one may be filial...
It is difficult even for one's own son to receive and comply with [such teachings], let alone others. This concludes the section on the benefits of clearly upholding the sutra. III.
Conclusion and Exhortation to Welcome and Honor: Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, as if honoring a Buddha.
As stated above, there are such benefits; therefore, one will certainly become a Buddha. Thus, it is urged that one should welcome and revere [the teaching].
This concludes the exhortation clarifying the benefits. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter.
When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being preached— up until the point where the bodhisattvas, as numerous as atoms, were fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra—
even those who, within their meditative contemplations, beheld Samantabhadra but once, attained such a revolving dharani-door and were able to uphold this sutra after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa;

it is already granted that such persons are endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra, let alone those who personally participated in the sublime assembly and received the profound texts face-to-face.
It is fitting that those who have attained this and possess this [should do so]. The Way is also practice. The detailed exposition of the method of cultivation is concluded.

△ Third, the dispersal after the ritual of the Great Assembly. When the Buddha spoke this sutra, Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas (down to) received and upheld the Buddha’s words, paid homage, and departed.
This concludes the assembly on Vulture Peak; the matters of teaching and listening are finished, and the benefit is ultimate. To explain the intent of the "Great Achievement" (Dacheng):
within this entire scripture, although both teacher and disciple are involved in the exposition, it is spoken from the perspective of the preeminent, and thus it is called "the Buddha’s teaching."

Samantabhadra and others represent the bodhisattvas within the assembly; Mañjuśrī is listed as the head of this assembly, while Samantabhadra is placed here because his significance as a symbol of the Dharma is evident, and also for the sake of following the logical sequence of the preceding text. Śāriputra and others represent the śrāvakas within the assembly;
although they have already received predictions of enlightenment and are thus all bodhisattvas, they are still referred to as "śrāvakas" in order to preserve [the conventional designation].
Because they occupy the stages [of the path], and because they cause all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, they are true śrāvakas.

The various devas and others are included among the eight classes within the assembly; the entire great congregation encompasses those from this world and other directions who have formed karmic connections, rejoice, and—following the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*—have entered the assembly according to their respective chapters. As for "those who rejoice," it means they celebrate what they have heard.
Therefore, having drifted through many kalpas without hearing this Dharma, now that one has heard it, one rejoices like a child meeting its mother; thus, there is joy.

"To receive and uphold" means to grasp what has been heard; therefore, one is earnestly entrusted with it and repeatedly praised and exhorted to do so, wearing the holy words upon oneself and engraving the supreme teaching in the heart;
thus, one receives and upholds it. "To prostrate" means to revere what has been heard; as if receiving it...
The King’s decree: "As if receiving my father’s command, with utmost reverence and trepidation, I prostrate myself and bow my head repeatedly; thus do I perform this rite.

As for those who depart, having heard [the teaching], they withdraw to cultivate it. Thus, the ancients would advance to hear the Way from their teachers and retreat to cultivate the Way within themselves;
they were not like people of today, who merely let it enter their ears and exit through their mouths.
Enduring those various hardships for the sake of this most supreme Dharma, may I be perfumed by the cause of outflow-free wisdom;
may I receive and uphold it in every birth. May my cultivation never be in vain, and through sympathetic joy, hearing, and seeing, may we together enter the inconceivable.
*Fahua Zhizhang Shu*, Scroll Seven (End). Phonetic Explanations:

*Zhěn* (cut with *zhǐrěn*; sound *zhěn*): the paths between the plots of a well-field. *Ào* (cut with *ègè*; sound *è*): whitewash; colored earth. *Tuánluán* (the second character cut with *lúwǎn*; sound *luán*): round. Anciently called *dàjiā*.

Gathered in a circle, they together speak of the discourse on non-arising (*anutpāda*). *Wéi* (cut by *yúfēi*, pronounced *wéi*): A gate within the palace. *Jiǒng* (cut by *gǔyíng*, pronounced *jǐng*): A personal name. *Lú* (cut by *lóngdū*, pronounced *lú*): The skull. *Dān* (cut by *duōhán*, pronounced *dān*):

To exhaust; to bring to an end. *Kàn* (cut by *kǔlàn*, pronounced *què*): To look down from above. *Xī* (cut by *jiànxī*, pronounced *xī*): Minced vegetables; to break into pieces. *Xún* (cut by *xiánglún*, pronounced *xún*):

Virtuous; compliant and submissive. *Qū*: Same as *qū* (to drive). *Qiàn* (cut by *qìzhàn*, pronounced *qiàn*): To reprimand; to question with censure. *Xuān-chí* (upper character cut by *xǔyún*, pronounced *xūn*; lower character *chénzhī*): Musical instruments. The upper is the *xuān* (a clay oboe); the lower is the *chí* (a bamboo oboe).
(Qieyun: chī; a type of wind instrument.)
